book: Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction
summary: Tetlock and Gardner show that forecasting skill can be measured, that some ordinary people forecast far better than experts, and that their habits of mind can be learned.

unitSummaries.Chapter 1: The case that forecasting is neither hopeless nor easy: experts do little better than chance, yet some people can forecast well, and measuring them shows how.
unitSummaries.Chapter 2: Why confident experts mislead us: the medical-testing parallel, and Kahneman's System 1 and System 2 thinking show how intuition produces certainty without evidence.
unitSummaries.Chapter 3: How to judge forecasts fairly: clear questions, probabilities, Brier scores and benchmarks, then the results of Tetlock's expert political judgment study, where foxes beat hedgehogs.
unitSummaries.Chapter 4: The Good Judgment Project's forecasting tournament, and how its best performers, the superforecasters, consistently beat the crowd, intelligence analysts and chance.
unitSummaries.Chapter 5: Superforecasters are smart but not geniuses: they break problems down Fermi-style, start from the outside view, then adjust with the inside view and synthesise opposing views.
unitSummaries.Chapter 6: Superforecasters are not math whizzes but think in finely graded probabilities, balancing the three settings of probability and avoiding both overconfidence and wishy-washy maybes.
unitSummaries.Chapter 7: Superforecasters update beliefs bit by bit as news arrives, avoiding both underreaction and overreaction, using Bayesian-style updating without the formal math.
unitSummaries.Chapter 8: Superforecasters keep improving through practice, timely feedback, honest postmortems and grit, adopting a growth mindset and treating beliefs as hypotheses to test.
unitSummaries.Chapter 9: Teams can outperform individuals when they share information, challenge each other respectfully and aggregate judgments, and superteams do this best.
unitSummaries.Chapter 10: Leaders need judgment-based humility and decisive action; the German Army's Auftragstaktik shows how to combine trust in subordinates with clear intent.
unitSummaries.Chapter 11: Taleb's black-swan critique of forecasting, and the authors' reply on how far forecasting can reach and where it cannot.
unitSummaries.Chapter 12: What the authors hope will change: adversarial collaboration, better questions and a more evidence-based forecasting culture, with the humanists' objection answered.
unitSummaries.Epilogue: The authors close with Bill Flack and precision, then distil the book's lessons into ten guidelines for aspiring superforecasters.
unitSummaries.Whole book: How the chapters build one argument: forecasting can be measured, some people do it well, and their habits can be learned.

concepts.title: Everyone forecasts
concepts.question: What counts as a forecast, and when do we hand forecasting to experts?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, every decision that rests on how we expect the future to unfold depends on a forecast, so we are all forecasters.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The chapter lists changing jobs, marrying, buying a home, investing, launching a product and retiring. Each choice depends on an expectation about what comes next. We often forecast for ourselves, but when markets crash or wars loom we turn to experts, such as the columnist Tom Friedman.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, an expectation about how the future will unfold is a forecast, whether we make it or an expert does.
card.limits: Calling an expectation a forecast says nothing about whether it is any good; the chapter goes on to ask how good forecasts actually are.

concepts.title: Bill Flack, remarkable forecaster
concepts.question: What makes an unknown retiree a remarkable forecaster?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: Bill Flack, a retired agriculture department worker, is a remarkable forecaster, and we know it because his record was kept and independently assessed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Bill answered about three hundred questions on world events, such as whether Russia would annex more Ukrainian territory. He is fifty-five, a Nebraska native with a science degree who left a math PhD. Each prediction was dated, recorded and assessed by independent scientific observers, and his record is excellent.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, when Bill meets an unfamiliar question he does his homework: he gathers facts, balances clashing arguments and settles on an answer.

card.rule: Judge a forecaster by a dated, recorded and independently assessed track record, not by fame or access.
card.limits: One person's record shows that good forecasting is possible; the chapter next turns to the thousands of others in the same program.

concepts.title: Superforecasters
concepts.question: What does the term superforecaster mean, and how common are they?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: About 2% of the volunteers who answered the same questions as Bill forecast as well as he does; the authors call them superforecasters.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Thousands of volunteers answered the same questions, and most were not as good as Bill. About 2% were. They include engineers, lawyers, artists, scientists, Wall Streeters, Main Streeters, professors and students. The authors say reliable evidence proves their skill.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Superforecasters: the authors' term for the roughly 2% of volunteer forecasters whose measured accuracy matches Bill's.

card.rule: According to the authors, a superforecaster is shown by a measured record of accuracy, not by a profession or a title.
card.limits: The 2% describes these volunteers; most volunteers were not as good as Bill.

concepts.title: Forecasts of unknown quality
concepts.question: Why can the chapter not say how good Tom Friedman's forecasting is?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Tom Friedman's forecasting accuracy has never been rigorously tested, so there are only opinions about it, and the same is true of most forecasts we rely on.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Friedman's fans and critics cite his hits and misses, such as the Arab Spring or the 2003 invasion of Iraq, but there are no hard facts about his record. The media deliver forecasts without asking how good the forecasters are, and governments and companies pay for forecasts that may be prescient, worthless or in between.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: Baseball managers would not hire a player without performance statistics, and fans expect to see player stats on scoreboards.

card.rule: According to the authors, the quality of a forecaster is known only from a rigorously tested record, not from opinions about hits and misses.
card.limits: The authors do not say Friedman forecasts badly; they say nobody can tell, so he cannot be compared with superforecasters.

concepts.title: A skill, not a gift
concepts.question: Is forecasting a talent you have or lack, or a skill you can build?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, forecasting is not a you-have-it-or-you-don't talent; it is a skill that can be cultivated.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The case offered is Bill Flack and his tested forecasting record. The authors promise that the book will show how such skill is cultivated.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, treat forecasting as a skill that can be cultivated, not as an inborn gift.
card.limits: At this point the claim is a promise; the chapter later offers tournament results as support.

concepts.title: The dart-throwing chimp
concepts.question: What did Tetlock's twenty-year study find about the average expert?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: In Tetlock's study, the average expert was roughly as accurate as a dart-throwing chimpanzee, which means about as good as random guessing.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tetlock gathered a big group of experts, academics and pundits among them, who made thousands of predictions about the economy, stocks, elections and wars. The study ran from 1984 to 2004, and the average expert did about as well as random guessing.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The dart-throwing chimpanzee: the famous joke, which Tetlock himself had used, for the average expert's accuracy.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Tetlock says he is the researcher; his study was the most comprehensive assessment of expert judgment in the scientific literature.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, the average expert did about as well as random guessing on the questions posed.
card.limits: The next ideas show that this is an average over many questions, not a verdict on every expert or every question.

concepts.title: Why pundits are on camera
concepts.question: Why do the authors think the joke makes a valid point about pundits?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the joke makes a valid point: experts are on camera because they tell a compelling story with conviction, not because of proven forecasting skill.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In newspapers and on television, some experts are cautious, more are bold and a handful claim to see decades ahead. Accuracy is seldom mentioned, old forecasts are forgotten like old news, and pundits are almost never asked to reconcile what they said with what happened.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, a pundit's visibility rests on storytelling and conviction, not on a checked record.
card.limits: The authors criticize a marketplace of untested forecasts; they do not say every expert in the media lacks skill.

concepts.title: The message that got garbled
concepts.question: What did Tetlock's research actually show, and what did retelling make of it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: Tetlock's research showed the average expert did little better than guessing on many questions, not all, and accuracy fell as the forecast horizon grew.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: It was easiest to beat chance on the shortest-range questions, those a year out, and accuracy fell off, approaching chimp level three to five years out. Like the children's game of telephone, the retelling garbled the message into the claim that all expert forecasts are useless, which Tetlock calls nonsense.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Telephone: the authors' comparison to a children's whisper game, for how a message changes in retelling.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Many does not equal all.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, the finding is about the limits of expertise on many questions, with accuracy highest at about one year and fading by three to five years.
card.limits: It does not show that every expert forecast is useless or that nothing can be predicted.

concepts.title: The optimistic skeptic
concepts.question: Where does Tetlock stand between the debunkers and the defenders of experts?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: Tetlock takes a position between debunkers and defenders: it is possible to see into the future in some situations and to some extent, though there are limits.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The debunkers have a point: there are shady peddlers of questionable insights, and limits to foresight that may not be surmountable. But they go too far when they dismiss all forecasting as a fool's errand. Tetlock calls himself an optimistic skeptic.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Optimistic skeptic: Tetlock's label for accepting real limits on foresight while believing some foresight can be cultivated.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, accept the limits on prediction, but do not conclude that all forecasting is futile.
card.limits: The label is Tetlock's own stance; the next two sections defend its skeptic half and its optimist half in turn.

concepts.title: One man and the Arab Spring
concepts.question: How did one street vendor's humiliation grow into the Arab Spring?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: One ordinary humiliation of a poor street vendor set off a chain of events that reshaped a region, and nobody could trace it forward in advance.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: On December 17, 2010, Tunisian police took the scales and cart of the vendor Mohamed Bouazizi, who then set himself on fire. Protests spread, President Ben Ali fled into exile, and unrest reached Egypt, Libya, Syria, Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain. In Egypt, Hosni Mubarak was driven from office.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The Arab Spring: the chapter's name for the wave of protests, rebellions and civil wars that began with Bouazizi.

card.rule: A small, ordinary event can start a chain of consequences far out of proportion to it, which is easy to trace afterward.
card.limits: The chapter uses one story to illustrate the limits on foresight; it does not claim every humiliation leads to revolt.

concepts.title: Looking back is not looking ahead
concepts.question: Why does a clear story after the fact not show the event could have been foreseen?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: It is one thing to sketch a narrative arc backward; no one, not even Tom Friedman present that morning, could have foreseen the self-immolation and all that followed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A knowledgeable observer might have said that poverty and unemployment were high, desperate young people were many, corruption was rampant and repression was relentless, so Tunisia was a powder keg. But an observer could have said the same the year before, and for decades, and the kegs never blew until that morning.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, an after-the-fact story that links causes to an event does not show the event could have been predicted.
card.limits: The authors do not say conditions are irrelevant; they say conditions that persist for decades do not tell you when, or whether, an explosion will come.

concepts.title: The butterfly effect
concepts.question: How can a tiny change in starting conditions lead to a very different outcome?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, in nonlinear systems like the atmosphere, tiny differences in starting conditions can grow to enormous proportions, which limits long-term prediction.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: About a decade before that 1972 paper, Edward Lorenz found by accident that replacing 0.506127 with 0.506 in weather simulation data produced dramatically different long-term forecasts. His 1972 paper asked whether a butterfly's wings in Brazil could set off a tornado in Texas. The insight inspired chaos theory.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The butterfly effect, and chaos theory.

card.rule: According to the authors, in nonlinear systems small changes in initial conditions can mushroom, so long-term prediction has limits.
card.limits: Lorenz did not mean the butterfly causes the tornado the way a hammer causes a glass to break; he meant the tornado might not have formed without that flap.

concepts.title: Laplace's demon and the clock
concepts.question: What did scientists once expect from growing knowledge, and how far did Laplace push it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: For centuries scientists supposed that growing knowledge must bring greater predictability, because reality was like a very big and complicated clock; Laplace took that dream to its extreme.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In 1814 the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace imagined an intellect that knew all forces and all positions of everything in nature and could analyze the data. For it, nothing would be uncertain and the future, like the past, would be present before its eyes. He called it a demon.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Laplace's demon: an imagined omniscient intellect that could predict everything about the future; Laplacean predictability is the clock's perfect predictability.

card.rule: Laplace's dream: complete knowledge of the present, plus enough power to analyze it, would allow perfect prediction of the future.
card.limits: The dream was shaken when Lorenz moved scientific opinion toward the view that predictability has hard limits.

concepts.title: The Lorenzian cloud
concepts.question: Why can more knowledge fail to predict the shape of a cloud?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, where equations are highly sensitive to tiny errors, even knowing all that is knowable does not allow us to predict outcomes; the cloud, not the clock, is the symbol.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Clouds form when water vapor coalesces around dust particles, but the shape of a particular cloud depends on complex feedback interactions among droplets. Computer models need equations highly sensitive to tiny butterfly-effect errors in data collection, so we can only wait and see how the cloud develops.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The Lorenzian cloud: the opposite of the Laplacean clock.

card.rule: According to the authors, where tiny data errors mushroom, learning more still cannot give a perfect prediction.
card.limits: The cloud is one image; the next section says the world holds clocks, clouds and much else.

concepts.title: Ripples reach everyone
concepts.question: Why do the authors say it is misguided to think anyone can see very far ahead?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: In a world where one nearly powerless man can start ripples that reach us all, the authors say it is misguided to think anyone can see very far into the future.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A woman in a Kansas City suburb may think Tunisia is another planet. But if her husband is an air force navigator, the Tunisian vendor's act led to protests, then riots, then the toppled dictator, then protests in Libya, civil war, a NATO intervention, and her husband dodging antiaircraft fire over Tripoli.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, because distant events can ripple into ordinary lives, long-range foresight is limited, which is the skeptic half of their stance.
card.limits: This is only the skeptic half; the optimist half follows in the next section.

concepts.title: A predictable day
concepts.question: How much of an ordinary day rests on predictions that turn out right?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, much of ordinary life is quite predictable, and we and others make predictions that shape our lives all the time without noticing.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The Kansas City woman leaves at 6:30 to beat rush hour, expects drivers to stop at red lights, expects colleagues on her 10:30 call, and trusts the restaurant's posted hours. Electricity producers anticipate the morning demand surge, Amazon forecasts what she will like, and her employer, an insurer, forecasts disability and death.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, alongside unpredictable influences, there is as much or more in our lives that is quite predictable.
card.limits: The chapter says predictability exists to some degree; the next ideas show it can be punctured.

concepts.title: Clocklike predictability
concepts.question: Which things can be predicted precisely, and why?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: Some things can be predicted with great precision far ahead, because they follow clocklike scientific laws.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The author Googled tomorrow's sunrise and sunset times for Kansas City and got them to the minute. Tides, eclipses and the phases of the moon are the same: all can be predicted from clocklike laws.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Clocklike: the chapter's word for phenomena governed by laws that allow precise prediction.

card.rule: Where clocklike scientific laws govern a phenomenon, precise prediction is possible.
card.limits: Clocklike cases are special; the next idea shows even these pockets can be punctured.

concepts.title: Pockets that can be punctured
concepts.question: Does a reliable prediction ever become certain?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, every pocket of predictability can be abruptly punctured, so there are no certainties, only high probabilities.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A good restaurant is very likely to open when it says it will, but it may not: a manager may sleep late, or there may be a fire, bankruptcy, pandemic or nuclear war. Even fifty-year sunrise forecasts could be off if a massive space rock bumps Earth off its orbit.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Pockets of predictability: the chapter's phrase for areas where prediction works well.

card.rule: Treat even highly predictable events as very probable, not certain.
card.limits: Puncturing is possible, not likely; the pockets of predictability are real and useful.

concepts.title: Clocks and clouds together
concepts.question: Is the future predictable or not, or is that the wrong question?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, asking whether reality is clocklike or cloud-like is a false dichotomy: predictability and unpredictability coexist, and how predictable something is depends on what, how far ahead and under what circumstances.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The chapter says we live in a world of clocks and clouds and a vast jumble of other metaphors. Predictability and unpredictability sit together in the interlocking systems of bodies, societies and the cosmos.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: False dichotomy: the chapter's name for an either-or framing that hides a mixture.

card.rule: Ask how predictable something is for what question, how far ahead and under what conditions, not whether the future is predictable.
card.limits: The chapter does not give a formula for sorting the predictable from the unpredictable; it calls that difficult work.

concepts.title: How far ahead can we see?
concepts.question: How does predictability change as the forecast reaches further ahead?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, predictability usually falls as forecasts look further ahead, but there are prolonged exceptions, and nothing is predictable or unpredictable without qualification.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Weather forecasts are quite reliable a few days ahead, less accurate three, four and five days out, and much beyond a week we might as well consult the dart-throwing chimpanzee. A long stock bull market can also be predicted profitably for years.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: Say that something is predictable to some extent under some circumstances, and be careful about being more precise than that.
card.limits: The distance rule is generally true, not universal: the chapter says laws of physics aside there are no universal constants.

concepts.title: Forecast, measure, revise
concepts.question: What explains why weather forecasts are good and slowly getting better?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: Meteorologists make many forecasts and routinely check their accuracy, then revise their models and try again; this loop explains why weather forecasts are good and improving slowly.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Because meteorologists measure results, we know one- and two-day forecasts are typically quite accurate and eight-day forecasts are not. The checking sharpens their understanding of how weather works and lets them tweak their models. The chapter sums it up: forecast, measure, revise, repeat.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Forecast, measure, revise, repeat: the chapter's phrase for the loop; no formal term.

card.rule: Improve forecasts by making many, measuring their accuracy and revising the method, over and over.
card.limits: Weather is nonlinear, so improvement hits limits: bigger computers and better models nudge the limit out, but payoffs shrink toward zero.

concepts.title: No measurement, no improvement
concepts.question: Why do most forecasters never learn how good they are?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: In most high-stakes forecasting accuracy is not measured, so there is no revision and no improvement; the authors call this mostly a demand-side problem.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Forecast, measure, revise operates only in high-tech settings, such as macroeconomists at central banks, marketing and financial professionals in large companies, and poll analysts like Nate Silver. Elsewhere forecasts are made and then nothing, because governments, business and the public do not demand evidence of accuracy.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Demand-side problem: the authors' description of why measurement is missing.

card.rule: According to the authors, without measurement there is no revision, and without revision there can be no improvement.
card.limits: The chapter says the loop operates in some places; it is rare, not absent.

concepts.title: Forecasts with other goals
concepts.question: Is the goal of every forecast to foresee the future accurately?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, accuracy is often not the sole goal of a forecast, and the jumble of goals is seldom acknowledged, which makes it hard to start measuring.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The chapter lists goals other than accuracy: to entertain, like Jim Cramer or the host of The McLaughlin Group; to advance political agendas, like activists warning of horrors; to impress, as when a bank pays a famous pundit to describe the 2050 economy; and to comfort an audience that its beliefs are correct.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Dress-to-impress forecasting: the chapter's phrase for forecasts bought to look impressive.

card.rule: According to the authors, ask what a forecast is for before judging it by accuracy.
card.limits: The authors do not say accuracy is unimportant; they say unacknowledged goals block progress toward measuring it.

concepts.title: The opportunity in missing rigor
concepts.question: What is the opportunity in forecasting's lack of rigor?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the lack of rigor in forecasting is a huge opportunity: to seize it, set a clear goal, accuracy, and get serious about measuring.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tetlock points to the quoted view of Bill Gates that measurement drives progress when there is a clear goal and a measure toward it. In forecasting, even that simple first step has not been taken.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: To improve forecasting, set accuracy as the goal and measure progress toward it.
card.limits: Gates also says measurement is often not done and hard to get right, so the step is simple to state, not easy to do.

concepts.title: The Good Judgment Project and the tournament
concepts.question: How was the tournament built so that forecasts could be compared fairly?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: Tetlock and Barbara Mellers launched the Good Judgment Project in 2011, and it competed in an IARPA tournament built so that teams could be compared fairly.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: More than twenty thousand volunteers forecast. IARPA, an intelligence research agency, ran a tournament with five scientific teams, each required to forecast the same questions at the same time each day from September 2011 to June 2015. About five hundred questions and over a million judgments produced a level playing field.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Good Judgment Project (GJP): Tetlock and Mellers's team; IARPA: the research agency that ran the tournament.

card.rule: Compare forecasters by having them forecast the same questions at the same time.
card.limits: Most questions looked more than one month and less than one year ahead, so the tournament does not speak to forecasts decades out.

concepts.title: What the tournament showed
concepts.question: How did the Good Judgment Project do against its rivals?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The Good Judgment Project beat the official control group and its rival university teams by wide margins.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In year 1 it beat the official control group by 60%, and in year 2 by 78%. It beat university-affiliated competitors, including Michigan and MIT, by 30% to 70%. After two years it was doing so much better that IARPA dropped the other teams.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, a team of volunteers using best practices can beat control groups and academic rivals in a fair tournament.
card.limits: The chapter gives the percentages without the details, which it promises to cover later.

concepts.title: Foresight is real, and learnable
concepts.question: What are the two key conclusions of the tournament research?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, foresight is real, and what makes superforecasters good is not who they are but what they do: particular ways of thinking, gathering information and updating beliefs.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Some people have a real, measurable skill at judging high-stakes events three months to a year and a half ahead. They are not gurus or oracles who see decades ahead. Their habits can be learned by any intelligent, thoughtful, determined person.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: A tutorial of about sixty minutes covering basic concepts improved accuracy by roughly 10% through the tournament year.

card.rule: According to the authors, foresight is a product of learnable habits of thought, not a mysterious gift.
card.limits: The skill is for roughly three months to a year and a half; it does not stretch to decades.

concepts.title: Why we do not measure
concepts.question: What stops us from measuring forecasts, and how did medicine solve a similar problem?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the psychology that convinces us we know things we do not explains why forecasts are not measured, and medicine shows that testing can replace trust in experience.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say we feel sure about things like whether Tom Friedman is accurate. For centuries a similar certainty hobbled medicine. When physicians accepted that their experience and perceptions were not reliable ways to tell whether a treatment works, they turned to scientific testing and medicine advanced rapidly.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, personal experience and perception are not reliable guides to what works; test it rigorously instead.
card.limits: Testing forecasting is a bigger challenge than it appears; the book returns to it in chapter 3.

concepts.title: How they think, not who they are
concepts.question: What separates forecasters with foresight from the rest: who they are, or how they think?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, what matters most is how the forecaster thinks, not intelligence, mathematics, hours or beliefs; commitment to self-improvement is the strongest predictor of performance.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Earlier, the experts with modest but real foresight had no mystical gift or special information, and within a wide range of views what they thought did not matter. Superforecasters are smart and numerate, yet intelligence, arcane math and endless hours on the news do not explain them.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, superforecasting demands thinking that is open-minded, careful, curious and above all self-critical.
card.limits: Minimum levels of intelligence, numeracy and knowledge are needed, but readers of serious books on psychology probably have them.

concepts.title: Algorithms against judgment
concepts.question: When should a well-validated statistical algorithm replace subjective judgment?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, when a well-validated statistical algorithm exists, use it: in most studies algorithms beat subjective judgment, and in the rest they usually tie.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In 1954 Paul Meehl reviewed twenty studies in which informed experts predicted outcomes, such as a student's college success or a parolee's return to prison. The experts were less accurate than simple algorithms adding up objective indicators like test scores and past conduct. Over two hundred studies since point the same way.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, when you have a well-validated statistical algorithm, use it.
card.limits: Well-validated algorithms are rare for the problem at hand, so subjective judgment has not been displaced.

concepts.title: Why machines have not replaced forecasters
concepts.question: Why is predicting the future harder for a computer than looking up the past?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, computers have beaten humans at chess and Jeopardy!, but the sort of forecasting superforecasters do is a long way off, because it calls for judgment about intentions and causes.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in 1997 and Watson beat Jeopardy! champions in 2011. Watson's chief engineer, David Ferrucci, noted that naming which two Russian leaders once traded jobs is a historical fact a computer can look up, while asking whether two will trade jobs again needs an informed guess about Putin's intentions, Medvedev's character and Russian politics.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: A question about the past can be looked up; a forecast needs a judgment call about intentions, character and causes.
card.limits: Ferrucci says computing is on an exponential curve and not sure subjective judgment will remain; the chapter says only that the day is far off.

concepts.title: Humans and machines together
concepts.question: What does the chapter expect from combining human judgment with computers?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors expect the future to blend computer-based forecasting and subjective judgment, as in freestyle chess, and the guru model of debate to fade.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In freestyle chess humans with computers compete as teams, the human drawing on the computer's strengths but sometimes overriding it, and the combination can sometimes beat both humans and machines. Ferrucci expects the guru model, where each side counters a famous columnist with another, to become obsolete.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Freestyle chess: humans with computers competing as teams. Guru model: debate that rests on dueling pundits.

card.rule: According to the authors, we will need to blend computer-based forecasting and subjective judgment, so it is time to get serious about both.
card.limits: The combination can only sometimes beat both humans and machines.

concepts.title: Cochrane and the unchecked verdict
concepts.question: Why did neither Cochrane nor his specialist wait for the pathologist before accepting a deadly diagnosis?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, neither Archie Cochrane nor the eminent specialist doubted the diagnosis, so neither thought to wait for the pathologist. People are quick to make up their minds and slow to change them, and unless we examine how we make these mistakes, we will keep making them.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In 1956 Cochrane, himself a physician, had a skin cancer removed from his hand. A renowned specialist then took out an armpit lump and a chest muscle, and said the armpit was full of cancer and Cochrane would not live long. Cochrane believed him. The pathologist later found no cancer in the tissue.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Cochrane's own account, written many years later and quoted by the authors.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: one case shows how the mistake happens; it does not say how often specialists are wrong.

card.rule: According to the authors, a confident verdict is not a verified one, so look for the evidence that could still settle the matter.
card.limits: The authors do not blame the two men harshly; they call the haste human nature. The case shows a habit, not a count of how often experts err.

concepts.title: What histories of medicine leave out
concepts.question: Why do the authors call the long history of medicine wretched, when most histories of it sound impressive?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, most histories of medicine report what people believed they were doing but almost nothing on whether they were right. Judged by modern science, most treatments were useless or worse, and treatments seldom improved however much time passed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Burch, a British physician, makes the complaint about histories. The authors ask whether Egyptian ostrich-egg poultices, Mesopotamian treatments and bloodletting worked. In 1799 George Washington's doctors bled him, dosed him with mercury, induced vomiting and raised blisters with hot cups, and he died.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Druin Burch, a British physician and author, quoted by the authors.

card.rule: According to the authors, a long record of confident treatment shows what people believed, not that the treatment worked.
card.limits: The authors say most, not all, treatments were useless or worse. They judge with modern science, not with the doctors' own confidence.

concepts.title: A single outcome proves little
concepts.question: Why can Washington's death not show whether his treatments helped or harmed him?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, observing one outcome cannot show whether a treatment helped, did nothing or harmed. Even many such observations can be hard to untangle, because too many factors and explanations are in play. If physicians already believe the treatment works, they read the ambiguity in its favour.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Washington died after his physicians' treatment. That proves only that the treatment failed to prevent his death. It may have helped but not enough, not helped at all, or hastened his death, and the single result cannot say which.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors do not say the treatments helped or hurt Washington; they say one result cannot tell.

card.rule: According to the authors, one outcome fits several explanations, and a belief that a treatment works tilts how the outcome is read.
card.limits: More observations do not always fix this; the authors say only strong evidence and rigorous experiment can overwhelm preconceptions.

concepts.title: Galen and the unlosable claim
concepts.question: How did Galen make every outcome confirm his treatment?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Galen was untroubled by doubt and so never ran anything like an experiment, because experiments are what people do when they are unsure of the truth. Each outcome seemed to him to confirm that he was right.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Galen, a second-century physician to Roman emperors, claimed that all who drink his treatment recover quickly, except those it does not help, who all die. His conclusion was that it fails only in incurable cases.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given in this passage; the authors later call this pattern confirmation bias.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors call Galen an extreme example, not the typical physician.

card.rule: According to the authors, a claim that treats every outcome as support can never be shown wrong, and certainty removes the reason to test it.
card.limits: Galen is described as extreme. The point is the structure of his reasoning, not that every physician was like him.

concepts.title: Confident men and untested theories
concepts.question: What do the authors mean by physicians arguing like blind men over the colours of a rainbow?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the history of medicine keeps producing men of strong conviction who embrace treatments, invent bold theories, denounce rivals as quacks and spread their ideas with evangelical passion. Fringe or mainstream, almost all of it was wrong, and ignorance and confidence stayed defining features.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The line runs from the Greeks to Galen, Paracelsus, Hahnemann and Benjamin Rush. In nineteenth-century America, orthodox physicians fought charismatic rivals such as Thomsonianism, which blamed illness on an excess of cold, and the orificial surgery of Edwin Hartley Pratt, which centred life on the rectum.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given; the surgeon and historian Ira Rutkow's image is of blind men arguing over the colors of the rainbow.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Ira Rutkow, surgeon and historian, quoted by the authors.

card.rule: According to the authors, loud and confident disagreement among experts who never test their claims is not progress.
card.limits: The image fits debates that no test can settle. It does not say that every disagreement among experts is empty.

concepts.title: Lind's missed chance
concepts.question: Why did James Lind's 1747 scurvy experiment not change medicine?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Lind's 1747 experiment came tantalizingly close to a cure for medicine's certainty, but it was not the eureka moment that ushered in modern experimentation. Lind did not fully understand what he was doing.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Lind, a British ship's doctor, took twelve scurvy-stricken sailors, split them into pairs and gave each pair a different treatment: vinegar, cider, sulfuric acid, seawater, a bark paste, and citrus fruit. The two given citrus recovered quickly. Yet he failed to make sense of his experiment and stayed unconvinced of the benefit of lemons and limes.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Druin Burch, quoted by the authors.

card.rule: According to the authors, running a comparison is not enough: someone must grasp what it shows and act on it.
card.limits: Lind did run a comparison, so it is not that he had no method. The authors say he lacked the understanding to use it.

concepts.title: Why random assignment works
concepts.question: How does randomly assigning people to groups let us conclude that a treatment caused a difference?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, if identical patients were split into two groups and treated differently, any difference in outcome would be caused by the treatment. No two people are alike, so the solution is to assign people to groups at random: differences among them should balance out if enough people take part.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The British statistician Austin Bradford Hill laid out the template for modern medical investigation. The experiment is confounded by differences among subjects, even identical twins, which random assignment is meant to balance.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors call the result a randomized controlled trial.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: It is not perfect, the authors say, because there is no perfection in a messy world.

card.rule: According to the authors, random assignment of enough people balances their differences, so a gap in outcomes can be traced to the treatment.
card.limits: It needs enough participants and is imperfect. The authors say only that it beats wise men stroking their chins.

concepts.title: Cargo cult science
concepts.question: What does it mean to say that medicine dressed up as science without being scientific?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, medicine before the randomized trial was not scientific. It occasionally reaped the fruits of science, such as germ theory and the X-ray, and it dressed up as science with educated men, titles, case studies and Latin-laden lectures, but it was cargo cult science.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The physicist Richard Feynman described islanders in the South Pacific who, after wartime American airbases were removed, built runways, lit fires beside them, and made a hut with wooden headphones and bamboo antennas for a controller. They waited for planes, which never returned.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Cargo cult science, Feynman's term.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: It has the outward form of science but lacks what makes it truly scientific.

card.rule: According to the authors, the look of science without its substance, such as testing, is not science.
card.limits: Medicine did gain from real science, such as germ theory and the X-ray. The charge is about its method, not its every result.

concepts.title: Doubt as the engine of science
concepts.question: According to Feynman, what drives the rate at which science develops?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, what medicine lacked was doubt, and doubt is what propels science forward. Feynman said the rate of scientific development depends not only on making observations but, more importantly, on the rate at which new things to test are created.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Feynman distinguished three states: a scientist who says he does not know is ignorant; one with a hunch is uncertain; and one who is pretty sure and says he will bet still has some doubt. He calls it of paramount importance to recognise this ignorance and doubt, if we are to make progress.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: The authors say the absence of doubt and scientific rigor made medicine stagnate for so long.

card.rule: According to Feynman, recognise your ignorance and doubt, because doubt is what generates new things to test.
card.limits: Doubt is not paralysis: even a scientist who is pretty sure still bets, with some doubt remaining.

concepts.title: The God complex
concepts.question: Why did the medical establishment resist testing even after the first serious trials gave excellent results?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, after the Second World War the first serious trials were attempted and gave excellent results, yet the medical establishment stayed uninterested or even hostile. Physicians and their institutions did not want to give up the idea that their judgment alone revealed the truth.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Archie Cochrane complained that in the 1950s and 1960s too much of health care lacked scientific validation, and that the British National Health Service showed far too little interest in proving and promoting what was effective.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Cochrane's name for the attitude was the God complex.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Cochrane's autobiography, quoted by the authors.

card.rule: According to the authors, an institution convinced that its judgment alone reveals the truth feels no need for validation.
card.limits: The label describes an attitude of the establishment Cochrane faced. The authors do not say every physician held it.

concepts.title: Cochrane's trick on the cardiologists
concepts.question: What did Cochrane's reversal of the trial results show about how the cardiologists reacted?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the cardiologists' reaction to Cochrane's preliminary results followed what they believed, not what the evidence showed. They said at first that the cardiac care units were obviously better and that denying them to patients would be unethical.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Cochrane proposed a randomized trial of cardiac care units against going home for monitoring and bed rest. Part-way through, he told cardiologists that the units seemed slightly better, though not by a statistically significant margin. They demanded the trial stop. He then revealed he had reversed the results: home care had done slightly better.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The difference was small and not statistically significant, so the story is about reactions, not about which care was better.

card.rule: According to the authors, strong confidence in a treatment can drive reactions to a result even when the result runs the other way.
card.limits: The result was preliminary and not statistically significant. The story shows beliefs at work; it does not prove home care is better.

concepts.title: The illusion of insight
concepts.question: Why can a policy rolled out everywhere never tell us whether it worked?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the only alternative to a controlled experiment that delivers real insight is an uncontrolled experiment that produces merely the illusion of insight. A policy introduced everywhere at once cannot be judged, because many causes could explain what follows.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Cochrane's example was the Thatcher government's short, sharp, shock approach to young offenders: brief incarceration in spartan jails under strict rules, applied across the whole justice system. If crime fell, the policy may have worked or crime may have fallen for another reason; if crime rose, the policy may have failed or prevented a bigger rise.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors do not say the policy failed. They say nobody could know.

card.rule: According to the authors, without a controlled comparison, politicians on each side can claim the same facts, and nobody knows.
card.limits: The authors do not say all policies can be randomized; their point is that without a comparison the result is an illusion of insight.

concepts.title: Two riddles about Cochrane
concepts.question: What are the two puzzles the authors raise, and why does the second matter?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, there are two riddles. First, Cochrane's modest point, that more than intuition is needed for firm conclusions, is so obviously true that it is odd that people resisted it. Second, Cochrane himself, who stressed not rushing to judgment, rushed to judgment about whether he had terminal cancer.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: When an eminent physician told him he was riddled with cancer he did not think it was one man's subjective judgment, could be wrong, or should await the pathologist. He treated the conclusion as fact and prepared to die.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The riddles are posed here. The authors answer them in the sections that follow.

card.rule: According to the authors, even people who know the rule against rushing to judgment break it, so the cause must lie in how minds work.
card.limits: Our reading: the two riddles are raised, not yet solved. The explanation comes later in the chapter.

concepts.title: Introspection sees little
concepts.question: How much of what drives our decisions can we reach by looking inward?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, we can only share our thoughts by introspecting, and introspection can capture only a tiny fraction of the complex processes inside our heads and behind our decisions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Asked to explain a choice, we examine the contents of our minds and report what we find there.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Introspection: turning attention inward to examine the contents of the mind.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors do not say the reasons people give are false, only that they cover a tiny fraction.

card.rule: According to the authors, the reasons we can state are only a small part of what is behind our decisions.
card.limits: The reasons given may be true as far as they go. The point is that they are not the whole story.

concepts.title: System 1 and System 2
concepts.question: What are System 1 and System 2, and in what order do they usually work?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, modern psychologists often describe thinking with a dual-system model. System 2 is conscious thought, everything we choose to focus on. System 1 is automatic perceptual and cognitive operation that we do not notice. System 1 is fast, always running and comes first. System 2 is charged with interrogating its answers, which takes time and effort.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Turning print into a meaningful sentence, or holding a book while reaching for a glass, are System 1 jobs. An answer you instantly know sprang from System 1. The usual routine is that System 1 delivers an answer first and only then can System 2 examine it.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: System 1 and System 2, terms associated with Daniel Kahneman.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Whether System 2 actually gets involved is another matter.

card.rule: According to the authors, an instant answer comes from System 1, and System 2 must choose to check it.
card.limits: System 2 involvement is not guaranteed. The authors show next how often it is skipped.

concepts.title: The bat and the ball
concepts.question: What does the bat-and-ball question reveal about how quickly we accept an answer?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the answer 'ten cents' appears instantly, without calculation, and feels right, but it is wrong. The question is an item in the Cognitive Reflection Test, which shows that most people, even very smart ones, are not very reflective and go with strong hunches.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A bat and ball together cost $1.10, and the bat costs a dollar more than the ball. Most people answer ten cents, write it down, and never discover the mistake. Thinking it through gives five cents.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The Cognitive Reflection Test.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors call this normal human behaviour, not stupidity.

card.rule: According to the authors, an answer that feels right is not shown to be right, and checking it takes sustained effort.
card.limits: The test shows a habit common even among smart people. It does not say that the instant answer is always wrong.

concepts.title: Why snap judgments exist
concepts.question: Why is jumping to conclusions from little evidence not always a flaw?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, going with strong hunches is not a bad way of making decisions in the world in which our brains evolved. Snap judgments are sometimes essential. Kahneman says System 1 is designed to jump to conclusions from little evidence.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A hunter-gatherer who consulted statistics on lions before deciding whether to worry about a moving shadow in the grass would be unlikely to live long enough to pass on his accuracy-maximising genes.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Daniel Kahneman, quoted by the authors.

card.rule: According to the authors, snap judgments are sometimes essential, so fast conclusions are not always a flaw.
card.limits: The authors do not say snap judgments suit every decision. Their next point is that System 1 can mislead.

concepts.title: The availability heuristic
concepts.question: How does System 1 decide a shadow in the grass is worth fearing?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, when you see a shadow move in long grass, System 1 asks whether you can recall a lion pouncing on someone. If the memory comes easily, you conclude lion attacks are common and start to worry. This can happen entirely within System 1, in a few tenths of a second.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors spell the process out to show it can sound ponderous but is automatic, fast and complete. It is the availability heuristic.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The availability heuristic.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: It is a mental shortcut, not a calculation of how often lion attacks occur.

card.rule: According to the authors, ease of recall stands in for how common something is, and it all happens without effort.
card.limits: The authors do not say it is wrong every time, only that it is automatic.

concepts.title: What You See Is All There Is
concepts.question: What does System 1 assume about the evidence in front of it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a defining feature of intuitive judgment is that it does not respond to the quality of its evidence. System 1 treats whatever evidence is at hand as reliable and sufficient, and never wonders whether it is flawed or whether better evidence exists elsewhere.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors present this as a defining feature of intuitive judgment, and Kahneman gave the tacit assumptions behind it a label.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: WYSIATI, Kahneman's label, short for What You See Is All There Is.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Kahneman's label for these tacit assumptions, as the authors describe it.

card.rule: According to the authors, System 1 treats the evidence it has as all the evidence there is, so its confidence does not reflect how thin that evidence is.
card.limits: The authors say System 1 needs this to do its job quickly. It is a feature of speed, not a defect that can be removed.

concepts.title: Inventing stories to make sense
concepts.question: What did Gazzaniga's split-brain patients show about our urge to explain?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the human brain demands order. We must be able to explain what we see and think, and we are creative confabulators hardwired to invent stories that impose coherence on the world.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Michael Gazzaniga studied split-brain patients, whose brain hemispheres cannot communicate. A picture of a snowstorm was shown to the left visual field and the patient pointed to a shovel. A chicken claw was shown to the right visual field, and when asked why he pointed at a shovel, the left hemisphere had no idea, yet he said a shovel was needed to clean out the chicken shed.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors call people creative confabulators.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The patients were otherwise remarkably normal; the authors use them to show a general tendency.

card.rule: According to the authors, when we lack the real reason we invent a sensible-sounding one rather than say we do not know.
card.limits: The split-brain setting is extreme. The authors use it to make visible something they say ordinary people do too.

concepts.title: The journalist's tidy story
concepts.question: Why is the explanatory urge both useful and risky?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the same compulsion to explain appears whenever a stock market closes and a journalist reports that it moved because of some news. The journalist conjures a plausible story from whatever is at hand. The trouble is moving too fast from confusion to a confident conclusion.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A line such as the Dow rose ninety-five points today on news that something happened is typical. A quick check often shows that the news came out after the market had risen. A journalist rarely says the market rose for any one of a hundred reasons, or a mix, so no one knows.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: The authors say the missing step is the middle ground: this is one possible explanation but there are others.

card.rule: According to the authors, pause between not knowing and a confident explanation to say that this is one possibility among several.
card.limits: The authors call the explanatory urge mostly good. Their complaint is about skipping the middle step.

concepts.title: Oslo: the plausible first guess
concepts.question: How does the Oslo attack show the pull of a plausible hypothesis?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, after the 2011 Oslo attack, speculation quickly settled on radical Islamists. Given the few facts known and the history of terrorism in the preceding decade, suspecting them was reasonable. A scientist would call it a plausible hypothesis, but would have handled it very differently.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A car bomb killed eight people and injured over two hundred, and a mass shooting at a Labour Party summer camp followed. People decided everything fit. In fact there was one perpetrator, Anders Breivik, who is not Muslim and hates Muslims, and who attacked a government he thought had betrayed Norway.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Plausible hypothesis, the scientist's term for such an early guess.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors do not defend those who blamed Muslims in general; they say the suspicion itself was reasonable.

card.rule: According to the authors, a plausible hypothesis can be reasonable and wrong; treat it as a guess to test, not as the answer.
card.limits: The authors say suspecting Islamist terrorists was reasonable at the time. The fault was in the certainty and in how the guess was handled.

concepts.title: How a scientist handles a hunch
concepts.question: How do scientists treat an idea that feels true?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, scientists have intuitions too and hunches have led to countless breakthroughs, but they are trained to be cautious. Alternative explanations must get a hearing, and they must seriously consider that their first hunch is wrong. They replace the feeling of certainty with finely measured degrees of doubt.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In science the best evidence that a hypothesis is true is often an experiment designed to prove it false that fails to do so. Scientists must be able to answer the question What would convince me I am wrong? If they cannot, they have grown too attached to their beliefs.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors say System 1 and System 2 can interact subtly and creatively in science.

card.rule: According to the authors, test a hunch by trying to prove it false and know what would convince you that you are wrong.
card.limits: The authors say such caution runs against human nature, so it takes training.

concepts.title: Confirmation bias and coherence
concepts.question: Why does a story that fits everything make us more confident than we should be?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, our natural inclination is to grab the first plausible explanation and gather supporting evidence without checking its reliability. We rarely seek evidence that undercuts it, and when it is pushed under our noses we become motivated skeptics who belittle or discard it. Tidy explanations satisfy the brain's desire for order.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The post-Oslo speculation showed this. So did Galen, who counted a cure as evidence for his treatment and a death as meaning nothing.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Confirmation bias, a psychologists' term; the authors call those who dismiss contrary evidence motivated skeptics.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors say this is a poor way to model a complicated world but a superb way to feel that everything is settled.

card.rule: According to the authors, the feeling that it all fits is not evidence that the story is true.
card.limits: The authors say the pull is strong because tidy explanations leave no loose ends. They do not say that a good fit is always misleading.

concepts.title: Bait and switch in the mind
concepts.question: What does the mind do when it faces a hard question it cannot answer?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, when faced with a hard question we often surreptitiously replace it with an easy one, and the answer to the easy question stands in for the answer to the hard one. It is usually an unconscious System 1 activity.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Should I worry about the shadow in the long grass? Without more data that may be unanswerable, so we ask instead whether we can easily recall a lion attacking someone from the long grass. If yes, the answer to the first question becomes yes.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Attribute substitution is the formal name; the author calls it bait and switch.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors say they are not offering anything startling: people often jump to judgment.

card.rule: According to the authors, check whether the question you answered is the one you were asked.
card.limits: The authors say the swap is usually unconscious, so noticing it takes deliberate effort.

concepts.title: Conscious and unconscious switches
concepts.question: Can we substitute questions knowingly, and what did the authors suspect Cochrane did?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, we are not always oblivious to the swap. Someone who lacks the knowledge may knowingly replace a hard question with an easier one about experts. The author suspects Cochrane did something similar unconsciously, in the case of his own diagnosis.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Asked whether climate change is real, a person without training may substitute whether most climatologists think so. An ordinary patient told by an eminent specialist may accept the verdict. The author suspects Cochrane replaced Do I have cancer? with Is this the sort of person who should know?

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Bait and switch, here done consciously or unconsciously.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The author says I suspect: this is a likely explanation, not a proven one.

card.rule: According to the authors, replacing a question by asking who should know can be sensible if done knowingly, and risky if unnoticed.
card.limits: The authors call the Cochrane account a suspicion. They do not claim to know what went on in his mind.

concepts.title: The tip-of-your-nose perspective
concepts.question: Why can we not switch off the fast, automatic way of seeing the world?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the quick, nearly effortless way of thinking cannot be called a default setting, because that suggests we can flip a switch to something else, and we cannot. System 1 keeps humming, nonstop. No one is immune, not even skeptics like Cochrane.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The instant we wake and look past the tip of our nose, sights and sounds flow to the brain and System 1 is engaged. This view is subjective and unique to each of us, because only you can see the world from the tip of your own nose.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The tip-of-your-nose perspective, the authors' term.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors say the view is imperfect but should not be discounted entirely.

card.rule: According to the authors, you cannot turn off your tip-of-your-nose perspective, so build checks around it.
card.limits: The authors do not say the perspective is useless. They say it is subjective and cannot be switched off.

concepts.title: Blink versus think
concepts.question: Should we trust intuition or analysis, and how did Kahneman and Klein resolve it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, popular books often set intuition against analysis, blink versus think. The authors call this a false dichotomy: the choice is how to blend them in evolving situations. Snap judgments can work astonishingly well, and Kahneman and Klein, who seemed to disagree, got together to solve the puzzle.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Gary Klein studied professionals such as firefighting commanders. One commander sent his men from a house just before the living-room floor collapsed, though the fire he was fighting seemed routine. Kahneman and Klein wrote in 2009 that they agreed on most of the issues that matter.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Blink versus think is the popular dichotomy; the authors call it false.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors say they are more of a thinker than a blinker.

card.rule: According to the authors, ask how to combine intuition and analysis, not which to pick.
card.limits: The authors say their conclusion is less inspiring than choosing a side, but it has the advantage of being true.

concepts.title: When intuition can be trusted
concepts.question: What decides whether intuition yields insight or delusion?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, an accurate intuition such as the commander's is pattern recognition. With training or experience, people store patterns in great number and detail. Intuition yields insight or delusion depending on whether the world offers valid cues that can be learned. Even when it can work, they advise caution and double-checking.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Kahneman and Klein reason that early signs of a collapsing building or an infant's infection exist, but public information that predicts a stock does not, since the price already reflects it. So trust a firefighter or a nurse more than a stockbroker.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Pattern recognition.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Pattern recognition also yields false positives, as when someone sees the Virgin Mary in burnt toast.

card.rule: According to the authors, trust intuition where valid cues can be learned, and even there double-check.
card.limits: The authors say it is often hard to know when enough valid cues exist. Pattern recognition also comes with false positives.

concepts.title: Noonan's vibrations and the tablespoon of doubt
concepts.question: Why do the authors compare forecasting today with nineteenth-century medicine?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, tip-of-your-nose illusions are so convincing that we ignore the advice to think before big decisions. Forecasting in the twenty-first century looks like nineteenth-century medicine: theories, assertions, arguments and confident famous figures, but little experimentation. The cure is a tablespoon of doubt.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The day before the 2012 election, Peggy Noonan forecast a Romney victory from big rally crowds, the candidate looking happy and a report of the crowd's joy. She wrote that the vibrations were right. The authors say many of us feel the same mistaken certainty.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors say bad forecasting rarely leads as obviously to harm as bad medicine.

card.rule: According to the authors, forecasting needs the doubt and testing that medicine once lacked.
card.limits: The authors say bad forecasting causes harm less obviously than bad medicine.

concepts.title: Why scoring forecasts is harder than it looks
concepts.question: Why is judging forecasts not as simple as collecting them and adding up the hits?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, once medicine learned to doubt itself and test treatments in trials, measuring forecasting seems easier: collect forecasts, judge their accuracy, add the numbers. They then say it is not nearly so simple.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The chapter opens with the medical comparison, then offers two famous forecasts (Steve Ballmer on the iPhone, an open letter to Ben Bernanke) that look clear but cannot be marked right or wrong without dispute.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, scoring forecasts takes more than gathering them and counting hits: a forecast has to be judgeable first.
card.limits: The point is about care, not despair. The authors go on to show how forecasts can be made testable, so the claim is not that scoring is impossible.

concepts.title: Ballmer’s iPhone line and the word “significant”
concepts.question: What makes Steve Ballmer’s famous iPhone forecast hard to declare wrong?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Ballmer’s 2007 forecast looks spectacularly wrong, but its key term is ambiguous: he never said what counts as significant, or which market he meant, so it cannot be judged without assumptions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: As Microsoft’s CEO, Ballmer said there was no chance the iPhone would get any significant market share. By 2013 a writer reported the iPhone held 42% of the US smartphone market and 13.1% worldwide. Yet Ballmer named no market and no threshold.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors’ term for the pile of such blunders is the “forecasting hall of shame”, where Ballmer’s line is often listed.

card.rule: According to the authors, a forecast must be free of ambiguity before it can be marked right or wrong.
card.limits: The authors do not say the forecast was right. They say a strong case can be made that it was wrong, but not beyond reasonable doubt.

concepts.title: The full Ballmer statement narrows the claim
concepts.question: What did the longer 2007 interview show Ballmer was actually forecasting?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Ballmer’s full statement shows he meant the global mobile phone market, so it is wrong to measure him against US or global smartphone share. Some ambiguity still remains.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the April 2007 USA Today interview he put the market at 1.3 billion phones, said he would rather have his software in 60% to 80% of them than 2% or 3%, “which is what Apple might get”, and added Apple may make a lot of money. Tetlock, using Gartner data, put the iPhone at roughly 6% of global mobile phone sales in late 2013.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, check the original statement in context, and then ask what is still undefined.
card.limits: Context fixes some terms, not all. The authors note that how far above 2% or 3% counts as significant, and how much is a lot of money, are still unstated.

concepts.title: The Bernanke letter and the missing time frame
concepts.question: Why could critics of quantitative easing never be shown wrong or right on inflation?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the November 2010 open letter to Fed chairman Ben Bernanke gave no time frame, so however many years passed, a defender could say the predicted debasement and inflation had not yet come.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Economists and commentators, including Niall Ferguson and Amity Shlaes, urged the Fed to stop quantitative easing as it risked currency debasement and inflation. The advice was ignored; the dollar was not debased and inflation did not rise in later years. Barry Ritholtz called the signers terribly wrong in 2013, but the letter set no deadline.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, a forecast with no time frame cannot be refuted, because it can always be said that the event is still to come.
card.limits: The authors do not say the letter writers were right. They say the missing deadline makes the claim untestable, not true.

concepts.title: “Risk” and unmeasured size in the letter
concepts.question: Read literally, what did the Bernanke letter forecast, and why does that matter?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the letter also left open how much the dollar must fall and inflation rise to count, and by calling these a “risk”, it literally said they may or may not follow, so non-occurrence is not necessarily wrong.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The letter said large-scale asset purchases risked currency debasement and inflation. Read literally, that is not a prediction that they would happen. The authors add that this is surely not what the signers meant or how people read it then, but it is what the text says.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, judge what a forecast says, and note when a hedge such as “risk” lets it escape failure.
card.limits: The authors say the literal reading is not how the letter was understood at the time. Their point is about testability, not about the signers’ intentions.

concepts.title: Fear of nuclear war and the 1984 panel
concepts.question: What was the setting in which Tetlock began to doubt confident expert forecasts?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, in the early 1980s many thoughtful people saw nuclear war coming, and in 1984 a National Research Council panel on preventing nuclear war heard from confident experts. Tetlock sat on it as its youngest, least impressive member.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Jonathan Schell wrote that unless nuclear arsenals were abolished a holocaust would occur, if not today then tomorrow. In June 1982 about seven hundred thousand people marched in New York. The panel included three Nobel laureates, Charles Townes, Kenneth Arrow and Herbert Simon, and Amos Tversky.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, the panel invited impressive, informed and confident experts, which is what made their later surprise instructive.
card.limits: This is scene-setting for the chapter, not evidence about forecasters in general. The authors use the panel as the start of their story, not as a result.

concepts.title: Experts right about Chernenko, wrong about what followed
concepts.question: What did the experts agree on in 1984, and what did almost none of them see coming?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the panel’s experts agreed on the basic facts and expected the next Soviet leader to be another stern party man, but they disagreed about why. Few saw Gorbachev’s reforms coming.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Liberal experts thought Reagan’s hard line was strengthening Kremlin hard-liners; conservative experts thought the Soviet system perfectly reproduced itself. Both were confident. They were right that Chernenko would die; he did, in March 1985, and the Politburo named the fifty-four-year-old Mikhail Gorbachev, who pursued glasnost and perestroika.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors use the Marx joke that when history hits a curve, the intellectuals fall off. No other name is given.

card.rule: According to the authors, experts with opposite reasons and equal confidence expected the same result and were jointly surprised by Gorbachev.
card.limits: The authors do not claim that every expert was wrong about everything. The experts were right about Chernenko’s death. The surprise concerned what came next.

concepts.title: Explaining it afterwards: retrospective light
concepts.question: How did experts who missed Gorbachev’s rise react afterwards, and what did Tetlock suspect?

blocks.label: Claim
