blocks.text: According to the authors, most experts who did not see it coming soon grew convinced they knew why it happened, and Tetlock suspected they would have explained away any outcome. He says intelligence and integrity are not enough.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Liberals said the Soviet economy was crumbling and the outcome was bound to happen, with no credit to Reagan. Conservatives said Reagan had called the Soviets’ bluff. Each side found it predictable in the right retrospective light. The authors compare these experts to renowned physicians of the prescientific era.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors’ term is “tip-of-your-nose delusions”, which can fool even the best and brightest.

card.rule: According to the authors, an explanation that is available after the event tells you little about whether the event was foreseen.
card.limits: Tetlock says he was not questioning the experts’ intelligence or integrity. His claim is about the limits of both, not about the experts’ character.

concepts.title: Kahneman’s lunchtime guess about expertise
concepts.question: What did Daniel Kahneman guess about how much intelligence and knowledge help forecasting?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, at a 1988 lunch his Berkeley colleague Daniel Kahneman speculated that intelligence and knowledge improve forecasting, but the benefits taper off fast, so experts may beat well-read laypeople only slightly.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Kahneman suggested people with PhDs and decades of experience may be only a tad more accurate than attentive readers of the New York Times. Tetlock notes it was only a guess, and that no one had seriously tested the forecasting accuracy of political experts.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: the lunchtime remark is a prompt for the study, not a finding of the study.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, Kahneman’s idea was a testable guess: skill might rise with knowledge, but flatten out quickly.
card.limits: It was a hypothesis, not a result. Tetlock says even Kahneman’s guesses are guesses, and the chapter goes on to test it.

concepts.title: Forecasts without time frames
concepts.question: Why do forecasts without time frames cause disputes, though they seem fine when made?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a forecast without a time frame is absurd, yet forecasters routinely make them because they rely on a shared, rough understanding of the timeline.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The forecasters are not usually dishonest. As time passes, memories fade and tacit time frames that once seemed obvious become less so. The result is a tedious dispute about the real meaning: this year or next, this decade or next. With no stated time frame, the dispute cannot be settled, especially when reputations are on the line.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, state the time frame in the forecast itself, since memory of an implied one will not last.
card.limits: The authors do not call forecasters dishonest. Their point is that an unstated deadline cannot settle a later argument.

concepts.title: Vague verbiage is the rule, not the exception
concepts.question: What does the chapter call a smaller obstacle to judging forecasts than probability, besides timelines?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, forecasts often rely on implicit understandings of key terms rather than explicit definitions, and this vague verbiage is more the rule than the exception. It makes forecasts untestable.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors point to Ballmer’s significant market share. They call timelines and vague terms among the smaller obstacles to judging forecasts. Probability is a much bigger one.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, a sentence is not yet a testable claim until its key terms are given explicit definitions.
card.limits: Explicit terms help only up to a point. The authors say probability is a bigger obstacle, so defined terms and a date are still not enough.

concepts.title: Probability makes judging much harder
concepts.question: Why is a forecast that says “very likely” harder to judge than one that says something will happen?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, forecasts that say something will or will not happen are easy to judge, but a probabilistic forecast is much harder, because one outcome cannot show whether the odds were right.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Jonathan Schell wrote that a holocaust would occur; there was no nuclear war that year or the next, so read literally he was wrong. Had he said very likely, the verdict would be unclear: he might have exaggerated the risk or been right and humanity lucky. Even if history were rerun and 63% of reruns ended in nuclear war, we could not say he was right without knowing what very likely meant.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, one outcome cannot judge a probability, and a probability needs a clear meaning to be judged at all.
card.limits: The idea of rerunning history is a thought experiment. The authors say we cannot do it, so we cannot know.

concepts.title: Sherman Kent and the words that meant different odds
concepts.question: What did Sherman Kent discover when he asked what serious possibility meant?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the CIA analyst Sherman Kent found that a phrase in a 1951 estimate meant very different odds to different people, so a seemingly informative phrase could be almost useless.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Kent led the Office of National Estimates and held that estimating is what you do when you do not know. NIE 29-51 said an attack on Yugoslavia in 1951 should be considered a serious possibility. A State Department official asked what odds that meant; Kent said about 65 to 35 for an attack, and the official had thought lower. Kent’s analysts answered from about 80 to 20 to 20 to 80.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The phrase is serious possibility. The authors call such estimates national intelligence estimates (NIE).

card.rule: According to the authors, a word like serious possibility hides disagreement because each reader fills it with a different probability.
card.limits: The authors say Kent was far from perfect, for example in the 1962 estimate that the Soviets would not deploy offensive missiles to Cuba. His rigor was not in doubt.

concepts.title: A fair chance at the Bay of Pigs
concepts.question: How did the phrase fair chance mislead President Kennedy before the Bay of Pigs?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, in 1961 the Joint Chiefs of Staff told President Kennedy the Bay of Pigs plan had a fair chance of success, and Kennedy read the phrase as more positive than its author intended.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The man who wrote the words later said he had in mind odds of 3 to 1 against success. Kennedy was never told precisely what fair chance meant and took it as much more positive. The authors cannot be sure he would have called off the plan had the odds been stated, but it would surely have made him think harder.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, a verbal estimate can lead a decision maker to act on odds the writer never meant.
card.limits: The authors say we cannot be sure the president would have changed his decision. They say only that it would have made him think harder.

concepts.title: Kent’s scheme: words with numerical meanings
concepts.question: What fix did Sherman Kent propose for vague words of probability?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Kent proposed that the terms analysts use should have designated numerical meanings, narrowing ranges wherever possible and reserving possible for important matters where no probability can reasonably be given.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: His table set certain at 100%, almost certain at about 93% (give or take 6), probable at about 75% (give or take 12), chances about even at 50% (give or take 10), probably not at 30% (give or take 10), almost certainly not at 7% (give or take 5), and impossible at 0%. So probable meant 63% to 87%.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, pinning words to numerical ranges greatly reduces the room for confusion.
card.limits: The authors say Kent’s scheme was simple but it was never adopted. A numerical meaning also does not by itself tell you the probability is correct.

concepts.title: Why Kent’s numbers were not adopted
concepts.question: Why did people refuse numbers even though they liked clarity in principle?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Kent’s scheme was never adopted: people liked precision in principle but disliked numbers in practice, finding them unnatural, awkward, or tacky.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Some said numbers felt unnatural, which the authors grant is true after a lifetime of vague language but call a weak argument against change. Others felt an aesthetic revulsion: language has its own poetry and talking of odds makes you sound like a bookie. Kent’s reply was legendary: “I’d rather be a bookie than a goddamn poet.”

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, feeling awkward about numbers is a weak argument against using them.
card.limits: Awkwardness is real. The authors grant that numbers feel unnatural but argue it is no reason to avoid them.

concepts.title: Do numbers pretend to be facts?
concepts.question: What reply do the authors give to the objection that numbers make estimates look like objective facts?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a number may suggest an objective fact, which is a danger, but the answer is not to drop numbers; it is to tell readers that numbers, like words, are only estimates and opinions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A second objection says a precise number implies the forecaster knows it exactly. The authors say that is not intended and should not be inferred. They add that words like serious possibility suggest the same thing numbers do, and that numbers only make it explicit, reducing the risk of confusion.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, inform readers that numbers are estimates, rather than avoiding numbers.
card.limits: The danger is real: the authors call it a danger. Their view is that the danger is better handled by explanation than by vagueness.

concepts.title: Numbers sharpen thinking: metacognition
concepts.question: Why does turning serious possibility into a number help a forecaster think better?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, when forecasters are forced to translate vague terms into numbers they have to think carefully about how they are thinking, and with practice they get better at telling finer degrees of uncertainty apart.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Vague thoughts are easily expressed in vague language. The authors compare the improvement to artists getting better at distinguishing subtler shades of gray.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors call thinking about one’s own thinking metacognition.

card.rule: According to the authors, practice with numbers trains finer judgment of uncertainty.
card.limits: The authors say practice is needed; they do not say that a number by itself improves a judgment.

concepts.title: The wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy
concepts.question: Why is a 70% chance of rain not proved wrong when it stays dry?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, people judge a probabilistic forecast by which side of maybe (50%) it was on: right if the likelier side happens, wrong if not. This simple mistake is extremely common, even among sophisticated thinkers.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A meteorologist who says 70% chance of rain also says 30% chance it will not rain, so a dry day may fit her forecast exactly. Only many reruns could show it. In 2012, prediction markets put 75% on the Supreme Court striking down Obamacare; when it was upheld, the New York Times reporter David Leonhardt declared the crowd wrong.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Tetlock calls it the wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, a single forecast of 70% cannot be called wrong because the event did not happen; judge many forecasts instead.
card.limits: The reasoning does not mean a 70% forecast can never be criticized. It means one result cannot do it.

concepts.title: Why rubbery words are safe for forecasters
concepts.question: Why might a forecaster prefer elastic words to numbers?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, because people commit the wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy, a forecaster who gives a number risks being pilloried for a miss, so the safe course is elastic language.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If an agency says 65% and the event does not happen, it may be attacked though the forecast gave a 35% chance of that. Words like a fair chance and a serious possibility can be stretched afterwards: if the event happens, they mean more than 50%; if not, much less. With such perverse incentives, people prefer rubbery words.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, vague words protect forecasters from accountability, which is why they persist.
card.limits: Tetlock calls the incentives perverse. He does not say forecasters are dishonest; their choices follow the rewards.

concepts.title: Numbers reach intelligence and weather
concepts.question: How did numbers finally gain ground in intelligence work, and where are vague words still common?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, studies kept showing people attach different meanings to words like could, might and likely, yet the intelligence community resisted numbers until reforms after the Iraq weapons failure.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In some fields numbers have become standard. In weather forecasts, for example, slight chance of showers has given way to 30% chance of showers.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, numbers have become standard in some fields, such as weather forecasting.
card.limits: The authors describe the shift as partial: it came late and only in some fields.

concepts.title: Niall Ferguson, Greece and the word may
concepts.question: Why could Niall Ferguson’s Greek default forecast not be judged either way?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Ferguson’s January 2012 forecast that a Greek default may be days away was ambiguous in two ways: the meaning of default, and the word may, which says nothing about probability.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: There is a popular meaning of default, a complete repudiation of debt, which Greece did not do, and a technical one, which Greece did shortly after. Even with no default of any kind, he said only that Greece may default, and almost anything may happen. The authors say the interviewer did not notice the fine print.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, may is a hollow word: it means something is possible and nothing about how likely it is.
card.limits: The authors say there is reason to think Ferguson was right under one definition. They do not say he was wrong.

concepts.title: Terms, numbers, and lots of forecasts
concepts.question: What three things do the authors say forecasts need if we want to measure and improve?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, forecasts must have clearly defined terms and timelines, must use numbers, and there must be lots of them, because we cannot judge one probabilistic forecast.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: We cannot rerun history, so a single 70% call cannot be judged. But a meteorologist who forecasts weather every day for months leaves a track record that can be tabulated. If she is perfect, rain falls 70% of the time when she says 70%, 30% of the time when she says 30%, and so on.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors call this match between stated chance and outcome frequency calibration.

card.rule: According to the authors, judge a forecaster on a large set of numerical forecasts with clear terms.
card.limits: Many forecasts do not rescue a forecast that is too vague to judge. All three requirements are needed together.

concepts.title: Reading a calibration chart in words
concepts.question: What do under- and overconfidence look like on a calibration chart?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, plot stated chance against how often the event happened: perfect calibration is a diagonal line. A curve far above it means underconfidence, and one far below it means overconfidence.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If a forecaster’s curve is far above the line, things she calls 20% likely actually happen 50% of the time, so she is underconfident. If it is far under the line, things she calls 80% likely happen only 50% of the time, so she is overconfident.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors name the two errors underconfident and overconfident, together miscalibrated.

card.rule: According to the authors, compare what a forecaster says with what happens: gaps from the diagonal show the direction of the error.
card.limits: The method needs many forecasts of the same kind to be read reliably.

media.alt: Square calibration chart: forecast on the horizontal axis, share of forecasts that came true on the vertical axis, each from 0 to 1. A thick straight diagonal from bottom-left to top-right marks perfect calibration, with dots at 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8. A dashed guide shows that forecasts of 0.8 come true 0.8 of the time.

Calibration chart: forecast on the horizontal axis, share of forecasts that came true on the vertical axis, each from 0 to 1. A thick curve bows above a faint dashed diagonal, touching it only at the ends. A dashed guide shows that forecasts of 0.2 came true about half the time: an underconfident forecaster.

Calibration chart: forecast on the horizontal axis, share of forecasts that came true on the vertical axis, each from 0 to 1. A thick curve sags below a faint dashed diagonal, touching it only at the ends. A dashed guide shows that forecasts of 0.8 came true only about half the time: an overconfident forecaster.

concepts.title: Where calibration works and where it does not
concepts.question: Why does calibration work well for weather but poorly for presidential elections?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, calibration works well for weather because new weather arrives daily and forecasts stack up fast, but it works poorly for rare events such as presidential elections.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: It would take centuries, undisturbed by wars, plagues and other shocks, to pile up enough election forecasts. A little creativity helps: judging at the state level gives fifty results per election, not one. But the many forecasts needed make it impractical to judge rare events.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, calibration needs many forecasts of the same kind, so use it where outcomes repeat quickly.
card.limits: It is a method with limits, not a flaw in forecasters. The authors suggest creativity, such as state-level results, to work around it.

concepts.title: Resolution: calibrated but cowardly
concepts.question: Why is perfect calibration not the same as perfect forecasting accuracy?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, perfect forecasting is godlike omniscience: saying this will happen and it does, or this won’t happen and it doesn’t. Its technical term is resolution, and calibration and resolution capture distinct facets of good judgment.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In one figure the forecaster is perfectly calibrated but never strays from the 40% to 60% zone, so resolution is poor. In the other she is equally calibrated but decisive, giving high probabilities to events that happen and low to those that do not.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors call the skill of making bold, correct calls resolution.

card.rule: According to the authors, a good forecaster is both calibrated and decisive.
card.limits: Resolution is not a license for boldness: a bold forecaster who is miscalibrated does not qualify. The two are judged together.

media.alt: Calibration chart with a faint dashed diagonal. Only a short thick stretch of dots, running from about 0.4 to 0.6 on both axes, lies on it, bracketed as ultra-cautious but well calibrated. The forecaster stays in the middle zone, and stated chances match outcomes there.

Calibration chart with a faint dashed diagonal. Thick dotted stretches on the diagonal appear only at the two ends, one from about 0 to 0.2 and one from about 0.8 to 1, each bracketed as decisive and well calibrated. The middle is empty: strong probabilities that match outcomes.

concepts.title: A score that rewards boldness and punishes hubris
concepts.question: How should a good scoring system treat 70%, 90% and 100% forecasts that come true or fail?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, combining calibration and resolution gives a scoring system that fits our sense of good forecasting: 90% should score better than 70% when the event happens, and 100% gets top marks, but hubris must be punished when the slam dunk fails.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Someone saying 70% should do fairly well if the event happens, someone saying 90% should do better, and someone correctly saying 100% gets top marks. The forecaster who says an event is a slam dunk should take a big hit if it does not happen. How big a hit is debatable.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, the more confident the call, the bigger the reward when right and the bigger the penalty when wrong.
card.limits: The authors say the size of the penalty is debatable. They give a betting analogy to make the point clear.

concepts.title: Odds as the price of confidence
concepts.question: What odds does an 80%, 90% or 95% forecast imply in the Yankees example?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a probability can be read as betting odds: 80% means 4 to 1, 90% means 9 to 1, and 95% means 19 to 1. The higher the confidence, the more a loss would cost.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the example, saying the Yankees will beat the Dodgers with 80% likelihood means offering 4 to 1: if you bet $100, you pay me $100 if they win and I pay you $400 if they lose. At 90% the odds are 9 to 1, and at 95% they are 19 to 1.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, a good score should capture the pain of an extreme forecast failing.
card.limits: It is an analogy. A forecast is not literally a bet, though it shows how fast the cost of confidence rises.

concepts.title: The Brier score
concepts.question: What does a Brier score measure, and what do 0, 0.5 and 2.0 mean?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Brier scores measure the distance between what you forecast and what happened. Like golf scores, lower is better.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A perfect score is 0. A hedged fifty-fifty call, or random guessing in the aggregate, scores 0.5. A forecast that is wrong to the greatest possible extent, saying 100% that something will happen and it does not, every time, scores a disastrous 2.0.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors call the results Brier scores.

card.rule: According to the authors, a lower Brier score is better; 0 is perfect, 0.5 is random, 2.0 is as bad as possible.
card.limits: A Brier score alone is not enough. The authors say its meaning depends on what is being forecast and who else is forecasting it.

concepts.title: A Brier score only means something against a benchmark
concepts.question: Why is knowing your Brier score not enough to say how good your forecasts are?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, to interpret Brier scores you need two more things: benchmarks and comparability. What a score means depends on what is being forecast.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Suppose your score is 0.2. That is far from godlike omniscience at 0 but much better than chimp-like guessing at 0.5. But the authors add that it is easy to imagine circumstances where 0.2 would be disappointing.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, read a Brier score against what a simple rule would have scored on the same questions.
card.limits: A benchmark does not replace the score. It gives the score a meaning, and the benchmark must be a fair one for the same questions.

concepts.title: Phoenix weather and the mindless rule
concepts.question: In Phoenix in June, why might a Brier score of 0.2 be a poor result?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, in a place where the answer rarely changes, a mindless rule can score extremely well, so skill means beating the rule that predicts no change.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Each June, Phoenix, Arizona gets very hot and sunny. A forecaster who followed a rule like always assign 100% to hot and sunny could earn a Brier score close to 0, leaving 0.2 in the dust. The right test of skill is whether you can do better than mindlessly predicting no change.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, the right test of skill is doing better than a mindless no-change prediction.
card.limits: The benchmark only works when no-change is a sensible baseline. The authors use it where the world changes little.

concepts.title: He called all fifty states: the no-change rule scored 48
concepts.question: How many states would a crude no-change rule have got right in the 2012 US presidential election?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the excited cry He called all fifty states! was a tad overwrought, because a crude no-change rule would have scored forty-eight out of fifty.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: After the 2012 presidential election Nate Silver, Princeton’s Sam Wang and other poll aggregators were hailed for correctly predicting all fifty state outcomes. A rule that said states would vote as in 2008, whether Democratic or Republican, would have got forty-eight right.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, praise for a forecast should be checked against what a no-change rule would have done.
card.limits: The authors do not belittle the aggregators. They say these are pros who know the gains are small.

concepts.title: Other forecasters as the benchmark
concepts.question: Besides a simple rule, what other benchmark do the authors name for a Brier score?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, another key benchmark is other forecasters: who can beat everyone else, who can beat the consensus forecast, and how do they pull it off.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Answering those questions requires comparing Brier scores, which requires a level playing field.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, comparing forecasters is only meaningful when they answer the same questions over the same time.
card.limits: Comparisons without a shared question set can mislead. The next idea gives an example.

concepts.title: Phoenix versus Springfield: a level playing field
concepts.question: Why would comparing a Phoenix and a Springfield, Missouri, meteorologist by Brier score be unfair?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, comparing forecasters needs a level playing field. Phoenix weather is just plain easier to forecast than that of Springfield, Missouri, so comparing their Brier scores would be unfair.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Springfield’s weather is notoriously variable. A 0.2 Brier score there could be a sign you are a world-class meteorologist.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, compare Brier scores only between forecasters facing the same questions.
card.limits: Level fields are rare outside designed studies; tournaments are what the authors turn to.

concepts.title: The recipe for a proper forecasting experiment
concepts.question: What steps do the authors say a proper test of forecasters must follow?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, like Archie Cochrane and the pioneers of evidence-based medicine, we must run carefully crafted experiments: assemble forecasters, ask many questions with precise time frames and unambiguous language, require numerical probabilities, and wait.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If researchers do their jobs, the data can be analyzed to answer how good the forecasters are, who the best are, and what sets them apart.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, test forecasting like a medical trial: same questions, clear wording, numbers, then time.
card.limits: The recipe needs patience, and it needs forecasters who agree to take part, which was a problem for the study that follows.

concepts.title: Recruiting experts and promising anonymity
concepts.question: Why did Tetlock have to promise anonymity to the experts in his study?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, the highest-profile pundits refused to take part, so he recruited 284 serious professionals and had to guarantee them anonymity, because even lesser-known experts did not want to risk their reputations for no professional payoff.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: These card-carrying experts earned their livelihoods analyzing political and economic trends: academics, government staff, workers at international organizations such as the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, and media figures. Anonymity also ensured they made their best guesses, uninfluenced by fear of embarrassment.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, promised anonymity let him recruit experts and gather their honest best guesses.
card.limits: The experts who took part were those willing to be anonymous; the highest-profile pundits declined.

concepts.title: Who the experts were and what they were asked
concepts.question: What kinds of questions did the experts answer, and why were some outside their expertise?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, the questions ranged over one, five and ten-year horizons and over political and economic topics drawn from the news, often outside the experts’ own zone, so he could compare true subject-matter experts with smart, well-informed laypeople.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The experts made roughly twenty-eight thousand predictions in total. The first questions were about the experts themselves: ideological leanings and preferred approaches to political problems.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, many topics outside specialty let the study compare experts with informed laypeople.
card.limits: The sample was not random. Tetlock does not claim it represents all experts.

concepts.title: Twenty-one years from panel to publication
concepts.question: How long did the study take, and what is it called?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, asking the questions took years, then came the waiting; the final results appeared in 2005, twenty-one years after the panel that got him thinking, in a book he calls EPJ for short.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: By the time he wrote up the results, the USSR existed only on historical maps. In those twenty-one years there were six presidential elections and three wars. The book is Expert Political Judgment: How Good Is It? How Can We Know?

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Tetlock calls the whole research program EPJ.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, testing forecasts takes patience: the clock is set by events, not by researchers.
card.limits: The length is a cost of the method. It limits how fast such a study can run.

concepts.title: The average expert and the dart-throwing chimp
concepts.question: What is the best-known result of the expert political judgment study, and why do averages mislead?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the punch line of EPJ is that the average expert was roughly as accurate as a dart-throwing chimpanzee. But they warn that averages can obscure.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say that as students are warned in introductory statistics classes, a single average can hide differences between groups. In the EPJ results, two statistically distinguishable groups of experts lay behind the average.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors call the result the dart-throwing chimpanzee punch line.

card.rule: According to the authors, the average expert did about as well as random guessing, but averages can hide differences between groups.
card.limits: The authors say forget the punch line. What matters is that EPJ found modest but real foresight in some experts.

concepts.title: Two groups of experts behind the average
concepts.question: What separated the two statistically distinguishable groups of experts?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, EPJ found two statistically distinguishable groups: one that failed to beat random guessing, and one that beat the chimp, though not by a wide margin.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The first group even lost to the chimp in longer-range forecasts. The second group had reason to stay humble. Still, however modest, they had some foresight.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, the second group showed real but modest foresight.
card.limits: Our reading of modest: the second group did beat the chimp, but the margin was small.

concepts.title: It was how they thought, not what they thought
concepts.question: What did not explain why one group of experts did better than the other?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the better group was not distinguished by PhDs, nor by what the experts thought, whether liberal or conservative, optimist or pessimist. The critical factor was how they thought.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tetlock asked about credentials and politics and found that neither separated the two groups. What did was the style of thinking.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, style of thinking separated forecasters, not credentials or ideology.
card.limits: This is a finding about the EPJ experts. The authors do not say credentials never matter.

concepts.title: Hedgehogs: Big Ideas and certainty
concepts.question: How did the first group organize their thinking, and what were the consequences?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, one group organized thinking around Big Ideas, squeezed problems into cause-effect templates, treated non-fitting facts as irrelevant, and were unusually confident and likelier to say impossible or certain.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: They disagreed over which Big Ideas were true: environmental doomsters versus cornucopian boomsters, socialists versus free-market fundamentalists. They were united by how ideological their thinking was. They piled up reasons with furthermore and moreover, and were reluctant to change their minds even when predictions clearly failed.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors call these experts hedgehogs.

card.rule: According to the authors, hedgehogs pushed one Big Idea to the limit and rarely changed their minds.
card.limits: Hedgehog is a label for a thinking style, not an ideology. Hedgehogs came from every side of the political spectrum.

concepts.title: Foxes: many tools and shades of maybe
concepts.question: How did the second group think, and how did they talk about the future?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the other group were pragmatic experts who drew on many analytical tools, chose each tool by the problem, and gathered information from as many sources as possible.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: They shifted mental gears and used transition words such as however, but, although and on the other hand. They spoke of possibilities and probabilities, not certainties, and more readily admitted being wrong and changed their minds.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors call these experts foxes.

card.rule: According to the authors, foxes combined many perspectives and revised their views.
card.limits: Like hedgehog, fox describes a style of thinking, not a fixed type of person.

concepts.title: Where the fox and the hedgehog come from
concepts.question: Who gave Tetlock the fox and hedgehog metaphor, and which animal did that thinker favor?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, he borrowed the metaphor from the philosopher Isaiah Berlin, who drew on a 2,500-year-old scrap of Greek poetry attributed to Archilochus. Berlin favored foxes; Tetlock took no side.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Berlin wrote an essay comparing the styles of great authors. The poetry line is “The fox knows many things but the hedgehog knows one big thing.” Tetlock liked the metaphor because it captured something deep in his data, and dubbed the Big Idea experts hedgehogs and the eclectic experts foxes.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors call the pair foxes and hedgehogs.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, the metaphor fits the data, but he claims no preference for either type.
card.limits: The poem does not say which side Archilochus favored; no one knows. Tetlock takes the metaphor as a label, not a verdict.

concepts.title: Foxes beat hedgehogs on calibration and resolution
concepts.question: Did foxes win just by playing safe with cautious probabilities?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, foxes beat hedgehogs, and not merely by acting like chickens with 60% and 70% forecasts while hedgehogs boldly went with 90% and 100%.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Foxes beat hedgehogs on both calibration and resolution. The authors conclude that foxes had real foresight and hedgehogs did not.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, the fox advantage was real foresight, not mere caution.
card.limits: This describes group results across EPJ, not any single forecast or forecaster.

concepts.title: Larry Kudlow: a hedgehog who denied the recession
concepts.question: How did Larry Kudlow keep forecasting a boom as a recession arrived?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Larry Kudlow, a CNBC host whose one Big Idea was supply-side economics, was certain the Bush tax cuts would bring a boom, and kept insisting on it as the economy weakened.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: He dubbed it the Bush boom and called it the biggest story never told, though growth was disappointing. In December 2007, he wrote that there is no recession and that the Bush boom was entering its seventh year. The National Bureau of Economic Research later dated the recession start to December 2007. He kept denying it, calling it a mental recession, until Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on September 15.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, Kudlow is a prototypical hedgehog.
card.limits: It is a single case. The authors use it to illustrate a pattern, not to prove one.

concepts.title: Green-tinted glasses: why more information did not help
concepts.question: Why did hedgehogs do worse on subjects they knew best?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a hedgehog’s Big Idea is like green-tinted glasses he never takes off: they may occasionally reveal something real, but far more often they distort. More information does not help, since it is seen through the same glasses.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Hedgehogs first see things from the tip-of-your-nose perspective, then apply the Big Idea. The glasses raise confidence, not accuracy. When hedgehogs in EPJ forecast on their own specialties their accuracy declined. The economy was Kudlow’s beat but in 2008 he did not see what others did.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors use the image of green-tinted glasses, from the Emerald City of The Wonderful Wizard of Oz.

card.rule: According to the authors, one Big Idea can distort what you see and raise confidence without raising accuracy.
card.limits: The glasses can help: they might reveal a trace of green in a tablecloth that the naked eye would miss. The problem is that they are never taken off.

concepts.title: Fame and accuracy moved in opposite directions
concepts.question: Why were the most famous experts the least accurate?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, EPJ revealed an inverse correlation between fame and accuracy: the more famous an expert, the less accurate he was, because media go looking for hedgehogs, who happen to be poor forecasters.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Kudlow’s new show The Kudlow Report premiered on CNBC in January 2009 despite his errors. Hedgehogs tell tight, simple, clear stories that grab audiences, and they are confident, likelier to say something definitely will or will not happen. Uncertainty is disturbing, and maybe underscores it with a bright red crayon. Simplicity and confidence impair foresight but calm nerves.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors call the pattern an inverse correlation between fame and accuracy.

card.rule: According to the authors, the audience rewards the same confidence and simplicity that hurts accuracy.
card.limits: The authors say editors do not go looking for bad forecasters. They go looking for hedgehogs, who happen to be bad forecasters.

concepts.title: Why foxes fare badly on television
concepts.question: Why do the traits that make foxes good forecasters make them bad guests?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, foxes are less confident and less likely to say something is certain or impossible, and their complex stories make bad TV but good forecasting.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: They look at a problem one way, then another, then another. The aggregation of many perspectives is bad TV, but the authors call it essential for good forecasting.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, what suits the camera does not suit forecasting, and vice versa.
card.limits: The authors speak of the media in general; they do not say every fox is ignored.

concepts.title: Galton’s ox and the wisdom of crowds
concepts.question: How accurate was the crowd at the 1906 fair, and why does luck not explain it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the average of many individual guesses beats the accuracy of the average member of the group, and is often startlingly accurate; but some individuals beating the group is mostly luck.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In 1906 Sir Francis Galton watched hundreds of people at a country fair guess the dressed weight of an ox. Their average, 1,197 pounds, was one pound short of the true 1,198. When such an exercise is repeated, individuals beat the group each time but tend to be different people each time.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The phenomenon was popularized by James Surowiecki’s bestseller The Wisdom of Crowds, and is named for it.

card.rule: According to the authors, aggregating many judgments beats the average member, but consistently beating the average takes rare skill.
card.limits: The group average is not always more accurate than every individual. Occasional bull’s-eyes say more about luck, as with chimps throwing many darts.

concepts.title: Why aggregation works: errors cancel, information adds
concepts.question: Why does averaging many guesses produce an accurate answer?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the key is that useful information is widely dispersed, with each person holding a scrap. In a crowd, valid information points one way while errors point in different directions and cancel.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At the fair, a regular customer added a little, and someone who remembered last year’s weight did the same. All valid information pointed toward 1,198 pounds. The myths and mistakes had different sources and pointed higher and lower, so they canceled each other out.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors say some reverently call it the miracle of aggregation, but it is easy to demystify.

card.rule: According to the authors, aggregation works because true signals add up and random errors cancel.
card.limits: Errors cancel only if they point in different directions. The card does not say what happens if everyone shares the same mistake.

concepts.title: What you aggregate matters: polls of polls and PollyVote
concepts.question: How does the quality of what you pool change the result?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, how well aggregation works depends on what is aggregated: many people who know nothing give nothing, those who know a little do better, and many who know lots about different things do best.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Aggregations of aggregations can be impressive. A poll of polls turns many information pools into one big pool, which is the core of what Nate Silver and Sam Wang did in 2012. PollyVote, run by an academic consortium, pools election polls, a panel of political experts and quantitative models, and often sticks with the eventual winner when the polls turn and the experts change their minds.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors name the combination of surveys a poll of polls.

card.rule: According to the authors, aggregate diverse, informed sources, and you can aggregate aggregations.
card.limits: Aggregation cannot create knowledge from nothing: the authors say pooling the judgments of many who know nothing produces nothing.

concepts.title: Foxes aggregate inside one skull
concepts.question: In what way is a fox like Galton’s crowd?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, foxes deploy many analytical ideas and seek information from many sources, then synthesize it into a single conclusion, which is aggregation done inside one head.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: What a fox does is in principle no different from what Galton’s crowd did: integrate perspectives and the information within them. The only real difference is that the process occurs within one skull.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, a fox is a crowd of perspectives in one mind.
card.limits: The authors note that foxes may be individuals working alone.

concepts.title: The guess-two-thirds game and the Financial Times contest
concepts.question: What number won the 1997 Financial Times contest, and what does it show?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, in a guess-the-number game on 0 to 100 where the winner is closest to two-thirds of the average guess, pure logic leads to 0, yet the actual winning guess was 13.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In 1997, at Richard Thaler’s urging, the Financial Times ran the contest. Reasoning from an average of 50 gives 33, then 22, then about 15, shrinking toward 0, which game theory calls the Nash equilibrium. Many contestants did reach 0, but the average guess was 18.91.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors call 0 the Nash equilibrium solution of the game.

card.rule: According to the authors, the winning answer reflects how real people think, not what perfect logic says.
card.limits: Logic is not wrong here. The authors say Tetlock’s logic was sound, but he looked at only one perspective.

concepts.title: Spock, McCoy and Kirk: combining perspectives
concepts.question: What did Tetlock do wrong in the game, and how would he fix it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, he got the game wrong because he used only the perspective of logic. He should have combined it with psycho-logic, how real, sometimes lazy humans think.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Many Financial Times readers are not Vulcans and would stop at 33 or 22. Using Star Trek, Spock’s answer is 0, McCoy’s is 33 or 22, and Captain Kirk, who considers both, synthesizes them. The gradations are fine-grained: should the guess be 10, 11 or 12?

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors call the synthesizing third view the Captain Kirk perspective.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, combine the rational view and the human view, and add a third that anticipates both.
card.limits: The authors admit the approach gets complicated: sophisticated thinkers may be few, and fine distinctions are hard.

concepts.title: The dragonfly eye
concepts.question: Why do the authors compare good forecasters to a dragonfly?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the best metaphor for aggregating many perspectives is dragonfly vision: thousands of tiny lenses, each with a unique view, synthesized into one clear picture. A fox with dragonfly eyes aggregates perspectives.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Each dragonfly eye is a huge bulging sphere covered with lenses, up to thirty thousand on one eye depending on the species. Each lens occupies a slightly different space, so it has a unique perspective. Information from all of them flows into the brain and is synthesized into vision so superb that the dragonfly sees in almost every direction at once.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors call this the dragonfly eye; they admit that a fox with the bulging eyes of a dragonfly is an ugly mixed metaphor.

card.rule: According to the authors, there is no theoretical limit to the number of perspectives you can merge.
card.limits: In practice there is a limit: in the guess game three or four perspectives is about as far as it is practical to go.

concepts.title: Why aggregating perspectives does not come naturally
concepts.question: What stops people from taking other perspectives, even at the poker table?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, aggregation does not come naturally: the tip-of-your-nose perspective insists it sees reality objectively and correctly, so people feel no need to consult others, even when they should.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At the poker table, seeing through an opponent’s eyes is critical, yet many do not. Annie Duke found that students assume a raised bet means a strong hand, though they would not raise with a strong hand themselves. Foxes are likelier to try, by temperament, habit or conscious effort.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors call the default view the tip-of-your-nose perspective.

card.rule: According to the authors, taking another view is a struggle, but foxes are more likely to do the hard work.
card.limits: The authors say this is not a quirk of poker players. The difficulty is general.

concepts.title: A spectrum, not a dichotomy: models are useful, not true
concepts.question: Does the fox and hedgehog model sort every person into one of two types?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, the fox and hedgehog model is a spectrum, not a dichotomy: people think differently in different circumstances, and thinking habits can change with effort. The model is a starting point, not the end.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In EPJ his analyses also covered hybrids: fox-hedgehogs, who are foxes closer to the hedgehog end, and hedgehog-foxes. Even four categories do not capture styles; someone may be cool and calculating at work but impulsive when shopping. Habits can evolve without awareness, or be shifted by choice.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors call the mixed cases fox-hedgehogs and hedgehog-foxes.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, treat the model as a useful simplification, and aim to shift your own gears.
card.limits: No model captures the richness of human nature. Tetlock quotes George Box: all models are wrong, but some are useful.

concepts.title: The 2002 estimate on Iraq
concepts.question: What did the intelligence community's October 2002 estimate say about Iraq, and why did it carry weight?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors present National Intelligence Estimate 2002-16HC, made public in October 2002, as a flatly worded consensus judgment: Iraq had continued its weapons of mass destruction (WMD) programs and would probably have a nuclear weapon within the decade.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: An NIE is the consensus view of the CIA, the National Security Agency, the Defense Intelligence Agency and thirteen other agencies. By one rough estimate this community has a budget above $50 billion and 100,000 staff, of whom 20,000 are analysts who make sense of collected information. Many found its conclusion persuasive.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: National Intelligence Estimate (NIE); the intelligence community, or IC, for the sixteen agencies together.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The budget and staff figures are a rough estimate, because the exact numbers are classified.

card.rule: According to the authors, the 2002 estimate was the shared judgment of sixteen agencies, and that scale led many to treat its claims as settled fact.
card.limits: Size and agreement made the estimate persuasive, but the authors go on to show it was wrong. An elaborate apparatus does not guarantee accuracy.

concepts.title: The weapons that were not there
concepts.question: What happened after the 2003 invasion, and how did the intelligence community's claims look afterwards?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say the 'facts' in the 2002 estimate were false, and that the Iraqi WMD episode was arguably the worst intelligence failure in modern history.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: After invading in 2003, the United States turned Iraq upside down looking for WMDs and found nothing. The IC was humiliated, with condemnation in the media, official investigations, and congressional hearings. Even caustic critics of the Bush administration had been convinced that Saddam Hussein was hiding something.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: That the claims were false does not yet answer whether the IC's judgment was reasonable. The authors take that question up next.

card.rule: According to the authors, no WMDs were found, so the 2002 estimate's key claims were false and the IC suffered a major failure.
card.limits: Being wrong settles only that the conclusion did not match reality. The authors go on to separate that from whether the judgment was reasonable.

concepts.title: Reasonable versus correct
concepts.question: Can a judgment be reasonable and still turn out wrong, and how should we judge it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors, following Robert Jervis, say the IC's WMD judgment was both reasonable and wrong. The right question is whether it was reasonable given the information available then, not whether it proved correct.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Official investigations rejected the claim that the IC caved to White House bullying, and so did Jervis, a scholar of intelligence with a four-decade nonpartisan record. Using only what was known then, nearly every major intelligence agency suspected Saddam was hiding something, because he was acting like someone hiding something.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: 'Mental time travel' is the authors' phrase for putting yourself in the position of the people at the time, which they call a struggle even for historians.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, judge by the evidence available when the call was made, and resist the pull of what you now know.

card.rule: According to the authors, ask whether a judgment was reasonable given what was known at the time, because asking only whether it was correct is easy and misleading.
card.limits: Reasonable does not mean blameless. Jervis still said the analysis had correctable errors, and the authors treat that as devastating criticism (next idea).

concepts.title: Good decision or good outcome
concepts.question: Why is it a mistake to judge a decision by how it turned out?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say replacing 'Was it a good decision?' with 'Did it have a good outcome?' is popular and pernicious. Good poker players, investors and executives avoid it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A novice overestimates the chance that the next card wins, bets big, gets lucky and wins; winning does not make the bet wise. A pro correctly sees a high chance of winning, bets big, gets unlucky and loses; the bet was not unwise. Those who judge by outcomes draw false lessons from experience and get worse over time.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: 'Bait and switch' is the authors' term, from chapter 2, for swapping a tough question for an easy one and then believing the tough one was answered.

card.rule: According to the authors, judge a decision by the reasoning and odds behind it, not by whether luck gave a good result.
card.limits: The point is about one bet or call. The authors' own tournament tracks accuracy over many forecasts, which is why one outcome should not settle a judgment.

concepts.title: Reasonable but not off the hook
concepts.question: Why did Jervis say the IC's errors mattered even if its conclusion was reasonable?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say Jervis did not excuse the IC: its errors were correctable, and better analysis would have made the assessment less certain, which may have changed history.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Jervis wrote: “Analysis could and should have been better.” Better work would have made the assessments less certain, not reversed their conclusion. If lawmakers had demanded “beyond a reasonable doubt” before backing an invasion, a 60% or 70% estimate might not have satisfied them, and the resolution might not have passed.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors say the resolution “might not have passed”. That is a possibility, not a certainty.

card.rule: According to the authors, a less confident conclusion can matter greatly even if the conclusion itself stays the same.
card.limits: Jervis said better analysis would have lowered confidence, not changed the conclusion. The effect on the vote is the authors' stated possibility only.

concepts.title: Flat certainty and no challenge
concepts.question: What was wrong with how the estimate expressed itself, apart from being wrong?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say the IC was not merely wrong; it was wrong when it said it could not be wrong. Intelligence analysis always involves uncertainty, yet the NIE showed hubris.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The NIE said “Iraq has…” and “Baghdad has…”, statements that admit no possibility of surprise. CIA director George Tenet used the phrase “slam dunk” on December 12, 2002. Postmortems found no red teams, no devil's advocates and no papers offering competing possibilities.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: 'Red teams' are groups that attack the prevailing views; the authors note there were none.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Tenet later protested that the phrase was taken out of context. The authors say that does not matter here, since it summed up the IC's attitude.

card.rule: According to the authors, flat statements with no probabilities and no one assigned to challenge the prevailing view are signs of hubris in an uncertain field.
card.limits: The authors do not say any one phrase proves the case. Their evidence is the estimate's own wording and the absence of any challenge to the prevailing view.

concepts.title: IARPA and the 2008 review
concepts.question: How did the intelligence community respond to the WMD failure with research on good judgment?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say the shock of the WMD failure moved the bureaucracy: IARPA was created in 2006, and in 2008 the Office of the Director of National Intelligence asked the National Research Council to review research on good judgment.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: IARPA's mission is to fund research that could make the IC smarter and more effective. It was modeled on DARPA, whose work helped lead to the Internet. The NRC committee was chaired by the psychologist Baruch Fischhoff, and Tetlock was in the room too, probably because of the stir from his 2005 book Expert Political Judgment.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: IARPA is the Intelligence Advanced Research Projects Activity; the NRC is the National Research Council; the book's earlier work is abbreviated EPJ.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors call asking the NRC a bold (or rash) move, since the report might have concluded that the bureaucracy was clueless.

card.rule: According to the authors, the WMD shock led the IC to create a research funder and to ask a scientific body what is known about good judgment.
card.limits: IARPA is a research funder, not a spy service or an analysis unit. Asking for a review shows willingness to be tested, not that the findings were already favorable.

concepts.title: Don't believe until you test
concepts.question: What did the National Research Council report say the IC should do about its analytical methods?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The NRC report was, in the authors' words, 100% Archie Cochrane: do not believe until you test. It said the IC should not rely on methods that lack evidence of efficacy beyond their intuitive appeal.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The report asked the IC to test its current and proposed methods rigorously. The authors give an example: the CIA gives analysts a manual by former analyst Richards Heuer, setting out psychology and the biases that can trip up thinking. It is fine work, but no one knows whether it improves judgment, because it has never been tested.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The report calls its approach 'an evidence-based approach to analysis'.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors do not call the manual poor. They say that sounding sensible is not evidence that it works.

card.rule: According to the authors, a method should be trusted only after it is tested, however convincing it seems.
card.limits: The principle does not say that untested methods are wrong, only that nobody knows whether they work.

concepts.title: The $50 billion question
concepts.question: Can anyone say how accurate the intelligence community's forecasts are, and what does that mean for accountability?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say the question 'How accurate are intelligence analysts' forecasts?' cannot be answered, because the IC's forecasts have never been systematically assessed.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Senior officials may claim the IC is right 80% or 90% of the time, but these are guesses, like the confident figures of nineteenth-century physicians. A director dragged before Congress after a blown call faces accountability of a sort, which may be ill informed or capricious. Meaningful accountability needs systematic tracking of accuracy.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: 'The $50 billion question' is the authors' phrase, a nod to the IC's budget of about $50 billion.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors do not say the IC is inaccurate; they say its accuracy is unknown and its claims are guesses.

card.rule: According to the authors, without systematic tracking of accuracy, there is no meaningful way to hold analysts accountable for accuracy.
card.limits: A congressional hearing after a failure is a form of accountability, but the authors call it possibly capricious. It does not tell anyone how accurate forecasts usually are.

concepts.title: Accountable for process, not accuracy
concepts.question: Why is holding analysts to a checklist of good process not enough?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say the IC has accountability for process but not for accuracy, and that the point of forecasting is to foresee what is coming, not to tick the boxes on a checklist.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Analysts are told what to do when researching, thinking and judging, and are held to those standards: did you consider alternative hypotheses, did you look for contrary evidence? The authors call this sensible. Yet the forecasts themselves are never checked against what happens.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The contrast is between accountability for process and accountability for accuracy.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: Process asks whether the analyst did the right things; accuracy asks whether the forecast was right.

card.rule: According to the authors, following a good process does not replace checking whether the forecasts turn out accurate.
card.limits: The authors do not call good process worthless. Their objection is that process alone never shows whether forecasts are accurate.

concepts.title: The IARPA forecasting tournament
concepts.question: What kind of tournament did IARPA sponsor, and why were its questions chosen as they were?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say IARPA acted on the NRC's recommendation by sponsoring a massive tournament to find the best methods of making the forecasts analysts make every day.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In summer 2010 IARPA officials Jason Matheny and Steve Rieber told Tetlock and Barbara Mellers of the plan. Questions looked like: Will the president of Tunisia flee in the next month? They sat in the Goldilocks zone, neither so easy that a careful reader could get them right nor so hard that no one could, with horizons shorter than those in Tetlock's earlier study. Teams had to beat an independent control group's combined forecast by 20% in year 1, rising to 50% by year 4.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: 'Goldilocks zone' is the authors' name for questions of just-right difficulty; 'wisdom of the crowd' is the combined forecast of the control group.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The tournament did not ask for what the authors call pretty much impossible: forecasting turning points in lives or nations years ahead.

card.rule: According to the authors, IARPA tested forecasting methods on moderately hard, shorter-range questions, with teams measured against a control group.
card.limits: The tournament covers questions in the Goldilocks zone only. The authors do not claim it shows anyone can forecast distant turning points.

concepts.title: Experiments inside the teams
concepts.question: How could a team find out whether a training exercise really improved forecasters' accuracy?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say each research team could run Archie Cochrane-style experiments with internal control groups, which avoids the problem that physicians faced throughout history.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: If you train all forecasters and accuracy rises, it might be the training, easier questions, or luck. If it falls, the training might have hurt, or accuracy might have fallen further without it. You cannot tell. The fix is to train one randomly chosen group and not another, keep all else constant, and compare.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The chapter calls them Archie Cochrane-style experiments with internal control groups.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: To exploit these experiments the authors needed a lot of forecasters, so they recruited volunteers.

card.rule: According to the authors, to learn whether a training works, give it to a randomly chosen group, hold everything else constant, and compare results.
card.limits: The method needs many participants, and it tests one thing at a time. It cannot tell you whether something works if everyone gets it.

concepts.title: The Good Judgment Project
concepts.question: Who took part in the authors' tournament entry, and how large was it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: Tetlock and his colleagues formed a research team and program to compete in the IARPA tournament, recruiting ordinary volunteers who forecast from home.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: They spread the word through blogs and professional networks. In the first year several thousand volunteers signed up and roughly 3,200 passed an initial gauntlet of psychometric tests and began forecasting. The project costs many millions of dollars a year, an anthill beside the IC's $50 billion budget.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The Good Judgment Project, or GJP, the name Tetlock's team gave itself and its program.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors say the cost was not what made IARPA's decision gutsy. What made it gutsy was what the tournament could reveal.

card.rule: According to the authors, the GJP recruited volunteers online, screened them with psychometric tests, and began forecasting at scale.
card.limits: Cost was small beside the IC's budget, so it was not the risk. The risk to the bureaucracy lay in the results.

concepts.title: How the tournament was won
concepts.question: What simple method let the authors beat every other group, including professional analysts?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say the method that won the tournament for Tetlock's team was nothing dazzlingly innovative: average the crowd, weight the best forecasters, then extremize.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Take a couple of hundred ordinary people. Use how often they revise and how accurate they prove to pick the forty or so best. Average everyone's forecasts, with extra weight on those forty, then push the result toward 100% or zero: a 70% might become 85%, a 30% might become 15%. These forecasts beat every other group and method, often by large margins, and beat professional analysts with classified information, by margins that remain classified.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: 'Wisdom of the crowd' is the average forecast of a group; to 'extremize' is to push it closer to 100% or zero.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The 70% to 85% shift is the authors' example of a possible bump, not a fixed rule.

card.rule: According to the authors, averaging many forecasts, weighting the best forecasters, and extremizing beat far costlier approaches.
card.limits: The authors' figures are illustrations (they say 'say, 85%'). Beating the analysts is reported, but the margins are classified.

concepts.title: Doug Lorch and real-time updating
concepts.question: Who is Doug Lorch, and how did the tournament count his many updates?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors introduce Doug Lorch, a retired IBM programmer with no special expertise in international affairs, and show how the tournament let forecasters update in real time.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Doug lives in Santa Barbara, reads the New York Times, and spent about an hour a day at his dining table forecasting. In year 1 he answered 104 questions and made roughly one thousand separate forecasts. Each update counted as a separate forecast, a forecast stood until changed, and all were rolled into one Brier score per question.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: In Tetlock's earlier EPJ research, experts made only one forecast per question, scored later.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Brier score, the measure of the gap between forecasts and reality.

card.rule: According to the authors, every update counted as its own forecast, and all of a question's forecasts fed one final Brier score.
card.limits: Doug's 104 questions understate his work. The count shown is a year-1 figure for one person.

concepts.title: Doug's first-year Brier score
concepts.question: How did Doug do in year 1, and what does a Brier score of 0.22 mean?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say Doug's year-1 Brier score of 0.22 was impressive, putting him fifth among the 2,800 competitors in the Good Judgment Project.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The Brier score measures the gap between forecasts and reality: 2.0 means forecasts are the perfect opposite of reality, 0.5 is random guessing and 0 is the center of the bull's-eye. On the question whether Italy would restructure or default on its debt in 2011, the answer was no. To score 0.22, Doug's average over eleven months had to be no at roughly 68% confidence.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Brier score. A lower score means more accurate forecasts.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors point out Doug had to be that accurate, on average, on all the questions, not just Italy.

card.rule: According to the authors, on the Brier scale 0 is perfect, 0.5 is random guessing and 2.0 is perfectly wrong, so lower is better.
card.limits: A score means little without the difficulty of the questions. The authors call 0.22 impressive given how hard the questions were.

concepts.title: Doug's second year
concepts.question: How far above his rivals did Doug rise in year 2, and which yardstick is unfair to him?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say Doug did astonishingly well by any mortal standard in year 2: he joined a superforecaster team and became the best of the 2,800 volunteers.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: His final Brier score was 0.14. He beat a prediction market of traders by 40%, was the only person to beat the extremizing algorithm, and surpassed the control group's wisdom of the crowd by more than 60%, exceeding the fourth-year target on his own.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: A prediction market is one where traders buy and sell futures contracts on the outcomes of the same questions.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Comparing Doug with omniscience, a score of 0, would be like belittling Tiger Woods in his prime for failing to hit holes in one.

card.rule: According to the authors, judge a forecaster against realistic benchmarks and rivals, not against godlike omniscience.
card.limits: These are one man's results in one year. The authors later warn against treating even Doug as infallible.

concepts.title: Why Doug was a threat
concepts.question: Why would a retiree's forecasting success threaten the status quo?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say Doug Lorch threatened the status quo: a man with no applicable experience or classified access did so well that little room was left for a salaried analyst to do better.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: His only payment was a $250 Amazon gift certificate, given to all volunteers at season's end. The authors imagine someone asking why the United States spends billions on geopolitical forecasting when it could give Doug a gift certificate. Doug was not unique: Bill Flack, a retired Department of Agriculture employee from Nebraska, and 58 others scored at the top in year 1.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Superforecasters: the authors' name for the top performers, here the first class.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Doug's performance on its own would pose little threat if he were a uniquely gifted oracle; there is only so much one man can do.

card.rule: According to the authors, the threat came from Doug being one of many ordinary people whose forecasts matched or beat professionals.
card.limits: The evidence so far does not prove the superforecasters are super; the chapter later tests that.

concepts.title: Superforecasters versus regulars
concepts.question: How much better than other forecasters were the superforecasters, and how far ahead could they see?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say the superforecasters, the top performers of year 1, beat all other forecasters, and that the gap grew in later years.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At the end of year 1 the superforecasters' collective Brier score was 0.25, against 0.37 for all other forecasters. By the end of the four-year tournament they had outperformed regulars by over 60%.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Superforecasters, the authors' name for the top performers of the first year; the others are 'regular' forecasters.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: These are group results from the tournament. The chapter later tests whether luck could explain them.

card.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters beat regular forecasters by a widening margin, ending the tournament more than 60% ahead.
card.limits: The numbers describe a group in one tournament. The authors do not say each superforecaster would beat each regular on each question.

concepts.title: What a 60 percent edge is worth
concepts.question: Does a large percentage advantage in Brier score matter in real life, and what did insiders report?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say a 60% improvement can change what you can do, as moving from 20/100 to 20/40 vision does, and that a report put superforecasters about 30% ahead of IC analysts with secret data.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Say a regular forecaster's Brier score is like 20/100 vision. Glasses that bring it to 20/40 are a 60% improvement. That is not hawkeyed, but it brings rows two to five of the Snellen chart into focus and eases catching baseballs, recognizing friends and reading fine print. Cumulatively that is life changing.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: In November 2013 the Washington Post editor David Ignatius reported that a participant in the project said superforecasters did about 30% better than the average for IC analysts who could read intercepts and other secret data.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The 30% figure is a secondhand report from an unnamed participant. The authors say a direct comparison would be closely guarded.

card.rule: According to the authors, a 60% improvement from a weak base is not elite, but it can change what a person can do.
card.limits: The vision numbers are an arbitrary illustration the authors choose. The 30% claim is reported, not an official comparison.

media.alt: Three eye charts side by side, from blurry to sharp. The left chart, 20/100, is so blurred that only two rows can be made out. The middle chart, 20/40, shows five rows, the lower ones fuzzy. The right chart, 20/20, is crisp through eight rows of shrinking letters.

concepts.title: Why testing is rare
concepts.question: Why do organizations avoid testing their own people's judgment, and why was IARPA unusual?

blocks.label: Claim
