blocks.text: The authors say testing may be in an organization's interest, yet the people inside it have interests of their own, above all a comfortable status quo, so tournaments are rare.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Famous, well-paid pundits are loath to risk their reputations by having accuracy tested. Power players are unlikely to try tournaments that test their own judgment. The authors' picture: Bob in the CEO suite does not want to hear that Dave in the mail room is better at forecasting the company's trends. IARPA put the IC's mission ahead of insiders who did not want to rock the boat.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors speak of insiders who preferred the status quo, not of everyone in the IC.

card.rule: According to the authors, testing accuracy threatens those whose standing rests on untested judgment, which is why few organizations do it.
card.limits: The authors' account is about incentives. They do not say every executive or analyst opposes testing.

concepts.title: Luck among many coin callers
concepts.question: Why can extreme results among many forecasters come from luck alone?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors urge readers not to be convinced yet. Extreme results among many people can arise from luck alone, so extremes do not prove skill.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Suppose 2,800 volunteers each predict 104 coin tosses. Results form a bell curve around 50% right, with some mostly wrong and some mostly right. Calling a coin toss correctly shows no skill, whether once or a hundred times, unless you believe in ESP. It takes a lot of luck to call 70% of 104 tosses, which is extremely unlikely for one person, but with 2,800 callers the unlikely becomes quite likely.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The chapter uses a coin-toss game and a bell curve.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The coin game shows the risk of misreading extremes. It does not show that the superforecasters were lucky.

card.rule: According to the authors, the more people who try, the more likely that someone gets extreme results by luck, so extremes alone do not show skill.
card.limits: The game is a pure-luck case. In real forecasting skill and luck mix, so the authors go on to test for luck.

media.alt: Symmetric bell curve of many people guessing coin tosses. The horizontal axis is the number of correct guesses, the vertical axis the number of guessers at each level. A dashed line at the peak is labelled 50/50. The thin left tail is labelled very bad guessers and the thin right tail very good guessers.

concepts.title: Langer's coin-flip experiment
concepts.question: What did Ellen Langer's experiment show about how an early run of hits changes people's beliefs?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors report that the psychologist Ellen Langer showed how poorly people grasp randomness: an early run of hits led students to think they could predict coin tosses.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Yale students watched someone flip a coin thirty times and predicted heads or tails; they could not see the flips but were told each result. The results were rigged: every student got fifteen right and fifteen wrong, but some had hits early and others misses. Those with early hits had a higher opinion of their skill and expected to shine again.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Langer called it the 'illusion of control'; the authors add that it is also an 'illusion of prediction'.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Every student ended with the same total. The difference was in the order of hits.

card.rule: According to the authors, an early streak of hits can make people sincerely believe they can predict outcomes that are entirely random.
card.limits: The experiment shows how streaks mislead. It does not show that every person is fooled.

concepts.title: Success stories and the missing denominator
concepts.question: Why do tales of one successful forecaster, investor or company tell us little about skill?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say stories of vivid success mislead when they ignore how many others tried and failed, and when luck is left out of the explanation.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: TV guests are introduced by a dramatic call, such as having called the crash of 2008, which tells little about their overall accuracy. A great investor who beats the market for six or seven years is profiled and the odds computed; journalists ignore how many others were trying. A lottery winner is not called a skilled ticket-picker. Business books recount a company's run and promise similar results without solid evidence of cause.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors say such stories may be true or fairy tales; they only note the evidence is seldom provided.

card.rule: According to the authors, judge a success story by how many people tried and by what evidence links the actions to the outcome.
card.limits: The authors do not say skill never exists. Most things involve both skill and luck, as they say next.

concepts.title: Skill and luck together
concepts.question: Are the superforecasters super or lucky, and why is that the wrong question?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say the evidence so far does not establish that superforecasters are super. 'Superforecasters or superlucky?' is a false dichotomy, since most outcomes involve both skill and luck.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The mix may be almost all luck, almost all skill, or one of a thousand variations, which makes it hard to say what to credit to which.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: 'False dichotomy': an either/or that hides the many mixes in between.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, ask how much skill and how much luck, and use regression to the mean to find out.

card.rule: According to the authors, ask how much of a result is skill and how much luck, not which of the two it is.
card.limits: The authors do not say luck and skill cannot be separated. They offer a test next.

concepts.title: Regression to the mean: fathers and sons
concepts.question: Why is the son of a six-foot father likely to be shorter than his father?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say that when two measures are linked imperfectly, the best prediction for an extreme case is a compromise between that case and the average. They call this regression to the mean.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Take men's average height of five feet eight and a father who is six feet tall. A quick System 1 hunch says his adult son is also six feet. But the father-son correlation is about 0.5, so the best guess is halfway between the father's height and the average: five feet ten. The son's height regresses two inches toward the mean.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Regression to the mean.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Five feet ten is a best guess, not a certainty. A son can still be six feet; it is just unlikely.

card.rule: According to the authors, with a correlation of about 0.5, predict a value halfway between the extreme case and the population average.
card.limits: The halfway guess follows from a correlation of 0.5. A different correlation gives a different compromise.

media.alt: Scatter plot of fathers' heights (horizontal) against sons' heights (vertical), in inches. Hundreds of hollow dots form a rising cloud with a thick upward line through it. Dashed guides show a six-foot father meeting the line at a son of about five feet ten, with many dots above and below.

concepts.title: Mistaking regression for a cure
concepts.question: How does forgetting regression to the mean lead people to believe in treatments that do nothing?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say regression to the mean is as easy to forget as to understand, and forgetting it leads people to credit treatments for improvements that would have happened anyway.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Suppose you have chronic back pain. Some days you feel fine, others some pain, and occasionally it is awful. You seek help, such as a homeopath, on an awful day. Next day you feel better, so the treatment seems to work. The placebo effect may help, but you would probably have felt better anyway, thanks to regression to the mean.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Regression to the mean.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors do not say all treatments fail. They say the explanation will not occur to you unless you stop and think carefully.

card.rule: According to the authors, an improvement after an extreme low point may be regression to the mean rather than the effect of the treatment.
card.limits: The point does not show a given treatment is useless. It shows that improvement after a bad day is weak evidence that the treatment worked.

concepts.title: Retesting the lucky callers
concepts.question: What should happen if the same coin-toss callers play again, and what does it show about luck?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say regression to the mean becomes a valuable tool when you retest. If results were luck, the top performers of round one fall back toward 50% in round two.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Have the 2,800 callers predict 104 tosses again. The curve looks the same, but the amazingly good results most likely belong to different people. The correlation across rounds is close to zero, so the best prediction for each is the average rate of 50%: total regression. If only round-one stars repeat, most do worse, the luckiest most; those at 90% right should expect a rapid descent to 50%.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Total regression to the mean.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: A few people may again get nine or ten right. The authors say not to call them coin-toss gurus; make them repeat until their luck runs out.

card.rule: According to the authors, if round-one stars fall back to the average when retested, their first-round results were luck.
card.limits: The pattern is for pure luck, where the correlation across rounds is zero. Skill produces less regression.

concepts.title: Regression as a gauge of luck
concepts.question: How does the amount of regression between two periods reveal how much luck was involved?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say regression to the mean is an indispensable tool for testing luck's role: the more results regress, the more luck was involved.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Mauboussin notes that slow regression is more often seen in skill-dominated activities, faster regression with chance. Take two forecasters, Frank in the bottom 1% of year 1 and Nancy in the top 99%. If luck alone decided, both regress fully to 50% in year 2. With equal parts luck and skill, Frank rises to around 25% and Nancy falls to around 75%. If skill alone decided, neither moves.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Regression to the mean; no new term.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The three cases are illustrations. Real results usually fall in between.

card.rule: According to the authors, the less results regress from one period to the next, the more skill and the less luck were involved.
card.limits: The three Frank and Nancy cases are illustrations of luck-only, equal mix and skill-only. Real mixes lie anywhere between.

media.alt: Four bell curves of forecasters' Brier scores. In year 1, one wide bell has an arrow spanning from a good forecaster A to a bad forecaster B. For year 2, three bells show that arrow: equally wide if results are all skill, about half as wide with half luck, and shrunk to almost nothing if all luck.

concepts.title: Superforecasters did not regress
concepts.question: Did the superforecasters regress toward the mean, and what do the authors think offset it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say superforecasters as a group held up across years, even widening their lead, which is the opposite of regression to the mean. They suspect an offsetting process pushed their performance up.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In years 2 and 3 superforecasters as a whole, including Doug, increased their lead. That hints at little or no luck, which the authors doubt. After year 1 they were congratulated, anointed super and put on teams with fellow superforecasters, and scores got better. In years 3 and 4 fresh crops of superforecasters joined elite teams and did as well or better.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The authors speak of an offsetting process.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The offsetting explanation is the authors' suggestion: recognition and stimulating teammates may have erased the regression we would otherwise see.

card.rule: According to the authors, regression can be hidden when something offsets it; here, recognition and elite teams may have lifted performance.
card.limits: The offsetting process is the authors' proposed reading. They do not claim to have isolated it.

concepts.title: Why luck must matter
concepts.question: Why do the authors doubt that luck played little or no part in the superforecasters' results?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say some questions hinge on unforeseeable events or on tangled systems, so irreducible uncertainty means luck must have played a significant role.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: One question asked whether vessels would have a fatal confrontation in the East China Sea. It resolved yes when, just before the deadline, a Chinese fishing boat captain stabbed a South Korean coast guard officer who had seized his boat. Oil prices depend on a huge number of factors, from US frackers to jihadists in Libya to battery designers, and on factors behind those. Many ties are nonlinear: as Edward Lorenz showed, even a butterfly's wing flaps can make a dramatic difference.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: 'Nonlinear' causal ties: small causes can have large effects.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors do not say forecasting is impossible. They say luck must play a part in some questions.

card.rule: According to the authors, quirky last-minute events and tangled nonlinear systems put a floor under uncertainty, so luck cannot be absent.
card.limits: The authors say 'some' questions, not all. Their point is that luck is not zero, not that skill is absent.

concepts.title: Turnover, consistency and the verdict
concepts.question: What do the year-to-year numbers say about skill and luck among superforecasters?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors say superforecasters were mostly skilled but not infallible: individuals regress, yet the group's consistency is far beyond what luck would give.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The correlation between an individual's results in successive years is about 0.65, a little above the 0.5 for fathers and sons, so considerable regression is expected. Each year roughly 30% fall out of the top 2%, and 70% remain. With a zero correlation, as among coin guessers, such consistency has less than a 1 in 100,000,000 chance; with 0.65 it is about 1 in 3.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, do not treat any year's superstars as infallible, even Doug Lorch, but conclude that they were not just lucky.

card.rule: According to the authors, some turnover plus strong year-to-year consistency means superforecasters were mostly skilled, though not infallible.
card.limits: The authors say mostly skill, not wholly skill. The chapter ends by asking why superforecasters are so good, which later chapters take up.

concepts.title: A star forecaster with a star mind
concepts.question: What made Sandy Sillman's first-year result striking, and what explanation does it tempt us to give?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors present Sandy Sillman as a case that tempts a simple explanation: his remarkable mind must explain his remarkable results, and the same for other superforecasters.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Sandy, an atmospheric scientist with several advanced degrees and fluency in several languages, had multiple sclerosis and joined the tournament as a gentle project once he had to stop working. In year 1 he forecast alone, in the control condition he was randomly assigned to, and tied for overall champion among roughly 2,800 forecasters with a Brier score of 0.19.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the temptation. The accuracy measure reported for Sandy is the Brier score.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: the authors raise the intelligence explanation as a hypothesis to test next, not as their conclusion.

card.rule: According to the authors, a brilliant star forecaster invites the guess that intelligence explains forecasting success, and that guess is only a starting point.
card.limits: One brilliant forecaster shows how the top performer looks, not what causes the result across all forecasters; the chapter turns to data on many people.

concepts.title: Putting 'smart people forecast better' to the test
concepts.question: Why do the authors test the idea that knowledge and intelligence drive foresight instead of accepting it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The idea that knowledge and intelligence drive foresight is plausible, say the authors, but plausibility is not enough: the hypothesis has to be tested.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Volunteers took a grueling battery of psychological tests, and those results were compared with their forecasting. That gave the data to check the hypothesis rather than assume it.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the idea. The authors treat it as a hypothesis, and mention Archie Cochrane as the person who showed why testing matters.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, state a tempting explanation as a hypothesis and look for data that could confirm or refute it.

card.rule: According to the authors, a plausible explanation is a hypothesis to test with data, not a conclusion.
card.limits: Testing does not mean the plausible idea is wrong; the test may confirm it, partly confirm it, or show it adds less than expected.

concepts.title: Fluid and crystallized intelligence
concepts.question: What two kinds of intelligence did the tests measure, and with what kinds of questions?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors measured two kinds of intelligence: fluid intelligence, or raw crunching power, and crystallized intelligence, which is knowledge.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Fluid intelligence was measured with puzzles that required finding the rules behind patterns in rows and columns of shapes, to fill the missing space. Crystallized intelligence was measured with knowledge questions, some US-centric, such as how many Justices sit on the Supreme Court, and some global, such as which nations are permanent members of the UN Security Council.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Fluid intelligence (raw crunching power) and crystallized intelligence (knowledge). Both are the authors' working labels in this chapter.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: the authors use these as the two measures behind their test; a puzzle score is not offered as a full picture of a person.

card.rule: According to the authors, fluid intelligence is raw reasoning power on puzzles and crystallized intelligence is accumulated knowledge.
card.limits: Neither score is the whole story: the authors go on to argue that what a person does with these abilities matters more than the abilities themselves.

media.alt: Three-by-three grid of outlined shapes, each holding a small symbol, with the bottom-right cell blank. Row 1 holds a rectangle, a star and a diamond, each with a minus. Row 2 holds a star, a diamond and a rectangle, each with a plus. Row 3 holds a diamond and a rectangle, each with an x, then the blank cell. Each row and column holds all three shapes once. Eight candidate figures sit below as possible answers.

concepts.title: Volunteers are not a random sample
concepts.question: Why can the authors not treat their 2,800 forecasters as typical of the general population?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the roughly 2,800 volunteers who completed the testing and made forecasts were far from a randomly selected sample, so they cannot be assumed to represent the general population.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Several thousand people volunteered in year 1, but only those motivated enough to work through the testing and forecast stayed. The motivated few who stayed are the ones tested.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Random selection is what makes a sample representative of the population it is drawn from. No further name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: self-selection limits what can be assumed about other people; it does not make the volunteers' test scores worthless.

card.rule: According to the authors, a self-selected group of volunteers cannot be assumed to reflect the population, so results must be compared with the general population.
card.limits: Without random selection, representativeness cannot be assumed; the comparison with the general population fixes the problem only for the intelligence and knowledge scores.

concepts.title: Smart enough, but not genius
concepts.question: Where do regular forecasters and superforecasters stand against the general population, and what does that suggest?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, intelligence and knowledge help forecasting but add little beyond a certain threshold, so superforecasting does not require genius.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Regular forecasters scored higher on the intelligence and knowledge tests than about 70% of the population. Superforecasters placed higher than about 80%. The big jump is from the public to the forecasters, not from forecasters to superforecasters, and most superforecasters fall well short of so-called genius territory (the top 1%, or an IQ of 135 and up).

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the threshold idea. The authors call the genius cut-off a problematic, arbitrarily defined concept.

card.rule: According to the authors, intelligence and knowledge help up to a point, but superforecasting does not call for genius-level scores.
card.limits: The authors do not say the traits are useless; they say the jump from forecasters to superforecasters is small compared with the jump from public to forecasters.

concepts.title: Brilliant people, bad forecasts
concepts.question: Why do the authors say intelligence and knowledge are not enough, and what does Robert McNamara show?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, having the needed intelligence and knowledge is not enough: many clever and informed forecasters fell short, and what counts is how you use your crunching power.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Robert McNamara, defense secretary under Kennedy and Johnson, was dubbed one of the best and the brightest. He and colleagues escalated the Vietnam war believing that if South Vietnam fell, all of Southeast Asia would follow. Their certainty rested on no serious analysis of that critical forecast.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The authors close the thought with the point that it is how you use crunching power, not the power itself.

card.rule: According to the authors, smart people can forecast badly; it is how intelligence is used, not the raw amount, that matters.
card.limits: One historical case shows that clever people can be wrong, not that cleverness is a handicap; the case does not say how often the clever fail.

concepts.title: Fermi-izing: from black box to open box
concepts.question: What does breaking a question down, as Enrico Fermi taught, change about a hard estimate?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, breaking a hard question into smaller ones separates the knowable from the unknowable and brings the guessing out where it can be inspected.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Enrico Fermi set students the puzzle of how many piano tuners work in Chicago, with no yellow pages or internet. Most people shrug and offer a number from a black box, 'it seems about right'. Fermi asked what would have to be true, or what information would allow an answer. Guessing is not removed, but the result tends to be a more accurate estimate.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Fermi estimates or Fermi problems; the authors use the verb 'to Fermi-ize'.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, ask 'What would have to be true for this to happen?' or 'What information would allow me to answer?'

card.rule: According to the authors, replace one question you cannot answer with several smaller ones whose guesses you can inspect.
card.limits: Fermi-izing does not remove guessing and may swap one unanswerable question for several; the gain is that the guesses are visible and checkable.

concepts.title: The piano-tuner breakdown
concepts.question: Which four facts does the piano-tuner estimate need, and how do they combine?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The number of piano tuners depends on how much piano-tuning work there is and how much work it takes to employ one tuner.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Four facts would settle it: the number of pianos in Chicago, how often pianos are tuned each year, how long one tuning takes, and how many hours a year the average tuner works. The first three give the total tuning work; dividing by the fourth gives the number of tuners.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for this particular breakdown; it is the Fermi estimate of the piano-tuner puzzle.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: the authors do not have any of the four facts to hand; the point is that the question can be broken down.

card.rule: According to the authors, total tuning work divided by one tuner's annual hours gives the number of tuners.
card.limits: Breaking the question into four unknowns exchanges one unanswerable question for four; the gain is that each is easier to guess than the original.

concepts.title: Rough guesses, laid out in the open
concepts.question: How do the authors fill in the piano-tuner numbers when they have no data?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a Fermi estimate fills each gap with an explicit rough guess, and a 90% confidence interval helps narrow a guess when you lack the number.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For Chicago's population they set a range they are 90% sure holds the answer, 1.5 to 3.5 million, and took the midpoint, 2.5 million. They guessed one in a hundred people owns a piano and doubled that to cover institutions, giving fifty thousand pianos. Tuning was once a year, two hours each. A tuner works 40 hours for 50 weeks, less 20% for travel: 1,600 hours.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Confidence interval: a range you are 90% sure contains the right answer. Guesses with no reasoning behind them are called black-box guesses.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: the authors admit many of these figures are black-box guesses; they are not research results.

card.rule: According to the authors, name each missing number, give it a rough value and keep the guesses visible.
card.limits: A midpoint of a confidence interval is a convenience when you cannot say where in the range the answer lies; it does not make the guess more certain.

concepts.title: Does Fermi estimation work?
concepts.question: How close did the piano-tuner estimate come, and why do the authors think the habit matters for forecasters?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Fermi estimates, though built on crude guesswork, can come impressively close, and the habit is a huge advantage for a forecaster.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Daniel Levitin found eighty-three piano-tuner listings in the Chicago yellow pages, but many were duplicates, such as one business with several phone numbers, so the true number is uncertain. The authors' estimate of sixty-three looks surprisingly close. They add that Fermi often made back-of-the-envelope estimates later confirmed by measurement.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Fermi estimates or Fermi problems.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The yellow-pages count is itself uncertain because of duplicates, so it is not a perfect benchmark.

card.rule: According to the authors, a visible chain of rough guesses can land near the truth, which is why the habit helps forecasters.
card.limits: The match with the yellow pages is one case, and the benchmark is imperfect; the authors present it as looking surprisingly close, not as proof of exactness.

concepts.title: The Arafat polonium question
concepts.question: What exactly did the tournament question about Yasser Arafat ask, and what was it not asking?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The tournament question was narrow: whether a French or Swiss inquiry would find elevated polonium in Arafat's remains. It did not ask who killed him.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Yasser Arafat, the 75-year-old Palestinian leader, fell ill on October 12, 2004 and died on November 11, 2004, cause uncertain. In July 2012 Swiss researchers found unnaturally high polonium-210, a radioactive element, on his belongings. His widow allowed exhumation and two agencies tested the body, in Switzerland and France. IARPA asked if either would find elevated polonium.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The question was posed by IARPA.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, reread the question's exact words before forming a view.

card.rule: According to the authors, read a forecasting question exactly as written, because it may ask less than the story it sits in.
card.limits: A question's wording can still leave room for ambiguity; the authors use this case to show a trap in answering, not to settle the Arafat mystery.

concepts.title: The tip-of-your-nose perspective
concepts.question: How do most people turn a hunch into a forecast, and why do the authors say it is no way to forecast?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, most people forecast from the hunch that comes the moment they read the question, and that is no way to make accurate forecasts.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For the Arafat question, a hunch might be a whisper for someone who knows little, or a shout for someone passionate about the region: 'Israel would never do that!' becomes 5% or zero, 'Of course Israel did it!' becomes 95% or 100%, and ambivalence becomes about 50%. The hunch comes from a black box, so an error in it cannot be caught. TV pundits do roughly this.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The tip-of-your-nose perspective.

card.rule: According to the authors, the strength of a hunch is not a forecast; an unexamined hunch cannot be checked for errors.
card.limits: The authors do not say hunches are always wrong; they say that if the hunch contains an error you will not catch it, because it came from a black box.

concepts.title: Bait and switch: answering a different question
concepts.question: What mistake do the authors find hidden in the common hunches about Arafat?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The common hunches answer a different, easier question than the one asked.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The question asked whether French or Swiss inquiries would find elevated polonium. 'Israel would never do that!' and 'Of course Israel did it!' do not respond to that; they answer 'Did Israel poison Yasser Arafat?' The hard question asked was replaced by the easy question that was not.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Bait and switch (the authors say System 1 pulled a classic bait and switch).

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: The authors attribute the swap to System 1, a term they use here without definition.

card.rule: According to the authors, check that your answer responds to the question actually asked, not a nearby easier one.
card.limits: Spotting the swap is not the same as getting the answer right; the authors say Fermi-izing helps avoid the trap, not that it solves the question.

concepts.title: Bill Flack unpacks the question
concepts.question: How did Bill Flack, a non-expert, get off to a great start on the Arafat question?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: Bill Flack, who had no expertise on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, got a strong start by unpacking the question into what it would take for yes and for no.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: His first step had nothing to do with politics. Polonium decays quickly, so could scientists detect it on remains years later? He read the Swiss team's report, learned the science and was satisfied they could. He then listed ways remains could be contaminated: Israel, Palestinian enemies, or postmortem contamination by a faction wanting to blame Israel.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Fermi-style unpacking (the authors say he thought like Fermi).

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, ask 'What would it take for the answer to be yes? What would it take for it to be no?'

card.rule: According to the authors, unpack a question into what it would take for yes and for no, and start with the step that comes first.
card.limits: This is a start, not an answer: the authors call it only the beginning, a road map for later analysis.

concepts.title: Outside view first: the base rate
concepts.question: What do superforecasters do first when asked about a specific case, and what is it called?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, superforecasters start with the outside view, the base rate for the broader class, and only then use the case's specifics to adjust it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Asked how likely the Renzetti family is to own a pet, most people seize on details: Italian names, one child, a grandmother, and build a story. Superforecasters first find what percentage of American households own a pet. That figure is the starting estimate, and the family's details then move it up or down.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Base rate: how common something is within a broader class (statisticians). Outside view: Daniel Kahneman's term for it. Inside view: the specifics of the particular case.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: Storytelling from details feels compelling, but it is the inside view and comes second.

card.rule: According to the authors, begin with how common the thing is in the broader class, then adjust for the particulars.
card.limits: The outside view is a starting point, not an answer; the authors immediately adjust it with the inside view.

concepts.title: Why the inside view tempts
concepts.question: Why do even smart people skip the outside view, and what does Peggy Noonan's example show?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the inside view is concrete and story-rich while the outside view is abstract and bare, so even smart, accomplished people routinely skip the outside view.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Columnist Peggy Noonan predicted trouble for the Democrats because George W. Bush's approval, rock-bottom at the end of his term, had risen to 47% four years after leaving office, equal to Obama's. She found this astonishing and deeply meaningful. But the outside view shows the rise is the usual pattern for former presidents, so it was no surprise and the meaning she drew was illusory.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The outside view, here the pattern in what happens to former presidents.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: the example is about missing a base rate, not about Noonan's politics.

card.rule: According to the authors, a vivid story about one case can hide a plain pattern across the class.
card.limits: The authors say the outside view is not the end of the analysis; it is the check that stops a vivid case from carrying more meaning than it has.

concepts.title: The recurrence model: base rates from history
concepts.question: How does Bill Flack turn the history of past events into an opening probability?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, for a question about whether an event will happen in the next period, a forecaster can use how often it happened before as the outside view.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Asked whether an armed clash between China and Vietnam would occur within twelve months, Bill Flack would look at how often clashes occurred in the past. If hostile conduct comes about every five years, he would use a five-year recurrence model, so in a given year the outside view is a 20% chance of a clash.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Recurrence model (Bill Flack's phrase for using how often something recurs as a forecast).

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, once the outside view is set, Bill looks at today's situation and adjusts the number up or down.

card.rule: According to the authors, use how often something has happened in the past to set the first probability, then adjust.
card.limits: A recurrence model assumes the past frequency is a fair starting point; it is not a prediction and the inside view must adjust it.

concepts.title: More than one outside view
concepts.question: When several outside views are available, which should you start from?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, there is often more than one outside view, and a narrower class that matches the case more closely makes a better starting point.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the Renzetti problem, the pet-ownership rate of all American households is one outside view. The authors refine it to single-family detached homes like the family's own, and say that second figure, perhaps 73%, is probably a better bet because it more closely matches the particular case.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Narrowing the lens: choosing the outside view whose class best matches the case.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: 73% is the authors' illustrative figure ('let's say'), not a measured statistic.

card.rule: According to the authors, choose the outside view whose class fits your case most closely.
card.limits: A narrower class is better only while it still matches the case; each narrowing leaves fewer examples to rely on, a point the authors do not discuss.

concepts.title: An outside view when there is no base rate
concepts.question: How do the authors find a starting point for the Arafat question when no base rate exists?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, when there is no handy base rate, you can still bound an outside view with Fermi-style reasoning and use its midpoint as a starting point.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Dead Middle Eastern leaders are not routinely exhumed, so a quick search will not give a rate. The authors reason: a famous person is dead and major investigators think suspicion is strong enough to exhume the body. The chance of finding poisoning must be well above zero, so at least 20%. It cannot be 100%, so at most 80%. The midpoint is 50%.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Outside view by bounds, a Fermi-style approach.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: the 20% and 80% limits are the authors' judgments, not data.

card.rule: According to the authors, when no base rate exists, reason about the lowest and highest sensible values and start in the middle.
card.limits: The range is wide and the midpoint is a convenience; the authors accept it as a starting point, not as a finding.

concepts.title: Why the outside view comes first: anchoring
concepts.question: Why must the outside view come before the inside view, rather than after it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, outside first is better because of anchoring: we start from a number and adjust, we tend to under-adjust, so a bad anchor can produce a bad estimate.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In classic experiments, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that merely exposing people to a number, even one obviously meaningless such as one from a spin of a wheel, influenced their judgment. A forecaster who dives into the inside view risks being swayed by a number with little meaning. Starting with the outside view gives a meaningful anchor.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Anchoring: the anchor is the number we start with; under-adjusting is stopping short of the right figure.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, set the outside view first so the anchor is meaningful.

card.rule: According to the authors, the first number you settle on pulls the estimate toward it, so choose a meaningful one first.
card.limits: Anchoring explains the order, not the answer: a good anchor still needs adjustment, and the authors do not claim it removes error.

concepts.title: The inside view is an investigation, not an amble
concepts.question: How should the inside view be explored once Fermi-izing and the outside view are done?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a good exploration of the inside view is targeted and purposeful, an investigation and not an amble, and does not mean soaking up any and all information.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: After Fermi-izing the Arafat question and finding the outside view, one might fill a small library with books on Middle Eastern politics and settle in for six months of reading. The authors call that admirable but misguided; a good exploration is targeted and purposeful.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, let the Fermi breakdown tell you what to look for.

card.rule: According to the authors, research the inside view with a purpose set by the breakdown, not by wandering through information.
card.limits: Targeted does not mean quick; the authors say real detective work is slow and demanding, and it still works far better than wandering.

concepts.title: Pathways become hypotheses
concepts.question: What do the several routes to a yes answer give the inside-view researcher?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the pathways found by Fermi-izing make ideal hypotheses, a framework for investigating the inside view.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: When Bill Flack Fermi-ized the Arafat question, he saw several routes to a yes, including that Israel poisoned Arafat and that Arafat's Palestinian enemies did.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Hypotheses: the candidate routes to the outcome.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, take the hypotheses one at a time, then move on to the next, and the next.

card.rule: According to the authors, turn each route to an outcome into a hypothesis and investigate them in turn.
card.limits: The hypotheses set the agenda but not the verdict; each one still has to be researched for evidence both for and against.

concepts.title: What would it take for a hypothesis to be true?
concepts.question: How do the authors test a single hypothesis such as 'Israel poisoned Arafat'?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a hypothesis is investigated by asking what it would take to be true, then researching each element for evidence for and against.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For the hypothesis that Israel poisoned Arafat with polonium, three things would have to be true: Israel had or could obtain polonium; Israel wanted Arafat dead badly enough to take a big risk; Israel had the ability to poison him with polonium. Each element can be researched for pro and con evidence, giving a sense of how likely it is and so how likely the hypothesis is.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the three elements.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: the three elements are a worked example, not the authors' verdict on whether Israel did it.

card.rule: According to the authors, break a hypothesis into the conditions it needs, and judge each with evidence on both sides.
card.limits: The method yields likelihoods for each element and the whole; it does not by itself deliver certainty.

concepts.title: David Rogg's base rate
concepts.question: How did David Rogg set his outside view on a question about attacks in Europe?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: Facing a flood of media coverage, David Rogg resisted the pull of the inside view and began by computing a base rate from a list of past attacks.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In early 2015, soon after the Charlie Hebdo killings, IARPA asked whether an attack by Islamist militants would occur in any of eight named European countries between 21 January and 31 March 2015. David found a list of Islamist terror attacks, counted six in those countries over the previous five years, and wrote that he calculated the base rate as 1.2 a year.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Base rate, expressed as attacks per year.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: a list on a public web page was good enough for his starting figure; the authors do not call it complete.

card.rule: According to the authors, count how often the event has occurred over a defined period in a defined place to set the base rate.
card.limits: The base rate is a starting point; David went on to adjust it, and a count over a short window can be rough.

concepts.title: Adjusting the base rate both ways
concepts.question: How did David Rogg adjust his base rate, and why in both directions?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: David Rogg moved from his base rate by weighing changes that pushed the probability up against changes that pushed it down.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: ISIS had surged and had repeatedly threatened Europe. He judged data from 2010 and earlier no longer relevant and dropped 2010, which raised the base rate to 1.5 a year, still low in his view. But security had been sharply increased after Charlie Hebdo, which cut the likelihood. Balancing both, he raised the rate by only a fifth, to 1.8 attacks a year.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Inside-view adjustment: changing the base rate for what is new about the case.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, a good adjustment considers forces pulling in both directions.

card.rule: According to the authors, adjust the base rate for what is different now, weighing forces up and down.
card.limits: The adjustment is a judgment; the numbers 1.5 and 1.8 are David's, and he suspected 1.5 was still low before he netted the security effect.

concepts.title: Synthesis: one number from two views
concepts.question: How did David turn his adjusted rate into a probability for the question period?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, David's work was a textbook merger of outside and inside views into one estimate.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: There were 69 days left in the forecast period. He divided 69 by 365 and multiplied by 1.8 attacks a year, getting 0.34. He concluded there was a 34% chance the answer to IARPA's question was yes.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Synthesis of outside and inside views (the section title also uses thesis and antithesis).

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: He was not saying '34%, final answer', like a contestant on a quiz show.

card.rule: According to the authors, merge the outside and inside views into one number, but treat it as a beginning.
card.limits: Scaling a yearly rate to a shorter period is one way to make the estimate; it is a rough merge and not a final answer.

concepts.title: Seeking other perspectives
concepts.question: Why do superforecasters share their reasoning and invite critiques, even after reaching a synthesis?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a synthesis is not the end but a good beginning; superforecasters constantly look for other views to fold into their own.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: David Rogg posted his analysis on a Good Judgment Project forum because he wanted to know what teammates were thinking. Ways to get new perspectives include asking what other forecasters think, what outside and inside views they found, and what experts say. Bill Flack explains his thinking to teammates and asks for critiques, hoping they will spot flaws and offer perspectives; writing it down also distances him from it.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Auto-feedback: Bill Flack's term for scrutinising his own written judgment.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, write your judgment down, then ask whether you agree and where it has holes.

card.rule: According to the authors, share your reasoning, invite critique, and keep looking for views to add.
card.limits: Seeking other views feeds the judgment; it does not replace it, and the final estimate is still the forecaster's own synthesis.

concepts.title: The crowd within
concepts.question: How can you get a second perspective from yourself that improves accuracy?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, you can improve your own accuracy by making a second judgment after assuming your first was wrong, and combining the two.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Researchers found that asking people to assume their initial judgment was wrong, consider why, and make another judgment gave a second estimate that, combined with the first, improved accuracy almost as much as a second estimate from another person. Letting several weeks pass before the second estimate had the same effect.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The crowd within, built on the wisdom-of-the-crowd concept.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, assume your first judgment is wrong, ask why, and combine the two estimates.

card.rule: According to the authors, a second estimate from yourself, made after assuming the first was wrong, improves the average.
card.limits: A second estimate from yourself helps almost as much as one from another person, not more; another person's view can still add independent information.

concepts.title: Turn the question on its head
concepts.question: How can rewording a question give you another perspective and counter confirmation bias?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, tweaking a question's wording is a simple way to get another perspective and to check the pull of confirmation bias.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The question was whether South Africa would grant the Dalai Lama a visa within six months. A naive forecaster seeks evidence he will get it; a sophisticated one seeks evidence both ways. Thinking only 'Will he get his visa?' tilts the mental playing field. Flip it to whether the government will deny him for six months and you lean the other way, finding reasons it might deny the visa.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Confirmation bias: looking mainly for evidence that supports your leaning.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, restate the question in the opposite form and see what evidence it brings out.

card.rule: According to the authors, ask the question in its opposite wording to find the evidence the first wording hides.
card.limits: Rewording changes the lean of your search, not the facts; the authors use it as a check, not as a replacement for weighing both sides.

concepts.title: Dragonfly eye: many hands
concepts.question: What does it look like when a superforecaster juggles many perspectives, and what does it cost?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, superforecasters synthesize many perspectives, which is mentally demanding, and keep at it past the point where most people give up.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: On forums they write 'on the one hand, on the other', and have more than two hands. One superforecaster weighing Saudi Arabia's response to OPEC production cuts in November 2014 weighed reserves, social spending and the drilling frenzy, and ended: 'Net answer: Feels no-ish, 80%.' The Saudis did not support cuts, to many experts' shock. Superforecasters also scored very well on the Cognitive Reflection Test.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Dragonfly eye. The chapter uses the label for this many-perspective synthesis and does not elaborate.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, forget the old advice to think twice; superforecasters often think thrice.

card.rule: According to the authors, keep weighing several views against one another, even when it is mentally demanding.
card.limits: More perspectives make the synthesis harder, not easier, and the authors do not claim it guarantees being right.

concepts.title: Why do they bother? Need for cognition and openness
concepts.question: What traits do the authors say make the hard work enjoyable for superforecasters?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, one reason superforecasters put so much effort into an unpaid hobby is that they enjoy it, helped by two features of psychology.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Need for cognition is the tendency to engage in and enjoy hard mental slogs, as with hard crosswords and Sudoku, and superforecasters score high on tests of it. Openness to experience is one of the Big Five personality traits, covering a taste for variety and intellectual curiosity. Asked about a hypothetical Ghana election, Doug Lorch said it was an opportunity to learn something about Ghana.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Need for cognition and openness to experience (one of the 'Big Five' traits).

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Their only rewards are a gift certificate and bragging rights, and the authors present these as likely contributors, not proven causes.

card.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters enjoy hard thinking and curiosity, which helps explain why they put in so much effort.
card.limits: The authors say ultimately this matters less as traits than as behavior, which they turn to next.

concepts.title: Active open-mindedness
concepts.question: What is active open-mindedness, and how does Doug Lorch put it into practice?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, what sets superforecasters apart is behavior, above all active open-mindedness: they treat beliefs as hypotheses to be tested, not treasures to be guarded.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Doug Lorch built a database of hundreds of information sources, tagged by ideological orientation, subject matter and geographic origin, and a program that picks what he should read next with diversity as a criterion. Jonathan Baron's test for the trait asks whether you agree with statements such as 'Changing your mind is a sign of weakness.' Superforecasters score highly on it.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Active open-mindedness (AOM), a concept coined by psychologist Jonathan Baron.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, the bumper-sticker version of superforecasting is that beliefs are hypotheses to test.

card.rule: According to the authors, treat beliefs as hypotheses to be tested, and arrange your habits so you meet views that differ.
card.limits: The authors admit it would be facile to reduce superforecasting to a slogan; they offer it as the single line they would choose.

concepts.title: Superforecasters have a way with numbers
concepts.question: What do superforecasters share when it comes to numbers?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, superforecasters have a way with numbers: they are almost uniformly numerate and comfortable using figures.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Most of them aced a brief test of basic numeracy, such as working out how many of 10,000 people would catch a virus if the chance is 0.05%. Many have a background in math, science or computer programming. The author has yet to find a superforecaster who is not comfortable with numbers.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Numeracy: comfort with numbers, checked here by a short quiz of basic questions. No further name is given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The chapter treats numeracy as a shared trait, not as the whole explanation of their results; it goes on to ask how it helps.

card.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters pass basic numeracy tests and often come from math, science or programming backgrounds.
card.limits: Being numerate is not the same as running arcane math models to divine the future; the authors say that is not how it helps.

concepts.title: There is no moat and no castle wall
concepts.question: Do superforecasters get their accuracy from running advanced math models?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, math does not explain superforecasters' results. They occasionally use explicit models, or other people's, but that is rare.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Most of their forecasts come from careful thought and nuanced judgment. Lionel Levine, a math professor, says math helped on a couple of questions only. Bill Flack builds a Monte Carlo model from past changes when asked about currency exchange rates.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Quants: Wall Street's math wizards. Monte Carlo model: the kind of model Flack builds, which the chapter calls basic stuff for the cognoscenti.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, someone who stopped doing calculus after high school is not walled off from superforecasting.

card.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters' accuracy rests mostly on careful thought and judgment, not on arcane math models.
card.limits: Some questions, such as exchange rates, do prompt a model; the claim is that this is rare, not that it never happens.

concepts.title: The compound in Abbottabad
concepts.question: What decision did intelligence analysts face about the compound in early 2011?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: In early 2011 US intelligence analysts had to judge whether a compound in the Pakistani city of Abbottabad housed Osama bin Laden, with an assault inside a volatile nuclear-armed country at stake.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: High walls were normal in that wealthy neighbourhood. Occupants who were unknown and wanted to stay unknown were unusual. Bits and strands of evidence together pointed to bin Laden, which the author calls approaching unique.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The judgments were later dramatized in the movie Zero Dark Thirty.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The author stresses that everyone knows the answer now, but the analysts did not know it then.

card.rule: According to the authors, the analysts faced a hard judgment on partial evidence, without the answer everyone has since learned.
card.limits: The film is a dramatization; the authors compare it with what the real people said and did.

concepts.title: The film director who wants agreement
concepts.question: What does the fictional CIA director want from his advisers, and is it reasonable?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: In Zero Dark Thirty the fictional Leon Panetta wants every adviser to reach the same conclusion so he can be sure it is right. The authors say that wish is mistaken.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the scene he asks whether bin Laden is there. The deputy director says 60%, the next adviser concurs, another says 80%, and so it goes around the table, with 60% and 80% recurring. He sighs that the result is a mess.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The authors call it a natural but wrong desire: agreement is reassuring, disagreement is not.

card.rule: According to the authors, the fictional director wants agreement as proof of correctness, but agreement is not proof.
card.limits: The scene is fiction; the authors use it as a foil and check it against the real Panetta.

concepts.title: A spread of judgments is a gift
concepts.question: Why should a smart executive welcome different probability estimates from advisers?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a spread of independent judgments should be welcomed, and unanimity should be treated as a warning flag that groupthink has taken hold.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Independent people with different educations, training, experiences and personalities are unlikely to reach precisely the same conclusion, even on the same evidence. Their spread is wisdom of the crowd, gift wrapped. The executive can synthesise it by simple averaging or by weighted averaging.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Wisdom of the crowd; groupthink; dragonfly eye (the chapter calls this synthesis dragonfly eye at work).

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, a good start is a simple average. Giving more say to those whose judgment you most respect is a weighted average.

card.rule: According to the authors, treat a spread of independent judgments as a resource to average, and unanimity as a warning flag.
card.limits: The advice is for independent judgments; it does not show that averaging fixes poor information.

concepts.title: The real Panetta thinks like a superforecaster
concepts.question: How did the real Leon Panetta react to the spread of estimates in the room?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the real Leon Panetta welcomed diverse judgments and thinks like a superforecaster, unlike his fictional counterpart.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: He confirmed a scene like the film's did happen and the room held much experience but little agreement. Estimates ranged from 30 to 40 percent to 90 percent and above. He told the author that he encouraged people to say what they believed, not what he wanted to hear. He said nothing is one hundred percent.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The authors cite his remark “Nothing is one hundred percent” as the heart of his attitude.

card.rule: According to the authors, the real Panetta asked for honest, varied estimates and rejected certainty.
card.limits: The authors rely on his own recollection of the meeting; the film's version is a dramatization.

concepts.title: Maya and the two-setting dial
concepts.question: How does the character Maya think about whether bin Laden is in the compound?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: In the film, Maya says bin Laden is there at 100%, reduced to 95% only because certainty freaks the others out. The fictional director backs her, seeing only yes and no.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: She wanted the compound bombed at once. As weeks passed she wrote the number of elapsed days on her superior's window: 21, later 98, 99, 100. The director says the others will not commit because they are cowed; probabilities are for weaklings.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Mental dial: the chapter's image of how a person sets a judgment. His dial has two settings, yes and no, with no maybe.

card.rule: According to the authors, the fictional director and Maya think with a two-setting mental dial: yes or no, with no degrees of maybe.
card.limits: The authors say this style feels bold and appealing in a film, but they go on to show it is unreasonable.

concepts.title: Right but unreasonable
concepts.question: Can a forecast be right in outcome yet unreasonable given the evidence?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Maya was right but unreasonable: bin Laden was there, but 100% was more extreme than the evidence could support.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The man in the compound could have been another terrorist, a trafficker, a warlord, an arms dealer or a wealthy Pakistani businessman with paranoid schizophrenia. Even tiny odds for each would add up to 1%, 2%, 5% or more. The mirror image is wrong but reasonable: the intelligence community scaling a slam dunk back to 60% or 70% on Saddam's weapons would have been wrong but reasonable.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Right but unreasonable; wrong but reasonable; process-outcome paradoxes.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors do not say 99% would have been correct; they say certainty is not supported.

card.rule: According to the authors, judge a forecast by whether it fits the evidence, since the outcome cannot show that.
card.limits: The authors still say outcomes matter in the long run; this idea is about judging one case.

concepts.title: Obama hears the CIA's confidence levels
concepts.question: How varied were the confidence levels the CIA officers gave the president?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Mark Bowden's account, the real Obama heard confidence levels from officers that ranged widely, and he called it a probability matter.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The CIA's team leader put his confidence at 95%, and a second CIA officer agreed. Four senior officers at the Directorate of National Intelligence put most estimates near 80%, with some as low as 40 or even 30%. Another officer said 60%. The president answered, “OK, this is a probability thing”.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. Source: Mark Bowden, The Finish: The Killing of Osama bin Laden.

card.rule: According to Bowden, the president heard estimates from about 30% to 95% and treated the matter as one of probability.
card.limits: The numbers come from Bowden's account, which the authors call sketchy.

concepts.title: Probabilities that disguised uncertainty
concepts.question: What did Bowden and Obama think the CIA's numbers achieved?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Bowden, Obama thought the CIA's elaborate numerical process produced more confusion, not more certainty.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: After the CIA's erroneous call on Saddam's weapons of mass destruction, it instituted an almost comically elaborate process for weighing certainty. Obama told Bowden that it gave “probabilities that disguised uncertainty as opposed to actually providing you with useful information”.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. Source: Bowden's account and Obama's later interview with him.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: This is Bowden's and Obama's view; the authors go on to test it.

card.rule: According to Bowden, Obama found the CIA's number-heavy process confusing rather than clarifying.
card.limits: The authors do not endorse this view; they ask whether Bowden's admiration is justified.

concepts.title: Fifty-fifty against a median of 70%
concepts.question: Was Obama's fifty-fifty a better estimate than the officers' median?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, if Obama meant fifty-fifty literally, he was misguided, because the officers' median estimate was higher.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Obama told the room this was fifty-fifty, a flip of the coin. From Bowden's sketchy information the median estimate, the wisdom of the crowd, was around 70%. On Bowden's account Obama had no reasonable basis for thinking 50% more accurate: it was a number plucked out of the air.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Wisdom of the crowd: the collective view of many judges; median: the middle estimate.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The 70% median is inferred from limited information; the authors say there are several possible meanings of fifty-fifty.

card.rule: According to the authors, a literal 50% against a crowd median near 70% has no reasonable basis in Bowden's account.
card.limits: The authors consider other meanings of fifty-fifty; the next idea covers the most likely.

concepts.title: Fifty-fifty as a stand-in for maybe
concepts.question: What do people often mean when they say fifty-fifty?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, researchers show that people who say fifty-fifty often do not mean 50% but I am not sure, or maybe. Obama may have meant that, which would be reasonable.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: As an executive making a critical decision, he may have felt he would order the strike if there was any significant possibility bin Laden was there. Whether the probability was 90%, 70% or even 30% did not matter. So rather than waste time on a number, he cut the discussion short.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Fifty-fifty used as maybe: no separate name is given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The author says he does not know if that was Obama's thinking.

card.rule: According to the authors, fifty-fifty often means maybe, and when a decision does not turn on the exact number a quick maybe can be reasonable.
card.limits: This holds when the action would follow from any significant chance; if the decision turned on the number, refining it would matter.

concepts.title: The ignorance prior
concepts.question: What is the ignorance prior, and why is retreating to it a mistake?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a much less defensible reading is that Obama was bothered by the spread, thought the estimates unreliable, and fell back on the ignorance prior.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The ignorance prior is the state of knowledge you are in before you know whether a coin will land heads or tails or, here, whether bin Laden will be in the master bedroom. Retreating to it was a mistake, say the authors, because Obama did not make full use of the information at the table.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Ignorance prior: the starting state of knowledge before an outcome is known.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: Unlike the fictional director, Obama had a third setting on his mental dial, maybe, and that is where he settled.

card.rule: According to the authors, falling back on the ignorance prior because estimates differ wastes the information on the table.
card.limits: The authors present this as one possible reading of Obama, not as what they believe he did.

concepts.title: Tversky and the three settings
concepts.question: What three settings does Tversky's remark say most people have for probabilities?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the author, Amos Tversky remarked that in dealing with probabilities most people have only three settings: gonna happen, not gonna happen and maybe.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tversky said it about thirty years earlier, when he and the author served on a National Research Council committee charged with preventing nuclear war. The author is 98% sure he was joking and 99% sure the joke captures a basic truth about human judgment.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Three-setting mental dial (also called the three-setting dial).

card.rule: According to the author, most people think in three settings: it will happen, it will not, or maybe.
card.limits: The remark was a joke; the author treats it as a basic truth, not as a measured finding.

concepts.title: Judging by the tip of your nose
concepts.question: How did people judge uncertainty before probability was studied seriously?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, before probability was studied seriously people relied on the tip-of-your-nose perspective, a System 1 judgment that gives a yes, a no or a maybe but not fine degrees.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Serious thought about probability came remarkably late, arguably as late as Jakob Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi in 1713. Seeing a shadow in long grass, you try to recall a lion attack. If an example comes easily, a strong response gives a binary conclusion; a weaker one gives maybe.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Tip-of-your-nose perspective; System 1 (from chapter 2); Ars Conjectandi, Bernoulli's 1713 work.

card.rule: According to the authors, the tip-of-your-nose perspective turns how easily an example comes to mind into yes, no or maybe.
card.limits: It is fast, not fine: it cannot tell a 60% chance from an 80% one.

concepts.title: Why a three-setting dial made sense
concepts.question: Why would a coarse dial have helped our ancestors survive?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, in the world our ancestors lived in, a three-setting dial gave quick, clear directions, so the preference for two or three settings makes sense.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Is that a lion? Yes means run, maybe means stay alert, no means relax. Pressing existential problems rarely required finer distinctions, and telling 60% from 80% would have added little.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Three-setting dial; the authors also speak of two- and three-setting mental dials.

card.rule: According to the authors, a coarse dial was a good fit for the quick decisions of ancestral life.
card.limits: Its fit for ancient dangers does not make it suit modern forecasting questions.

concepts.title: The premium on certainty
concepts.question: Why do 0% and 100% weigh more in our minds than the models say they should?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, both 0% and 100% weigh far more heavily in our minds than economists' mathematical models say they should.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A parent willing to pay something to cut a child's risk of a serious disease from 10% to 5% may pay two to three times as much to cut it from 5% to 0%, because the second step delivers certainty and not only a 5% reduction.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, people pay a premium for removing a risk altogether, more than the size of the reduction explains.
card.limits: The authors describe a tendency, not a rule that holds for every person or every risk.

concepts.title: We reward confident answers
concepts.question: Why do people prefer a confident answer even when it is no more accurate?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, confidence and accuracy are positively correlated, but people exaggerate the correlation, so confident forecasters are trusted more than their records justify.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Answers to a question like whether France has more people than Italy are likelier to be right when we are confident. Yet people trust more confident financial advisers over less confident ones even when their track records are identical. The media often turn to hedgehogs who are sure.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Hedgehogs: the chapter's term for forecasters sure they know what is coming.

card.rule: According to the authors, confidence tells you a little about accuracy, but people read much more into it than is there.
card.limits: Confidence does carry some information; the claim is about the size of the correlation, not its sign.

concepts.title: A middling probability looks like weakness
concepts.question: What do people think of a forecaster who gives a middling probability?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, people equate confidence with competence, so a forecaster who says something has a middling probability earns less respect.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: One study found that people read such middling judgments as a sign the forecasters were incompetent, ignorant of the facts, or too lazy to gather the information that would justify more confidence.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, hedged forecasts are often read as a flaw in the forecaster, not as honest uncertainty.
card.limits: The study reports how people judge; it does not show the hedged forecasters were worse.

concepts.title: What a 70% chance of rain means
concepts.question: What does a forecast of a 70% chance of rain tell you?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a 70% chance of rain means that, across 100 days on which such forecasts are made, good forecasts should see rain on 70 of them and dry weather on the rest.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Some people read it as rain over 70% of the day, rain over 70% of Los Angeles, or 70% of forecasters expecting rain. The authors say the underlying problem is more basic: our natural leaning is to think it will rain, it will not, or maybe.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, a probability forecast describes how often such outcomes occur across many similar cases.
card.limits: A single day gives one outcome, so one forecast alone cannot show whether the forecaster is good.

concepts.title: The 75% that did not come true
concepts.question: Does an outcome that was forecast at 75% to be unlikely show the forecast was wrong?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the author, even sophisticated people make elementary mistakes with probability, such as calling a forecast wrong because a likely event did not occur.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: David Leonhardt said a prediction market's forecast was wrong because it had put a 75% chance on a law being struck down and it was not. Later he wrote a column warning that a 74% chance the Republicans win the Senate also means a 26% chance they will not.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the author, a forecast of 75% that fails to come true is not shown wrong, since it also meant a 25% chance of the other outcome.
card.limits: A run of such misses across many forecasts would show a problem; a single miss does not.

concepts.title: Eighty percent heard as certain
concepts.question: How do educated policy makers tend to treat a high probability?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Robert Rubin, as the authors report, policy makers tend to translate a high probability into this will happen.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Rubin said that he and his deputy Larry Summers were often frustrated when briefing top people in the White House and Congress, who treated an 80% probability as a certainty. He said you almost had to pound the table to remind them it might not happen.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to Rubin, even accomplished people slip from a high probability to a certainty when dealing with real issues.
card.limits: Rubin says they grasp it in a classroom, so the failure is one of habit, not knowledge.

concepts.title: Science is tentative, not carved in granite
concepts.question: How do scientists regard certainty, and how does that differ from the popular picture?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, scientists relish or at least accept uncertainty, because in scientific models of reality certainty is illusory and all scientific knowledge is tentative.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The popular picture is nineteenth-century: scientists chisel facts into granite tablets and push uncertainty back until it is eradicated. Twentieth-century science showed that uncertainty is ineradicable, and facts that look solid to one generation can be crushed by the next. The mathematician William Byers writes that “It is the dream of total certainty that is an illusion.”

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Invisible asterisk: the unspoken caveat attached when scientists say this is true.
