card.rule: According to the authors, treat every scientific claim as carrying an invisible asterisk, because nothing is certain.
card.limits: The asterisk does not make all claims equal; some are held with high confidence and others not.

concepts.title: Dividing maybe into degrees
concepts.question: If nothing is certain, what must replace the yes, no and maybe settings?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, if nothing is certain, yes and no must go. Maybe remains, but it must be divided into finely graded numerical degrees of probability. This is probabilistic thinking.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A one-setting dial is useless: Is that a lion? Maybe. So maybe is subdivided. Vague terms like probably and unlikely carry dangerous ambiguity, so scientists prefer numbers, as fine as forecasters can manage, provided the steps capture real distinctions: outcomes said to be 11% likely should happen 1% less often than 12% ones.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Probabilistic thinking; granularity (how fine the steps are).

card.rule: According to the authors, replace yes, no and maybe with numbers as finely graded as real distinctions allow.
card.limits: Granularity helps only if each step reflects a real difference; empty precision adds nothing.

concepts.title: Rubin, the probabilistic thinker
concepts.question: How did Robert Rubin turn the idea of uncertainty into a working habit?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Robert Rubin is a probabilistic thinker who treats everything as a matter of probability and wants as much precision as possible.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: As a Harvard student he heard a philosophy professor argue that nothing is provably certain, and it just clicked. It guided him for twenty-six years at Goldman Sachs and as a Clinton adviser and Treasury secretary. A Treasury aide who told him a bill would pass absolutely was corrected; now the aide says 60%, and they argue over 59 or 60.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Probabilistic thinker.

card.rule: According to the authors, Rubin rejects certainty and demands numbers, even to the point of arguing over a single point.
card.limits: The authors take no position on whether Rubin was a hero or a villain; they use him as an example of thinking.

concepts.title: Fish and birds
concepts.question: Why did many people find Rubin's way of thinking surprising, even startling?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the author, probabilistic thinking and the two- and three-setting dials are like fish and birds: fundamentally different creatures resting on different assumptions about reality.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: When a 1998 New York Times feature laid out Rubin's thinking, many found it startlingly counterintuitive; professionals pinned it to cubicle walls beside inspirational messages and photos of their kids. Rubin was bemused. His autobiography got the same reaction.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Fish and birds: the author's comparison.

card.rule: According to the author, each style of thinking can seem surpassingly strange to someone used to the other.
card.limits: The comparison is an image, not a finding; it does not say which creature is better suited to every environment.

concepts.title: Superforecasters as probabilistic thinkers
concepts.question: Are superforecasters probabilistic thinkers, and why?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, thanks partly to superior numeracy, superforecasters, like scientists and mathematicians, tend to be probabilistic thinkers.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Rubin would not have to pound the table to make them see that an 80% chance of something happening implies a 20% chance it will not. The core of probabilistic thinking is an awareness of irreducible uncertainty, which is tricky to measure.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Probabilistic thinker; irreducible uncertainty.

card.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters grasp that high probability leaves a real chance of the opposite.
card.limits: The claim is a tendency across the group, not a trait every member shows on every question.

concepts.title: Epistemic and aleatory uncertainty
concepts.question: What is the difference between uncertainty you could resolve and uncertainty you cannot?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, epistemic uncertainty is something you do not know but could in theory know; aleatory uncertainty is unknowable even in theory.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A mystery machine is epistemic: skilled engineers could in theory pry it open and work it out, a clocklike challenge. Whether it will rain in Philadelphia a year from now is aleatory: no meteorologist can outguess the seasonal averages, a cloud-like problem.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Epistemic uncertainty; aleatory uncertainty; clocklike; cloud-like.

card.rule: According to the authors, sort a question by whether more knowledge could in theory settle it.
card.limits: Real questions mix both kinds; the distinction guides how much to expect from more research.

concepts.title: Cautious with cloudy questions
concepts.question: How do superforecasters start when a question is loaded with irreducible uncertainty?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, when superforecasters sense a question is loaded with irreducible uncertainty, they are cautious: they keep initial estimates inside the 35% to 65% shades-of-maybe zone and move out tentatively.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A currency-market question is an example. They know the cloudier the outlook, the harder it is to beat the dart-throwing chimpanzee.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Shades-of-maybe zone (35% to 65%); dart-throwing chimpanzee (from earlier chapters).

card.rule: According to the authors, when a question is cloudy, start near the middle and move out slowly.
card.limits: The zone is for questions with irreducible uncertainty; clearer questions allow bolder starts.

concepts.title: Frequent fifties and accuracy
concepts.question: What does a forecaster's frequent use of 50% reveal about accuracy?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, forecasters who use 50% often are less accurate, because it tends to be a stand-in for maybe.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: To careful probabilistic thinkers, 50% is one setting among a huge range, no likelier than 49% or 51%. Forecasters who think in three settings use it much more often, as maybe. The authors expect frequent users to be less accurate, and the tournament data show exactly that.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Fifty-fifty as a stand-in for maybe.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: starting inside 35% to 65% is not the same as using 50% as maybe.

card.rule: According to the authors, a forecaster who leans on 50% is probably thinking in three settings and is less accurate.
card.limits: One use of 50% when evidence is truly balanced is fine; the finding is about frequent use.

concepts.title: Brian Labatte and finer steps
concepts.question: How finely do superforecasters grade their probabilities, compared with ordinary forecasters?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, superforecasters grade probabilities much more finely than ordinary forecasters, who tend to stick to the tens.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Asked how much he read of fiction and nonfiction, Brian Labatte paused and corrected 70% to 65/35. Ordinary tournament forecasters said 30% or 40%, not 35% or 37%. A third of superforecasters' forecasts used single percentage points. They debate 5% versus 1% because moving from extremely improbable to impossible can matter: an Ebola outbreak, funding the next Google.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Granularity: how fine the steps are.

card.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters think in single percentage points when the question rewards it.
card.limits: Fine steps pay off when consequences are large; they do not matter for every question.

concepts.title: Granularity is not bafflegab
concepts.question: How do we know superforecasters' fine steps carry real information?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, granularity predicts accuracy, so the fine steps of superforecasters are precision and not bafflegab.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Barbara Mellers found that forecasters who use tens are less accurate than those who use fives, who are less accurate than those who use ones. She also ran a rounding test on their forecasts.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Granularity; bafflegab (precision meant to impress); Brier score.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The test shows fine steps in this tournament go with accuracy; it is the authors' evidence that they are meaningful.

card.rule: According to the authors, check whether fine steps are meaningful by seeing if rounding them away costs accuracy.
card.limits: Rounding costs accuracy only if the precision was real; for ordinary forecasters it cost little.

concepts.title: Even the best organizations stop short
concepts.question: How granular are the scales used inside the intelligence community, and what do the authors suggest?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, even sophisticated organizations do not push to superforecasters' level of granularity, and they could.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The National Intelligence Council, which produces National Intelligence Estimates that inform decisions such as whether to invade Iraq or negotiate with Iran, asks analysts for judgments on a five- or seven-degree scale. That beats a two- or three-setting dial but falls short of what committed superforecasters achieve. The author suspects the NIC is selling itself short.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: National Intelligence Council (NIC); National Intelligence Estimates.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, the NIC or any organization with top-flight people could get similar results if it valued and encouraged granularity.

card.rule: According to the authors, organizations should value and encourage fine-grained probability, as the NIC could.
card.limits: The scale is an improvement over two or three settings; the authors say it still falls short.

media.alt: Two horizontal gradient bars, pale to dark, each labelled with verbal probability steps from remote to almost certain and no numbers. The upper bar has five steps, with even chance in the middle. The lower bar divides the same range into seven steps, adding very unlikely and very likely.

concepts.section: But What Does It All Mean?
concepts.title: Why we ask why
concepts.question: Why do people look for meaning when something unlikely and important happens?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the author, it is deeply human to ask why when something unlikely and important happens, and the search for meaning is a basic human need that religious and secular people share.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In Slaughterhouse-Five, a guard answers a prisoner's Why me? with Vy anybody? Oprah Winfrey says there is no failure and no coincidence, only divine order. Many atheists also see meaning in major life events, and a majority said they believe in fate. Among survivors of the 9/11 attacks, those who saw meaning were less likely to suffer post-traumatic stress responses.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Fate: the view that events happen for a reason and an underlying order to life determines how events turn out.

card.rule: According to the author, finding meaning in events is a mark of a healthy, resilient mind.
card.limits: The author does not call this need bad; he says it sits uneasily with a scientific worldview.

concepts.section: But What Does It All Mean?
concepts.title: Science asks how, not why
concepts.question: Why do chance and fate not mix in probabilistic thinking?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the author, science asks how, about causation and probabilities, and not why, about purpose. Probabilistic thinking and divine-order thinking are therefore in tension, and moving toward fate undermines probabilistic thinking.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Snow built up on a mountainside may slip and start an avalanche or may not; until it happens it could go either way. It is not predetermined and not meant to be. Maybe suggests that, contrary to Einstein, God does play dice. Chance and fate, like oil and water, do not mix.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Probabilistic thinking versus divine-order thinking.

card.rule: According to the author, the more you think in terms of fate, the less you can think in terms of probability.
card.limits: The author does not claim that meaning is wrong or false; he says it conflicts with probabilistic accuracy.

concepts.section: But What Does It All Mean?
concepts.title: Imagining alternatives adds meaning
concepts.question: What happens to the sense of fate when people imagine how things could have turned out differently?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the author, counterfactual thinking, picturing how something might have turned out differently, makes people see what did happen as more meaningful and more fated.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In his experiments with Laura Kray, Northwestern students who wrote about how they chose Northwestern and then listed ways things could have turned out differently saw the decision as more meaningful. Imagining a different path with a close friend deepened the relationship's significance. People who described life without a turning point saw the path taken as fated.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Counterfactual thinking.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The experiments show an effect on how people rate meaning; they do not show that fate is real.

card.rule: According to the author, imagining alternatives tends to raise the sense that what happened was meant to be.
card.limits: The three experiments are the author's evidence for a tendency, not a law for every person.

concepts.section: But What Does It All Mean?
concepts.title: Improbable, therefore meant to be?
concepts.question: What is wrong with reasoning that something improbable happened and so was meant to happen?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the author, people take the sheer improbability of an event and the fact that it happened as proof it was meant to happen, and this reasoning is incoherent.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Meeting the love of your life depended on countless chance events, yet most people say it was meant to be rather than lucky. On a cosmic scale, finely tuned laws allowed stars and life; most people suspect something, perhaps God, was behind it, though some physicists think of many parallel universes. Written out, the chain runs: the chance was tiny, it happened, so it was meant to be, so the chance was 100%.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Psycho-logic: the pull of thinking that conflicts with logic.

card.rule: According to the author, improbable and happened do not add up to meant to happen.
card.limits: The author calls the reasoning incoherent, not the feeling of wonder.

concepts.section: But What Does It All Mean?
concepts.title: Why me? Why not me?
concepts.question: How does a probabilistic thinker respond to profound events, such as tragedy?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the author, a probabilistic thinker asks how, not why. Why leads to metaphysics, and how sticks with physics. Even toward tragedy, he takes the outside view and sees quasi-random draws from once-possible worlds.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The economist Robert Shiller tells how Henry Ford's $5-a-day wage brought both of his grandfathers to Detroit; one change in countless events and he would not exist. He does not see fate but how indeterminate the future is, and calls looking back as if it was logical an illusion of hindsight. The author ends with Vonnegut: Why me? Why not me?

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Outside view (Kahneman's term); illusion of hindsight.

card.rule: According to the author, replace why with how: events took one of many possible paths, and this one is the path they took.
card.limits: The author notes this is not a comfort; he says the book is not about being happy.

concepts.section: But What Does It All Mean?
concepts.title: Measuring belief in fate
concepts.question: How did the researchers measure fate thinking, and how did superforecasters score?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, superforecasters are much less inclined than other groups to see things as fated.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Researchers gave pro-fate statements (Events unfold according to God's plan; Everything happens for a reason; There are no accidents or coincidences) and pro-probability ones (Nothing is inevitable; even World War II or 9/11 could have turned out very differently; randomness is often a factor in our personal lives). On a 9-point fate score, adult Americans were mid-scale, Penn undergraduates a little lower, regular forecasters a little lower still, and superforecasters lowest.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Fate score: a 9-point scale where 1 rejects it-was-meant-to-happen thinking and 9 embraces it.

card.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters score lowest on fate and sit firmly on the side that rejects it.
card.limits: Scores describe averages for groups; individuals within each group vary.

concepts.section: But What Does It All Mean?
concepts.title: Fate thinking and forecasting accuracy
concepts.question: Do forecasters who believe in fate forecast less accurately?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the more a forecaster inclined toward it-was-meant-to-happen thinking, the less accurate her forecasts were; the more she embraced probabilistic thinking, the more accurate she was.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: For both superforecasters and regulars, the researchers compared individual fate scores with Brier scores and found a significant correlation.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Fate score; Brier score.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors report a correlation; they say they do not know whether misery is the price of accuracy.

card.rule: According to the authors, the more a forecaster embraces probabilistic thinking, the more accurate she is.
card.limits: The authors leave the happiness question to others; the book is about accuracy, not happiness.

concepts.title: The opening process is only the beginning
concepts.question: What do superforecasters do before they update, and why is that only the start?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, superforecasting is not paint-by-numbers, but superforecasters often tackle questions in a roughly similar way that anyone can follow. Done well, the process is demanding, and it is only the beginning of the work on a question.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors list the steps: unpack the question into components; separate the known from the unknown and scrutinize every assumption; take the outside view, which treats the problem as a case of a wider class; then the inside view, which plays up its uniqueness; compare your views with those of others; synthesize them; state a judgment on a finely grained probability scale.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors liken the synthesis step to a single vision as acute as that of a dragonfly. The outside view and the inside view are the two comparison steps.

card.rule: According to the authors, the opening process of unpacking, comparing views and stating a precise probability is demanding, yet it only starts the work on a question.
card.limits: The authors call this a roughly similar way of working, not a fixed recipe. It describes what superforecasters often do and leaves room for judgment.

concepts.title: Forecasts are judgments to be updated
concepts.question: Why do the authors say a forecast should not be filed away once it is made?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, forecasts are not like lottery tickets that you buy and file away until the big draw. They are judgments built on the information available, and they should be updated when the information changes.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the IARPA tournament, Bill Flack did his hard initial work on whether polonium would be detected in Yasser Arafat's remains and settled on 60% yes. He then followed the news and updated whenever he saw good reason. The authors reason that a forecast reflecting the latest information is likely to be closer to the truth than one that does not.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The chapter later calls the act belief updating.

card.rule: According to the authors, a forecast is a judgment to be revised as information changes, and an updated forecast is likely to be closer to the truth.
card.limits: Updating helps only when the new information is read well. The rest of the chapter is about reading it neither too weakly nor too strongly.

concepts.title: Devyn Duffy, a frequent updater
concepts.question: How often do superforecasters update compared with regular forecasters, and what does Devyn Duffy show?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, superforecasters update much more frequently, on average, than regular forecasters, and this is another big reason why they are super.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Devyn Duffy, a Pittsburgh caseworker who joined the Good Judgment Project while unemployed, sets Google alerts on each question, daily if events may change fast and weekly otherwise. In the third season he made 2,271 forecasts on 140 questions, more than 16 per question on average.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The tool he uses is the Google alert.

card.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters update much more often than regular forecasters, and Devyn Duffy shows how: alerts on each question and a revision whenever the news bears on it.
card.limits: The authors call Devyn a fantastic updater, but they also warn in the next pages that how often someone updates is not the whole explanation.

concepts.title: Is it only about watching the news?
concepts.question: Do superforecasters win only because they watch the news more closely, and what do the authors say?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: The authors take up the suspicion that superforecasters win mainly by spending more time watching the news and updating. They say that is not the whole story and that it is a huge mistake to belittle belief updating, which is not mindless adjustment to whatever is on CNN.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Superforecasters' initial forecasts were at least 50% more accurate than those of regular forecasters, so they would have won decisively even if the tournament had asked for one forecast and allowed no updating. The suspicion came up when a famous political scientist who runs a lucrative forecasting consultancy was interested in the tournament until he learned it required updating.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The chapter title plays on the word newsjunkies.

card.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters' lead does not come from news-watching alone: their first forecasts were already at least 50% more accurate, and updating well is itself skilled work.
card.limits: The authors concede that careful monitoring gives superforecasters a big advantage over the less attentive. Their point is that it is not the decisive factor.

concepts.title: News everyone can see
concepts.question: Why does updating on headline news not give a forecaster an edge?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a development like a major announcement, and the update it calls for, are clear to everyone. No one can produce superior forecasts by staying on top of what everyone knows.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: On September 10, 2014, President Obama said in a televised address that the United States would take action against ISIL in Syria as well as Iraq. A tournament question asked whether a foreign military would carry out operations in Syria before December 1, 2014. The announcement made a yes all but certain, and superforecasters updated in a flurry.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, updating on news everyone can see is necessary but gives no edge; the difference lies elsewhere.
card.limits: The authors do not say to ignore headline news. Missing it is a mistake, as the next section shows, but catching it does not set a forecaster apart.

concepts.title: Reading the Swiss delay
concepts.question: How did Bill Flack extract a signal from a delay in the Arafat test results?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Bill Flack's move on the Arafat question is a model of smart updating. He spotted subtly diagnostic information and moved his forecast cautiously in the right direction before everyone else.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: After Bill's 60% forecast on polonium in Arafat's remains, the Swiss team said results would be late because of more, unspecified, testing. But polonium can be introduced or can arise from natural lead, so Bill read the delay as a sign the team had found polonium and was ruling out lead. It was one explanation among several, so he raised his forecast to 65%. The Swiss found polonium.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Brier score: the accuracy measure. His was 0.36, which the authors say has meaning only relative to the difficulty of the problem.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The delay could have been irrelevant. The authors stress that Bill moved only a few points because it was one possible explanation.

card.rule: According to the authors, smart updating reads subtly diagnostic information and moves the forecast in proportion to how much the signal supports one explanation.
card.limits: The delay might have meant nothing, and no one could check. Bill's small move reflects that: a signal open to several explanations earns only a small shift.

concepts.title: Bill's miss on Yasukuni
concepts.question: What went wrong when Bill Flack heard that Shinzo Abe would visit the Yasukuni Shrine?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, even the best updaters make mistakes. Bill Flack had a reasonable forecast that Shinzo Abe would not visit the Yasukuni Shrine, but he failed to update when evidence to the contrary arrived.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The shrine honors Japan's war dead, including about a thousand war criminals; visits by Japanese leaders outrage China and Korea, and the United States urges against them. Bill strongly believed Abe would not go. Then someone close to Abe said, unofficially, that he would. Bill thought a visit made so little sense that he discounted the statement. Abe visited on December 26, and Bill's Brier score took a hit.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The authors later class this kind of error as underreaction.

card.rule: According to the authors, a forecaster who dismisses new evidence because it conflicts with a reasonable forecast can underreact, even if the forecast was sound.
card.limits: The initial forecast was reasonable. The failure lay in the update, which should have weighed the tip rather than discounting it because it seemed to make little sense.

concepts.title: Doug Lorch and the Arctic ice
concepts.question: What did Doug Lorch do after finding a convincing report, and how did it turn out?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Bill's miss does not mean any insightful-looking evidence should send you hard over. Doug Lorch moved sharply on a single convincing report and was punished for it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: IARPA asked whether Arctic sea ice extent on September 15, 2014 would be less than a year earlier. Doug Lorch opened at a prudent 55% yes. Two days later a teammate found a Sea Ice Prediction Network report: twenty-eight projections by four methods, all but three predicting less ice. It was a month old. Doug found it pretty convincing and spun the ship's wheel hard to 95% yes.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The authors soon call this kind of error overreaction.

card.rule: According to the authors, one convincing but dated report can tempt even a top forecaster into a sharp move that the evidence does not support.
card.limits: The report was not worthless: the projections favoured yes. The authors' point is the size of Doug's move and the age of a report on a daily-changing reality.

concepts.title: Underreaction and overreaction
concepts.question: After the initial call, what are the two dangers, and how does each damage a forecast?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a forecaster faces two dangers after making the initial call. Either of them can diminish accuracy.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: One danger is not giving enough weight to new information. The other is overreacting: seeing new information as more meaningful than it is and adjusting a forecast too radically. The chapter's two cases line up: Bill Flack discounted a tip about Abe, and Doug Lorch lurched to 95% on a stale report.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Underreaction (too little weight on new information) and overreaction (too much).

card.rule: According to the authors, after the first forecast you can err by giving new information too little weight or too much, and both errors cost accuracy.
card.limits: The names describe errors of weight, not of how often someone updates. Frequent small updates are not overreaction, as the later sections show.

concepts.title: Underreaction from being too busy
concepts.question: Is all underreaction caused by bias, or can it have ordinary causes?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, underreaction can happen for any number of reasons, some of them prosaic, such as simple neglect.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: After US Air Force attacks on Syria on September 22, 2014 closed the foreign-intervention question, Joshua Frankel reviewed his updating. He had seen President Obama announce action against ISIL but never raised his forecast from 82% to the 99% he later said it should have been, because events moved quickly and he was too swamped with work to stay on top of them.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

card.rule: According to the authors, some underreaction is plain neglect, such as being too busy to revise a forecast after decisive news.
card.limits: Prosaic neglect is the easy case. The authors say it is the subtler, psychological causes that are hard to spot.

concepts.title: A bait and switch on himself
concepts.question: What question did Bill Flack actually answer when he dismissed the tip about Abe?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a subtler cause of Bill Flack's underreaction was psychological. By his own account he answered a different question from the one asked, and so he dismissed information that was irrelevant to the question he had substituted.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The question was whether Abe would visit Yasukuni. Bill reasoned from the political costs and the negligible benefit that not going looked rational. Reflecting later, he said he had really been answering what he would do as prime minister, which left out Abe's own feelings.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Bait and switch: substituting an easy question for a hard one, a term from chapter 2 that the authors recall here.

card.rule: According to the authors, replacing the hard question with an easier one can make real evidence look irrelevant, causing underreaction.
card.limits: The substitution is hard to see from inside. It is a psychological bias, so the authors call these errors always a challenge to spot.

concepts.title: Belief perseverance
concepts.question: What is belief perseverance, and what does the 1942 internment show about it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, one psychological source of underreaction is particularly tenacious: belief perseverance, in which people rationalize to avoid acknowledging new information that upsets their settled beliefs.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: After Pearl Harbor, California's attorney general Earl Warren warned that Japanese Americans might be civil defense's Achilles' heel. In 1942, 112,000 people, two-thirds born in the United States, were interned. No sabotage occurred in the ten weeks before, in the rest of 1942 or in 1943, yet hard-liners insisted the danger had not lessened. General DeWitt called the absence of sabotage a disturbing, confirming sign that it would come.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Belief perseverance, the psychologists' term.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors call this an extreme case; such obstinacy is rare.

card.rule: According to the authors, belief perseverance is the pull to rationalize away facts that upset a settled belief, and in extreme cases absent evidence is read as confirmation.
card.limits: Extreme obstinacy is rare. The usual pattern is a grudging budge that falls short of what the evidence calls for.

concepts.title: The Keynes quotation
concepts.question: What happened when one of the authors tried to trace the famous Keynes line about changing your mind?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the line about changing your mind when the facts change is cited in countless books, including one by each of them, yet it may never have been said by Keynes. One of them tried to track it to its source and could not.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: He found a post by a Wall Street Journal blogger saying that no one has ever discovered where the line comes from and that the two leading experts on Keynes think it is apocryphal. He concluded that he had been wrong and confessed it publicly.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The word apocryphal means of doubtful authorship.

card.rule: According to the authors, a well-known line attributed to Keynes could not be traced and may be apocryphal, and one author publicly admitted he was wrong to repeat it.
card.limits: The authors do not say the idea behind the line is wrong. They say only that its attribution to Keynes is doubtful.

concepts.title: Commitment freezes belief
concepts.question: Why does publicly committing to a belief make it harder to change?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, social psychologists have long known that getting people to publicly commit to a belief is a great way to freeze it in place, making it resistant to change. The stronger the commitment, the greater the resistance.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Jean-Pierre Beugoms is a superforecaster who prides himself on changing his opinions faster than his teammates. He is a West Point graduate writing a PhD dissertation on American military history. He admits that changing his mind is a challenge, especially on questions in which he has an investment, which for him means military questions.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Commitment. The authors use the word for any kind of investment in a belief.

card.rule: According to the authors, the more a person is committed to a belief, the harder it is to change, which makes updating hardest on questions one cares about.
card.limits: Commitment is not the only cause of poor updating, and it can come in many forms, not only public statements.

concepts.title: The Jenga tower of beliefs
concepts.question: How does the Jenga image explain why some beliefs are easier to change than others?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, beliefs about ourselves and the world are built on each other like the blocks of a Jenga tower. A belief near the top supports nothing and is easy to remove; one near the core is hard to pull out without upsetting others.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The author's belief in the Keynes line was a block at the apex that supported nothing else, so he could toss it away. When Jean-Pierre Beugoms makes a forecast in his specialty, that block sits lower in the tower, beside a block of self-perception near the core, so he is reluctant to tamper with it.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Jenga is the children's game in which players take turns removing blocks from a stacked tower until someone topples it. The authors use it as a metaphor.

card.rule: According to the authors, the nearer a belief sits to the core of one's self-perception, the more it supports, and the harder it is to remove.
card.limits: It is a metaphor, not a measurement. It illustrates why commitment varies, and the authors give no way to count blocks.

concepts.title: Identity over evidence
concepts.question: What does Dan Kahan's research suggest about how we judge risks?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Dan Kahan's research shows that our judgments about risks, such as whether gun control makes us safer, are driven less by a careful weighing of evidence than by our identities.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Kahan, a Yale professor, finds that people's views on gun control often correlate with their views on climate change. Asked to imagine conclusive evidence that shows they are wrong, and then whether they would change their position if given it, people who feel strongly typically say no.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The authors sum it up as psycho-logic trumping logic.

card.rule: According to the authors, strongly held views on risk often follow identity rather than evidence, so people will not change them even for conclusive proof.
card.limits: The authors report a typical response, not a universal one, and the finding concerns views on contested risks.

concepts.title: Little ego in the game
concepts.question: Why might being non-professionals help superforecasters avoid underreaction?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, superforecasters may have a surprising advantage: they are not experts or professionals, so they have little ego invested in each forecast. That makes it easier to admit a forecast is off track and to adjust, which helps them avoid underreaction.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Except in rare cases, such as Jean-Pierre Beugoms on military questions, they are not deeply committed to their judgments. The authors add that superforecasters do not have zero ego investment.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The advantage comes from low ego investment.

card.rule: According to the authors, low ego investment makes it easier for superforecasters to admit an offtrack forecast and so avoid underreaction.
card.limits: The advantage is relative, not absolute: the authors say superforecasters are not free of ego investment.

concepts.title: The dilution effect
concepts.question: What happens to a judgment when irrelevant information is added?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, irrelevant information sways us. When we judge from evidence that fits a stereotype, adding irrelevant facts weakens the judgment.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In a 1989 study building on work by Richard Nisbett, randomly selected participants read either bare facts or the facts plus irrelevant ones, then estimated a student's grade point average or a patient's proclivity for child abuse. Robert studied about thirty-one hours a week; David's fantasies fit the stereotype. The irrelevant facts were tennis, a short relationship, jokes and a skiing injury. Those who got them lost confidence.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The dilution effect: irrelevant information weakens the fit with a stereotype, so judgments lose confidence.

card.rule: According to the authors, adding irrelevant facts about a person dilutes a stereotype-based judgment, even though those facts should be ignored.
card.limits: The authors note that stereotypes are a source of bias, so diluting them can look beneficial.

concepts.title: Overreaction in the market
concepts.question: What does the stock market show about the cost of overreacting?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, overreaction is a common and costly mistake. Looking at a typical day in the stock market, it seems clear that at least some of the volume and volatility of trading is due to traders overreacting to new information.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Burton Malkiel notes that many investors move between stocks or funds as if they were selecting and discarding cards in a game of gin rummy. He cited a study of 66,000 American households over a five-year period in the 1990s, when the market returned 17.9% a year. The households that traded the most earned only 11.4% a year.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Gin rummy is Malkiel's metaphor for traders who treat holdings as cards to be discarded.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors say the reasons for market volume and volatility are complex and debated. Their claim is that at least some of it is overreaction.

card.rule: According to the authors, frequent trading on new information tends to earn less than old-fashioned buy-and-hold, a sign of costly overreaction.
card.limits: The figures concern one cited study of households, and the authors treat overreaction as one contributor among others.

concepts.title: Between Scylla and Charybdis
concepts.question: How can a forecaster avoid both under- and overreaction?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, superforecasters avoid both errors; they would not be superforecasters if they did not. Good updating is about finding the middle passage between the two.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Traders who buy and sell constantly lack commitment to their stocks and so overreact. Superforecasters also have modest commitment to their forecasts, so the authors would expect overreaction to be the greater risk for them than underreaction.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Scylla and Charybdis: the authors' image for the two opposing dangers, under- and overreaction.

card.rule: According to the authors, good updating means steering a middle course between giving new information too little weight and too much.
card.limits: The image says that a middle course exists, not what it is. The next section shows how Tim Minto finds it.

concepts.title: Tim Minto's routine
concepts.question: How does Tim Minto work, and why might his many forecasts mislead an observer?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Tim Minto won top spot in the third season with a final Brier score of 0.15, and a big reason was his skill at updating. He is a forty-five-year-old Vancouver software engineer.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: He spends five to fifteen minutes on an initial forecast, about an hour when a batch of six or seven questions opens. The next day he comes back, takes another look and forms a second opinion. He also trawls the Internet for contrary evidence, five days a week.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The authors nickname him Captain Minto.

card.rule: According to the authors, Tim Minto's routine is a quick first pass followed by daily revisits, a second opinion and a search for contrary evidence.
card.limits: The authors call his routine common among top forecasters, but they warn it is not a rule for every case.

concepts.title: Many small updates
concepts.question: How do many small updates keep a forecaster between underreaction and overreaction?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, superforecasters not only update more often than other forecasters but in smaller increments. Updating often but bit by bit is the best way to carry the value of both old and new information.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In January 2014 the tournament asked whether the number of registered Syrian refugees reported by the UN refugee agency as of 1 April 2014 would be under 2.6 million. Tim Minto changed his forecast thirty-four times over three months. The trend was mostly in the right direction and his final Brier score was 0.07. The average update was only 3.5%, with no swings of thirty or forty percentage points.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The authors say Tim's style is common among superforecasters.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Some of Tim's new forecasts led him away from the correct answer. The claim is about the trend.

card.rule: According to the authors, many small updates let a forecaster keep the value of both the prior forecast and the new information.
card.limits: The authors say tournament data show the pattern, but not that small steps are always right; the last section shows a case where they are the wrong approach.

media.alt: Line chart of one forecaster’s probability on the vertical axis, 0 to 1, from January to March, with a dashed line at 1. The line starts a little above 0.5 and wobbles between about 0.6 and 0.75 through January and early February. It dips to near 0.55 in mid-to-late February, jumps back to about 0.72, then climbs in many small steps to almost 1 by the end of March.

concepts.title: Thinking in units of doubt
concepts.question: How can a forecaster decide how much a piece of news should move a forecast?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, thinking granularly makes tiny changes, or units of doubt, natural. The forecaster bounds the update and narrows the range with questions about the news until a figure emerges.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Nate Silver, a poll aggregator, gave Republicans a 60% chance of winning the Senate. A new poll shows Republican support in Colorado rising from 45% to 55%. The update must exceed zero, but many other races must tip too, so you might cap it at 10%. Questions narrow the range to 2% to 9%, then 3% to 7%; you settle on 4% and go from 60% to 64%.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Units of doubt, the authors' phrase for these small increments.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The numbers illustrate a way of reasoning, not a formula.

card.rule: According to the authors, bound the size of the update, then narrow the range with questions until a figure emerges, however boring the result.
card.limits: The authors call the result a tad boring. The numbers are illustrative, and different forecasters may settle on slightly different figures.

concepts.title: The billiard table
concepts.question: How can a series of trivial clues narrow in on the truth?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, an old thought experiment shows how small scraps of information add up. Each scrap shifts the probabilities a little, and repeating the process slowly narrows the range, though uncertainty is never eliminated entirely.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: You sit with your back to a billiard table while a friend rolls a ball onto it. You want to locate it. The friend rolls a second ball and tells you whether it stopped left or right of the first. Say it is to the left. Repeat with more balls and each answer narrows the range.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The authors say a version of this thought experiment was dreamt up by Thomas Bayes.

card.rule: According to the authors, many small bits of information, each slightly favouring one answer, can slowly narrow the range of the truth without ever removing uncertainty.
card.limits: The thought experiment shows a direction, not certainty. The authors say you never eliminate uncertainty entirely.

concepts.title: Bayes' theorem in words
concepts.question: What two things should a new belief depend on, according to Bayes' theorem?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, in simple terms Bayes' theorem says your new belief should depend on two things: your prior belief, with all the knowledge that informed it, and the diagnostic value of the new information. The two are multiplied.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Thomas Bayes was a Presbyterian minister educated in logic. The theorem is written as posterior odds equal the likelihood ratio times prior odds. The authors call this head-scratchingly abstract and turn to a concrete case.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Prior: the belief before new information. Posterior odds: the updated belief. Likelihood ratio: the diagnostic value of the new information.

card.rule: According to the authors, a new belief combines the prior belief with the diagnostic value of the new information, rather than replacing one with the other.
card.limits: The authors present the theorem as an abstract formula that most forecasters do not use explicitly; what matters is its insight.

concepts.title: Hagel and the base rate
concepts.question: How did Jay Ulfelder use a base rate and Bayes' theorem on Hagel's confirmation?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the superforecaster Jay Ulfelder shows the theorem in use: start with the base rate as the prior, then adjust it for the diagnostic value of the new information.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Chuck Hagel was nominated for defense secretary in 2013. Only one of 24 earlier nominees had been rejected by the Senate and none had withdrawn, so the prior was 96%. Hagel did badly at his hearing. Ulfelder assumed one in five nominees bound for success does poorly in hearings but 19 of 20 bound for failure do. His forecast fell to 83%. Hagel was confirmed two weeks later.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Base rate: how often something happens among comparable cases. Prior: the estimate made before the new information.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Ulfelder did not have the true figures; he assumed them, so 83% illustrates the method and is not a measurement.

card.rule: According to the authors, an experienced forecaster starts from the base rate and lets bad news pull the figure down by only as much as the news is diagnostic.
card.limits: The hearing performance numbers were assumptions. A different assumption about how diagnostic a poor hearing is would give a different posterior.

concepts.title: A Bayesian who does not use the theorem
concepts.question: Do superforecasters need to use Bayes' theorem to update well?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, forecasters do not have to understand, memorize and use the algebraic formula. What matters far more to superforecasters is Bayes' core insight of gradually getting closer to the truth by constantly updating in proportion to the weight of the evidence.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tim Minto knew Bayes' theorem but did not use it once to make his hundreds of updated forecasts.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Minto is a Bayesian who does not use Bayes' theorem, a paradoxical description the authors say applies to most superforecasters.

card.rule: According to the authors, you can update the Bayesian way by weighing evidence in proportion to its strength, without writing the formula.
card.limits: The authors do not say numbers are useless: they say superforecasters could deploy the theorem when it is worth the trouble.

concepts.title: Not a skeleton key
concepts.question: When is the many-small-updates rule the wrong thing to do?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, lots of small updates is the winning formula for many cases but not a skeleton key that opens all locks. Sometimes it is exactly the wrong thing to do, and there is no magical formula, only broad principles with caveats.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Doug Lorch, at 95% on the Arctic sea ice report, later saw a big and widening gap between its projections and reality. Instead of lowering his forecast gradually, he ditched the report and made a new forecast: first back to his opening 55%, then down to 15%. After that he resumed many small updates. The authors call it the right call.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The authors invoke Orwell's last rule as an analogy.

card.rule: According to the authors, the many-small-updates guideline is a principle with caveats: when the basis of a forecast fails, make a fresh forecast.
card.limits: The authors give no test for when to break the rule beyond judgment, and say that superforecasters know applying principles needs nuance.

concepts.title: Failure that started a forecaster
concepts.question: What made Mary Simpson set out to improve her forecasting?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Mary Simpson set out to improve her forecasting because she missed the financial crisis of 2007-08, and felt that with her background she should have done better.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Simpson held an economics PhD and had managed regulatory and financial affairs for a utility. Like most experts in her field, she grasped the size of the crisis only when Lehman Brothers collapsed in September 2008, and her retirement savings fell sharply. She then volunteered for the Good Judgment Project and became a superforecaster.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for her motive. The authors call the top performers in their tournament superforecasters.

card.rule: According to the authors, a clear miss in a field you know well can be the push to get better at foresight.
card.limits: One story shows one motive, not a law that every miss produces improvement. The chapter ties progress to what a person does after the miss.

concepts.title: Growth versus fixed mindset
concepts.question: What is the difference between a growth mindset and a fixed mindset, and why does it matter for forecasters?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a top-flight forecaster needs a growth mindset: the belief that abilities are largely the product of effort, so you can grow by working hard and learning.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors cite the psychologist Carol Dweck's research. Many people hold the opposite view, which she calls a fixed mindset: the belief that we are who we are and that abilities can only be revealed, not created or developed. Such people say things like I am bad at math, as if it were an unchangeable trait.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Growth mindset and fixed mindset, both terms from Carol Dweck.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, Mary Simpson shows a growth mindset, and the authors call it essential to being a top-flight forecaster.

card.rule: A growth mindset treats ability as something effort and learning can build; a fixed mindset treats it as something to be revealed.
card.limits: Dweck's definition says abilities are largely the product of effort, not wholly. The authors do not claim effort erases every difference between people.

concepts.title: How a fixed belief fulfils itself
concepts.question: Why does the belief I am bad at math tend to come true?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the belief that you are bad at math, held as a fixed fact, becomes self-fulfilling.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors reason in steps. A person who thinks he is bad at math and always will be sees no point in trying hard. If he is forced to study, he reads any setback as more proof that his limits are revealed and wants to stop wasting time. Whatever potential he had is never realized.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Self-fulfilling is the authors' word for the belief; the underlying idea is the fixed mindset.

card.rule: A fixed belief about ability cuts off the effort that would have changed the ability, so the belief proves itself.
card.limits: This is the authors' reasoning about what the fixed belief leads to. They do not say that every person with the belief ends up failing.

concepts.title: Dweck's puzzle experiment
concepts.question: What separated the children who loved harder puzzles from those who lost interest?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, mindset, not puzzle-solving talent, separated children who relished a tougher challenge from those who gave up.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Dweck gave fifth graders fairly easy puzzles, which they enjoyed, and then harder ones. Some children lost interest and turned down an offer to take puzzles home. Others liked the harder puzzles even more. Even among equally adept children, some were turned off and others intrigued.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the experiment. The authors describe the two groups as fixed-mindset and growth-mindset children.

card.rule: Facing difficulty, fixed-mindset children gave up and growth-mindset children knuckled down, whatever their talent.
card.limits: The authors report this as one of many experiments by Dweck. It involved fifth graders and puzzles; the chapter does not say it applies identically to adults.

concepts.title: Brain scans and feedback
concepts.question: Which information held the attention of fixed-mindset volunteers, and which held growth-mindset volunteers?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, fixed-mindset people care whether they were right or wrong, but not about information that would help them improve; only growth-mindset people attend to that.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In one of Dweck's experiments, volunteers answered hard questions while their brains were scanned. They were told whether each answer was right or wrong and given information that could help them improve. Fixed-mindset volunteers were fully engaged by the verdict but not by the improving information.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the experiment.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: The authors quote Dweck for the conclusion that only growth-mindset people paid close attention to information that could stretch their knowledge.

card.rule: Fixed-mindset people attend to the verdict; growth-mindset people also attend to what would help them improve.
card.limits: The chapter reports one experiment. It does not say the fixed-mindset volunteers could not learn, only that they paid little attention to the helping information.

concepts.title: Keynes, consistently inconsistent
concepts.question: Why does the chapter call John Maynard Keynes consistently inconsistent?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Keynes was a very successful investor who changed his mind readily and took pride in admitting mistakes. His one constant belief was that he could do better.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: From World War I to World War II he managed his own money and that of family, friends, two insurance companies, funds and King's College, Cambridge. His returns were astounding in the stagnant 1920s and the Depression 1930s. A 1945 profile said he contradicted colleagues and himself whenever circumstances warranted, and called him consistently inconsistent.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Consistently inconsistent, from the 1945 profile the authors quote.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors say his record was far from unblemished, so the point is how he handled mistakes, not that he never made them.

card.rule: Keynes's willingness to reverse himself was a strength, held together by one steady belief: he could do better.
card.limits: The Churchill cable is described as legend. The authors offer Keynes as a model of mindset, not as proof that changing your mind always pays.

concepts.title: Keynes turns failure into method
concepts.question: How did Keynes respond to his big investing failures?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Keynes treated failure as an opportunity to learn: he identified mistakes, looked for new alternatives, and tried again, and he came back stronger each time.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In 1920 his foreign currency forecasts were horribly wrong and he was nearly wiped out. He recovered and made a fortune in the 1920s. He did not foresee 1929 and lost heavily, then examined his thinking and decided one theoretical assumption was wrong: stock prices do not always reflect a company's true value. So an investor should study a company's business, capital and management. He then did better than before.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Value investing, the name Benjamin Graham gave to a similar approach developed in the United States around that time.

card.rule: After a failure, look for the faulty assumption, adopt a better approach and try again.
card.limits: The authors tell this as one man's story. It shows a way to respond to failure, not a guarantee that scrutiny will find the right fix.

concepts.title: Try, fail, analyze, adjust, try again
concepts.question: What cycle do the authors say underlies how all of us learn?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, try, fail, analyze, adjust, try again is fundamental to how everyone learns, and skills are learned and improved by doing.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A baby learning to sit up tilts her head back and flops onto a pillow; the mother lets it happen because the flop teaches her not to tilt so far. Adults do the same: a middle-aged accountant new to golf will fail often. Even modern fighter pilots need hours in the air; classroom instruction and flight simulators are not enough.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given; the authors list the steps and Keynes, they say, cycled through them ceaselessly.

card.rule: We learn a skill by doing it, failing, working out why, adjusting, and trying again.
card.limits: The authors say the cycle is not enough alone: later in the chapter they add that practice must be informed and come with clear feedback.

concepts.title: Tacit knowledge and the bicycle
concepts.question: Why can't a perfect written description of riding a bicycle teach you to ride?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, some knowledge can't be fully captured in words and passed on. This tacit knowledge comes only from bruising experience.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The philosopher Michael Polanyi wrote a precise account of the physics of cycling: turn the handlebars toward the direction you are falling, and the curve's tightness depends on your speed. He then asked whether this tells you how to ride, and said no: you cannot compute it while riding, and the rule leaves out other factors.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Tacit knowledge.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, to learn to ride you must try to ride, and even a rider who knows how cannot explain it better than Polanyi did.

card.rule: Knowledge gained by doing cannot be fully handed over in words, so you must try the thing to learn it.
card.limits: Polanyi's example makes the point for riding. The authors carry it to forecasting, where books still help but cannot replace trying.

concepts.title: Practice needs to be informed
concepts.question: Why do the authors say practice is not enough on its own, and what should be added?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, not all practice improves skill: it needs to be informed. Books help, so they say, don't burn your books.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Randomized controlled experiments found that mastering one tiny booklet, the authors' training guidelines, can improve accuracy by roughly 10%. The experiments also showed that people who read the booklet gained more from practice, and people who practiced gained more from the booklet.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the interaction; the authors use the saying Fortune favors the prepared mind.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, learn which mistakes to look out for and which best practices really are best, then practise.

card.rule: Combine knowledge of best practices with practice, because each makes the other work better.
card.limits: The roughly 10% gain is the authors' report from their experiments on one booklet. It does not mean books alone make a superforecaster.

concepts.title: Experience needs clear, timely feedback
concepts.question: Why don't police officers get better at spotting lies with experience?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, effective practice also needs clear and timely feedback. Experience alone is not enough, and without feedback people grow more confident without growing more accurate.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors' collaborator Don Moore points out that police officers spend much time judging who is lying, yet research finds they are not nearly as good as they think and do not improve with experience. An officer rarely learns quickly whether a judgment was right: any trial or plea bargain takes months or years. In controlled tests, the gap between confidence and skill grows as officers gain experience.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Overconfidence, the authors' word for confidence growing faster than accuracy.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Don Moore, whom the authors call a research collaborator.

card.rule: Practice improves judgment only when feedback is clear and arrives soon enough to connect to the judgment.
card.limits: The authors say officers assume, not unreasonably, that experience has made them better. The point is that experience without feedback misleads, not that officers are careless.

concepts.title: Calibration and clear feedback
concepts.question: Which groups avoid overconfidence, and what do they have that officers lack?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, overconfidence is not an immutable law of human nature. People who receive clear, prompt feedback, such as meteorologists and seasoned bridge players, are not overconfident.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Research on calibration, how closely your confidence matches your accuracy, routinely finds people too confident. Meteorologists generally do not suffer from it, nor do seasoned bridge players. A meteorologist who calls for torrential rain and wakes to sunshine knows he was off. Bridge players estimate the tricks they will win and see the result at the end of each hand.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Calibration: how closely your confidence matches your accuracy.

card.rule: Good calibration follows clear, prompt feedback; when forecasts are scored soon, confidence stays honest.
card.limits: The chapter says people are routinely too confident, so calibration is the exception that feedback makes possible. It does not say every meteorologist is perfect.

concepts.title: Vague language blocks feedback
concepts.question: Why do words like could and might make forecasts impossible to learn from?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, ambiguous language is a big reason most forecasters lack the clear feedback that helps meteorologists and bridge players.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Chapter 3 showed that vague terms like probably and likely make it impossible to judge forecasts. When a forecaster says something could, might or may happen, she could be saying almost anything. Terms like Steve Ballmer's reference to significant market share sound precise but prove as fuzzy as fog. Often the judge is the forecaster herself, which makes it worse.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the problem; the authors speak of ambiguous language.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, put forecasts in terms that can be checked.

card.rule: A forecast you cannot score gives you nothing to learn from, so state it clearly.
card.limits: The authors list ambiguity as one of two main barriers to feedback. Precise wording solves only this one: time lag remains.

concepts.title: The Forer effect
concepts.question: Why did students rate a profile written for everyone as a good fit for them?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, vague language is elastic: people stretch it to fit their self-image even when they think they are judging objectively.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Bertram Forer had students complete a personality test, then gave each an individual-looking profile and asked how well the test captured their personality. They gave it an average of 4.2 out of 5. He had built the profile from vague statements in an astrology book and given the same profile to everyone.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The Forer effect.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, forecasters who judge their own vague forecasts should not kid themselves.

card.rule: Elastic wording lets any reader see a good fit, so vague forecasts cannot be fairly judged by the one who made them.
card.limits: The authors use the effect to show why vague forecasts mislead. They do not say people are gullible in general.

concepts.title: Hindsight bias
concepts.question: What does knowing the outcome do to your memory of what you once expected?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a long wait for results lets flaws of memory creep in. Once we know an outcome, that knowledge skews our perception of what we thought before.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Baruch Fischhoff first documented the effect. People estimated the likelihood of major world events at the time, such as whether Nixon would personally meet with Mao, then later recalled their estimate after the event did or did not happen. Knowing the outcome consistently slanted the estimate, even when people tried to prevent it.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Hindsight bias, sometimes known as the I knew it all along effect.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Baruch Fischhoff, who first documented the effect.

card.rule: Knowing how things turned out changes your memory of your earlier estimate, usually toward the result.
card.limits: The effect can be subtle or large. The authors present it as a barrier to learning from long-range forecasts, not as a defect that effort alone removes.

concepts.title: The Soviet forecast recalled
concepts.question: How large was the hindsight effect in Tetlock's study of experts on the Soviet Union?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, hindsight bias can be quite big, even among experts: after the Soviet collapse they remembered their earlier forecasts as far more confident than they were.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In 1988 Tetlock asked experts how likely it was that the Communist Party would lose its monopoly on power in the Soviet Union within five years. After the Soviet Union disintegrated in 1991, he returned in 1992-93 and asked them to recall their estimates. On average they recalled a number 31 percentage points higher than the figure they gave. An expert who thought 10% might remember 40% or 50%.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Hindsight bias.

card.rule: Even experts misremember their earlier estimates once the outcome is known, and the error can be large.
card.limits: The 31-point gap is an average from this one study of experts on one question. It shows the size of the effect that Tetlock found, not a fixed amount.

concepts.title: Turning the lights on
concepts.question: What does the free-throw-in-the-dark picture say about learning from forecasts?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, forecasters who use ambiguous language and trust flawed memory are like free-throw shooters in the dark: they do not get clear feedback, so they cannot learn from experience.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the dark, a shooter hears only a clang, a thunk or a swish, and a novice cannot tell what each means. The shooter may grow more confident without improving. Tim Minto's forecast on Syrian refugee flows in 2014 scored 0.07 on the Brier score, an excellent result, while his forecast on whether Shinzo Abe would visit the Yakusuni Shrine scored 1.46, a miss. Clear wording left no room to hide.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Brier score, the measure used to score forecasts in the tournament.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, state forecasts clearly and score them so you know when you missed.

card.rule: Clear, scoreable forecasts turn the lights on, so you can see your hits and misses and learn from them.
card.limits: A score tells you that you missed, not why. Analysis after the score is a further step.

concepts.title: No shortcuts to calibration
concepts.question: Why won't playing bridge make you a better political or business forecaster?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, there are no shortcuts: judgment calibrated in one context transfers poorly, if at all, to another.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Bridge players may be well calibrated when bidding on tricks, but research shows calibration in one context does not carry over. So if you wanted to become a better political or business forecaster by playing bridge, forget it.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors, to get better at a type of forecasting, do that type over and over, with good feedback, and a cheerful willingness to say you got one wrong.

card.rule: Practise the specific kind of forecasting you want to improve, with feedback on that kind.
card.limits: The authors say transfers poorly, if at all; they do not say it never happens. Their advice is to practise the target skill directly.

concepts.title: Postmortems and checked assumptions
concepts.question: How do superforecasters learn from a closed question?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, whenever a question closes, superforecasters are as keen to know how they can do better as how they did, and they hold careful, self-critical postmortems.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Devyn Duffy's team took a drubbing on whether Arafat's remains would test positive for polonium. He posted that the team had assumed polonium's half-life made detection nearly impossible and had not questioned it, for example by asking an expert or considering decay products. Jean-Pierre Beugoms found his old comments so sparse that he could not tell why he had made a forecast, so he began leaving longer comments.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Postmortem, the authors' word for the review after a question closes.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: According to the authors: be careful about assuming expertise, ask experts if you can, and reexamine your assumptions from time to time.

card.rule: Review each closed question for what went wrong or right in your thinking, and leave notes that make that review possible.
card.limits: The postmortem is only as good as the record you kept. And a postmortem on a result still has to ask whether luck, not skill, explains it.

concepts.title: Good outcome, bad decision
concepts.question: Why can a good outcome hide a flawed decision?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a good outcome does not prove the decision was good, and thinking so can be dangerous if it blinds us to flaws in our thinking.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Devyn Duffy's team aced a question about elections in Guinea. In his postmortem he said they were more inclined to believe that protests wouldn't prevent the elections, but the protests nearly did, so we lucked out, too. The authors call this deeply perceptive.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given; Duffy's words are that the team lucked out.

card.rule: Judge a decision by the reasoning behind it as well as by how it turned out.
card.limits: The authors do not say good outcomes always come from luck. They say a good result alone does not show the thinking was sound.

concepts.title: Almost right, never almost wrong
concepts.question: Which what-if stories do experts welcome after a forecast, and which do they reject?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, experts are open to I was almost right stories after a failed forecast but reject I was almost wrong stories after a correct one.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In his late-1980s research on expert political judgment, Tetlock had experts forecast three political outcomes. He then offered what-if scenarios. Those implying a failed forecast would have been right were welcomed like old friends; those implying a correct forecast could easily have been wrong were dismissed as speculative.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the pattern; the authors speak of I was almost right and I was almost wrong scenarios.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors report the experts' tendency, not a law for every forecaster. Duffy shows that admitting luck is possible.

card.rule: Watch for the urge to accept what-ifs that excuse your misses and to reject those that threaten your hits.
card.limits: This is a tendency Tetlock found in experts on three questions. It does not mean every counterfactual should be accepted; the lesson is to judge them evenly.

concepts.title: Where the bicycle analogy breaks
concepts.question: Where does the forecasting-as-bicycling analogy stop fitting?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the analogy between forecasting and bicycling is pretty good but imperfect: the feedback loop is slower and chance plays a bigger role. Our reading: that makes forecasting harder to improve at.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: On a bicycle, the cycle of try, fail, analyze, adjust, try again typically takes seconds. In forecasting it can take months or years. Chance also plays a bigger role: cyclists following best practices can usually expect excellent outcomes, but forecasters should be more tentative.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Following best practices still improves the odds, just less reliably than in games where chance plays a smaller role.

card.rule: In forecasting the learning loop is slower and chance is larger, so progress takes patience.
card.limits: The authors call the analogy pretty good. The gaps are the length of the loop and the role of chance, not a reason to drop practice.

concepts.title: Grit in practice
concepts.question: What is grit, and how do Sloane and Kilkenny show it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, grit is passionate perseverance of long-term goals, even in the face of frustration and failure. Married with a growth mindset, it is a potent force for personal progress.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Elizabeth Sloane endured chemotherapy, a failed stem-cell transplant, recurrence and two more years of chemo, and volunteered for the Good Judgment Project to re-grow her synapses. Anne Kilkenny, a housewife in an Alaskan town, forecast all 150 questions in year 3 with an inert team, kept going when high-confidence forecasts ended badly, and chased data sources for answers.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Grit, a term of the authors' colleague Angela Duckworth.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Kilkenny is not a superforecaster, at least not yet.

card.rule: Grit is staying with a long goal through failures, and it drives improvement together with a growth mindset.
