card.limits: The authors call Kilkenny impressive but not yet a superforecaster. Grit supports progress; it does not by itself guarantee top results.

concepts.title: Perpetual beta
concepts.question: What does perpetual beta mean, and how well does it predict who becomes a superforecaster?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the strongest predictor of rising into the ranks of superforecasters is perpetual beta: the degree of commitment to belief updating and self-improvement.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Programmers use the term for a program meant to be used, analyzed and improved without end rather than released in final form. The authors say perpetual beta is roughly three times as powerful a predictor as its closest rival, intelligence. Paraphrasing Thomas Edison, they say superforecasting is roughly 75% perspiration and 25% inspiration.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Perpetual beta, borrowed from computer programmers.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Becoming a superforecaster is only the end of the beginning, and not every superforecaster has every attribute.

card.rule: Commitment to updating beliefs and improving yourself predicts success in forecasting better than raw intelligence does.
card.limits: The authors paint with a broad brush. Many paths lead to success, and strengths can offset weaknesses.

concepts.title: The modal superforecaster
concepts.question: What traits make up the authors' composite portrait of a superforecaster?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a rough composite portrait of the modal superforecaster can be drawn from what they have learned about their lives, scores and habits.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Outlook: cautious (nothing is certain), humble (reality is infinitely complex), nondeterministic (what happens does not have to happen). Thinking: actively open-minded, intelligent and knowledgeable with a need for cognition, reflective, numerate. Methods: pragmatic, analytical, dragonfly-eyed, probabilistic, thoughtful updaters, good intuitive psychologists. Work ethic: growth mindset and grit.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Modal superforecaster, the typical case the sketch describes.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors paint with a broad brush: not every attribute is equally important and not every superforecaster has every one.

card.rule: The portrait groups fifteen traits into outlook, thinking style, method and work ethic, with perpetual beta weighing most.
card.limits: It is a sketch of the modal case. The authors note it leaves out other people, since we seldom judge the future in isolation.

concepts.section: To Team or Not to Team?
concepts.title: The Bay of Pigs: a plan nobody tested
concepts.question: Did the Bay of Pigs fail in the execution or in the plan, and what shows it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the Bay of Pigs invasion of 1961 failed because of the plan, not its execution. Historians on the left and the right agree that it had problems the White House should have spotted, so calling it a hindsight judgment does not fit.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The New York Times exposed the secret CIA training of Cuban exiles, yet planning went ahead. About 1,400 men landed and were surrounded by 20,000 soldiers. The fallback was a retreat to the Escambray Mountains, but that idea came from an earlier landing site; the site was switched and the fallback never rechecked.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the failure; it is called the Bay of Pigs invasion.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr., an adviser to President Kennedy and part of the inner circle that approved the mission, recalled the blunders with amazement.

card.rule: According to the authors, the Bay of Pigs failed because of a flawed plan whose faults were visible beforehand, not because it was carried out badly.
card.limits: Our reading: The authors use this one case to open a question about groups. It does not show that every secret operation fails.

concepts.section: To Team or Not to Team?
concepts.title: One team, two outcomes
concepts.question: How could mostly the same advisers botch the Bay of Pigs and then handle the missile crisis well?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the team that bungled the Bay of Pigs was largely the team that performed brilliantly in the Cuban missile crisis. So who sits in a group does not settle how well it thinks.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Over thirteen days in October 1962, Kennedy's team weighed a range of dangerous options, including invasion, before choosing a naval blockade. Each side read the other through actions and back-channel messages. War was averted. Kennedy had not cleaned house after the Bay of Pigs; the cast was mostly the same.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The authors say the group is its own animal.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: James Surowiecki's 2004 bestseller on the wisdom of crowds plays on an 1841 classic about collective folly. The authors conclude that groups can be wise, mad, or both.

card.rule: According to the authors, a group's quality depends on how it works as a group, not only on who is in it.
card.limits: Our reading: One pair of cases cannot show how much of the difference comes from process alone. The authors present it as an illustration, not a measurement.

concepts.section: To Team or Not to Team?
concepts.title: Groupthink as Janis meant it
concepts.question: What did Janis mean by groupthink, and how does it let a bad plan go ahead?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, groups that get along too well do not question assumptions or confront uncomfortable facts. Everyone agrees, which is pleasant, and the agreement itself is taken as proof that the group is on the right track.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Irving Janis argued in 1972 that members of a small cohesive group keep up team spirit by unconsciously building shared illusions and norms that get in the way of critical thinking and reality testing. He applied this to the planning of the Bay of Pigs invasion.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Groupthink, a term coined by Janis in his book Victims of Groupthink. The authors say he meant something more precise than the vague catchphrase it has become.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Janis was one of Tetlock's PhD advisers at Yale.

card.rule: According to the authors, groupthink is cohesion that replaces questioning with shared illusions, so that agreement is mistaken for proof.
card.limits: Our reading: The term describes a specific mechanism, not every case of agreement; a group can agree because the plan is sound.

concepts.section: To Team or Not to Team?
concepts.title: Kennedy's fixes after the fiasco
concepts.question: What changes did Kennedy make to how his advisers debated before the missile crisis?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, after the Bay of Pigs inquiry named cozy unanimity as the key problem, Kennedy rebuilt the decision process around skepticism and open give-and-take.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Participants spoke not only as specialists but as generalists licensed to question anything. Theodore Sorensen and Robert Kennedy were named intellectual watchdogs, and Robert often played devil's advocate. Protocol and hierarchy were set aside, new advisers were sometimes brought in, and the president sometimes left the room.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Intellectual watchdogs: the role given to Sorensen and Robert Kennedy to press every bone of contention.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors stress it was never easy. There were constant disagreements, and the stress was brutal.

card.rule: According to the authors, Kennedy's team improved its decisions by licensing questions, assigning watchdogs, setting rank aside and sometimes leaving the room.
card.limits: These steps fit a small group facing one hard decision. The authors say the process was stressful and do not claim it guarantees success.

concepts.section: To Team or Not to Team?
concepts.title: The case against teams
concepts.question: What two tendencies made the authors worry that teams might drag forecasters down?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: Tetlock and Gardner say the research literature, and Tetlock's decades of experience on university committees, suggested that teams might make forecasters worse. Two tendencies could feed each other.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The first is cognitive loafing: why labor over a hard problem when others will do the heavy lifting? Widespread, this can sink a team. The second is groupthink: forecasters grow too friendly and everyone agrees, so ill-founded agreement leads the group into self-righteous complacency.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Cognitive loafing, a term for easing off because others will do the work.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: The research literature on teams, and Tetlock's experience on university committees.

card.rule: According to the authors, cognitive loafing and groupthink are the two risks of teams, and each can make the other worse.
card.limits: These are risks, not certainties; the authors note the case for teams was equally strong and chose to test the question.

concepts.section: To Team or Not to Team?
concepts.title: Why aggregation needs independence
concepts.question: Why can averaging many judgments fail once people discuss in a group?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, aggregation can only do its magic when people form judgments independently. Independence keeps errors more or less random, so they cancel. Group discussion can destroy independence, and then mistakes pile up instead of cancelling.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The model is the fairgoers guessing the weight of the ox: separate guesses, random errors, a good average. In a discussion, one member may dominate and the rest abandon their own judgment, so the same error is repeated across the group.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the loss of independence. The authors call its result collective folly.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Loss of independence is not inevitable. Forecasters who keep questioning themselves and welcome vigorous debate can make the group more than the sum of its parts, as Kennedy's team did.

card.rule: According to the authors, averaging cancels errors only when judgments are independent, and group discussion can make errors pile up instead.
card.limits: Independence is a risk to protect, not a certainty lost the moment people talk; good debate habits can keep a group more than the sum of its parts.

concepts.section: To Team or Not to Team?
concepts.title: The year-1 experiment
concepts.question: How did the authors test whether teams help forecasters, and why did they run the test?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, strong arguments existed on both sides and they could only guess, so they ran an experiment on teams. Groups let people share information and perspectives, which helps aggregation, but they can also erode independence.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In year 1, 2011 to 2012, several hundred forecasters were randomly assigned to work alone and several hundred others to work in teams. Teams used online forums, e-mail, Skype or whatever else they liked. Accuracy was the goal, and teams could organise as they wished.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the design; the authors followed Archie Cochrane's advice to run an experiment.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: The Good Judgment research in the IARPA tournament, as described by the authors.

card.rule: According to the authors, when arguments for and against teams were both strong, they randomly assigned forecasters to work alone or in teams and compared results.
card.limits: Our reading: The teams did not meet face to face, and the test was of forecasters in an online tournament, so it cannot say how office teams would fare.

concepts.section: To Team or Not to Team?
concepts.title: The teamwork primer
concepts.question: What advice did the authors give teams to avoid both groupthink and rancor?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the primer warned of two dangers: groupthink, and its opposite, rancor and dysfunction. Teams should disagree without being disagreeable.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Against groupthink: be cooperative but not deferential, and if you happen to agree, do not take that agreement as proof you are right. Never stop doubting. Against rancor: team members should disagree without being disagreeable.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: “constructive confrontation”, a phrase from Andy Grove, the former CEO of Intel.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: The primer drew on research in group dynamics and was given to the year-1 teams.

card.rule: According to the authors, a team should cooperate without deferring and disagree without being disagreeable, and should not treat agreement as proof.
card.limits: Our reading: A primer states intentions; the authors show it needs practices such as precision questioning to work.

concepts.section: To Team or Not to Team?
concepts.title: Precision questioning
concepts.question: How can you challenge a vague claim without insulting the speaker or being vague yourself?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, tactful challenge works best as precise questions that dissect a vague claim. They do not settle the matter, but they reveal the thinking behind a conclusion so that it can be probed and tested.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Suppose someone says the world's favorite pastime, soccer, is declining. A personal shot adds heat, not light. Saying you do not think so voices disagreement without why. Asking what the person means is too vague. Zeroing in works: ask what is meant by a word, what evidence shows the decline, over what time frame.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Precision questioning, drawn from the work of Dennis Matthies and Monica Worline.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: Pick the loose word or number in the claim and ask about it directly.

card.rule: According to the authors, challenge a vague claim with specific questions about its terms, evidence and time frame, not with a personal shot or a vague query.
card.limits: Precise questions will not settle the matter by themselves; they open the thinking behind the claim to testing.

concepts.title: Year 2: the risk of hubris
concepts.question: Why did the authors fear that putting superforecasters together might backfire?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, year-1 teams were on average 23% more accurate than individuals, so teams stayed in the design. But grouping freshly identified superforecasters risked swelling their egos.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tell someone they are exceptionally good and surround them with similar people, and he may think his judgment must be right because it is his. The paradox: success can bring acclaim that undermines the habits of mind that produced it. The year-2 teams were a dozen people each, with extra guidance and special online forums.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: “CEO disease”, the business name for hubris in highly accomplished people.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors say they rolled the theoretical dice: the risk was real, and the result was not known in advance.

card.rule: According to the authors, success can breed acclaim that undermines the habits behind it, which is why grouping top performers was a risk.
card.limits: Our reading: The risk was a possibility the authors weighed, not an outcome they found.

concepts.title: Intimidation and dancing around
concepts.question: Why did superforecasters hold back in new teams, and what eased it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, new superteam members found it hard to question strangers, and excessive politeness hindered the critical examination of views. It eased when people made clear that criticism was welcome.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Elaine Rich, a pharmacist, was intimidated by teammates' impressive credentials and at first made forecasts but rarely gave opinions. Questions on sensitive subjects felt like walking through a minefield, and one on Arafat and polonium was almost taboo. Marty Rosenthal called the careful circling of a disagreement dancing around.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: “dancing around”, Rosenthal's phrase for couching disagreement in careful words.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: Say that push-back is welcome, and thank people for constructive criticism. Gradually, the dancing around diminished.

card.rule: According to the authors, a team where politeness blocks challenge improves when members say push-back is welcome and thank those who give it.
card.limits: Our reading: Experience helped here, and the account comes from a few superforecasters rather than a measured study.

concepts.title: Usual fixes and the premortem
concepts.question: What are the usual fixes for team problems, and what is a premortem?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, research on teams usually assumes there are leaders and norms, and aims to stop these from hindering performance. The usual remedies are the ones Kennedy's team used after the Bay of Pigs.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Those remedies are to bring in outsiders, suspend hierarchy, and keep the leader's views under wraps. A further remedy is the premortem: the team is told to assume that a course of action has failed and to explain why.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: “premortem”, the authors' term for the assume-it-failed exercise.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: Our reading: a postmortem looks back at a failure that has happened, while a premortem asks for the explanation before the plan is carried out.

card.rule: According to the authors, standard team fixes are outsiders, suspended hierarchy, a leader who withholds a view, and the premortem.
card.limits: These fixes assume a leader and norms already exist, which the superteams did not have at the start.

concepts.title: Leading from behind
concepts.question: How can someone shape a leaderless team without seeming to take over?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, in a team of strangers with no structure, stepping forward to give directions can backfire. Marty Rosenthal shaped his team by example instead.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Rosenthal, a semiretired management consultant who specialized in building teams, saw gaps in how his team was forming but did not want to seem to take over. When people were not explaining their forecasts enough to get good discussions going, he explained his in greater detail and invited comments.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: “leading from behind”, Rosenthal's phrase for leading by example.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Rosenthal's own account to the authors.

card.rule: According to the authors, in a leaderless team a member can lead from behind by modelling the behaviour he wants and inviting others in.
card.limits: Our reading: It is one member's account in one setting; the authors present it as an example, not a formula that works for everyone.

concepts.title: Meeting in person and belonging
concepts.question: How did occasional in-person meetings and a growing sense of belonging change superteam behaviour?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a small human dimension helped teams push back on one another and share information, and a sense of belonging deepened members' sense of responsibility.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: At the end of the second and third years the project manager hosted conferences at the Wharton School and the University of California, Berkeley. The official goal was to share knowledge; the unofficial goal was to add a human dimension. Rosenthal invited teammates to his house for a barbecue and beer, and he thinks this helped push-back and commitment.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the effect; Rosenthal describes it as commitment to step up and share information.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The effort was modest, and the judgment is Rosenthal's own impression rather than a measured result.

card.rule: According to the authors, even modest personal contact can strengthen a remote team's willingness to challenge each other and share.
card.limits: Our reading: Rosenthal says it made a difference, but it is his view; most contact was online, and the authors give no measure of the effect.

concepts.title: Commitment raises effort
concepts.question: Did dividing the work reduce how much effort each superteam member put in?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, on the best teams the work was divided but effort did not fall. As commitment grew, the amount of effort members gave grew too.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Most teams have a nucleus of five or six members who do most of the work. A division of labor might be expected to lower each person's effort, but the best teams showed the opposite. Elaine Rich said being on the team was tons more work, yet she found it more stimulating than working alone.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The expected drop in effort applies at least where forecasting is approached as work rather than play.

card.rule: According to the authors, on the best teams commitment made members work harder even though the work was shared.
card.limits: The authors tie the expected fall in effort to those who see forecasting as work, not play, so the pattern may depend on attitude.

concepts.title: Digging as a team: Honduras
concepts.question: How did one superforecaster's research on Honduras benefit his whole team?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, committed superteams did impressive digging, and because findings were shared, one member's effort lifted the whole team.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: On who would win Honduras's 2013 presidential election, Paul Theron, a South African investment manager, found a political scientist who specialises in Honduran politics. The expert said that although polls gave a candidate named Castro a slight lead, the polls were dodgy. Theron also found a thorough analysis on an obscure website, e-mailed the author and learned more, then moved his forecast to favour Castro's opponent Hernández.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Paul Theron, a superforecaster interviewed by the authors.

card.rule: According to the authors, on a good team one member's deep research, once shared, benefits everyone.
card.limits: Our reading: It is one example from the authors' conversations, and it shows the pattern at work, not how often it happens.

concepts.title: Superteams: 50% more accurate
concepts.question: How much more accurate did superforecasters become on superteams, and why was it a surprise?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a forecaster who qualified as a superforecaster in year 1 and joined a superteam in year 2 became on average 50% more accurate.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: This is a separate figure from the 23% by which year-1 teams beat individuals. The authors call the gain startling for collections of strangers tenuously connected in cyberspace.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Superteams, the authors' name for teams of superforecasters.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: the figure is an average across forecasters, not a promise for every member.

card.rule: According to the authors, putting year-1 superforecasters on superteams in year 2 made them on average 50% more accurate.
card.limits: Our reading: It is an average over a group of forecasters in one tournament, and the authors still call the work on superteams young.

concepts.title: How prediction markets aggregate
concepts.question: How does a prediction market turn many traders' views into a probability?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, most economists see markets as the best way to collect dispersed information, and a prediction market's price should in theory closely track the true probability of an outcome.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In a prediction market traders buy and sell contracts on a specified outcome. A contract pays $1 if the outcome occurs and nothing if not. If it sells at 40 cents and you think the chance is 60% or 70%, you buy; enough buying pushes the price up until traders think it about right. New bad news prompts a rush to sell.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Prediction market, such as the Iowa Electronic Markets. Efficient market hypothesis (EMH): the strong version holds that markets are such efficient aggregators that no one should aspire to beat them.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors say the strong EMH is hard to square with psychology and experience, though consistently beating markets is still very hard.

card.rule: According to the authors, in a prediction market the contract price tracks the probability because traders buy when the price is too low and sell when it is too high.
card.limits: Trades sometimes happen for other reasons, such as different financial needs, so price is not a perfect read of probability.

concepts.title: Superteams versus prediction markets
concepts.question: How did superteams, ordinary teams, prediction markets and the crowd rank against one another?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, most economists expected prediction markets to mop the floor with superteams. Instead superteams beat the markets, though the markets forecast complex global events pretty well.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Regular forecasters were randomly placed alone, in teams, or as traders in markets run by companies such as Inkling and Lumenogic. The solo forecasts were combined as an unweighted average, called the wisdom of the crowd. Each year, ordinary teams beat that average by about 10%, markets beat ordinary teams by about 20%, and superteams beat markets by 15% to 30%.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Wisdom of the crowd: here, the unweighted average of all forecasts made by people working alone.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Finance colleagues may object that the markets were thin; the authors call that a testable idea and say it may be right.

card.rule: According to the authors, from lowest to highest accuracy: the crowd average, ordinary teams, prediction markets, then superteams.
card.limits: The markets used no real money and lacked a critical mass of traders, so the ranking may not carry over to deep real-world markets.

concepts.title: Psychological safety and shared purpose
concepts.question: What features let superteams avoid both groupthink and internet flame wars?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, superteams did so well by avoiding the extremes of groupthink and flame wars, and by building minicultures in which people challenge each other respectfully, admit ignorance and ask for help.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Harvard's Amy Edmondson found that the best surgical teams were ones in which a nurse tells the surgeon without hesitation that a sponge was left behind the pancreas, because it is psychologically safe to correct higher-ups. Her best teams also had a shared purpose, and so did the superteams.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Psychologically safe: the phrase the authors take from Edmondson's work for a team where correcting higher-ups carries no penalty.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Amy Edmondson of Harvard, as cited by the authors.

card.rule: According to the authors, superteams resembled the best surgical teams: members felt safe to challenge, admit ignorance and ask for help, around a shared purpose.
card.limits: Our reading: The authors compare the teams; they do not claim superteams matched surgical teams in every respect.

concepts.title: Team open-mindedness is emergent
concepts.question: Is a team's open-mindedness just the sum of its members' open-mindedness?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a team's actively open-minded thinking (AOM) correlated with its accuracy, but it is not the sum of its members' AOM. It is an emergent property of the group.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors surveyed individuals for AOM, as in chapter 5, and also surveyed teams about attitudes toward the group and patterns of interaction. Putting high-AOM people together did not by itself yield a high-AOM team. How the group thinks is a property of the communication patterns among members, not only the thought inside each.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Actively open-minded thinking (AOM); the team version is an emergent property of the group.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: A group of open-minded people who do not care about one another will be less than the sum of its open-minded parts.

card.rule: According to the authors, a team's open-mindedness arises from how its members communicate, so it cannot be read off the individuals alone.
card.limits: Our reading: The authors found a correlation between team AOM and accuracy; correlation does not show which way the effect runs.

concepts.title: Givers and a culture of sharing
concepts.question: Why do givers tend to come out on top, and what did superteam givers do?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a final feature of winning teams is a culture of sharing. Adam Grant's research shows that givers tend to come out on top, because a giver's example improves the behaviour of others, which helps everyone including the giver.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Grant sorts people into givers, who contribute more to others than they receive; matchers, who give as much as they get; and takers, who give less than they take. Cynics call givers chumps. Marty Rosenthal gave deliberately, to change the behaviour of others for the benefit of all.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Giver, matcher and taker: Adam Grant's categories.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Adam Grant, the authors' Wharton colleague.

card.rule: According to the authors, deliberate giving can set an example that improves the behaviour of others, so givers need not lose out.
card.limits: Givers can be exploited by those who freeload; the authors rely on Grant's finding that, overall, their example tends to pay off.

concepts.title: Why superteams are not a recipe
concepts.question: Why do the authors warn against treating superteams as a simple recipe for organizations?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a busy executive might imagine a recipe: shop for top performers, put them in collaborative teams, strain out groupthink, add givers. They say it is not that simple.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Replicating the superteams in an existing organization would be a challenge. Singling out people for super status may be divisive, and moving people into cross-functional teams can be disruptive. There is no guarantee of results.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors call the work on superteams in its infancy; solid conclusions take time and there are many questions they have only begun to explore.

card.rule: According to the authors, superteam findings are promising but not a recipe, because replication in organizations is hard and results are not guaranteed.
card.limits: Our reading: The caution is the authors' own reading of early work, and it does not say that organizational teams cannot work.

concepts.title: Diversity versus ability
concepts.question: Is it ability or diversity that makes a team's combined judgment better?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, aggregating perspectives improves judgment only when the perspectives differ; combining uniform perspectives produces more of the same. Their key word is different.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Scott Page coined the phrase diversity trumps ability. The superteams were fairly diverse because superforecasters are, but the authors put ability first and did not design for diversity. If Page is right, making diversity the key to membership might have improved the results.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: “diversity trumps ability”, coined by Scott Page, a colleague and former competitor in the IARPA tournament.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors call it a false dichotomy: the choice is the mix of ability and diversity that works best in a given situation.

card.rule: According to the authors, aggregation depends on differing perspectives, and the useful question is how to mix ability and diversity.
card.limits: The authors did not test Page's claim directly; they say they might have done better had diversity been the key to membership.

concepts.title: Extremizing and the bin Laden advisers
concepts.question: Why can plain averaging of a team's probabilities be improved, and when does extremizing help?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, when team members hold different scraps of information, the plain average understates what they would conclude if they pooled everything. The extremizing algorithm corrects for this and works superbly, but its effectiveness depends on diversity.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Obama's advisers rated the chance that the tall man in the Pakistan house was bin Laden from 30% to 95%, most well over 50%, averaging roughly 70%. Most missing scraps pointed to bin Laden, so if each adviser had every scrap, each would raise an estimate, lifting the crowd figure perhaps to 80% or 85%.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Extremizing algorithm, mentioned in chapter 4.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: The authors say these tools should be on decision makers' desks, but will not replace analysts or advisers.

card.rule: According to the authors, extremizing helps most when team members hold different pieces of information, so the more diverse the team, the more it helps.
card.limits: A team of clones should not be extremized at all, and superteams that share information got little from it.

concepts.title: The leader's dilemma
concepts.question: Why might the habits of a superforecaster seem to make someone a worse leader?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, experts agree that leaders need confidence, decisiveness and a vision. The style of thinking behind superforecasting seems to undercut all three, so being a forecaster and being a leader look like rival jobs.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors ask how leaders can inspire confidence if they see nothing as certain, avoid analysis paralysis if their thinking is slow and self-critical, or act with determination if they readily revise or admit error. They add that humility is not a trait people link with great leaders, and that the superteams had no formal leader.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The chapter title names it the leader's dilemma. Endless deliberation is called “analysis paralysis”.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors state the dilemma in order to dissolve it: they say the contradiction is more apparent than real.

card.rule: According to the authors, leaders must be both forecasters and leaders, and the clash between the two roles is more apparent than real.
card.limits: The dilemma is only the setup. Treat it as a question the rest of the chapter answers, not as the authors' conclusion.

concepts.title: Moltke: nothing is certain
concepts.question: What did Moltke conclude from the idea that everything in war is uncertain?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Moltke treated “everything is uncertain” as an axiom, and drew from it the most urgent lesson: never entirely trust your plan. He was no Napoleon moving an army like chess pieces.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Moltke wrote that no plan of operations extends with certainty beyond the first encounter with the enemy's main strength. He also wrote that binding rules for all circumstances are impossible, because two cases never are exactly the same. So improvisation is essential.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Soldiers today say “no plan survives contact with the enemy”, a snappier version of Moltke's more nuanced wording.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Helmuth von Moltke led Prussian forces to victory over Denmark, Austria and France, which unified Germany.

card.rule: According to the authors, Moltke held that plans are provisional, since no two situations are exactly alike and improvisation is essential.
card.limits: Our reading: Moltke's original limits the claim to what lies beyond the first clash, so it does not say that planning is useless.

concepts.title: Schools that taught officers to think
concepts.question: How did German war academies train officers differently from other armies?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Moltke trusted his officers because they were trained to think hard. In German war academies disagreement was expected, not only permitted.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Scenarios were laid out and students were invited to suggest solutions and discuss them as a group. Instructors could be challenged, since each saw himself as a comrade among others. Junior officers criticised the outcome of a large maneuver before the attending general had the floor. Other nations, including the United States, told students the right answer.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: The historian Jörg Muth is quoted for the classroom practice.

card.rule: According to the authors, Moltke's officers were taught to propose, debate and criticise, not to memorise answers.
card.limits: The authors say this independence was balanced by elements that demanded action; it does not describe an organisation without discipline.

concepts.title: Seydlitz and the king's head
concepts.question: What does the story of Seydlitz at Zorndorf teach about obeying orders?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the Prussian officer corps passed on a message: think, and if necessary discuss your orders. Even criticise them. And if you absolutely must, and have a good reason, disobey.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In 1758, at Zorndorf, Frederick the Great sent a messenger three times telling the young cavalry general Seydlitz to attack. Seydlitz refused each time, judging the moment wrong, and the third time was warned of the king's anger. He attacked when he judged the time right and turned the battle. The king congratulated him and let him keep his head.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The story supports disobedience only for good reason; it does not say that officers may ignore orders freely.

card.rule: According to the authors, the lesson is to think and challenge orders, and to disobey only when there is a good reason.
card.limits: Our reading: Seydlitz was vindicated by the result, and the authors do not say how a failed refusal would have been judged.

concepts.title: Decide in time, not perfectly
concepts.question: How long should a leader deliberate before deciding, on the Wehrmacht's view?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the German military let circumstances set the time for a decision: leisurely and complex when time allowed, abrupt and simple under fire. An imperfect decision made in time was better than a perfect one made too late.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The Wehrmacht command manual of 1935, in force throughout World War II, called clarifying the enemy situation a necessity. It also said that waiting for information in a tense situation is seldom a sign of strong leadership, more often of weakness.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: The Wehrmacht, the German military, published the manual in 1935.

card.rule: According to the authors, let the situation set the time for a decision, and accept a less-informed choice made in time over a perfect one made late.
card.limits: The manual still calls clarifying the situation a necessity. The rule does not say to skip information when time allows.

concepts.title: Deliberate first, then act with resolve
concepts.question: How can a leader be resolute and still ready to change course?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the Wehrmacht drew a sharp line between deliberation and implementation. Before the decision, think about uncertainty and complexity. Once it is made, the mindset changes and the leader acts with resolve.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Moltke wrote that half measures are out of place when one attacks. The command manual said a course of action, once begun, must not be abandoned without overriding reason, yet clinging to it inflexibly can lead to failure. Its test of leadership is the timely recognition of when a new decision is needed.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: Be unwavering in carrying out the plan while staying open to the chance that it must be thrown out.

card.rule: According to the authors, deliberate before deciding, act resolutely after, and watch for the moment when circumstances demand a new decision.
card.limits: Our reading: the text sets no number for what counts as an overriding reason, so the judgment stays with the leader.

concepts.title: Auftragstaktik: say what, not how
concepts.question: What command principle joins “nothing is certain” with “unwavering determination”?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the principle of Auftragstaktik ties the two together. Decision-making power is pushed down the hierarchy so that people on the ground can respond fast. Commanders tell subordinates the goal but not how to reach it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Moltke wrote that war cannot be conducted from the green table, and that frequent, rapid decisions can be shaped only on the spot, according to local conditions. The authors add that people on the ground do not see the bigger picture. If they made strategic decisions, the army would lose coherence and become tiny units each seeking its own ends.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Auftragstaktik, usually translated today as “mission command”. The “green table” refers to top commanders at headquarters.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: Give the goal and keep strategy at the top; leave the choice of method to those closest to events.

card.rule: According to the authors, tell subordinates what the goal is but not how to achieve it, so that action is local and the whole stays coherent.
card.limits: Subordinates choose the how, not the strategic aim. Without a shared goal from above, units drift apart.

concepts.title: The captain and the town
concepts.question: Why does knowing the purpose of an order help a captain adapt?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, an order that gives only a route leaves a subordinate helpless when conditions differ. An order that gives the goal and the reason lets him adapt on the spot.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors imagine a captain ordered to take a town by a set route, not told why, who can only ask headquarters when the town differs from what was expected. In the Wehrmacht version he is told to take the town because that cuts a key road for enemy reinforcements. Finding a bridge HQ thought destroyed, he can wreck it himself.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The top-down style is called command and control; the other is Auftragstaktik.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: This is the authors' imagined illustration, not a recorded event.

card.rule: According to the authors, giving the purpose with the goal lets subordinates improvise toward the aim without asking permission.
card.limits: The example is made up to show the contrast. The authors do not claim every order-following unit freezes.

concepts.title: Eben Emael: improvising under loss
concepts.question: What does the attack on Eben Emael show about how the Wehrmacht handled setbacks?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the attack on the Belgian fortress of Eben Emael shows initiative working at every level. It was no obedient machine. When the plan was damaged, those on the spot improvised.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: On 10 May 1940 gliders came in by night. The commander, Lieutenant Rudolf Witzig, made an emergency landing in Germany, 100 kilometres off target. A sergeant took charge of the troops on the fort's roof and knocked out the guns. Witzig then arrived by a second plane and glider. Another sergeant, whose glider landed 60 kilometres away, commandeered two vehicles and improvised an attack that took 121 prisoners.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Case Yellow was the German invasion of Belgium and France that began that day.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors tell the story to show initiative, not to claim that every German operation went like this.

card.rule: According to the authors, when plans break down, units that know the aim and can use their judgment can still succeed.
card.limits: The case is one celebrated operation. The authors say not all Wehrmacht officers had these qualities.

concepts.title: The Wehrmacht was not a machine
concepts.question: Was the Wehrmacht the mindless machine that many people picture?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the common picture of a mindless, obedient war machine is the opposite of the Wehrmacht's real nature. The Nazi regime preached total obedience, but the Nazis inherited the Wehrmacht; they did not create it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The Wehrmacht manual asked for soldiers who think and act independently. The authors say enough officers, especially at the operational and tactical levels, were both superforecasters and superleaders. The German military, heavily outnumbered and outgunned, conquered most of Europe and held it for years.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The authors' pairing is superforecasters who are also superleaders, used in their terms.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: The historian James Corum is quoted: man for man, the German army was one of the most effective fighting forces ever seen.

card.rule: According to the authors, the Wehrmacht's strength came from judgment spread through the ranks, not from mindless obedience.
card.limits: The authors add that not all officers had these qualities, and they stress the evil nature of the regime the army served.

concepts.title: Hitler, Normandy and Moltke's rule
concepts.question: What happened at Normandy when Moltke's principles were broken?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the Wehrmacht failed partly because of its enemies' superior resources, and partly because Hitler took direct control of operations in violation of Moltke's principles. Normandy was the worst case.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The Allies feared that German tanks would drive their troops back into the sea. Hitler had directed that the reserves could move only on his personal command. He slept late, and for hours after the landings his aides refused to wake him to ask whether he wanted to order the tanks into battle.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors name two causes, resources and blunders. They do not claim Hitler alone lost the war.

card.rule: According to the authors, centralising decisions in one person, against Moltke's rule, left reserves waiting when speed mattered most.
card.limits: Hitler's interference was one reason among others. The authors also credit the Allies' greater resources.

concepts.title: The American army that discouraged thinking
concepts.question: How did the United States army of Eisenhower's youth treat independent thinking?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, in contrast with the Wehrmacht, the free and democratic American army of the same era had little use for independent thinking. Subordinates were to salute and obey without question.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: After World War I, the junior officer Dwight Eisenhower published an article arguing that tanks should be seen as speedy and efficient. He was told his ideas were wrong and dangerous and to keep them to himself, or face a court-martial. Orders were long and detailed; those for the North Africa landings were the size of a Sears Roebuck catalogue.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: The historian Jörg Muth supplies the catalogue comparison; Eisenhower recalls the reprimand himself.

card.rule: According to the authors, the American army of that era valued obedience and detailed orders over initiative, even though it was a democracy.
card.limits: The authors say there were smart, creative American officers; they valued initiative despite their training, not because of it.

concepts.title: Eisenhower understood Moltke
concepts.question: Which of Moltke's habits did Eisenhower practise as a leader?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Eisenhower, like Moltke, knew that nothing is certain, projected calm so as to spread confidence, and welcomed open debate. He shows that the Moltke model can work in a democracy's army.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: After giving the irrevocable order for the D-Day invasion, his first act was to write a note taking personal responsibility, to be released in the event of failure. In private he could be moody and brooding. With the troops he kept a smile and a steady word. He respected well-founded criticism and readily acknowledged mistakes.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors do not say Eisenhower copied Moltke, only that he held the same philosophy.

card.rule: According to the authors, a leader can act decisively and look assured while privately accepting that nothing is certain and that blame may be his.
card.limits: The calm face was a choice for the troops' sake. It does not mean he lacked doubts in private.

concepts.title: Israel, NATO and the 1982 doctrine
concepts.question: How did mission command reach official American doctrine?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the US military was slow to learn the lessons of the Wehrmacht after World War II. The new Israeli military valued individual initiative first, and in 1982 mission command became official American doctrine.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: An Israeli slogan of the era said plans are a platform for change, and the Israeli system was not openly patterned on a foreign model, since German Auftragstaktik could never be acknowledged. In the early 1980s, with the Soviets far ahead in men and tanks, NATO had to do more with less. American generals combed the writings of historians and theorists, studied Israeli experience and even consulted old Wehrmacht generals.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: “Mission command”, the official American name from 1982.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Israeli officers' remarks and Wehrmacht generals' advice are the sources the authors cite.

card.rule: According to the authors, a numerical disadvantage pushed NATO and the US army to adopt mission command in 1982.
card.limits: The authors say it is debatable whether the army is as decentralised as it should be.

concepts.title: Thunder runs and Mosul
concepts.question: What did on-site initiative achieve in Iraq?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the initiative of on-site commanders has produced big successes in the modern era. Two cases in Iraq show it: the thunder runs on Baghdad in 2003 and David Petraeus's command in Mosul.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In a thunder run a heavily armoured column raced to the captured airport and lost one vehicle; two days later a brigade ran the same route, turned into the government district, seized it and held it, though low on ammunition. Ground commanders made those calls. In Mosul, Petraeus improvised strategies from his knowledge of history, informed Baghdad but did not ask permission, and the insurgency was starved of oxygen there.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: “thunder run” is the name given to the 2003 raid.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors say it is never clear how much credit any one person deserves for the later fall in violence.

card.rule: According to the authors, empowering commanders on the spot let them seize chances that a distant headquarters would have missed.
card.limits: The authors call the successes big, not complete: the insurgency itself had not been forecast.

concepts.title: Training flexible leaders
concepts.question: How does Petraeus build leaders who are both thoughtful and bold?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Petraeus holds that flexible thinking must be trained by pushing people out of their intellectual comfort zone. He also holds that the divide between doers and thinkers is a false dichotomy: leaders must be both.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: He said it is easy to spout platitudes such as “no plan survives contact with the enemy”, and asked what a leader does to prepare for that beyond the bumper sticker. As a brigade commander he disliked live-fire exercises so choreographed that nothing surprising happened, and worked to make them safe but surprising.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The authors report that he calls the split between doers and thinkers a false dichotomy.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: He says: figure out the right move and then execute it boldly. He also says to preserve and promote the iconoclasts.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: Ralph Peters wrote that Hamlet thinks too much and that the army needs doers like Henry V, not thinkers.

card.rule: According to the authors, Petraeus trains officers on surprises and holds that leaders should work out the right move and then carry it out boldly.
card.limits: He admits that building safe but surprising exercises with real weapons was a huge challenge, and his stress on thinking is still controversial.

concepts.title: Mission command in companies
concepts.question: Which companies voice the same principle as Moltke, and in what words?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, bosses everywhere feel the tension between control and innovation, so Moltke's spirit appears in organisations that have nothing to do with bullets and bombs.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: William Coyne of 3M said the company tells people what to accomplish but not how. Amazon's Jeff Bezos set the principle “Have backbone; disagree and commit”. When Walmart built stores faster than it could develop managers, it created a leadership academy modelled on military academies, with mission command at its base.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: “disagree and commit” is Amazon's name for challenging a decision first and then backing it fully.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Coyne was senior vice president of research and development at 3M; the Walmart academy was designed by McKinney Rogers, headed by the former Royal Marine Damian McKinney.

card.rule: According to the authors, successful firms tell people the goal, invite challenge before a decision and commit fully after it.
card.limits: The authors call Bezos's language a little blunt for Moltke. The firms share the principle, not the vocabulary.

concepts.title: Business is more command-and-control than the army
concepts.question: Which organisations, armies or companies, are more command-and-control than people assume?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the common view of the military as strictly hierarchical, with salutes and mechanical obedience, is laughably out of date. Companies are often the more command-and-control side.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Many former officers advise corporations. Damian McKinney told the Financial Times that, ironically, companies are much more focused on what he calls command and control than their military counterparts.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: “command and control” is the top-down style that mission command replaces.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The remark comes from a former Royal Marine who advises companies. The authors report it; they do not measure it.

card.rule: According to the authors, bosses in business often hold tighter control than modern military leaders, who give their people the goal and room to choose how.
card.limits: The claim concerns the modern military and the firms the advisers meet, not every army or every company.

concepts.title: Self-assured judges
concepts.question: Were the leaders and thinkers the authors admire humble people?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, many of the leaders and thinkers whose judgment they single out were strongly self-assured. So the humility that forecasting needs cannot be a humble temperament.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Petraeus believed from his West Point days that he had the right stuff. Keynes thought he was the smartest man in the room. Cochrane had the chutzpah to call out eminent authorities. Soros, under extreme pressure, shorted the British pound in 1992, selling almost $10 billion of sterling and earning an estimated $1.1 billion.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Helmuth von Moltke and Sherman Kent are also listed among the self-assured.

card.rule: According to the authors, strong self-assurance and good judgment can go together in the same person.
card.limits: The point leaves open how such leaders manage their confidence. The next idea explains the kind of humility they have.

concepts.title: Intellectual humility, not self-doubt
concepts.question: What kind of humility does good judgment need, and how does it differ from self-doubt?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the humility needed for good judgment is not self-doubt. It is intellectual humility: a recognition that reality is complex, that seeing reality accurately is a constant struggle, and that human judgment is therefore full of mistakes, for fools and geniuses alike.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Annie Duke, a poker champion, is confident she can compete with most opponents. Yet she warns against the shortcut of reasoning that a successful person with good judgment must be right because she believes it, which looks at reality from the tip of the nose. She keeps apart what she is confident about and what she is not.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Intellectual humility, in the authors' own term.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: The authors say this humility drives careful reflection, while confidence in one's abilities drives determined action.

card.rule: According to the authors, you can think highly of yourself and still be intellectually humble, and the combination is fruitful.
card.limits: Our reading: the authors say the combination can be fruitful, not that it comes easily; Duke notes that humility about the game differs from humility about opponents.

concepts.title: Why use the Wehrmacht at all?
concepts.question: Why did the authors teach this lesson through the Wehrmacht, an army that served an evil cause?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, understanding what worked in the Wehrmacht means acknowledging that something we despise has impressive qualities. Forecasters who cannot cope risk the gravest error in a conflict: underestimating the opponent.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: There is no divinely mandated link between morality and competence. Milton portrayed Satan as both evil and resourceful in Paradise Lost. Forecasters who see illusory correlations and assume moral and cognitive weakness go together will fail when most needed. Analysts should not assume jihadist groups must be inept or vicious regimes cannot be creatively vicious.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: A “psycho-logical tension”: the authors say there is no logical contradiction in the Wehrmacht being horrific and effective.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: Separate your feelings about the Nazi regime from your factual judgments about the Wehrmacht's resilience.

card.rule: According to the authors, a forecaster must hold two opposed ideas at once: the Wehrmacht was horrific and also effective.
card.limits: The authors say the tension is psychological, not logical. The lesson judges competence, not the cause the army served.

concepts.title: When values leak into forecasts
concepts.question: How can even a superforecaster let feelings distort a forecast?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, even superforecasters who excel at aggressive self-criticism sometimes conflate facts and values. A strong feeling about the question can push the forecast toward the wished-for outcome.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Early in the Syrian civil war, Doug Lorch got a question wrong on whether rebels would take Aleppo. He saw that his loathing of the Assad regime had led him to the wishful conclusion that the rebels would win, though they were outgunned. Joshua Frankel got a question wrong on whether North Korea would detonate a nuclear weapon, influenced by optimism and hope for progress.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given; the authors call it conflating facts and values.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors report two cases; they do not say how often this happens.

card.rule: According to the authors, check whether a hoped-for outcome is shaping a forecast, and separate your feelings from the evidence.
card.limits: Frankel did not sense the influence at the time. The check works after the fact; it cannot be relied upon in the moment.

concepts.title: Different people, or different habits?
concepts.question: Are superforecasters a different kind of person, or people who do different kinds of things?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, the answer to Kahneman is a bit of both. Superforecasters score above average on intelligence and open-mindedness, though not off the charts. What makes them good is less what they are than what they do.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tetlock lists what they do: hard research, careful thought and self-criticism, gathering and combining other perspectives, granular judgments and relentless updating. He answers a question Kahneman put to him in conversation.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the answer. The chapter's term for the top performers is superforecasters.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: Tetlock points to habits of work that others could copy, not to a rare personality type.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, superforecasters are good mainly because of the work they do, helped by somewhat above-average intelligence and open-mindedness.
card.limits: The text gives no figures for how much traits and habits each contribute. Tetlock says only that it is a bit of both.

concepts.title: Can careful thinking be kept up?
concepts.question: Why might even the best forecasters slip back into easy, intuitive thinking?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, superforecasters use conscious System 2 reflection to catch mistakes from rapid, unconscious System 1 operations. But continuous self-scrutiny is exhausting, and the feeling of knowing is seductive, so even the best will tend to slip back into easier intuitive modes.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: This is Tetlock's reasoning about how the mind works, not a new experiment. He notes that superforecasters put enormous effort into catching their own errors, and he and Kahneman agree on the risk.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: System 1 (rapid, unconscious) and System 2 (slow, conscious reflection), terms Tetlock introduced earlier in the book.

card.rule: According to Tetlock and Kahneman, self-scrutiny tires, and a feeling of knowing is seductive, so superforecasters stay close to a slipup.
card.limits: Tetlock and Kahneman agree about the risk. They do not agree about how far training can lower it.

concepts.title: Flynn, WYSIATI and a claim that can be checked
concepts.question: How can a sweeping claim about the world be tested, and why did Flynn not test his?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, General Michael Flynn's remark that the world faced a prolonged, pretty unprecedented period of societal conflict is an empirical claim that can be checked. The available data point the other way, and Flynn fell for Kahneman's WYSIATI.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In a 2014 interview, shortly before leaving the Defense Intelligence Agency, Flynn said he spent two to three hours each morning on intelligence reports. Reports that quantify global violence since World War II show interstate wars declining since the 1950s, civil wars declining since the early 1990s, and battle deaths per year falling with a few blips. Flynn did not look them up.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: WYSIATI: What You See Is All There Is. Tetlock calls it the mother of all cognitive illusions, an egocentric view that blocks any world beyond the one at the tip of the nose.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Tetlock says he is not belittling Flynn. The error is notable because so accomplished a man made it, and he says everyone is vulnerable.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, a claim that feels true because of what is on your desk should be checked against the wider record before you state it.
card.limits: Tetlock says much of what Flynn said was too vague to judge. Only the last line was checkable, and WYSIATI explains the error without excusing it.

concepts.title: An illusion you cannot switch off
concepts.question: Why does knowing that an illusion is an illusion not make it disappear?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, we cannot make ourselves bulletproof against the tip-of-the-nose perspective. We can only monitor the answers that bubble up into consciousness and use a ruler to check them.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the Müller-Lyer illusion, two horizontal lines are the same length, yet the top one looks longer. Measure them with a ruler and you know they are identical, but you still see them as different. Knowing it is an illusion does not turn it off.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The Müller-Lyer illusion. The tip-of-your-nose perspective is Tetlock's name for the egocentric view that produces cognitive illusions.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: Watch the answers that come up, and measure where you can.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, you cannot stop an illusion from appearing, but you can check what it tells you.
card.limits: A check does not remove the illusion. The line still looks longer after you measure it.

media.alt: Two horizontal lines of equal length, one above the other. The upper line has pairs of short strokes at each end flaring outward, away from the line. The lower line has pairs of strokes at each end sweeping back toward the line, like arrowheads. The upper line looks longer.

concepts.title: Tetlock's optimism about training
concepts.question: Where does Tetlock part from Kahneman on biases, and what follows for organizations?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, he is more optimistic than Kahneman that smart, dedicated people can inoculate themselves to some degree against certain cognitive illusions. If he is right, organizations gain by recruiting and training talented people to resist biases.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tetlock cites no study in this passage. He goes on to a test with Kahneman and the psychologist Barbara Mellers on scope insensitivity, a bias that matters a great deal in forecasting.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for his optimism. The word he uses is inoculate.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: He and Kahneman agree that superforecasters are always a System 2 slipup from a blown forecast. They differ on how far training can protect.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, talented people can resist some biases to some degree, so organizations should recruit and train for that.
card.limits: The claim is hedged: some degree and certain illusions. Tetlock does not say anyone can become immune.

concepts.title: Scope insensitivity: lakes and birds
concepts.question: What happened when people were told that more lakes or more birds were at stake?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, citing Kahneman, people are insensitive to the scope of a problem: how large it is barely changes what they will pay. They answer how bad it makes them feel, not what it is worth.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In Toronto, one group was asked what they would pay to clean up the lakes of a small region of Ontario, and said about $10. Another group was asked about all 250,000 lakes in Ontario, and also said about $10. In a bird study, people told 2,000, 20,000 or 200,000 migratory birds drown yearly in oil ponds each said about $80.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Scope insensitivity. Tetlock calls the switch to an easier question a classic bait and switch.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Kahneman first documented it thirty years ago and later work got similar results.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, people respond to a prototype image and its feeling, so the size of the problem is mostly ignored.
card.limits: These cases are about money values for things we never price. The chapter does not say every judgment ignores scope.

concepts.title: The Assad question and the time frame
concepts.question: What did the Assad experiment show about superforecasters and the time frame of a question?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, the time frame of a forecast is its scope. A forecaster who ignores it gives the same probability whatever the deadline. Regular forecasters mostly did that, while superforecasters adjusted much more.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In an early-2012 question about whether the Assad regime would fall, one randomly chosen group was given a three-month window and another a six-month window, for superforecasters and regular forecasters alike. Barbara Mellers ran several such studies. Regular forecasters said 40% for three months and 41% for six. Superforecasters said 15% for three months and 24% for six.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Scope insensitivity, Kahneman's term from the lakes and birds studies; here the scope is the time frame.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Tetlock says this is not perfect scope sensitivity, which is tricky to define, but it was good enough to surprise Kahneman, who had expected the bias.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, a probability should change with the time frame asked about, and superforecasters' answers did while regular forecasters' barely moved.
card.limits: Tetlock calls the result short of perfect sensitivity. It shows superforecasters shook off much of the bias, not all of it.

concepts.title: Tinkering with the question
concepts.question: How can forecasters keep their answers sensitive to scope?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, his team's advanced training guidelines urge forecasters to mentally tinker with the question asked and see how the answer would change. These thought experiments stress-test the mental model and help keep a forecaster scope sensitive.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Examples from the guidelines: move the cutoff date to six months out instead of twelve, or make the target price for oil 10% lower. Tetlock says he cannot take credit, because superforecasters were talking about scope problems, without that term, before his team studied them.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the exercise. The chapter calls it running thought experiments inside your head.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: Change the date, the price or another relevant detail in your head and ask how your answer would change.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, run small thought experiments on the question asked to test whether your model responds to the details.
card.limits: Our reading: the chapter gives the guideline and the Assad result but does not test the guideline on its own.

concepts.title: From effort to habit
concepts.question: How can a careful correction become less tiring to carry out?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, some superforecasters practise System 2 corrections, such as stepping back to take the outside view, so well that they become habitual and part of System 1. Software tools that some of them built also lighten the load. The work stays hard, and good forecasters expect to stumble.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tetlock's analogy is a golfer told how to stand at the tee: bend the knees, tilt the head, raise one shoulder. The first, second and third tries need a mental checklist and she still forgets something. Slowly it gets easier, and she buries the steps in System 1. Cooking, sailing, surgery, singing and flying fighter jets work the same way, as does a child learning to read.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the process. Tetlock says deliberative practice can make a task second nature.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Tetlock introduces this with My sense is, so it is his judgment, and he adds that how long they can sustain it depends on how heavy their cognitive loads are.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, practice can turn a conscious System 2 correction into an automatic System 1 habit, though forecasting remains hard work.
card.limits: Tetlock presents the idea as his sense, not a tested result, and says the load still decides how long the effort can last.

concepts.title: What a black swan is
concepts.question: What does the black swan metaphor describe, and what else must a black swan be?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, the black swan is a brilliant metaphor for an event so far outside experience that we cannot even imagine it until it happens. Taleb adds that a black swan must also be impactful, not merely surprising.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tetlock's story: a European four centuries ago has seen many swans, all white, and so pictures every possible swan as white, however varied in size and shape. Then a ship returns from Australia carrying a black swan, and he is stunned.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Black swan, the term Nassim Taleb made a common English phrase.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Taleb is a former Wall Street trader whose thinking about uncertainty and probability has produced three influential books.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, a black swan is an impactful event so far beyond experience that it could not be imagined beforehand.
card.limits: Tetlock goes on to test this strict reading and finds that many events called black swans do not meet it.

concepts.title: Taleb's challenge to the tournament
concepts.question: Why does Taleb think the forecasting research is a fool's errand?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, Taleb holds that black swans, and black swans alone, determine the course of history. If so, what matters cannot be forecast and what can be forecast does not matter, so the IARPA tournament is a fool's errand. Tetlock respects the critique but sees a false dichotomy.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tetlock reports Taleb's line that history and societies do not crawl but make jumps. In this view the Good Judgment Project rests on misconceptions, panders to desperation and fosters foolish complacency. Tetlock says Taleb's critique makes deep points that future tournaments must struggle to address.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: False dichotomy is Tetlock's phrase for the choice between forecasting works if you follow my formula and forecasting is bunk.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: Tetlock rejects both extremes: the formula claim and the dismissal.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, Taleb's critique is serious but offers a false choice between forecasting working by formula and forecasting being bunk.
card.limits: This is Tetlock's account of Taleb's position. It is not a direct statement from Taleb beyond one quoted line.

concepts.title: Is 9/11 really a black swan?
concepts.question: Does the strict definition of a black swan survive a check against 9/11?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, on the stringent definition, something literally inconceivable before it happens, many events called black swans are actually gray. The 9/11 attacks, the prototypic black swan, were not unimaginable.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In 1994 a plot to hijack a jet and crash it into the Eiffel Tower was broken up. In 1998 the US Federal Aviation Administration examined a scenario of terrorists hijacking FedEx cargo planes and crashing them into the World Trade Center. In August 2001 a government official asked Harvard terrorism expert Louise Richardson why no group had used an airplane as a flying bomb.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Gray swan is the colour Tetlock gives to events that were called black but could be conceived beforehand.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The argument works against the stringent definition only. Tetlock says Taleb has implied that definition on occasion and also offers a more modest one.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, if a black swan must be inconceivable beforehand, a rare kind of event becomes rarer, because events like 9/11 fail the test.
card.limits: The argument holds only for the stringent definition. Taleb also defines a black swan more modestly, and the next ideas treat that.

concepts.title: What a tournament cannot show
concepts.question: What can a tournament of short-term forecasts tell us about rare, consequential events?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, Taleb also defines a black swan more modestly, as a highly improbable consequential event, and here his critique holds. The first IARPA tournament tells us nothing about how good superforecasters are at spotting gray or black swans.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Hundreds of forecasts looking out a few months soon give enough data to judge how well calibrated forecasters are. But highly improbable events almost never happen. If that means a 1%, 0.1% or 0.0001% chance, it may take decades, centuries or millennia to pile up enough data. Superforecasters may be as clueless as anyone or astonishingly adept; Tetlock says we do not know and should not fool ourselves.

blocks.label: Name it
