blocks.text: No name given for the gap. The modest definition is Taleb's phrase, a highly improbable consequential event.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: This limits what the evidence shows. It is not a finding that superforecasters fail at spotting rare events.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, short-term tournaments cannot show skill at spotting rare, high-impact events, and we should not pretend they do.
card.limits: The gap lies in the evidence, not in the forecasters. Tetlock says they may be clueless or astonishingly adept, and nobody knows.

concepts.title: History crawls as well as jumps
concepts.question: Does history only jump, or does slow change matter too?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, if only black swans mattered in the long run, the Good Judgment Project would interest only short-term thinkers. But history is not just black swans: it sometimes jumps, but it also crawls, and slow incremental change can be profoundly important.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tetlock points to average global economic growth of about 1% a year in the nineteenth century and 2% in the twentieth. Those slow rates turned the squalor of the eighteenth century, and of all the centuries before, into the unprecedented wealth of the twenty-first.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. Taleb's side of the contrast is that history makes jumps.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: Taleb: only jumps decide history. Tetlock: jumps and slow crawls both matter.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, history jumps and crawls, and the slow changes can matter profoundly, so not only black swans deserve forecasting.
card.limits: Tetlock concedes that history does sometimes jump. His argument shows that slow change matters, not that black swans do not.

concepts.title: Two ways to invest
concepts.question: In what two ways can an investor seek a profit in uncertain markets, and which is better?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, black swan investing and beating competitors by forecasting more accurately are two different ways to succeed. Neither is superior or inferior to the other. It is different.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Venture capitalist Vinod Khosla, a cofounder of Sun Microsystems and a fan of Taleb, knows he cannot specify the next big thing. He spreads his investments around, expecting most to fail and hoping for one or two start-ups that yield a Google-size fortune. Taleb traded this way, very successfully, before becoming an author. The other way is to forecast more accurately than rivals, for example judging a 68% chance where others see 60%, as the best poker players do. It pays off more often, but returns are modest and fortunes grow slowly.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Black swan investing is Tetlock's name for the spread-your-bets approach.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: Black swan investing wins rarely and hugely. Accurate forecasting wins often and modestly.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, black swan investing and accurate forecasting are different strategies, and neither is better than the other.
card.limits: The comparison is Tetlock's description of two styles. The chapter gives no figures comparing their returns.

concepts.title: Consequences make the swan
concepts.question: Why do an event's consequences, not the event alone, make it a black swan, and what follows?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, what lifts a surprise to black swan status is its consequences, and consequences take time to develop. Many links in those chains of consequences are questions forecasters can answer, so to that extent black swans can be forecast.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: On July 14, 1789 a mob took the Bastille prison, but the storming of the Bastille means that day plus the events it triggered that spiraled into the French Revolution. Today the black swan of 9/11 means the attacks plus the consequences, including the invasion of Afghanistan. That sequence could have gone differently: the Taliban might have handed over bin Laden, or he might have fled, and there might have been no invasion or ten-year hunt.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The sociologist Duncan Watts puts it that the more you want to explain about a black swan, the broader you must draw the boundaries around the event.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Tetlock says there may be no evidence that superforecasters can foresee events like 9/11 themselves. His claim is about the forecastable consequences.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, black swans owe their status to chains of consequences, and many links in those chains are forecastable questions.
card.limits: The claim reaches the consequences and not the shock itself. Tetlock admits the shock may be beyond foresight.

concepts.title: The ten-year horizon
concepts.question: How far ahead can forecasters see beyond the obvious, and why does it matter?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, he, Taleb and Kahneman agree there is no evidence that geopolitical or economic forecasters can predict anything ten years out beyond the excruciatingly obvious, such as that there will be conflicts, apart from the odd lucky hit. These limits follow from the butterfly dynamics of nonlinear systems.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In Tetlock's EPJ research, the accuracy of expert predictions declined toward chance five years out. Lucky hits are inevitable whenever lots of forecasters make lots of forecasts.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The butterfly dynamics of nonlinear systems is Tetlock's phrase for why small causes can have large and unpredictable effects.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The claim is about long-range geopolitical and economic forecasts. It does not cover the shorter questions the tournament tests.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, there is no evidence that anyone can forecast the long run beyond the excruciatingly obvious.
card.limits: The claim concerns horizons of about ten years in geopolitics and economics, and says nothing against short-range forecasts.

concepts.title: Planning beyond the horizon
concepts.question: If forecasting stops at a horizon, how should we plan beyond it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, if you have to plan for a future beyond the forecasting horizon, plan for surprise. That means planning for adaptability and resilience. Taleb goes further and asks for critical systems to be antifragile, strengthened by shocks.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In an April 2001 memo to the president and vice president, Defense Secretary Rumsfeld passed on a piece by Linton Wells. Wells wrote that he was not sure what 2010 would look like but was sure it would be very little like what we expect, so we should plan accordingly. Richard Danzig advises planning for adaptability and resilience. Eisenhower said plans are useless but planning is indispensable.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Antifragile is Taleb's term for a system that is resilient to shocks and strengthened by them, such as international banking or nuclear weapons systems.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: Prepare responses to several kinds of blows instead of betting on one forecast.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, beyond the forecasting horizon, plan for adaptability and resilience instead of betting on a single prediction.
card.limits: Tetlock agrees with Taleb in principle but says such preparation is costly, which brings back the need to judge probabilities.

media.alt: A scanned one-page typed memo made of bullets, one for each decade from 1900 to 2000, each noting how the strategic world differed from ten years earlier. A final bullet concludes that the future will differ from expectations and calls for planning. A handwritten note and a declassification stamp appear.

concepts.title: Preparing costs, so odds still count
concepts.question: Why does preparing for surprises still depend on judging probabilities?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, preparing for surprises, whether through resilience or antifragility, is costly. So we must set priorities, which puts us back in the forecasting business. Probability judgments sit at the heart of all long-term planning, and they should be explicit.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In Tokyo, big new buildings must use advanced engineering to withstand megaquakes. Seismologists cannot time earthquakes but know where they tend to occur and how big they are likely to be, so the expensive standard makes sense there, and less sense in regions less prone to big quakes, particularly poorer countries. For decades the US kept the capacity to fight two wars at once, a judgment that the likelihood was high enough to justify the expense, but not three wars, four wars or an alien invasion.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given for the point.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: Make the probability judgments behind a plan explicit, so they can be examined.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, every plan for surprise rests on probability judgments, so make them explicit.
card.limits: The argument is about priorities under cost. It does not deny that adaptability and resilience are worth having.

concepts.title: Hindsight makes the future look easy
concepts.question: How does hindsight bias lead people to overrate how predictable the future is?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, our minds crave certainty and impose it when they cannot find it. In forecasting, hindsight bias is the cardinal sin. Brushing off surprises makes the past look more predictable than it was, which encourages the belief that the future is much more predictable than it is.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In the 1980s and early 1990s many believed that Japan would soon dominate the global economy. Its later decline should give pause to those who are sure China will lead the world economy in the mid-twenty-first century. Looking back, it seems strange that anyone thought Japan would take the lead, as if its falter was obvious in hindsight, just as the prediction that China will not seems obvious today.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Hindsight bias.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Tetlock says China might become the leading economic power. His point is about certainty, not about the answer.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, hindsight bias makes the past look predictable and so inflates our confidence about the future.
card.limits: Tetlock grants that China might indeed lead. The Japan case warns against certainty, not against the prediction.

concepts.title: Bell curves and fat tails
concepts.question: Why does the shape of a distribution change how likely extreme events are?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, many recurring events in daily life fit the classic bell curve, but not everything does. Wealth has a fat-tailed distribution, which permits far more extreme outcomes than a bell curve would. Taleb's hardest-to-grasp view is that historical probabilities are distributed like wealth, not height.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Most men are between five and six feet tall, far fewer are around four or seven feet, and tiny numbers are near three or eight feet. For US household wealth, suppose the median is about $100,000 and 95% of households fall between $10,000 and $1,000,000. On a bell curve, a household worth over $10 million would almost never turn up and a billionaire would be a one-in-trillions event. In fact nearly five hundred people have over $1 billion, and the chance of a billionaire is roughly one in 700,000.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Bell curve for the classic normal distribution, and fat-tailed distribution for one that permits far more extreme outcomes.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Tetlock calls Taleb's step from wealth to history the hardest part to grasp. The card reports it as Taleb's view.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, a fat-tailed distribution makes extreme outcomes far likelier than a bell curve would, and Taleb says history's possibilities are fat-tailed.
card.limits: A bell curve fits height well and wealth badly, so the shape has to be checked for each quantity.

media.alt: Chart of number of households (vertical axis) against a quantity, with two curves. A shaded symmetric bell, labelled normal distribution such as height, has a dashed median line at its peak. A thick curve labelled fat tail, such as net worth, peaks lower and further left, then trails in a long stretch to the right, far above the bell, which has dropped to the floor there.

concepts.title: The 1914 policy maker
concepts.question: What would a Foreign Office official have done differently if he had used a fat-tailed view of war?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, if historical probabilities are fat-tailed like wealth, the world is more volatile than most of us realize and we risk grave miscalculation. An official who wrongly assumed a bell curve for war deaths would dismiss a warning of world war as absurd.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In summer 1914 an imagined senior British Foreign Office official assumes wars are normally distributed around an average of 100,000 deaths, so his worst case is about a million. A forecaster warns of a world war killing ten million, then another killing sixty million. The official puts this at one chance in several million and dismisses him. Under a fat-tailed distribution the warning would still seem improbable but thousands of times more probable. Tetlock compares it to Powerball odds rising from one in five million to one in five hundred.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The fat-tailed distribution, as in the previous idea.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The official is Tetlock's imagined figure, built to show the effect of an assumption. He is not a real person.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, assuming a bell curve for war deaths makes catastrophes look absurdly unlikely, while a fat-tailed view makes them thousands of times likelier.
card.limits: The story shows what an assumption does to a judgment. It does not give the true odds of any particular war.

concepts.title: One world among many possible
concepts.question: What does it mean to see the actual world as one of many possible worlds?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, Taleb's idea is that the world we live in emerged, quasi-randomly, from a vast population of once-possible worlds. Tetlock says Kahneman and he see history this way, and that counterfactuals give a feel for it and instill humility.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Kahneman's thought experiment takes three leaders of enormous impact: Hitler, Stalin and Mao. Each came to power backed by a movement that would not have accepted a woman as leader, and each began with an egg that had a 50% chance of producing a female baby. So there was only a 12.5% chance that all three would be male and an 87.5% chance that at least one would be female. Had Anna Hitler been born in 1889, World War II might never have happened, or a smarter dictator might have done worse.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Counterfactuals, or what-if history. The once-possible worlds are Taleb's idea of a statistical distribution of possible worlds.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Tetlock says the idea can feel like eggheaded nonsense. Counterfactuals are a way to feel it, not a proof.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, the actual world is one draw from many possible worlds, and counterfactuals teach humility about the future.
card.limits: Tetlock presents counterfactuals as a way to feel the point and to build humility, not as evidence that the future is random.

concepts.title: Humility without giving up
concepts.question: What is Tetlock's final position on how far foresight can reach?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, humility should not hide the fact that people can, with considerable effort, make accurate forecasts about at least some developments that really matter. In the big scheme human foresight is puny, but on the human scale it is nothing to sniff at.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tetlock calls Kahneman's and Taleb's critiques the strongest challenges to superforecasting, and he agrees with them on the limits: no evidence of foresight ten years out, and a fat-tailed, radically open history. His positive case rests on the forecasting questions that superforecasters do answer, not on the long run.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Contrast
blocks.text: Kahneman stresses minds' craving for certainty. Taleb stresses black swans and fat tails. Tetlock adds effortful accuracy on some questions.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, humility about the long run and effortful accuracy on some questions are both warranted.
card.limits: Tetlock says some developments, not all, and only with considerable effort. The chapter does not say which ones or how far ahead.

concepts.title: The Scottish vote and the hindsight trap
concepts.question: Why do the authors treat after-the-fact explanations of the Scottish vote as a dead end?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the explanations pundits give right after a major event are a dead end, because many factors were at work. Every event is better used as a chance to improve the mental models that shape our expectations of the future.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Before the 2014 referendum on Scotland leaving the United Kingdom, the polls moved back and forth. Pundits split between nationalist identity and economic calculation as the likely winner. No won, 55.3% to 44.7%, and the one highly probable outcome had been that pundits would explain the result at once.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The authors call the post-event commentary hindsight-tainted.

card.rule: According to the authors, treat a surprising outcome as a chance to revise your model of the world, not as proof of a ready-made story.
card.limits: The authors do not say that events teach nothing. They say that a story built after the fact is a poor way to learn from an event.

concepts.title: Drezner’s confession: keep score
concepts.question: What did Daniel Drezner decide to do differently after the Scottish referendum, and why?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, effective learning from experience cannot happen without clear feedback, and clear feedback needs forecasts that are unambiguous and scorable.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The day after the vote, the political scientist Daniel Drezner confessed he had been unsure of the outcome and surprised by the margin. He had thought no would win, but had written a post on why yes might win, so what he had forecast was unclear. He resolved to make a clear prediction, with a confidence interval, and so to keep score.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. Drezner’s own phrase for his resolve is that he wants to keep score.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Tetlock calls this the reaction he hoped for. Drezner, writing on a Washington Post blog, linked it to the IARPA tournament.

card.rule: According to the authors, state what you predict and how confident you are, so the outcome can tell you how to revise.
card.limits: The chapter reports Drezner’s resolution only. It does not say how his later forecasts turned out.

concepts.title: Real stakes and the path to seeing better
concepts.question: Why do the authors say forecasting tournaments matter even though they look like games?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, tournaments with scores and leaderboards may look like games, but the stakes are real. They help researchers learn what improves forecasting and help forecasters sharpen their skills through practice and feedback.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Good forecasting can mark the difference between prosperity and bankruptcy in business, between helpful and harmful policies in government, and between peace and war in national security. The authors point to Iraq: had US intelligence not told Congress it was certain Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction, a disastrous invasion might have been averted.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The short formula is: forecast, measure, revise.

card.rule: According to the authors, forecast, measure, revise is the surest path to seeing better.
card.limits: The authors say an invasion might have been averted, not that it would have been. They do not say tournaments alone prevent bad decisions.

concepts.title: The hoped-for evidence-based forecasting revolution
concepts.question: What change does Tetlock hope readers will bring about, and does he say it will happen?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: Tetlock hopes for an evidence-based forecasting revolution, similar to the evidence-based medicine revolution. He also says that nothing may change, and that things may go either way.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In his daydream, consumers of forecasting stop being gulled by pundits with good stories. They ask how past predictions fared and reject answers made only of anecdotes and credentials. Just as people expect a pill to have been tested in peer-reviewed experiments, they expect forecasters to prove their accuracy by rigorous testing.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Evidence-based forecasting, modelled on evidence-based medicine.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: Forecasters benefit too, says Tetlock: clear feedback from rigorous testing is the only way they can improve their foresight.

card.rule: Tetlock hopes buyers will demand tested track records from forecasters as they demand tested pills, while admitting change may not come.
card.limits: This is a hope stated with a superforecaster’s caution. Tetlock does not claim the revolution is certain.

concepts.title: Kto-kogo: forecasting as a contest for power
concepts.question: What does the kto-kogo view say the goal of forecasting is?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the kto-kogo view holds that the goal of forecasting is not to see what is coming but to advance the interests of the forecaster and the forecaster’s tribe. Accuracy is welcome when it helps and pushed aside when power requires.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Like many hardball operators, Lenin saw politics as a struggle for power. He summed it up as kto, kogo, which literally means who, whom: who does what to whom. On this view arguments and evidence are adornments. What matters is being the kto, not the kogo.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Kto-kogo, Lenin’s shorthand for who does what to whom.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors describe the view and the force it exerts. They do not adopt it.

card.rule: On the kto-kogo view a forecast is a move in a power contest, judged by whether it helps the forecaster’s side.
card.limits: The authors say Lenin had a point but call him a tad dogmatic. They treat kto-kogo as a strong force, not the whole truth.

concepts.title: When accuracy is not the goal
concepts.question: Which real cases show that accuracy is often only one of many goals in forecasting?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, accuracy is often only one of many goals in forecasting, and sometimes it is irrelevant. Tetlock says he swept this under the rug in chapter 1, when he said accuracy would be the sole concern.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Nate Silver’s 2012 forecasts never put Obama below a 61% chance of winning, and Democrats praised him while Republicans reviled him. In March 2014 his forecast favoured Republican control of the Senate, and many Democrats turned on him. Same forecaster, same record. At Santander Brasil, an analyst who warned of a market fall was fired at once.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given. The authors link these cases to kto-kogo.

card.rule: According to the authors, people often judge a forecast by whether it suits their side, not by whether it is accurate.
card.limits: Two cases do not show that no one cares about accuracy. The authors use them to show it is one goal among several.

concepts.title: Why Lenin was a tad dogmatic
concepts.question: Where do the authors judge the kto-kogo view to go too far?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Lenin had a point: self and tribe matter. But he was a tad dogmatic, because people want power yet value other things too, and that can make all the difference.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tetlock says one need not be a Marxist-Leninist to concede that forecasting can be bent to serve self and tribe. His reply is that other motives, such as the aim of making the sick well in medicine, can win. The next section tests this.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: the authors concede that co-option happens. They deny only that it is the sole force.

card.rule: According to the authors, power-seeking is real but not the only motive, so kto-kogo overstates the case.
card.limits: The authors do not deny that forecasting can be co-opted. They deny that nothing else moves people.

concepts.title: Codman and his outcome records
concepts.question: How did Ernest Codman’s system for recording hospital outcomes win through despite fierce resistance from hospitals?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Codman’s core insight, that hospitals should record and publish the end results of treatment, met entrenched resistance but ultimately won. They use this to show that kto-kogo is not the decisive force in human affairs.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A century ago the Boston doctor Ernest Amory Codman proposed that hospitals record each patient’s ailment, treatment and end result, and release statistics so consumers could choose on evidence. Hospitals balked at the cost and physicians feared for their reputations. Codman was pushed out of Massachusetts General, yet the uproar over his 1915 cartoon spread his ideas, and hospitals adopted them.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The End Result System (the book also writes End Results System), Codman’s name for his proposal.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: The historian Ira Rutkow, quoted by the authors, describes Codman’s plan and its reception.

card.rule: According to the authors, a score-keeping idea that threatens the powerful can still win when reason and a clear goal back it.
card.limits: The authors note that much of what Codman advocated was never adopted. His core insight won, not every proposal he made.

concepts.title: Evidence-based thinking spreads
concepts.question: In which fields does the chapter say evidence-based thinking has spread, and what lies behind the shift?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, an evidence-based forecasting movement would not spring up from nothing. It would be another sign of a broad shift away from decisions based on experience, intuition and authority, toward quantification and analysis, catalysed by information technology.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Evidence-based policy, modelled on evidence-based medicine, subjects government policies to rigorous analysis, and there is probably more top-quality policy analysis than ever. Charitable foundations tie funding to stringent evaluation, expanding programmes that deliver and shuttering those that fail. The Gates Foundation is renowned for rigor. Sports training has become data-driven.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Evidence-based policy. The sports case also draws on ‘Moneyball’-style analytics.

card.rule: According to the authors, evidence-based forecasting would be one more case of a broad shift from authority to quantification.
card.limits: Tetlock says politics will always be politics: politicians still weigh partisan advantage and ideological conviction.

concepts.title: Why intelligence agencies resist scoring
concepts.question: Why does the authors’ reasoning make scorekeeping dangerous for the intelligence community in the short run?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, scorekeeping is dangerous in the short run for the intelligence community. Numbers leave it open to the wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy, while phrases as fuzzy as a puff of smoke keep it safe.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The fallacy is to conclude that a forecast of a 70% chance is wrong because the event did not happen. It was a big reason why Sherman Kent’s proposal to attach numerical ranges to forecasts went nowhere. The community has been blamed for missing the dots before 9/11 and for connecting unconnected dots before Iraq, and each time lurches to the opposite extreme.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy; the authors call the swings blame-game ping-pong.

card.rule: According to the authors, numbers expose forecasters to unfair blame, so organisations under constant blame prefer fuzzy words.
card.limits: Tetlock says this thinking is tempting in many organisations but irresistible in the intelligence community.

concepts.title: The IARPA tournament as a reason for hope
concepts.question: Why does Tetlock treat the intelligence community’s funding of the tournament as a reason for hope?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, perhaps the best reason to hope for change is the IARPA tournament itself. A decade earlier, Tetlock would have put the intelligence community at the top of organisations that most needed to get serious about forecasting but were least likely to.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The reason for that doubt was kto-kogo: evidence-based forecasting would improve the community’s work in the long run, but it is dangerous in the short run. Yet the community did fund the tournament, and Tetlock has seen strong interest from the director of National Intelligence in making scorekeeping an integral part of intelligence analysis.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: the funding and the interest are evidence of a shift. They are not proof that scorekeeping will become routine.

card.rule: According to the authors, a reform backed by the organisation least likely to want it is a better reason for hope than one backed by friends.
card.limits: One agency’s funding and one director’s interest are not a movement. The authors do not claim they are.

concepts.title: The humanists’ objection to counting
concepts.question: What would a humanist say against measuring forecasts, and how seriously does Tetlock take it?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, humanists would object that numbers are being applied to things that cannot be captured by numbers. He says there is a lot of truth in this perspective.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tetlock imagines how he would have reacted had he taken a different path in 1976. As a twenty-two-year-old graduate he could have gone to Oxford to study the humanities, but his adviser Peter Suedfeld urged him toward the scientific method. In that other life he would cite the cultural critic Leon Wieseltier, who complained that metrics are assigned to phenomena that cannot be measured.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Naive positivism is the label the imagined humanist Tetlock uses for the over-trust in numbers.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Tetlock voices the objection in the person of his alternate self. It is not his own conclusion.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, the humanists’ warning has truth in it: numbers can be applied where they do not belong.
card.limits: Tetlock imagines the objection and agrees with part of it. He does not give up measuring forecasts.

concepts.title: Numbers are tools that need scrutiny
concepts.question: What does Tetlock say numbers are, and how should forecasters treat scoring systems as a result?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, the truly numerate know that numbers are tools, nothing more, and their quality ranges from wretched to superb. They must be constantly scrutinised and improved. Progressive improvement is attainable; perfection is not.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A crude version of Codman’s system that tracked only patient survival could let a hospital boast that 100% of its patients live. It would do so by turning away the sickest patients.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: Treat each scoring system as a work in progress and keep checking what it fails to capture.

card.rule: Treat numbers as tools to be tested and improved, not as sacred insight.
card.limits: Tetlock warns against bad measures, not against measuring. He still prefers a flawed score to none.

concepts.title: Fixing Brier scores and the credit-score comparison
concepts.question: What flaw does Tetlock admit in Brier scoring, and why does he still call it a big improvement?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, Brier scoring is a work in progress. A scoring system that needs tweaking can still be a big improvement on how forecasters are judged today.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Brier scores treat false alarms the same as misses, though for things like terrorist attacks people care far more about misses. The fix is easy: tell forecasters the ground rules in advance, for example that false positives cost one-tenth as much as false negatives. Credit scores are flawed too, yet they are a huge advance on loan officers who once decided almost whimsically.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Brier score, the authors’ measure of forecast accuracy.

card.rule: A scoring system can be imperfect and still a big improvement; adjust it by announcing in advance how errors are weighted.
card.limits: Tetlock does not claim his scoring system is perfect; he claims it is far better than the alternatives.

concepts.title: Big questions versus scorable questions
concepts.question: What dilemma did Paul Saffo’s challenge expose about questions that matter and questions that can be scored?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, there is a dilemma. What matters is the big question, but the big question cannot be scored. The little question does not matter as much, but it can be scored, so the tournament used little questions.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In spring 2013 Tetlock described the tournament to Paul Saffo, a Silicon Valley futurist, and mentioned an IARPA question: would North Korea attempt a multistage rocket launch between 7 January and 1 September 2013? Saffo thought it trivial and said the real question is ‘How does this all turn out?’ His long answer was impressive, but too vague for Tetlock to judge, even later.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Tetlock calls it unfair to say the tournament counted what does not count. The dilemma is that the big questions are broader.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, the questions that matter most are the hardest to score, and the ones that can be scored are narrower.
card.limits: Tetlock says there is a way out of the box, which the next idea sets out. The dilemma is not a ban on scoring.

concepts.title: Bayesian question clustering
concepts.question: How can many small, scorable questions help answer a big question that cannot be scored?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, a big question is composed of many small questions. Asking many tiny but pertinent questions lets us close in on an answer to the big one, even though no single small question settles it.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Saffo’s question implied recent events in Korea: a rocket launch, a new nuclear test, renouncing the 1953 armistice, a cyber attack, a severed hotline and a threatened nuclear attack. Small questions follow: another nuclear test? Rebuffed talks? Artillery fire? A ship firing on a ship? The answers are cumulative: the more yeses, the likelier the answer is ‘This is going to end badly.’

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Bayesian question clustering, which Tetlock compares to Bayesian updating from chapter 7 and to the painter’s technique of pointillism.

card.rule: Answer an unscorable big question by scoring a cluster of small, pertinent questions whose answers add up.
card.limits: One small question nails nothing down. Tetlock wants to test how well clustering works in future research.

media.alt: Tree diagram: a dark oval at the top asks whether there will be another Korean war. Arrows point down from it to four lighter ovals in a row, each a smaller question: missile launches, nuclear tests, cyber attacks and artillery shelling.

concepts.title: Foresight is not all of good judgment
concepts.question: How does Tetlock distinguish foresight from good judgment as a whole?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, foresight is one element of good judgment, but there are others, including some that cannot be counted and run through a scientist’s algorithms, such as moral judgment.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tetlock called his research program the Good Judgment Project, which seems to imply that accurate forecasting and good judgment are one and the same. That is not what he intended. He expects the Leon Wieseltiers of the world still to be unmollified, which is why he separates the two.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The Good Judgment Project, Tetlock’s research program.

card.rule: Foresight is one element of good judgment, not the whole of it.
card.limits: The name of the project does not claim that forecasting accuracy equals good judgment. Tetlock disowns that reading.

concepts.title: The smack-the-forehead test
concepts.question: What makes a question good, and why does Tom Friedman’s 2002 Iraq question pass Tetlock’s test?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, a good question is one that gets us thinking about something worth thinking about. One way to identify it is the smack-the-forehead test: when you read the question after time has passed, you smack your forehead and say ‘If only I had thought of that before!’

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In September 2002 Tom Friedman wrote that one question gnawed at him: is Iraq the way it is because Saddam Hussein is the way he is, or the reverse? Is it an artificial, tribalised state, or a real nation? His questioning pointed to what we now know were key drivers of later events, including the sectarianism that has devastated Iraq. So it passes the test.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The smack-the-forehead test, Tetlock’s own name.

card.rule: A good question is one that, after time has passed, makes you wish you had thought of it before.
card.limits: Tetlock offers this as one way to identify a good question. It can be applied only after time has passed.

concepts.title: Superforecasters and superquestioners
concepts.question: Does Tetlock think a superforecaster is also a superquestioner?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, we may assume a superforecaster is also a superquestioner, and the reverse, but we do not actually know. His best scientific guess is that they often are not.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: He suggests the psychological recipe for the ideal superforecaster may prove quite different from that for the ideal superquestioner. The evidence is a hunch about how minds work, not a test result.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Superquestioner, Tetlock’s counterpart to the superforecaster.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Tetlock presents this as a best scientific guess. It is not a finding from the tournament.

card.rule: According to Tetlock, superb forecasting and superb question-asking are different skills, and one should not assume they come together.
card.limits: It is a guess, not a result. Tetlock says we do not actually know.

concepts.title: Friedman’s oil column and the Tom-Bill symbiosis
concepts.question: Why does Tetlock say superforecasters and superquestioners should work together instead of competing?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, superforecasters and superquestioners need to acknowledge each other’s complementary strengths. Friedman’s provocative questions sharpen forecasters’ foresight, and forecasters’ well-calibrated answers fine-tune, and sometimes overhaul, questioners’ mental models.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Tetlock reads a December 2014 Friedman column on plunging oil prices. Friedman noted that the 1986 to 1999 oil slump had profound consequences and predicted ‘a lot of surprises’ in Venezuela, Iran and Russia if today’s fall is sustained. As a forecast it is vague. Read as a pointer to something forecasters should think about, it is a question, not an answer.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The Tom-Bill symbiosis. Tetlock calls the ‘Tom versus Bill’ frame from the start of the book his final false dichotomy.

card.rule: Read a vague warning as a question for forecasters to answer, and pair questioners with forecasters.
card.limits: Tetlock says the column is not a helpful forecast, and he knows some see Friedman as slippery. The point is to use it differently.

concepts.title: The Bernanke letter, four years on
concepts.question: How did the signatories of the 2010 letter to Bernanke answer when asked in hindsight, and why does it matter?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, the signatories’ replies capture what is wrong with so many public debates: those who replied said unanimously that they were right and would not change a word.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: In November 2010 a letter warned Fed chairman Ben Bernanke that his asset purchases ‘risk currency debasement and inflation’. He went ahead; the dollar did not weaken and inflation did not rise. In October 2014 Bloomberg reporters asked the signatories how they felt. Their reasons fell into two kinds: the wrong measure was being looked at, and the letter’s wording meant it had not been proved wrong.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: No name given.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.text: Bloomberg reporters collected the signatories’ replies in 2014, after Tetlock wrote about the letter in chapter 3.

card.rule: A forecast worded loosely enough can never be proved wrong, so its authors need never change their minds.
card.limits: Tetlock does not say the signatories were wrong on substance. His point is about how they responded.

concepts.title: Keynesians, Austerians and a failure of process
concepts.question: Why does Tetlock call the Keynesian-Austerian aftermath a failure even though he takes no side on the substance?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, the aftermath of the 2010 letter illustrates a failure of process, not necessarily of substance. One group spelled out its beliefs in writing, another disagreed vehemently, four years passed and no one budged. That should be unsatisfactory to everyone.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: After the turmoil of 2008 and 2009, two camps formed. Keynesians urged bold central-bank action and heavy deficit spending. Austerians urged budget cuts and warned the Keynesian policies would ignite inflation and sink currencies. Governments struck compromises. What should have followed was a comparison of predictions with outcomes, and updating. Instead, people so rarely changed their minds that when a Minneapolis Fed president, an Austerian, said the Keynesians were closer to the truth, it made headlines.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The Keynesians and the Austerians, the two camps.

card.rule: Judge a debate by whether anyone updated after the facts came in, not by who sounds the more convincing.
card.limits: Tetlock says he is agnostic on issues outside his field. His complaint is about process, not about who was right.

concepts.title: Adversarial collaboration for forecasters
concepts.question: How could rival camps design forecasts that test their disagreement?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, when a debate like Keynesians versus Austerians emerges, key figures could work with trusted third parties to identify what they disagree about and which forecasts would meaningfully test it. The key is precision.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The model is the adversarial collaboration between Daniel Kahneman and Gary Klein, two psychologists with apparently contradictory schools who got together to discuss why their views differed and how to reconcile them. In forecasting, it is not enough to say a policy will cause inflation. How much, measured by what benchmark, over what period? The result must be a question with ambiguity reduced to an absolute minimum.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Adversarial collaboration, as in the Kahneman-Klein case.

card.rule: Rivals should agree in advance on precise forecast questions that would meaningfully test what they disagree about.
card.limits: This is Tetlock’s proposal, not something that has been done at scale. It needs willing participants.

concepts.title: Learning, not gloating: the catch of good faith
concepts.question: What outcome of adversarial forecasting does Tetlock welcome, and what does it require of the participants?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to Tetlock, a split decision across many questions is a feature, not a bug: it shows reality is more mixed than either side thought. If learning, not gloating, is the goal, that is progress. The catch is that it presumes good faith.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A single dot on a canvas is not a painting, and a single bet cannot resolve a complex theoretical dispute, so it takes many questions and clusters. A major point of view rarely has zero merit. In noisy public arenas strident voices dominate and have no interest in adversarial collaboration, but there are less voluble and more reasonable voices.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: A split decision, which Tetlock calls a feature, not a bug.

card.rule: Measure success by what the participants learn, and look for reasonable voices who want the truth more than a win.
card.limits: The approach needs good faith. Strident voices will not join, and Tetlock only bets on the quieter ones.

concepts.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.title: Precision and intellectual humility
concepts.question: Which two habits of Bill Flack does the epilogue offer as reasons he is a superforecaster?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, precision and intellectual humility are two of the reasons Bill Flack is a superforecaster.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Flack told the author he was not quite a native Cornhusker: he was born in Kansas City, Missouri, and moved to Nebraska at seven. He also said he does not belong at Davos, because he would have to search the web for basic facts about a country that experts on it know by heart.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Intellectual humility is the epilogue's label for knowing what you do not know. Precision is named too, but not as a technical term.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Humility here does not mean a weak record. The epilogue says Flack has an outstanding record on tough real-world questions, shown by his Brier score.

card.rule: According to the authors, a superforecaster is exact about small facts and honest about what he does not know.
card.limits: Our reading: the epilogue shows these traits in one man and offers them as reasons, not as a complete recipe for superforecasting.

concepts.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.title: Using pundits like lawyers
concepts.question: How does Flack use pundits, and what does the baseball image add?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a superforecaster can use pundits without dismissing them or deferring to them: Flack treats the good ones as advocates and builds his own forecast from their arguments.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Flack calls a pundit bad when the forecast comes with no argument or only anecdotes. Good pundits argue their case, like lawyers in an adversarial court. He weighs everyone's arguments, digs into background where needed, and forms a forecast that is a weighted sum of theirs.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Dragonfly eye is the authors' phrase for the view in which Flack and a big strategic thinker complement each other.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: The authors add a baseball image: strategic thinkers may never be scored on batting averages, but they could pitch forecasting questions to aspiring batters.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Our reading: the text gives no formula for the weights in the weighted sum; the weighing is Flack's own judgment.

card.rule: According to the authors, treat a pundit's argument as evidence to weigh, not as a pronouncement to obey or ignore.
card.limits: The method needs an argument to weigh; a bare pronouncement or an anecdote gives a forecaster little to work with.

concepts.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.title: Luck, slumps and perpetual beta
concepts.question: Why does Flack expect his success may not last, and how does he respond to feedback?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, Flack stays a superforecaster because he accepts that luck helped him and keeps adjusting to feedback. They call this being perpetual beta.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The authors say slumps are inevitable: history often passes through phases of irreducible uncertainty, where luck beats skill and statistics point to regression to the mean. Flack says luck played a part in his success. An overconfident forecast that goes wrong can hit the Brier score hard, and a few could separate a terrific season from a terrible one.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Perpetual beta is the authors' name for the cycle of try, fail, analyze, adjust and try again, with the grit to keep improving.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Flack does not predict failure. A bad run would not shatter his image of himself as a reasonably competent superforecaster, but would make him more cautious and less prone to extreme forecasts.

card.rule: According to the authors, treat success as partly luck, expect slumps, and let score feedback change how you forecast.
card.limits: Flack expects to become more cautious after overconfident misses; the epilogue does not say to avoid extreme forecasts altogether.

concepts.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.title: Triage: the Goldilocks zone
concepts.question: Which questions does the first commandment say are worth effort, and which are not?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, concentrate on questions where hard work is likely to pay off, and skip those that are too easy or too hopeless.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Clocklike questions can be answered close to right with simple rules of thumb. Cloudlike questions defeat even fancy statistical models. A presidential winner twelve years out is hopeless: nobody in 1940 could have named Eisenhower as the 1952 winner, and thinking so is hindsight bias.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Triage is the commandment's name. The middle band is the Goldilocks zone of difficulty, between clocklike and cloudlike.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Triage gets harder closer to home. In March 2015 the 2016 field could be narrowed to a few plausible contenders, far better than for 2028.

card.rule: According to the authors, put effort into the Goldilocks zone, where questions are neither clocklike nor cloudlike.
card.limits: Triage calls are judgment calls and get harder close to home. The authors add that how unpredictable a class is often shows only after trying.

concepts.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.title: Break problems apart: Fermi-izing
concepts.question: How does the second commandment make an impossible-seeming question tractable?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, break an intractable problem into sub-problems, in the playful but disciplined spirit of Enrico Fermi, and make best guesses so that errors surface early.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Peter Backus, a lonely man in London, started from about six million people and narrowed by the share who are women, single, in the right age range, graduates, found attractive by him, finding him attractive, and compatible. He reached roughly twenty-six women: a daunting but not impossible search.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Fermi-izing is the authors' word for this habit, and a Fermi estimate is the number it produces.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: There is no objectively correct answer to a true-love question. Superforecasters' Fermi estimates in the IARPA tournament can be scored, and good estimates often come from crude assumptions.

card.rule: According to the authors, split a hard question into parts, guess each part in the open, and let the pieces build a number you can check.
card.limits: Backus's estimate cannot be scored, so it shows the method only; the authors score accuracy where questions resolve, as in the tournament.

concepts.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.title: Balancing the outside and inside views
concepts.question: How does the third commandment balance the outside view with the inside view?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, nothing is entirely unique, so first ask how often things of this sort happen in situations of this sort, then adjust for what is special about this case.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Superforecasters search for comparison classes even for seemingly unique events, such as the hunt for Joseph Kony or Greece's standoff with its creditors. Larry Summers, aware that employees underestimate project time by factors of two or three, doubled an estimate and moved to the next higher time unit.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The outside view starts from the comparison class. The planning fallacy is the habit of underestimating how long a project will take. The inside view is evidence about the particular case.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Summers would adjust if an employee astonished him by delivering on time. He balances his outside-view expectation against inside-view evidence, because each of us is to some degree unique.

card.rule: According to the authors, set your expectation from the comparison class, then adjust for evidence about the particular case.
card.limits: Uniqueness is a matter of degree, so no comparison class fits perfectly and a particular case may be an exception.

concepts.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.title: Updating and degrees of doubt
concepts.question: How finely should a forecaster update beliefs and distinguish degrees of doubt?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, update neither too little nor too much, and tell apart as many degrees of doubt as the problem permits but no more.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The best forecasters tend to update in small steps, such as 0.4 to 0.35 or 0.6 to 0.65, differences too fine for words like might or maybe. Yet they also jump when a signal is diagnostic. The authors imagine Obama hearing the bin Laden estimates as basketball odds: not fifty-fifty, but between three to one and four to one.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Belief updating is compared to brushing and flossing: boring, sometimes uncomfortable, and worthwhile in the long run. Vague verbiage is the authors' name for hedging words.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Superforecasters are not perfect Bayesian updaters, only better than most. The line between a subtle clue and a misleading one is fine, and the aim is not infinite fineness.

card.rule: According to the authors, move estimates in small steps on weak signals, jump on diagnostic ones, and use more than three settings of doubt.
card.limits: Finer distinctions help only as far as the problem permits, and a subtle clue can be a misleading one.

concepts.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.title: Clashing causal forces and synthesis
concepts.question: What does the fifth commandment ask of a dove or a hawk, and why is synthesis hard?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, look for the clashing causal forces in each problem, grant the best counterargument, and then synthesize the competing views into one judgment.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: A devout dove who thinks threats never bring peace, or a devout hawk who thinks appeasement never pays, should be open to being wrong about Iran. Each side should list, in advance, the signs that would nudge it toward the other side.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Dragonfly eye is the view in which one view meets another and another and all merge into one image. Someone who does this well can become a dove-hawk.

blocks.label: In practice
blocks.text: List in advance the evidence that would move you toward the opposing view, and keep a counterargument in sight.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors say there are no paint-by-number rules: synthesis is an art that reconciles irreducibly subjective judgments.

card.rule: According to the authors, name the best counterargument and the signs that would move you, then merge the views into one judgment.
card.limits: No formula exists for the merger; it rests on subjective judgment, so two careful forecasters may merge the same views differently.

concepts.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.title: Balancing errors and learning from mistakes
concepts.question: Which balances do the seventh and eighth commandments ask a forecaster to strike?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, balance prudence against decisiveness, and learn from mistakes and from successes without learning too little or too much.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: Superforecasters know the risk of rushing to judgment and the risk of dawdling near maybe. Long-term accuracy needs good scores on both calibration and resolution. After a failure, own it and run an unflinching postmortem. Do postmortems on successes too, since you may have lucked out through offsetting errors.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Calibration and resolution are the two scores named in the seventh commandment; the text does not define them. A postmortem is a hard look at where reasoning went wrong.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The authors say the more common error is to learn too little from failure. Learning too much is also possible, as when a minor technical mistake is mistaken for a flaw in a basically sound approach.

card.rule: According to the authors, avoid both rushing and dawdling, and run postmortems on failures and successes alike.
card.limits: Learning too much from one failure is also possible, and a success can come from offsetting errors, so it does not prove the reasoning.

concepts.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.title: Bringing out the best in others
concepts.question: Which three skills does the ninth commandment name for working with others?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, a forecaster should bring out the best in others and let others bring out the best in them, by mastering the fine arts of team management.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: The commandment names three skills: perspective taking, understanding the other side's arguments so well that you could state them to its satisfaction; precision questioning, helping others clarify arguments so they are not misunderstood; and constructive confrontation, disagreeing without being disagreeable.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: Perspective taking, precision questioning and constructive confrontation are the three names, each defined as above.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: Wise leaders know the lines are fine: a helpful suggestion versus micromanaging, a rigid group versus a decisive one, a scatterbrained group versus an open-minded one.

card.rule: According to the authors, practise perspective taking, precision questioning and constructive confrontation, and mind the fine lines in leading.
card.limits: The lines are thin: the same behaviour can be helpful or meddling, and a group can look decisive or rigid depending on its balance.

concepts.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
concepts.title: The error-balancing bicycle
concepts.question: Why can a forecaster not learn from a manual, and why are the commandments not commandments?

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.text: According to the authors, each commandment requires balancing opposing errors, skill comes from doing with clear feedback, and the list is a set of guidelines, not binding rules.

blocks.label: Evidence
blocks.text: You cannot learn to ride a bicycle by reading a physics textbook, and you cannot become a superforecaster by reading training manuals. Practice needs feedback that leaves no doubt about success or failure, and it is not just making casual forecasts after reading the news.

blocks.label: Name it
blocks.text: The error-balancing bicycle is the tenth commandment's image. Deep, deliberative practice is the authors' name for the practice that builds expertise.

blocks.label: Do not overread
blocks.text: The eleventh item says not to treat commandments as commandments. Guidelines are the best that can be done where nothing is certain or exactly repeatable, and they require constant mindfulness.

card.rule: According to the authors, practise with unambiguous feedback, balance opposing errors, and treat the list as guidelines.
card.limits: Guidelines cannot cover cases that are never exactly alike, so even following them dutifully needs constant mindfulness.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: The thesis in one claim
concepts.question: What one claim does the whole book set out to support, and how wide is it?

paragraphs: According to the authors, chapter 1 states the book's two conclusions. One: foresight is real, meaning some people show a measurable skill at judging how high-stakes events will unfold. Two: what makes them good is what they do, not who they are, so the habits behind the skill can be learned by an intelligent, determined person.

The claim is bounded. The skill the authors measured covers roughly three months to a year and a half ahead, and they say superforecasters are not oracles who see decades out. Our reading: the rest of the book supports these two conclusions, with chapters 2 to 4 on measuring, chapters 5 to 9 on habits, and chapters 10 to 12 on leadership, black swans and scorekeeping.
card.rule: According to the authors, foresight is real and learnable: a measurable skill, over months to about a year and a half, that comes from habits of thought rather than a gift.
card.limits: The claim covers roughly three months to a year and a half ahead and says nothing about decades; chapter 11 adds that there is no evidence of foresight ten years out beyond the obvious.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: The argument in four steps
concepts.question: In what order do the chapters build the case, and what does each step need from the one before?

paragraphs: Our reading: the book argues in four steps, and this order is ours, not the authors' outline. First, forecasts can be scored, but only if they are precise and judged against a benchmark (chapters 2 and 3, where the Brier score appears). Second, a fair tournament shows some forecasters beating the rest by a wide margin, and a luck check says skill explains most of it (chapter 4).

Third, the skilled share habits: starting from base rates, weighing many views, updating in small steps, practising with feedback and working in teams (chapters 5 to 9). Fourth, the authors test their own claim against leadership, black swans and scorekeeping (chapters 10 to 12), and the epilogue gathers the habits as guidelines.
Each step leans on the one before. Habits mean little unless the skill is real, and the skill is not shown unless forecasts are scored fairly.
card.rule: To judge the book's case, ask of each step what it assumes from the steps before it: scoring, then the tournament result, then the habits, then the limits.
card.limits: The four-step order is our reading aid. The chapters also loop back, for example chapter 8 returns to feedback and measurement while explaining how forecasters improve.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Measurement as the hinge
concepts.question: Which point about testing and scoring recurs in the chapters on medicine, vague words, intelligence agencies and feedback?

paragraphs: One proposition can appear in many sentences. Here it runs through the book: a belief about what works, or what will happen, earns trust only after a fair test. Chapter 1 says that without measurement there is no revision and no improvement. Chapter 2 shows medicine advancing only after random assignment replaced confident experience.

Chapter 3 adds that a forecast must be precise enough to score: vague terms and missing time frames make judging impossible. Chapter 4 reports that the intelligence community is held to its process, not to its accuracy. Chapter 8 says practice needs clear, timely feedback, and in chapter 12 Daniel Drezner resolves to keep score.
Our reading: the authors treat this as the lever for everything else, since the claims about habits and teams rest on forecasts that were scored.
card.rule: According to the authors, trust a method or a forecaster only after a fair test, which needs precise forecasts, a comparison and clear feedback.
card.limits: The authors do not say untested methods are wrong, only that nobody knows if they work; chapter 12 adds that numbers are tools that need scrutiny too.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Why skill rather than luck
concepts.question: Which separate findings combine to show superforecasters' results reflect skill, and what do the authors say stays luck?

paragraphs: The book argues for skill with several strands that point the same way. In Tetlock's earlier expert study, foxes beat hedgehogs on calibration and resolution, so the edge was real foresight and not mere caution. In the tournament, the superforecasters' lead over regular forecasters widened, ending more than 60% ahead.

A luck check follows. If top scorers were lucky, they would fall back toward the average the next year. Individuals do slip: roughly 30% leave the top group each year. But about 70% stay, a consistency that guessers would almost never show. The authors conclude superforecasters were mostly skilled, though not infallible.
The authors do not say luck is absent. Last-minute events and tangled systems put a floor under uncertainty. Our reading: the case is cumulative, and no single strand settles it.
card.rule: According to the authors, a lead over rivals, year-to-year consistency and a luck check together show mostly skill, not pure skill.
card.limits: The strands describe groups in one earlier study and one tournament. The authors say mostly skilled, not infallible, and say luck must have played a part on some questions.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Many views, one recurring idea
concepts.question: Which recurring idea do the fox, the crowd, the dragonfly eye, teams and adversarial collaboration all express?

paragraphs: One proposition can appear in different sentences. Our reading: several chapters express a similar one, that judgment improves when separate views are combined. Chapter 3 shows foxes drawing on many tools, and the average of many guesses at Galton's ox landing within a pound of the true weight. The dragonfly eye is the authors' picture of one clear image built from thousands of lenses.

Chapter 5 applies the idea inside one head, with the crowd within, and in superforecasters weighing many perspectives. Chapter 9 applies it to teams: aggregation works only when judgments are independent, and the key word is different. Chapter 12 proposes that rivals agree on joint forecast tests, and the epilogue has the forecaster weigh pundits as advocates.
The authors do not state this link in one sentence; it is our reading of how these parts fit.
card.rule: Our reading: judgment gains when differing views are combined, whether inside one head, across a crowd or within a team, provided the views are independent and different.
card.limits: Combining helps only when views differ and errors are independent. Chapter 9 warns that group discussion can destroy independence, and the fox and hedgehog model is a spectrum, not a strict dichotomy.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: From chapters to guidelines
concepts.question: Which habits from the middle chapters does the epilogue gather into guidelines, and what does it add?

paragraphs: The book's practical answer is a set of habits. Break a hard question into parts and guess each one (Fermi-izing, chapter 5). Start from the base rate, then adjust for the case (outside and inside views, chapter 5). Tell apart more than three degrees of doubt (chapter 6). Update in small steps, and jump when a signal is strong (chapter 7).

Learn from outcomes through postmortems and clear feedback (chapter 8), and bring out the best in others through perspective taking, precision questioning and constructive confrontation (chapter 9). The epilogue adds triage: spend effort on questions in the Goldilocks zone, neither clocklike nor cloudlike.

According to the authors, each guideline asks you to balance opposing errors, such as updating too little or too much, and the list ends by telling the reader not to treat commandments as commandments.
card.rule: According to the authors, apply the habits as guidelines that balance opposing errors, and practise them with clear feedback rather than learning them from a manual.
card.limits: Guidelines cannot cover cases that are never exactly alike. The last item warns against treating them as binding rules, and the authors say even dutiful use needs constant mindfulness.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Optimistic skeptic, first page to last
concepts.question: What does the book claim to have solved, and what does it leave open?

paragraphs: According to Tetlock, he is an optimistic skeptic. Chapter 1 gives the skeptic's reasons, the butterfly effect and nonlinear systems that limit long-range foresight, and the optimist's, the pockets of predictability and the tournament results. Predictability exists, it says, to some degree and in some circumstances.

Chapter 11 ends in the same place. Tetlock agrees with Kahneman and Taleb that there is no evidence of foresight ten years out beyond the obvious, yet holds that careful work yields accurate forecasts about some developments that matter. The problem the book claims to solve is therefore bounded: seeing better over months to about a year and a half.

By the authors' own account, two things stay open: whether superforecasters can spot rare, high-impact events, which a short-term tournament cannot show, and how to score the biggest questions. Chapter 12 offers question clustering as a way forward, not a finished answer.
card.rule: According to the authors, the book solves a bounded problem, seeing better at short horizons, and leaves long-run foresight and rare events open.
card.limits: Our reading: the authors give no complete inventory of what remains open; the open points here are the ones chapters 11 and 12 name.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: What the book asks of those who use forecasts
concepts.question: What does the book ask of organisations and readers who rely on forecasts, and why does it expect resistance?

paragraphs: According to the authors, the problem is partly on the demand side: governments, business and the public rarely ask for evidence of accuracy. Tetlock hopes for an evidence-based forecasting revolution, in which buyers expect forecasters to show tested track records as they expect a pill to have passed peer-reviewed trials. He adds that nothing may change.

The book names reasons for resistance. People whose standing rests on untested judgment have little to gain from testing (chapter 4), and numbers expose intelligence analysts to blame, so fuzzy words feel safer (chapter 12). Codman's hospital results show that such resistance can still be overcome.
For readers, the epilogue's advice is to treat a pundit's argument as evidence to weigh, like a lawyer's case, not as a pronouncement to obey or ignore.
card.rule: According to the authors, ask forecasters for a tested track record, expect resistance from those whose standing depends on untested judgment, and weigh arguments instead of obeying pundits.
card.limits: This is Tetlock's hope, stated with caution; he says the change may not come. Codman shows that resistance can be beaten once, not that it will be again.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: What the evidence supports
concepts.question: Which limits on the tournament evidence does the book itself state, and which one is our own reading?

paragraphs: Judging soundness means asking what the evidence can carry. The book states several limits itself. Most tournament questions looked more than one month and less than one year ahead. The forecasters were volunteers who stayed through testing, not a random sample. The report that superforecasters beat intelligence analysts with secret data by about 30% is secondhand, from an unnamed participant.

The authors also warn against over-reading their own findings. Superteam results are promising but not a recipe for organizations, and many small updates is not a skeleton key. A short-term tournament cannot show skill at spotting rare, high-impact events.

Our reading: the headline results come from the authors' own team, though the tournament was run by an outside agency, IARPA, with a control group and rival teams. That outside design is a point in the book's favour.
card.rule: Judge the book by asking what each result can support: short horizons, volunteers, group averages and secondhand figures, as the authors themselves note.
card.limits: Naming a limit is not the same as refuting the case. The authors still hold that foresight is real at short horizons; a limit narrows the claim without removing it.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Objections the book raises, and its replies
concepts.question: How does the book answer Taleb and the humanists, and where do the replies concede rather than refute?

paragraphs: The book raises objections against itself. Taleb holds that black swans determine history, so what matters cannot be forecast. Tetlock calls this a false dichotomy but agrees a short-term tournament cannot show skill at rare events. Imagined humanists say numbers are applied where they do not belong; Tetlock finds truth in this and replies that numbers are tools to be scrutinised.

Saffo's challenge is that the questions that matter are hard to score, while scorable ones are narrow. Tetlock's reply is to score clusters of small, pertinent questions. The kto-kogo view says forecasts serve power; the authors grant that co-option happens but deny that it is the only motive.

Our reading: on rare events, the humanists and the cluster method, the replies concede or propose rather than refute. The cluster method comes with an illustration about Korea, not a scored test, and the book says the approach has conditions it cannot guarantee.
card.rule: To judge the book fairly, separate the objections it answers from those it concedes, and notice where a reply is a proposal rather than a result.
card.limits: The replies are Tetlock's account of the critics, not their own words, so a critic might frame them differently. Judging soundness also presumes the claims were understood first.

questions.q: According to the authors, what are we doing when we decide to change jobs or buy a home?
options: Gambling, because the outcome of such a choice is uncertain and cannot be known beforehand
Planning, which the chapter keeps apart from forecasting because planning needs no expectations
Forecasting, because the choice rests on an expectation of how the future will unfold
Guessing, because ordinary people lack the data that professional forecasters would use
optionExplain: Uncertainty is real, but the chapter calls the underlying expectation a forecast.
Planning depends on expectations about what comes next, which are forecasts.
Right: the expectation behind the choice is a forecast.
The chapter does not say ordinary expectations are guesses; it says they are forecasts.
questions.explain: The authors treat any expectation about the future that guides a decision as a forecast. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an expectation about how the future will unfold is a forecast, whether we make it or an expert does.

questions.q: The authors say that our expectations about how the future will unfold are ____.
questions.explain: Expectations that drive decisions about jobs, homes and investments are forecasts.
questions.rule: Expectations about the future are forecasts.

questions.q: A couple sign a two-year lease because they expect rents in their city to climb. What is that expectation?
options: A forecast, because it is a belief about how the future will unfold that guides a decision
A fact about the present, because rents in the city are already visible to everyone
Not a forecast, because only an expert asked to predict events produces a forecast
A forecast only once it has been written down, dated and scored by someone else
optionExplain: Right: it is an expectation about what comes next.
Present rents are fact; the expectation about next year is not.
The chapter says we often do our own forecasting.
Scoring matters for judging a forecast, not for being one.
questions.explain: A forecast is an expectation about the future that a decision rests on; writing and scoring come later.
questions.rule: Decisions rest on forecasts.

questions.q: Sort each item: does it rest on a forecast, or not?
