items.t: Buying a home because you expect prices to rise
Retiring this year because you expect savings to last
Launching a product because you expect demand
Recalling what you had for breakfast
Reading the temperature on a thermometer
Adding up the lines on a receipt

questions.explain: The first three depend on an expectation about the future. The others concern the past or the present.
questions.rule: A forecast looks forward.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says we are all forecasters and often do our own forecasting.
questions.explain: It opens by saying so, before turning to experts for big events.
questions.rule: Everyone forecasts.

questions.q: A regional war flares near a firm's factories. According to the chapter, whom do people tend to look to in such moments?
options: Their own judgment alone, since the authors say big events are too rare for experts to understand
Statistical models alone, because the chapter says experts are replaced once markets crash
No one, because the chapter says forecasts of war cannot be made by anyone
Experts and commentators in the know, such as Tom Friedman, whose columns and books reach millions
optionExplain: The chapter says we turn to experts for big events.
The chapter names no such replacement here.
The chapter later argues for limits, but here it says we look to experts.
Right: when big events happen we turn to those in the know.
questions.explain: At moments of crisis the chapter says people look to experts, and Friedman is its example of a widely read one.
questions.rule: In a crisis we turn to the expert voice.
questions.teaches: When big events happen, people turn to experts in the know; Friedman's columns and bestselling books reach millions of readers.

questions.q: What makes the book call Bill Flack a remarkable forecaster?
options: He is a famous commentator regularly consulted by presidents and chief executives about world events
His many forecasts were dated, recorded and assessed by independent scientific observers, with an excellent record
He holds a doctorate in mathematics and spent his career working for an intelligence agency
He once foresaw a single dramatic event that made his name and drew a large public following
optionExplain: The chapter says the opposite: no one asks him for his thoughts on CNN.
Right: the credibility comes from the measured record.
He left a math PhD program and worked for the Department of Agriculture.
The chapter rests on a record of about three hundred forecasts, not one event.
questions.explain: The authors rest their praise on a measured record, not on a reputation. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Judge a forecaster by a dated, recorded and independently assessed track record, not by fame or access.

questions.q: Bill Flack's forecasts count as credible because each was dated, recorded and ____ for accuracy by independent scientific observers.
questions.explain: The independent assessment of every dated forecast is what makes his record credible.
questions.rule: A record needs independent assessment.

questions.q: A neighbor claims to forecast local elections well but keeps no notes. What would make her claim checkable, by Bill's example?
options: Gathering a reputation for speaking confidently at meetings and being quoted in the local paper
Holding a degree in political science from a respected university and citing it often
Asking friends and family whether they remember her being right in the past few years
Dating and recording each forecast so an independent party can score it later
optionExplain: Confidence and quotation are the kind of fame the chapter says proves nothing.
Bill's credibility did not come from credentials.
Memory is not a dated, independent record.
Right: Bill's forecasts were dated, recorded and assessed.
questions.explain: Checkability needs a dated, recorded forecast and an outside judge.
questions.rule: Date it, record it, have it scored.

questions.q: Bill meets a question about the Shanghai Free Trade Zone and has no clue. According to the chapter, what does he do?
options: He declines to answer, because he lacks expertise in Chinese politics and trade rules
He does his homework: gathers facts, balances clashing arguments and settles on an answer
He waits for a respected commentator to publish a view and adopts that view as his own
He gives a quick instinctive guess drawn from his years of watching birds in the field
optionExplain: He answers about three hundred questions, many obscure.
Right: that is the process the chapter describes.
The chapter describes his own research, not borrowing a view.
The bird-watching is background; the method is homework and weighing arguments.
questions.explain: Even on obscure questions Bill researches and weighs arguments before settling on an answer.
questions.rule: Do the homework, weigh the arguments, commit.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says no one bases decisions on Bill Flack's forecasts, even though his record is excellent.
questions.explain: It calls this unfortunate: his forecasts are tested and good, but he has no platform.
questions.rule: Skill and attention are different things.

questions.q: A friend says Bill's questions must be easy because he is only a retiree. Which chapter detail answers that?
options: Corporations, banks, embassies and intelligence agencies struggle with the same kind of question
Bill took roughly three hundred questions, and the authors say a large number proves each was easy
The questions came from a newspaper his parents owned, which kept them local and simple
Bill studied ornithology, which the chapter says trains the mind for geopolitical questions
optionExplain: Right: the chapter calls the questions difficult for large institutions.
Volume does not show ease; the chapter calls the questions difficult.
His parents' paper is background; the questions were about world events.
Ornithology is background, not an explanation of the questions' difficulty.
questions.explain: The chapter says institutions with large staffs struggle with questions like Bill's, so they are hard.
questions.rule: Retired does not mean unqualified; difficulty is in the question.
questions.teaches: The questions Bill answers are ones that corporations, banks, embassies and intelligence agencies struggle with, so they are difficult.

questions.q: Among the thousands of volunteers forecasting the same questions, roughly what share were as good as Bill Flack?
options: About 20%
About half
About 2%
Almost none
optionExplain: Too large; most volunteers were not as good as Bill.
Far too large; the chapter says most are not as good as Bill.
Right: the chapter says most are not as good as Bill, but about 2% are.
Not so: the chapter says about 2% are, and calls them superforecasters.
questions.explain: A small group stood out. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a superforecaster is shown by a measured record of accuracy, not by a profession or a title.

questions.q: The authors call the roughly 2% of volunteers who forecast as well as Bill Flack ____.
questions.explain: The authors coined the term for this small group, with reliable evidence behind it.
questions.rule: The top 2% are superforecasters.

questions.q: A tournament has 1,000 volunteer forecasters. Using the chapter's figure, about how many would be superforecasters?
options: About 200
About 20
About 500
About 2
optionExplain: That would be 20%, ten times the chapter's figure.
Right: 2% of 1,000 is 20.
That would be half of them, far above the chapter's 2%.
That would be 0.2%, ten times too small.
questions.explain: Two percent of 1,000 volunteers is 20 people.
questions.rule: 2% of a pool.

questions.q: Sort each item: does it fit the chapter's description of superforecasters?

items.t: Volunteers who answered the same questions as Bill
Include engineers, lawyers, artists and students
About 2% of the volunteer pool
A group chosen for fame as television commentators
Only professors from leading universities
Most of the volunteers

questions.explain: The chapter describes a small, varied group of volunteers, identified by reliable evidence of accuracy.
questions.rule: Rare, varied, measured.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says the superforecasters include engineers, lawyers, artists, scientists and students.
questions.explain: It lists them, to show that the skill is not tied to a profession.
questions.rule: Skill is not tied to a profession.

questions.q: A company assumes strong forecasters must be full-time analysts. Which chapter detail challenges that view?
options: The superforecasters described all hold full-time jobs in intelligence agencies and banks
Most of the volunteers outperformed Bill Flack after a few weeks of practice with the questions
Superforecasters were chosen from a list of famous pundits who agreed to be scored
The superforecasters the book introduces include a mathematician, a filmmaker and retirees with underused talents
optionExplain: The chapter says they include students, artists and retirees.
The chapter says most were not as good as Bill.
They were volunteers, not pundits chosen for fame.
Right: the chapter says we will meet people of such varied backgrounds.
questions.explain: The chapter says the authors will introduce a mathematician, a filmmaker and some retirees.
questions.rule: Do not assume a type.
questions.teaches: Among the superforecasters we will meet are a mathematician, a filmmaker and some retirees eager to share their underused talents.

questions.q: According to the chapter, how good is Tom Friedman's forecasting record?
options: Excellent, because he is read by millions and is said to have foreseen the Arab Spring
Poor, because critics point to his mistakes about the 2003 invasion of Iraq
Unknown, because the accuracy of his forecasting has never been rigorously tested
Average, matching the typical expert in the researcher's twenty-year study of experts
optionExplain: Fans cite this, but the chapter calls it opinion.
Critics cite this, but the chapter calls it opinion too.
Right: there are only opinions about his record.
Friedman was not scored, so no such comparison exists.
questions.explain: The chapter says the question cannot be answered, because no rigorous test exists. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the quality of a forecaster is known only from a rigorously tested record, not from opinions about hits and misses.

questions.q: In the chapter, Friedman's fans and critics trade opinions because nobody has rigorously ____ his forecasting accuracy.
questions.explain: Without a rigorous test there are only opinions on opinions.
questions.rule: No test, no facts.

questions.q: A pundit's fans say he nailed one crisis; critics say he missed another. What does the chapter's reasoning say this shows?
options: Nothing reliable about his overall accuracy, without a systematic and scored record
That his accuracy is probably about average, since the hit and the miss offset each other
That critics should win, since a single miss counts for more than a single success
That the fans are right, since one clear success proves the pundit has real foresight
optionExplain: Right: single hits and misses are opinions, not a record.
Two cases cannot set an average; no record exists.
The chapter does not weigh misses over hits.
One success may be luck; the chapter wants a tested record.
questions.explain: Selected hits and misses do not make a track record.
questions.rule: Records, not anecdotes.

questions.q: Match each case to how its forecasting quality is known in the chapter.
pairs: Delivered without asking how good the forecaster is
questions.explain: Only baseball and Bill Flack have measured records; the media and Friedman's record rest on opinion.
questions.rule: Know the record before trusting the voice.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter concludes that Tom Friedman forecasts worse than the superforecasters.
questions.explain: It says the comparison cannot be answered, since his accuracy has never been rigorously tested.
questions.rule: Untested is not the same as poor.

questions.q: A government buys yearly economic forecasts and does not check them later. What does the chapter suggest about their value?
options: They may be prescient, worthless or something in between, and the buyer cannot tell which
They are probably prescient, because paying a high price signals that the forecasts are of high quality
They are probably worthless, because forecasts about the economy are rarely right in the long run
They are probably average, because unchecked forecasts drift toward the typical level over the years
optionExplain: Right: unchecked forecasts have unknown quality.
Price is not a measure of accuracy.
The chapter does not say that; it says quality is unknown.
No such drift is described; quality is simply unknown.
questions.explain: The chapter says corporations and governments pay for forecasts that may be prescient, worthless or in between.
questions.rule: Unmeasured means unknown.
questions.teaches: Every day corporations and governments pay for forecasts that may be prescient or worthless or something in between.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say forecasting is a skill that can be cultivated.
questions.explain: They reject the idea that it is a talent some have and others lack. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, treat forecasting as a skill that can be cultivated, not as an inborn gift.

questions.q: The authors say forecasting is not a talent you have or don't, but a ____ that can be cultivated.
questions.explain: Skills can be built; the authors argue forecasting is one.
questions.rule: Forecasting can be cultivated.

questions.q: An office manager says: 'Some people are born forecasters, so training is a waste.' Which reply matches the chapter?
options: Training helps only those already in the top 2%, since the rest cannot improve at all
Training is a waste, but only because computers will replace human forecasters soon
Everyone becomes a superforecaster after reading a book, so the manager is mistaken
Forecasting is not an all-or-nothing talent; it is a skill that can be cultivated
optionExplain: The chapter says many readers may become reasonable to rely on.
That is a different claim; the authors do not say training is a waste.
The chapter promises to show how, not that reading guarantees it.
Right: that is the authors' claim.
questions.explain: The authors reject the born-forecaster view and say the book shows how to cultivate the skill.
questions.rule: Skill, not destiny.

questions.q: If the authors are right, what should happen to accuracy when readers practice the habits the book describes?
options: It stays fixed, because accuracy is set by inborn talent that practice cannot change
It can improve, because forecasting is a skill that can be cultivated
It falls, because overthinking forecasts makes them worse than natural intuition
It improves only for readers who already hold a mathematics degree and work in finance
optionExplain: That is the view the authors reject.
Right: skills grow with the right practice.
No such claim appears in the chapter.
The chapter says readers of many backgrounds may become reliable.
questions.explain: A cultivable skill can be improved.
questions.rule: Skills improve with practice.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter treats Bill Flack's success as proof that only rare, gifted individuals can forecast well.
questions.explain: It uses Bill to argue the opposite: forecasting is a skill, and many readers may become reliable.
questions.rule: One strong case is not a gift.

questions.q: A hospital must choose between a volunteer with a tested record and a celebrity with none. What does the chapter's reasoning favor?
options: The celebrity, because fame shows that audiences have found his forecasts useful over time
Neither, because the authors say no forecaster can be trusted with decisions that matter
The volunteer, since a tested record makes relying on his forecasts look quite reasonable
Whoever sounds more confident, since confidence is the best sign of forecasting skill
optionExplain: Fame is not a record.
They say relying on Bill looks reasonable.
Right: the authors say this about Bill Flack.
Confidence is what the chapter says pundits use instead of a record.
questions.explain: A tested record is a reasonable basis for reliance; fame is not.
questions.rule: Prefer the record.
questions.teaches: Given his tested record, the authors say that relying on Bill Flack's forecasts looks quite reasonable.

questions.q: In Tetlock's twenty-year study, how did the average expert's accuracy compare with random guessing?
options: Much better, since experts hold specialist knowledge that chance cannot match
Far worse, since experts were overconfident and often pointed in the wrong direction
Slightly better on every question, with the gap growing as the forecasts looked further out
About the same
optionExplain: The study found otherwise.
The study did not find experts worse than chance on average.
Accuracy fell with distance, not rose.
Right: the average expert did about as well as random guessing.
questions.explain: The headline result is the chimp joke. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to Tetlock, the average expert did about as well as random guessing on the questions posed.

questions.q: The joke sums up Tetlock's finding: the average expert was about as accurate as a dart-throwing ____.
questions.explain: The joke stands for random guessing.
questions.rule: Average expert, near chance.

questions.q: A pundit says: 'The study proved my forecasts are random.' What is wrong with that claim?
options: The study measured only experts in economics, so it says nothing about political pundits
The study found that pundits score better than chance, so the claim reverses its result
The study reported the average across many experts and questions, so it does not settle any one pundit
The study was done by a researcher with no access to the pundits' forecasts at all
optionExplain: It covered the economy, stocks, elections and wars.
The study found the average expert near chance.
Right: an average does not describe each individual.
He gathered the experts' predictions and checked their accuracy.
questions.explain: An average across experts leaves room for individuals to differ; Tetlock's later point is that one group had modest foresight.
questions.rule: Averages are not individuals.

questions.q: Sort each item: was it part of the study as the chapter describes it?

items.t: Thousands of predictions on the economy, elections and wars
Experts including academics and pundits
Accuracy checked after time had passed
Volunteer amateurs recruited online
A tournament run by an intelligence agency
A project launched in the summer of 2011

questions.explain: The chimp study used experts and checked their predictions over about twenty years. The tournament with volunteers came later.
questions.rule: Know which study is which.

questions.q: True or false: According to Tetlock, his study showed the average expert did about as well as random guessing.
questions.explain: That is the finding behind the chimp joke, not a result of worse than chance.
questions.rule: Near chance, not below it.

questions.q: A columnist says the whole message of the study was the chimp joke. How does Tetlock describe its results?
options: Entirely captured by the joke, which he still enjoys telling at every opportunity
Far richer and more constructive than the punch line suggested
Mostly negative, with no useful finding beyond the one that experts match chance
Unimportant, because the study was too small to say anything about expert judgment
optionExplain: He says he tired of the joke.
Right: he says so.
He says the results were constructive.
He calls it the most comprehensive assessment of its kind.
questions.explain: Tetlock says the joke understated the study; later parts of the chapter give the richer findings.
questions.rule: The joke is not the study.
questions.teaches: Tetlock says the results were far richer and more constructive than the punch line suggested.

questions.q: According to the authors, why are most forecasting experts on camera?
options: They tell a compelling story with conviction, not because they have proven forecasting skill
Networks check their records and put the most accurate forecasters on the air
Their forecasts are tested against outcomes each year, so the best are invited back
Their cautious tone earns viewers' trust, so networks prefer experts who hedge
optionExplain: Right: that is the talent the chapter names.
Accuracy is seldom even mentioned.
Pundits are almost never asked to reconcile forecasts with outcomes.
More experts are bold than cautious.
questions.explain: The authors say accuracy has little to do with it. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a pundit's visibility rests on storytelling and conviction, not on a checked record.

questions.q: The one talent the authors say talking heads reliably have is telling a compelling ____ with conviction.
questions.explain: Storytelling with conviction is enough to get airtime, the authors say.
questions.rule: Conviction sells.

questions.q: A panel host does not revisit last year's confident predictions. Which part of the chapter's account does this fit?
options: Pundits claim to see decades into the future, so last year's forecasts are too short to matter
Old forecasts are like old news, and pundits are seldom asked to reconcile them with what happened
Cautious experts are preferred, so the host avoids bold predictions that could be checked
Media experts are scored by independent observers, who say last year's forecasts were fine
optionExplain: A few claim long vision, but that is a different point.
Right: the host illustrates that pattern.
More experts are bold, not cautious.
The chapter says no such scoring happens.
questions.explain: Forgetting old forecasts is the habit the authors describe.
questions.rule: Ask for the follow-up.

questions.q: Which statements does the chapter make about media forecasters? Select all that apply.
options: Accuracy is seldom even mentioned
Some are cautious, but more are bold and confident
A handful claim to see decades into the future
Most are asked to reconcile earlier forecasts with outcomes
Their forecasts are scored publicly each year
optionExplain: Right: the chapter says so.
Right: the chapter says more are bold.
Right: it calls them Olympian visionaries.
The chapter says they almost never are.
No such scoring is described.
questions.explain: Accuracy goes unmentioned and boldness dominates; pundits are not held to account.
questions.rule: Notice what is missing: a record.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the chimp joke makes a valid point, though retelling later distorted it.
questions.explain: They say it makes a valid point about experts without proven skill, and that the retold message mutated.
questions.rule: A valid point can still be overstated.

questions.q: Why do the authors compare some forecasts sold to executives with elixirs sold from the back of a wagon?
options: Buyers who would never take medicine of unknown efficacy and safety routinely pay for forecasts of untested value
Both are sold by persuasive speakers, and the authors say persuasion is always a sign of fraud
Both have been banned in most countries after studies showed they did harm to customers
Both rely on ancient methods that modern science has replaced with statistical tests
optionExplain: Right: the comparison is about untested products.
The authors do not say persuasion proves fraud.
No bans are mentioned.
The comparison is about lack of testing, not antiquity.
questions.explain: The chapter contrasts our care about medicine with our carelessness about forecasts.
questions.rule: Test before you buy.
questions.teaches: People who would never swallow medicine of unknown efficacy and safety routinely pay for forecasts as dubious as elixirs sold from the back of a wagon.

questions.q: In Tetlock's research, how did expert accuracy change as forecasts looked further ahead?
options: Accuracy rose with distance, since long-range questions give events more time to unfold
Accuracy stayed at chimp level for every horizon, from one month to ten years
Beating chance was easiest about a year out, and accuracy fell toward chimp level by three to five years
Experts did best three to five years out, where their deep knowledge of trends mattered most
optionExplain: The opposite happened.
Short-range questions were easiest to beat chance on.
Right: accuracy fell with distance.
Chimp level was approached there.
questions.explain: Distance mattered a great deal. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to Tetlock, the finding is about the limits of expertise on many questions, with accuracy highest at about one year and fading by three to five years.

questions.q: Tetlock says his message was garbled, like the children's game of ____.
questions.explain: In telephone a whispered phrase changes as it passes along.
questions.rule: Retelling distorts.

questions.q: A blogger writes: 'Tetlock proved all expert forecasts are useless.' Which correction fits his research?
options: It showed experts beat chance on every question, but only by a small margin
It showed expert forecasts are useless at every horizon, short or long, though only for economics
It showed experts are useless on average but excellent when they are confident
It showed little better than guessing on many questions, not all, with short-range ones easiest
optionExplain: It showed the average was near chance.
Short-range questions were easier to beat chance on.
Confidence was not what the chapter credits.
Right: many does not equal all.
questions.explain: The blogger's version drops the limits on many questions and the effect of horizon.
questions.rule: Check the retelling.

questions.q: Based on the research, which question should experts find easiest to beat chance on?
options: What will happen four years from now, as the long view lets patterns show up
What will happen five years from now, because experts can reason about trends
What will happen within the next year
All horizons equally, since expertise does not depend on how far ahead one looks
optionExplain: Four years is near chimp level.
Five years is near chimp level.
Right: the shortest-range questions were easiest.
Accuracy fell with distance.
questions.explain: Accuracy was best at about a year and fell off with distance.
questions.rule: Shorter is easier.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says it was easiest to beat chance on the shortest-range questions, those one year out.
questions.explain: Accuracy fell off as experts looked further out, so the claim of no skill at any horizon is wrong.
questions.rule: Horizon matters.

questions.q: A speaker waves away a climate briefing by citing the chimp study. Whose use of the study does this resemble?
options: Know-nothing populists who put the phrase so-called in front of the word expert
Debunkers who gather evidence from tournaments and revise their models each year
Meteorologists who compare forecasts with outcomes and adjust their models afterwards
Insurance actuaries who estimate life spans from large samples of past records
optionExplain: Right: the chapter names them among those who turned the study into a backstop.
That describes the authors' method, not the garbled use.
Meteorologists test forecasts; they do not dismiss all expertise.
Actuaries use data; the speaker waves expertise away.
questions.explain: The chapter says nihilists and know-nothing populists made the study a backstop reference.
questions.rule: Do not use the study as a slogan.
questions.teaches: The garbled message became a backstop reference for nihilists who see the future as inherently unpredictable and for know-nothing populists.

questions.q: Which view does Tetlock say he holds about forecasting?
options: Prediction is a fool's errand, and the sensible course is to stop trying to forecast
Confident experts are the most reliable, so their forecasts deserve our trust by default
With enough data and effort, anyone can see decades ahead with reasonable accuracy
Some foresight is possible in some situations and to some extent, though there are limits
optionExplain: He rejects the debunkers on this.
He finds experts' confidence is no proof of skill.
He says there are limits to foresight.
Right: that is his optimistic skeptic stance.
questions.explain: He sits between two camps. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to Tetlock, accept the limits on prediction, but do not conclude that all forecasting is futile.

questions.q: Tetlock's label for his stance is optimistic ____.
questions.explain: The skeptic half stresses limits; the optimist half stresses what can be learned.
questions.rule: Limits and hope together.

questions.q: A strategist says: 'Forecasting is a fool's errand, so we will plan for nothing.' What does Tetlock's stance say?
options: The strategist is right, since the limits of foresight mean no forecast can be useful
Debunkers go too far when they dismiss all forecasting, since some foresight is possible
The strategist should trust the nearest expert, since experts see further than ordinary planners
The strategist must forecast ten years ahead, since long horizons are the most informative
optionExplain: Tetlock rejects that conclusion.
Right: the dismissal overshoots.
That is the defenders' error, not his stance.
Accuracy falls with distance.
questions.explain: Tetlock accepts limits but rejects the claim that all forecasting is futile.
questions.rule: Limits are not a reason to give up.

questions.q: Sort each item: does Tetlock accept it, or reject it?

items.t: Some forecasting peddlers sell insights of questionable value
There are limits to foresight that may not be surmountable
Some foresight is possible in some situations
All forecasting is a fool's errand
No one can cultivate forecasting skill

questions.explain: He agrees with the debunkers about peddlers and limits, but not about futility.
questions.rule: Concede the limits, keep the hope.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says the debunkers have a point, but go too far when they dismiss all forecasting.
questions.explain: He agrees about shady peddlers and limits, and disagrees only with the dismissal of everything.
questions.rule: Partial agreement is still agreement.

questions.q: A reader doubts they have a gift for forecasting. Which qualities does Tetlock say are enough to cultivate the skills?
options: A degree in statistics and years of experience as a television pundit
Access to classified information that ordinary readers do not normally have
A natural gift together with a mentor who is a recognised expert in the field
Being intelligent, open-minded and hardworking
optionExplain: He names no such credentials.
Access is not what he names.
He rejects the gift idea.
Right: any such person can cultivate the skills.
questions.explain: Tetlock says any intelligent, open-minded and hardworking person can cultivate the requisite skills.
questions.rule: Effort and openness count.
questions.teaches: Tetlock believes that any intelligent, open-minded and hardworking person can cultivate the requisite forecasting skills.

questions.q: According to the chapter, what event started the Arab Spring?
options: A coup organized by Tunisia's army officers against the long-serving President Ben Ali
A Tunisian street vendor, humiliated by police, set himself on fire
Mass student demonstrations in Cairo over a disputed election, which spread to Tunisia later
A civil war in Libya that drew in NATO and then set off protests across the Arab world
optionExplain: Ben Ali fled after protests; no coup is described.
Right: Bouazizi's act began the protests.
The unrest began in Tunisia and spread outward.
Libya came later in the chain.
questions.explain: The chapter begins the story with one poor man. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A small, ordinary event can start a chain of consequences far out of proportion to it, which is easy to trace afterward.

questions.q: The chapter traces the Arab Spring to a Tunisian street vendor named Mohamed ____.
questions.explain: Bouazizi's self-immolation on December 17, 2010 sparked the protests.
questions.rule: Small start, huge consequence.

questions.q: Put these links of the Arab Spring chain in the order the chapter gives them.
items: Police take the vendor's scales and cart
The vendor sets himself on fire
Protests spread and Ben Ali flees Tunisia
Protests erupt in Egypt, Libya, Syria and other countries
Mubarak is driven from office after three decades
questions.explain: The chain runs from a petty police shakedown through self-immolation and protests to the fall of two rulers.
questions.rule: Trace the chain forward.

questions.q: According to the chapter, what followed after Ben Ali fled Tunisia?
options: Protests erupted in Egypt, Libya, Syria, Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain
The protests faded in Tunisia, and neighboring governments ruled without challenge for years
Tunisia's neighbors sent troops to restore order, which ended the unrest within a month
The vendor's family led a new government, which the other Arab states then recognized
optionExplain: Right: the unrest spread across the Arab world.
The chapter says the opposite.
No such intervention is described.
The chapter describes protests, not such a government.
questions.explain: The unrest grew and spread to several countries, with Mubarak driven from office.
questions.rule: Ripples spread.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says police humiliations of street vendors like Bouazizi were a daily occurrence, with no apparent ripple effects before or since.
questions.explain: It says countless vendors suffered the same treatment, which mattered to no one aside from the police and their victims, until this one.
questions.rule: Most small injustices ripple nowhere, which is why the one that did was unforeseeable.
questions.teaches: Countless poor street vendors across the Arab world suffered such police humiliations daily, and these mattered to no one but the police and their victims.

questions.q: A newsroom asks how fast the Tunisian unrest toppled its ruler. Based on the chapter, which answer is closest?
options: Ben Ali stayed for two more years, until a negotiated settlement led to his retirement
Ben Ali fled within hours of the self-immolation, before Bouazizi had even died
Ben Ali fled ten days after Bouazizi died, ending a rule of twenty-three years
Ben Ali stayed in office a decade and fled only after a civil war reached the capital
optionExplain: He fled within days.
He fled after Bouazizi's death.
Right: Bouazizi died on January 4, 2011, and Ben Ali left on January 14.
He fled in January 2011.
questions.explain: Bouazizi died on January 4, 2011, and Ben Ali fled on January 14, ending his twenty-three-year kleptocracy.
questions.rule: Chains can move fast.
questions.teaches: Bouazizi died on January 4, 2011, and Ben Ali fled on January 14, ending his twenty-three-year kleptocracy.

questions.q: Could even Tom Friedman, present that morning, have foreseen the Arab Spring, according to the authors?
options: Yes, because his deep knowledge of the Middle East would have shown him the coming unrest
No; no one could have foreseen the self-immolation and all that followed
Yes, but only the self-immolation itself, not the later protests and the fall of the dictator
Probably, if he had been given access to police and intelligence reports from that region
optionExplain: The authors say knowledge alone would not have been enough.
Right: the authors say so plainly.
They say he could not have foreseen any of it.
No such condition is mentioned.
questions.explain: The chapter says no. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an after-the-fact story that links causes to an event does not show the event could have been predicted.

questions.q: A knowledgeable observer might have called Tunisia a ____ keg, but could have said so for decades.
questions.explain: Poverty, corruption and repression had lasted for decades without an explosion.
questions.rule: Conditions are not triggers.

questions.q: After a company collapses, analysts list every warning sign it showed. By the chapter's logic, what does the list show?
options: That the collapse could have been foreseen by anyone who read the signs carefully enough
That the analysts are skilled forecasters, since they identified the causes of the collapse
That the warning signs were absent before the event, since only hindsight has revealed them
A story can be told in hindsight, which does not show the collapse could have been foreseen
optionExplain: Hindsight makes signs look decisive.
Explaining the past is a different skill.
The signs could have existed all along; the point is they did not single out the event.
Right: backward stories are not forward forecasts.
questions.explain: Looking backward, causes line up; looking forward, many equally plausible stories exist.
questions.rule: Do not mistake a story for a forecast.

questions.q: An observer in 2009 calls Tunisia a powder keg. What does the chapter say about the same claim a year earlier?
options: It would have been false, because conditions in Tunisia only turned bad in 2010
It would have been more accurate, since an earlier warning shows greater foresight
It could have been made, and the keg did not blow
It would have been impossible to make, since earlier observers lacked data on the region
optionExplain: The conditions had held for decades.
The chapter does not reward an earlier warning that is equally true each year.
Right: the same claim fit the year before, and the year before that.
The chapter says the claim could have been made for decades.
questions.explain: The same description fit year after year until the trigger.
questions.rule: A condition that persists cannot time an event.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says the conditions cited as signs of a powder keg held in several Arab countries for decades without exploding.
questions.explain: It says the kegs never blew until December 17, 2010.
questions.rule: Persistent conditions do not date the explosion.

questions.q: A newsroom praises a columnist's tidy explanations of a crisis after it happened. What skill does the chapter say this shows?
options: Skill at reconstructing a narrative arc backward, which differs from foreseeing events
Skill at foreseeing events, because a good explanation of a crisis implies advance knowledge
Skill at the same kind of forecasting that superforecasters do, only from a different angle
No skill, because the chapter says that explanations given afterward are always invented
optionExplain: Right: the chapter says elite pundits are skilled at such reconstruction.
The chapter says explaining and foreseeing are different.
The chapter does not equate the two.
The chapter says the reconstruction is skilled, not invented.
questions.explain: The chapter says Tom Friedman, like many elite pundits, is skilled at reconstructing events backward, particularly in the Middle East.
questions.rule: Explaining the past is not predicting the future.
questions.teaches: Tom Friedman, like many elite pundits, is skilled at backward reconstruction of events, particularly in the Middle East, which he knows well.

questions.q: What did Lorenz discover by accident about computer simulations of weather?
options: Tiny data entry variations, such as 0.506127 versus 0.506, could produce dramatically different long-term forecasts
Weather simulations always produce the same long-term forecast, whatever small changes are made to the inputs
Larger computers always give more accurate long-term forecasts, which proved weather is a predictable clock
Rounding in data entry cancels out over time, so small errors do not affect long-term results
optionExplain: Right: small input changes grew into big differences.
He found the opposite.
He found sensitivity, not predictability.
Rounding did not cancel; it mushroomed.
questions.explain: A rounding difference changed everything. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, in nonlinear systems small changes in initial conditions can mushroom, so long-term prediction has limits.

questions.q: Lorenz's insight inspired the field known as ____ theory.
questions.explain: Chaos theory studies systems where small changes in conditions grow enormously.
questions.rule: Small changes can mushroom.

questions.q: A modeler rounds one input from 0.8123 to 0.81, and a weeks-long weather simulation gives a very different result. Which idea fits?
options: Rounding errors cancel over long runs, so the model must contain a mistake of another kind
The model had too little computing power, so a bigger machine would have removed the difference
Weather follows no laws at all, so any forecast is as good as any other
Small differences in initial conditions can grow enormously in a nonlinear system
optionExplain: Cancelling is the opposite of what Lorenz found.
Lorenz found the sensitivity in the system, not just in the machine.
Lorenz's point concerns sensitivity, not lawlessness.
Right: that is the butterfly effect.
questions.explain: Weather simulations are sensitive to starting values, so a tiny rounding can change the long-term result.
questions.rule: Sensitivity, not randomness.

questions.q: Which best states how Lorenz meant the butterfly 'causes' a tornado?
options: The flap pushes enough air to reach Texas and directly spin up the tornado there
Without that flap at that moment, the network of atmospheric actions would have behaved differently and the tornado might not have formed
The flap is the usual cause of tornadoes, so meteorologists should watch butterflies
The flap is one of many equal causes, so each butterfly flap carries the same weight as another
optionExplain: Lorenz did not mean a direct push.
Right: it is counterfactual, not direct.
He meant a possibility, not a usual cause.
The chapter says most flaps cause no noticeable gust.
questions.explain: The butterfly does not cause the tornado the way a hammer breaks a glass.
questions.rule: Sensitive dependence is not direct causation.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says Lorenz found the sensitivity to small changes by designing an experiment to test it.
questions.explain: He discovered it by accident, when replacing a number with a rounded version changed the forecasts.
questions.rule: Discovery can be accidental.

questions.q: A friend says: 'If butterflies can cause tornadoes, every flap matters equally.' Which chapter fact corrects this?
options: Lorenz showed that each flap sets off a small gust, and a gust is the first step toward a tornado
Lorenz showed that a flap in Brazil changes the weather of Texas only in computer simulations
Swarms of other Brazilian butterflies could flap frantically their whole lives and never cause a noticeable gust a few miles away
Lorenz showed that butterflies cause tornadoes only when they flap together in very large swarms
optionExplain: The chapter says most flaps never cause a noticeable gust.
The chapter says it could in principle in the real atmosphere.
Right: most flaps lead nowhere noticeable.
The chapter says swarms flapping frantically need not cause a gust.
questions.explain: The chapter says a lone butterfly could set off a tornado, even though swarms of others could flap and never cause a gust.
questions.rule: Sensitivity does not make every small event matter.
questions.teaches: Swarms of other Brazilian butterflies could flap frantically their whole lives and never cause a noticeable gust a few miles away.

questions.q: In 1814 Laplace imagined an intellect that knew every force and position in nature. What did he think it could do?
options: Predict only the motions of the largest bodies, since the tiniest atoms would stay uncertain
Explain the past but not forecast the future, since the future depends on chance events
Calculate probabilities for each outcome, since no mind can be certain about the future
Predict everything about the future from its knowledge of the present
optionExplain: He said it would embrace the greatest bodies and the tiniest atom alike.
He said the future would be as present as the past.
He said nothing would be uncertain for it.
Right: for it nothing would be uncertain.
questions.explain: Laplace pushed determinism to its limit. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Laplace's dream: complete knowledge of the present, plus enough power to analyze it, would allow perfect prediction of the future.

questions.q: Laplace called his imaginary all-knowing intellect a ____.
questions.explain: The demon would know everything about the present and so predict the future.
questions.rule: Perfect knowledge, perfect prediction.

questions.q: A researcher says: 'With every measurement and enough computing power, I will predict this system perfectly.' Whose view is this?
options: Lorenz's, who held that small changes in conditions make long-term prediction limited
The optimistic skeptic's, who holds that some foresight is possible within limits
Laplace's, who held that complete knowledge of the present allows complete prediction
The debunkers', who hold that all forecasting is a fool's errand and cannot succeed
optionExplain: That is the opposite view.
That stance accepts limits.
Right: it is the Laplacean dream.
That is the opposite of the researcher's confidence.
questions.explain: The researcher assumes perfect knowledge leads to perfect prediction, which is the Laplacean view.
questions.rule: Know all, predict all: Laplace's dream.

questions.q: Before Lorenz, what did scientists expect to happen to predictability as knowledge grew?
options: It would stay the same, because the clock's complexity was believed to cancel any new knowledge
It would grow, because learning how the clock works would let them predict what it does
It would shrink, because every discovery was expected to reveal new sources of uncertainty
It would depend on chance, because scientists accepted that dice govern events in nature
optionExplain: The clock image meant knowledge would help.
Right: knowledge was expected to bring predictability.
That is the later, Lorenzian view.
The clock image was deterministic.
questions.explain: A clock's gears and springs, once understood, determine its operation.
questions.rule: More knowledge, more prediction: the old assumption.

questions.q: True or false: Laplace believed that an intellect knowing all forces and positions would see the future as plainly as the past.
questions.explain: That is why the chapter calls his dream the extreme of the clock view.
questions.rule: Laplace was a determinist.

questions.q: A student says mechanical clocks prove nature can be captured by exact equations. Which view does the chapter attribute to the old scientists?
options: They supposed knowing the clock's gears, weights and springs would let deterministic equations capture its operations
They supposed nature is mostly random, but that clocks nevertheless show averages can be predicted
They supposed equations could describe only the past, since the future is open to human choice
They supposed equations were useful only for very small systems, not for the universe
optionExplain: Right: that is the old assumption.
They supposed nature was deterministic.
They supposed equations would predict the future.
Laplace extended the dream to the universe.
questions.explain: The chapter says the more scientists learned about the gears, weights and springs, the better they could capture the operations with deterministic equations.
questions.rule: Deterministic equations were the old hope.
questions.teaches: The old view held that learning how the gears grind, and how the weights and springs function, would let scientists capture reality's operations with deterministic equations.

questions.q: In the chapter, what is the opposite of the clock as a symbol of predictability?
options: The Laplacean demon, which stands for the idea that nature has no hidden laws at all
The Lorenzian cloud
The tornado in Texas, which stands for the final result of every long chain of events
The butterfly in Brazil, which stands for the quiet stretches when nothing changes at all
optionExplain: The demon is the clock's perfect predictor, not its opposite.
Right: the cloud stands for unpredictability.
The tornado is the butterfly example.
The butterfly is the small cause, not the opposite symbol.
questions.explain: The chapter names the opposite. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, where tiny data errors mushroom, learning more still cannot give a perfect prediction.

questions.q: The shape of a particular cloud depends on complex feedback interactions among ____.
questions.explain: Droplet interactions are what make cloud shapes sensitive to small data errors.
questions.rule: Feedback among droplets.

questions.q: A modeler says: 'Collect every detail of a cloud's formation and its shape is known in advance.' What does the chapter say?
options: Not so; the equations are highly sensitive to tiny data errors, so we can only wait and see
Correct, since the chapter says growing data-crunching power will remove the uncertainty soon
Correct, but only for large clouds whose droplets are too numerous to have an individual effect
Not so, because clouds form without any physical cause that models could capture
optionExplain: Right: the shape cannot be predicted even with all knowable facts.
The chapter says more data does not remove it.
Nothing in the chapter makes that distinction.
Clouds form from water vapor and dust; the problem is sensitivity.
questions.explain: Even complete knowledge of how clouds form will not give the shape of a specific cloud.
questions.rule: Sensitivity limits foresight.

questions.q: Computing power grows tenfold. According to the chapter, what happens to prediction of a particular cloud's shape?
options: It becomes perfect, because the chapter says power is the only thing standing in the way
It gets worse, because more computing power amplifies the errors in the data collected
It does not become perfect, because the equations stay sensitive to tiny data errors
It is no longer needed, because clouds can be forecast without equations once power is high
optionExplain: The chapter says the opposite.
Nothing says computing power makes it worse.
Right: sensitivity remains.
The chapter does not say that.
questions.explain: Sensitivity to tiny errors, not computing power, is the obstacle.
questions.rule: Power does not cure sensitivity.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says that even knowing all that is knowable about cloud formation, we cannot predict a given cloud's shape.
questions.explain: Sensitivity to tiny data errors means we can only wait and see.
questions.rule: Some limits are not about data.

questions.q: A historian asks how scientists' confidence in perfect predictability changed over the past century as knowledge grew. What does the chapter say?
options: They became more confident, because each decade of new data brought the clock image closer to reality
Their confidence stayed the same, because knowledge and doubt grew at the same pace
They became confident only for weather, while remaining doubtful about every other field
They know vastly more and have far more computing power, yet are much less confident about perfect predictability
optionExplain: The chapter says confidence fell.
The chapter says confidence fell.
The chapter says nothing of the kind.
Right: the chapter calls this one of history's great ironies.
questions.explain: The chapter calls it one of history's great ironies.
questions.rule: More knowledge can mean less confidence in perfect prediction.
questions.teaches: Scientists today know vastly more than their colleagues a century ago, and have vastly more data-crunching power, but are much less confident in the prospects for perfect predictability.

questions.q: Why does the chapter follow a Kansas City woman's husband from Tunisia to Tripoli?
options: To show that the Arab Spring was caused by American military policy in the region
To show that air force navigators are among the best forecasters of conflicts abroad
To show that distant events can reach ordinary lives through chains of consequences
To show that suburban households ignore world events because those events do not affect them
optionExplain: The chapter says it began with a vendor's act.
No such claim appears.
Right: the link is traceable.
The chapter says the opposite.
questions.explain: The chain is a skeptic's argument. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, because distant events can ripple into ordinary lives, long-range foresight is limited, which is the skeptic half of their stance.

questions.q: The chapter's example links the Tunisian vendor to a US air force navigator flying over ____.
questions.explain: The chain ran through the Libyan civil war and the NATO intervention.
questions.rule: Chains of consequence.

questions.q: A factory worker is laid off after a coup in a country he had not heard of. Which point does this support?
options: Distant events can reach ordinary lives, so far-ahead forecasting is hard
Only experts need to track foreign events, since ordinary lives are insulated from them
Coups are always predictable, since the chain of consequences can be read in advance
Layoffs are random, so no event can be said to cause another in the economy
optionExplain: Right: it matches the ripple-effects argument.
The chapter says the opposite.
The chapter does not say that.
The chapter says connections exist but are often hard to spot.
questions.explain: The authors say connections between distant events and our lives are all around us.
questions.rule: Everything is connected, and the links are hard to see.

questions.q: Put the links from the Tunisian vendor to the husband's mission in the order the chapter gives them.
items: A Tunisian vendor's act leads to protests
The protests lead to riots
The riots topple a dictator
Protests spread to Libya, then civil war
NATO intervenes, and the navigator flies over Tripoli
questions.explain: Each link followed from the one before; the chain is easy to trace backward.
questions.rule: Trace the chain.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says the connection between the Tunisian vendor and the Kansas City couple was impossible to trace.
questions.explain: It calls it an easily traceable connection.
questions.rule: Some links are easy to trace; others are not.

questions.q: Besides a husband's mission, which everyday things does the chapter say distant events can touch?
options: The weather forecast and the speed limit on the road to work each morning
The fare on the local bus and the hours posted at a favorite restaurant
The sunrise time and the tides, which shift when events abroad disturb the planet
The price we pay at the gas station and layoffs down the street
optionExplain: Neither is named.
Neither is named.
Those are among the clocklike pockets, not ripple effects.
Right: both are named.
questions.explain: The chapter says connections are often harder to spot, but they are around us in gas prices and layoffs.
questions.rule: The links are often invisible.
questions.teaches: Often the connections are harder to spot than in the Libya example, but they are all around us, in the price we pay at the gas station or the layoffs down the street.

questions.q: Why did the Kansas City woman leave home at 6:30 in the morning, according to the chapter?
options: Her employer required an early start, since the insurance company opens its doors before dawn
She predicted that traffic would be much heavier later, since rush hour is highly predictable
She expected the roads to be empty then, because few workers in her suburb leave early
She needed time to browse online before her call, and she scheduled the drive around that
optionExplain: The reason given is traffic.
Right: she forecast rush hour.
She expected heavier traffic later.
Browsing came after she reached her desk.
questions.explain: A routine choice rests on a prediction. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, alongside unpredictable influences, there is as much or more in our lives that is quite predictable.

questions.q: Electricity producers vary their output because they anticipate the weekday morning demand ____.
questions.explain: Workers turning on computers cause a predictable surge each non-holiday weekday morning.
questions.rule: Routine patterns are predictable.

questions.q: A commuter checks the bus timetable and reaches the stop at the posted time. In the chapter's terms, what is this?
options: A guess, since a timetable gives no evidence about what the bus will do on a given day
A certainty, since a posted timetable cannot fail in the way an uncontrolled event can
A forecast only an expert is able to make, since ordinary riders lack the data to judge a timetable
A mundane prediction that posted times are a reliable guide
optionExplain: The chapter treats posted hours as a reliable guide.
Even posted hours can fail; the next idea covers this.
The chapter says we all make mundane predictions routinely.
Right: like the woman trusting the restaurant's hours.
questions.explain: Trusting a posted schedule is a routine prediction that usually comes true.
questions.rule: We predict constantly.

questions.q: Sort each item from the woman's day: predictable, or unpredictable?

items.t: Rush hour traffic building later in the morning
Drivers stopping at a red light
Colleagues joining the 10:30 call
The restaurant opening at its posted hour
Her lottery ticket winning
The price of gas rising after a coup abroad

questions.explain: The chapter lists the lottery ticket and the Arab Spring effects among unpredictable influences, and routine patterns among predictable ones.
questions.rule: Mix of predictable and unpredictable.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says the woman's life is shaped almost entirely by unpredictable factors.
questions.explain: It says her life has many unpredictable influences, but as much or more that is quite predictable.
questions.rule: Do not overstate unpredictability.

questions.q: A life insurer cannot say when you will die. According to the chapter, what can it forecast well?
options: The exact date of death for each policyholder, once enough personal data has been collected
How long someone of your age and profile is likely to live
Nothing useful, since death is the outcome with the highest uncertainty of any life event
Only the average life span of the whole population, with no use of sex, income or lifestyle
optionExplain: The chapter says it does not know precisely when.
Right: that is what actuaries do.
The chapter says it does a good job and has lasted since 1895.
The chapter says it uses sex, income and lifestyle.
questions.explain: The insurer does not know precisely when a person will die, but has a good idea of life expectancy for a given age and profile.
questions.rule: Forecast groups, not individuals.
questions.teaches: An insurer cannot say precisely when you will die, but it has a good idea of how long someone of your age and profile (sex, income, lifestyle) is likely to live.

questions.q: Which of these does the chapter say can be predicted precisely from clocklike scientific laws?
options: Sunrise times, tides, eclipses and the phases of the moon
Election results, stock prices and the outbreak of wars during the next several years
The shape of a particular cloud, the path of a tornado and the weather three weeks ahead
The winners of football matches, the demand for new gadgets and the timing of market crashes
optionExplain: Right: all four are named.
Those are cloud-like questions.
Those are sensitive to tiny errors.
Those are not clocklike.
questions.explain: Some pockets of the world run like clocks. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Where clocklike scientific laws govern a phenomenon, precise prediction is possible.

questions.q: Sunrise, tides, eclipses and the phases of the ____ can be predicted from clocklike scientific laws.
questions.explain: These four are the chapter's examples of clocklike predictability.
questions.rule: Clocklike laws allow precision.

questions.q: An almanac prints the times of high tide for a harbor ten years ahead. Why can it do so?
options: Tide times are averaged from many years of random variation, which makes them look regular
Almanac writers have a gift for foresight that most forecasters lack across fields
Tides follow clocklike scientific laws that permit precise prediction
Tides depend on weather, and weather can be forecast reliably for years in advance
optionExplain: The chapter says they follow scientific laws.
The chapter does not say that.
Right: that is the chapter's explanation.
Weather is not reliable years ahead, as the chapter later says.
questions.explain: The tide's regularity comes from physical laws, not from luck.
questions.rule: Laws, not luck.

questions.q: According to the chapter, how does a sunrise forecast for fifty years ahead compare in reliability with tomorrow's?
options: It is much less reliable, since reliability falls with every year added to the forecast horizon
It is reliable too; such forecasts hold for tomorrow, the day after or fifty years from now
It is slightly less reliable, since the chapter says tomorrow's is best by a small margin
It is unknowable, since no one can check a forecast fifty years ahead
optionExplain: For sunrise, the horizon does not matter.
Right: the chapter says so.
The chapter does not rank them.
The chapter calls such forecasts reliable.
questions.explain: Clocklike laws make the horizon matter little.
questions.rule: Clocklike means distance does not erode accuracy.
questions.teaches: Sunrise and sunset forecasts are reliable whether they are for tomorrow, the day after, or fifty years from now.

questions.q: Sort each item: clocklike or cloud-like?

items.t: Sunrise times
Tides
Eclipses
Phases of the moon
The shape of a particular cloud
Whether a tornado forms in Texas

questions.explain: The chapter calls the first four predictable from scientific laws; the cloud's shape and a tornado are sensitive to tiny errors.
questions.rule: Know which kind you face.

questions.q: A physicist says eclipse predictions meet an exacting standard. In the chapter's words, how precise are such predictions?
options: Precise to within a few days, which the chapter calls good enough for planning
Precise only when the sky is clear, since weather affects the timing of eclipses
Not precise at all, since the chapter says no natural event can be predicted exactly
Precise enough to satisfy Laplace's forecasting demon
optionExplain: The chapter says to the minute.
No weather condition is mentioned.
The chapter says these can.
Right: the chapter says so.
questions.explain: The chapter says clocklike laws allow precision that would satisfy the demon.
questions.rule: Some predictions are as exact as Laplace dreamed.
questions.teaches: Sunrise, tide, eclipse and moon-phase forecasts can be made with enough precision to satisfy Laplace's forecasting demon.

questions.q: A good restaurant says it will open at noon. What does the chapter say about that prediction?
options: It is certain, because posted hours are a guide that has no exceptions in practice
It is unreliable, because restaurants close for many reasons that cannot be foreseen
It is very likely right, but it may fail for any number of reasons
It is meaningless, because no event in life can be predicted at all with any confidence
optionExplain: The chapter lists reasons it may fail.
The chapter calls posted hours a reliable guide.
Right: reliable, not certain.
The chapter says much is predictable.
questions.explain: Even good predictions can be punctured. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Treat even highly predictable events as very probable, not certain.

questions.q: The chapter says each pocket of predictability can be abruptly ____.
questions.explain: A sudden event can puncture a pocket of predictability.
questions.rule: Pockets can be punctured.

questions.q: Your train has run on time every day for years. What attitude to tomorrow's schedule fits the chapter?
options: Expect it to run on time, while accepting it may not for some reason
Treat it as certain, because years of punctual trains remove any chance of a delay
Treat it as unknowable, because any prediction about trains could fail tomorrow
Treat it as a coin flip, because the past gives no information about the future
optionExplain: Right: high probability, not certainty.
No pocket is immune from puncturing.
The pocket is real; plan on it.
The chapter says the past is a guide to routine patterns.
questions.explain: The track record supports a high probability; it cannot support certainty.
questions.rule: High, not certain.

questions.q: A massive space rock bumps Earth off its orbit. What does the chapter say would happen to fifty-year sunrise forecasts?
options: They could be off somewhat
They would remain exact, because sunrise times depend only on the laws of physics
They would become useless, because every astronomical prediction depends on the orbit
They would improve, because the new orbit would be easier to measure than the old one
optionExplain: Right: the chapter says so.
The chapter says they could be off.
The chapter says off somewhat, not useless.
No such claim appears.
questions.explain: A shift in orbit would change the timing somewhat.
questions.rule: Even clocks can be knocked.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says that, because pockets can be punctured, predictions are worthless.
questions.explain: It says the pockets are real and punctures are possible; it still treats routine predictions as reliable.
questions.rule: Fragile is not worthless.

questions.q: How does the chapter treat the saying that death and taxes are certain?
options: As certain, because the chapter says death and taxes are the two events that can be predicted
As false, because the chapter says death can be delayed forever and taxes are already voluntary
As irrelevant, because the chapter limits its examples to weather, tides and rush hour
As not strictly certain, if we assign a nonzero probability to brain uploading and a society funded by donations
optionExplain: The chapter says there are no certainties.
The chapter treats it as a matter of probability.
The chapter addresses it explicitly.
Right: the chapter makes this playful point.
questions.explain: The chapter says there are no certainties if we allow nonzero probability for unlikely technologies and social changes.
questions.rule: Nonzero probability means not certain.
questions.teaches: There are no certainties in life, not even death and taxes, if we assign a nonzero probability to uploading brains into a cloud and to a society so public-spirited that the state is funded by charity.

questions.q: How does the chapter answer the question of whether the future is predictable?
options: It answers no, because Lorenz showed that the future of every system is cloud-like
It calls the question a false dichotomy: predictable and unpredictable things coexist
It answers yes, because clocklike laws govern the cosmos and clouds are only apparent exceptions
It answers that the question cannot be asked, because science has no tools for the future
optionExplain: It rejects the either-or.
Right: it depends on what, how far and under what circumstances.
It rejects the either-or.
It answers the question by reframing it.
questions.explain: The chapter reframes the question. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Ask how predictable something is for what question, how far ahead and under what conditions, not whether the future is predictable.

questions.q: The chapter calls the choice between a clocklike and a cloud-like reality a false ____.
questions.explain: Both clocks and clouds exist.
questions.rule: No either-or.

questions.q: A manager asks whether the sales forecast is predictable or not. Which reframing fits the chapter?
options: Ask whether the sales team has been trained in statistics, since training decides predictability
Ask whether sales are clocklike, and if they are not, drop the forecast as a waste of effort
Ask how predictable it is for which measure, how far ahead and under what conditions
Ask whether the competitors publish forecasts, since only shared forecasts can be accurate
optionExplain: The chapter points to the question, horizon and circumstances.
That keeps the either-or the chapter rejects.
Right: the three things the chapter says matter.
Nothing like that appears in the chapter.
questions.explain: Predictability is a matter of degree, depending on what, how far ahead and under what circumstances.
questions.rule: Ask how, not whether.

questions.q: Match each factor the chapter says predictability depends on to an example.
pairs: Sunrise time versus the shape of a cloud
Tomorrow versus fifty years from now
A restaurant opening, unless there is a fire or a pandemic
questions.explain: The chapter names these three factors, and the examples come from its earlier discussion.
questions.rule: Three questions to ask.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter concludes that reality is a clock, so every event is in principle predictable with enough data.
questions.explain: It says we live in a world of clocks and clouds, and predictability depends on what, how far and under what circumstances.
questions.rule: Do not collapse the mixture.

questions.q: A doctor notes that the heartbeat is regular, but the course of an illness is hard to time. Which chapter point does this match?
options: Clocks govern the body and clouds govern society, so the two never meet in one system
Medicine can eliminate unpredictability by measuring the body more finely than Lorenz could
Only bodies are predictable; societies and the cosmos are cloud-like through and through
Predictability and unpredictability coexist in the interlocking systems of our bodies
optionExplain: The chapter says they coexist in the same systems.
The chapter does not say that.
It names all three as mixed.
Right: bodies are named in the chapter.
questions.explain: The chapter says predictability and unpredictability coexist uneasily in our bodies, our societies and the cosmos.
questions.rule: Mixed systems are normal.
questions.teaches: Predictability and unpredictability coexist uneasily in the intricately interlocking systems that make up our bodies, our societies and the cosmos.

questions.q: Roughly how far ahead are weather forecasts typically quite reliable, according to the chapter?
options: A few weeks, since modern models track the atmosphere in great detail
A whole season, since seasonal patterns repeat from year to year
A few days
A single day only, since every longer forecast is little better than a guess
optionExplain: Beyond a week they approach chimp level.
Not according to the chapter.
Right: reliability fades by three to five days.
One- and two-day forecasts are typically quite accurate; reliability extends a few days.
questions.explain: Weather is the chapter's test case. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Say that something is predictable to some extent under some circumstances, and be careful about being more precise than that.

questions.q: Much beyond a week, the chapter says we might as well consult the dart-throwing ____.
questions.explain: The chapter reuses the joke to describe weather forecasts a week or more out.
questions.rule: Weather fades beyond a week.

questions.q: A farmer wants to plan around a weather forecast for twelve days from now. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Treat it as reliable, since modern models make forecasts a fortnight ahead quite accurate
Treat it as little better than guessing, since forecasts much beyond a week are weak
Treat it as impossible to produce, since the chapter says weather beyond a day cannot be forecast
Treat it as exactly as good as a forecast for tomorrow, since horizon does not matter
optionExplain: The chapter says accuracy falls well before that.
Right: it matches the weather horizon.
Forecasts are reliable a few days out.
Horizon matters for weather.
questions.explain: Weather loses accuracy rapidly beyond a week.
questions.rule: Check the horizon.

questions.q: By about how many days out does the chapter say weather forecasts become increasingly less accurate?
options: Three, four and five days out
Twenty, thirty and forty days out, where the long-range models are said to give up
One hour and two hours out, where the atmosphere is too sensitive for any forecast
Never, because the chapter says weather models keep their accuracy at every horizon
optionExplain: Right: accuracy falls from about the third day.
Much too far.
Too short; one- and two-day forecasts are accurate.
The chapter says accuracy falls off.
questions.explain: Accuracy declines from about three to five days out.
questions.rule: Weather has a horizon.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says weather should be called predictable or unpredictable, with no need for qualification.
questions.explain: It says weather is predictable to some extent under some circumstances, and we must be careful about being more precise.
questions.rule: Qualify predictions.

questions.q: A fund manager's rule of buying every dip has worked for fifteen years. What lesson does the chapter's dinosaur example offer?
options: Rules that worked for fifteen years will work for fifteen more, since long runs show a law at work
A rule that held for a very long time can still fail abruptly, as dinosaurs' reign ended with an asteroid
Rules based on markets never work, since the dinosaurs lost out to a more intelligent mammal
Rules should be changed every year, since the chapter says no prediction holds beyond a season
optionExplain: The dinosaurs show a long run ending.
Right: long runs end.
The dinosaurs' fall is the lesson, not market rules.
The chapter says some rules hold for tens of millions of years.
questions.explain: The chapter says predicting that dinosaurs would remain on top was a safe bet for tens of millions of years, until an asteroid.
questions.rule: Long streaks can end.
questions.teaches: Predicting that dinosaurs would continue to preside at the top of the food chain was a safe bet for tens of millions of years, until an asteroid set off a cataclysm.

questions.q: What explains why weather forecasts are good and slowly getting better?
options: Meteorologists make many forecasts, check their accuracy and revise their models, repeatedly
Weather has become more predictable in recent decades as the atmosphere itself has grown calmer
Meteorologists have discovered a formula that removes the effect of tiny errors on long forecasts
Forecasters trust one famous expert whose judgment is more reliable than any model
optionExplain: Right: the loop explains the progress.
The chapter says nothing of the kind.
The chapter says the limits remain.
The chapter credits measurement, not a guru.
questions.explain: The answer is a loop. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Improve forecasts by making many, measuring their accuracy and revising the method, over and over.

questions.q: The chapter sums up the improvement loop as forecast, measure, ____. Repeat.
questions.explain: Revising follows measuring, then the loop restarts.
questions.rule: Forecast, measure, revise.

questions.q: A cafe owner logs each week's predicted customers beside the actual count and adjusts the next prediction. Which idea is this?
options: The butterfly effect, since the small weekly change in counts is magnified over months
A Laplacean demon, since the owner now knows every detail of the cafe's customers
The forecast, measure, revise loop
A dress-to-impress forecast, since the log is meant to look careful to the cafe's investors
optionExplain: That concerns sensitivity, not improvement.
She does not claim complete knowledge.
Right: she forecasts, measures and revises.
Nothing indicates a show.
questions.explain: She records forecasts, measures them against outcomes and revises.
questions.rule: Close the loop.

questions.q: Put the steps of the loop in the order the chapter gives them.
items: Make forecasts
Measure their accuracy
Revise the model
Repeat
questions.explain: The chapter's sequence is forecast, measure, revise, repeat.
questions.rule: Loop, don't stop.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says weather forecasts can improve without limit, because bigger computers keep pushing the limit further.
questions.explain: It says there may be limits because weather is nonlinear, and the payoffs of better models shrink toward zero.
questions.rule: Loops have limits.

questions.q: A team finds its monthly sales forecasts lose accuracy beyond three months and cannot be improved. How does the weather discussion frame this?
options: As a failure, since the chapter says only forecasts that improve forever have any value
As proof that sales are cloud-like, so the team should stop measuring accuracy altogether
As a reason to trust the loudest expert, since measurement has nothing more to offer
Knowing the current limits is itself a success
optionExplain: The chapter says limits are themselves informative.
Stopping would stop learning.
The chapter says measure and learn.
Right: the chapter says so.
questions.explain: The chapter says that while no one knows how good weather forecasts can get, knowing the current limits is itself a success.
questions.rule: Limits found are progress made.
questions.teaches: How good weather forecasting can get is unknown, but knowing the current limits is itself a success.

questions.q: According to the chapter, why is accuracy seldom determined after forecasts are made?
options: Forecasters refuse to share their outcomes, since the chapter says they fear being exposed
No method exists to measure accuracy, since forecasts are too vague to be scored at all
The consumers of forecasts do not demand evidence of accuracy
Measuring is too expensive for anyone but large governments to afford in any case
optionExplain: The chapter blames the lack of demand.
The chapter says it can be done.
Right: it is mostly a demand-side problem.
Cost is not the reason given.
questions.explain: The problem sits with buyers. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, without measurement there is no revision, and without revision there can be no improvement.

questions.q: Without measurement there is no revision, and without revision there can be no ____.
questions.explain: The chain runs measure, revise, improve.
questions.rule: Measure to improve.

questions.q: A city budget office publishes revenue forecasts and does not compare them with actual revenue. What does the chapter predict?
options: Little improvement, because without measurement there is no revision
Steady improvement, because careful budget staff learn from each year's experience by instinct
Rapid decline, because forecasts that are never checked drift further from reality each year
No effect, because revenue forecasts in cities are as accurate as weather forecasts a day out
optionExplain: Right: the chain breaks at measurement.
The chapter says experience without measurement does not drive improvement.
Nothing says they drift; they simply do not improve.
The chapter gives no such comparison.
questions.explain: No measurement means no revision and no improvement.
