questions.rule: Close the loop.

questions.q: Sort each item: is forecast-measure-revise typical there, or rare?

items.t: Macroeconomists at central banks
Marketing and financial professionals in big companies
Poll analysts like Nate Silver
Pundits on television talk shows
Most forecasts bought by governments and companies

questions.explain: The chapter says the loop operates within high-tech forecasting; elsewhere forecasts are made and then nothing happens.
questions.rule: The loop is the exception.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says the lack of measurement is mostly a demand-side problem: consumers do not ask for evidence of accuracy.
questions.explain: That is the chapter's explanation.
questions.rule: Demand drives measurement.

questions.q: Imagine runners with no agreed track, start signal, distance or timekeepers. What does the chapter suggest about their times?
options: They are likely improving, since runners learn from every race even without recorded times
They are certainly improving, since competition between runners makes everyone faster
They cannot be judged at all, since the chapter treats running as unrelated to forecasting
They are unlikely to be improving, and the best may not be running as fast as is humanly possible
optionExplain: The chapter says improvement is unlikely.
The chapter says not very likely.
The analogy is about forecasting.
Right: the chapter gives this as its analogy.
questions.explain: Without ground rules and independent timekeepers, nobody knows how fast runners go or could go.
questions.rule: Rules and timekeepers enable progress.
questions.teaches: In a world of runners without agreed ground rules or independent timekeepers, running times are unlikely to be improving, and the best may not be running as fast as humanly possible.

questions.q: According to the chapter, is accuracy the only goal a forecast can have?
options: Yes; any forecast that aims at anything else is not a real forecast
No; forecasts may aim to entertain, advance agendas, impress or comfort
Yes; but media forecasts are the only ones that sometimes fall short of that goal
No; forecasts aim only to persuade, since accuracy cannot be known in advance
optionExplain: The chapter says other goals are common.
Right: accuracy is often not the sole goal.
Other goals reach beyond media.
The chapter lists several goals, not one.
questions.explain: The chapter lists several goals. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, ask what a forecast is for before judging it by accuracy.

questions.q: A bank pays a famous pundit to tell wealthy clients about the 2050 economy: the chapter calls this dress-to-____ forecasting.
questions.explain: Such forecasts are bought for show.
questions.rule: Know the purpose.

questions.q: Match each forecast to the goal the chapter's list would give it.
pairs: An activist warns of looming horrors unless we change our ways
A host demands odds on a scale from zero to ten
A bank buys a famous pundit's outlook for its wealthy clients
A partisan assures supporters that events will go their way
questions.explain: Each of the four goals matches one of the chapter's examples.
questions.rule: Match the forecast to its purpose.

questions.q: Why does an unacknowledged jumble of goals make progress harder, according to the chapter?
options: Forecasters with mixed goals always give inaccurate forecasts, so they cannot be measured
Buyers with mixed goals refuse to pay for forecasts, so the market for forecasting disappears
Mixed goals cannot be measured by any method, since accuracy is not one of them
It is difficult to start working toward measurement when the goal is not clear
optionExplain: The chapter does not say mixed goals mean inaccuracy.
The chapter says buyers pay.
Accuracy can be measured if it is the goal.
Right: measurement needs a stated goal.
questions.explain: A clear goal is the first step toward measurement.
questions.rule: Name the goal.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says all forecasting is meant to foresee the future accurately.
questions.explain: It says the goal is often not accuracy, or not the sole goal.
questions.rule: Purpose differs.

questions.q: A partisan reader enjoys forecasts that confirm what they already believe. How does the chapter describe such forecasts?
options: A form of entertainment, like the shouting on a television panel show about future events
The cognitive equivalent of slipping into a warm bath
A way to advance a political agenda, like an activist's warning of looming horrors
The most accurate kind of forecast, because partisans know their own side's plans best
optionExplain: The chapter keeps comfort and entertainment apart.
Right: the chapter's image for comfort forecasts.
That is a separate goal.
The chapter does not say that.
questions.explain: The chapter says partisans are fond of forecasts that assure the audience their beliefs are correct.
questions.rule: Comfort is not accuracy.
questions.teaches: Forecasts meant to comfort are described as the cognitive equivalent of slipping into a warm bath, and partisans are fond of them.

questions.q: What does Tetlock say all we have to do to seize the opportunity in forecasting?
options: Set a clear goal, accuracy, and get serious about measuring
Hire more famous experts and ask them to forecast on a wider range of subjects
Build larger computers that can model every system with more detail than Laplace imagined
Stop forecasting altogether until a perfect method for prediction has been discovered
optionExplain: Right: that is his two-part answer.
Fame is not accuracy.
He does not propose that.
He proposes the opposite.
questions.explain: The answer is short. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: To improve forecasting, set accuracy as the goal and measure progress toward it.

questions.q: Tetlock says the goal to set is ____, and then to get serious about measuring.
questions.explain: Accuracy is the clear goal he proposes.
questions.rule: Goal, then measure.

questions.q: A hospital wants fewer missed appointments. By the Gates passage the authors quote, what should it do first?
options: Ask the most experienced staff what they think will work and apply their combined opinion
Wait until the problem is better understood, and then decide which targets to track
Set a clear goal and find a measure that drives progress toward it
Publish a bold forecast about next year's missed appointments to motivate the staff
optionExplain: Opinion is not a measure.
The passage says to set the goal first.
Right: goal, then measure.
A forecast is not a goal-and-measure step.
questions.explain: Gates's advice is to set a clear goal and find a measure.
questions.rule: Goal and measure.

questions.q: Gates says progress comes from a clear goal and a measure. What does Tetlock say has not been done in forecasting?
options: Only the final step, publishing the results, since the goal and measures are already agreed
Even the simple first step of setting a clear goal
Any forecast at all, since forecasters have been silent about the future for centuries
Running tournaments, which the authors say are the only way to set a clear goal
optionExplain: The first step is missing.
Right: the goal itself is unclear.
Forecasts are everywhere.
The goal-setting step is the point.
questions.explain: The goal of forecasting is a jumble of purposes.
questions.rule: Start with the goal.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says that for scientists, not knowing is exciting because the more that is unknown, the greater the opportunity.
questions.explain: Tetlock says not knowing is an opportunity to discover, which is why he is an optimistic skeptic.
questions.rule: Unknowns are opportunities.
questions.teaches: For scientists, not knowing is exciting: it is an opportunity to discover, and the more that is unknown, the greater the opportunity.

questions.q: A lab director finds that almost no one in her field measures results. How would Tetlock's reasoning frame this?
options: As proof that measurement is impossible in her field, since no one has managed to do it
As a reason for pessimism, since a field that is not measured cannot improve at all
As evidence that her field is already at its limit, because everyone has stopped trying
As a large opportunity, since it is easy to improve where no one measures
optionExplain: He treats lack of measurement as a gap, not a proof.
He sees it as an opportunity.
No limit is implied.
Right: it echoes his optimistic stance.
questions.explain: Tetlock calls the lack of rigor in many forecasting domains an opportunity, and the authors quote Bill Gates saying measurement is amazingly often not done and hard to get right.
questions.rule: Gaps are opportunities.
questions.teaches: Bill Gates, quoted by the authors, says measurement is amazingly often not done and hard to get right.

questions.q: What was the Good Judgment Project?
options: A government agency that employs twenty thousand analysts to forecast world events each day
A study of experts from 1984 to 2004 that found the average expert matched random guessing
A team of volunteer forecasters led by Tetlock and Mellers in a tournament run by IARPA
A company that sold forecasts to banks and charged more for predictions about the far future
optionExplain: That describes the intelligence community, not the project.
That was Tetlock's earlier study.
Right: one of five teams.
No such company is described.
questions.explain: The project is the second phase of Tetlock's research. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Compare forecasters by having them forecast the same questions at the same time.

questions.q: Because all teams forecast the same questions at the same time, the tournament created a level playing ____.
questions.explain: Same questions, same moment, so teams can be compared fairly.
questions.rule: Fair comparison.

questions.q: A company wants to compare three vendors' forecasts fairly. Which tournament feature applies?
options: Have every vendor forecast the same questions at the same time
Let each vendor choose its own questions, so that it forecasts what it knows best
Ask each vendor for one big forecast at the end of the year, with no earlier submissions
Pick the vendor with the most famous name, since fame signals past accuracy
optionExplain: Right: that is what created the level playing field.
That would hide differences.
The tournament used daily submissions.
Fame is not a comparison.
questions.explain: Same questions at the same time allow a fair comparison.
questions.rule: Level the field.

questions.q: Match each quantity in the tournament to its figure.
pairs: Volunteers in the Good Judgment Project
questions.explain: These are the figures the chapter gives for the tournament.
questions.rule: Know the scale.

questions.q: True or false: The tournament's forecasts mostly extended three to five years ahead.
questions.explain: The vast majority extended more than one month and less than one year, shorter than in Tetlock's earlier research.
questions.rule: Know the horizon.

questions.q: A skeptic asks why IARPA ran a tournament at all. Which chapter fact supports the need?
options: The intelligence community had about twenty thousand analysts but little evidence of how good its forecasting was
The intelligence community already knew its forecasts were excellent and wanted to share its method
The intelligence community had too few analysts and needed volunteers to fill the gap
The intelligence community had measured every forecast and wanted an outside check on the result
optionExplain: Right: it had never been keen to measure.
The chapter says little could be said about quality.
It had about twenty thousand.
The chapter says it had not.
questions.explain: The chapter says the community has not been keen to spend money to find out how good its forecasting is.
questions.rule: Measure large operations too.
questions.teaches: The United States has about twenty thousand intelligence analysts, yet little can be said with confidence about how good their forecasting is, because the intelligence community has not been keen to measure it.

questions.q: How did the Good Judgment Project do against the official control group?
options: It tied with it in year 1 and beat it by a small margin only in year 2
It beat it by 78% in year 1 and by 60% in year 2, with the margin shrinking
It lost to it in year 1 and caught up in year 2 after learning the questions
It beat it by 60% in year 1 and by 78% in year 2
optionExplain: It won by wide margins in both years.
The margin grew, not shrank.
It won in both years.
Right: the margin widened.
questions.explain: The results were strong. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a team of volunteers using best practices can beat control groups and academic rivals in a fair tournament.

questions.q: After two years, IARPA dropped the other teams because the Good Judgment Project was doing so much ____.
questions.explain: The gap was large enough that continuing the rivals was pointless.
questions.rule: A clear win.

questions.q: A forecasting team beats the control group by 60% in year one and by 78% in year two. What trend does that show?
options: Its lead narrowed, since the second-year result shows regression toward the group average
Its lead over the control group widened
Its lead was stable, since both numbers describe a large margin over the control group
Its lead cannot be compared, since the two years used different control groups
optionExplain: 78% is above 60%.
Right: 78% is larger than 60%.
The margin grew.
The chapter compares them.
questions.explain: The second-year margin of 78% is larger than the first-year 60%.
questions.rule: Compare the margins.

questions.q: Which comparison group did the chapter say the Good Judgment Project beat by margins of 30% to 70%?
options: The official control group, which it beat by 60% and then 78% in the first two years
The professional analysts with classified data, whom the chapter says it narrowly beat
University-affiliated competitors, including Michigan and MIT
Tetlock's earlier panel of experts from the 1984 to 2004 study of political forecasts
optionExplain: Those are the control group margins.
No range is given for them here.
Right: that range applies to the rival university teams.
That panel was in a different study.
questions.explain: Two different comparison groups had two different margins.
questions.rule: Keep the groups apart.

questions.q: True or false: The chapter says the Good Judgment Project beat the control group by a smaller margin in year 2 than in year 1.
questions.explain: The margin was 60% in year 1 and 78% in year 2.
questions.rule: The margin grew.

questions.q: A critic says the volunteers had only public information, so the win means little. Which result addresses this?
options: The project drew volunteers from many professions, including lawyers, engineers and artists
The project submitted forecasts every day at 9 a.m. eastern standard time for four years
The project's volunteers were later hired by the intelligence agencies that ran the tournament
The project also outperformed professional intelligence analysts with access to classified data
optionExplain: That addresses variety, not information.
That addresses fairness, not information.
The chapter does not say that.
Right: the chapter says so.
questions.explain: The chapter says GJP even outperformed professional intelligence analysts with access to classified data.
questions.rule: Rival information does not decide the result.
questions.teaches: The Good Judgment Project even outperformed professional intelligence analysts with access to classified data.

questions.q: What do the authors say makes superforecasters so good?
options: Who they are, meaning a rare mix of intelligence and luck that cannot be taught to others
The information they hold, meaning access to classified sources that ordinary people lack
What they do, meaning their ways of thinking, gathering information and updating beliefs, not who they are
The hours they spend, meaning they follow the news more than anyone else in the world
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite.
The chapter says the project beat analysts with such access.
Right: the second key conclusion.
Hours are not the explanation.
questions.explain: The chapter gives two conclusions. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, foresight is a product of learnable habits of thought, not a mysterious gift.

questions.q: A tutorial of about sixty minutes improved accuracy by roughly ____ through the tournament year.
questions.explain: A short tutorial brought a modest but real gain.
questions.rule: Learning helps.

questions.q: A new analyst asks whether she needs a special gift to forecast. Which conclusion applies?
options: Foresight is bestowed at birth, but she can still earn a place among the best by working hard
Foresight is the product of habits of thought that can be learned and cultivated
Foresight needs access to classified data, so she should seek a job in an intelligence agency
Foresight comes from watching the news constantly, so she should follow more sources
optionExplain: The authors reject the gift view.
Right: no mysterious gift is needed.
The project beat analysts with such access.
Hours of news are not the explanation.
questions.explain: The authors say foresight is not a mysterious gift but the product of learnable habits.
questions.rule: Habits, not a gift.

questions.q: Sort each item: does the chapter make this claim, or not?
groups: The chapter does not claim this

items.t: Some people have a real, measurable skill at judging events months ahead
The habits behind good forecasting can be learned
A short tutorial improved accuracy by about 10%
Superforecasters can see decades into the future
Foresight is a mysterious gift bestowed at birth
A short tutorial made forecasters perfect

questions.explain: The chapter says the skill is real and learnable but limited to months, not decades, and the tutorial's gain was modest.
questions.rule: Real, learnable, limited.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say superforecasters are gurus or oracles able to peer decades into the future.
questions.explain: They say the opposite: superforecasters have a real skill over three months to a year and a half, not decades.
questions.rule: Skill has a horizon.

questions.q: A manager says a 10% accuracy gain is too small to bother with. What point does the chapter make in reply?
options: Modest improvements, if sustained, add up to the difference between a consistent winner and a loser
Ten percent is never worth the cost, but a sixty-minute tutorial is cheap enough to try
A ten percent gain is a dramatic improvement that anyone would notice immediately
A ten percent gain matters only for hedge funds with more than a hundred billion dollars
optionExplain: Right: Aaron Brown's point.
The chapter says it is worth it, because it is sustained.
Brown says it is hard to see because it is not dramatic.
The point applies to any sustained edge.
questions.explain: Aaron Brown says it is hard to see because it is not dramatic, but if sustained it separates a winner from someone going broke.
questions.rule: Small edges compound.
questions.teaches: Aaron Brown, a Wall Street risk manager, says a sustained modest improvement in foresight is hard to see because it is not dramatic, yet it separates a consistent winner from someone who is going broke all the time.

questions.q: What do the authors say explains why measuring is not standard practice in forecasting?
options: A lack of any method for scoring forecasts, since no one has ever designed a scoring rule
A psychology that convinces us we know things we really do not
A shortage of volunteers, since few people would agree to be scored on their forecasts
A belief that the future is wholly unpredictable, which makes any scoring a waste of effort
optionExplain: The chapter says measurement can be done.
Right: the feeling of knowing blocks testing.
Over twenty thousand volunteered.
The authors say the future is partly predictable.
questions.explain: The answer is about minds. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, personal experience and perception are not reliable guides to what works; test it rigorously instead.

questions.q: Medicine advanced rapidly once physicians turned to scientific ____ instead of trusting their experience.
questions.explain: Testing replaced trust in perceptions.
questions.rule: Test, don't trust.

questions.q: A clinic's doctors are sure a remedy works because patients seem to improve. Which chapter lesson applies?
options: Experience and perceptions are unreliable for judging whether a treatment works, so test it
Doctors' certainty is a good guide, so the remedy should be kept if most of them agree
Patients' reports are worthless, so the remedy should be dropped and never studied again
Remedies cannot be tested, so doctors should rely on the opinions of senior colleagues
optionExplain: Right: the medicine lesson.
The chapter says certainty misleads.
The lesson is to test, not to drop.
Medicine advanced by testing.
questions.explain: Medicine progressed when physicians accepted that experience alone does not show what works.
questions.rule: Test, don't trust.

questions.q: Match each case to what the chapter says about it.
pairs: Progress hobbled by trust in experience and perception
The same revolution still needs to happen
An example of thinking we know what we do not
questions.explain: The chapter pairs medicine's history with the present state of forecasting.
questions.rule: History offers a template.

questions.q: True or false: The authors compare forecasting today with medicine before it adopted scientific testing.
questions.explain: They say the same revolution needs to happen in forecasting.
questions.rule: Testing is the way out.

questions.q: A student asks who tested expert forecasting rigorously before the tournament. Which chapter fact answers?
options: In the late 1980s IARPA ran a tournament in which five scientific teams competed on the same questions
In the 1950s Meehl compared experts with algorithms in a test of thousands of political forecasts
In the late 1980s Tetlock worked out a methodology and ran what was then the biggest test of expert political forecasting accuracy
In the 1990s physicians tested forecasts of epidemics and compared them with outcomes
optionExplain: That was 2011 to 2015.
Meehl's work compared experts with algorithms in other settings.
Right: that was his earlier research.
No such test is mentioned.
questions.explain: The chapter says Tetlock worked out the methodology in the late 1980s; chapter 3 examines it.
questions.rule: Rigorous testing has a history.
questions.teaches: In the late 1980s Tetlock worked out a methodology and conducted what was, at the time, the biggest test of expert political forecasting accuracy ever.

questions.q: What does the chapter say is the strongest predictor of forecasting performance?
options: Raw intelligence, measured by tests, since the smartest forecasters tend to be the best
Advanced mathematical training, since many superforecasters hold degrees in math and science
Hours spent reading the news, since staying on top of developments produces better updates
Commitment to self-improvement
optionExplain: The chapter says intelligence is not the secret.
Even mathematicians rarely use much math.
The chapter calls that explanation a mistake.
Right: the analyses found it so.
questions.explain: The answer is about attitude. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, superforecasting demands thinking that is open-minded, careful, curious and above all self-critical.

questions.q: Above all, superforecasting demands thinking that is open-minded, careful, curious and ____.
questions.explain: Self-criticism is the quality the chapter stresses most.
questions.rule: Be self-critical.

questions.q: A firm hires only people with top test scores, expecting the best forecasts. What does the chapter say?
options: It is right, since intelligence explains almost all differences in forecasting performance
It is wrong, since intelligence is of no use at all in forecasting well
Intelligence alone is not what separates the best; how a person thinks matters most
It is right if the hires also work long hours, since hours explain the rest
optionExplain: The chapter says it is not the secret.
Minimum levels of intelligence are needed.
Right: thinking style beats raw ability.
Hours are not the explanation.
questions.explain: The authors say smart people are not automatically superforecasters.
questions.rule: How, not how smart.

questions.q: Within a quite wide range of views, what mattered for the earlier experts who had real foresight?
options: How they thought, not what they thought
What they thought, since certain political beliefs gave an edge in reading events
Whom they knew, since access to insiders gave them information others lacked
How famous they were, since media exposure forced them to be careful
optionExplain: Right: beliefs did not matter within a wide range.
The chapter says what they thought did not matter.
Special access was not the difference.
Fame was not the difference.
questions.explain: Style of thinking separated those with foresight from those who dragged the average down.
questions.rule: How, not what.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the experts with real foresight owed it to access to information others lacked.
questions.explain: They say it was not a mystical gift or access to information others lacked.
questions.rule: Not access.

questions.q: A mathematician joins a forecasting team. How much math does the chapter say to expect her to use?
options: A great deal, since the chapter says arcane math is the secret of superforecasting
None at all, since the chapter says mathematicians are poor forecasters
Only statistics, since the chapter says it is the one branch of math forecasters need
Little; even superforecasters who are card-carrying mathematicians rarely use much math
optionExplain: The chapter says the secret is not arcane math.
It does not say that.
Not mentioned.
Right: the chapter says so.
questions.explain: The chapter says the secret is not arcane math.
questions.rule: Thinking beats calculation.
questions.teaches: Even superforecasters who are card-carrying mathematicians rarely use much math.

questions.q: What did Paul Meehl's 1954 review find about experts and simple algorithms?
options: Experts were more accurate than algorithms, because they weigh subtle details that formulas miss
Well-informed experts were less accurate than simple algorithms that added up objective indicators
Experts and algorithms were equally accurate, so the choice between them was a matter of cost
Algorithms were accurate only for students, and failed on every question about parolees
optionExplain: Meehl found the reverse.
Right: algorithms did better.
Experts did worse.
Both kinds of question were reviewed.
questions.explain: The result upset many experts. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, when you have a well-validated statistical algorithm, use it.

questions.q: Meehl found that experts did worse than simple ____ that added up objective indicators.
questions.explain: Simple rules adding up objective indicators beat expert judgment.
questions.rule: Use validated algorithms.

questions.q: A bank has a well-validated scoring formula for loan defaults. What does the chapter advise?
options: Use it only as a second opinion, with the loan officer's hunch as the deciding vote
Ignore it, because a formula cannot capture the character of a borrower as a person
Test it against hunches each month, since the formula is unlikely to stay accurate for long
Use it
optionExplain: The advice is to use the algorithm.
The evidence points the other way.
The advice is to use it.
Right: the point is indisputable, in the authors' words.
questions.explain: A well-validated algorithm should be used.
questions.rule: Validated beats hunch.

questions.q: In the more than two hundred studies since Meehl, what is the usual result?
options: Experts beat algorithms in most cases, and the algorithms catch up only when data are plentiful
Algorithms beat subjective judgment in most cases and usually tie in the rest
Algorithms and experts split the wins evenly, with the winner depending on the subject
Algorithms win only where outcomes are numbers and lose wherever outcomes are choices
optionExplain: The reverse is reported.
Right: that is the chapter's summary.
Algorithms win most.
No such split is described.
questions.explain: Algorithms usually win, or tie.
questions.rule: Most studies favor algorithms.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say well-validated algorithms exist for most forecasting problems, so subjective judgment is obsolete.
questions.explain: They say we so rarely have well-validated algorithms for the problem at hand that subjective judgment was never threatened.
questions.rule: Algorithms are rare.

questions.q: In a study, an algorithm and expert judgment tie in accuracy. Which does the chapter's reasoning favor, and why?
options: The algorithm, because it is quick and cheap, so a tie supports using it
The expert, because a tie means the algorithm has failed to show any added benefit
Neither, because ties show the problem cannot be forecast by anyone
Both together, because a tie means each fills the gap in the other's reasoning
optionExplain: Right: cost decides a tie.
A tie supports the algorithm.
The chapter favors the cheaper tool.
The chapter's reasoning is about cost.
questions.explain: The chapter says algorithms are quick and cheap, unlike subjective judgment, so a tie supports using the algorithm.
questions.rule: Ties favor the cheap tool.
questions.teaches: Because algorithms are quick and cheap, unlike subjective judgment, a tie in accuracy supports using the algorithm.

questions.q: Why is asking whether two Russian leaders will trade jobs again harder for Watson than asking which two once did?
options: The first question concerns Russia, and Watson cannot read Russian news sources well enough
The first question has too many possible answers, and Watson can only answer yes or no questions
The first needs a judgment about intentions and causes; the second is a fact to look up
The first question needs a longer computation, which Watson's hardware could not run in time
optionExplain: Language is not the reason given.
That is not the reason.
Right: look-up versus judgment call.
Speed is not the issue.
questions.explain: The two questions differ in kind. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A question about the past can be looked up; a forecast needs a judgment call about intentions, character and causes.

questions.q: Deep Blue beat the chess champion Garry ____ in 1997.
questions.explain: It was a landmark of machine progress, one of two the chapter cites.
questions.rule: Machines have made great progress.

questions.q: A machine can instantly answer which country hosted the last Olympic Games. Why is that not forecasting?
options: It is looking up a number, whereas forecasting needs words, which machines still process poorly
It is looking up a historical fact; a forecast needs a judgment about what will happen
It is answering too fast, whereas forecasting needs a slow review of competing arguments
It is answering a question about sport, whereas forecasting concerns politics only
optionExplain: The contrast is fact versus judgment.
Right: the look-up versus judgment-call contrast.
Speed is not the contrast.
Subject is not the contrast.
questions.explain: The chapter says the first kind of question is a historical fact; the second needs an informed guess.
questions.rule: Fact versus judgment.

questions.q: Sort each question: can a computer look it up, or does it need a judgment call?

items.t: Who won the last football World Cup?
Which two Russian leaders traded jobs?
What was last year's GDP growth?
Will two top Russian leaders trade jobs in the next ten years?
Who will win the next football World Cup?
Will GDP growth rise next year?

questions.explain: Questions about the past can be looked up; questions about the future require integrating intentions and causes into a judgment.
questions.rule: Past: look up. Future: judge.

questions.q: True or false: According to the chapter, the kind of forecasting superforecasters do is still a long way from being done by computers.
questions.explain: The chapter says that even with computers making galloping advances it is a long way off.
questions.rule: Forecasting remains hard for machines.

questions.q: A startup promises machines will soon do all human forecasting. Which chapter episode counsels caution?
options: In 1954 Paul Meehl found algorithms beat experts, which proved machines had already won
In 1997 Deep Blue beat Kasparov, which proved that machines had reached the limit of progress
In 2011 Watson beat Jeopardy! champions, which proved computers can forecast world events
In 1965 Herbert Simon predicted machines would do any work a man can do within twenty years
optionExplain: Meehl's finding is about validated algorithms, not about machines taking over.
That shows progress, not a limit.
Watson answered questions about facts.
Right: the chapter calls it naively optimistic.
questions.explain: The chapter calls Simon's prediction naively optimistic and says it is one reason Ferrucci is more cautious today.
questions.rule: Beware confident timelines.
questions.teaches: In 1965 Herbert Simon thought machines were twenty years from doing any work a man can do, a naively optimistic view that makes Ferrucci cautious today.

questions.q: In freestyle chess, who competes?
options: Computers only, with humans watching and choosing which machine plays on their behalf
Humans only, with computers banned so that the players rely on their own judgment
Humans paired with computers, as teams
Humans against computers, in a match between a pure-human side and a pure-machine side
optionExplain: Humans take part in the team.
Computers are part of the team.
Right: the human draws on the computer but may override it.
That describes the older man versus machine contest.
questions.explain: It is a model for forecasting too. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, we will need to blend computer-based forecasting and subjective judgment, so it is time to get serious about both.

questions.q: The authors expect more syntheses like freestyle ____, where humans and computers compete as teams.
questions.explain: The chess example stands for the human and computer combination.
questions.rule: Teams beat either alone, sometimes.

questions.q: A hospital lets software suggest diagnoses while a doctor may override it. Which chapter model does this resemble?
options: Freestyle chess, where a human draws on the computer's strengths but sometimes overrides it
The guru model, where a single famous expert's opinion settles the matter for everyone else
The Laplacean demon, where a single all-knowing mind is able to predict every outcome
A dress-to-impress forecast, where the software is bought to look advanced for the hospital's donors
optionExplain: Right: human plus machine.
Not what is described.
Not what is described.
Nothing indicates showmanship.
questions.explain: The doctor and software work as a team, each covering the other's weaknesses.
questions.rule: Combine strengths.

questions.q: What does Ferrucci predict will become obsolete?
options: The guru model, in which each side counters a famous pundit with another
Human forecasters of every kind, who will be replaced by computers within a few decades
Statistical algorithms, which will be replaced by judgment in the cases that matter most
Chess tournaments, which have lost their audience now that computers beat every human
optionExplain: Right: it is the model of puerile policy debates.
He sees humans paired with computers.
He values the pairing.
He uses chess as a model of pairing.
questions.explain: Ferrucci sees it getting stranger to listen to experts informed only by subjective judgment.
questions.rule: The guru model fades.

questions.q: True or false: According to the chapter, Ferrucci expects computers soon to replace human judgment entirely in forecasting.
questions.explain: He expects more and more syntheses of human and computer, and pairs the expert with a computer to overcome human limitations.
questions.rule: Pairing, not replacement.

questions.q: Machines may get better at predicting human behavior by mimicking meaning. What limit does Ferrucci name?
options: Machines cannot mimic meaning at all, so their predictions of behavior will never improve
Machines can originate meaning, but they cannot yet process enough data to show it
Machines can reflect meaning only in chess and Jeopardy!, where the rules are fixed
Mimicking and reflecting meaning differs from originating it, a space human judgment will always occupy
optionExplain: He says they may get better.
He denies that they originate it.
He draws a general distinction.
Right: that is his argument.
questions.explain: According to Ferrucci, there is a difference between mimicking and reflecting meaning and originating meaning.
questions.rule: Humans originate meaning.
questions.teaches: According to Ferrucci, machines may get better at mimicking human meaning, but there is a difference between mimicking and reflecting meaning and originating it, a space human judgment will always occupy.

questions.q: In Archie Cochrane's 1956 story, what did the pathologist find in the tissue removed during his surgery?
options: No cancer at all
A cancer that was confined to the armpit
The same basal cell carcinoma found on his hand
A cancer too advanced for treatment
optionExplain: Right: the specialist's grim verdict was wrong, and Cochrane had no cancer.
A confined cancer would still make the specialist right, which the story denies.
The hand carcinoma was a separate, earlier finding, confirmed before the specialist was seen.
This repeats the specialist's verdict, which the pathologist's report overturned.
questions.explain: Cochrane had been told he was dying, yet the pathologist found no cancer. The card next shows why neither man waited for that report.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a confident verdict is not a verified one, so look for the evidence that could still settle the matter.

questions.q: Cochrane did not doubt the surgeon's words, and nobody thought to wait for the ____ report before closing the books on his life.
questions.explain: The pathologist's examination of the removed tissue could have settled the question, but neither man considered that the diagnosis might be wrong.
questions.rule: Pending evidence should be awaited before a verdict is final.

questions.q: Which situation most closely repeats the mistake in Cochrane's case?
options: A manager hears a respected analyst predict a sales boom and cancels the data check that was due next week
A manager asks two analysts for forecasts and compares both with the data check due next week
A manager rejects an analyst's sales forecast because analysts have been wrong before and trusts the data check
A manager follows a forecast only after the data check, due next week, has been read and discussed
optionExplain: Right: a respected voice replaces a check that was already on its way.
Comparing sources is the kind of checking Cochrane skipped, so this does not repeat his mistake.
This distrusts the expert and uses the check, so it is the opposite error.
Waiting for the check is exactly what neither Cochrane nor the specialist did.
questions.explain: The mistake is letting one confident judgment stand in for evidence that is still to come.
questions.rule: Do not let a confident verdict replace the check that is pending.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Cochrane and his specialist should not be judged too harshly, since being quick to decide is human nature.
questions.explain: The authors call the haste human nature: we have all been too quick to make up our minds and too slow to change them.
questions.rule: The haste is a human habit, not a flaw peculiar to two men.

questions.q: According to the authors, what happens if we do not examine how we make such mistakes?
options: They fade as training improves, because each generation of doctors corrects the last
We keep making them, and the stagnation can last years, a lifetime or centuries
They stay within one profession and do little harm outside medicine's walls
They are repeated only by people who lack the specialist's rank or experience
optionExplain: Medicine's long history, which the authors go on to tell, shows no such steady correction.
Right: the authors say the stagnation can go on for years, a lifetime or even centuries.
The authors later apply the same pattern to policing policy and to forecasting, so it does not stay in medicine.
Cochrane himself was a prominent physician, and the specialist was renowned, so rank did not protect them.
questions.explain: Unexamined habits of judgment persist, and the authors point to medicine's history as proof of how long.
questions.teaches: The authors say unexamined overconfidence can last for centuries, as the long history of medicine shows.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a confident verdict is not a verified one, so look for the evidence that could still settle the matter.

questions.q: A school head hears a respected inspector call a teacher failing. A classroom-observation report is due next week. What do the authors' lessons suggest?
options: Act now, since the inspector's rank makes a further report redundant
Act now but tell the teacher the verdict may change after the report
Wait for the report, since even a respected verdict is a judgment
Ignore the inspector, because experts' verdicts carry no information at all
optionExplain: Rank is what led Cochrane to accept the specialist without waiting.
Softening the delivery still acts on an unchecked verdict, as the specialist did.
Right: the pending report is the evidence that could settle the matter.
The authors do not say experts' verdicts are worthless; they say a verdict is not a fact.
questions.explain: Cochrane knew the pathologist had not yet reported, and accepted the verdict anyway; the report was exactly the evidence that could have settled the matter.
questions.teaches: Cochrane knew the pathologist had not yet reported, so the evidence that could settle the question was pending when he accepted the verdict.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a confident verdict is not a verified one, so look for the evidence that could still settle the matter.

questions.q: True or false: Until quite recently in historical terms, a sick person was often better off if no physician was available.
questions.explain: The authors say letting an illness run its course was often less dangerous than what a physician would inflict. The card next gives the reasoning.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a long record of confident treatment shows what people believed, not that the treatment worked.

questions.q: Burch said histories of medicine describe what people believed they were doing but give almost no account of whether they were ____.
questions.explain: Burch's complaint is that histories give a clear account of belief but none of whether the treatments worked.
questions.rule: A history of belief is not a history of results.

questions.q: A book describes in detail how village healers used one root for centuries. What question do the authors' points say to ask next?
options: Did the root actually work, when judged by evidence?
Which healer's account of the root is the oldest?
How many healers used the root over the centuries?
How confident were the healers in their account of it?
optionExplain: Right: the missing piece in most histories is whether the practice worked.
Age of an account tells you about records, not about whether the root worked.
Counting users repeats the belief-focused kind of account the authors criticise.
Confidence is what the authors say physicians had in abundance, so it does not test the root.
questions.explain: Ask for evidence of effect, not for details of practice or the confidence of those who practised it.
questions.rule: Ask whether it worked, not only what people did.

questions.q: Sort each item: does it show what people believed, or whether a treatment worked?

items.t: Doctors swearing that bloodletting was restorative
A detailed account of how poultices were applied
Washington's physicians trusting their regimen
A modern-science judgment of a treatment's efficacy
A finding that a patient does better without the treatment
A trial comparing treated and untreated patients

questions.explain: Confident statements and detailed descriptions record belief and practice. Only a test of the effect, judged by modern science, shows whether a treatment worked.
questions.rule: Belief and practice are not evidence of effect.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say treatments seldom got better, no matter how much time passed.
questions.explain: They say treatments seldom improved however much time passed.
questions.rule: Time alone did not improve treatment.

questions.q: Washington's 1799 care was bleeding, mercury, induced vomiting and blistering. What does the authors' account say about medicine over earlier centuries?
options: The regimen was a modern revision of ancient methods that had finally proved effective
Washington's doctors had invented methods that no earlier physician would have recognised
Each earlier century had added to the regimen until it became the best then known
Physicians in Athens, Rome, Paris or London would have nodded at much of it
optionExplain: The authors judge the methods useless or worse, so they were not proved effective.
The regimen was old, not new; the authors stress its lack of change.
This suggests progress, which the authors deny.
Right: the authors say physicians in all those places would have nodded at much of the regimen.
questions.explain: Washington's treatment matched what physicians had done in Athens, Rome, Paris and London, which shows how little treatment changed.
questions.teaches: Physicians in Aristotle's Athens, Nero's Rome, medieval Paris or Elizabethan London would have nodded at much of Washington's 1799 regimen.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a long record of confident treatment shows what people believed, not that the treatment worked.

questions.q: Washington died after heavy treatment. What do the authors say that proves about the treatments?
options: That they were too weak to matter to the outcome
That they hastened his death, since the outcome points that way
That they were harmless to him but unable to help
Only that they failed to prevent his death
optionExplain: Weakness is a guess; the death cannot show strength or weakness of the treatment.
Hastening is one possibility among several, not something the death proves.
Harmless is another possibility, but the death does not show it.
Right: his death proves only that the treatments did not prevent it.
questions.explain: A single death fits several explanations, so it proves little. The card next sets out the reasoning.
questions.rule: According to the authors, one outcome fits several explanations, and a belief that a treatment works tilts how the outcome is read.

questions.q: It is impossible to know which explanation is true by observing only that one ____.
questions.explain: With one outcome, the treatment may have helped, done nothing or hurt, and the outcome cannot say which.
questions.rule: One outcome underdetermines the cause.

questions.q: A shop owner redesigns the window and sales rise next month. What does the authors' reasoning say about that rise?
options: It shows the window worked, because sales followed the change
It shows the window did nothing, because sales may rise anyway
It fits several explanations, so one result cannot show it worked
It shows other causes were absent, because the change came first in time
optionExplain: Following the change is the tempting but weak reasoning the authors warn about.
This swings to the opposite certainty; the rise also leaves the window possibly helpful.
Right: the rise fits the window helping, doing nothing or other causes at work.
Order in time does not rule out other causes; the authors list too many factors involved.
questions.explain: The rise is compatible with many causes, and the owner's hope for the window tilts how it is read.
questions.rule: A result that fits many causes proves none of them.

questions.q: True or false: Physicians who already think a treatment works will tend to read an ambiguous outcome in its favour.
questions.explain: The authors say they are already inclined to think the treatments work, or they would not prescribe them, so the ambiguity is likely read in favour of the happy conclusion.
questions.rule: Prior belief tilts how ambiguous results are read.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Washington's treatments may have helped, done nothing or hastened his death, and one outcome cannot tell which.
questions.explain: They list these as possibilities and say it is impossible to know which is true from the one outcome.
questions.rule: Do not turn a possibility into a finding.

questions.q: A coach tries a routine for one season and the team wins the title. What do the authors say is needed to credit the routine?
options: Another title next season, which would settle the question once the routine is seen working twice
The opinions of respected coaches in other sports, who can judge the routine without bias
Stronger, more rigorous testing than one season, enough to overcome the coach's preconceptions
A longer explanation from the coach of why the routine should help, since the logic matters
optionExplain: More loose observations can still be hard or impossible to untangle, as the authors say.
Respected opinion is the kind of authority the authors say medicine leaned on.
Right: the authors say it takes strong evidence and rigorous experimentation to overwhelm preconceptions.
A theory of why a treatment works is what confident physicians already supplied.
questions.explain: Bleed-and-see tests cannot beat preconceptions; the authors say rigorous experimentation was needed and, in medicine, was never done.
questions.teaches: The authors say overwhelming physicians' preconceptions takes strong evidence and more rigorous experiment than bleeding the patient and seeing whether he gets better, and that this was never done.
questions.rule: According to the authors, one outcome fits several explanations, and a belief that a treatment works tilts how the outcome is read.

questions.q: How did Galen explain patients who took his treatment and died?
options: They had taken it in the wrong dose or at the wrong time
They had delayed too long before taking the treatment
They were incurable cases, where it is said to fail
They were failed by physicians who misapplied his method
optionExplain: The quoted claim names no dose or timing.
Galen's own claim, quoted by the authors, does not mention delay.
Right: Galen said it fails only in incurable cases.
The claim lays no blame on other physicians; it turns every death into an incurable case.
questions.explain: Galen counted deaths as incurable cases, so no death could count against him. The card next explains why that matters.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a claim that treats every outcome as support can never be shown wrong, and certainty removes the reason to test it.

questions.q: Galen ran no experiments because they are what people do when they are not ____ what the truth is.
questions.explain: Galen was untroubled by doubt, so he saw no reason for experiments.
questions.rule: Experiments begin where certainty ends.

questions.q: A diet guru says everyone who follows his plan slims down, except those whose bodies resist it. What is wrong with that claim?
options: It promises far too much weight loss to be believable to anyone
It relies on followers who are not trained in nutrition
It ignores the people who gave up the plan early
Any result counts as support, so nothing could refute him
optionExplain: The size of the promise is not the flaw; the structure is.
The followers' training is irrelevant to whether the claim can be tested.
Dropouts matter in other ways, but the guru's logic would explain them away too.
Right: success confirms the plan and failure is blamed on the body, so the claim cannot lose.
questions.explain: Like Galen's claim, it wins either way, so it never has to be tested.
questions.rule: If every result confirms a claim, the claim says nothing.

questions.q: A patient taking Galen's treatment does not recover. What would Galen conclude?
options: The treatment may be flawed and needs testing
The patient was probably misdiagnosed from the very start
The patient was incurable, so his treatment is untouched
The treatment needs revising and another trial
optionExplain: That is the doubt Galen lacked; the authors say he was untroubled by it.
Nothing in Galen's reasoning questions the diagnosis; it questions the patient's curability.
Right: his stated rule turns every failure into an incurable case.
Revising and testing are what a doubter does, not what Galen did.
questions.explain: Galen's reasoning protects his treatment from every failure.
questions.rule: A claim protected from every failure cannot be tested.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Galen's writings were the indisputable source of medical authority for more than a thousand years.
questions.explain: They write that his writings were the indisputable source of medical authority for more than a thousand years.
questions.rule: Untested authority can last a very long time.

questions.q: How long, per the authors, did Galen's writings remain the indisputable source of medical authority, though he conducted nothing like a modern experiment?
options: About one hundred years
More than a thousand years
About three hundred years
About five hundred years in all
optionExplain: Far too short; his influence ran on through the Middle Ages.
Right: more than a thousand years.
This is still short of the authors' figure.
Closer, but the authors say more than a thousand years.
questions.explain: A claim that cannot lose can survive for an extremely long time, which is part of why medicine stagnated.
questions.teaches: The authors say Galen's writings were the indisputable medical authority for more than a thousand years, though he never did anything like a modern experiment.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a claim that treats every outcome as support can never be shown wrong, and certainty removes the reason to test it.

questions.q: What did the surgeon-historian Ira Rutkow compare debating physicians to?
options: Blind men arguing over the colors of the rainbow
Sailors arguing over where the shore lies
Travelers quarrelling over a map that no one can read
Merchants bargaining over goods that nobody has seen
optionExplain: Right: with no test to decide, the argument cannot be settled.
The image is of blindness to colour, not of navigation.
The image is about arguing over what cannot be seen, not about a map.
Bargaining is not the image; arguing about unseen properties is.
questions.explain: Rutkow's image is of arguing about something no one in the argument can perceive. The card next explains the point.
questions.rule: According to the authors, loud and confident disagreement among experts who never test their claims is not progress.

questions.q: Rutkow likened physicians who furiously debated the merits of treatments to blind men arguing over the ____ of the rainbow.
questions.explain: Blind men cannot see the colours, so their debate cannot be settled, like debates with no test.
questions.rule: Debates without tests cannot be settled.

questions.q: Two pundits furiously dispute whether a tax cut helped growth. Neither offers a test; each cites events that favour their side. Which phrase fits?
options: Galen's claim: every result is read as support for one's side
Cochrane's case: a verdict accepted before the evidence arrived
Blind men arguing: heated debate with nothing to decide it
Washington's case: a single outcome read as proof of a cause
optionExplain: Galen's pattern is about a claim that cannot lose; here the two sides each count different events, with nothing to decide between them.
Cochrane's case is about a verdict taken as fact before a pending report, not an endless debate.
Right: the debate has confidence but no test.
Washington's case is about a single outcome, while this dispute lacks any test to settle it.
questions.explain: Confident argument without a test is the pattern Rutkow's image describes.
questions.rule: Confidence plus no test equals argument that cannot end.

questions.q: Sort each item: how the confident figures behaved, or what was missing?

items.t: Embracing treatments with strong conviction
Denouncing rivals as quacks
Spreading insights with evangelical passion
Experiments to test the theories
Doubt about their own judgment
Evidence able to separate rival claims

questions.explain: The figures were certain, combative and evangelical. What the authors say was missing is doubt and experiment that could separate rival claims.
questions.rule: Conviction is not evidence.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that, fringe or mainstream, almost all of these medical theories and treatments were wrong.
questions.explain: They write that, fringe or mainstream, almost all of it was wrong.
questions.rule: Being mainstream did not make a treatment effective.

questions.q: A clinic's doctors privately suspect their standard therapy may be useless. According to the authors' account of earlier physicians, what did most do?
options: Dropped the therapy at once and tested alternatives
Published their fears so rivals could correct them
Carried on with business as usual
Asked patients to choose their own treatments instead
optionExplain: That is the doubt-driven response the authors say medicine lacked.
Publishing doubts would have started the scrutiny that the authors say was missing.
Right: the authors say some feared as much but most carried on.
Nothing in the authors' account has patients choosing for themselves.
questions.explain: Fear of being wrong did not lead to change; habit and confidence won.
questions.teaches: The authors say some physicians feared their treatments were worthless, but most carried on with business as usual.
questions.rule: According to the authors, loud and confident disagreement among experts who never test their claims is not progress.

questions.q: In James Lind's 1747 experiment on sailors with scurvy, which treatment led to quick recovery?
options: Seawater
Cider
A bark paste
Citrus fruit
optionExplain: Seawater was one of the six and did not help.
Cider was one of the six treatments tried, but it did not produce the recovery.
The bark paste was one of the six, with no recovery reported.
Right: the pair given citrus recovered quickly.
questions.explain: Citrus worked, yet the world did not change. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, running a comparison is not enough: someone must grasp what it shows and act on it.

questions.q: Lind divided his twelve sailors into ____ and gave each a different treatment.
questions.explain: Twelve sailors in pairs gave six treatments, each tried on two men.
questions.rule: Lind compared six treatments, two sailors each.

questions.q: A lab's test shows one method beats five others, yet the lead researcher shrugs and keeps the old method. Which part of Lind's story repeats?
options: Dividing patients into pairs without any comparison between them
Using treatments drawn from a stock of folk remedies of the time
Reporting a success that later experiments could not reproduce
Failing to make sense of his own result and staying unconvinced
optionExplain: Lind did compare the pairs; the problem lay in understanding the result.
The mix of treatments is not the failing that the authors single out.
The authors do not say later work failed to reproduce citrus recovery.
Right: Lind got a result he did not grasp.
questions.explain: A result unused is no better than no result, which is what the authors say happened to Lind's.
questions.rule: A result only changes practice if someone understands it.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Lind's experiment was not the eureka moment that ushered in the modern era of experimentation.
questions.explain: They say that, contrary to popular belief, it was not.
questions.rule: Doing something that looks modern is not the same as understanding it.

questions.q: According to the authors, what prompted Lind to run his experiment?
options: Curiosity about citrus, which sailors had long used as a flavouring on their voyages and in port
A request from naval officers that he prove the worth of a remedy that was already in use
A new statistical template for comparing treatments between groups of patients, laid out in a journal
Desperation: scurvy was a mortal threat at sea and nothing the physicians tried seemed to work
optionExplain: Nothing in the account has Lind interested in citrus beforehand.
The account gives no sign of such a request; the treatments were shots in the dark.
Statistical templates came in the twentieth century, much later.
Right: the authors call it an experiment born of desperation.
questions.explain: Scurvy killed sailors and nothing worked, which pushed Lind to try several treatments.
questions.teaches: Lind's experiment was born of desperation: scurvy was a mortal threat on long voyages and the physicians' confidence could not hide the futility of their treatments.
questions.rule: According to the authors, running a comparison is not enough: someone must grasp what it shows and act on it.

questions.q: A manager tests six sales scripts on two customers each and keeps the winner. Which phrase from the authors' account of Lind fits?
options: Galen's claim, which fails only in incurable cases
Six shots in the dark, with one hit
Blind men arguing over the colors of the rainbow
Cochrane's verdict, accepted before the pathologist reported
optionExplain: That is a claim built to win whatever happens, not a hit-or-miss trial.
Right: with no basis for knowing which would work, Lind tried six and one hit.
That image is about debate without a test, not about a trial.
That is a verdict taken on trust, not a set of attempts made in the dark.
questions.explain: The authors say Lind took six shots in the dark and one hit, and the result still did not convince him.
questions.teaches: The authors describe Lind's six treatments as six shots in the dark, one of which hit.
questions.rule: According to the authors, running a comparison is not enough: someone must grasp what it shows and act on it.

questions.q: Why do researchers assign patients to treatment groups at random?
options: So every patient is given the best treatment known at the time
So differences among patients should balance out across groups
So the two groups are identical in every way
So the doctors cannot be blamed for poor results
optionExplain: The point of a trial is to find the best treatment, not to give it.
Right: with enough people, chance spreads differences across both groups.
Groups cannot be identical, since no two people are alike; random assignment balances differences.
Blame is not the purpose; random assignment supports causal conclusions.
questions.explain: Random assignment lets chance spread personal differences across groups. The card next sets out the logic.
questions.rule: According to the authors, random assignment of enough people balances their differences, so a gap in outcomes can be traced to the treatment.

questions.q: Hill's template is flawed in practice because no two people are exactly alike, so the experiment is ____ by differences among subjects.
questions.explain: Differences among people confuse the comparison, so assignment must balance them.
questions.rule: Individual differences confound a comparison.

questions.q: A school wants to know whether a tutoring programme raises grades. Which design follows the authors' logic?
options: Pupils are assigned to tutoring or not by lottery, with enough pupils in each group
Parents who sign up their children form the tutoring group, and the rest form the comparison group
The weakest pupils are tutored and the strongest form the comparison group
Teachers pick who they think will gain the most and compare them with the others
optionExplain: Right: a lottery balances differences among pupils across the two groups.
Self-selection brings differences, such as parental effort, into the comparison.
Choosing by strength makes the groups differ systematically before tutoring starts.
Teacher picks bring in their expectations and differences that tilt the comparison.
questions.explain: Only chance assignment avoids building differences into the groups.
questions.rule: Let chance, not choice, decide who gets the treatment.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say random assignment balances out differences if enough people take part in the experiment.
questions.explain: They write that differences should balance out if enough people participate, so a very small group gives less protection.
questions.rule: The balancing needs numbers.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say randomized controlled trials are imperfect, because there is no perfection in our messy world.
questions.explain: They write that it isn't perfect but beats wise men stroking their chins.
questions.rule: A good method can still be imperfect.

questions.q: In 1921 the Lancet asked whether counting patients was a trivial ingenuity or an important stage in medicine. How did Hill answer?
options: That it was a trivial ingenuity, since patients vary too much
That it was useful only for diseases of the skin or blood
Emphatically that it was an important stage
That it mattered less than the judgment of senior physicians
optionExplain: Variation is the problem random assignment answers, not a reason to dismiss counting.
Nothing in the authors' account limits it to particular diseases.
Right: Hill answered emphatically that the numerical method was an important stage.
That would be the authority-first view the authors criticise.
questions.explain: The authors present Hill's answer as the start of modern medical investigation.
questions.teaches: The Lancet asked in 1921 whether the numerical method was trivial or an important stage in medicine, and Hill responded emphatically that it was the latter.
questions.rule: According to the authors, random assignment of enough people balances their differences, so a gap in outcomes can be traced to the treatment.

questions.q: In Feynman's story, what did the islanders do after the American airbases were removed?
options: Rebuilt the planes from scrap metal left behind
Sent messengers to the outside world to ask for goods
Built imitation runways, fires and a control hut, then waited
Burned the runways so that the planes would not return to the island
optionExplain: The story is about copying the airbase's appearance, not rebuilding planes.
They had lost contact with the outside world and did not send messengers.
Right: they copied the outward form of an airbase.
They wanted the planes to return, not to stop them.
questions.explain: They copied the form and waited for the result. The card next shows what that has to do with medicine.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the look of science without its substance, such as testing, is not science.

questions.q: The authors say medicine before randomized trials was cargo cult ____.
questions.explain: The phrase means the outward form of science without what makes it scientific.
questions.rule: Form without substance is cargo cult science.

questions.q: A startup holds data-driven meetings and builds dashboards but does not test whether any decision worked. How would the authors' term describe it?
options: Real science, because it uses charts and measurement
The look of science without the testing that makes it scientific
Real science, because it gathers more data than rivals
Poor science only because no famous scientist or university backs it
optionExplain: Charts and measurement words are outward form.
Right: the rituals imitate science, but nothing is tested.
Volume of data is not testing; the islanders also had many rituals.
Fame does not make a method scientific or unscientific.
questions.explain: Outward trappings do not make a method scientific.
questions.rule: Look for the test, not the trappings.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say medicine had occasionally reaped the fruits of science, such as the germ theory of disease and the X-ray.
questions.explain: They say so, and still call the medicine of the time cargo cult science.
questions.rule: Gaining from science is different from working scientifically.

questions.q: Sort each item: outward form of science, or what makes it truly scientific?

items.t: Educated men with impressive titles
Latin-laden lectures at august universities
A wooden hut with headphones and bamboo antennas
Doubt that leads to new things to test
Randomly assigned groups compared by outcome
Willingness to learn a hunch is wrong

questions.explain: Titles, lectures and mock equipment are form. Doubt, testing and comparison are what make a practice scientific.
questions.rule: Do not mistake titles for method.

questions.q: Which statement about the term cargo cult science is supported by the authors' account?
options: Feynman coined it as praise for physicians who borrowed methods from physics
Physicians used it themselves in the nineteenth century to describe quacks
Lind used it to explain why his citrus trial had failed to persuade
Feynman coined it much later, as mockery, and the authors apply it to older medicine
optionExplain: The authors describe it as mockery, not praise.
The term did not exist then; it was coined much later.
Lind is not linked to the term in the account.
Right: Feynman's term of mockery was coined much later.
questions.explain: The authors borrow a later label to describe earlier medicine.
questions.teaches: Feynman coined cargo cult science much later, as a term of mockery, and the authors apply it to the medicine of earlier times.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the look of science without its substance, such as testing, is not science.

questions.q: According to Feynman, what matters most for the rate at which science develops?
options: The rate at which new things to test are created
How certain scientists feel about their results
The number of observations made
How quickly rival theories are rejected by the field
optionExplain: Right: observation alone is not enough; new tests drive progress.
Certainty is what doubt replaces; it does not drive progress.
Observation matters, but Feynman says it is not the most important thing.
Quick rejection is not what Feynman's passage describes.
questions.explain: Feynman puts new things to test at the centre. The card next gives his reasoning.
questions.rule: According to Feynman, recognise your ignorance and doubt, because doubt is what generates new things to test.

questions.q: Feynman said doubt is not a fearful thing but a thing of very great ____.
questions.explain: He treats doubt as valuable because it propels science.
questions.rule: Doubt is valuable.

questions.q: A researcher says she has a hunch the drug works, would bet on it, and still has some doubt. How does Feynman's passage treat that?
options: As the normal state of a scientist who is pretty sure: a bet with some doubt
As a weakness, since a scientist should be certain before speaking in public
As ignorance, since she does not know the answer for sure
As dishonesty, since a hunch is no evidence at all
optionExplain: Right: Feynman describes being pretty sure as still being in some doubt.
Feynman values doubt; he does not ask for certainty.
Ignorance is his term for someone who says he does not know; she has a hunch.
Nothing suggests dishonesty; a hunch is a proper state of uncertainty.
questions.explain: Hunch, bet and lingering doubt are the stages he describes.
questions.rule: Pretty sure still leaves room for doubt.

questions.q: A lab doubles its observations but proposes no new tests. According to Feynman, what governs how fast its field develops?
options: The confidence of the most senior scientists
The total number of observations made across the whole field
The rate of creating new tests, not observations alone
The agreement reached among the leading laboratories
optionExplain: Confidence is what doubt replaces.
Feynman says the rate is not observation alone.
Right: more observation without new tests does not raise the rate.
Agreement is not the driver he names.
questions.explain: New tests are what move a field forward.
questions.rule: Observation alone is not the engine.

questions.q: True or false: Feynman says a scientist who is pretty sure of how it will work is still in some doubt.
questions.explain: He says that even then the scientist is still in some doubt.
questions.rule: Betting is not certainty.

questions.q: A team is certain its strategy is right. According to Feynman's reasoning, what is missing?
options: Doubt, which prompts people to look in new directions
Rivals, since doubt arises only from outside challenge
Observations, since doubt follows from more data alone
Time, since new ideas come only after a longer wait
optionExplain: Right: because we have the doubt, we propose looking in new directions.
Doubt can be one's own; the passage does not make it depend on rivals.
Observation alone is not the driver; doubt comes first.
Feynman does not tie doubt to waiting.
questions.explain: Doubt creates the demand for new ideas and tests.
questions.teaches: Feynman says that because we have doubt, we propose looking in new directions for new ideas.
questions.rule: According to Feynman, recognise your ignorance and doubt, because doubt is what generates new things to test.

questions.q: What did Cochrane call the physicians' belief that their own judgment alone revealed the truth?
options: The surgeon's pride
The healer's creed
The God complex
The authority trap
optionExplain: Surgeon's pride sounds plausible, but it is not the name used.
This is not Cochrane's term; his label for the attitude refers to divinity.
Right: Cochrane despised the attitude and gave it that name.
Authority trap sounds close, but Cochrane did not use it.
questions.explain: Cochrane named the attitude the God complex. The card next explains what it did to medicine.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an institution convinced that its judgment alone reveals the truth feels no need for validation.

questions.q: Cochrane called the attitude that a physician's judgment alone reveals the truth the God ____.
questions.explain: The attitude is the God complex.
questions.rule: Judgment alone, not tested, is the God complex.

questions.q: A senior engineer refuses an A/B test of a design: 'Twenty years in this job; I know which one works.' Which attitude is this?
options: Healthy skepticism of data that might mislead the team
A God-complex attitude: judgment alone is taken as truth
Reasonable thrift in avoiding a test whose result is already known
Doubt directed at his own judgment, as Feynman recommends
optionExplain: Skepticism of data is not the stance; he refuses to test at all.
Right: experience is used in place of a test.
Thrift would require that the result be known; here only his belief is offered.
Feynman's doubt is about one's own judgment, which this engineer does not show.
questions.explain: Declaring that judgment alone suffices, and so no test is needed, is the attitude Cochrane named.
questions.rule: If judgment alone is enough, nothing is ever tested.

questions.q: After the war the first serious trials gave excellent results. How did the medical establishment respond, according to the authors?
options: It adopted randomized trials at once across its hospitals
It often showed no interest, or even hostility
It funded further trials but kept practice unchanged
It welcomed the results but asked for more years of study
optionExplain: The authors say adoption was painfully slow.
Right: promoters of modernization met disinterest or hostility.
The account has no funding of trials; it describes disinterest.
The reception was not warm; it was uninterested or hostile.
questions.explain: Good results alone did not win over the establishment.
questions.rule: Evidence does not persuade those who think they already know.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the first serious trials after the war delivered excellent results, yet the establishment was still uninterested or hostile.
questions.explain: They write that the trials delivered excellent results but the establishment stayed uninterested or even hostile.
questions.rule: Resistance did not follow from poor results.

questions.q: Why did physicians say they did not need scientific validation, according to the authors?
options: They lacked the money for trials and the hospitals to run them
They did what they had done for years, backed by respected authority
They had already tested their treatments in small private studies
They believed trials were unethical in every circumstance
optionExplain: Cost is not the reason the authors give.
Right: tradition plus respected authority stood in for validation.
The authors say they just knew; they did not test.
Ethics was raised in a particular trial, but the general reason was habit and authority.
questions.explain: Habit and respected authority replaced evidence.
questions.teaches: Physicians kept doing what they did because they had always done it that way, and they were backed up by respected authority, so they did not feel they needed scientific validation.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an institution convinced that its judgment alone reveals the truth feels no need for validation.

questions.q: What trick did Cochrane play on the cardiologists during his cardiac care unit trial?
options: He ran the trial in secret so that nobody could object
He gave them the results the wrong way round, then revealed it
He asked them to guess the results before the trial had even begun
He swapped the patients between the two groups halfway through
optionExplain: The trial was proposed openly, and the cardiologists tried to stop it.
Right: he reversed the figures and later told them.
The account has no guessing exercise.
The trick concerned the reported results, not the assignment of patients.
questions.explain: Cochrane flipped the results to test their reaction. The card next explains what happened.
questions.rule: According to the authors, strong confidence in a treatment can drive reactions to a result even when the result runs the other way.

questions.q: In the trial, patients not sent to the cardiac care units were sent home for monitoring and ____ rest.
questions.explain: The old treatment was monitoring and bed rest at home.
questions.rule: The comparison was cardiac units against home monitoring and bed rest.

questions.q: Managers insist a new scheduling system is better and call a trial unfair to the wards without it. Which feature of Cochrane's story is this?
options: Treating belief that something is better as a reason not to test it
