Hiding results from those affected so that they cannot object later
Choosing groups by hand so that the new system wins
Stopping a trial early because its results are not significant
optionExplain: Right: the physicians used belief in the units to oppose the trial.
Cochrane's trick hid the true result only briefly to test reactions; the objection here is to testing at all.
The cardiologists did not choose groups; they argued against the trial.
The group-picking and results issues are not what the objectors did.
questions.explain: A conviction that one option is superior is turned into an argument against testing it.
questions.rule: Belief that a treatment is better is not a reason to skip the trial.

questions.q: Cochrane told cardiologists the units seemed slightly better. How did they respond?
options: They demanded he stop the trial at once, calling it unethical
They asked him to run it longer to confirm
They asked to see the data before drawing any conclusion
They accepted it as only a preliminary, non-significant result
optionExplain: Right: they abused him and demanded he stop.
Their reaction was to stop, not to extend.
They did not ask for the data; they were vociferous in their abuse.
Cochrane himself stressed the result was not significant; they ignored that.
questions.explain: Convinced of the units' benefit, they treated the preliminary result as enough to end the trial.
questions.rule: Confidence turns weak evidence into a verdict.

questions.q: True or false: Cochrane emphasised to the cardiologists that the difference in outcomes was not statistically significant.
questions.explain: He told them the difference was not statistically significant, though the units appeared slightly better.
questions.rule: A small, non-significant difference is not a verdict.

questions.q: A team lead swaps the figures in a briefing to test colleagues' convictions. Per the story, what followed when Cochrane revealed the truth?
options: A public debate about the ethics of the trial's design
Applause for the trick, followed by a vote to continue the trial to its end
A written apology to Cochrane for their earlier abuse
Dead silence, and Cochrane felt sick because they were his colleagues
optionExplain: The account reports silence, not a debate.
Applause is not in the account.
The account reports no apology.
Right: the story reports dead silence and Cochrane felt sick.
questions.explain: The reaction was silence, and Cochrane did not enjoy it.
questions.teaches: After Cochrane revealed the reversal there was dead silence, and he felt rather sick because the cardiologists were his medical colleagues.
questions.rule: According to the authors, strong confidence in a treatment can drive reactions to a result even when the result runs the other way.

questions.q: Why could nobody tell whether the short, sharp, shock policy for young offenders worked?
options: It covered the whole justice system, so there was nothing to compare
Crime statistics were not collected after the policy began in any court
Judges refused to apply the policy in most courts
It was tried in one prison and the results were lost
optionExplain: Right: with no comparison group the outcome has many possible causes.
The problem was not missing statistics but missing comparison.
The policy was applied throughout; refusal is not the problem.
It was applied widely, not in one prison.
questions.explain: Applying a policy everywhere at once leaves nothing to compare. The card next sets this out.
questions.rule: According to the authors, without a controlled comparison, politicians on each side can claim the same facts, and nobody knows.

questions.q: The only alternative to a controlled experiment that gives real insight is an ____ experiment, which gives the illusion of insight.
questions.explain: An uncontrolled experiment has no comparison, so it only seems to teach.
questions.rule: No control, no insight.

questions.q: A city launches a new bus network everywhere at once and ridership rises. What follows from the authors' reasoning?
options: Ridership rose, so the new network must have worked as the planners intended
Ridership rising shows only that fares were too low
It may have risen for many reasons, as nothing was compared with the old system
A rise in ridership means the old network was a failure
optionExplain: Rising after the change is exactly the post hoc reading the authors warn about.
The reasoning does not single out fares as the cause.
Right: with no comparison, a rise has many possible causes.
Nothing shows the old network failed; a rise could come from other reasons.
questions.explain: Without a comparison, the rise proves nothing about the network.
questions.rule: No comparison means no insight.

questions.q: Crime rises after the policy. What could supporters of the policy argue, per the authors?
options: That the policy had worked in other countries
That crime figures were collected wrongly after the policy began
That crime would have risen even more without the policy
That the rise proves the policy needs more time to act
optionExplain: Other countries are not mentioned.
The authors' point is about the interpretation of a rise, not about faulty figures.
Right: the authors say a rise might mean it prevented a bigger rise.
That is not what the authors give as the supporters' argument.
questions.explain: Either result can be read as success or failure, since nothing is controlled.
questions.rule: A result with no comparison can be spun either way.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that without a controlled trial of the policy, nobody would really know whether it worked.
questions.explain: Those in power said it worked and opponents said it failed, but nobody would really know.
questions.rule: Politicians argue; without a trial nobody knows.

questions.q: A district bans phones in every school at once. Which design would let it learn whether the ban worked?
options: Asking every principal to report whether the ban is working
Comparing this year's results with those from ten years ago in the same schools
Choosing some schools at random to start the ban first, then comparing
Counting how many parents approve of the ban
optionExplain: Principals' impressions are opinion, not comparison.
Ten years apart, many other things changed.
Right: a random start with a comparison group gives a controlled test.
Approval measures opinion, not effect.
questions.explain: Cochrane argued a controlled trial of the policy might by now have shown its true worth.
questions.teaches: Cochrane said that if the government had subjected its policy to a randomized controlled trial we might by now have known its true worth.
questions.rule: According to the authors, without a controlled comparison, politicians on each side can claim the same facts, and nobody knows.

questions.q: What is the puzzle of Cochrane himself, according to the authors?
options: A man who urged slow judgment yet rushed to judge his own cancer
A man who proposed trials for others but did not run one himself in his career
A man who hated doctors yet became one in later life, after the war
A man who trusted pathologists less than surgeons did, when it mattered
optionExplain: Right: his own behaviour contradicted his message.
Cochrane did run trials, including one on cardiac care units.
He was a physician from the start; the puzzle is about his reaction.
He wanted the pathologist's report but never asked for it; the puzzle is about acceptance.
questions.explain: The riddle is the gap between what Cochrane preached and what he did. The card next lays it out.
questions.rule: According to the authors, even people who know the rule against rushing to judgment break it, so the cause must lie in how minds work.

questions.q: Cochrane treated the physician's conclusion as ____ and prepared to die.
questions.explain: He did not think it was just one man's judgment.
questions.rule: A confident verdict was treated as fact.

questions.q: A statistician who teaches the danger of small samples decides to buy a house from one neighbour's anecdote. Which riddle does this repeat?
options: The first riddle: why people resist a point that is so plainly true
The pathologist's riddle: why a report arrives late
Cochrane's: an expert on the rule against haste breaks it himself
Galen's riddle: why every outcome confirms a theory
optionExplain: The first riddle concerns resistance by others; here the same person knows the rule.
No report is involved.
Right: knowing the rule did not prevent breaking it.
Galen's pattern is about unfalsifiable claims, not about knowing a rule and breaking it.
questions.explain: The statistician is like Cochrane: expert on the rule, yet caught by his own habit.
questions.rule: Knowing the rule does not guarantee following it.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Cochrane thought the specialist's verdict was one man's subjective judgment and waited for the pathologist.
questions.explain: He did not think that; he treated the conclusion as fact.
questions.rule: Cochrane did not apply his own skepticism.

questions.q: How did Cochrane describe other people's resistance to the idea that intuition alone is not a basis for firm conclusions?
options: As understandable, since intuition is usually right
As bewildering
As a minor irritation that would fade as trials spread
As deliberate dishonesty on the part of physicians
optionExplain: He thought the resistance wrong, not understandable.
Right: Cochrane found it bewildering.
His frustration is described as palpable, not minor.
The authors do not say Cochrane called it dishonest.
questions.explain: Cochrane's bewilderment makes his own lapse the more striking.
questions.teaches: Cochrane's frustration is palpable in his autobiography, where he calls people's failure to see that intuition alone is no basis for firm conclusions bewildering.
questions.rule: According to the authors, even people who know the rule against rushing to judgment break it, so the cause must lie in how minds work.

questions.q: Besides Cochrane's own puzzle, what question do the authors pose about the specialist?
options: Why he removed flesh before the pathologist had reported
Why he failed to notice the carcinoma on the patient's hand
Why he had refused to consult other specialists
Why he trusted a pathologist more than his own eyes
optionExplain: Right: the authors ask why the specialist did not wait for the pathologist.
The hand carcinoma was already found.
The account does not mention consulting others.
The specialist trusted himself, not the pathologist.
questions.explain: The riddle concerns both men: neither waited for the report.
questions.teaches: The authors ask why the specialist did not think to wait for the pathologist before removing a swath of Cochrane's flesh.
questions.rule: According to the authors, even people who know the rule against rushing to judgment break it, so the cause must lie in how minds work.

questions.q: According to the authors, how much of what whirls inside your head can introspection capture?
options: None of it at all
Roughly half of what goes on
Nearly all of it
Only a tiny fraction
optionExplain: None goes too far; it captures a tiny fraction.
Half overstates what looking inward can reach.
Nearly all would make the rest of the chapter unnecessary.
Right: introspection captures a tiny fraction of the processes.
questions.explain: Looking inward reveals little. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the reasons we can state are only a small part of what is behind our decisions.

questions.q: Introspection means turning your attention ____ to examine the contents of your mind.
questions.explain: Introspection is looking inward.
questions.rule: Introspection looks inward.

questions.q: A hiring manager says she picked a candidate for her résumé and interview. What do the authors' points suggest about that account?
options: It is probably a lie that hides the real motive
It is complete, because the manager knows her own mind
It reports what introspection can reach, a tiny share of the causes
It is useless, since reasons given afterward are not accurate at all
optionExplain: The authors do not suggest dishonesty.
Introspection does not give completeness, per the authors.
Right: the stated reasons are only part of the picture.
The authors do not say such reasons are never accurate.
questions.explain: The manager's reasons are real but cover a small part of what drove the choice.
questions.rule: Stated reasons are a small part of the story.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say introspection gives a full account of the causes of our decisions.
questions.explain: It captures a tiny fraction of the processes behind decisions.
questions.rule: Looking inward is not complete.

questions.q: Asked why they bought a car, what kind of answer does introspection typically supply?
options: The hidden processes that actually produced the choice
A memory of every earlier car and what was learned from each purchase
A list of rival cars considered and the odds of each
Stated reasons such as good mileage, cute style and a great price
optionExplain: The hidden processes are exactly what introspection does not reach.
The authors do not describe memory of earlier cars.
The authors' example is a list of reasons.
Right: people trot out reasons like these, and the authors say introspection captures only a tiny fraction of what drives the choice.
questions.explain: What gets reported is the set of reasons a person can state, which is only a small part of what drove the choice.
questions.teaches: Asked why they bought a car, people trot out reasons such as good mileage, cute style and great price.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the reasons we can state are only a small part of what is behind our decisions.

questions.q: Why does a person's list of reasons feel like the whole account of their thinking?
options: Other people confirm our reasons before we accept them
We test each reason against the evidence before stating it
We have access to the processes that run in the background of the mind
We identify thinking with what flows through consciousness
optionExplain: Confirmation by others is not part of the authors' point.
Testing each reason is careful checking, which the authors say people seldom do.
The processes that run in the background are the ones we cannot reach.
Right: the conscious flow seems to be the whole of thinking.
questions.explain: The feeling of completeness comes from identifying thinking with what we are aware of.
questions.teaches: It is natural to identify our thinking with the ideas, images, plans and feelings that flow through consciousness, which is why a list of reasons feels complete.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the reasons we can state are only a small part of what is behind our decisions.

questions.q: True or false: In the dual-system model, System 2 delivers an answer first and System 1 then checks it.
questions.explain: System 1 comes first and System 2 can then examine its answer. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an instant answer comes from System 1, and System 2 must choose to check it.

questions.q: In the dual-system model, the realm of conscious thought is System ____.
questions.explain: System 2 is everything we choose to focus on.
questions.rule: System 2 is conscious thought.

questions.q: Which of these is a System 1 operation?
options: Working out a fifteen percent tip step by step on paper
Deliberately weighing two job offers on a list of pros and cons
Checking a budget line against last year's invoices
Instantly sensing from a colleague's tone that she is annoyed
optionExplain: Deliberate arithmetic uses effort and focus, which marks System 2.
Weighing lists takes focus and effort.
Checking invoices is deliberate work, so it is System 2.
Right: an instant, effortless answer comes from System 1.
questions.explain: System 1's answers arrive without effort. System 2's work takes time and effort.
questions.rule: Instant and effortless points to System 1.

questions.q: Sort each item: System 1 or System 2?

items.t: Turning print into a meaningful sentence
Instantly knowing the answer to a question
Holding a book while reaching for a glass
Checking whether an answer is backed by evidence
Everything we choose to focus on
Slowly scrutinizing an answer with effort

questions.explain: System 1 covers automatic, instant operations. System 2 is conscious, slower and examines System 1's answers.
questions.rule: System 1 answers; System 2 checks.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say System 2 usually answers first and System 1 then checks the answer.
questions.explain: System 1 delivers an answer first and System 2 can then examine it.
questions.rule: The order is System 1, then System 2.

questions.q: Someone proposes eliminating System 1 to avoid its errors. What do the authors say would happen?
options: We would think more slowly but with fewer mistakes
We could not function, and would shut down
We would rely wholly on System 2 and do better
We would lose only the ability to guess
optionExplain: System 1 runs perception and many routine tasks; losing it would not be a mere slowdown.
Right: we could not function without it.
The authors say the opposite: we would shut down.
System 1 is far more than guessing.
questions.explain: System 1 runs the rapid-fire processes that daily life needs.
questions.teaches: We have no awareness of System 1's rapid-fire processes, but we could not function without them and would shut down.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an instant answer comes from System 1, and System 2 must choose to check it.

questions.q: A bat and ball together cost $1.10, and the bat costs a dollar more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?
options: One cent
Ten cents
Fifteen cents
Five cents
optionExplain: One cent makes the bat $1.01 and the total $1.02.
Ten cents is the instant answer; the bat would then cost $1.10 and the total would be $1.20.
Fifteen cents makes the bat $1.15 and the total $1.30.
Right: if the ball costs five cents, the bat costs $1.05, which is a dollar more, and the total is $1.10.
questions.explain: Five cents fits both facts. The card next explains why the wrong answer feels right.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an answer that feels right is not shown to be right, and checking it takes sustained effort.

questions.q: The bat-and-ball question is one item in a psychological measure called the ____ Reflection Test.
questions.explain: The measure is the Cognitive Reflection Test.
questions.rule: The test measures reflection, not knowledge.

questions.q: A notebook and pen cost $2.20 together. The notebook costs $2 more than the pen. How much does the pen cost?
options: Twenty cents
Ten cents
Five cents
Two cents
optionExplain: Twenty cents is the instant answer; the notebook would then cost $2.20 and the total $2.40.
Right: pen $0.10 and notebook $2.10 total $2.20 and differ by $2.
Five cents gives a notebook of $2.05 and a total of $2.10.
Two cents gives a notebook of $2.02 and a total of $2.04.
questions.explain: The instant answer subtracts $2 from $2.20. Setting up the two facts gives ten cents.
questions.rule: Check an instant answer against every fact given.

questions.q: Put in order what the authors say usually happens with the bat-and-ball question.
items: You read the question
The answer 'ten cents' appears at once, without calculation
You write it down as your final answer without reflection
You never discover the mistake
questions.explain: The answer arrives from System 1, and without System 2 checking it, the mistake goes unnoticed.
questions.rule: No check, no discovery of the error.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say even very smart people tend to answer ten cents without reflecting.
questions.explain: They say most people, including very smart people, are not very reflective.
questions.rule: Intelligence does not prevent unreflective answers.

questions.q: A manager says, 'My gut says this plan is sound, so it is.' Which feature of System 1 does this show?
options: A careful weighing of evidence by System 2
A calibrated estimate of the plan's chances
A primitive psycho-logic: if it feels true, it is
A test of the plan against competing explanations
optionExplain: Careful weighing is the opposite of the manager's reasoning.
Calibration involves checking numbers; the manager offers none.
Right: feeling true is taken as being true.
Testing against alternatives is the scientist's move, not the manager's.
questions.explain: System 1's logic treats the feeling of truth as truth.
questions.teaches: System 1 follows a primitive psycho-logic: if it feels true, it is.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an answer that feels right is not shown to be right, and checking it takes sustained effort.

questions.q: A hunter-gatherer consults lion statistics before reacting to a shadow moving in the grass. What do the authors say is likely?
options: He would judge the danger correctly and survive the encounter
He would not live long enough to pass on his genes
He would waste time but come to no harm
He would teach others to check statistics first
optionExplain: Accuracy is of no help if one is eaten while calculating.
Right: slowness could be fatal.
The cost of delay may be fatal, not merely wasted time.
The authors do not suggest teaching.
questions.explain: Quick reaction served survival. The card next sets out the point.
questions.rule: According to the authors, snap judgments are sometimes essential, so fast conclusions are not always a flaw.

questions.q: Kahneman says System 1 is designed to jump to ____ from little evidence.
questions.explain: System 1 produces conclusions from little evidence.
questions.rule: System 1 is built for speed.

questions.q: A driver sees a ball roll into the road and brakes at once. How do the authors' points describe this?
options: A mistake caused by the availability heuristic
A System 2 calculation of the child's likely path
A failure to gather all the evidence before acting
A snap judgment from little evidence that works
optionExplain: The scenario involves no recalled frequency; it is a quick response.
Braking at once is fast, so it is System 1.
Gathering all evidence would be too slow.
Right: speed matters more than accuracy here.
questions.explain: Snap judgments are essential when delay is costly.
questions.rule: When delay is costly, a snap judgment is justified.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say snap judgments are sometimes essential.
questions.explain: They say gathering all evidence may be best for accuracy but snap judgments are sometimes essential.
questions.rule: Speed has its uses.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say System 1's habit of jumping to conclusions is a design defect with no benefit.
questions.explain: They say the habit served our ancestors well, since snap judgments are sometimes essential.
questions.rule: The habit has a purpose.

questions.q: An investor has three weeks and no danger. According to the authors, which approach gives the most accurate answer?
options: Gathering all the evidence and mulling it over
Acting on the first hunch to save time
Asking the person with the most confidence
Waiting until a clear feeling of certainty arrives
optionExplain: Right: with time, gathering evidence is the best way to produce accurate answers.
A hunch suits an emergency, not a case with time.
Confidence is not evidence.
Certainty can arise from System 1 alone.
questions.explain: When time allows, the authors grant that fuller evidence yields better accuracy.
questions.teaches: The authors grant that gathering all the evidence and mulling it over may be the best way to produce accurate answers.
questions.rule: According to the authors, snap judgments are sometimes essential, so fast conclusions are not always a flaw.

questions.q: According to the authors, what leads a person to conclude that lion attacks are common?
options: Easily recalling a lion attack from memory
Reading statistics on lion attacks
Having been attacked by a lion
Being told by a hunter that they are common
optionExplain: Right: easy recall is the cue.
Statistics are what the hunter-gatherer in the story does not consult.
The authors do not require personal experience; easy recall is enough.
The cue described is the person's own memory.
questions.explain: Easy recall leads to a feeling that something is common. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, ease of recall stands in for how common something is, and it all happens without effort.

questions.q: Judging how common something is by how easily examples come to mind is the ____ heuristic.
questions.explain: That is the availability heuristic.
questions.rule: Easy recall is taken as frequency.

questions.q: After seeing news of a plane crash, a traveller judges flying dangerous. Which is at work?
options: Availability: the crash is easy to recall
A calculation of the yearly number of flights
Careful System 2 comparison of flying and driving
A deliberate search for evidence against the hunch
optionExplain: Right: a vivid memory stands in for the frequency of danger.
No calculation is involved.
Careful comparison would use statistics.
A deliberate search for contrary evidence is not what this traveller does.
questions.explain: Ease of recall drives the judgment, not data.
questions.rule: Ask whether a feeling of commonness is just ease of recall.

questions.q: A person cannot easily recall any lion attack. What would the heuristic lead them to conclude about the shadow?
options: That attacks are not common, so there is little to worry about
That lions are extinct in the area
That the shadow must be a lion in disguise
That they should consult the statistics on lion attacks before deciding
optionExplain: Right: no easy memory, no worry. This follows the described logic.
That goes well beyond the heuristic's logic.
It is the memory that is missing, not the shadow's identity.
Consulting statistics is the slow route the heuristic skips.
questions.explain: The heuristic follows the ease of recall in both directions.
questions.rule: The cue is ease of recall, whichever way it points.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the availability heuristic requires slow, calculating reasoning.
questions.explain: It can happen entirely within System 1, automatic, fast and complete within a few tenths of a second.
questions.rule: The shortcut is automatic.

questions.q: What does the authors' account say about the availability heuristic and System 1's other operations?
options: One of many System 1 heuristics found by Kahneman, Tversky and others
It is a conscious technique taught by psychologists
It is a rare error found only in people under stress
It is the only heuristic System 1 uses to judge any kind of risk or danger
optionExplain: Right: it is one of many.
They describe it as unconscious.
Nothing links it to stress.
The authors say many operations, not one.
questions.explain: The availability heuristic is a single example of a family of shortcuts.
questions.teaches: The availability heuristic is one of many System 1 operations, or heuristics, discovered by Kahneman, Tversky and other researchers in the science of judgment and choice.
questions.rule: According to the authors, ease of recall stands in for how common something is, and it all happens without effort.

questions.q: According to the authors, what does System 1 assume about the evidence at hand?
options: That it is probably incomplete and needs checking
That it is reliable and sufficient
That it is reliable but still needs more support
That it is of unknown quality and should be tested
optionExplain: Assuming incompleteness would slow it down; the authors say it never pauses to wonder.
Right: those tacit assumptions are vital to System 1.
Needing support would also require a pause.
Treating quality as unknown would require the doubt System 1 lacks.
questions.explain: System 1 takes its evidence as enough. The card next gives the label.
questions.rule: According to the authors, System 1 treats the evidence it has as all the evidence there is, so its confidence does not reflect how thin that evidence is.

questions.q: WYSIATI is short for What You ____ Is All There Is.
questions.explain: The label is Kahneman's.
questions.rule: What you see is all there is.

questions.q: A buyer sees one glowing review and feels sure the product is excellent, without wondering about reviews she cannot see. Which idea fits?
options: A test of the product against competing explanations
WYSIATI: the evidence in view is taken as sufficient
A fair weighing of the glowing review against possible doubts
A scientist's careful lowering of her confidence
optionExplain: No test is run; she does not seek alternatives.
Right: she treats the visible evidence as all there is.
She does not weigh doubts; she has none.
A scientist's lowering of confidence is the opposite of what she does.
questions.explain: She feels sure from one review because System 1 does not ask what it is missing.
questions.rule: Ask what evidence you cannot see.

questions.q: A person has only two facts about a stranger and feels she knows him well. What does the idea predict about her confidence?
options: It will drop to match the small amount of evidence she has
It will depend on how long she thinks about it
It will rise only after she checks a third fact
It will not fall to reflect how thin the evidence is
optionExplain: That would mean sensitivity to evidence, which System 1 lacks.
Duration of thought is not the factor named.
Confidence does not wait for a third fact.
Right: judgment is insensitive to the quality of its evidence.
questions.explain: Confidence is built from what is seen, however little.
questions.rule: Thin evidence can feel like enough.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say System 1 can deliver fast conclusions while also checking the quality of its evidence.
questions.explain: It can deliver conclusions at lightning speed only because it never pauses to wonder.
questions.rule: Speed and checking trade off.

questions.q: An engineer designs an alarm that audits its sensor data every time before sounding. What would the authors' logic predict?
options: It would gain accuracy and lose nothing of value in return
It would sound more often but sooner
It would ignore its sensors
It would lose the speed that makes alarms useful
optionExplain: Accuracy gains come with the cost of time.
The authors link pausing to slower conclusions.
Nothing suggests the alarm would ignore its sensors.
Right: pausing to question evidence costs speed.
questions.explain: The authors say System 1 delivers strong conclusions fast only by not pausing.
questions.teaches: The authors say System 1 can deliver strong conclusions at lightning speed only if it never pauses to wonder whether its evidence is flawed or inadequate or whether better evidence exists elsewhere.
questions.rule: According to the authors, System 1 treats the evidence it has as all the evidence there is, so its confidence does not reflect how thin that evidence is.

questions.q: When asked why his hand pointed at a shovel, what did Gazzaniga's split-brain patient do?
options: He made up a story about cleaning out a chicken shed
He said he did not know why
He changed his answer and pointed to the chicken
He asked the researcher to show him the picture again
optionExplain: Right: he explained his choice with an invented story.
The authors stress that he did not say I don't know.
Nothing in the account has him changing the pointing.
He gave an explanation instead of asking for more.
questions.explain: The patient filled the gap with a story. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, when we lack the real reason we invent a sensible-sounding one rather than say we do not know.

questions.q: In split-brain patients, the connection between the hemispheres that was surgically severed is the corpus ____.
questions.explain: The corpus callosum links the two hemispheres.
questions.rule: No link, no shared knowledge.

questions.q: Asked why a project failed, a manager does not know but offers a tidy account at once. Which idea fits?
options: A scientist testing the hypothesis against several alternatives
A calibrated estimate of the project's chances
A creative confabulator inventing a story for coherence
A careful survey of all the evidence
optionExplain: Testing against alternatives is the opposite of an instant tidy story.
No estimate is given; it is an account.
Right: a tidy story replaces I don't know.
A survey would take time, not happen at once.
questions.explain: The pressure to give sensible reasons produces stories.
questions.rule: Be ready to say I don't know.

questions.q: Match each part of Gazzaniga's setup to what happened.
pairs: A shovel is needed to clean out the chicken shed
questions.explain: The right hemisphere saw the snowstorm; the left saw the claw and invented the explanation.
questions.rule: One side invents what the other side knows.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the split-brain patient admitted that he had no idea why he pointed at the shovel.
questions.explain: He did not say I don't know; he made up a story.
questions.rule: The urge to explain overrides admitting ignorance.

questions.q: Why is admitting to having no idea why hard for a person at a table with neuroscientists, according to the authors?
options: Researchers punish people who admit ignorance in front of their colleagues
Admitting ignorance would invalidate the experiment
The person truly knows the real reason but hides it
Sane people are expected to have sensible reasons for their actions
optionExplain: The authors mention awkwardness, not punishment.
The experiment does not depend on the answer in that way.
The patient does not know; the story is invented.
Right: social expectation pushes toward a reason.
questions.explain: A norm that people have reasons feeds the urge to explain.
questions.teaches: Sane people are expected to have sensible-sounding reasons for their actions, so saying I have no idea is awkward, especially in front of white-coated neuroscientists.
questions.rule: According to the authors, when we lack the real reason we invent a sensible-sounding one rather than say we do not know.

questions.q: What does a quick check often reveal about the news that journalists say moved the market?
options: That the news was false and had been invented by the reporter
That the news came out after the market had risen
That the news was reported by only one outlet
That the news was too small to matter to investors
optionExplain: The authors do not say the news was false.
Right: the supposed cause arrived after the effect.
The number of outlets is not mentioned.
The size of the news is not the issue.
questions.explain: Timing can undo the story. The card next gives the reasoning.
questions.rule: According to the authors, pause between not knowing and a confident explanation to say that this is one possibility among several.

questions.q: The authors liken the journalist to a split-brain patient asked why he is pointing at a picture of a ____.
questions.explain: Both conjure a plausible story from whatever is at hand.
questions.rule: Both explain without knowing.

questions.q: A local paper says house prices fell because of new bike lanes. What do the authors' points suggest you ask?
options: How many readers agree with the paper's explanation?
Did the cause come first, and could other reasons explain it?
Which journalist wrote the report and how long has she worked there?
Whether bike lanes are popular in other cities?
optionExplain: Agreement among readers is not evidence of cause.
Right: check the timing and the alternatives.
Seniority does not test the story.
Popularity elsewhere does not test this case.
questions.explain: A plausible story needs timing and alternatives checked.
questions.rule: Check order and alternatives.

questions.q: A journalist adds the missing middle step to a market story. What would the report most likely say?
options: The market rose because of one clear cause that I can name
The market rose for no reason at all
The market rose, but nobody should read any report about it at all
The market rose; this is one possible explanation among others
optionExplain: That is the confident conclusion the authors criticise.
They say any of a hundred reasons, not none.
The authors do not say reports are worthless.
Right: it names a possibility without claiming certainty.
questions.explain: The missing step is a sentence of honest uncertainty.
questions.rule: Add the middle step: possible, but there are others.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the explanatory urge is a bad thing that should be suppressed.
questions.explain: They say it is mostly a good thing, the propulsive force behind efforts to comprehend reality; the problem is moving too fast to a confident conclusion.
questions.rule: Keep the urge; slow the conclusion.

questions.q: Why do the authors not tell people to stop explaining events outright?
options: Explanations are true whenever they come to mind quickly and easily
The urge to explain drives all efforts to comprehend reality
Scientists do not offer explanations
Journalists cannot be trained to avoid them
optionExplain: Quick explanations are often wrong, per the Oslo and market cases.
Right: the urge is valuable; speed to confidence is the problem.
Scientists do offer explanations, with caution.
The authors do not say training is impossible.
questions.explain: The authors target the haste, not the urge.
questions.teaches: The authors call the explanatory urge the propulsive force behind all human efforts to comprehend reality.
questions.rule: According to the authors, pause between not knowing and a confident explanation to say that this is one possibility among several.

questions.q: Who carried out the 2011 Oslo bomb and the Labour Party summer-camp shooting, according to the authors?
options: Two groups acting in coordination
A cell of radical Islamists linked to al-Qaeda
One man, Anders Breivik, who hates Muslims
A homegrown group backed by a foreign state
optionExplain: The authors say there was only one perpetrator.
That was the early guess that proved wrong.
Right: there was only one perpetrator.
Nothing in the account suggests a foreign state.
questions.explain: The early guess was wrong. The card next explains how it held.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a plausible hypothesis can be reasonable and wrong; treat it as a guess to test, not as the answer.

questions.q: A scientist would describe the early suspicion of Islamist terrorists as a plausible ____.
questions.explain: A plausible hypothesis is a reasonable guess still to be tested.
questions.rule: Plausible is not proved.

questions.q: After a factory fire, social media says a rival set it, and a few supporting facts turn up. Which stance fits the authors?
options: Accept it as fact because supporting facts have already turned up
Reject it since social media is unreliable
Wait for a confession before thinking about it
Treat it as a plausible hypothesis and look for others
optionExplain: Supporting facts can be found for almost any guess.
Rejecting it outright is as unscientific as accepting it.
Waiting for a confession is not what a scientist does.
Right: keep it as a guess and look for others.
questions.explain: Hold the guess lightly and test it.
questions.rule: A plausible guess is still a guess.

questions.q: A second, bigger attack follows the first. What effect does that have on the speculators' certainty, according to the account?
options: They became more cautious about the early guess and wanted more facts
They concluded that everything fit and felt more sure
They gave up speculating until the facts arrived
They split into rival theories of equal strength
optionExplain: The account has them more sure, not more cautious.
Right: the camp shooting seemed to fit the coordinated-attack story.
The account has them certain.
There is no sign of rival theories.
questions.explain: Each new event was folded into the story.
questions.rule: New events can be bent to fit a favored story.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say it was unreasonable to suspect Islamist terrorists given the facts known at the time.
questions.explain: They say it was reasonable, a plausible hypothesis.
questions.rule: Reasonable and correct are different.

questions.q: A manager suspecting a theft searches only for facts that support the suspicion. Which feature of the Oslo reaction does this repeat?
options: Looking for evidence that would disprove the suspicion of the group
Waiting for the arrest before forming any view
Dismissing the hypothesis as implausible
Rushing to find supporting information, and finding some
optionExplain: Disproof is the scientist's move.
Waiting is not what people did.
They found it plausible.
Right: people rushed to Google for support and found it.
questions.explain: Searching for support will usually find some.
questions.teaches: After the Oslo bombing people rushed to Google for supporting information and found it, such as Norway's soldiers in Afghanistan and a radical preacher charged the week before.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a plausible hypothesis can be reasonable and wrong; treat it as a guess to test, not as the answer.

questions.q: Which question, according to the authors, must scientists be able to answer?
options: How soon can I publish my result?
What would convince me I am wrong?
Who else supports my hypothesis?
How strongly do I feel it is true?
optionExplain: Publication speed is not the test.
Right: if they cannot answer it, they have grown too attached.
Support from others is not what the authors test for.
Feeling is what the scientist sets aside.
questions.explain: The question probes attachment to a belief. The card next sets out the reasoning.
questions.rule: According to the authors, test a hunch by trying to prove it false and know what would convince you that you are wrong.

questions.q: Scientists replace the feeling of certainty with finely measured degrees of ____.
questions.explain: Doubt, reduced by better evidence from better studies.
questions.rule: Replace certainty with measured doubt.

questions.q: A founder is asked what would convince her the product idea is wrong, and can name nothing. What do the authors' points suggest?
options: She is correct in her idea and needs no test to show it
She has probably grown too attached to her belief
She is showing healthy confidence in her plan
She is demonstrating the scientist's caution
optionExplain: Being unable to name a refuter does not make the idea correct.
Right: inability to name a refuting result signals attachment.
Confidence of that kind is not a virtue here.
The scientist's caution is the opposite.
questions.explain: A belief with no possible refuter cannot be tested.
questions.rule: If nothing could change your mind, you are attached.

questions.q: A team designs a test to show its hypothesis false, and the test fails to do so. How do the authors view that outcome?
options: As proof that the hypothesis is certainly and finally true
As worthless because the test was meant to fail
As often the best evidence that the hypothesis is true
As evidence that the team should stop testing
optionExplain: Doubt can be reduced but never to zero, so not proof.
The authors value such a test.
Right: surviving a serious attempt to refute counts as strong evidence.
Nothing in the account says stop.
questions.explain: A failed attempt to disprove is strong support.
questions.rule: Test by trying to refute.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say scientists have no intuitions, because training removes them.
questions.explain: They say scientists have intuitions too, and hunches have been behind countless breakthroughs.
questions.rule: Scientists differ in handling intuitions, not in having them.

questions.q: A study strongly supports a claim. What do the authors say about a scientist's remaining doubt?
options: It should drop to zero as soon as the study is published
It can be reduced by better evidence but never to zero
It should rise whenever new evidence arrives
It is unaffected by evidence and stays the same
optionExplain: Zero doubt would be certainty, which the authors rule out.
Right: better studies lower doubt but never remove it.
Evidence for the claim lowers doubt.
Evidence does change doubt.
questions.explain: Doubt shrinks with evidence but is never eliminated.
questions.teaches: Scientific doubt can be reduced, although never to zero, by better evidence from better studies.
questions.rule: According to the authors, test a hunch by trying to prove it false and know what would convince you that you are wrong.

questions.q: What do psychologists call grabbing the first plausible explanation and gathering supporting evidence without checking it?
options: Confirmation bias
Hindsight bias
Anchoring
The overconfidence effect
optionExplain: Right: the authors use this term for the habit.
Hindsight bias is a different effect; the authors use confirmation bias for this habit.
Anchoring is a different effect; it is not the term the authors use here.
Overconfidence is a related word, but the authors name this habit confirmation bias.
questions.explain: The habit has a name. The card next explains why it persists.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the feeling that it all fits is not evidence that the story is true.

questions.q: When contrary evidence is pushed under their noses, people become motivated ____.
questions.explain: They find reasons, however tenuous, to belittle or discard it.
questions.rule: Motivated skeptics argue against evidence they dislike.

questions.q: A fan counts every call against his team, ignores calls in its favour, then dismisses a stats sheet over a small error. Which idea fits?
options: Confirmation bias, with motivated skepticism toward contrary facts
A calibrated judgment of the referee's fairness over the season
A scientist's attempt to disprove his own hunch about the referee
Availability, with easy recall of a rare and vivid event
optionExplain: Right: he collects support and discards the rest.
He is not calibrated.
The scientist's move is the opposite.
The fan is selective, not recalling rare events.
questions.explain: He gathers support and discards contrary evidence.
questions.rule: Look for how you treat evidence you dislike.

questions.q: Sort each item: confirmation bias or scientific caution?

items.t: Searching only for facts that fit a first theory
Dismissing a contrary study over a tenuous flaw
Counting a cure as proof and a death as meaningless
Designing a test that could prove the theory false
Letting alternative explanations get a hearing
Asking what would convince me I am wrong

questions.explain: Confirmation bias seeks support and discards contrary evidence. Scientific caution invites refutation.
questions.rule: Seek what could show you wrong.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that the fact that a story all fits is good evidence that it is true.
questions.explain: They say it gives confidence, not evidence of truth.
questions.rule: Coherence is not truth.

questions.q: A consultant declares total confidence in a forecast. According to Kahneman, what does high confidence mainly tell you?
options: That he has checked the forecast against many independent sources
That the forecast is more likely than not to be right
That he has no stake in the outcome
That he has built a coherent story, not necessarily a true one
optionExplain: Checking would show doubt.
Confidence does not raise accuracy.
Stake is not mentioned.
Right: confidence signals a coherent story.
questions.explain: Kahneman advises taking admissions of uncertainty seriously.
questions.teaches: Kahneman says it is wise to take admissions of uncertainty seriously, while declarations of high confidence mainly tell you that someone has constructed a coherent story, not necessarily that it is true.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the feeling that it all fits is not evidence that the story is true.

questions.q: When faced with a hard question, what do the authors say we often do?
options: Quietly replace it with an easier question
Postpone the answer until more data arrives
Break the question into smaller parts and answer each
Ask others to answer the hard question for us
optionExplain: Right: an easy question quietly stands in for the hard one, and its answer is taken as the answer.
Postponing sounds prudent, but it is a deliberate choice; the swap the authors describe happens without notice.
Splitting a question is a deliberate System 2 technique; the authors describe an unnoticed replacement by a different question.
Asking others is a conscious move; bait and switch usually happens inside the mind without the person noticing.
questions.explain: The swap is the core of bait and switch. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, check whether the question you answered is the one you were asked.

questions.q: The formal name for bait and switch is attribute ____.
questions.explain: Attribute substitution is the formal term.
questions.rule: Bait and switch is attribute substitution.

questions.q: Asked whether a stock is a good investment, an investor answers whether she likes the company's products. What is this?
options: A careful System 2 analysis of the company's value and prospects
A bait and switch: an easy question replaces a hard one
A proper test of the stock against alternatives
A calibrated estimate of the stock's risk
optionExplain: A careful analysis of company value would be System 2 work; here she answers about the products instead.
Right: liking the products is easy to judge, and it stands in for the hard question about the stock.
Testing against alternatives would be a deliberate step; she takes none.
A calibrated risk estimate would need numbers; she offers only a feeling about products.
questions.explain: The easy question quietly stands in for the hard one.
questions.rule: Ask which question you actually answered.

questions.q: Match each term to the shadow example.
pairs: Should I worry about the shadow in the long grass?
Can I easily recall a lion attacking someone from the grass?
questions.explain: The hard question is swapped for an easy one, with two names for the process.
questions.rule: Hard question out, easy question in.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say bait and switch is usually a deliberate System 2 tactic.
questions.explain: They say it is usually an unconscious System 1 activity.
questions.rule: The swap is usually automatic.

questions.q: A researcher lists several of Kahneman's heuristics. What do the authors say they share?
options: Each needs slow, effortful System 2 reasoning
Each is learned from experience with valid cues
Each is essentially a bait-and-switch maneuver
Each applies only to questions about danger
optionExplain: Heuristics are largely automatic System 1 operations, so slow reasoning is not what they share.
Learning from valid cues describes pattern recognition, which the authors treat later and separately.
Right: the availability heuristic, like the others Kahneman found, swaps an easy question for a hard one.
The shadow example concerns danger, but nothing limits the heuristics to questions about danger.
questions.explain: Heuristics are ways of answering an easy question in place of a hard one.
questions.teaches: The availability heuristic, like Kahneman's other heuristics, is essentially a bait-and-switch maneuver.
questions.rule: According to the authors, check whether the question you answered is the one you were asked.

questions.q: What does the author suspect Cochrane unconsciously substituted for the question 'Do I have cancer?'
options: Is the surgery the best treatment for cancer?
Is the pathologist likely to agree with this surgeon?
Is this the sort of person who should know?
Is my family history likely to include cancer?
optionExplain: Which treatment is best is not the question the authors suspect; they point to who should know.
Cochrane did not weigh the pathologist; the authors stress that he never doubted the surgeon's words.
Right: the specialist seemed exactly the sort of person who should know, so his verdict stood in for the answer.
Family history is not in the account; the suspected substitute concerns the person giving the verdict.
questions.explain: The easy question was about the person, not the disease. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, replacing a question by asking who should know can be sensible if done knowingly, and risky if unnoticed.

questions.q: In the climate-change example, the person substitutes the question 'Do most ____ think climate change is real?'
questions.explain: The knowledgeable people are climatologists.
questions.rule: Substitute who knows for what is true.

questions.q: With no medical training, a woman asks whether a supplement works and replaces that with whether doctors recommend it. What is this?
options: An unconscious swap she cannot notice
A knowing swap to a question she can answer
A test of the supplement against placebo pills
A System 2 survey of all the evidence
optionExplain: She notices what she is doing, so the swap is not unconscious.
Right: she knowingly replaces the question with one about what experts say, which she can answer.
A placebo test would answer the hard question itself, which she cannot do.
A survey of all the evidence would be the hard route she is avoiding.
questions.explain: A conscious swap to a question about experts can be reasonable.
questions.rule: Know when you are swapping.

questions.q: Sort each swap: knowing or unconscious?

items.t: A layperson says she will go by what climatologists think
A patient deliberately accepts what the cancer specialist says
Cochrane's likely replacement, as the author suspects
Fear after easily recalling a lion attack
A hunch that feels like an answer, with no sense of a swap
An investor who admits she is going by experts

questions.explain: In a knowing swap you are aware of replacing the question. In an unconscious one you only experience an answer.
questions.rule: A swap noticed can be judged.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say they know for certain that Cochrane made an unconscious swap.
questions.explain: The author writes that this is what he suspects.
questions.rule: Treat a suspicion as a suspicion.

questions.q: A veteran safety auditor warns of overconfident managers yet accepts a manager's all-clear unchecked. Which part of Cochrane's account does this repeat?
options: Mistaking the pathologist for the surgeon who operated
Refusing every verdict until a trial
Knowing experts are too sure, yet accepting one's word
Preferring a layperson's judgment to an expert's
optionExplain: The pathologist and the surgeon are different people in the story; the lapse is accepting an expert's word despite knowing experts' flaws.
Cochrane did not refuse every verdict; he accepted this one at once.
Right: Cochrane knew physicians are often too sure of themselves, yet accepted the specialist.
Cochrane did not prefer laypeople; he deferred to the eminent specialist.
questions.explain: Knowing the danger does not prevent the swap.
questions.teaches: Cochrane knew better than anyone that physicians are often too sure of themselves and that the God complex can lead to terrible mistakes, yet he accepted the specialist's word at once.
questions.rule: According to the authors, replacing a question by asking who should know can be sensible if done knowingly, and risky if unnoticed.

questions.q: Why do the authors reject calling System 1 the 'default setting'?
options: A default suggests we can switch to something else; we cannot
System 1 is rarely used in everyday life or in routine tasks
A default setting is chosen consciously by the person using it
System 1 turns off when we concentrate hard on a problem
optionExplain: Right: a default suggests a switch to something else, and the authors say we cannot flip it.
System 1 is in constant use, so this contradicts the authors' point.
A default is not necessarily conscious; this misses why the authors reject the word.
System 1 does not turn off with concentration; it keeps humming nonstop.
questions.explain: The authors reject the word because it implies a switch. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, you cannot turn off your tip-of-your-nose perspective, so build checks around it.

questions.q: The authors call the subjective view from System 1 the tip-of-your-____ perspective.
questions.explain: Only you can see the world from the tip of your own nose.
questions.rule: The view is yours alone.

questions.q: A manager proudly claims to ignore gut feelings. What do the authors' points imply?
options: He is right, since training can switch System 1 off in time
System 1 keeps running; even skeptics are not immune
He is wrong only about decisions under pressure
He is right, if he checks every decision twice
optionExplain: Training can add checks but cannot switch System 1 off, so he is mistaken.
Right: System 1 never stops, and even skeptics like Cochrane are not immune.
System 1 runs in all conditions, not only under pressure.
Checking every decision twice is System 2 work added on top; System 1 still runs.
questions.explain: The manager can add checks but cannot remove System 1.
questions.rule: Build checks; do not claim immunity.

questions.q: True or false: System 1 operations stop whenever you concentrate on a hard problem.
questions.explain: The authors say System 1 operations keep humming nonstop beneath consciousness.
questions.rule: System 1 does not pause.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say skeptics like Archie Cochrane are immune to jumping to judgment.
questions.explain: They say no one is immune, not even skeptics like Cochrane.
questions.rule: Skepticism is not immunity.

questions.q: Which best describes the tip-of-your-nose perspective?
options: A rare state found only in untrained people
An objective record shared by everyone
A slow, deliberate review of the evidence
A subjective view unique to each of us
optionExplain: It is not rare: everyone has it, trained or not.
An objective, shared record sounds neutral, but the authors call the view subjective.
A slow review is System 2; this perspective is System 1's quick view.
Right: only you can see the world from the tip of your own nose.
questions.explain: The perspective is personal and automatic.
questions.rule: The view is subjective and universal.

questions.q: A colleague proposes that staff use only System 2 on important decisions. What image do the authors use against such a switch?
options: System 1 is a switch that can be set to off when needed
System 1 is a muscle that tires and rests
System 1 is a map that must be redrawn
System 1 operations hum nonstop beneath consciousness
optionExplain: A switch is the image the authors reject, since we cannot flip it.
A muscle that rests is not their image; System 1 never rests.
A map is not their image; the metaphor is of constant background activity.
Right: the operations hum on, nonstop, beneath conscious thought.
questions.explain: System 1 cannot be turned off.
questions.teaches: System 1 operations keep humming, nonstop, beneath the babbling brook of consciousness.
questions.rule: According to the authors, you cannot turn off your tip-of-your-nose perspective, so build checks around it.

questions.q: What do the authors say of the choice between intuition and analysis, blink versus think?
options: It is a false dichotomy; the task is to blend them
Analysis beats intuition in every case
Intuition beats analysis in every case
The choice depends on a person's personality type alone
optionExplain: Right: the authors reject choosing one side and say the task is how to blend them.
The authors say they lean toward thinking, but not that analysis wins in every case.
Intuition can work astonishingly well, but the authors do not say it beats analysis in every case.
Personality is not the factor the authors name; the situation and its cues matter.
questions.explain: The authors reject either-or. The card next gives the example.
questions.rule: According to the authors, ask how to combine intuition and analysis, not which to pick.

questions.q: The authors call the choice between blink and think a false ____.
questions.explain: A false dichotomy offers two choices where both are needed.
questions.rule: Both intuition and analysis matter.

questions.q: A hospital debates whether nurses should follow their gut or follow protocols only. What would the authors say?
options: Follow protocols only, since gut feelings mislead
Let each nurse choose a side and stick to it
Follow gut feelings only, since nurses know best
Blend them, since the task is to combine both
optionExplain: Protocol-only picks analysis alone, the either-or the authors reject.
Letting each person pick a side keeps the false choice; it is not a blend.
Gut-only picks intuition alone, also the either-or the authors reject.
Right: the task is to combine intuition and analysis.
questions.explain: The task is to combine intuition and analysis.
questions.rule: Blend intuition and analysis.

questions.q: In Klein's story, the commander ordered everyone out of the house. What happened next?
options: The floor collapsed; the real fire was in the basement
The fire went out once the men left the building
The kitchen fire flared up again and spread into the living room
The commander found the fire was smaller than he thought
optionExplain: Right: the floor collapsed because the real fire was in the basement.
The fire did not go out; it continued below the house.
The kitchen was not the real source; the fire was in the basement.
The fire was worse than he thought, not smaller; hence the danger.
questions.explain: His unease was well founded.
questions.rule: Intuition can be right.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Kahneman and Klein fired off rival polemics and found no agreement.
questions.explain: They got together to solve the puzzle and agreed on most issues that matter.
questions.rule: Good scientists collaborate to resolve disagreement.

questions.q: An experienced nurse cannot explain why but is sure a baby looks unwell. Which hallmark of the commander's case does this show?
options: She applies a rule from a handbook
She computes the odds from statistics
She asks other nurses and follows the majority view
She senses it without knowing how she knows
optionExplain: Looking up a rule would be deliberate; the nurse cannot explain her feeling.
Computing odds is System 2 work; her feeling arrives without calculation.
Following the majority is not an intuition; hers comes without asking anyone.
Right: like the commander, she knows without knowing how.
questions.explain: The commander told Klein it was ESP, a story covering that he did not know how he knew.
questions.teaches: The commander told Klein he had ESP, but that was a story he told himself to cover the fact that he did not know how he knew; he just knew, the hallmark of an intuitive judgment.
questions.rule: According to the authors, ask how to combine intuition and analysis, not which to pick.

questions.q: What do the authors say an accurate intuition like the fire commander's is?
options: A sudden flash of insight that cannot be explained
Extrasensory perception that trained people develop
Pattern recognition built from experience
A guess that happens to be lucky in many cases
optionExplain: Intuition feels like a flash, but the authors trace it to stored patterns, not to something unexplainable.
The commander said he had ESP, but the authors call that a story covering the fact that he did not know how he knew.
Right: with training or experience, people store patterns, and accurate intuition is recognising them.
Luck would not explain repeated accuracy in people who have had the chance to learn the cues.
questions.explain: Accurate intuition has an ordinary source. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, trust intuition where valid cues can be learned, and even there double-check.

questions.q: The authors say an accurate intuition is not mystical but pattern ____.
questions.explain: Experts detect that something does not fit a stored pattern.
questions.rule: Intuition is pattern recognition.

questions.q: Whose intuition do the authors' reasoning trust most?
options: A day trader's hunch about tomorrow's share price
An investor's gut sense of which share will beat the market
An emergency nurse's sense that an infant is becoming ill
A broker's feeling about a currency's next-week rate
optionExplain: A trader's price hunch fails the test: the price already reflects public information that could predict it.
Picking winners is like predicting a price: public information is already in it.
Right: an infant shows early signs of infection that a nurse can learn to recognise.
Currency rates also lack publicly available predictive cues by the same logic.
questions.explain: Valid cues make intuition reasonable to trust.
questions.rule: Ask whether valid cues exist and can be learned.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say pattern recognition comes at the cost of susceptibility to false positives.
questions.explain: They give the Virgin Mary seen in burnt toast or mold as an example.
questions.rule: Pattern recognition cost: false positives.

questions.q: About how many hours of practice does it take to learn the thousands of chess patterns, according to the estimate quoted?
options: Ten thousand hours
One hundred hours
One hundred thousand hours
One thousand hours
optionExplain: Right: the estimate is about ten thousand hours.
One hundred hours would be a few weeks of part-time practice, far below the estimate.
One hundred thousand is close to the number of patterns, not the hours.
One thousand hours is a tenth of the estimate quoted.
questions.explain: Some patterns take huge effort to learn.
questions.rule: Learning cues takes opportunity and effort.
questions.teaches: Learning the fifty thousand to one hundred thousand chess patterns is estimated to take about ten thousand hours of practice, while a child needs far fewer examples to tell dogs from cats.

questions.q: Carlsen usually knows his move after ten seconds. What does he do with the rest of his time?
options: Double-check, because intuition can let him down
Look for a stronger intuition to replace the first
Stop thinking and rest his mind
Study the position for an hour without result
optionExplain: Right: he double-checks because he knows intuition can let him down.
He keeps his intuition and checks it; he does not seek a replacement.
He does not stop; the remaining time is for double-checking.
Carlsen says an hour of study tends to go in loops, so he does not spend it that way.
questions.explain: Even great experts double-check.
questions.rule: Use intuition and check it.
questions.teaches: Carlsen says he usually knows his move after ten seconds and the rest is double-checking, since studying an hour tends to go in loops.

questions.q: On what did Peggy Noonan base her forecast that Romney would win in 2012?
options: Polling averages across the swing states in the final week
Big rally crowds and the joy people reported at them
Interviews with campaign strategists on both sides
Past results in similar elections held in earlier years
optionExplain: Polling is not what she cited; her reasoning rested on impressions.
Right: she cited crowds, the candidate's look and the crowd's joy.
She cited what she saw and heard, not interviews with strategists.
Past results are not in her column as the authors report it.
questions.explain: Her evidence was impressions. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, forecasting needs the doubt and testing that medicine once lacked.

questions.q: Noonan predicted a Romney win because, she wrote, the ____ were right.
questions.explain: That was her summing-up.
questions.rule: Vibrations are not evidence.

questions.q: A coach predicts a win because the team looked happy and the crowd was loud. Whose reasoning does this resemble?
options: Cochrane's trial: a forecast from a control group
Feynman's: a forecast from a failed disproof
Noonan's: a forecast from impressions of mood
Klein's: a forecast from stored chess patterns
optionExplain: Cochrane's reasoning ran a trial; this coach relies on impressions.
Feynman's point concerns trying to disprove; this coach does not.
Right: she predicts from mood and impressions.
Chess patterns are stored cues from long practice; the coach's mood impressions are not.
questions.explain: Mood impressions are weak cues.
questions.rule: Beware vibrations.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say bad forecasting causes harm as obvious and direct as bad medicine.
questions.explain: They say it rarely leads as obviously to harm.
questions.rule: Harm can be subtle.

questions.q: What do the authors say is the cure for the certainty in forecasting?
options: A dose of conviction
More famous experts to consult
Faster gut calls on each decision
A tablespoon of doubt
optionExplain: More conviction is the problem, not the cure.
Famous experts are the confident figures the authors criticise.
Faster gut calls would feed the tip-of-your-nose illusions.
Right: the authors say the cure is a tablespoon of doubt.
questions.explain: Doubt is the remedy.
questions.rule: Take doubt.

questions.q: A think tank issues confident predictions for years without testing them. What cost do the authors say this can carry?
options: No cost, since no one acts on predictions
Obvious harm of the same kind that bad medicine causes
Subtle steering toward bad decisions and their costs
Harm only to the tank's own reputation
optionExplain: People do act on predictions, which is why they matter.
The authors say bad forecasting rarely leads as obviously to harm as bad medicine.
Right: bad forecasts steer subtly toward bad decisions.
Harm spreads beyond reputation: decisions follow forecasts.
questions.explain: Bad forecasts lead to costly decisions.
questions.rule: Test forecasts.
questions.teaches: Bad forecasting steers us subtly toward bad decisions and all that flows from them, including monetary losses, missed opportunities, unnecessary suffering, even war and death.

questions.q: True or false: Judging how accurate a pundit is takes more than collecting his forecasts and counting the hits.
questions.explain: The authors say it looks easy but is not nearly so simple. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Judging forecasts takes more than counting.

questions.q: Doctors turned to ____ controlled trials to test which treatments work; the authors say measuring forecasts seems easier than that.
questions.explain: The chapter opens with physicians who learned to doubt themselves and used randomized controlled trials.
questions.rule: Medicine tested what works; forecasting needs the same rigor.

questions.q: A magazine plans to rank its columnists by tallying how many predictions came true. According to the authors, what must it check first?
options: Whether each prediction was worded so that anyone could tell if it came true
Whether the columnist is better known than the other writers
Whether the columnist had more years of experience than rivals
Whether the predictions were printed on the front page rather than inside the magazine
optionExplain: Right: the authors show that a forecast that cannot be judged cannot be tallied.
Fame matters to readers, but the chapter later finds it unrelated to accuracy.
Experience seems relevant, but it does not make a prediction testable.
Placement matters to attention, not to whether a forecast can be judged.
questions.explain: The tally only works if each forecast can be marked right or wrong. The two opening examples show how often it cannot.
questions.rule: Make the forecast testable before you count.

questions.q: True or false: The authors expect that checking a famous forecast, such as Ballmer’s, will give a clean right-or-wrong verdict once enough time has passed.
questions.explain: They show that Ballmer’s forecast and the Bernanke letter stay disputable even years later, because of what they say, not how much time passes.
questions.rule: Time passing does not fix an unclear forecast.

questions.q: A reader says: Ballmer’s forecast looks wrong, and a forecast that looks wrong is wrong. Which reply fits the authors’ view?
options: Only the forecaster can say whether his own forecast was right or wrong
A forecast that looks wrong should be scored as wrong with no further check
Ballmer’s forecast was right because looks are not evidence either way
Looking wrong is not proof; the meaning must be pinned down before judging
optionExplain: Self-judgment is the problem, not the solution; the test must not depend on later reinterpretation.
This is the very shortcut the authors question: appearance is not a judgment.
The authors do not say it was right; they say it cannot be declared wrong with certainty.
Right: the authors say it looks wrong and may be, but not beyond reasonable doubt.
questions.explain: The authors accept a strong case that Ballmer was wrong but insist on knowing what he meant before calling it.
questions.rule: Seeming wrong is not the same as being shown wrong.

questions.q: A health agency announces: The flu season will be bad. In March, staff disagree on whether it was. Which idea from the chapter explains this?
options: Agencies cannot be scored because they are not individuals
The forecast was set too far in the future for anyone to evaluate it in March
The forecast never defined bad, so staff apply different private meanings
Flu forecasts are random, so no outcome could confirm them
optionExplain: The chapter judges forecasts, not who made them; groups can be scored too.
Distance in time is not the issue; the issue is the undefined term.
Right: like “significant” in Ballmer’s line, an undefined key term lets each person read the outcome their own way.
Randomness is a different matter; the dispute here comes from wording.
questions.explain: An undefined key term lets everyone decide afterwards what the forecast meant.
questions.rule: Define the key terms before the outcome is known.
questions.teaches: The authors say an undefined term such as “significant” is what lets people argue forever about whether a forecast came true.

questions.q: Which part of Ballmer’s iPhone forecast do the authors say makes it hard to judge?
options: He gave no year in which the iPhone would go on sale in the largest markets
He never said what counted as significant market share, or which market
He predicted the iPhone would make Apple lose money
He relied on sales figures later found to be false
optionExplain: The iPhone sale date is not what the chapter questions.
Right: the key term and the market were both left undefined.
Ballmer said Apple might make a lot of money, so this misreads him.
Nothing in the chapter suggests false sales figures.
questions.explain: The card next explains how undefined terms block a verdict.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a forecast must be free of ambiguity before it can be marked right or wrong.

questions.q: Ballmer’s forecast turns on the key term significant ____ share, which he did not define.
questions.explain: The undefined phrase is “significant market share”.
questions.rule: Find the key term before judging.

questions.q: A CEO says: Our rival will not gain meaningful ground next year. Which question would the authors want answered before scoring this?
options: What share or growth counts as meaningful, in which market?
Was the statement made in a calm tone of voice?
Was the rival larger than the CEO’s own firm?
Did the CEO have a good reputation for earlier forecasts?
optionExplain: Right: like “significant”, “meaningful” needs a threshold and a market.
Tone shapes how it reads, but the authors say the words matter more.
Size may matter for the business but does not settle what the words mean.
Reputation is a different topic and does not define the forecast’s terms.
questions.explain: The same two gaps appear: no threshold and no stated market.
questions.rule: Ask for a threshold and a scope.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Ballmer’s forecast cannot be declared spectacularly wrong with certainty.
questions.explain: It looks wrong, but its terms are too ambiguous to call it wrong beyond reasonable doubt.
questions.rule: Ambiguity blocks a verdict both ways.

questions.q: Sort each question: does it help define Ballmer’s forecast, or does it only reflect how the forecast felt?

items.t: Which market was he talking about?
How much share counts as significant?
Smartphones or all mobile phones?
Did his tone sound dismissive?
Does the line look foolish today?
Is it listed in a hall of shame?

questions.explain: Scope and thresholds can be checked against data; tone and reputation cannot settle what was claimed.
questions.rule: Judge the words, not the impression.

questions.q: Ballmer is often quoted with only the line no chance … significant market share. What does this suggest about judging forecasts from quotes alone?
options: Context matters only for forecasts about technology
Short quotes are more accurate because they are less wordy
Quotes are reliable once a journalist has printed them in a respected newspaper
A short quote can drop the context that sets the forecast’s meaning
optionExplain: The chapter shows the problem in politics and economics too.
Brevity is not accuracy; the cut version changes what is being judged.
Printing does not preserve the context that gives the words their meaning.
Right: the full statement gave the market and the 2% or 3% figure, which a truncated version loses.
questions.explain: The authors show that the full interview narrowed the meaning, which the famous clipped version hid.
questions.rule: Read the whole statement before scoring it.
questions.teaches: The truncated version often quoted leaves out the rest of Ballmer’s sentence, which reveals he was talking about the global mobile phone market.

questions.q: From the full 2007 interview, which market was Ballmer talking about?
options: The US market for smartphones only
The worldwide market for smartphones only
The global market for mobile phones of all kinds
The market for software used in schools
optionExplain: This is how the clipped line is often read, but his number shows otherwise.
Smartphones alone are not what 1.3 billion phones describes.
Right: he cited 1.3 billion phones sold.
Software in phones was his aim, not schools.
questions.explain: The 1.3 billion figure in his own words shows the scope. The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: According to the authors, check the original statement in context, and then ask what is still undefined.

questions.q: In context, Ballmer preferred software in most phones to the 2% or ____% he said Apple might get.
questions.explain: He spoke of Apple getting 2% or 3%.
questions.rule: Context supplies numbers the clipped quote hides.

questions.q: Following the authors, you want to score Ballmer using later data. Which figure is the fair comparison?
options: The iPhone’s share of all computers sold worldwide
The iPhone’s share of global mobile phone sales
The iPhone’s share of US smartphone sales
Apple’s revenue compared with Microsoft’s revenue
optionExplain: Computers are a different market from the one he named.
