Right: his scope was global mobile phones, which the authors use.
US smartphones is a common but mismatched benchmark, as the authors point out.
Revenue is a separate claim; he even said Apple might make a lot of money.
questions.explain: A fair score uses the market the forecaster named.
questions.rule: Match the data to the forecast’s scope.

questions.q: True or false: The authors’ 6% figure lies above the 2% or 3% Ballmer mentioned, yet they do not call his forecast laughably wrong.
questions.explain: The figure is higher than what Ballmer said Apple might get but, unlike the clipped quote, not laughably wrong; the threshold for significant is still unspecified.
questions.rule: Closer data can leave the verdict open.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the longer quotation removes every ambiguity, so Ballmer’s forecast can now be graded cleanly.
questions.explain: They say some questions remain: how much above 2% or 3% would be significant, and how much money is a lot.
questions.rule: Some ambiguity may survive context.

questions.q: A sports pundit predicts the team will do well this year. Her full radio interview mentions a playoff spot. How should you use that context?
options: Treat the playoff spot as the likely meaning but note what stays unstated
Accept any outcome as proof that she was right
Wait another full year before trying to judge it at all, whatever the interview said
Ignore the interview and use only the clipped line
optionExplain: Right: context narrows the claim but, as with Ballmer, leaves gaps such as which round counts.
Accepting any outcome would remove the test.
Waiting does not help if the terms are still unclear.
The clipped line is the thing that lost the detail.
questions.explain: Context can supply scope, yet the authors still ask what remains undefined.
questions.rule: Use context, then list what is still open.
questions.teaches: Ballmer also said Apple “may make a lot of money”, so he did not forecast that the iPhone would be a bust for Apple.

questions.q: True or false: The 2010 letter to Bernanke on quantitative easing said nothing about a time frame.
questions.explain: It named no time frame. The card next shows why that matters for judging it.
questions.rule: No deadline, no test.

questions.q: The letter’s problem was the lack of a ____ frame, so it could be said at any time that the predicted outcome was still coming.
questions.explain: The letter says nothing about the time frame.
questions.rule: Set a deadline.

questions.q: An analyst said in 2020 that a housing crash would follow low interest rates. By 2026 none has come. What can fairly be said?
options: The analyst has been shown to have poor judgment overall
The claim has no deadline, so it can still be defended and cannot be tested
The claim was proved wrong in 2021 because no crash came
The claim is proved right as long as a crash remains possible at some later date
optionExplain: One untestable claim says nothing about overall judgment.
Right: like the Bernanke letter, an open-ended claim stays alive indefinitely.
No deadline was set, so there is no date by which it failed.
Possibility does not confirm a claim either.
questions.explain: Without a date no outcome can count against the claim, so it never fails or succeeds.
questions.rule: Add a date to make a claim testable.

questions.q: Suppose critics waited until 2016 and still saw no inflation. According to the authors, what would defenders of the letter be able to say?
options: That inflation had been delayed by exactly six years
That the Federal Reserve had followed the letter’s advice after all
That the letter had not set a date, so the effect might still come
That the letter had been proved right all along
optionExplain: No such period is stated in the letter.
The Fed ignored the advice and kept the policy going.
Right: the authors say no matter how much time passed, someone could say it is still coming.
Nothing in 2016 would confirm the letter.
questions.explain: The open ending protects the claim from any date of failure.
questions.rule: An open end protects a claim from failing.

questions.q: True or false: The authors argue that Barry Ritholtz was entitled to call the signers terribly wrong in 2013 because enough time had passed.
questions.explain: The letter set no time frame, so the authors say that however much time passed the writers could still say the event was coming.
questions.rule: You cannot prove wrong what has no deadline.

questions.q: A forecaster says: The stock market will fall sharply. What single addition would make this testable in the authors’ sense, beyond a time frame?
options: A famous colleague who agrees with the forecast
A promise to retract the forecast if it fails
A longer explanation of the forecaster’s reasons for expecting the market to fall
A clear size of fall and a date by which it should happen
optionExplain: Agreement of others does not set terms or deadline.
Retracting is a gesture; it does not define the claim.
Reasons explain a view but do not define what counts as failure.
Right: the authors ask for clear terms and a time frame together.
questions.explain: Fall “sharply” is as vague as “significant”, so a threshold is needed alongside the date.
questions.rule: Pair a deadline with a threshold.
questions.teaches: A deadline is only one missing piece: the letter also left unclear how far the dollar would have to fall and how far inflation would have to rise.

questions.q: True or false: Read literally, the open letter called currency debasement and inflation a risk, not a certainty.
questions.explain: It called them a risk. The card next explains the consequence.
questions.rule: A risk is not a promise.

questions.q: The authors note the letter called debasement and inflation a ____, which suggests they were not certain to follow.
questions.explain: The word “risk” is the hedge they point to.
questions.rule: Notice the hedge word.

questions.q: A report says a new tax risks causing job losses. Jobs grow after the tax. Following the authors, was the report wrong?
options: Yes, because growing jobs prove that the tax had no effect on employment at all
Not necessarily: read literally, it said losses might follow, or might not
Yes, because a risk means a forecast of certain loss
Yes, because such reports must use numbers to be right
optionExplain: Growing jobs fit the “or might not” half of the claim.
Right: a literal “risk” leaves room for the outcome not happening.
A risk is not a certainty, which is the point of the card.
Numbers help later, but they do not make this report wrong.
questions.explain: The report is not testable as written, so job growth does not prove it wrong.
questions.rule: A hedge can make a forecast unfalsifiable.

questions.q: Which statement is more exposed to being shown wrong?
options: This policy could eventually raise prices somewhere in the economy at some point
This policy may lead to inflation
This policy risks inflation
Inflation will exceed 5% within two years of this policy
optionExplain: “Could eventually” has neither limit nor deadline.
“May” leaves room to escape.
A “risk” leaves room to escape.
Right: it has a threshold and a deadline, so reality can contradict it.
questions.explain: Only the first statement gives reality a way to show it wrong.
questions.rule: Specific claims can fail; hedged ones cannot.

questions.q: True or false: The authors claim the Bernanke letter’s signers intended only to say that inflation was possible.
questions.explain: They say the opposite: it is surely not what the signers meant to communicate, and not how people read it then. The literal wording is the problem.
questions.rule: Literal text and intention can differ.

questions.q: A manager writes: Layoffs may follow if sales do not improve. Sales stay flat and no layoffs come. What does the chapter’s view imply?
options: The statement was not wrong, because may promised nothing either way
The statement should be counted as a 50% forecast, so it was half right
The statement shows that the manager lacks foresight
The statement was wrong because sales stayed flat
optionExplain: Right: “may” is a hollow word that allows both outcomes.
No probability is given, so it cannot be scored as 50%.
One hedged line shows nothing about foresight.
The statement did not say layoffs would follow; the condition matches what happened.
questions.explain: The chapter later says almost anything “may” happen, so “may” says nothing about probability.
questions.rule: “May” tells you nothing about likelihood.
questions.teaches: The chapter later calls “may” a hollow word, since almost anything may happen and the word says nothing about how likely it is.

questions.q: In the early 1980s Jonathan Schell warned that unless nuclear arsenals were abolished, what would happen?
options: A holocaust would occur, if not today then tomorrow
The cold war would end with a treaty within a year
Both superpowers would soon disarm voluntarily
Nuclear weapons would be used only in small wars
optionExplain: Right: this is his claim in The Fate of the Earth.
He predicted catastrophe, not a treaty.
Disarmament is what he hoped for, not what he predicted.
He wrote of a holocaust, not limited wars.
questions.explain: The card next gives the setting and the panel.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the panel invited impressive, informed and confident experts, which is what made their later surprise instructive.

questions.q: In June 1982 about seven hundred ____ people marched in New York against the arms race.
questions.explain: About seven hundred thousand marched, in one of the biggest US demonstrations.
questions.rule: The fear was widespread and public.

questions.q: A panel of senior experts sounds confident about a major threat. Following the authors’ story, how should that confidence be read?
options: It proves they have no foresight about political events, since they sound so sure
It shows the experts all share one political ideology
It tells you how the experts feel, not yet how accurate they are
It proves they have accurate foresight about the future
optionExplain: Nothing here shows they lack foresight.
The experts differed in views; confidence is a separate matter.
Right: the later chapter checks accuracy against outcomes.
Confidence can accompany error, as the chapter goes on to show.
questions.explain: Confident and impressive does not equal accurate; accuracy must be tested.
questions.rule: Confidence is not evidence of accuracy.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock describes himself as by far the least impressive member of the panel.
questions.explain: He was a thirty-year-old, newly promoted associate professor among Nobel laureates.
questions.rule: Know who is speaking in each part of the story.

questions.q: True or false: The authors present the panel as the scene where Tetlock’s doubts about expert forecasts began.
questions.explain: It is the start of his story; the evidence comes later, from his long-running study.
questions.rule: A scene is not a result.

questions.q: Tetlock says he got his seat on the panel because of a quirky research program. What does the authors’ telling suggest about expertise?
options: Younger members of a panel contribute more than older ones
Only Nobel laureates are invited to join such national panels on nuclear war
Credentials alone were not the reason for the invitation in his own case
Experts are chosen for panels purely by their fame
optionExplain: No claim about contribution is made.
Tversky and others were also on the panel.
Right: he says he owed the seat to his research program, not to a glorious career.
His own case shows another route in.
questions.explain: He tells the reader he was there for a research program germane to the mission.
questions.rule: A seat at the table is not proof of authority.
questions.teaches: Tetlock says he owed his seat to a quirky research program that happened to bear on the panel’s mission.

questions.q: True or false: In 1984 liberal and conservative experts, for different reasons, both expected the next Soviet leader to be another stern party man.
questions.explain: They agreed on the outcome but disagreed on the cause. The card next gives the account.
questions.rule: According to the authors, experts with opposite reasons and equal confidence expected the same result and were jointly surprised by Gorbachev.

questions.q: The experts were right that ____ would soon die; he did, in March 1985.
questions.explain: Konstantin Chernenko died in March 1985 as expected.
questions.rule: They got the easy call right.

questions.q: Two analysts predict the same election winner for opposite reasons and both sound certain. What does the Soviet case suggest?
options: Confident analysts are usually right when they agree
Agreement on the outcome does not show either explanation is correct
Disagreement over causes shows the forecast is useless
Agreement shows that the outcome is certain to occur whatever each side’s reasons are
optionExplain: The Soviet case shows the opposite of this.
Right: liberals and conservatives agreed on a leader for opposing reasons, and both were surprised.
Different reasons for one expectation tell nothing about its usefulness by themselves.
Agreement of confident people did not make the outcome certain.
questions.explain: Two opposed theories can predict the same event, and both can fail on the next turn.
questions.rule: Shared prediction does not validate either reason.

questions.q: Within hours of Chernenko’s death, who was named the next general secretary?
options: Mikhail Gorbachev, an energetic fifty-four-year-old
A military officer chosen by the Politburo
Leonid Brezhnev, returning to office after illness
Another frail veteran in his seventies, as before
optionExplain: Right: the Politburo anointed Gorbachev.
The text names Gorbachev, not a military officer.
Brezhnev had died in 1982.
This is the sort of leader the experts expected, not who came.
questions.explain: The man named was the opposite of what the experts expected.
questions.rule: Expect surprises at turns in history.

questions.q: True or false: The experts at the panel were right about Chernenko, yet few of them saw Gorbachev’s turn coming.
questions.explain: They were right about Chernenko. The failure was on the larger turn that followed.
questions.rule: Be exact about what experts got wrong.

questions.q: Which part of Tetlock’s story points to a limit of expert confidence?
options: The experts having all studied exactly the same subject
The panel meeting for only a single day of talks before the experts were sent home
Equal confidence from opposed views, then a shared surprise in both camps
The experts disagreeing about the cause of Brezhnev’s death
optionExplain: Their shared field does not make confidence a limit.
The meeting length is not in the story.
Right: both camps were confident and few anticipated the turn.
The text does not discuss Brezhnev’s cause of death.
questions.explain: Both camps were confident in opposed explanations, and the actual path matched neither.
questions.rule: Confidence does not shield you from a turn in events.
questions.teaches: Gorbachev changed direction swiftly, sought to normalize relations with the United States and reverse the arms race, and Reagan responded cautiously, then enthusiastically.

questions.q: After Gorbachev rose, how did most experts who had not seen it coming react?
options: They stopped giving forecasts for a decade
They agreed Reagan alone deserved the credit
They admitted at once that their field was useless
They grew convinced they knew why it happened
optionExplain: No such pause is described.
Liberals denied Reagan credit; conservatives gave it.
The chapter shows no such admission.
Right: both camps found it predictable in hindsight.
questions.explain: The card next shows the pattern.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an explanation that is available after the event tells you little about whether the event was foreseen.

questions.q: Both camps said the outcome looked predictable when viewed in the right ____ light.
questions.explain: The text says it was predictable “when you look at it in the right retrospective light”.
questions.rule: Hindsight makes any outcome look expected.

questions.q: After a surprise election result, commentators who predicted the other side now say it was inevitable. Following Tetlock, what should you suspect?
options: They have gained new insight that makes them reliable now
They would have found a story for any result, so the story proves little
Surprises are forecastable if one studies the warning signs of an event closely enough
Their earlier forecasts are now proved correct
optionExplain: A convincing story afterwards is not new proof of foresight.
Right: this is Tetlock’s inner cynic at work.
The chapter does not say surprises are always forecastable.
They did not predict this result, so their forecasts are not confirmed.
questions.explain: An explanation available for every outcome fails to separate good foresight from bad.
questions.rule: Ask what the story would have said had the opposite happened.

questions.q: True or false: Liberal experts denied Reagan credit for Gorbachev’s rise, while conservative experts credited him.
questions.explain: Liberals pointed to Soviet weakness; conservatives credited Reagan calling the Soviets’ bluff.
questions.rule: Different stories, same retrospective certainty.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says the experts at the panel lacked integrity and intelligence.
questions.explain: He says he was not questioning their intelligence or integrity, only saying those are not enough.
questions.rule: Distinguish character from method.

questions.q: Why do the authors compare the national security elites to renowned physicians from the prescientific era?
options: Both relied on rigorous tests of their claims, which later proved the claims reliable
Both were mainly interested in public fame and reward
Both worked without any formal training in their fields
Both had great intelligence and integrity yet could be fooled by delusions
optionExplain: Neither group is said to have tested its claims; that is the point of the comparison.
Fame is not the point of the comparison.
Elites were highly trained, so this does not fit.
Right: the comparison is about able people lacking a method of testing.
questions.explain: Ability and honesty alone do not protect against tip-of-your-nose delusions; testing does. The experts the panel heard were deeply informed, intelligent and articulate, and pretty confident, yet few saw the Soviet change coming.
questions.rule: Method, not brilliance, guards against delusion.
questions.teaches: The panel Tetlock sat on in 1984 invited experts who were deeply informed, intelligent and articulate, and pretty confident they knew where things were heading.

questions.q: At a 1988 lunch, what did Kahneman guess about experts versus attentive newspaper readers as forecasters?
options: Experts would be only slightly more accurate than attentive readers
Attentive readers would be far more accurate than experts
Experts would be far more accurate than attentive readers
Experts and readers would be exactly equal in accuracy
optionExplain: Right: he said the benefits taper off fast, leaving experts a tad ahead.
He did not say readers would beat experts.
He did not predict a large expert edge.
He said experts may be a tad ahead, not equal.
questions.explain: The card next gives the guess in full.
questions.rule: According to Tetlock, Kahneman’s idea was a testable guess: skill might rise with knowledge, but flatten out quickly.

questions.q: Kahneman guessed that experts with PhDs would be only a ____ more accurate than attentive readers of the New York Times.
questions.explain: The text says only a tad more accurate.
questions.rule: Expertise may flatten quickly.

questions.q: A company hires a panel of senior economists to forecast sales. Following Kahneman’s guess, what would you expect compared with well-informed staff?
options: An edge only on topics outside their specialty
A large edge over the staff, since more training steadily adds more accuracy
No edge or worse, since training tends to harm forecasts
A small edge at best, since added knowledge helps less and less
optionExplain: The guess says nothing about specialties.
This is the view the guess doubts.
The guess says benefits are small, not negative.
Right: this is the tapering-off idea.
questions.explain: Gains from knowledge are real but taper fast, per the guess.
questions.rule: Added expertise has diminishing returns.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman’s remark about expert forecasting was a guess, since no one had seriously tested political experts.
questions.explain: It was a guess; Tetlock notes no one had seriously tested political experts.
questions.rule: Do not confuse a hypothesis with a finding.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman suggested that intelligence and knowledge improve forecasting but that the benefits taper off fast.
questions.explain: He said they improve it, but the benefits taper off fast.
questions.rule: Read the claim exactly.

questions.q: Why had no one tested the accuracy of political experts before Tetlock? Choose the reason the chapter gives or points to.
options: Governments classified every expert forecast for decades
Experts refused to share their predictions publicly for fear of damaging their careers
Forecasts were hard to judge: no time frames, vague terms and probabilities
No forecast could be scored with numbers of any kind
optionExplain: Not stated.
Not stated; later Tetlock did recruit 284 experts.
Right: the chapter next lists these obstacles.
The chapter later shows scoring is possible.
questions.explain: The next ideas explain why judging forecasts was the barrier.
questions.rule: The barrier to testing was judging.
questions.teaches: Tetlock says the more he pondered how to test experts, the more he realized why no one had: forecasts are hard to judge.

questions.q: True or false: Forecasts without time frames do not appear absurd to the people who hear them when they are first made.
questions.explain: They do not appear absurd at the time, because people assume a shared timeline. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, state the time frame in the forecast itself, since memory of an implied one will not last.

questions.q: As time passes, the ____ time frames that once seemed obvious become less so.
questions.explain: The text says tacit time frames fade as memories fade.
questions.rule: Unstated assumptions decay.

questions.q: A consultant says in 2022 that a retailer will fail. In 2025 she says she meant 2030. What problem does this show?
options: Consultants must give their reasons before they are allowed to make any prediction
Without a stated deadline her meaning can be changed afterwards
Retail forecasts are too complex to state in plain terms
A forecast cannot be judged in less than a decade
optionExplain: Reasons are a different matter.
Right: the tacit time frame can be stretched.
The issue is the missing deadline, not complexity.
No such minimum period is claimed.
questions.explain: The chapter shows tacit time frames drift with memory and interest.
questions.rule: Write the deadline down.

questions.q: Two colleagues each remember a forecast as meant for different years. According to the authors, what usually happens next?
options: A tedious dispute over the real meaning that cannot be settled
The forecast is scored as correct by default
The forecast is judged by an outside referee
Both accept the earlier date without any discussion because memories are reliable
optionExplain: Right: with reputations at stake, the argument has no way to end.
No default scoring applies.
No referee exists without a written deadline.
Reputations make quick agreement unlikely.
questions.explain: Without a written deadline there is no referee between memories.
questions.rule: Memories will not settle it.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say forecasters who omit a time frame are usually not being dishonest.
questions.explain: They rely on an implicit shared understanding of the timeline.
questions.rule: Separate honesty from testability.

questions.q: Which rewrite fixes the timeline problem for the statement: housing prices will fall?
options: Housing prices will fall once interest rates change
Housing prices will fall eventually, as they often do
Housing prices may fall in the next cycle of the market
Housing prices will fall by 10% or more by 31 December 2027
optionExplain: Once rates change depends on an undated event.
Eventually is not a deadline.
May and the next cycle add nothing definite.
Right: it adds a threshold and a date.
questions.explain: A date plus a threshold lets anyone check the result later.
questions.rule: Date it and size it.
questions.teaches: The authors say this problem alone renders many everyday forecasts untestable.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say vague verbiage in forecasts is more the rule than the exception.
questions.explain: They say vague verbiage is more the rule than the exception. The card next gives the point.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a sentence is not yet a testable claim until its key terms are given explicit definitions.

questions.q: The authors say vague verbiage is more the rule than the ____.
questions.explain: The text says it is more the rule than the exception.
questions.rule: Expect vagueness.

questions.q: A report forecasts that the new road will ease traffic. Which edit makes the sentence testable?
options: Traffic will be eased in a meaningful way within a few years
Drivers will notice a real improvement before too long
Rush-hour travel time on the route falls 15% within two years
Congestion on the route will likely be somewhat lower soon
optionExplain: Meaningful and soon are undefined.
Notice and before long are undefined.
Right: it defines the measure, the size and the date.
Likely and somewhat are undefined.
questions.explain: Make each key term measurable.
questions.rule: Replace soft words with measures.

questions.q: Sort each phrase: explicit enough to test, or too vague to test?

items.t: Unemployment above 7% in March 2026
At least 3 named countries default by 2030
Prices fall 10% by year-end
A significant slowdown soon
Serious trouble ahead
Notable growth in the medium term

questions.explain: The explicit phrases fix a measure and a limit; the vague ones leave both to the reader.
questions.rule: Measures and limits make claims testable.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that once timelines are fixed and terms defined, a forecast can be fully judged whatever its form.
questions.explain: They call these smaller obstacles and say probability is a much bigger one.
questions.rule: Fix terms, then handle probability.

questions.q: A columnist writes: the party will do badly in the election. Which question is the authors’ kind of check?
options: Would the party agree with what the columnist wrote?
What counts as badly: seats lost, vote share, or something else?
Does the columnist write for a widely respected national paper with many readers?
Has the columnist been right on earlier elections?
optionExplain: Agreement does not define the term.
Right: it asks for the definition of the key term.
Reputation does not define the term.
Track record is useful later, once terms are fixed.
questions.explain: Any soft word like badly needs a measure before scoring.
questions.rule: Define the soft word.
questions.teaches: The authors call timelines and vague terms the smaller obstacles, and the next one, probability, is the much bigger one.

questions.q: True or false: If a forecast says war is very likely and war does not happen, the forecast has been shown wrong.
questions.explain: A very likely event can fail to happen and the forecast still be sound. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, one outcome cannot judge a probability, and a probability needs a clear meaning to be judged at all.

questions.q: In the authors’ thought experiment, history is rerun hundreds of times and ____ percent of reruns end in war; what very likely meant still matters.
questions.explain: The text uses 63%.
questions.rule: The reruns give a frequency, not a meaning.

questions.q: A forecaster says there is a 90% chance of a flood this year, and no flood comes. What do the authors say?
options: One miss cannot show the 90% was wrong; one call in ten should miss
The forecaster was right because floods are rare events in most places and years
Percentages cannot be used for forecasting floods
The forecaster was wrong and should be marked down for it
optionExplain: Right: a single outcome cannot judge a probability.
The rarity of floods does not settle it.
Nothing in the chapter bars probabilities for any topic.
One miss is expected about one time in ten.
questions.explain: A probability of 90% leaves a 10% chance for the other result.
questions.rule: One outcome cannot judge a probability.

questions.q: Suppose a forecaster gives 80% to events and later is right on 80% of them. What does this say about the forecaster?
options: That nothing can be said without rerunning history
That the forecaster looks well matched to reality across many calls
That the forecaster was wrong on 20% of calls and should be penalized for each of them
That each forecast was exactly 80% correct
optionExplain: Many forecasts together do give a test.
Right: patterns across many forecasts are what tell.
Missing 20% is expected from an 80% claim.
Each single forecast cannot be called 80% correct.
questions.explain: Many forecasts give a track record even without reruns.
questions.rule: Judge sets of probabilistic forecasts.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that, read literally, Schell’s holocaust forecast was wrong.
questions.explain: Neither superpower scrapped its arsenal and there was no war, so read literally he was wrong.
questions.rule: Test the claim as worded.

questions.q: A doctor says a patient is very likely to need surgery. The patient recovers without it. Which conclusion fits the chapter?
options: The doctor is proved right because surgery was possible
The doctor failed because the claim lacked a date by which the surgery was expected
The doctor may have been wrong or may have met the unlikely case
The doctor is proved wrong by the recovery
optionExplain: Possibility does not prove it right.
A missing date is a separate issue.
Right: one case cannot decide it.
One recovery does not prove the forecast wrong.
questions.explain: To judge a probability you need many cases and a clear meaning of the words.
questions.rule: One case is a weak test.
questions.teaches: The authors say the only way to settle a probabilistic claim definitively would be to rerun history hundreds of times, which we cannot do.

questions.q: Kent asked his analysts what odds serious possibility meant. What did he find?
options: All of them said about 65 to 35
All of them said it meant a probability below 10%
They refused to give numbers at all
Answers ranged from about 80 to 20 to 20 to 80
optionExplain: 65 to 35 was Kent’s own view.
No such agreement existed.
They answered; the answers disagreed.
Right: the answers were scattered between those extremes.
questions.explain: The card next gives the story.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a word like serious possibility hides disagreement because each reader fills it with a different probability.

questions.q: Kent wrote that estimating is what you do when you do not ____.
questions.explain: The quote is estimating is what you do when you do not know.
questions.rule: Estimates replace certainty.

questions.q: Four managers each agree the project has a good chance of finishing on time. One means 60%, another 90%. What does Kent’s story show?
options: Their agreement proves the project will finish on time
Agreement on words can hide disagreement on odds
Good chance is the best phrase for managers
Managers should avoid probabilities
optionExplain: Agreement on a phrase proves nothing about the odds.
Right: the same phrase carries different numbers.
Kent found such phrases unreliable.
Kent moved the other way, toward numbers.
questions.explain: The same words stood for very different probabilities.
questions.rule: Shared words can mask different odds.

questions.q: Suppose the official had been told 65 to 35 for attack rather than serious possibility. What would the authors expect?
options: Nothing would change because words and numbers are equal
The official would have ignored the estimate altogether and asked for another one
The official would have read the risk as lower than before
The official would likely have read the risk as higher than before
optionExplain: The story shows numbers clarify.
Nothing indicates he ignored it.
Numbers would have raised, not lowered, his reading.
Right: he had taken serious possibility to mean much lower odds, and was startled.
questions.explain: The numbers would have removed the gap between writer and reader.
questions.rule: Numbers prevent misreading.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Kent upheld high standards of rigor, yet confusion still seeped into the estimates.
questions.explain: The vague phrase fooled a rigorous team.
questions.rule: Rigor does not prevent vagueness.

questions.q: Besides analysts’ disagreement, what bigger worry did Kent raise?
options: That readers and producers took the same words to mean very different things
That estimates leaked to enemies before the readers saw them
That analysts lacked the formal degrees the work required
That national estimates were published too slowly to be of any use to senior officials
optionExplain: Right: he feared months of estimates seemed to agree with no real agreement.
Nothing about leaks.
The chapter highlights his PhD, not any lack of degrees.
Speed is not the concern.
questions.explain: Kent asked whether five months of estimates were agreement in name only.
questions.rule: Hidden disagreement is the danger.
questions.teaches: Kent wondered whether his team had been seeming to agree on five months of estimative judgments with no real agreement at all.

questions.q: What odds did the author of the phrase fair chance say he had in mind for the Bay of Pigs invasion?
options: About 3 to 1 against success
Even odds of success
About 3 to 1 in favor of success
Almost certain success
optionExplain: Right: he said 3 to 1 against.
Even odds does not match his claim.
The reading was positive but the intended odds were not.
Far more positive than intended.
questions.explain: The card next gives the story.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a verbal estimate can lead a decision maker to act on odds the writer never meant.

questions.q: The Joint Chiefs said the plan had a ____ chance of success.
questions.explain: The phrase was fair chance.
questions.rule: Fair chance meant poor odds to its author.

questions.q: A safety team says there is a reasonable chance the new system fails, meaning about 30%. What risk do the authors illustrate?
options: The manager will ask for a number before deciding
The manager will cancel the project at once
The manager may take reasonable chance to mean something far lower
The team will be sued for the failure of the system once the manager reads the report
optionExplain: Legal outcomes are not discussed.
Asking for a number is the fix, not the risk.
Right: the reader can miss the writer’s meaning.
Nothing makes cancelling certain.
questions.explain: The words carry the writer’s meaning only if the reader shares it.
questions.rule: State the odds in numbers.

questions.q: True or false: Kennedy was not told precisely what fair chance meant.
questions.explain: He took the phrase to be much more positive than its author intended.
questions.rule: The reader never saw the intended odds.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say they cannot be sure Kennedy would have called off the invasion had the odds been stated.
questions.explain: They say they cannot be sure, but a stated 3 to 1 would surely have made him think harder.
questions.rule: Do not overstate counterfactuals.

questions.q: Which point about this episode fits the authors’ view of vague phrases?
options: Odds are irrelevant to wartime planning and decisions
Vague phrases matter only in academic papers and not in government decisions of this kind
Vague wording can cost more than confusion: it can steer a bad decision
Presidents should not rely on military advice in wartime
optionExplain: Odds are central.
The example comes from a real decision.
Right: the authors call the invasion an unmitigated disaster.
The chapter does not say that.
questions.explain: The same problem Kent found in one estimate appeared in a presidential decision.
questions.rule: Vagueness has real costs.
questions.teaches: The authors describe the invasion that went ahead as an unmitigated disaster.

questions.q: In Kent’s scheme, roughly what range of probability did probable cover?
options: Exactly 100%
About 63% to 87%
About 40% to 60%
About 5% to 20%
optionExplain: 100% is certain.
Right: 75% give or take 12.
That range matches chances about even.
That range is closer to almost certainly not.
questions.explain: The card next gives the table in words.
questions.rule: According to the authors, pinning words to numerical ranges greatly reduces the room for confusion.

questions.q: In Kent’s scheme the term ____ was reserved for important matters where analysts must judge but cannot reasonably assign any probability.
questions.explain: The word possible was to be reserved for that case.
questions.rule: Keep possible for the truly unquantifiable.

questions.q: Under Kent’s table, which term fits a forecast that an event has about a 30% chance?
options: Probably not
Probable
Chances about even
Almost certainly not
optionExplain: Right: probably not is 30% give or take 10.
Probable is about 75%.
Chances about even is about 50%.
Almost certainly not is about 7%.
questions.explain: The table assigns a number range to each term.
questions.rule: Match words to the table.

questions.q: Order Kent’s terms from lowest to highest probability.
items: Impossible
Almost certainly not
Probably not
Chances about even
Probable
Almost certain
questions.explain: The central values rise: 0%, about 7%, 30%, 50%, 75%, 93%, with certain at 100%.
questions.rule: Scale words by their numbers.

questions.q: True or false: In Kent’s scheme each term had a central value with a give-or-take range around it.
questions.explain: For example, probable was 75% give or take 12.
questions.rule: Ranges express uncertainty.

questions.q: Why does a table of this kind help a decision maker who reads a report?
options: It guarantees that events called probable will happen
It removes all uncertainty from forecasting for the reader
The same word then means the same odds to writer and reader
It lets analysts avoid giving the reasons for a view
optionExplain: Probable events can fail.
It does not remove uncertainty.
Right: this removes room for confusion.
Reasons are still needed.
questions.explain: The scheme shares meaning; it does not guarantee truth.
questions.rule: Shared meaning, not certainty.
questions.teaches: Kent said the word possible alone covers a range from almost zero to almost 100%, so analysts should narrow their estimates whenever they can.

questions.q: True or false: The intelligence community did not adopt Kent’s numerical scheme.
questions.explain: It was never adopted. The card next gives the reasons.
questions.rule: According to the authors, feeling awkward about numbers is a weak argument against using them.

questions.q: Kent said he would rather be a ____ than a goddamn poet.
questions.explain: The legendary reply is I’d rather be a bookie than a goddamn poet.
questions.rule: Kent chose clarity over style.

questions.q: A team resists using percentages because it sounds crude. Which reply fits the authors?
options: Percentages are certain facts, so the awkwardness is justified
The resistance proves that percentages are wrong
Percentages should be replaced by poetry
Feeling awkward is a weak argument; one gets used to numbers
optionExplain: Numbers are estimates, not facts.
Resistance is not evidence of error.
The chapter argues for numbers over poetry.
Right: the authors call awkwardness a weak argument.
questions.explain: Habit explains the unease; it is not an argument.
questions.rule: Unease is not evidence.

questions.q: Which reasons for resisting numbers does the chapter report? Select all that apply.
options: Numbers felt unnatural or awkward
Language has its own poetry
Numbers made analysts sound like bookies
Numbers cost too much to print
optionExplain: Right: some said it felt unnatural.
Right: some felt aesthetic revulsion.
Right: it makes you sound like a bookie.
Not mentioned.
questions.explain: Awkwardness, poetry and the bookie image were the reasons reported.
questions.rule: Name the objections to be able to answer them.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Kent’s scheme was not adopted because people disliked using numbers.
questions.explain: It failed because people did not want to use numbers, not because tests showed it inaccurate.
questions.rule: Distinguish rejection from refutation.

questions.q: Which later development does the chapter use to show the resistance eased?
options: After a treaty on nuclear weapons, numbers were banned in reports
After the failure over Saddam Hussein’s supposed weapons of mass destruction
After Kent died, his scheme was adopted unchanged by every agency
After the Bay of Pigs, numbers were adopted at once in all national estimates
optionExplain: No such ban.
Right: reforms after that debacle made numbers more acceptable.
Not described that way.
The Bay of Pigs did not produce adoption.
questions.explain: It took a serious failure before the intelligence community shifted.
questions.rule: Failures can change norms.
questions.teaches: Only after the debacle over Saddam Hussein’s supposed weapons of mass destruction, and the reforms that followed, did it become more acceptable to give probabilities as numbers.

questions.q: True or false: The authors accept that a numerical probability may mislead readers into treating it as an objective fact.
questions.explain: They call it a danger, though not a reason to drop numbers. The card next gives the reply.
questions.rule: According to the authors, inform readers that numbers are estimates, rather than avoiding numbers.

questions.q: According to the authors, numbers, like words, only express ____ and nothing more.
questions.explain: The text says numbers express estimates, opinions, nothing more.
questions.rule: A number is an opinion with a value.

questions.q: A report says 70% chance of delay and a reader complains it sounds too exact. What reply fits the authors?
options: Delete the number because it implies a certainty it lacks
Round it to 100% so that the reader sees no false precision
Replace it with a probable delay, since words sound less exact
It is an estimate, as words would be; say so and keep the number
optionExplain: It is an opinion, not a falsehood.
Rounding to 100% changes the claim.
Words carry the same suggestion, with more confusion.
Right: label it as an estimate.
questions.explain: Fix the misreading with explanation, not vagueness.
questions.rule: Explain; do not hide.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say words like serious possibility suggest the same thing that numbers do.
questions.explain: Numbers only make explicit what such words already suggest.
questions.rule: Words imply odds too.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a precise number should not be read as meaning the forecaster knows it is exactly right.
questions.explain: That is not intended and should not be inferred.
questions.rule: A number is not a claim of certainty.

questions.q: Which benefit of numbers do the authors give besides reducing confusion?
options: They make predictions come true more often than words do
They force forecasters to think carefully about how they are thinking
They protect forecasters from being blamed when they are wrong
They make forecasts agree with each other across agencies and across the years
optionExplain: Numbers do not change events.
Right: this is metacognition, covered next.
Numbers expose forecasters rather than protect them.
Numbers do not force agreement.
questions.explain: Translating into numbers requires thought that vague words let one skip.
questions.rule: Numbers sharpen thinking.
questions.teaches: Vague thoughts are easily expressed in vague language, but translating them into numbers forces a forecaster to think about thinking, which the authors call metacognition.

questions.q: Thinking about how you are thinking is called ____.
questions.explain: The authors name it metacognition. The card next explains why numbers invite it.
questions.rule: According to the authors, practice with numbers trains finer judgment of uncertainty.

questions.q: Forecasters forced to turn vague terms into numbers must think carefully about how they are ____.
questions.explain: The authors say they have to think carefully about how they are thinking, which is metacognition.
questions.rule: Numbers force a check on your own thinking.

questions.q: A planner says a delay is possible. Asked for a number, she pauses and settles on 35%. What process do the authors describe?
options: She is avoiding responsibility for the claim she made
She is switching to a different forecasting model that suits the problem better
She is checking her own thinking and refining a vague thought
She is copying the opinion of a group of colleagues
optionExplain: A number increases accountability.
No model switch occurred.
Right: asked for a number she examines her thought.
No group is involved.
questions.explain: The number request prompted a closer look at her belief.
questions.rule: Ask for a number to sharpen a thought.

questions.q: True or false: The authors expect forecasters who practice giving numbers to get better at telling finer degrees of uncertainty apart.
questions.explain: They compare this to artists distinguishing subtler shades of gray.
questions.rule: Practice builds resolution of thought.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a forecaster who writes a number automatically improves, with no practice needed.
questions.explain: They say forecasters who practice get better.
questions.rule: Skill grows with practice.

questions.q: An agency analyst writes 65% for an event, and it does not happen. Why might she fear being blamed?
options: Readers will find the number too precise to be believed
Readers will assume she did not think about the question
Readers may treat the miss as proof she was wrong, though 65% allowed a 35% chance
Readers will blame the agency for not using plain words that everyone can understand
optionExplain: Precision was an earlier objection and is a separate issue.
A number shows more thought, not less.
Right: this is the accountability worry the chapter turns to next.
The blame is about the miss, not the format.
questions.explain: The 65% forecast itself said there was a 35% chance of the event not happening.
questions.rule: A miss on a 65% call is not proof of error.
questions.teaches: The authors say a more fundamental obstacle to adopting numbers is accountability, which they link to what they call the wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy.

questions.q: True or false: A forecaster who says 70% chance of rain has been shown wrong if it does not rain.
questions.explain: The forecast also said there was a 30% chance of no rain. The card next names the mistake.
questions.rule: According to Tetlock, a single forecast of 70% cannot be called wrong because the event did not happen; judge many forecasts instead.

questions.q: Tetlock calls judging a forecast by whether it landed on the right side of 50% the wrong-side-of-____ fallacy.
questions.explain: The name is the wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy.
questions.rule: Name the fallacy.

questions.q: A news site says: the pollsters said a 65% chance of a win, the team lost, so the pollsters were wrong. What is the flaw?
options: A 65% forecast also allowed a 35% chance of a loss, so one loss proves little
Pollsters should avoid giving percentages in public
The site should have trusted the team, not the pollsters
A single loss proves that the true chance of a win was below 50% all along
optionExplain: Right: this is the fallacy.
The problem is the judging, not the percentage.
The flaw is not about whom to trust.
One loss tells nothing sure about the true chance.
questions.explain: A 65% call expects a miss about a third of the time.
questions.rule: One result cannot judge a probability.

questions.q: If Leonhardt’s view that a 75% forecast was wrong were applied to many 75% calls, what would that approach wrongly punish?
options: Forecasters who made only a single forecast and then stopped forecasting
Forecasters who gave 50% to everything and so never took a stand on any question
Forecasters who used vague words, not numbers, to describe what they expected
Well-calibrated forecasters, since about a quarter of their 75% calls should miss
optionExplain: A single forecast is judged the same way.
The 50% forecaster is judged differently.
Words are not the issue here.
Right: a correct 75% forecaster misses one in four.
questions.explain: A fair 75% forecaster should miss about 25% of the time.
questions.rule: Expect misses at the stated rate.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says even sophisticated thinkers commit the wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy.
questions.explain: He cites David Leonhardt of the New York Times as an example.
questions.rule: The error is common.

questions.q: Which fact helps judge a weather service saying 30% chance of showers?
options: Whether it rained at least once during that month
Whether it rained on the day after one such forecast was issued by the service
Whether showers fell on about 30% of the days it said that
Whether the service predicted more rain than sun
optionExplain: A monthly shower says little about a daily percentage.
One day cannot judge it.
Right: track the frequency across many such days.
The balance of forecasts is not the test.
questions.explain: The authors say a meteorologist’s track record comes from tabulating many forecasts.
questions.rule: Compare stated odds with frequencies.
questions.teaches: Tetlock says the only way to know for sure would be to rerun the day hundreds of times, and a 70% forecast would be right if it rained in 70% of the reruns.

questions.q: Why does vague wording protect a forecaster, according to the card’s story?
options: It cannot be quoted by journalists in their stories or repeated by anyone later
It can be stretched after the event to fit whichever outcome occurred
It is required by law in intelligence work
It sounds more confident than numbers do to most readers
optionExplain: Journalists can quote words easily.
Right: it can mean more or less than 50% afterwards.
No such law is mentioned.
Vague words sound less confident.
questions.explain: The card next explains the incentives.
questions.rule: According to Tetlock, vague words protect forecasters from accountability, which is why they persist.

questions.q: Words like a fair chance can be stretched or shrunk afterwards, so the forecaster can say he ____ it either way.
questions.explain: The text says the forecaster nailed it in either case.
questions.rule: Elastic words never lose.

questions.q: A strategist repeatedly says a downturn is a distinct possibility. Whatever happens, she says she was right. What explains her habit?
options: Elastic wording lets her claim success after any outcome
She is using Kent’s scheme of fixed numerical meanings
She is giving a probability of exactly 50% each time
She has excellent foresight about the economy
optionExplain: Right: this is the safe course.
Kent’s scheme uses fixed numbers.
No number is given.
Her claim cannot be tested, so it shows no foresight.
questions.explain: Words with no number can be read to match any result.
questions.rule: Beware claims that cannot lose.

questions.q: True or false: Under the wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy, a forecaster who gives a number is more exposed to blame than one who uses elastic words.
questions.explain: A number can be checked against the outcome, while elastic words can be stretched.
questions.rule: Numbers expose; words hide.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock blames the incentives, which he calls perverse, for the preference for elastic wording.
questions.explain: He does not accuse forecasters of lying; the avoidance follows from the incentives.
questions.rule: Blame the incentives, not the people.

questions.q: Which change would reduce the pull of elastic language, following this card?
options: Letting forecasters revise their wording as they like after the outcome is known
Banning all forecasts about politics in the media
Rewarding the boldest-sounding forecaster each year
Judging forecasters on many forecasts instead of single outcomes
optionExplain: Revising wording is the very escape.
Banning forecasts removes the information.
Boldness is not accuracy.
Right: this removes the single-miss risk.
questions.explain: Tracking many forecasts makes a single miss expected, not damning.
questions.rule: Fix the judging, and numbers become safer.
questions.teaches: Tetlock says Kent could not overcome such political barriers, even though the case for numbers only grew as the years passed.

questions.q: What finally made numbers more acceptable in the intelligence community, according to the authors?
options: A new law requiring numerical probabilities in every briefing sent to the president
A study showing that numbers were correct more often than words
The failure over Saddam Hussein’s supposed weapons and the reforms that followed
Kent’s retirement in 1967, after which his scheme was adopted
optionExplain: No such law is mentioned.
Numbers are estimates, not always correct.
Right: the failure led to wholesale reforms.
His retirement came in 1967.
questions.explain: The card next gives the sequence.
questions.rule: According to the authors, numbers have become standard in some fields, such as weather forecasting.

questions.q: Weather forecasts shifted from slight chance of showers to ____% chance of showers.
questions.explain: The text says 30% chance of showers.
questions.rule: Weather moved to numbers.

questions.q: A news anchor says experts think a recession is quite possible. Following the authors, what should a careful viewer do?
options: Assume the anchor has given a probability above 50%
Ask what probability and time frame the phrase stands for
Treat it as a firm forecast that a recession will come
Ignore forecasts on television as a habit
optionExplain: The phrase fixes no number.
Right: such phrases slip by without meaning.
The phrase is not firm.
The point is to ask for meaning, not to ignore.
questions.explain: Vague language is common in the media and rarely noticed.
questions.rule: Ask what the vague phrase means.

questions.q: Sort each example: fits the shift toward numbers, or the older vague style?

items.t: Thirty percent chance of showers
Sixty percent chance of rain
Twenty percent chance of snow
Slight chance of showers
A serious possibility of attack
A fair chance of success

questions.explain: The first three give numbers; the others use phrases open to different readings.
questions.rule: Numbers fix meaning.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Kent saw his numerical scheme adopted during his lifetime.
questions.explain: The authors say it was never adopted in his time; change came only after the later debacle.
questions.rule: Change came late.

questions.q: What had study after study shown about words like could, might and likely?
options: People attach very different meanings to them
They mean the same as the word certain
They are more accurate than numbers
People agree closely on what they mean
optionExplain: Right: this supports the case for numbers.
They are not equal to certainty.
No such claim is made.
The studies showed the opposite.
questions.explain: Different readings of the same word are the problem Kent found.
questions.rule: Words are read in different ways.
questions.teaches: The authors say that when CIA analysts told President Obama they were 70% or 90% sure the man in a Pakistani compound was Osama bin Laden, it was a small posthumous triumph for Kent.

questions.q: True or false: The word may in a forecast says only that something is possible, not how likely it is.
questions.explain: It says only that something is possible. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, may is a hollow word: it means something is possible and nothing about how likely it is.

questions.q: The authors call may a ____ word, since it says nothing about the probability of the possibility.
questions.explain: The text says may is a hollow word.
questions.rule: May carries no odds.

questions.q: A fund manager says: oil prices may double next year. They fall. What follows?
options: He gave a 50% forecast of doubling, so he was exactly half right either way
Nothing: may allowed both outcomes, so he cannot be shown wrong
He was proved wrong by the fall in oil prices
He was proved right because a doubling was possible
optionExplain: No percentage was stated.
Right: may carries an or-may-not clause.
May does not claim doubling will happen.
Possibility alone proves nothing.
questions.explain: Almost anything may happen, so may cannot be tested.
questions.rule: May cannot lose.

questions.q: Which statement could a later result contradict?
options: A Greek default is on the cards for the coming months
Greece is close to serious trouble with its creditors
There is a 60% chance Greece defaults by 30 June 2012
Greece may default on its debts at some stage soon
optionExplain: On the cards is vague and has no date.
Close to trouble has no clear event.
Right: it names a probability, an event and a date.
May never fails.
questions.explain: Only the first has a definition, a date and odds.
questions.rule: Testable forecasts name event, date and odds.

questions.q: True or false: The authors conclude Ferguson was definitely wrong because Greece did not repudiate its debt completely.
questions.explain: They say Greece defaulted in the technical sense shortly after, so there is reason to think he was right; the meaning was unclear.
questions.rule: Check the definition used.

questions.q: The authors say they can forecast that the Earth may be attacked by aliens tomorrow. What point does this make?
options: Alien attack is more likely than most people think
Forecasts about space cannot be tested but forecasts about earthly events can be
The authors believe aliens are a real risk
Almost any event may happen, so a may statement is no real forecast
optionExplain: The example is a joke, not a probability claim.
The point is about the word may, not subject area.
Not their view.
Right: the example shows may is hollow.
questions.explain: May covers everything, including the absurd, so it conveys nothing.
questions.rule: May covers everything.
questions.teaches: The authors say every may carries an asterisk, with the words or may not buried in the fine print.

questions.q: Which set best matches what the authors say forecasts need, to be measured?
options: One bold forecast made by a famous name
Clear terms and timelines, numbers, and many forecasts
Short wording and a confident tone of voice
A long essay explaining the reasoning in detail
optionExplain: One forecast cannot be judged.
Right: these are the three requirements.
Confidence and brevity do not make it testable.
Reasoning is useful but does not make it measurable.
questions.explain: The card next gives the three requirements.
questions.rule: According to the authors, judge a forecaster on a large set of numerical forecasts with clear terms.

questions.q: The match between stated chances and how often events occur is called ____.
questions.explain: The authors call it calibration.
questions.rule: Name the measure.

questions.q: A trader makes ten forecasts in a year. Which fix best follows the authors for judging him?
options: Ask him to explain the reasoning behind each forecast
Rely on his reputation among colleagues in the same firm
Pick his best forecast and judge him on that one alone
Gather many more forecasts with clear terms and numbers
optionExplain: Explanations do not test accuracy.
Reputation is what testing replaces.
Picking the best is a biased sample.
Right: more forecasts with terms and numbers make a track record.
questions.explain: Ten loosely worded forecasts give too little to tabulate.
questions.rule: Track record needs volume and clarity.

questions.q: Order what the meteorologist does to build a judgeable record.
items: Give a numerical chance of rain each day
Wait while the days pass
Record whether it rained each day
Group days by stated chance and compare frequencies
questions.explain: Forecasts stack up, outcomes are recorded, and the groups are compared with the stated chance.
questions.rule: Record first, compare after.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a single 70% forecast cannot be judged on its own.
questions.explain: They say only a set of forecasts can be judged.
questions.rule: One forecast is not enough.

questions.q: Which forecaster can be judged most fairly?
options: One who gives dated, numerical odds on 200 defined questions
One who issues a yearly letter of warnings
One who gives a likely call on 20 broad topics
One who gives a vivid and memorable story about a single big event of the decade
optionExplain: Right: many numerical, dated forecasts.
Letters of warnings are vague.
Likely is a vague word.
A story on one event has no volume.
questions.explain: Terms, numbers and volume together give a record.
questions.rule: All three requirements together.
questions.teaches: The authors say calibration can be plotted on a simple chart, where perfect calibration is a diagonal line.

questions.q: A forecaster says 80% for events that happen only 50% of the time. How do the authors describe her?
options: Overconfident
Perfectly calibrated
Underconfident
Uninformative but accurate
optionExplain: Right: she claims more than the results support.
Perfect calibration would show 80%.
Underconfident means events happen more than she says.
The term does not fit.
questions.explain: The card next explains the chart.
questions.rule: According to the authors, compare what a forecaster says with what happens: gaps from the diagonal show the direction of the error.

questions.q: Perfect calibration appears as a ____ line on the chart.
questions.explain: The authors describe a diagonal line.
questions.rule: Diagonal means stated chance matches frequency.

questions.q: A forecaster’s 20% calls happen half the time. Which description fits?
options: Underconfident: the curve lies below the diagonal
Overconfident: the curve lies below the diagonal
Underconfident: the curve lies above the diagonal
Overconfident: the curve lies above the diagonal
optionExplain: Underconfident curves are above the line, not below.
Overconfident means below, but this case is above.
Right: events occur more often than she says.
Overconfident is the opposite case.
questions.explain: Above the line means more happens than stated.
questions.rule: Above is underconfident; below is overconfident.

questions.q: Sort each pattern: underconfident or overconfident?

items.t: Events called 20% happen 50% of the time
Events called 10% happen 30% of the time
Events called 90% happen 60% of the time
Events called 80% happen 50% of the time

questions.explain: The first two happen more often than claimed; the last two less often.
questions.rule: Compare claim with frequency.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a curve far below the diagonal shows a forecaster is overconfident.
questions.explain: Below the line is overconfident; above is underconfident.
questions.rule: Above and below are easy to swap.

questions.q: Across 100 calls of 60%, only 30 happened. What does the authors’ chart logic say?
options: No chart can be drawn from 100 calls
The curve sits above the diagonal: underconfident
The curve sits below the diagonal: overconfident
The curve is on the diagonal
optionExplain: Enough calls exist for one point at least.
That would need more than 60% to occur.
Right: events happened less often than stated.
The match would need 60%.
questions.explain: Apply the same comparison at any stated chance.
questions.rule: Compare claim with frequency at every level.
questions.teaches: The authors say this method works well for weather, where forecasts stack up fast, but less well for events such as presidential elections.

questions.q: Why is calibration easier to measure for weather than for presidential elections?
options: Meteorologists are more honest than election forecasters
Weather gives new outcomes every day, so forecasts stack up fast
Elections cannot be forecast with numbers of any kind
Weather is perfectly predictable, so there is little to measure
optionExplain: Honesty is not the issue.
Right: volume is the difference.
Numbers can be used for elections.
Weather is not perfectly predictable.
questions.explain: The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: According to the authors, calibration needs many forecasts of the same kind, so use it where outcomes repeat quickly.

questions.q: Judging elections at the state level gives ____ results per election, not one.
questions.explain: The text says fifty results per election.
questions.rule: Break big events into smaller ones.

questions.q: You want to check how well a hospital predicts rare complications. What limit from the card applies?
options: Too few events to build a track record, so judging is impractical
The test needs a presidential election to have any meaning
Complications cannot be assigned numerical probabilities by doctors
Calibration only works for weather forecasts and nothing else
optionExplain: Right: rare events pile up slowly.
Elections are only an example.
Numbers can be given.
The method works elsewhere with enough events.
questions.explain: Rare events give few cases and the statistics do not work.
questions.rule: Rare events need creative framing.

questions.q: True or false: If a forecaster only ever predicts one-off events, the authors would expect it to be easy to judge her calibration.
questions.explain: They say a one-off event yields too few forecasts to judge calibration.
questions.rule: No volume, no calibration.

questions.q: A reader claims the authors say calibration is useless. Which reply fits?
options: They say it is the whole story of forecasting accuracy
They say it is useless for weather and for every other kind of forecast as well
They call it important, but it needs many forecasts and careful reading
They say it is impossible to compute from real forecasts
optionExplain: The next idea shows it is not the whole story.
It works well for weather.
Right: it is important but limited.
It is computable.
questions.explain: The authors call it important but not the whole story.
questions.rule: Know a method’s scope.

questions.q: A league wants to judge a tipster across 40 matches in a season. What does the card suggest?
options: Forty matches give a perfect measure of the tipster’s skill
The tipster should be judged by one match, the biggest one
Forty is too few to judge anything about the tipster
Forty matches is a modest set, so read the record with caution
optionExplain: Small sets give noisy measures.
One match gives no calibration.
The card does not set a minimum so strict.
Right: patient data collectors, cautious interpreters.
questions.explain: Common events help, but the authors still ask for patience and caution.
questions.rule: Be patient and cautious with small samples.
questions.teaches: The authors say that even with common events one must be patient collecting data and cautious interpreting it.

questions.q: A forecaster says 50% for everything and 50% of events occur. Which is true?
options: She has perfect resolution because every call she makes is correct
She is well calibrated but shows poor resolution
She is overconfident because she claims too much certainty
She is underconfident because events happen more than she says
optionExplain: Resolution requires bold correct calls.
Right: she never commits.
Her stated and actual chances match.
Her stated and actual chances match.
questions.explain: The card next explains resolution.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a good forecaster is both calibrated and decisive.

questions.q: The technical term for saying this will happen, and it does, is ____.
questions.explain: The authors call it resolution.
questions.rule: Resolution is bold and right.

questions.q: Forecaster A says 40% or 60% on every question; B says 5% or 95%. Both are well calibrated. Who has better resolution?
options: Neither, because calibration is equal for both
A, because 60% is a safer call than 95% when the forecaster may turn out wrong
A, who stays cautious and avoids bold calls
B, who separates events that happen from those that do not
optionExplain: Resolution differs even when calibration is equal.
Safety is not the measure.
Caution lowers resolution.
Right: B is decisive and still calibrated.
questions.explain: Equal calibration can hide very different resolution.
questions.rule: Calibration plus decisiveness.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a forecaster who stays between 40% and 60% can still be perfectly calibrated.
questions.explain: The top figure shows exactly this: perfect calibration with poor resolution.
questions.rule: Calibration alone is not enough.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say bold forecasters with high resolution are better even when their stated chances do not match outcomes.
questions.explain: Good judgment needs both calibration and resolution.
questions.rule: Boldness without calibration is not good.

questions.q: Which pair best fits the authors’ picture of the bottom figure?
options: Poor calibration and poor resolution
Superb calibration and superb resolution
Superb calibration and poor resolution
Poor calibration and superb resolution
optionExplain: Neither is poor there.
Right: the bottom figure is calibrated and brave.
That describes the top figure.
Both are superb there.
questions.explain: The bottom figure combines both skills.
questions.rule: Seek both.
questions.teaches: The authors say combining calibration and resolution gives a scoring system that fully captures our sense of what good forecasters should do.

questions.q: True or false: A fair scoring system would reward a 100% forecast that fails more than a 70% forecast that fails.
questions.explain: It should punish the failed 100% forecast more. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the more confident the call, the bigger the reward when right and the bigger the penalty when wrong.

questions.q: The forecaster who says X is a slam dunk should take a big ____ if X does not happen.
questions.explain: The text says a big hit.
questions.rule: Hubris is punished.

questions.q: Two analysts both predict a merger. Analyst A says 70%, B says 99%. The merger fails. Under the authors’ logic, who should be penalized more?
options: Both equally, because both were wrong
Neither, because one miss tells nothing
B, who was far more confident
A, who was less sure
optionExplain: The penalty grows with confidence.
A miss still costs; the cost scales with confidence.
Right: bigger confidence, bigger penalty.
A gave a lower chance of success.
questions.explain: The confident miss is the costliest.
questions.rule: Confidence raises both prize and penalty.

questions.q: Order these by the score a good system would give if the event happens, best first.
items: 100% forecast
90% forecast
70% forecast
50% forecast
questions.explain: The closer to certainty the correct call, the better the score.
questions.rule: Right and bold scores best.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a forecaster who calls an event a slam dunk should take a big hit if it fails.
questions.explain: They say hubris must be punished.
questions.rule: Do not excuse extreme misses.

questions.q: Why does a scoring system need both rewards and penalties for confidence?
options: Without rewards, nobody would bother to make forecasts
Without penalties, the scores would be harder to read
Without penalties, forecasters could claim certainty on everything
Without rewards, calibration would be impossible to compute from any set of forecasts
optionExplain: Rewards matter, but the key point is gaming.
Scores can be clear without penalties.
Right: costless boldness would be gamed.
Calibration does not depend on rewards.
questions.explain: A penalty keeps boldness honest.
questions.rule: Make overconfidence expensive.
questions.teaches: The authors say it is reasonable to think of the penalty in betting terms: saying 80% and being willing to bet means offering 4 to 1 odds.

questions.q: At 95% confidence in a Yankees win, what odds does the authors’ betting example imply?
options: 19 to 1
2 to 1
4 to 1
9 to 1
optionExplain: Right: 19 to 1.
Smaller than 95% implies.
This is the 80% odds.
This is the 90% odds.
questions.explain: The card next gives the arithmetic.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a good score should capture the pain of an extreme forecast failing.

questions.q: An 80% confidence in a Yankees win is the same as offering ____ to 1 odds.
questions.explain: The text says 4 to 1.
questions.rule: Convert probability to odds.

questions.q: At 90%, a bettor stakes $100 on the other side. If the Yankees lose, how much does the 90% forecaster owe?
optionExplain: That is the 80% case.
That is the stake.
That is the 95% case.
Right: 9 to 1 odds means $900.
questions.explain: The odds multiply the stake.
questions.rule: Odds scale the cost.

questions.q: As stated confidence rises from 80% to 95%, what happens to the payout owed if the forecast fails?
options: It falls
It stays the same
It becomes zero
It rises steeply
optionExplain: Higher confidence means a larger payout.
Odds change with confidence.
A loss is never free.
Right: from $400 to $1,900 per $100.
questions.explain: The cost of being wrong grows faster than the confidence.
questions.rule: Extreme confidence is costly.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say an 80% forecast means offering 1 to 4 odds.
questions.explain: It means 4 to 1 odds.
questions.rule: Check the direction.

questions.q: Why does the authors’ betting picture justify a heavy penalty for failed extreme forecasts?
options: It shows 50% is the best forecast to give
It shows bettors are wrong more often than forecasters
It shows extreme confidence puts a lot at stake
It shows odds cannot be computed from probabilities
optionExplain: 50% scores worse when right.
Bettors are not always wrong.
Right: the stake is the cost of hubris.
Odds are computed in the text.
questions.explain: A score should capture the pain that a real bet would.
questions.rule: Capture the pain.
questions.teaches: The authors say that at 95% a $100 bet would mean owing $1,900 if the Yankees lose, which is extreme and is the pain a scoring system should capture.

questions.q: On a Brier score, which value is perfect?
optionExplain: Right: zero distance from the truth.
This is the worst possible.
Not a landmark value in the text.
This is random guessing.
questions.explain: The card next gives the scale.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a lower Brier score is better; 0 is perfect, 0.5 is random, 2.0 is as bad as possible.

questions.q: Brier scores are like golf scores: ____ is better.
questions.explain: The authors compare them to golf scores.
questions.rule: Lower wins.

questions.q: A forecaster hedges every question at 50%. What Brier score do the authors say she gets?
options: About 0.5
About 2.0
About 0
About 1.5
optionExplain: Right: hedged fifty-fifty scores 0.5.
That requires being 100% sure and wrong every time.
Zero is perfect.
Not a figure in the text.
questions.explain: Always hedging earns the random-guessing score.
questions.rule: Hedging earns 0.5.

questions.q: Order these Brier scores from best to worst.
questions.explain: Lower is better, so 0 is best and 2.0 is worst.
questions.rule: Lower is better.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a Brier score of 2.0 is the worst possible score.
questions.explain: 2.0 is the worst possible; 0 is perfect.
questions.rule: Check the direction.

questions.q: Who did the authors name as the developer of the scoring math, and when?
options: Nate Silver in 2012
Glenn W. Brier in 1950
Daniel Kahneman in 1988
Sherman Kent in 1951
optionExplain: Silver was a poll aggregator.
Right: hence Brier scores.
Kahneman made the 1988 guess.
Kent proposed words with numbers.
questions.explain: The scoring system takes its name from the person who developed the math.
questions.rule: Name the origin.
questions.teaches: The authors say the math was developed by Glenn W. Brier in 1950, hence the name.

questions.q: True or false: A Brier score of 0.2 means the same level of skill whatever was being forecast.
questions.explain: The meaning depends on what is forecast. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, read a Brier score against what a simple rule would have scored on the same questions.

questions.q: To interpret Brier scores the authors say you need benchmarks and ____.
questions.explain: The two things are benchmarks and comparability.
questions.rule: Two tools to interpret a score.

questions.q: A forecaster scores 0.2 on questions where almost nothing ever changes. Following the authors, what is the key question?
options: Could a mindless rule have done as well on the same questions?
Does the forecaster work for a famous and respected firm?
Is 0.2 below 0.5, which proves skill on its own?
Did the forecaster give numbers in whole percentages?
optionExplain: Right: that is the benchmark test.
Fame is not a benchmark.
Beating 0.5 only beats guessing; an easy question set can do that.
Rounding is not the issue.
questions.explain: A score has a meaning only relative to what was easy or hard to get.
questions.rule: Compare with a simple rule.

questions.q: If the questions are very hard, what would you expect a skilled forecaster’s Brier score to look like compared with an easy set?
options: Exactly 0.5
Lower (better), because skill always helps more on hard questions
Exactly 0
Higher (worse), even though the forecaster is skilled
optionExplain: Random guessing alone gives 0.5.
Skill helps, but hard questions limit scores.
Perfect scores are not expected.
Right: hard questions produce worse scores for anyone.
questions.explain: Scores depend on the difficulty of the questions.
questions.rule: Difficulty moves the scores.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a score of 0.2 is disappointing in every circumstance.
questions.explain: They say it is easy to imagine circumstances where it would be disappointing, not all circumstances.
questions.rule: Context decides.

questions.q: A student scores 85% on a test. What does the benchmark idea suggest you ask?
options: Did the student study for many hours before the test day, and in what subjects?
Is 85% above half marks, which is the usual passing line?
What would a blind guesser or a simple rule have scored on this test?
Is the student well liked by the teachers and classmates?
