optionExplain: Effort is not a benchmark.
Beating half marks can still be easy.
Right: score against a baseline.
Popularity is irrelevant.
questions.explain: The same logic applies to any score: compare with a baseline.
questions.rule: Ask what the baseline would score.
questions.teaches: The authors say a score of 0.2 falls in the range one might expect from a human being.

questions.q: In Phoenix each June, what Brier score could a rule that assigns 100% to hot and sunny every day get?
options: About 0.5
Close to 0
About 1.0
About 2.0
optionExplain: That is random guessing.
Right: the weather rarely changes.
Not a figure the authors give.
That is the worst possible.
questions.explain: The card next gives the point.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the right test of skill is doing better than a mindless no-change prediction.

questions.q: The right test of skill is whether a forecaster can beat mindlessly predicting no ____.
questions.explain: The text says no change.
questions.rule: Beat the no-change rule.

questions.q: A forecaster says a store’s sales will rise in December, as they do every year, and scores very well. What do the authors suggest?
options: Check whether repeating last year’s pattern would have scored as well
Assume the store has been lucky this year and wait to see what next December brings
Ignore the score because December is an unusual month
Treat the score as proof of rare forecasting skill
optionExplain: Right: this is the no-change benchmark.
Luck is not the point.
December is a regular pattern, not unusual.
A strong score on an easy question proves little.
questions.explain: A repeating pattern is beaten by a simple rule.
questions.rule: Check the simple rule first.

questions.q: True or false: Beating a Brier score of 0.2 is equally impressive in Phoenix in June and in a place with variable weather.
questions.explain: It is easy in Phoenix and harder where weather varies.
questions.rule: Difficulty differs.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say beating a mindless no-change rule is the right test of skill.
questions.explain: They say beating no change is the right test of skill.
questions.rule: Beating the baseline matters.

questions.q: In which setting would a no-change baseline be a weak benchmark?
options: Where a sunny day is almost certain every day
Where nothing varies from year to year at all
Where the same event repeats each June without fail
Where outcomes swing widely from one period to the next
optionExplain: That is the Phoenix case too.
No change is a strong baseline there.
That is the Phoenix case.
Right: no change would often be wrong, so the baseline is weak.
questions.explain: The baseline is only as strong as the stability of the world.
questions.rule: Choose a baseline that fits.
questions.teaches: The authors say that in the 2012 US presidential election a crude no-change rule would have called forty-eight of fifty states correctly.

questions.q: After the 2012 election, how many states would a rule of same-as-2008 have called correctly?
options: Thirty of fifty
Twenty-five of fifty
Forty-eight of fifty
All fifty
optionExplain: That is too low.
That is chance level.
Right: forty-eight.
Then no skill would show; it was forty-eight.
questions.explain: The card next gives the context.
questions.rule: According to the authors, praise for a forecast should be checked against what a no-change rule would have done.

questions.q: A crude no-change rule would have scored ____ out of fifty states in 2012.
questions.explain: The text says forty-eight out of fifty.
questions.rule: A baseline can be strong.

questions.q: A pundit boasts that he picked 46 of 50 winners in a league whose champion rarely changes. How do you weigh it?
options: Ask whether he is famous enough to be believed
Compare it with the score from picking last year’s champions
Accept it as proof of exceptional skill in that league and reward him for it
Reject it because he missed four of the fifty winners
optionExplain: Fame is not evidence.
Right: use the no-change baseline.
The baseline may score as well.
Four misses may still beat the baseline.
questions.explain: A strong result on a stable question may be easy.
questions.rule: Check against no change.

questions.q: True or false: If most states vote as they did four years earlier, improving on a no-change rule is a game of inches.
questions.explain: With 48 of 50 already right, only small gains remain.
questions.rule: The easy part is already scored.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Silver and Wang were wrong to call all fifty states.
questions.explain: They did call them; the authors only say praise was overwrought without the baseline.
questions.rule: Praise needs context.

questions.q: Which result from a forecasting tournament would impress the authors most?
options: Beating a no-change baseline on questions where change is likely
Giving the most confident forecasts of all the entrants in the tournament this year
Winning the tournament with the fewest forecasts
Matching the baseline on questions where nothing changes
optionExplain: Right: this shows real foresight.
Confidence is not accuracy.
Fewer forecasts give less evidence.
Matching a baseline shows little.
questions.explain: Value lies in beating a baseline where there is something to beat.
questions.rule: Beat a baseline that bites.
questions.teaches: The authors say poll aggregators know that improving predictions tends to be a game of inches.

questions.q: True or false: The authors name other forecasters as a benchmark for interpreting Brier scores.
questions.explain: They ask who can beat everyone else and the consensus. The card next gives the setting.
questions.rule: According to the authors, comparing forecasters is only meaningful when they answer the same questions over the same time.

questions.q: Besides beating everyone else, the authors ask who can beat the ____ forecast.
questions.explain: The text asks who can beat the consensus forecast.
questions.rule: Consensus is a benchmark.

questions.q: Two analysts publish yearly forecasts on different topics. A reader compares their Brier scores. What is wrong?
options: Yearly forecasts cannot be given a Brier score at all
They answered different questions, so the comparison may be unfair
Brier scores cannot be compared between two different people
Analysts should not be compared with one another in public
optionExplain: Any forecast set can be scored.
Right: the playing field is not level.
Scores can be compared on the same questions.
Comparing is exactly the benchmark idea.
questions.explain: Comparisons need the same questions.
questions.rule: Level the field.

questions.q: True or false: Outside tournaments, real-world forecasters usually predict the same developments over the same period.
questions.explain: Outside tournaments they seldom do, which is why comparisons there are hard.
questions.rule: Real forecasts differ in scope.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say comparing Brier scores is meaningful whichever questions each forecaster answered.
questions.explain: It needs a level playing field.
questions.rule: Same questions matter.

questions.q: What setup would give the fairest comparison of fifty forecasters?
options: Each forecaster answering a different number of questions
Each forecaster using a different scoring rule
The same questions with the same deadlines for all of them
Each forecaster choosing their own best topic to answer
optionExplain: Different numbers break comparability.
Different scoring breaks comparability.
Right: that is a tournament.
Choice of topic breaks comparability.
questions.explain: A tournament sets the same questions for all forecasters.
questions.rule: Use a tournament.
questions.teaches: The authors say dredging up old forecasts from newspapers will seldom yield apples-to-apples comparisons.

questions.q: Which city’s meteorologist faces easier forecasting, according to the authors?
options: Springfield, Missouri
Both are equal
Neither can be compared
Phoenix, Arizona
optionExplain: Springfield is notoriously variable.
They differ in difficulty.
The point is they differ, not that comparison is impossible.
Right: Phoenix weather is much more stable.
questions.explain: The card next gives the example.
questions.rule: According to the authors, compare Brier scores only between forecasters facing the same questions.

questions.q: The authors call weather in ____, Missouri notoriously variable.
questions.explain: The text names Springfield, Missouri.
questions.rule: Difficulty varies.

questions.q: Two fund managers have Brier scores of 0.18 and 0.22. One covers stable bonds, the other volatile startups. What should you conclude?
options: The first is better because 0.18 is the lower score
Little: the questions differ in difficulty, so the scores are not comparable
The second is better because startups are harder to call
Scores always favor the larger fund because a larger fund has far more data behind it
optionExplain: Lower is better only for comparable questions.
Right: no level playing field.
Harder questions do not make the manager better.
No such rule is claimed.
questions.explain: Different questions, different baselines.
questions.rule: Compare like with like.

questions.q: A 0.2 Brier score appears in Springfield. How might the authors read it?
options: Meaningless, since weather cannot be scored with numbers
Average, since all places are equally hard to forecast
Poor, since 0.2 is well above a perfect 0
Possibly world-class, given how variable the weather is
optionExplain: Weather can be scored.
Places differ.
The meaning depends on the difficulty.
Right: the authors say it could be world-class.
questions.explain: Variable weather lifts the baseline for all.
questions.rule: Judge against difficulty.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say old newspaper forecasts usually allow neat apples-to-apples comparisons.
questions.explain: They say such forecasts will seldom allow it.
questions.rule: Archives are messy.

questions.q: Why do the authors recommend designed experiments over old forecasts?
options: Designed studies give all forecasters the same questions and time frames
Forecasters prefer experiments because they get paid for taking part
Experiments are cheaper than collecting forecasts from archives
Old forecasts are mostly wrong, so only new ones are worth scoring
optionExplain: Right: the playing field can be made level.
Preferences are not discussed.
Cost is not discussed.
Old forecasts are not necessarily wrong.
questions.explain: Tournaments solve the comparability problem.
questions.rule: Design for comparability.
questions.teaches: The authors say the answer is to assemble forecasters, ask them large numbers of questions with precise time frames, and require numerical probabilities.

questions.q: In the authors’ proposed forecasting experiment, which step comes first?
options: Assemble a group of forecasters
Analyze the scores of the group
Wait for time to pass before scoring
Publish the results of the study
optionExplain: Right: the experiment starts with the forecasters.
Analysis comes last.
Waiting comes after the questions are asked.
Publishing comes after analysis.
questions.explain: The card next gives the order.
questions.rule: According to the authors, test forecasting like a medical trial: same questions, clear wording, numbers, then time.

questions.q: The authors compare the proposed experiments to the work of Archie ____ and evidence-based medicine.
questions.explain: The text names Archie Cochrane.
questions.rule: Borrow medicine’s rigor.

questions.q: A think tank wants to test its analysts. Which design best follows the authors?
options: A survey asking analysts to rate their own past accuracy and confidence
One long essay from each analyst explaining their view of the future
Many dated, precisely worded questions answered with numbers, scored later
A panel discussion in which the audience votes on who sounded best
optionExplain: Self-rating is not testing.
An essay cannot be scored.
Right: same questions, clear wording, numbers, then time.
Sounding best is not accuracy.
questions.explain: The design follows the card.
questions.rule: Design the test before collecting.

questions.q: Put the steps of the authors’ proposed experiment in order.
items: Assemble forecasters
Ask many precisely worded questions
Require numerical probabilities
Wait for time to pass
Analyze the data
questions.explain: Forecasters come first, then questions and numerical answers, then time, then analysis.
questions.rule: Test in a set order.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say waiting for time to pass is optional if the questions are worded precisely.
questions.explain: They list waiting as part of the design: forecasts can only be scored after events occur.
questions.rule: Time is needed.

questions.q: Why does the authors’ recipe ask for precise time frames and unambiguous language?
options: So that the questions are more fun for volunteers to answer
So that forecasts are shorter and cheaper to collect in bulk
So that outcomes can be marked right or wrong without dispute
So that forecasters feel more confident when committing to numbers
optionExplain: Fun is not the aim.
Length is not the aim.
Right: this answers the earlier problems.
Confidence is not the aim.
questions.explain: The recipe answers each obstacle raised earlier.
questions.rule: Fix wording first.
questions.teaches: Tetlock says he set out to do exactly this in the mid-1980s but ran into rough spots early on.

questions.q: What did Tetlock offer the experts to get them to take part?
options: A book contract
Anonymity
Public ranking of the best
Payment for each forecast
optionExplain: Not mentioned.
Right: he guaranteed anonymity.
Public competition was left for later.
Payment is not mentioned.
questions.explain: The card next gives the reasons.
questions.rule: According to Tetlock, promised anonymity let him recruit experts and gather their honest best guesses.

questions.q: Tetlock recruited ____ serious professionals for the study.
questions.explain: The text says 284.
questions.rule: Know the sample.

questions.q: A study of pundits promises that names will be published. Following Tetlock, what might happen?
options: Experts may decline or play it safe to avoid embarrassment
More famous pundits will join because of the publicity
Experts will be more honest since their names are on record
Experts will give better forecasts because they are watched
optionExplain: Right: Tetlock says reputations were at risk.
The highest-profile pundits refused even so.
Anonymity ensured honest guesses; publication risks the reverse.
Fear of embarrassment can distort guesses.
questions.explain: Public exposure changes behavior.
questions.rule: Anonymity protects honesty.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says anonymity also made the experts give their best guesses without fear of embarrassment.
questions.explain: He lists this as a second benefit of anonymity.
questions.rule: Two benefits: participation and honesty.

questions.q: True or false: None of the highest-profile pundits agreed to take part in Tetlock’s study.
questions.explain: None participated, despite his pleading.
questions.rule: Fame stayed out.

questions.q: What did Tetlock say about testing the effects of public competition?
options: It showed that fame improved accuracy
It was done within the same study
It would have to wait for a future study
It was impossible by its very nature
optionExplain: Not reported.
Not in this study.
Right: left for later.
Not said to be impossible.
questions.explain: Public competition was not part of this study.
questions.rule: Know the limits of a study.
questions.teaches: Tetlock says the effects of public competition would have to wait for a future study.

questions.q: Roughly how many predictions did the experts make in total?
options: About two thousand predictions in all
About two million predictions in all
About two hundred predictions in all
About twenty-eight thousand predictions in all
optionExplain: Too low.
Too high.
That is too low.
Right: roughly twenty-eight thousand.
questions.explain: The card next gives the design.
questions.rule: According to Tetlock, many topics outside specialty let the study compare experts with informed laypeople.

questions.q: The questions covered time frames of one, five and ____ years.
questions.explain: The horizons were one, five and ten years.
questions.rule: Know the horizons.

questions.q: Why would Tetlock ask an economist to forecast events outside economics?
options: To embarrass the economist before the other participants
To compare subject-matter experts with well-informed laypeople
To test whether economists can explain topics in plain terms
To shorten the survey by using fewer specialist questions
optionExplain: Not the aim.
Right: this allowed the comparison.
Not the aim.
Not the aim.
questions.explain: Out-of-field questions create a layperson comparison.
questions.rule: Mix in and out of expertise.

questions.q: True or false: If experts are asked about topics in their own field, the study can still compare them with laypeople on topics outside it.
questions.explain: The mix allows both comparisons.
questions.rule: Mix topics.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says every question fell inside each expert’s specialty.
questions.explain: The experts were sometimes asked in their zone of expertise but more often not.
questions.rule: Not all in-field.

questions.q: What did Tetlock ask the experts about themselves first?
options: Their predictions about how well the other experts in the study would do
Their favorite countries and the places they had visited
Their salaries, savings and investments in the markets they forecast
Age, experience, education, ideological leanings and preferred approaches
optionExplain: Not mentioned.
Not mentioned.
Not mentioned.
Right: those background and style questions.
questions.explain: The study collected background to later test what mattered.
questions.rule: Collect the background.
questions.teaches: The experts averaged forty-three years of age and 12.2 years of relevant work experience, and almost all had postgraduate training, half with PhDs.

questions.q: In which year did the final results of Tetlock’s study appear?
optionExplain: Not the year.
Right: 2005.
Not the year.
That is when the study began.
questions.explain: The card next gives the timeline.
questions.rule: According to Tetlock, testing forecasts takes patience: the clock is set by events, not by researchers.

questions.q: Tetlock calls his whole research program ____ for short.
questions.explain: EPJ stands for Expert Political Judgment.
questions.rule: Know the abbreviation.

questions.q: A researcher wants to test 10-year forecasts. Following Tetlock, what must she accept?
options: That the experts must be named in print
That only laypeople can take part
A long wait before results can be scored
Instant results if the questions are precise
optionExplain: Anonymity was used.
Experts were the subjects.
Right: events set the clock.
Clear questions still need time.
questions.explain: Long horizons need long waits.
questions.rule: Plan for time.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock’s project spanned several wars and presidential elections.
questions.explain: He says six presidential elections and three wars.
questions.rule: Time shows.

questions.q: True or false: The results of Tetlock’s study appeared in 2005.
questions.explain: The panel was in 1984; the results appeared in 2005.
questions.rule: Do not mix dates.

questions.q: What had changed by the time Tetlock wrote up the results?
options: The Cold War was starting to heat up
Gorbachev was taking office as general secretary
The USSR existed only on historical maps
Chernenko was still in power in Moscow
optionExplain: That was the starting situation.
That was 1985.
Right: the world had changed.
He died in 1985.
questions.explain: The question set was rooted in a world that vanished.
questions.rule: Time changes the questions.
questions.teaches: Tetlock says that by the time he wrote up the results Gorbachev was doing commercials for Pizza Hut.

questions.q: In the EPJ results, how accurate was the average expert?
options: About as accurate as a dart-throwing chimpanzee
Perfectly calibrated across all questions
Far more accurate than informed laypeople
Worse than any simple rule by a wide margin
optionExplain: Right: this is the punch line.
Calibration was not perfect on average.
The average did not show a big edge.
The authors do not describe it that way.
questions.explain: The card next gives the result and its limit.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the average expert did about as well as random guessing, but averages can hide differences between groups.

questions.q: The punch line is that the average expert was roughly as accurate as a dart-throwing ____.
questions.explain: The text says a dart-throwing chimpanzee.
questions.rule: Remember the headline.

questions.q: A school’s average student scored exactly the national mean. A teacher says all students must be average. What does the authors’ warning suggest?
options: Averages are not reported in serious statistics
An average is the score of the typical student in the school
The school has no strong students if the mean is average
An average can hide groups that are far above and far below it
optionExplain: Not what the authors say.
The mean need not describe anyone.
Not implied.
Right: averages obscure.
questions.explain: Look under the average.
questions.rule: Averages can obscure.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the chimpanzee result applied equally to every expert in the study.
questions.explain: It was an average; there were two distinguishable groups.
questions.rule: The average hides groups.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say EPJ found that experts had no foresight at all.
questions.explain: They say it found modest but real foresight.
questions.rule: Do not overread the punch line.

questions.q: Which joke do the authors use to show how averages can mislead?
options: A fox and a hedgehog arguing over who knows more about weather
A chimpanzee choosing stocks at random and beating every analyst
Statisticians with feet in an oven and head in a freezer, comfortable on average
A meteorologist in a desert who predicts sunshine every single day of the year
optionExplain: Fox and hedgehog come later.
The chimp is the result, not the joke.
Right: the average hides the extremes.
Not used.
questions.explain: The joke shows an average can describe no one.
questions.rule: Check the spread.
questions.teaches: The joke they tell is the old one about statisticians sleeping with their feet in an oven and their head in a freezer because the average temperature is comfortable.

questions.q: How did the second group of experts fare compared with simple algorithms?
options: They beat them by a wide margin
They only barely beat them
They lost to them badly
They were never compared
optionExplain: The margin was narrow.
Right: they barely beat them.
They beat the chimp, and barely the algorithms.
They were compared.
questions.explain: The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the second group showed real but modest foresight.

questions.q: The first group of experts failed to do better than ____ guessing.
questions.explain: The text says random guessing.
questions.rule: Know group one.

questions.q: A hiring panel’s forecasts beat a coin flip in short-range calls but lose to it in long-range calls. Which group does this resemble?
options: The first group, who lost to the chimp in longer-range forecasts
A group that never forecasts on long horizons
Neither group, since their record is mixed by horizon
The second group, who beat all simple rules by a wide margin
optionExplain: Right: longer-range calls were where the first group lost.
They do forecast.
The first group matches.
The second group only barely beat simple rules.
questions.explain: Long-range forecasting was where group one fell behind.
questions.rule: Check horizons.

questions.q: Sort each description: first group or second group of EPJ experts?

items.t: Failed to beat random guessing
Lost to the chimp on longer-range forecasts
Beat the chimp, not by a wide margin
Had some foresight, however modest
Showed some modest foresight

questions.explain: The first group did no better than chance; the second had modest foresight.
questions.rule: Two groups, two results.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the second group beat simple algorithms by a wide margin.
questions.explain: They only barely beat them.
questions.rule: Modest means small.

questions.q: A forecaster beats the chimp by a small margin. What does the second group’s result suggest about her against a mechanical rule?
options: A mechanical rule cannot be compared with a person in this way, so nothing follows
She will beat it by a wide margin, as the chimp is weak
She will lose to it badly, as the second group did
She may beat it only barely, so she has reason to stay humble
optionExplain: Rules were used as baselines.
A wide margin is not what the group showed.
The group beat the chimp, so not badly.
Right: the second group had modest foresight.
questions.explain: Even good experts had little margin over mechanical rules.
questions.rule: Respect the baseline.
questions.teaches: The authors say the second group only barely beat simple algorithms such as always predict no change or predict the recent rate of change.

questions.q: Which factor does the chapter say separated better from worse forecasters in EPJ?
options: Whether they had PhDs
Whether they were liberal or conservative
How they thought
Whether they had classified information
optionExplain: Credentials did not separate them.
Politics did not separate them.
Right: the style of thinking.
Access did not separate them.
questions.explain: The card next gives the finding.
questions.rule: According to the authors, style of thinking separated forecasters, not credentials or ideology.

questions.q: The critical factor, say the authors, was not what the experts thought but ____ they thought.
questions.explain: The text says how they thought.
questions.rule: Style over content.

questions.q: A company wants to hire the best forecaster. Following EPJ, what should it check first?
options: The candidate’s access to confidential data
How the candidate reasons about problems
The candidate’s degrees
The candidate’s political outlook
optionExplain: Access did not separate groups.
Right: the style of thinking.
Degrees did not separate groups.
Politics did not separate groups.
questions.explain: Style of thinking outperformed credentials.
questions.rule: Check how, not what.

questions.q: True or false: If the authors are right, a PhD-holding expert and a non-PhD expert could land in the same group.
questions.explain: Having a PhD did not decide the group.
questions.rule: Credentials are not sorted by group.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say liberals forecast better than conservatives in EPJ.
questions.explain: Neither political camp was set apart; style of thinking was.
questions.rule: Politics did not decide it.

questions.q: Which pair were united by style despite disagreeing on content, according to the card’s logic?
options: A socialist and a free-market fundamentalist who both squeeze problems into one big idea
A pessimist and a statistician who both study the economy
A liberal and a conservative who both change their minds readily
A socialist and a family doctor who both work in busy public hospitals
optionExplain: Right: opposites in content, alike in style.
Not in the text.
This is a fox pairing, not the hedgehog.
Not a style pairing in the text.
questions.explain: Opposing views can share a way of thinking.
questions.rule: Look past content.
questions.teaches: The authors say that access to classified information did not separate the better group from the worse one.

questions.q: What united the group that organized thinking around Big Ideas?
options: They were all economists working in the same field
How ideological their thinking was, not which ideas they held
They all agreed on which Big Ideas were true
They were all conservatives with broadly the same political outlook on the economy
optionExplain: Their fields varied.
Right: opposed ideas, same style.
They disagreed on the Big Ideas.
They came from several camps.
questions.explain: The card next gives the profile.
questions.rule: According to the authors, hedgehogs pushed one Big Idea to the limit and rarely changed their minds.

questions.q: Hedgehogs were likelier to declare things impossible or ____.
questions.explain: The text says impossible or certain.
questions.rule: Hedgehogs claim certainty.

questions.q: A commentator explains every economic event by a single theory and calls failures temporary. Which EPJ group does this resemble?
options: Neither
Laypeople
Hedgehogs
Foxes
optionExplain: It fits hedgehogs.
Not a lay type.
Right: Big Idea, resistant to revision.
Foxes use many tools.
questions.explain: One Big Idea plus certainty is the hedgehog signature.
questions.rule: Spot the template.

questions.q: Sort each trait: more typical of hedgehogs or of foxes?

items.t: Squeezes problems into one template
Likelier to say impossible or certain
Reluctant to change mind when predictions fail
Uses different tools for different problems
Often says however and on the other hand
Readily admits being wrong

questions.explain: Hedgehogs push one idea; foxes switch tools and revise.
questions.rule: Contrast the two styles.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say hedgehogs shared the same Big Ideas, which is why they were united.
questions.explain: They disagreed on which Big Ideas were true; they were united by how ideological their thinking was.
questions.rule: Style, not content.

questions.q: Which words did hedgehogs use while piling up reasons?
options: However and although
Perhaps and maybe
On the other hand and but
Furthermore and moreover
optionExplain: These are fox words.
Not highlighted.
These are fox words.
Right: these stack reasons for one view.
questions.explain: Hedgehog language adds; fox language contrasts.
questions.rule: Listen for connectors.
questions.teaches: The authors say hedgehogs, committed to their conclusions, would tell Tetlock when their predictions failed: just wait.

questions.q: Which description fits the better forecasters in EPJ?
options: Experts who stuck to one theory and defended it
Pragmatic experts who used many tools and many sources
Experts who avoided all forecasts to protect themselves
Experts with access to secret government data
optionExplain: That is the hedgehog.
Right: many tools, many sources.
They forecast.
Access was not the factor.
questions.explain: The card next gives the profile.
questions.rule: According to the authors, foxes combined many perspectives and revised their views.

questions.q: Foxes talked about possibilities and ____, not certainties.
questions.explain: The text says possibilities and probabilities.
questions.rule: Foxes speak in odds.

questions.q: An analyst picks a different method for each problem and often says however. Which style is this?
options: Layperson
Chimp
Hedgehog
Fox
optionExplain: Not the best label.
The chimp is a baseline.
Hedgehogs use one template.
Right: this is the fox style.
questions.explain: Switching tools by problem is the fox signature.
questions.rule: Spot the switch.

questions.q: Order these statements from most hedgehog-like to most fox-like.
items: It is certain to happen
It is very likely, but there are risks
It could go either way
It might happen, however much depends on other factors
questions.explain: The first is certainty; the later ones increasingly add doubts and caveats.
questions.rule: Count the caveats.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say foxes more readily admitted being wrong and changed their minds.
questions.explain: No one likes to say I was wrong, but foxes more readily did.
questions.rule: Foxes revise.

questions.q: What did foxes do with information, according to the authors?
options: Gathered it from as many sources as they could
Avoided it to prevent bias in their thinking
Ignored data that conflicted with their view
Relied on a single trusted source for it
optionExplain: Right: many sources.
They sought more.
That is the hedgehog.
That is not the fox.
questions.explain: Foxes collected widely before concluding.
questions.rule: Collect from many sources.
questions.teaches: The authors say that, even so, no one likes to say I was wrong, yet foxes more readily admitted it.

questions.q: Whose essay gave Tetlock the fox and hedgehog metaphor?
options: Isaiah Berlin
Sherman Kent
Daniel Kahneman
Glenn Brier
optionExplain: Right: Berlin.
Kent proposed number words.
Kahneman guessed about expertise.
Brier developed the score.
questions.explain: The card next gives the source.
questions.rule: According to Tetlock, the metaphor fits the data, but he claims no preference for either type.

questions.q: The fox knows many things but the hedgehog knows one ____ thing.
questions.explain: The line is the fox knows many things but the hedgehog knows one big thing.
questions.rule: Know the line.

questions.q: A speaker says: fox and hedgehog are labels Tetlock dubbed from the data. What is accurate?
options: He took Berlin’s side in favor of foxes
He found the groups in Berlin’s own data on the styles of great authors
He named the groups with Berlin’s metaphor after seeing the data
He discovered the groups in ancient Greek poems
optionExplain: Berlin favored foxes; Tetlock took no side.
The data were Tetlock’s.
Right: he dubbed the groups.
The poem is the source of the metaphor, not data.
questions.explain: The metaphor was borrowed; the groups came from his data.
questions.rule: Borrowed metaphor, original data.

questions.q: True or false: Berlin favored foxes, but Tetlock felt no need to take sides.
questions.explain: The text says exactly this.
questions.rule: Different stances.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Archilochus favored the fox.
questions.explain: No one will ever know whether Archilochus favored the fox or the hedgehog.
questions.rule: Do not assume the poet’s side.

questions.q: What had Berlin’s essay compared?
options: The accuracy of the astronomers of the ancient world
The economies of ancient Greece and ancient Rome
The styles of thinking of great authors through the ages
The predictions made by oracles of the ancient world
optionExplain: Not in the text.
Not in the text.
Right: styles of great authors.
Not in the text.
questions.explain: Berlin’s essay organized observations with the poetry scrap.
questions.rule: Know the origin.
questions.teaches: The authors say Berlin’s essay was much acclaimed but rarely read.

questions.q: True or false: The foxes’ edge in EPJ came only from staying near 60% and 70% where hedgehogs went to 90% and 100%.
questions.explain: Foxes beat hedgehogs on both calibration and resolution. The card next gives the point.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the fox advantage was real foresight, not mere caution.

questions.q: Foxes beat hedgehogs on both calibration and ____.
questions.explain: The text says calibration and resolution.
questions.rule: Two measures.

questions.q: A forecaster is well calibrated but says 50% on everything. Compared with EPJ foxes, what is missing?
options: Use of probabilities: she should state numbers rather than words
Resolution: bold calls that separate what happens from what does not
Humility: she should admit uncertainty more often than she does
Calibration: her stated chances must match how often events occur
optionExplain: She uses probabilities.
Right: foxes had resolution too.
She is humble.
She is calibrated.
questions.explain: Foxes beat hedgehogs on both measures, not by hedging.
questions.rule: Seek both.

questions.q: If foxes had won only by playing safe, which measure would they have lost on?
options: Resolution
Neither
Both would be equal
Calibration
optionExplain: Right: safe forecasts lack resolution.
They beat on both.
They beat hedgehogs on both measures.
Safe forecasts can be calibrated.
questions.explain: The authors rule out the caution explanation.
questions.rule: Caution is not the explanation.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say foxes had real foresight and hedgehogs did not.
questions.explain: Foxes beat hedgehogs on both calibration and resolution.
questions.rule: Check direction.

questions.q: Which is the authors’ reading of how hedgehogs did against random guessing?
options: Exactly equal to random guessing
Much better than random guessing
Slightly worse than random guessing
Impossible to say from the data
optionExplain: They did slightly worse.
They did not do better.
Right: slightly worse.
The authors state it.
questions.explain: Hedgehog results were a shade below chance.
questions.rule: Know the size.
questions.teaches: The authors say hedgehogs managed to do slightly worse than random guessing.

questions.q: What was Larry Kudlow’s one Big Idea?
options: State control of the economy
Game theory
Environmental limits to growth
Supply-side economics
optionExplain: This is a socialist idea.
Not his.
This is a doomster idea.
Right: supply-side economics.
questions.explain: The card next gives the story.
questions.rule: According to the authors, Kudlow is a prototypical hedgehog.

questions.q: Kudlow called the boom he expected after the tax cuts the Bush ____.
questions.explain: He dubbed it the Bush boom.
questions.rule: Name the boom.

questions.q: A manager insists, as sales fall, that the growth plan is working and nobody has noticed. Which Kudlow behavior does this resemble?
options: Revising the forecast at once when the new data arrived
Insisting a boom was happening though others did not see it
Giving a 50% probability to each of the possible outcomes
Seeking contrary data from people who disagreed with him
optionExplain: Kudlow did not revise.
Right: the biggest story never told.
He did not hedge.
He did not seek contrary data.
questions.explain: He stuck to his guns.
questions.rule: Stay alert to doubling down.

questions.q: Order the Kudlow events from earliest to latest.
items: Calls the Bush boom the biggest story never told
Writes in December 2007 that there is no recession
Writes in April 2008 that Bush may be the top economic forecaster
Lehman Brothers files for bankruptcy
questions.explain: The sequence runs through the years of boom claims, then the recession, then the Lehman collapse.
questions.rule: Follow the timeline.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Kudlow admitted the recession soon after it began.
questions.explain: He kept denying it, calling it a mental recession, until Lehman Brothers failed.
questions.rule: He did not budge.

questions.q: What did the National Bureau of Economic Research later decide about December 2007?
options: It was the start of a boom that Kudlow was the first commentator to see
It was a month in which the economy neither grew nor shrank
It was the end of the Bush boom that Kudlow had predicted
It was the official start of the Great Recession of 2007 to 2009
optionExplain: It was not a boom.
It was a recession start.
Kudlow said it continued.
Right: the recession started then.
questions.explain: The official date contradicted Kudlow’s December 2007 claim.
questions.rule: Check the official record.
questions.teaches: In April 2008 Kudlow wrote that President George W. Bush may turn out to be the top economic forecaster in the country, when the White House also denied a recession.

questions.q: What happened to hedgehogs’ accuracy when they forecast within their own specialty?
options: It matched the foxes
It declined
It stayed the same
It rose sharply
optionExplain: Foxes were better.
Right: accuracy declined.
It did not stay equal.
The authors say the opposite.
questions.explain: The card next gives the metaphor.
questions.rule: According to the authors, one Big Idea can distort what you see and raise confidence without raising accuracy.

questions.q: The authors compare a hedgehog’s Big Idea to ____-tinted glasses.
questions.explain: The text says green-tinted glasses.
questions.rule: Know the image.

questions.q: An investor with one favorite theory reads more reports, and becomes more certain without becoming more accurate. Which part of the metaphor fits?
options: Glasses that change colour each day with the latest news
Glasses that were rarely worn but still gave the investor a perfectly clear view of all facts
More information seen through the same tint raises confidence, not accuracy
Glasses that shrink the world so fewer facts come into view
optionExplain: The tint is constant.
The hedgehog never takes them off.
Right: the same tint colors all the data.
Not part of the metaphor.
questions.explain: Extra data does not fix a distorted lens.
questions.rule: More information does not cure bias.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the glasses can sometimes help by accentuating something real that might be overlooked.
questions.explain: They give the trace of green in a tablecloth as an example.
questions.rule: The lens can sometimes help.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say hedgehogs became more accurate as they gathered more information.
questions.explain: They say it increased confidence but not accuracy.
questions.rule: Info does not fix a lens.

questions.q: According to the authors, why was the Emerald City not even emerald in the fable?
options: It was built of green stone quarried near the city gates
It was painted green each year to welcome the visitors
People thought so only because they wore green-tinted glasses
It glowed in the dark when the Wizard turned on the lights
optionExplain: Not so in the fable.
Not so.
Right: the glasses supplied the color.
Not so.
questions.explain: The color was in the glasses, not the city.
questions.rule: The lens supplies the color.
questions.teaches: The authors say that in the fable the Emerald City was not emerald; people thought it was because they were forced to wear green-tinted glasses.

questions.q: What did EPJ find about fame and accuracy?
options: More famous experts were less accurate
Fame doubled accuracy
Fame and accuracy were unrelated
More famous experts were more accurate
optionExplain: Right: an inverse correlation.
No such claim.
They were related.
The reverse.
questions.explain: The card next gives the reason.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the audience rewards the same confidence and simplicity that hurts accuracy.

questions.q: The authors say media go looking for ____, who happen to be bad forecasters.
questions.explain: The text says hedgehogs.
questions.rule: Media prefer hedgehogs.

questions.q: A TV producer picks a guest who gives a simple, confident story. Following the authors, what is the risk?
options: The guest will give probabilities that confuse viewers
The guest will be too humble to hold an audience
The guest will list many caveats and lose the thread
The guest may be a hedgehog with poor foresight
optionExplain: Hedgehogs rarely do.
Hedgehogs are not humble.
Hedgehogs rarely do.
Right: the confidence appeals but may hide poor accuracy.
questions.explain: Simple and confident sells, but does not predict.
questions.rule: Beware polish.

questions.q: True or false: If audiences prefer simplicity and confidence, the authors would expect foxes to be less welcome on television.
questions.explain: They say the aggregation of many perspectives is bad TV.
questions.rule: Media rewards the wrong trait.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say editors deliberately look for bad forecasters.
questions.explain: They look for hedgehogs, who just happen to be bad forecasters.
questions.rule: Selection by style, not by badness.

questions.q: According to the authors, why does a hedgehog’s confidence calm audiences?
options: Audiences check the hedgehog’s record before trusting him
Hedgehogs give longer answers that fill more airtime
Hedgehogs explain probabilities in a way viewers understand
People find uncertainty disturbing and maybe underscores it
optionExplain: Audiences seldom check.
Length is not the reason.
Hedgehogs do not.
Right: certainty soothes.
questions.explain: Certainty soothes; doubt disturbs.
questions.rule: Comfort is not accuracy.
questions.teaches: The authors say the first rule of media training is keep it simple, stupid.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say foxes’ complex, qualified stories make them popular on television.
questions.explain: Their complexity is bad TV. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, what suits the camera does not suit forecasting, and vice versa.

questions.q: The authors say aggregating many perspectives is bad ____ but good forecasting.
questions.explain: The text says bad TV.
questions.rule: Know the trade-off.

questions.q: A fox-style analyst says: it could go either way, however, there are risks, but also upsides. Why is this a poor guest?
options: Her style is hedgehog, so audiences distrust its single theory
Her facts are probably wrong, since fox analysts hedge so much on every question
Her answer is complex and uncertain, which audiences find unsatisfying
Her answer is too confident, which audiences dislike on TV
optionExplain: This is a fox style.
Nothing says her facts are wrong.
Right: bad TV, good forecasting.
She is not confident.
questions.explain: Complexity does not sell.
questions.rule: What sells differs from what predicts.

questions.q: If a broadcaster wants the most accurate guests, what should it expect to give up?
options: Some simplicity and confidence in what the guests say
Number of guests, since fewer people can be booked each week
Variety of topics, since only a few subjects suit cautious guests
Some accuracy, since sounding uncertain lowers forecasting quality
optionExplain: Right: foxes sound less certain.
Not implied.
Not implied.
Accuracy is the gain.
questions.explain: Accuracy and polish pull apart.
questions.rule: There is a price.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a forecaster who sounds sure at every turn is the best sort.
questions.explain: They say confidence and simplicity impair foresight, though they calm nerves.
questions.rule: Sounding sure is not accuracy.

questions.q: Which advice follows from the authors’ view for a reader of pundits?
options: Trust a pundit’s accuracy record over how confident the story sounds
Prefer the speaker who avoids caveats and sounds decisive on air
Prefer the simplest explanation on offer, as it is likely best
Prefer the most famous speaker, since fame signals real insight
optionExplain: Right: track record, not confidence.
Caveats are a fox trait.
Simplicity is the hedgehog trap.
Fame correlates negatively.
questions.explain: A record on scored forecasts beats polish.
questions.rule: Check the record.
questions.teaches: The authors say foxes are likelier to settle on shades of maybe, and their stories are full of howevers and on-the-other-hands.

questions.q: At Galton’s fair, how close was the crowd’s average guess to the ox’s true weight?
options: One pound short
About a hundred pounds over
About fifty pounds short
It was exactly right
optionExplain: Right: 1,197 against 1,198.
Much too far.
Much too far.
It was one pound off.
questions.explain: The card next gives the story.
questions.rule: According to the authors, aggregating many judgments beats the average member, but consistently beating the average takes rare skill.

questions.q: The popular book that named the phenomenon is The ____ of Crowds.
questions.explain: The book is The Wisdom of Crowds by James Surowiecki.
questions.rule: Name the book.

questions.q: A class guesses the beans in a jar. The average is very close, though one student was closer. What do the authors say about her?
options: The average cannot be accurate if even one guess in the class turns out to be better
The student is more skilled than the crowd as a whole
The crowd must have copied the student’s answer
The student’s hit says more about luck than skill, unless repeated
optionExplain: The average can be accurate while an individual is closer.
Repeating the exercise would show whether it is skill.
Copying is not discussed.
Right: one bull’s-eye may be luck.
questions.explain: Check whether the same individuals win again.
questions.rule: Repeat to separate luck from skill.

questions.q: The exercise is repeated many times. If one person keeps beating the group each time, what does that suggest?
options: That luck is the only explanation for such repeated wins
That the group is bad at guessing and should be replaced
That the person may have skill, since luck would not repeat
That the average of the guesses is useless as a benchmark
optionExplain: Luck does not repeat.
The group may still be accurate.
Right: consistent winning takes rare skill.
The average is still a strong benchmark.
questions.explain: Consistency distinguishes skill from luck.
questions.rule: Repeat the test.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the collective judgment is more accurate than every individual in the group.
questions.explain: They say there are likely individuals who beat the group.
questions.rule: The average can lose to some individuals.

questions.q: Why might different individuals beat the group each time the exercise is repeated?
options: The group changes its collective mind in each new round of guessing
Single bull’s-eyes are largely luck, which changes from round to round
The ox gains or loses weight between the rounds of guessing
The guessers learn from each other and copy the previous winner
optionExplain: The group guess is an average, not a mind.
Right: luck does not repeat.
The ox is the same each time in the story.
Not described.
questions.explain: Different winners each time is what luck predicts.
questions.rule: Luck rotates; skill repeats.
questions.teaches: The authors say beating the average consistently requires rare skill.

questions.q: According to the authors, what happens to the errors in a crowd’s guesses?
options: They point in different directions and cancel out
They disappear because the guessers share facts
They are corrected by the butcher who knows the ox
They add up to a larger error as guesses pile up
optionExplain: Right: errors cancel.
Not described.
Not described.
Valid information adds; errors cancel.
questions.explain: The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, aggregation works because true signals add up and random errors cancel.

questions.q: Some reverently call aggregation the ____ of aggregation.
questions.explain: The text says the miracle of aggregation.
questions.rule: Know the phrase.

questions.q: A panel of ten doctors each notes a different clue about a patient. Why might their combined judgment beat any one doctor?
options: They discuss until they agree, which removes their differences
They all use the same method, so their errors are the same
They share the same mistakes, so the errors reinforce each other
Each holds a different scrap of valid information, which adds up
optionExplain: Agreement is not what the card describes.
Same method would give correlated errors.
Shared mistakes would not cancel.
Right: dispersed information combines.
questions.explain: Dispersed clues pool into a bigger set.
questions.rule: Collect different scraps.

questions.q: True or false: In the ox story, valid information pointed toward 1,198 pounds, while errors pointed in various directions.
questions.explain: That is why the errors canceled.
questions.rule: Signals align; errors scatter.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the crowd was accurate because everyone had the same accurate information.
questions.explain: Information was dispersed: each person held a scrap.
questions.rule: Pooling, not sameness.

questions.q: Suppose all guessers read the same wrong tip and guessed too high. What would the card’s logic predict?
options: The errors would still cancel out as in the ox story
The crowd would still be accurate to within a pound
The errors would point the same way and would not cancel
The butcher would correct them with his experience
optionExplain: They share a direction.
Accuracy would suffer.
Right: cancellation needs different directions.
No fix is described.
questions.explain: Cancellation needs independent errors.
questions.rule: Shared errors do not cancel.
questions.teaches: The authors say that when the butcher looked at the ox he contributed the information he had from years of training and experience.

questions.q: According to the authors, what does aggregating the judgments of many people who know nothing produce?
options: A perfect answer
A lot of nothing
A surprisingly good answer
A moderately good answer
optionExplain: Not described.
Right: a lot of nothing.
Not if nobody knows anything.
Not described.
questions.explain: The card next gives the ranking.
questions.rule: According to the authors, aggregate diverse, informed sources, and you can aggregate aggregations.

questions.q: Combining surveys, the authors call this a poll of ____.
questions.explain: The text says a poll of polls.
questions.rule: Name it.

questions.q: Which crowd should give the best aggregate estimate of next year’s rainfall?
options: A thousand people who each know different things about climate and weather
Ten people who all share the same sources and the same views
A hundred people who all repeat the same expert’s forecast word for word each time
A thousand people who know nothing at all about the weather
optionExplain: Right: informed and diverse.
Few and alike.
Alike repeats the same information.
Nothing in, nothing out.
questions.explain: Aggregation rewards diverse, informed inputs.
questions.rule: Diversity plus knowledge.

questions.q: Order these crowds by expected usefulness of their combined judgment, least to most.
items: People who know nothing
People who know a little
People who know lots about the same thing
People who know lots about many different things
questions.explain: Knowing nothing gives nothing; more diverse knowledge gives a bigger pool.
questions.rule: Diverse and informed wins.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say PollyVote relies on polls alone.
questions.explain: It aggregates polls, a panel of political experts and quantitative models.
questions.rule: Many sources.

questions.q: Why does PollyVote often stick with the eventual winner when polls turn and experts change their minds?
options: It relies on one well-tested model that is rarely revised
It pools several different sources, so no single swing dominates
It ignores polls and follows only the quantitative models
It uses only expert opinion, which stays steady over time
optionExplain: It uses several models.
Right: diverse sources steady it.
It uses polls too.
It uses more than experts.
questions.explain: A mix of sources damps swings in one.
questions.rule: Mix sources.
questions.teaches: The authors say PollyVote has been in operation since the 1990s and has a strong record.

questions.q: What do the authors say is the main difference between a fox and Galton’s crowd?
options: The fox ignores outside information
The crowd is less accurate
The aggregation occurs within one skull
The fox uses numbers while the crowd does not
optionExplain: Foxes seek many sources.
Not claimed.
Right: same process, one mind.
Not the difference.
questions.explain: The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a fox is a crowd of perspectives in one mind.

questions.q: A fox, like the crowd, does what the authors call ____: combining many perspectives.
questions.explain: The text says they aggregate.
questions.rule: Name the process.

questions.q: An analyst forecasts sales by combining a statistical model, interviews with customers and a rival’s data into one number. What is she doing?
options: Following a single Big Idea, as a hedgehog does
Averaging several identical sources of data
Ignoring evidence that does not fit her view
Aggregating perspectives, as a fox does
optionExplain: That is the hedgehog.
The sources differ.
She uses evidence.
Right: many tools, one conclusion.
questions.explain: Many inputs, one synthesis.
questions.rule: Synthesize many views.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a fox is a crowd of perspectives in one mind.
questions.explain: That is the point of the parallel with Galton’s crowd.
questions.rule: Same process, different location.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say aggregating inside your own head is easy.
questions.explain: They call it challenging, and later say aggregation does not come to us naturally.
questions.rule: Inner aggregation takes effort.

questions.q: Which of the following does a fox do that a hedgehog does not?
options: Applies one favorite theory to every case that comes up
Seeks information from many sources and integrates the perspectives
Repeats the same argument using moreover and furthermore as often as possible
Declares outcomes certain or impossible with great conviction
optionExplain: That is a hedgehog.
Right: many sources, integrated.
That is a hedgehog.
That is a hedgehog.
questions.explain: Integration across sources is the fox skill.
questions.rule: Integrate.
questions.teaches: The authors say that doing this sort of inside-your-head aggregation can be challenging.

questions.q: In the 1997 Financial Times game, what was the winning guess?
optionExplain: 33 is the first step.
22 is a step of the logic.
0 is the Nash equilibrium but did not win.
Right: 13, close to two-thirds of 18.91.
questions.explain: The card next gives the contest.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the winning answer reflects how real people think, not what perfect logic says.

questions.q: In the guess-the-number game, the winner is closest to ____ of the average guess.
questions.explain: The rule is two-thirds of the average.
questions.rule: Know the rule.

questions.q: If everyone guessed 50 at random, the average would be 50. What would a contestant who guessed two-thirds of that choose?
optionExplain: Right: two-thirds of 50 is about 33.
Not two-thirds.
That is the average.
Not two-thirds.
questions.explain: This is the first step in the chain.
questions.rule: Work out step one.

questions.q: Order the guesses as the logic chain runs.
questions.explain: Each step takes two-thirds of the one before, ending at 0.
questions.rule: Follow the chain.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say 0 was the winning guess because it is the logical answer.
questions.explain: The winning guess was 13; many reached 0 but the average guess was 18.91.
questions.rule: Logic did not win.

questions.q: Why did reaching 0 fail to win?
options: Many contestants stopped at 33 or 22, so the average stayed well above 0
Zero is not between 0 and 100, so it was outside the range
The contest forbade a guess of 0, so the logical answer was disqualified
Logic is unreliable in games, so nobody should use it here
optionExplain: Right: other contestants did not follow the logic all the way.
0 was within the range.
0 was allowed.
The logic was sound.
questions.explain: The winner had to account for how others actually think.
questions.rule: Model the other players.
questions.teaches: The authors say that 33 and 22 were popular answers in the contest.

questions.q: Sort each: a step of the logic chain, or the real result?

items.t: Average 50, so guess 33
Average 33, so guess 22
Average 22, so guess about 15
Average guess was 18.91
Winning guess was 13
Many people stopped at 33 or 22

questions.explain: The first three follow the reasoning; the last three are what happened.
questions.rule: Separate theory from outcome.

questions.q: According to Tetlock, why was his answer of 0 wrong?
options: He misread the rules about two-thirds of the average
He guessed at random instead of reasoning it through
He looked at the problem from only one perspective, logic
His logic had a flaw in one of the steps of the chain
optionExplain: He read the rules correctly.
He did not guess.
Right: logic alone.
The logic was sound.
questions.explain: The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to Tetlock, combine the rational view and the human view, and add a third that anticipates both.

questions.q: In the Star Trek analogy, the synthesizing perspective is that of Captain ____.
questions.explain: Kirk considers both Spock and McCoy.
questions.rule: Name the synthesizer.

questions.q: Match each Star Trek character to the guess or approach.
questions.explain: Spock is the Vulcan, McCoy the human, Kirk the synthesis.
questions.rule: Three perspectives.

questions.q: If many more contestants think like Captain Kirk, what happens to the math?
options: The answer jumps to 100, because they push the average up
Nothing can change, because the math is fixed by the rules
Their sophisticated thinking can shift the answer a little
The answer jumps to 0, because everyone then reasons alike
optionExplain: Not stated.
A few Kirks change little, many change more.
Right: more Kirks make a difference.
Not stated.
questions.explain: The number of sophisticated thinkers matters.
questions.rule: Count the other thinkers.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says his logic was flawed, which is why he lost.
questions.explain: He says his logic was sound; he looked at one perspective.
questions.rule: One lens, not wrong logic.

questions.q: Which approach does Tetlock say would have improved his answer?
options: Ignoring the other contestants and trusting his own logic even more than before
Merging logic and psycho-logic, and perhaps a third view that combined them
Guessing the same number as most other readers of the newspaper
Choosing whichever answer lies farthest from the logical answer of 0
optionExplain: Ignoring others misses the point.
Right: merge perspectives.
Copying is not the method.
Not what he says.
questions.explain: More perspectives give a better estimate.
questions.rule: Merge perspectives.
questions.teaches: Tetlock says such fine distinctions, such as whether to guess 10, 11 or 12, can be the difference between good and great, as the book shows later with superforecasters.

questions.q: What does the dragonfly eye represent in the authors’ argument?
options: Combining many perspectives into one clear judgment
Ignoring information that conflicts with a favored theory
Looking only at the far future and ignoring the near term
Focusing on one detail until it is fully understood
optionExplain: Right: many lenses, one picture.
Not the point.
Not the point.
That is the opposite.
questions.explain: The card next gives the metaphor.
questions.rule: According to the authors, there is no theoretical limit to the number of perspectives you can merge.

questions.q: A single dragonfly eye can have as many as thirty ____ lenses.
questions.explain: The text says thirty thousand.
questions.rule: Know the scale.

questions.q: A team forecasts a product launch by asking marketing, finance, engineering, customers and rivals, then combining their views. Which metaphor fits?
options: Dart-throwing chimp
Green-tinted glasses
Dragonfly eye
Hall of shame
optionExplain: That is the average result.
That is the hedgehog.
Right: many perspectives synthesized.
That is a list of bad forecasts.
questions.explain: Many lenses, one view.
questions.rule: Use many lenses.

questions.q: Sort each: dragonfly eye or green-tinted glasses?

items.t: Many perspectives combined
Information from thousands of lenses synthesized
Sees nearly all directions at once
One Big Idea colors everything
Extra information seen through the same tint
Never taken off

questions.explain: Dragonfly vision merges many views; the glasses impose one.
questions.rule: Compare the metaphors.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say there are theoretical limits of two or three on how many perspectives you can merge.
questions.explain: In theory there is no limit, though three or four is practical in the game.
questions.rule: No limit in theory.

questions.q: The authors admit a flaw in their metaphor. What is it?
options: Dragonflies cannot see forward, only to the sides and back
Foxes have eyes too small to be compared with insects
Dragonflies have only one lens, unlike a fox’s two eyes
A fox with dragonfly eyes is an ugly mixed metaphor
optionExplain: They see almost every direction.
Not the point.
Dragonflies have thousands.
Right: they call it ugly.
questions.explain: They note the mix but keep it for its meaning.
questions.rule: Know the caveat.
questions.teaches: The authors say a fourth, fifth and sixth perspective can further sharpen a judgment in other contexts.

questions.q: According to the authors, what does the dragonfly’s synthesized vision let it do?
options: Detect the body heat of its prey in total darkness, as night hunters do
Pick off flying insects at high speed, with clarity and precision
See sharply in a single direction while the rest of its view stays blurred
Hear the wingbeats of insects from far across a field and hunt by sound
optionExplain: Heat sensing is not mentioned; the passage is about vision.
Right: the authors say the vision is superb enough to pick off flying insects at high speed.
The authors say it sees in almost every direction at once, so no direction is blurred.
Hearing is not mentioned; the passage is about vision.
questions.explain: The authors say information from thousands of lenses is synthesized into vision clear and precise enough to pick off flying insects at high speed.
questions.rule: Diverse inputs add.
questions.teaches: The authors say the dragonfly’s vision is clear and precise enough for it to pick off flying insects at high speed.

questions.q: In Annie Duke’s poker seminars, what did students assume when an opponent raised?
options: That the opponent was weak
That the opponent would fold
That the opponent was bluffing
That the opponent had a strong hand
optionExplain: Not what they said.
Not what they said.
Not what they said.
Right: universally they said strong hand.
questions.explain: The card next gives the story.
questions.rule: According to the authors, taking another view is a struggle, but foxes are more likely to do the hard work.

questions.q: The default view that insists it sees reality objectively is the tip-of-your-____ perspective.
questions.explain: The text says tip-of-your-nose.
questions.rule: Name the default.

questions.q: A manager sees a rival cut prices and assumes it is desperate, though she would cut prices to win share. What is she missing?
options: Faster reports on competitor prices
Seeing the situation from the rival’s side
A bigger forecasting model of the market
More data on her own costs and prices
optionExplain: Speed is not the issue.
Right: she did not take the rival’s perspective.
Models are not the issue.
Her data is not the issue.
questions.explain: Duke’s students did the same with raises.
questions.rule: Ask what you would do in their seat.

questions.q: True or false: Duke’s students were holiday beginners trying poker for the first time.
questions.explain: They were serious players paying a thousand dollars for a seminar.
questions.rule: Experience did not prevent the error.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the difficulty of seeing other views is a quirk of poker players only.
questions.explain: They say it is not a quirk of poker players.
questions.rule: The difficulty is general.

questions.q: According to Duke, why would a student with a very strong hand call rather than raise?
options: Strong hands should be played quietly to avoid any risk of loss
Calling wins more often than raising, whatever the cards are
A raise might scare the opponent into folding, shrinking the pot
Raising is against the rules of poker in the early rounds
optionExplain: No such rule.
No such claim.
Right: they want to expand the pot.
Raising is allowed.
questions.explain: The same behavior, seen from their own seat, reverses the inference.
questions.rule: Reverse the roles.
questions.teaches: Duke says her students would never raise with really great hands, because they do not want to chase her away and want to expand the pot as much as possible.

questions.q: How does Tetlock describe the fox and hedgehog model?
options: A strict split of every person into two types
A discarded model
A spectrum, not a strict two-type split
A purely historical metaphor
optionExplain: He says it is not a dichotomy.
He keeps it.
Right: a spectrum.
He uses it for data.
questions.explain: The card next gives the nuance.
questions.rule: According to Tetlock, treat the model as a useful simplification, and aim to shift your own gears.

questions.q: Tetlock calls foxes who sit closer to the hedgehog end ____-hedgehogs.
questions.explain: The text says fox-hedgehogs.
questions.rule: Name the hybrid.

questions.q: An analyst is methodical at work but impulsive when shopping. What does Tetlock’s spectrum idea say?
options: People can think differently in different circumstances
Thinking style is fixed by temperament from birth
Thinking style cannot change once it is set in adulthood
She must be a hedgehog at work and a fox at home
optionExplain: Right: style varies by setting.
Not claimed.
Habits can change.
The model does not assign fixed types.
questions.explain: Style depends on circumstances.
questions.rule: Style varies.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says thinking habits are immutable.
questions.explain: He says they are not immutable and can change with effort.
questions.rule: Habits can shift.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock claims the fox and hedgehog model captures the full richness of human nature.
questions.explain: He says no model does, but this one is a useful starting point.
questions.rule: Models simplify.

questions.q: Which summary of EPJ do the authors give at the end of the chapter?
options: Foresight depended mainly on political outlook, liberal or conservative, optimist or pessimist
No expert had any foresight, so the study found nothing to explain
Foresight depended mainly on degrees and years of experience
Modest but real foresight existed; the critical ingredient was style of thinking
optionExplain: Politics did not decide.
Real but modest foresight existed.
Degrees did not decide.
Right: style of thinking.
questions.explain: The chapter ends on style of thinking.
questions.rule: Style matters.
questions.teaches: Tetlock says that after EPJ the next step was figuring out how to advance the insight about style of thinking.

questions.q: True or false: In October 2002 the intelligence community's consensus supported the administration's key claims about Iraqi weapons of mass destruction.
questions.explain: The estimate backed the claims, and many people found that persuasive. The card next shows how the estimate was built.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the 2002 estimate was the shared judgment of sixteen agencies, and that scale led many to treat its claims as settled fact.

questions.q: The CIA, NSA, DIA and thirteen other agencies are together called the intelligence ____, or IC.
questions.explain: The sixteen agencies are known collectively as the intelligence community.
questions.rule: IC means the sixteen agencies together.

questions.q: A city report is signed by sixteen departments backed by a large budget. What does the 2002 case suggest about trusting it?
options: Its scale shows it was bent by politics, because large groups follow whoever leads them
Its scale guarantees accuracy, because so many experts would catch any error between them
Its scale is irrelevant, so it should be set aside whatever its content says
Scale makes it persuasive, but agreement alone does not show it is correct
optionExplain: The authors report that investigations rejected the claim that the IC caved to pressure.
This is the pull of authority; the 2002 estimate had that scale and was still false.
Scale is a reason people find a report persuasive, so it cannot be waved away.
The case shows a huge, expert, agreed estimate that was wrong.
questions.explain: The IC was large, expert and in agreement, and many people took its judgment as fact. It was wrong, so agreement is not proof.
questions.rule: Persuasive is not the same as correct.

questions.q: Match each term to what the chapter says it means.
pairs: The consensus view of the agencies
Someone who judges what collected information implies
questions.explain: An NIE is the consensus view; the IC is the sixteen agencies together; analysts are the staff who interpret what is collected.
questions.rule: Keep apart the product, the community and the people.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the IC's analysts make sense of collected information and judge what it implies for national security.
questions.explain: The authors say the analysts' job is not to collect information but to make sense of it and judge its implications.
questions.rule: Analysts interpret; they do not mainly collect.

questions.q: A hospital's independent safety board, not its manager, reports that a drug is unsafe. Why might many treat the report as settling the facts?
options: A board's report always proves the drug is unsafe, whatever evidence the board used or ignored
The manager would have had no reason to read the report, so only the board's view counts
People assume large bodies are always more cautious than managers, so they discount optimism
People expect such a body to speak truth to power, so its finding reads as fact
optionExplain: A report from an independent body is trusted, but the 2002 case shows it can be wrong.
Readers settle on the board because of its independence, not because the manager is ignored.
The chapter makes no claim that large bodies are more cautious.
The authors say this is why the NIE settled the matter for many.
questions.explain: Per the authors, the job of intelligence is to speak truth to power, not to tell leaders what they want to hear. For those who saw the NIE that way, it settled the facts.
questions.rule: Independence makes a finding persuasive; it does not make it right.
questions.teaches: The authors say intelligence is meant to speak truth to power, which is why many saw the NIE as settling the facts; what to do about them was a separate question.

questions.q: What did the United States find when it searched Iraq for weapons of mass destruction after invading in 2003?
options: Small stockpiles of chemical weapons only
Missiles with ranges above the UN limit
Biological weapons but no nuclear program
Nothing
optionExplain: The authors say nothing like this was found.
The estimate claimed these; no such finding is reported.
No weapons of any kind were found.
The search found no WMDs.
questions.explain: Nothing was found, even though the estimate had been sure. The card next sets out the fallout.
questions.rule: According to the authors, no WMDs were found, so the 2002 estimate's key claims were false and the IC suffered a major failure.

questions.q: After the 2003 invasion, the search of Iraq for weapons of mass destruction found ____.
questions.explain: The United States turned Iraq upside down and found no WMDs.
questions.rule: The search found nothing.

questions.q: A friend says everyone, even harsh critics of the White House, believed Iraq had WMDs, so it must have been true. What answers this?
options: Critics are always less reliable than officials, so their agreement counts for little
Only intelligence staff can judge such claims, so what critics believed is beside the point
The belief was true until 2003, and the weapons were destroyed after the invasion began
Widespread belief proved false once the search found nothing, so agreement is not proof
optionExplain: The authors treat the critics' belief as notable, not as unreliable.
The point is that belief was near universal and still wrong.
The authors say the claims were false, not that they stopped being true.
Even critics like Tom Friedman believed it, and it was still false.
questions.explain: The search found nothing, though belief was widespread. Agreement is not evidence of truth by itself.
questions.rule: According to the authors, no WMDs were found, so the 2002 estimate's key claims were false and the IC suffered a major failure.

questions.q: Sort each item: was it in place before the 2003 invasion, or learned after it?

items.t: The NIE released in October 2002
The 9/11 attacks thirteen months earlier
Critics such as Tom Friedman suspecting Saddam was hiding something
A search of Iraq that found no WMDs
Congressional hearings with sweating intelligence officials
The description of it as arguably the worst intelligence failure in modern history

questions.explain: The estimate, the 9/11 attacks and the critics' belief came before the invasion; the empty search, the hearings and the label 'worst failure' came after.
questions.rule: Separate what people believed from what the search revealed.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the 2003 search found no WMDs, so the key claims of the 2002 estimate were false.
questions.explain: The search found nothing, and the authors call the claims false facts.
questions.rule: Nothing was found.

questions.q: A national agency's flagship forecast fails in public. According to the Iraq episode, what followed for the IC?
options: A pause in its work while the White House took over all analysis for a year
An immediate rise in its budget, as officials argued more money would prevent a repeat
A quiet internal review that the public never heard about, as with earlier failures
Media condemnation, official investigations and congressional hearings
optionExplain: No such takeover is described.
The chapter reports condemnation, not a reward.
This was a very public failure with hearings.
The authors list these as the reaction to the failure.
questions.explain: The IC was humiliated: media condemnation, official investigations, and hearings in which committees tore into officials.
questions.rule: A public failure brings public accountability.
questions.teaches: The failure brought media condemnation, official investigations and hearings in which congressional committees took turns tearing into intelligence officials.

questions.q: What did Robert Jervis conclude about the IC's WMD judgment?
options: It was reasonable and, in substance, correct on the weapons
It was insincere and bent by White House pressure
It was wrong, so it must have been unreasonable too
It was sincere and reasonable, though wrong
optionExplain: No weapons were found.
The authors report that Jervis and the official inquiries rejected politicization.
The authors insist that wrong and unreasonable are different.
This is Jervis's verdict, as the authors report it.
questions.explain: Jervis judged the conclusion sincere and reasonable but wrong. The card next explains how that can be.
questions.rule: According to the authors, ask whether a judgment was reasonable given what was known at the time, because asking only whether it was correct is easy and misleading.

questions.q: The authors say the key test of a judgment is whether it was ____ given what was known at the time.
questions.explain: Reasonableness is judged by the information available at the time.
questions.rule: Judge reasonableness at the time.

questions.q: A manager reviews a hire made on a thin but sensible CV who later quit. Which question fits the authors' view?
options: Since the hire quit, was the decision a mistake in hindsight?
How many people who share this CV have quit, and was it more than half?
