Who would have blamed the manager if the hire had worked out well?
Given what was known at hiring, was the decision a sensible one?
optionExplain: This replaces the tough question with the easy one.
Sensible odds matter, but this ignores the evidence available then.
Blame is not the same as the quality of the call.
It asks for a time-of-decision judgment.
questions.explain: Putting yourself in the position of the decider, with only the then-available information, is the reasonable-judgment test.
questions.rule: According to the authors, ask whether a judgment was reasonable given what was known at the time, because asking only whether it was correct is easy and misleading.

questions.q: Suppose Saddam had cooperated openly with UN inspectors. By the authors' reasoning, how would that change what agencies suspected?
options: Suspicion would be unchanged, since agencies had already seen the weapons directly
Agencies would have ignored it, since they relied on White House briefings alone
Suspicion would rise, because open cooperation is the usual way to hide a program
Suspicion would likely have eased, since it came from his hide-and-seek behavior
optionExplain: The authors say agencies had not glimpsed what he was hiding.
The authors say politicization was rejected as the explanation.
The text says the hiding behavior drove the suspicion.
Their suspicion came from his behavior, not from sight of the weapons.
questions.explain: The text says agencies suspected Saddam not because they had glimpsed the weapons but because he acted like someone hiding something. This is our reading of a changed condition.
questions.rule: According to the authors, ask whether a judgment was reasonable given what was known at the time, because asking only whether it was correct is easy and misleading.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that because Iraq had no WMDs, the IC's conclusion must have been unreasonable.
questions.explain: They say the conclusion was reasonable and wrong. Judging by outcome swaps the hard question for the easy one.
questions.rule: Wrong does not mean unreasonable.

questions.q: A court judges a doctor's decision years later with full records. Why is that harder than it looks, per the authors?
options: The records are always incomplete, so no sound judgment of the doctor is possible
Courts favor doctors, so they accept any decision that was made sincerely
Mental time travel is hard: hindsight sways our view of what was reasonable
The outcome is irrelevant, so the court should ignore what happened to the patient
optionExplain: The difficulty is bias from hindsight, not missing records.
The authors say sincerity and reasonableness are separate points.
The authors call it a struggle even for historians.
The outcome is not ignored; it just does not settle whether the call was good.
questions.explain: The authors say few things are harder than mental time travel: not being swayed by what you know happened later. Our reading applies this to a new field.
questions.teaches: The authors say that even historians struggle to put themselves in the position of someone at the time, without being swayed by their knowledge of what happened later.
questions.rule: According to the authors, ask whether a judgment was reasonable given what was known at the time, because asking only whether it was correct is easy and misleading.

questions.q: True or false: A poker player who makes a sound bet and loses has made a mistake.
questions.explain: A bet can be sound and still lose, because luck plays a part. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, judge a decision by the reasoning and odds behind it, not by whether luck gave a good result.

questions.q: Swapping the hard question for an easy one and believing you answered the hard one is called a bait and ____.
questions.explain: The authors use this phrase from chapter 2 for substituting a tough question with an easy one.
questions.rule: Bait and switch.

questions.q: A firm launched a product on weak market research, and it succeeded. According to the authors, what should the board conclude?
options: The research must have been strong, since good results come from good judgment
The research should be copied, since its results are now proven
A win does not make weak research wise; judge the decision by its reasoning
The research is irrelevant, since the market decided the matter in the end
optionExplain: This is the outcome-based swap the authors warn about.
Copying a lucky result draws a false lesson from experience.
A lucky win does not make a foolish bet wise.
The research is exactly what the decision should be judged on.
questions.explain: Like the novice poker player who bets big and gets lucky, the firm's win does not retroactively make the decision wise.
questions.rule: According to the authors, judge a decision by the reasoning and odds behind it, not by whether luck gave a good result.

questions.q: If a fund manager judges every trader only by last quarter's profit, what do the authors predict about the manager's judgment over time?
options: It will improve, as the profit numbers give a steady stream of clear feedback
It will stay the same, since luck evens out within a single quarter
It will worsen, as lucky wins and unlucky losses teach false lessons
It will improve only for the traders who lost money, who will learn most
optionExplain: The authors say outcome-based learning makes judgment worse.
A quarter is too short to remove luck.
Judging by outcomes teaches false lessons.
Both lucky wins and unlucky losses mislead.
questions.explain: Without separating the quality of the decision from luck, they will draw false lessons from experience, making their judgment worse over time.
questions.rule: According to the authors, judge a decision by the reasoning and odds behind it, not by whether luck gave a good result.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a pro who bets big on a likely win and loses has not necessarily made an unwise bet.
questions.explain: She correctly saw a high chance of winning; losing does not make the bet unwise.
questions.rule: A good bet can lose.

questions.q: A candidate wins an election after a campaign built on a gamble. Which view fits the authors' account of good decisions?
options: The gamble cannot be judged, since each election is unique and has no odds
The win proves the gamble was wise, because elections are the final test of strategy
The gamble was wise only if the candidate had been certain it would work
The win alone does not show the gamble was wise; judge the odds beforehand
optionExplain: The authors treat decisions as judgeable by the odds known then.
The authors warn against this swap.
Certainty is not the test; the odds at the time are.
This applies the novice-poker lesson to politics.
questions.explain: A decision is judged by the odds and reasoning at the time, not by the result. The authors call this mental time travel and say it is hard even for historians. Our reading extends the poker example to a new field.
questions.teaches: Judging a call fairly means putting yourself in the position of those at the time, which the authors say is a struggle even for historians.
questions.rule: According to the authors, judge a decision by the reasoning and odds behind it, not by whether luck gave a good result.

questions.q: Per Jervis, what would better analysis by the IC have changed?
options: It would have shown that Iraq had no WMD programs at all
It would have made the assessments more certain and so more useful
It would have made the assessments less certain
It would have changed nothing, because the errors were not correctable
optionExplain: Jervis said it would not have produced a fundamentally different conclusion.
The opposite is true: more care meant less certainty.
Jervis said confidence would fall rather than the conclusion reversing.
He said the errors were correctable.
questions.explain: Better analysis would have lowered confidence. The card next shows why that matters.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a less confident conclusion can matter greatly even if the conclusion itself stays the same.

questions.q: Jervis wrote that the IC's analysis could and should have been ____.
questions.explain: He held the IC to account for correctable errors even while calling its judgment reasonable.
questions.rule: Reasonable and correctable.

questions.q: A jury convicts only if sure 'beyond a reasonable doubt'. How does that standard relate to the authors' point about a 60% estimate?
options: A 60% estimate would meet that bar, since it is more likely than not
The bar and the estimate are unrelated, since law and intelligence use different words
Only a 100% estimate could meet it, so the vote was never in doubt
A 60% estimate would fall short of that bar, so honest odds could change the vote
optionExplain: More likely than not falls short of beyond a reasonable doubt.
The authors link the two to show why confidence matters.
The authors discuss 60% or 70% as falling short; they do not say only 100% would do.
It is the authors' own illustration.
questions.explain: The authors say that if some in Congress had set the bar at beyond a reasonable doubt, a 60% or 70% estimate would not have satisfied them.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a less confident conclusion can matter greatly even if the conclusion itself stays the same.

questions.q: Suppose the IC had reported 65% confidence instead of flat statements. Per the authors, which outcome becomes possible?
options: The invasion would certainly have been prevented
The conclusion would have flipped to 'no WMDs'
Congress might not have authorised the use of force
Nothing could change, because the votes were already fixed
optionExplain: The authors say 'might', not 'would certainly'.
Jervis said the conclusion would not have fundamentally differed.
The authors say it might not have passed.
The authors suggest a lower figure could have mattered.
questions.explain: The authors say the resolution authorizing force might not have passed. The change is a stated possibility.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a less confident conclusion can matter greatly even if the conclusion itself stays the same.

questions.q: True or false: Jervis wrote that the IC's analysis could and should have been better, even though he found its conclusion reasonable.
questions.explain: He held the IC to account for correctable errors while calling its judgment reasonable.
questions.rule: Reasonable does not mean flawless.

questions.q: The authors say the IC’s confidence level mattered a great deal in the Iraq case. According to them, why?
options: A lower confidence would have reversed the IC’s conclusion that Saddam had weapons of mass destruction
The sixteen agencies disagreed sharply, so a confidence figure showed which agency deserved trust
Public trust in the IC had fallen after 9/11, so any estimate needed a higher figure to be believed
The stakes were huge: thousands of lives and trillions of dollars hung on the invasion decision
optionExplain: The authors say the IC would still have concluded that Saddam had WMDs, only with less confidence.
The estimate was a consensus of the agencies; the authors do not describe such a split.
The authors report no such fall in trust; their point is the stakes of the decision.
Right: the authors say stakes rarely get much higher, so how confident the IC sounded mattered.
questions.explain: The authors say a less confident conclusion may have made a huge difference to the vote, because thousands of lives and trillions of dollars were at stake.
questions.teaches: The authors say stakes rarely get much higher: thousands of lives and trillions of dollars hung on the invasion decision, so the level of confidence mattered.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a less confident conclusion can matter greatly even if the conclusion itself stays the same.

questions.q: How did the 2002 NIE express its claims about Iraq's weapons?
options: As estimates of 60% to 70%, with a clear margin of doubt
As ranges, with the CIA and NSA offering different views
As flat statements, with no stated chance of error
As questions for Congress to settle with its own evidence
optionExplain: The authors contrast the actual wording with such figures.
The estimate was presented as a consensus view.
Statements like 'Iraq has' admit no surprise.
The estimate made flat claims.
questions.explain: The estimate said 'Iraq has'. The card next explains why that matters.
questions.rule: According to the authors, flat statements with no probabilities and no one assigned to challenge the prevailing view are signs of hubris in an uncertain field.

questions.q: A group assigned to attack the prevailing view is called a ____ team.
questions.explain: Postmortems found there were no red teams, no devil's advocates and no papers with competing possibilities.
questions.rule: Red teams challenge the consensus.

questions.q: A launch memo states that customers will love the product, with no figures and no dissent. Which flaw matches the 2002 estimate?
options: Too much detail about the market, which hides the main point from busy readers
Too many dissenters in the room, who prevent the team from reaching a decision
Flat certainty, with no stated doubt and nobody assigned to challenge it
Too little time spent on it, as any rushed memo will prove unreliable
optionExplain: The 2002 flaw was too little doubt, not too much detail.
The estimate lacked dissenters.
Same pattern as 'Iraq has'.
The text does not blame rushing.
questions.explain: Admitting no possibility of surprise and having no red team are the two signs the authors point to.
questions.rule: According to the authors, flat statements with no probabilities and no one assigned to challenge the prevailing view are signs of hubris in an uncertain field.

questions.q: Suppose the IC had commissioned a red team to argue Saddam had ended his programs. What would likely differ, per the authors?
options: Someone would have at least considered the true view
The conclusion would certainly have reversed to 'no WMDs'
The IC's budget would have been cut for its disloyalty
The estimate would have gained false precision from extra numbers
optionExplain: The investigation said not even considering it was another matter.
Jervis said confidence would fall, not that the conclusion would flip.
Nothing in the text suggests this.
The authors want honest probabilities, not false precision.
questions.explain: The presidential investigation said that failing to conclude Saddam had ended the program was one thing; not even considering it was another. Our reading extends this to a red team.
questions.rule: According to the authors, flat statements with no probabilities and no one assigned to challenge the prevailing view are signs of hubris in an uncertain field.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Tenet's 'slam dunk' remark proves the IC knowingly misled the public.
questions.explain: They say the phrase summed up the IC's attitude, whatever its context; they do not accuse it of lying.
questions.rule: Hubris, not deceit.

questions.q: An engineer declares that a new bridge cannot fail. By the authors' standard, what is wrong with that statement?
options: It is too short to be useful and should include design details
It should be stated more quietly, to avoid frightening the public
It should leave the question to politicians, who decide what is safe
It admits no possibility of surprise in a field full of uncertainty
optionExplain: Length is not the issue.
Tone is not the issue; the claim is unqualified.
The issue is the unqualified certainty.
Like the NIE, it is wrong in the very act of saying it cannot be wrong.
questions.explain: Intelligence analysis, like most expert work, always involves uncertainty, and the authors treat refusing to admit it as hubris.
questions.teaches: Postmortems found the IC never seriously explored the idea that it could be wrong; the investigation said not even considering a view is worse than rejecting it.
questions.rule: According to the authors, flat statements with no probabilities and no one assigned to challenge the prevailing view are signs of hubris in an uncertain field.

questions.q: What is the mission of IARPA, created in 2006?
options: To fund research that could make the intelligence community smarter
To run spies and covert operations on behalf of the sixteen agencies
To write the National Intelligence Estimates that the president reads
To develop new weapons for the military through contractors
optionExplain: This is the mission as the authors state it.
The authors say IARPA has no cloak-and-dagger work.
Estimates come from the agencies as a consensus.
That fits DARPA, the agency it was modeled on, more than IARPA.
questions.explain: IARPA funds research. The card next says what it did and why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the WMD shock led the IC to create a research funder and to ask a scientific body what is known about good judgment.

questions.q: IARPA was modeled after the famous defense research agency known as ____.
questions.explain: DARPA's military-related research has had a huge influence on the modern world, and contributed to the invention of the Internet.
questions.rule: IARPA copies DARPA's research-funding idea.

questions.q: A hospital board pays a university to review its safety methods, knowing the report might be harsh. Which feature of 2008 does this echo?
options: A minister overriding the experts to protect an agency from any outside criticism
A bureaucracy paying a scientific body for a report that might call it clueless
A department building a rival body that mirrors the older one in size and role
A firm announcing its results before any outside group has had a chance to check them
optionExplain: The 2008 step invited outside criticism.
The same risk the authors describe.
IARPA is a research funder, not a rival.
The 2008 step asked outsiders to check.
questions.explain: The authors say it is not every day that a bureaucracy pays one of the world's most respected scientific institutions to produce an objective report that might find it clueless.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the WMD shock led the IC to create a research funder and to ask a scientific body what is known about good judgment.

questions.q: Match each body or person to its role in this chapter.
pairs: Funds high-risk, high-payoff research for the IC
Office of the Director of National Intelligence
Sits atop the sixteen agencies and asked for the review
The scientific institution asked to form a committee
The psychologist who chaired the committee
questions.explain: IARPA funds research, the ODNI sits atop the agencies, the NRC was asked to form a committee, and Fischhoff chaired it.
questions.rule: Know who funds, who asks, who reviews and who chairs.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the 2008 request to the National Research Council carried no risk, because a favorable report was assured.
questions.explain: They call it a bold or rash move because the report might have concluded that the bureaucracy was clueless.
questions.rule: Asking for an objective review is a risk.

questions.q: A firm shrugged off a small recall but reformed after a deadly failure. Which part of the IC story matches?
options: Both failures led to the same large reforms, since every shock is taken to heart in the same way
Neither failure led to reform, since a bureaucracy cannot change in response to shocks
After 1979 a promised follow-up never happened; after the WMD failure, it was taken to heart
The 1979 failure led to IARPA, and the WMD failure led to no change
optionExplain: Jervis contrasts the two cases.
Jervis says the second shock shook the bureaucracy to its foundation.
Jervis told the authors the two failures led to very different responses.
IARPA followed the WMD failure, in 2006.
questions.explain: Jervis said that after his postmortem on 1979, the promised big meeting never happened; the WMD shock shook the bureaucracy to its foundation and, he said, they took it to heart.
questions.rule: Only a big enough shock moved the bureaucracy.
questions.teaches: After Jervis's postmortem on the 1979 Iranian revolution failure, a CIA office head promised a big meeting that never happened; the WMD shock, by contrast, shook the bureaucracy to its foundation.

questions.q: True or false: The CIA's psychology manual for analysts has been tested and shown to improve their judgment.
questions.explain: The authors say it has never been tested. The card next explains why that matters.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a method should be trusted only after it is tested, however convincing it seems.

questions.q: The NRC report followed Archie Cochrane: don't believe until you ____.
questions.explain: Cochrane's maxim from medicine became the report's core message.
questions.rule: Believe after testing.

questions.q: A company trains staff in a popular course that people enjoy, but nobody has measured its effect on results. What fits the report's view?
options: It works, because people enjoy it and it sounds sensible
It fails, because no test has proven that it works
It should be cancelled at once, since training cannot be tested
It may be fine, but whether it works is unknown until tested
optionExplain: Intuitive appeal is not evidence.
Untested is not the same as failed.
The authors say methods can be tested.
This is the manual's position as the authors describe it.
questions.explain: The manual is fine work but untested; the same holds for any course that has intuitive appeal and no measured effect.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a method should be trusted only after it is tested, however convincing it seems.

questions.q: Suppose a test showed that analysts trained on the Heuer manual forecast no better than untrained ones. What would the report's stance imply?
options: The IC should stop treating the manual as proven, whatever its appeal
The IC should add more of the same training, to make the effect stronger
The test must be flawed, since the manual is fine work
The result should be kept secret, to protect the analysts' morale
optionExplain: Evidence should override intuitive appeal.
The report asks for evidence of efficacy.
The authors accept that tests can overturn plausible ideas.
The report asks for evidence-based learning.
questions.explain: The authors say the manual's psychology is fine work, yet whether it improves judgment is unknown. If tested and found useless, the report would not support relying on it. This is our reading.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a method should be trusted only after it is tested, however convincing it seems.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the Heuer manual is poor work that should be dropped.
questions.explain: They call it fine work. Their point is that it has never been tested, so no one knows whether it helps.
questions.rule: Sensible is not the same as tested.

questions.q: A school adopts a reading method because teachers find it compelling. What would the NRC report ask the school to do?
options: Wait for teachers to agree on a ranking, then use the top method
Test it under conditions as realistic as possible
Copy the method used by the school with the best exam results
Rely on a psychologist's manual that explains why the method works
optionExplain: Agreement among teachers is the intuitive appeal the report doubts.
The report asked for rigorous testing under realistic conditions.
A single outcome is the kind of evidence the authors distrust.
A manual of insights can also go untested, as the Heuer example shows.
questions.explain: The report urged the IC to test methods rigorously under conditions as realistic as possible. Our reading applies the advice to a school.
questions.teaches: The NRC report asked the IC to test its methods under conditions as realistic as possible, so that continuous learning would keep it smarter and more agile than its adversaries.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a method should be trusted only after it is tested, however convincing it seems.

questions.q: True or false: Senior intelligence officials can state the IC's forecast accuracy rate from systematic records.
questions.explain: The authors say no such records exist; claims of 80% or 90% are guesses. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, without systematic tracking of accuracy, there is no meaningful way to hold analysts accountable for accuracy.

questions.q: Meaningful accountability for accuracy requires systematic ____ of accuracy.
questions.explain: Getting upset when something goes awry is not enough.
questions.rule: Track accuracy to hold anyone accountable for it.

questions.q: A minister summons a forecaster to explain one wrong call, with no records of any of her other calls. How do the authors see this?
options: As meaningful accountability, since a public hearing shows the matter is taken seriously
As accountability of a sort, but not meaningful, since accuracy is not tracked
As unfair, because no forecaster should ever be called to account for a wrong call
As proof that the forecaster is inaccurate, since she failed in public
optionExplain: The authors say it may serve no purpose beyond grandstanding.
The authors draw this line between kinds of accountability.
The authors do not argue against accountability; they ask for the meaningful kind.
One blown call tells little about her overall accuracy.
questions.explain: A single blown call is an anecdote; meaningful accountability requires a record of all calls.
questions.rule: According to the authors, without systematic tracking of accuracy, there is no meaningful way to hold analysts accountable for accuracy.

questions.q: Suppose the IC began scoring every forecast and kept the results. What would become possible, per the authors' argument?
options: Proving that senior officials' 80% to 90% claims were true all along
Removing all uncertainty from the work of intelligence analysts for good
Answering how accurate analysts are and holding them to account
Replacing analysts with the wisdom of a control group of volunteers
optionExplain: Tracking might confirm or refute them; the authors say they are only guesses.
Analysis would still involve uncertainty.
Tracking makes both possible.
The authors do not draw that conclusion here.
questions.explain: With systematic scoring, the $50 billion question gets an answer. Our reading follows the authors' demand for tracking.
questions.rule: According to the authors, without systematic tracking of accuracy, there is no meaningful way to hold analysts accountable for accuracy.

questions.q: True or false: The authors call the claims of senior officials that the IC is right 80% or 90% of the time guesses.
questions.explain: Without accuracy metrics those figures are guesses, like the confident claims of nineteenth-century physicians.
questions.rule: Unmeasured claims are guesses.

questions.q: A company buys market forecasts each year without checking them against what happened. According to the authors, how unusual is that?
options: Rare, since most organizations score forecasts to decide which provider to keep
Unique to government, since firms face the market's discipline
Reasonable, since forecasts cannot be checked against the facts
Common: many organizations produce or buy forecasts without checking accuracy
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite.
The authors list other organizations too.
The tournament shows they can.
The IC is not alone.
questions.explain: The authors say the IC is not alone: the list of organizations that produce or buy forecasts without bothering to check for accuracy is astonishing.
questions.teaches: The IC is not alone: the authors call the list of organizations that produce or buy forecasts without checking their accuracy astonishing.
questions.rule: According to the authors, without systematic tracking of accuracy, there is no meaningful way to hold analysts accountable for accuracy.

questions.q: What is the IC held accountable for, according to the authors?
options: The measured accuracy of each analyst's forecasts over time
The profits the agencies earn from their estimates
Following expected steps in research and judging
The speed with which it answers the president's questions
optionExplain: The authors say accuracy has never been systematically assessed.
Nothing like this is mentioned.
Process, such as considering alternative hypotheses.
Speed is not mentioned.
questions.explain: It is held to process standards. The card next says why that falls short.
questions.rule: According to the authors, following a good process does not replace checking whether the forecasts turn out accurate.

questions.q: Analysts are held accountable for process, but not for ____.
questions.explain: The point of making forecasts is to foresee what is coming.
questions.rule: Check accuracy as well as process.

questions.q: A weather service audits whether forecasters filled in every form, but does not compare forecasts with the weather. What is the flaw?
options: It checks process only, so it never learns if forecasts were right
It checks too many forms, which wastes the forecasters' time
It compares with the weather too often, which punishes honest misses
It lets forecasters choose their own forms, which spoils fairness
optionExplain: This matches the IC's situation.
The flaw is not volume.
No comparison is made at all.
The flaw is that accuracy is never checked.
questions.explain: A process audit can be perfect while accuracy is poor or unknown.
questions.rule: According to the authors, following a good process does not replace checking whether the forecasts turn out accurate.

questions.q: An analyst follows every process step perfectly, yet her forecasts are usually wrong. What does process accountability show, per the authors?
options: That she is a good forecaster, because she did everything she was told
That the process itself is useless, because her forecasts were wrong
Nothing about the problem, because only a check on accuracy would reveal it
That she should be dismissed, since process has failed to guard against error
optionExplain: Process compliance is not accuracy.
Our reading: it may help, but it is not enough alone.
Process accountability cannot catch it.
The text does not say this.
questions.explain: Process accountability would clear her; only a check on accuracy would show the problem.
questions.rule: According to the authors, following a good process does not replace checking whether the forecasts turn out accurate.

questions.q: True or false: The authors call the process questions analysts are held to, such as considering alternative hypotheses, sensible.
questions.explain: They call it sensible stuff, and object only that process is not a substitute for accuracy.
questions.rule: Good process is sensible, not sufficient.

questions.q: Which analogy do the authors use for accountability for process without accuracy?
options: A runner who is timed at every training session but is never entered in a race
Doctors who follow every routine step but never check if treatment works
A banker who audits every loan form carefully but never reads the final contract
A pilot who flies by a checklist and never looks outside the cockpit window
optionExplain: This is not the authors' analogy.
The analogy from the chapter.
This is not the authors' analogy.
This is not the authors' analogy.
questions.explain: The authors liken the IC to physicians who follow routine steps but never check whether the treatment works.
questions.teaches: The authors liken process-only accountability to ensuring that physicians wash their hands, examine the patient and consider all symptoms, but never checking to see whether the treatment works.
questions.rule: According to the authors, following a good process does not replace checking whether the forecasts turn out accurate.

questions.q: What kind of questions did IARPA want in its tournament?
options: Questions of middling difficulty, neither too easy nor too hard to answer
Questions with answers already known to the research teams in advance
Questions about turning points in the fortunes of nations several years ahead
Questions so hard that only intelligence analysts with clearances could try them
optionExplain: The Goldilocks zone.
The questions concerned future events.
The authors say such forecasting is pretty much impossible.
Questions were meant to be answerable by many people.
questions.explain: IARPA chose a middle zone. The card next names it.
questions.rule: According to the authors, IARPA tested forecasting methods on moderately hard, shorter-range questions, with teams measured against a control group.

questions.q: IARPA wanted questions in the ____ zone of difficulty.
questions.explain: The zone is neither too easy nor too hard.
questions.rule: Goldilocks questions find talent and test methods.

questions.q: A forecasting contest wants fair questions. Which fits the Goldilocks zone?
options: Will the sun rise tomorrow over the capital of Tunisia, as usual?
Who will be the richest person in the whole world in the year 2060?
Did a famous treaty get signed at some point in the previous century?
Will a named currency drop below a set rate within six months?
optionExplain: Too easy; anyone gets it right.
Too hard and too far ahead.
A known past fact, not a forecast.
Hard enough to be uncertain, close enough to be answerable.
questions.explain: The zone has uncertainty but a horizon short enough to forecast. The first three options are too easy, too far, or not forecasts.
questions.rule: According to the authors, IARPA tested forecasting methods on moderately hard, shorter-range questions, with teams measured against a control group.

questions.q: Suppose IARPA had asked forecasters to name turning points in nations several years away. What would likely happen, per the authors?
options: The best forecasters would shine more, as long horizons reward deep thinking
Effort would be wasted, since no search for talent can fix this limit
The control group would win easily, since crowds beat experts at long horizons
Nothing would change, as forecast length does not affect accuracy
optionExplain: The authors say it is pretty much impossible.
They liken it to reading a chart 100 meters away.
No such claim is made.
The chapter says horizon matters.
questions.explain: The authors say IARPA did not want to waste money pushing people to do what is pretty much impossible, like reading eye-chart letters from 100 meters.
questions.rule: According to the authors, IARPA tested forecasting methods on moderately hard, shorter-range questions, with teams measured against a control group.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say IARPA's longest questions would usually be shorter than the shortest questions in Tetlock's earlier tournament.
questions.explain: IARPA kept horizons short to avoid pushing people to do what is pretty much impossible.
questions.rule: Short horizons in the IARPA tournament.

questions.q: A league sets a rising bar for entrants. Which describes IARPA's target for research teams?
options: Beat the control group by 20% in year 1, rising to 50% by year 4
Beat every other team in each of the four years
Reach a Brier score of zero within two years
Match the intelligence analysts' average by the end of the tournament
optionExplain: The targets were intimidating.
The target was set against the control group.
A zero score is perfect omniscience, not the target.
The target was set against the control group.
questions.explain: The target was set against the control group's wisdom of the crowd and rose over the years.
questions.teaches: Research teams had to beat the control group's combined forecast, the wisdom of the crowd, by 20% in year 1, growing to 50% by year 4; the authors found the margins intimidating.
questions.rule: According to the authors, IARPA tested forecasting methods on moderately hard, shorter-range questions, with teams measured against a control group.

questions.q: A team trains all its forecasters and accuracy improves. What can it conclude?
options: The training worked, since accuracy rose after it
Nothing firm: easier questions or luck could explain the change
The training was useless, since it was given to everyone
The forecasters were already good, since training cannot change them
optionExplain: Other causes could explain the rise.
Without a comparison group, the cause is unknown.
Giving it to everyone does not prove it useless.
No such claim is made.
questions.explain: Without a control group the result is ambiguous. The card next gives the fix.
questions.rule: According to the authors, to learn whether a training works, give it to a randomly chosen group, hold everything else constant, and compare results.

questions.q: The fix is to give the training to one ____ chosen group of forecasters and not to another.
questions.explain: Random choice makes the groups comparable.
questions.rule: Randomize, then compare.

questions.q: Order the steps of a fair test of a training exercise, as the authors describe it.
questions.explain: The authors say to give the training to one randomly chosen group but not another, keep all else constant, and compare results.
questions.rule: According to the authors, to learn whether a training works, give it to a randomly chosen group, hold everything else constant, and compare results.
items: Choose one group of forecasters at random to receive the training
Give the training to that group and not to the other
Keep everything else constant
Compare the results of the two groups

questions.q: Suppose the control group's questions were harder than the trained group's. What happens to the comparison, per the authors' logic?
options: It becomes more reliable, because harder questions test the training harder
It becomes unreliable, because the gap could come from the questions
It is unaffected, since random assignment fixes every difference
It shows the training failed, because the control group scored lower
optionExplain: Fairness needs the same conditions.
All else must be constant.
Random assignment does not equalize unequal questions.
A lower score may be due to harder questions.
questions.explain: The authors say to keep all else constant. Our reading applies this to a changed condition.
questions.rule: According to the authors, to learn whether a training works, give it to a randomly chosen group, hold everything else constant, and compare results.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that if accuracy falls after training, the training was counterproductive.
questions.explain: It might be, or accuracy might have fallen even more without it; without a control group there is no way to know.
questions.rule: Falls can be ambiguous too.

questions.q: Why did Tetlock and his colleagues need a lot of forecasters for these experiments?
options: To have enough people to split into trained and control groups
To reduce the cost of each forecaster, which would fall as numbers grew
To make sure every question received at least one forecast per day
To outnumber the intelligence analysts in the contest
optionExplain: Their recruiting call explains it.
Cost is not the reason given.
The text gives a different reason.
No such reason is given.
questions.explain: The research possibilities were limited only by imagination, but to exploit them the authors needed a lot of forecasters. Our reading links this to splitting groups.
questions.teaches: The research possibilities were limited only by imagination, but exploiting them took a lot of forecasters, so they put the word out through blogs and professional networks.
questions.rule: According to the authors, to learn whether a training works, give it to a randomly chosen group, hold everything else constant, and compare results.

questions.q: How did Tetlock and his colleagues recruit forecasters for their team?
options: They put the word out through blogs and professional networks
They hired retired intelligence analysts through the sixteen agencies and paid salaries
They sampled voters at random and required a security clearance
They asked the National Research Council to assign the committee's staff
optionExplain: This is how the call went out.
The volunteers were ordinary people, not hired analysts.
No clearance was involved.
The committee was separate from the project.
questions.explain: The authors recruited volunteers online. The card next gives the name and scale.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the GJP recruited volunteers online, screened them with psychometric tests, and began forecasting at scale.

questions.q: Tetlock and his colleagues called their team and program the ____ Judgment Project.
questions.explain: The Good Judgment Project, or GJP, the name Tetlock's team gave itself and its program.
questions.rule: GJP is the authors' tournament program.

questions.q: A lab wants many volunteers who can forecast with little time. Which step did the GJP use after sign-up?
options: A paid audition with real money bets placed on world events
A security check carried out by the intelligence community
A degree check in international relations or related subjects
A gauntlet of psychometric tests before forecasting began
optionExplain: No betting is described.
The volunteers had no classified access.
Volunteers like Doug had no special expertise.
Roughly 3,200 volunteers passed it.
questions.explain: Several thousand signed up, and roughly 3,200 passed the tests and started forecasting.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the GJP recruited volunteers online, screened them with psychometric tests, and began forecasting at scale.

questions.q: Suppose the project had cost nothing. Would the authors still call IARPA's decision gutsy?
options: No, since cost was the only real risk in sponsoring a tournament like this
Yes: the daring lay in what the tournament could reveal, not in its cost
No, since a free project could reveal nothing important to anyone
Yes, but only because free projects always attract more volunteers
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite.
They say cost was an anthill.
They treat the revelations as the point.
The text says nothing like this.
questions.explain: The authors say the cost was not what made it gutsy; what it could reveal did.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the GJP recruited volunteers online, screened them with psychometric tests, and began forecasting at scale.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say IARPA's decision was gutsy mainly because the project cost more than the IC's whole budget.
questions.explain: The IC's budget is about $50 billion; the project's cost was an anthill beside that mountain.
questions.rule: The risk was in what it might reveal.

questions.q: A foundation wants to test forecasting skill cheaply. What made the GJP's large scale possible?
options: A staff of professional analysts working full time for the project
A small number of experts who made each question's forecast once
Volunteers needed little time each day and could work from home
Access to classified data supplied by the intelligence agencies
optionExplain: The forecasters were volunteers.
The project had thousands of forecasters who updated often.
Doug's hour at his dining table is one example.
Volunteers had no classified access.
questions.explain: Volunteers working a little each day at home, over four years and nearly 500 questions, produced well over a million judgments.
questions.teaches: Over four years the tournament asked nearly five hundred questions about international affairs and drew well over one million judgments from thousands of GJP forecasters.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the GJP recruited volunteers online, screened them with psychometric tests, and began forecasting at scale.

questions.q: Which method won IARPA's tournament for Tetlock's team?
options: Relying on one panel of area experts and asking it for a single agreed view of each question
Averaging many forecasters, weighting the best, then pushing the result toward 100% or zero
Hiring professional analysts with access to classified information and paying them for accuracy
Choosing one forecaster at random for each question and using that forecaster's number
optionExplain: The winning method used many ordinary forecasters.
This is the method the chapter describes.
Professionals were beaten by the method.
Averaging, not random choice, was key.
questions.explain: A weighted crowd average that is extremized. The card next explains its parts.
questions.rule: According to the authors, averaging many forecasts, weighting the best forecasters, and extremizing beat far costlier approaches.

questions.q: Pushing a crowd's average forecast closer to 100% or zero is called to ____ it.

options: About 45%
About 50%
About 15%
About 30%, since extremizing leaves the numbers alone

questions.rule: According to the authors, averaging many forecasts, weighting the best forecasters, and extremizing beat far costlier approaches.

The best forty or so count for more in the average
Pushing the result closer to 100% or zero

questions.q: Each of 200 residents knows part of the picture about a flood risk. Why might extremizing the average make sense?

Extremizing corrects the residents' tendency to guess too high about risks
Extremizing makes the forecast easier for newspapers to print and explain
Extremizing replaces the average with the view of the single most confident resident

questions.rule: According to the authors, averaging many forecasts, weighting the best forecasters, and extremizing beat far costlier approaches.

questions.q: In the IARPA tournament, how many forecasts could a forecaster make on one question?

It is replaced by the crowd average automatically after a week
It stands as her forecast and goes into the question's Brier score
It is counted once, on the day she made it, and then dropped entirely

A forecast stays until it is changed. This is our reading.

questions.q: True or false: After a forecaster updated in the tournament, her earlier forecasts still counted as separate forecasts.

questions.q: One weather service issues a single storm forecast scored later; another revises hourly. Which resembles the tournament?

Hourly revision resembles the tournament; one forecast resembles the earlier EPJ
Both resemble the tournament, since each forecasts the future
Neither resembles it, since weather is not geopolitics

The comparison is about updating method.

questions.rule: According to the authors, every update counted as its own forecast, and all of a question's forecasts fed one final Brier score.

questions.q: On the Brier scale as the chapter describes it, which score is a perfect forecast?

Zero is the center of the bull's-eye.

Not described as perfect; it lies between guessing and the opposite.

questions.q: Three forecasters score 0.50, 0.22 and 0.31 over the same questions. Which pattern is right?
options: The 0.50 forecaster did best, since it is the highest number of the three
The 0.31 forecaster did best, as the middle score is the safest of the three
The 0.22 forecaster did best; the 0.50 one did no better than guessing
All three did equally well, since Brier scores cannot be compared

The lowest score wins.
Lower is better.
They are on the same scale.
questions.explain: 0.22 is the lowest of the three, and 0.50 is the random-guessing level.
questions.rule: According to the authors, on the Brier scale 0 is perfect, 0.5 is random guessing and 2.0 is perfectly wrong, so lower is better.

questions.q: A forecaster scores 2.0 on a question. What does that say about the forecasts?
options: They were the perfect opposite of what happened
They were perfect, matching what happened exactly
They were no better than a coin flip
They were slightly better than guessing
optionExplain: 2.0 is the worst possible score on this scale.
That would be 0.
That would be 0.5.
Better than guessing is below 0.5.
questions.explain: Per the chapter, 2.0 is the result if your forecasts are the perfect opposite of reality.
questions.rule: According to the authors, on the Brier scale 0 is perfect, 0.5 is random guessing and 2.0 is perfectly wrong, so lower is better.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a Brier score of 0.22 is poor because it is far from the maximum of 2.0.
questions.explain: Lower is better, so far from 2.0 is good; 0.22 put Doug fifth of 2,800.
questions.rule: Closer to zero is better.

questions.q: A forecaster averages about 68% confidence on the correct side of a question over months. Which Brier score does the chapter link to that?
options: 0.22, the score on the Italy question
0.50, the random-guessing score
0, the perfect score
0.68, since the score equals the confidence

Random guessing is much less confident.
A perfect score needs near certainty on the right side.
The score is not the same as the confidence.

questions.rule: According to the authors, on the Brier scale 0 is perfect, 0.5 is random guessing and 2.0 is perfectly wrong, so lower is better.

questions.q: What was Doug's final Brier score in year 2?
optionExplain: That was year 1.
Better than his 0.22 in year 1.
That was the score of regular forecasters in year 1.
No one reached perfection.

questions.q: A critic says Doug is unimpressive because his score is not zero. How do the authors answer?
options: Zero is reachable with practice, so Doug did not try hard enough
Doug's score is zero if the rounding is generous

The critic is right, and Doug should be compared only with the average forecaster

questions.rule: According to the authors, judge a forecaster against realistic benchmarks and rivals, not against godlike omniscience.

questions.q: Doug scored 0.22 in year 1 and 0.14 in year 2. What does that change mean?
options: He became more accurate, since a lower Brier score is better
He became less accurate, since the number fell

He became luckier, since scores cannot show skill

Falling Brier scores are an improvement.
0.22 and 0.14 differ in accuracy.
The authors treat scores as informative, though luck is discussed later.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Doug was the only person to beat the extremizing algorithm in year 2.

questions.rule: Doug beat the algorithm.

questions.q: A coach is judged by results against rival coaches, not against a perfect season. Which of Doug's results fits this kind of yardstick?
options: Scoring exactly zero on a single question late in the year, as a perfect forecaster would
Beating a prediction market by 40% and the control group by 60%
Being right on every single question he attempted over the whole season
Receiving a gift certificate at season's end

Real rivals are the benchmark.
No one is said to have done this.
That was his payment, not a performance measure.

questions.teaches: Doug surpassed the control group's wisdom of the crowd by more than 60%, which meant that on his own he exceeded IARPA's fourth-year target.

A salary from the intelligence community

An unpaid outsider matching salaried professionals

questions.q: At the end of year 1, how did the superforecasters' collective Brier score compare with the other forecasters'?

options: It had shrunk as regulars learned from the leaders

options: Superforecasters answered three times as many questions as regulars

20/40 is not hawkeyed.
The authors use percentage gains as a measure.

questions.rule: According to the authors, a 60% improvement from a weak base is not elite, but it can change what a person can do.

questions.q: A weekend hobbyist beats paid engineers at a contest. Which point do the authors make about superforecasters?

questions.q: According to the authors, why might power players avoid forecasting tournaments?

The chapter does not say this.

questions.rule: According to the authors, testing accuracy threatens those whose standing rests on untested judgment, which is why few organizations do it.

options: It would have been sponsored sooner, to protect their own positions inside the IC

questions.q: True or false: Among 2,800 people calling 104 fair coin tosses, someone will probably get about 70% right by luck alone.

That is a method of pooling forecasts.

questions.explain: Early hits led students to believe they could predict random outcomes.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an early streak of hits can make people sincerely believe they can predict outcomes that are entirely random.

questions.q: Suppose Langer rigged results so all students started with a string of misses. What would you expect about their opinion of their skill?
options: It would be higher, since misses teach more than hits
It would be unchanged, since the totals of hits and misses were equal
It would vanish, since the flips were hidden from the students
It would be lower, as early misses lowered it in the study
optionExplain: The study found early misses lowered opinion.
The order mattered even with equal totals.
Their opinion still formed.
The study found the order mattered.
questions.explain: The students who started with misses had a lower opinion than those who started with hits, with the same totals.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an early streak of hits can make people sincerely believe they can predict outcomes that are entirely random.

questions.q: True or false: In Langer's experiment every student got fifteen right and fifteen wrong, whatever their early run.
questions.explain: The results were rigged so that all totals were equal; only the order differed.
questions.rule: Beliefs differed, skill did not.

questions.q: Why does the authors' use of Yale students strengthen the lesson?
options: They are bright students facing a symbol of randomness, yet were fooled
Yale students are less intelligent than the public, so they were easy to fool
Yale students were paid to answer wrongly
Yale students could see the coin, which made the hits visible
optionExplain: Langer's own expectation.
The reverse is stressed.
No such payment is mentioned.
They could not see the flips.
questions.explain: These were students at an elite university, in a task symbolizing randomness, and Langer wrote that you would expect them to be super-rational.
questions.teaches: The students were at an elite university and the task was the very symbol of randomness, so Langer said you would expect them to be super-rational, yet the first pattern fooled them.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an early streak of hits can make people sincerely believe they can predict outcomes that are entirely random.

questions.q: A TV guest is introduced as having called the crash of 2008. What does that tell viewers about his accuracy?
options: A great deal, since calling a crash is a rare thing to do correctly
Nothing, since no one can call a crash in advance by any method at all
That he is more accurate than anyone who happened to miss it
Very little, since one correct call does not show overall accuracy
optionExplain: Rare events can be called by chance.
The authors do not say that.
Others may have had different overall records.
A single success is weak evidence.
questions.explain: One call says little about overall accuracy. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, judge a success story by how many people tried and by what evidence links the actions to the outcome.

questions.q: A great investor's streak looks like proof of skill when journalists ignore how many others were ____.
questions.explain: The odds look long only if you forget the many who tried.
questions.rule: Count the others who tried.

questions.q: A magazine profiles a fund manager who beat the market seven years running, calling the odds astronomically small. What is the flaw?
options: It overstates the odds, which are actually quite small for one person
It ignores how many managers tried, so some lucky winner is likely
It uses too few years, since seven is not enough to measure anything
It trusts the manager, who may be lying
optionExplain: The flaw is ignoring the numbers who tried.
Same flaw as the lottery winner.
Years are not the main issue.
No dishonesty is alleged.
questions.explain: With many thousands trying, some people are bound to get lucky.
questions.rule: According to the authors, judge a success story by how many people tried and by what evidence links the actions to the outcome.

questions.q: Match each story to the flaw the authors find in it.
pairs: A pundit introduced as having called the crash of 2008
One success says little about overall accuracy
An investor who beat the market six or seven years in a row
It ignores how many others were trying
A business book on a company's run of successes
It seldom shows the actions caused the results
questions.explain: A single dramatic call ignores overall accuracy, a long streak ignores how many tried, and a business book ignores luck and cause.
questions.rule: Name the missing piece in each story.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the stories in business books may be true or fairy tales, and that it is impossible to know.
questions.explain: These books seldom provide solid evidence that the highlighted actions caused the outcomes.
questions.rule: Unproven, not disproven.

questions.q: Which comparison do the authors use to show that predicting a crash proves little?
options: A dart-throwing chimp hits a bull's-eye if it throws enough darts
A broken clock is right twice a day, so every forecaster is a clock
A weather vane points the right way when the wind blows
A coin lands heads half the time, so forecasts are coin tosses
optionExplain: Their own comparison.
Not the authors' comparison.
Not the authors' comparison.
Not the authors' comparison.
questions.explain: A chimp throwing enough darts will hit the bull's-eye, and anyone can predict a crash by incessantly warning of one.
questions.teaches: Even a dart-throwing chimp will hit the occasional bull's-eye if it throws enough darts, and anyone can easily predict the next stock market crash by incessantly warning that one is coming.
questions.rule: According to the authors, judge a success story by how many people tried and by what evidence links the actions to the outcome.

questions.q: Do the authors say the evidence so far shows that superforecasters are truly skilled?
options: No: it does not yet establish that, and readers should not be convinced yet
Yes, since the Brier scores prove it beyond any reasonable doubt
Yes, but only for the single best forecaster, Doug Lorch, whose scores stood out
No, because skill cannot exist in forecasting events that are this uncertain
optionExplain: They want the reader skeptical.
The authors say the opposite.
They do not say this.
They go on to find skill.
questions.explain: The chapter pauses to test the claim. The card next gives the frame.
questions.rule: According to the authors, ask how much of a result is skill and how much luck, not which of the two it is.

questions.q: The authors call 'superforecasters or superlucky?' a false ____.
questions.explain: Most things in life involve skill and luck in varying proportions.
questions.rule: Most results mix skill and luck.

questions.q: A coach asks whether a star athlete's season was skill or luck. What does the authors' view suggest?
options: It was all skill, since top athletes train hard
It was all luck, since sports are unpredictable
Ask how much of each, since results usually mix both
It cannot be judged, since skill and luck are inseparable
optionExplain: Most outcomes mix both.
Most outcomes mix both.
False dichotomy.
The authors offer a test.
questions.explain: The mix may range from mostly luck to mostly skill and anything in between.
questions.rule: According to the authors, ask how much of a result is skill and how much luck, not which of the two it is.

questions.q: Suppose a forecaster's results came from almost all luck and a little skill. How do the authors say that mix fits the picture?
options: It is impossible, since a skilled forecaster would show all skill
It is the usual mix for every superforecaster
It means skill is irrelevant
It is one of many possible mixes, so a test is needed
optionExplain: Mixes vary widely.
The authors do not say.
A little skill still counts.
Hence regression to the mean.
questions.explain: The authors say the mix could be almost all luck and a little skill, or the reverse, or many variations.
questions.rule: According to the authors, ask how much of a result is skill and how much luck, not which of the two it is.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say retiring to Santa Barbara and driving a little red convertible will let readers forecast as accurately as Doug Lorch.
questions.explain: They say the evidence does not establish that; they are warning against that sort of overreach.
questions.rule: Do not overread success stories.

questions.q: Which rule of thumb does Mauboussin offer for sorting skill from luck?
options: Regression to the mean
The wisdom of the crowd
Extremizing
The illusion of control
optionExplain: The rule applies to athletes, CEOs, stock analysts and superforecasters.
That is pooled forecasting.
That is a method of adjusting forecasts.
That is a bias.
questions.explain: Mauboussin's rule of thumb is regression to the mean.
questions.teaches: Michael Mauboussin, a global financial strategist and author of The Success Equation, offers regression to the mean as an elegant rule of thumb for athletes, CEOs, stock analysts and superforecasters alike.
questions.rule: According to the authors, ask how much of a result is skill and how much luck, not which of the two it is.

questions.q: Average male height is five feet eight and a father is six feet. What is the best guess for his adult son's height?
options: Five feet ten
Six feet, the same as his father
Five feet eight, exactly the population average
Six feet two, since sons tend to outgrow fathers

The authors say this is possible but unlikely.
That ignores the father's height.
Nothing supports this.
questions.explain: Halfway between father and average. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, with a correlation of about 0.5, predict a value halfway between the extreme case and the population average.

questions.q: With a father-son correlation of about 0.5, the son's height is predicted halfway between his father's height and the population ____.
questions.explain: A correlation of 0.5 gives a halfway compromise.
questions.rule: Predict between the extreme and the mean.

questions.q: Average height is five feet eight, a father is five feet four, and the correlation is 0.5. What is the best guess for his son?
options: Five feet four, the same as his father
Five feet six
Five feet eight, the population average
Five feet two, shorter than his father
optionExplain: That ignores regression.
Halfway between five feet four and the average.
That ignores the father's height.
That moves away from the mean.
questions.explain: The guess is pulled halfway toward the average, from below.
questions.rule: According to the authors, with a correlation of about 0.5, predict a value halfway between the extreme case and the population average.

questions.q: A father is exactly five feet eight, the average. What does the compromise rule suggest for his son's best guess?
options: Five feet ten, since sons tend to be taller than fathers
Five feet six, since sons are shorter
Five feet eight, as the father equals the average
Six feet, since a mean father has no effect
optionExplain: No pull exists.
No pull exists.
No pull in either direction.
The rule does not give this.
questions.explain: When the father is at the average, the compromise is the average. This is our reading of the rule.
questions.rule: According to the authors, with a correlation of about 0.5, predict a value halfway between the extreme case and the population average.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say it is unlikely, though possible, that a six-foot father's adult son is also six feet tall.
questions.explain: The best guess is five feet ten, halfway toward the average.
questions.rule: Regression pulls toward the average.

questions.q: A manager sees a salesperson's record sale and assumes next month will match it. Which thinking produces that hunch?
options: System 2, the slow reasoning that weighs the average against the case
Extremizing, which pushes the guess toward the extreme of the range
The wisdom of the crowd, which averages the views of the whole team
System 1, the quick hunch, which System 2 reasoning must correct
optionExplain: That is the system that corrects the hunch.
That is a different tool.
The hunch is not a crowd average.
The same two systems as in the height example.
questions.explain: The authors say the hunch that the son is also six feet comes from System 1, and seeing why it is unlikely takes strenuous System 2 reasoning.
questions.teaches: The hunch that a six-foot father has a six-foot son is a System 1 reaction; seeing why that is unlikely takes strenuous System 2 reasoning about the correlation of about 0.5.
questions.rule: According to the authors, with a correlation of about 0.5, predict a value halfway between the extreme case and the population average.

questions.q: You have your worst back-pain day, visit a homeopath, and feel better the next day. What may explain this?
options: The homeopath's treatment cured the condition within a day
Regression to the mean: a terrible day is usually followed by a better one
Your pain always improves after any visit to a clinic, whatever is done there
The placebo effect is the only possible explanation of the improvement
optionExplain: That is the tip-of-your-nose conclusion.
The authors' point.
No such rule exists.
The authors say placebo may help but regression is likely too.
questions.explain: A bad day tends to be followed by a better one. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an improvement after an extreme low point may be regression to the mean rather than the effect of the treatment.

questions.q: People most often seek treatment on an extreme day, so the next day tends to ____ toward average.
questions.explain: Extreme days are followed by less extreme ones.
questions.rule: Extremes fade toward the mean.

questions.q: A coach scolds the team after its worst game of the season, and the next game improves. What does the authors' logic suggest?
options: The scolding worked, since the improvement followed straight after it
The team improved because it practised harder in the days between
It may be regression to the mean, so the scolding is weak evidence
Scolding is harmful, since it only works by luck
optionExplain: That is the tip-of-your-nose conclusion.
Nothing supports this.
Same logic as the back-pain case.
The authors do not say that.
questions.explain: After an extreme low, improvement is expected anyway, so credit to the scolding is hard to claim. This is our reading in a new setting.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an improvement after an extreme low point may be regression to the mean rather than the effect of the treatment.

questions.q: Suppose you seek treatment on a typical day rather than your worst. How does regression change what you can expect afterwards?
options: The same regression effect, since every kind of day regresses equally toward the average
A larger effect, since typical days are least stable
No effect from the treatment either way
Less room to improve by regression alone, so a gain would be stronger evidence
optionExplain: The pull is stronger from extremes.
Typical days are closer to the average.
That does not follow.
Our reading of the logic.
questions.explain: Regression pulls extreme days toward the average; a typical day has little to regress. This is our reading, not a claim in the text.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an improvement after an extreme low point may be regression to the mean rather than the effect of the treatment.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the placebo effect cannot help when someone treats an awful back-pain day.
questions.explain: They say the placebo effect may have helped, but regression to the mean probably explains the improvement.
questions.rule: Placebo and regression can both be at work.

questions.q: How do the authors describe the mistake of forgetting regression to the mean?
options: A modest little mistake behind many things people believe but should not
A rare lapse that only trained experts ever make in their work
A deliberate trick used by sellers of unproven treatments to attract buyers
A harmless error that has no effect on what people go on to believe
optionExplain: Their own words.
They say it is common.
They treat it as an error, not a trick.
They say it is responsible for many beliefs.
questions.explain: The authors call it a modest little mistake responsible for many of the things people believe but shouldn't.
questions.teaches: The authors call forgetting regression to the mean a modest little mistake responsible for many of the things people believe but shouldn't.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an improvement after an extreme low point may be regression to the mean rather than the effect of the treatment.

questions.q: In a repeat of the coin-toss game, what happens to people who scored 90% in round one?
options: Most keep scoring about 90%, since they found a method
Most score below 50%, to balance their luck
Most fall rapidly back toward 50%
They are removed from the game as ineligible
optionExplain: Coin tosses cannot be predicted.
Luck does not balance in that way.
Their first-round results were luck.
Nothing like this is described.
questions.explain: They drift back to 50%. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, if round-one stars fall back to the average when retested, their first-round results were luck.

questions.q: With coin tosses, the correlation between round one and round two results is close to ____.
questions.explain: Round-one stars do not carry their luck into round two.
questions.rule: Luck does not repeat.

questions.q: A cohort of 100 people guessed coin flips and 90% of one subgroup got most right. Retested, what should we expect?
options: All of them to stay near the top, because their skill persists
Most to regress toward the average; a few may stay high by luck
All of them to fall far below the average, to balance out their luck
Half of them to improve further, as practice sharpens their guessing
optionExplain: That would signal skill, not luck.
The luckiest decline the most.
They regress to average, not below it.
Chance gives no such pattern.
questions.explain: Most go back to 50%; a few may repeat by luck. Make them repeat again and their luck runs out.
questions.rule: According to the authors, if round-one stars fall back to the average when retested, their first-round results were luck.

questions.q: Suppose a retest showed round-one stars scoring as high again. What would that suggest?
options: Skill is likely involved, since luck would have regressed
The game is still pure luck, since luck tends to repeat itself
The stars cheated in round two
The questions were easier in round two
optionExplain: Our reading of the authors' logic.
Luck regresses.
Nothing suggests this.
A different explanation, not the main inference.
questions.explain: If the top performers do not regress, results are less likely to be pure luck. The authors build on this later.
questions.rule: According to the authors, if round-one stars fall back to the average when retested, their first-round results were luck.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the best prediction for any coin-toss caller in round two is that she repeats her round-one result.
questions.explain: The best prediction is the average accuracy of 50%: total regression.
questions.rule: Predict 50% for coin callers.

questions.q: If a few round-one stars do get nine or ten right again, what do the authors advise?
options: Crown them champions, since repeating is proof of skill beyond any doubt
Ignore them completely, since every result in a luck game is meaningless
Pay them to forecast, since luck is as good as skill for that purpose
Hesitate to call them gurus; make them repeat until their luck runs out
optionExplain: A few repeats can be luck.
More rounds would reveal.
The authors say the opposite.
A few repeats do not prove skill.
questions.explain: The authors say that since everyone else is rapidly regressing, we should hesitate to declare the repeaters coin-toss gurus.
questions.teaches: Even if a few round-one stars get nine or ten right again, the authors say to make them repeat the exercise, because eventually their luck will run out.
questions.rule: According to the authors, if round-one stars fall back to the average when retested, their first-round results were luck.

questions.q: If Nancy's year-1 success was entirely luck, where would she be expected in year 2?
options: Still near the top, at about 99%
Back at the middle, around 50%
Around 75%
Near the bottom, to balance her luck
optionExplain: That is the skill-only case.
Total regression.
That is the equal-mix case.
Luck does not balance this way.
questions.explain: Pure luck regresses all the way. The card next gives the other cases.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the less results regress from one period to the next, the more skill and the less luck were involved.

questions.q: If results were equal parts luck and skill, the regression would be ____ of the way back to the mean.
questions.explain: Frank to about 25% and Nancy to about 75%.
questions.rule: Equal mix means halfway.

questions.q: Match each assumed mix of luck and skill to Nancy's expected year-2 rank (year 1 was top 99%).
questions.explain: Luck alone sends her to 50%, equal parts to about 75% and skill alone leaves her at about 99%.
questions.rule: More regression means more luck.

questions.q: Order the three cases by how much regression to the mean you expect from year 1 to year 2, most first.
questions.explain: Luck alone sends everyone back to 50%; equal parts give halfway regression; skill alone gives none.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the less results regress from one period to the next, the more skill and the less luck were involved.
items: Results entirely decided by luck
Results of equal parts luck and skill
Results entirely decided by skill

questions.q: True or false: The authors report that slow regression is more often seen in activities dominated by skill.
questions.explain: Faster regression is more associated with chance.
questions.rule: Slow regression points to skill.

questions.q: A sports league sees last year's top ten teams stay near the top this year. Which reading fits the authors' gauge?
options: Much regression, so the results were mostly luck
No information, since sports are unpredictable
Little regression suggests skill played a large part
Only luck, because the same teams cannot win twice running
optionExplain: The teams did not regress.
Regression is informative.
Slow regression goes with skill.
That does not follow.
questions.explain: The less regression, the more skill. Our reading applies the gauge to sports.
questions.teaches: If results were entirely decided by skill there would be no regression: Frank would be just as awful in year 2 and Nancy just as spectacular.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the less results regress from one period to the next, the more skill and the less luck were involved.

questions.q: In years 2 and 3, what did the superforecasters as a group do relative to other forecasters?
options: They fell back toward the average
They tied with the regular forecasters
They were dropped from the study
They widened their lead
optionExplain: That would be regression.
They widened the lead.
They continued.
The opposite of regression to the mean.
questions.explain: They widened their lead. The card next gives the authors' puzzle.
questions.rule: According to the authors, regression can be hidden when something offsets it; here, recognition and elite teams may have lifted performance.

questions.q: Instead of regressing, the superforecasters as a group actually ____ their lead in years 2 and 3.
questions.explain: The opposite of regression to the mean.
questions.rule: Their lead grew.

questions.q: A company's top sales team, after being praised and given the best colleagues, keeps improving. What explains the lack of regression?
options: No luck was involved in the original result, so nothing could regress
An offset: recognition and strong teammates can mask regression
The sales numbers must be wrong, because teams cannot improve results
Regression to the mean does not exist in sales, only in sports
optionExplain: The authors doubt that in their own case.
The same story as the superforecasters.
No basis.
It exists but can be offset.
questions.explain: Recognition and a team of stimulating colleagues can offset regression.
questions.rule: According to the authors, regression can be hidden when something offsets it; here, recognition and elite teams may have lifted performance.

questions.q: Suppose the new crops of superforecasters in years 3 and 4 had regressed sharply. What would that say about the first group's gains?
options: It would show the teams were harmful to those who joined them
It would show regression to the mean does not apply to forecasters
It would suggest the first group's gains owed more to luck than to teams
It would show the control group got better over the same years
optionExplain: No basis.
It would suggest the opposite.
Our reading.
No basis.
questions.explain: The authors use fresh crops for apples-to-apples comparisons; they did as well or better, against the regression hypothesis.
questions.rule: According to the authors, regression can be hidden when something offsets it; here, recognition and elite teams may have lifted performance.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the superforecasters' lead growing proves there was no luck at all in their results.
questions.explain: They say they deeply doubt that, given irreducible uncertainty; they suspect an offsetting process.
questions.rule: A growing lead is not proof of zero luck.

questions.q: Why did the authors use fresh crops of superforecasters in years 3 and 4?
options: To give a fresh apples-to-apples comparison of new top performers
To replace the first group, who had all failed by the second year
To reduce costs by hiring cheaper volunteers in place of the first group
To remove the elite teams from the study
optionExplain: A way to test regression again.
The first group did not fail.
Cost is not the reason.
The fresh crops were put on elite teams.
questions.explain: Each new cohort was a fresh test of whether newly identified stars regress.
questions.teaches: In years 3 and 4 the authors harvested fresh crops of superforecasters and put them in elite teams, which gave more apples-to-apples comparisons; the new cohorts did as well or better than the year before.
questions.rule: According to the authors, regression can be hidden when something offsets it; here, recognition and elite teams may have lifted performance.

questions.q: How did the East China Sea question about a fatal confrontation between vessels resolve?
options: No: the vessels avoided one another until the question closed
Yes: a fishing boat captain stabbed a coast guard officer
Yes: a collision between two ships sank a navy vessel
It was annulled for lack of evidence of the event
optionExplain: The answer was yes.
A quirky last-minute event.
A stabbing resolved it.
It was resolved yes.
