questions.explain: A stabbing just before the deadline. The card next explains the point.
questions.rule: According to the authors, quirky last-minute events and tangled nonlinear systems put a floor under uncertainty, so luck cannot be absent.

questions.q: The authors call the oil price a long-time graveyard topic for forecasting ____.
questions.explain: Many factors affect it, and many more affect those.
questions.rule: Oil is hard to forecast.

questions.q: A forecast question depends on a chain of interacting factors, each affected by many others. Which authors' term fits?
options: Linear ties, where effects are proportional to causes
Regression ties, where extremes fade
Extremized ties, where results are pushed to the poles
Nonlinear ties, where tiny changes can matter hugely
optionExplain: The authors contrast it.
That is a different idea.
That is a pooling tweak.
Lorenz's point.
questions.explain: Many causal ties are nonlinear, so small causes can have big effects.
questions.rule: According to the authors, quirky last-minute events and tangled nonlinear systems put a floor under uncertainty, so luck cannot be absent.

questions.q: Suppose all questions were stable and simple. How would the amount of luck in forecasting change, per the authors' logic?
options: Luck would matter less, with less irreducible uncertainty
Luck would matter more, since easier questions have more chance
Luck would be unchanged
Luck would disappear entirely
optionExplain: Our reading.
The reverse.
The authors link luck to irreducible uncertainty.
Some uncertainty remains.
questions.explain: The authors tie luck to irreducible uncertainty in some questions. This is our reading.
questions.rule: According to the authors, quirky last-minute events and tangled nonlinear systems put a floor under uncertainty, so luck cannot be absent.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Edward Lorenz showed that butterfly wings are the main driver of oil prices.
questions.explain: They cite Lorenz to show that in nonlinear systems tiny things can have big effects, not that butterflies drive oil.
questions.rule: Small causes can matter in nonlinear systems.

questions.q: Which factors do the authors list as influencing the price of oil?
options: Only OPEC decisions and the weather in producing regions around the world
Only the price of gold and the euro, which move together with oil
US frackers, Libyan jihadists and Silicon Valley battery designers
Only central bank rates and exchange rates among the major economies
optionExplain: The listed examples differ.
The listed examples differ.
The three examples.
The listed examples differ.
questions.explain: The authors list these three, and say the factors influencing those factors are an even bigger number.
questions.teaches: The authors list frackers in the United States, jihadists in Libya and battery designers in Silicon Valley as drivers of the oil price, and say the factors that influence those factors are even more numerous.
questions.rule: According to the authors, quirky last-minute events and tangled nonlinear systems put a floor under uncertainty, so luck cannot be absent.

questions.q: Each year, roughly what share of superforecasters fall out of the top 2%?
options: About 30%
About 70%
About 5%
About 100%
optionExplain: The remaining 70% stay.
That share remains.
Too few.
Then there would be no consistency.
questions.explain: About 30% leave. The card next gives the verdict.
questions.rule: According to the authors, some turnover plus strong year-to-year consistency means superforecasters were mostly skilled, though not infallible.

questions.q: Each year about 70% of superforecasters remain ____.
questions.explain: Thirty percent fall out of the top 2%.
questions.rule: Consistency with some turnover.

questions.q: A league's top 20 players keep about 70% of their places from one year to the next. How do the authors' numbers help read this?
options: Turnover proves the players are lucky, so skill is absent from the pattern
Consistency beyond chance suggests skill; turnover shows luck remains
Consistency proves the players are infallible and cannot have a bad year
The pattern proves nothing, since every league differs from the others
optionExplain: Turnover is expected even with skill.
The same pattern as the superforecasters.
The authors reject infallibility.
Comparison to chance is informative.
questions.explain: Some regression is expected with a correlation like 0.65, while 70% staying is far from a luck-only pattern.
questions.rule: According to the authors, some turnover plus strong year-to-year consistency means superforecasters were mostly skilled, though not infallible.

questions.q: Which statements about superforecasters' year-to-year results are true? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: The authors report about 30% leaving and 70% staying. The correlation of 0.65 is a little above the father-son figure, and regression is still expected.
questions.rule: According to the authors, some turnover plus strong year-to-year consistency means superforecasters were mostly skilled, though not infallible.
options: About 30% fall out of the top 2% each year
About 70% remain superforecasters the next year
Their year-to-year correlation is lower than for fathers and sons
With a 0.65 correlation, no regression to the mean is expected
optionExplain: True: roughly 30% drop out each year.
True: 70% remain, which shows considerable consistency.
False: 0.65 is modestly higher than the 0.5 for fathers and sons.
False: considerable regression is still expected at 0.65.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the superforecasters' results were mostly skill, so no superforecaster should ever have a bad year.
questions.explain: They say luck plays a role and superstars will occasionally have a bad year, like superstar athletes.
questions.rule: Mostly skill is not infallible.

questions.q: What big question does the chapter leave open at its end?
options: Whether the IC will fund another tournament
Why superforecasters are so good
Whether luck exists at all
How the Brier score is calculated
optionExplain: Not the closing question.
The question is stated at the close.
The authors have just shown luck plays a role.
Not the closing question.
questions.explain: Having concluded the superforecasters were not just lucky, the authors ask why they are so good.
questions.teaches: Having concluded that superforecasters were mostly skilled, the authors close by asking the big question: why are superforecasters so good?
questions.rule: According to the authors, some turnover plus strong year-to-year consistency means superforecasters were mostly skilled, though not infallible.

questions.q: In year 1, how did Sandy Sillman, forecasting on his own, place among roughly 2,800 tournament forecasters?
options: He finished mid-table, then rose after he joined a team
He tied for overall champion despite having no team
He placed second behind a team that pooled its forecasts
He placed low, because working alone is a handicap
optionExplain: Plausible, since teams helped many forecasters, but the text puts him at the top in year 1.
Sandy's score tied him with the best, even though he worked alone.
Teams did well in the project, but Sandy was in a solo condition and tied for first.
Working alone can sound like a handicap, yet he tied for the top spot.
questions.explain: He forecast alone in a control condition and still tied for overall champion. The card next shows what explanation this tempts.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a brilliant star forecaster invites the guess that intelligence explains forecasting success, and that guess is only a starting point.

questions.q: Sandy was randomly assigned to forecast alone, in what the tournament called the ____ condition.
questions.explain: In year 1 he worked in the control condition, forecasting by himself, and still tied for the top.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a brilliant star forecaster invites the guess that intelligence explains forecasting success, and that guess is only a starting point.

questions.q: A colleague with three degrees wins the office sports-forecast pool. Which explanation does the chapter say is tempting in a case like this?
options: Her results are pure luck, so the win tells us nothing about skill
She wins because she spends the most hours on the pool of anyone
She wins because the pool was designed to favour well-educated people
Her mind explains her results, and the same holds for other top forecasters
optionExplain: Luck is possible in any one contest, but the chapter's temptation is about intelligence, not luck.
Effort may matter, yet the chapter's tempting suspicion is about the mind itself.
Nothing in the case suggests rigged conditions; the temptation is about her mind.
The authors say people readily suspect a brilliant mind explains a brilliant forecasting record.
questions.explain: The suspicion that a remarkable mind explains remarkable results is the natural one the chapter sets up before testing it.
questions.rule: A star with a star mind makes intelligence the first suspect.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Sandy's case makes it hard not to suspect his mind explains his results.
questions.explain: They say so, and then treat the suspicion as a hypothesis to put to the test.
questions.rule: A suspicion is not a finding.

questions.q: Most of the roughly 2,800 forecasters Sandy beat worked in other conditions. What does that detail add to his result?
options: He tied for first despite lacking the extra stimulation most others had
It shows he cheated the conditions by seeing other forecasters' work in advance
It shows solo work is always better than team work
It shows the conditions did not affect anyone's accuracy at all
optionExplain: Most others worked in more stimulating conditions, so his solo result was the harder one.
Nothing says he saw others' forecasts; he was in the solo control condition.
The detail concerns one result, not a general ranking of solo against team conditions.
The text only says most others had livelier conditions, not that conditions made no difference.
questions.explain: Sandy forecast alone, while most of those he beat worked in more stimulating conditions.
questions.teaches: Sandy beat roughly 2,800 others, most of whom worked in more stimulating conditions than his solo one.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a brilliant star forecaster invites the guess that intelligence explains forecasting success, and that guess is only a starting point.

questions.q: A music school's best violinist also speaks four languages. A newsletter says her mind explains her playing. What does the chapter's approach suggest next?
options: Accept it, since an exceptional individual is the best evidence available
Reject it, since language skill cannot affect music at all
Treat that as a hypothesis and look for data across many players
Ask only the violinist, since she knows her own reasons best
optionExplain: One striking case is the source of the guess, not a test of it.
The chapter does not dismiss the guess; it tests it.
The authors say a plausible hypothesis must be put to the test, not accepted.
Her own account is one source, and the chapter turns to data on many people instead.
questions.explain: Plausibility is not enough, so the authors go to data from many forecasters rather than one star.
questions.teaches: Plausibility is not enough for the authors: a hypothesis such as intelligence explaining success is checked against data.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a brilliant star forecaster invites the guess that intelligence explains forecasting success, and that guess is only a starting point.

questions.q: How did the research team check whether intelligence and knowledge help people forecast?
options: They interviewed the top forecasters about how they think about problems
They asked experts to name the forecasters who looked smartest to them
They compared forecasters' degrees and awards as listed on their résumés
Volunteers took psychological tests that were compared with forecasting
optionExplain: Interviews might suggest ideas, but they do not compare results across forecasters.
Expert impressions would be a judgment, not a measurement of intelligence.
Credentials are a rough guide at best and are not what the card describes.
The team had test data from volunteers to set against forecast accuracy.
questions.explain: The volunteers took a battery of tests that gave measured data. The card next explains the logic.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a plausible explanation is a hypothesis to test with data, not a conclusion.

questions.q: The authors say a plausible idea is not enough; the hypothesis must be put to the ____.
questions.explain: Plausibility alone does not settle a question; the authors go to the data.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a plausible explanation is a hypothesis to test with data, not a conclusion.

questions.q: A school says its new reading app lifts scores because pupils find it engaging. What does the authors' approach ask for?
options: Reading scores for many pupils, with and without the app, to compare
A handful of cheerful pupils' quotes, since engagement is hard to count
Nothing further, since an engaging app plainly raises scores
The head teacher's view, since she knows the school best
optionExplain: Testing means gathering data that could confirm or refute the claim.
Quotes may suggest the idea, but they cannot test it against other pupils.
Plausible does not mean true; that is the authors' point.
Authority is not data; the hypothesis needs measures across pupils.
questions.explain: The hypothesis becomes testable once there are measurements on many people to compare.
questions.rule: Turn a plausible story into a comparison of data.

questions.q: True or false: The authors argue that because the intelligence explanation is plausible, no test is needed.
questions.explain: They say the opposite: plausibility is not enough, and the hypothesis must be tested.
questions.rule: Plausible is not proven.

questions.q: Why does the answer matter to ordinary readers who hope to forecast well?
options: If intelligence mattered, readers could raise it through study
If intelligence mattered, knowledge would become irrelevant
If foresight needed top-1% genius, most people could never qualify
If it mattered, only those with elite degrees could be tested at all
optionExplain: The authors say adult intelligence is felt to be relatively fixed, and knowledge grows only slowly.
The authors treat knowledge and intelligence together as the hypothesis, not as rivals.
The authors say that outcome would leave most readers with little reason to try.
Nothing in the text links testing to degrees; the worry is about who could qualify.
questions.explain: Knowledge can be increased only slowly and intelligence feels fixed, so a genius requirement would shut out most people.
questions.teaches: Knowledge grows only slowly and adult intelligence feels relatively fixed, so if foresight required genius (the top 1%) most people could never qualify.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a plausible explanation is a hypothesis to test with data, not a conclusion.

questions.q: A firm wants to know whether a trait predicts trainee success. When should it measure the trait to follow the tournament's design?
options: After the programme ends, once success is known and can be counted
Before trainees begin, so results cannot colour the measure
At the midpoint, so both stages can be compared
Whenever convenient, since timing does not affect a test
optionExplain: Measuring afterwards risks the outcome shaping the measure; the tournament tested first.
In the tournament volunteers sat the tests before they started forecasting.
The text describes the tests as coming before any forecasting.
Timing matters; the volunteers were tested before they forecast.
questions.explain: The tournament tested volunteers before they forecast, so the trait scores could be set against later accuracy.
questions.teaches: The volunteers took the batteries of psychological tests before they started forecasting, and project coleader Barbara Mellers supplied the data.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a plausible explanation is a hypothesis to test with data, not a conclusion.

questions.q: Which kind of question would measure what the authors call knowledge?
options: Finding the rule behind rows and columns of shapes
Estimating how many pianos a city holds from scratch
Naming the permanent members of the UN Security Council
Naming the best strategy for a game after one practice round
optionExplain: This is the pattern puzzle used to gauge raw crunching power.
This is a Fermi-style estimate, a different skill the chapter discusses later.
This is a factual question about the world, which tests stored knowledge.
Nothing in the chapter measures intelligence like this.
questions.explain: Knowledge questions are factual. The card next names the two kinds the authors measured.
questions.rule: According to the authors, fluid intelligence is raw reasoning power on puzzles and crystallized intelligence is accumulated knowledge.

questions.q: The authors call raw crunching power, measured by pattern puzzles, ____ intelligence.
questions.explain: Fluid intelligence is raw reasoning power on puzzles; crystallized intelligence is knowledge of facts about the world.
questions.rule: According to the authors, fluid intelligence is raw reasoning power on puzzles and crystallized intelligence is accumulated knowledge.

questions.q: A job test asks applicants to find the missing shape in a grid. Which measure does this correspond to?
options: Crystallized intelligence, because it rewards stored facts about the world
Fluid intelligence, because it tests spotting rules in patterns
Fermi estimation, because it breaks a puzzle into parts
Active open-mindedness, because it welcomes other views
optionExplain: Nothing in a shape grid depends on stored facts; the puzzle is rule-finding.
The puzzle in the chapter has this form and was used to gauge raw crunching power.
Fermi estimation is a different method that the chapter describes next.
That is a later concept about attitudes, not about puzzle-solving ability.
questions.explain: Spotting rules in rows and columns is the fluid intelligence puzzle of the chapter.
questions.rule: Rule-finding puzzles measure fluid intelligence; factual questions measure crystallized intelligence.

questions.q: Sort each test item by the kind of intelligence it measures.

items.t: Fill the missing shape in a 3-by-3 grid
How many Justices sit on the Supreme Court?
Work out which rule each column of shapes follows
Which nations are permanent members of the UN Security Council?

questions.explain: Puzzle items test pattern reasoning (fluid); factual questions test knowledge (crystallized).
questions.rule: According to the authors, fluid intelligence is raw reasoning power on puzzles and crystallized intelligence is accumulated knowledge.

questions.q: True or false: The authors measured both fluid intelligence and crystallized intelligence.
questions.explain: They used puzzles for fluid intelligence and knowledge questions for crystallized intelligence.
questions.rule: Two measures: crunching power and knowledge.

questions.q: A hiring test has only pattern puzzles. By the authors' reasoning, what could it miss for a role needing judgment about world events?
options: The applicant's fluid intelligence, which only knowledge tests reveal
Their active open-mindedness, which puzzles measure directly
Nothing, since pattern skills are enough for real-world judgment
Knowledge to say where to look for patterns in the real world
optionExplain: Puzzles do measure fluid intelligence; what they miss is knowledge.
Puzzles do not measure open-mindedness; the mismatch the card describes is knowledge.
The authors say pattern skills fall short without knowing where to look.
High-powered pattern recognition skills do not get far without knowing where to look.
questions.explain: Raw puzzle power needs knowledge of where to look for patterns in the real world.
questions.teaches: High-powered pattern recognition does not get far if you do not know where to look for patterns in the real world, which is why knowledge was measured too.
questions.rule: According to the authors, fluid intelligence is raw reasoning power on puzzles and crystallized intelligence is accumulated knowledge.

questions.q: Why would the authors say the 2,800 forecasters might not be typical of the general population?
options: They were motivated volunteers, not a randomly selected sample
They were all already professional analysts of world events by trade
They were too few for any comparison to be possible
They were chosen by the authors for their high test scores
optionExplain: Random selection is what makes a sample representative; these people chose themselves.
The text describes volunteers who read a blog or article, not paid professionals.
Numbers are not the issue; how they were chosen is.
They were not chosen by test score; they volunteered and stayed with the work.
questions.explain: These people chose themselves, which a random draw does not do. The card next explains why that matters.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a self-selected group of volunteers cannot be assumed to reflect the population, so results must be compared with the general population.

questions.q: Random ____ is what ensures a sample is representative of the population it is drawn from.
questions.explain: The authors say random selection makes a sample representative; their volunteers lacked it.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a self-selected group of volunteers cannot be assumed to reflect the population, so results must be compared with the general population.

questions.q: A gym surveys only members who stay to fill in a long form. Using the authors' logic, what follows about the results?
options: They cannot be assumed to reflect all members, let alone the public
They reflect all members, since each answered for themselves
They reflect the public, since gym members come from the general public
They are worthless, so nothing can be drawn from them
optionExplain: A self-selected sample lacks the random selection that makes it representative.
Self-report does not cure self-selection; those who stayed may differ from those who left.
Members of one gym are a particular slice, and the form-fillers a narrower one.
The authors do not say the data are useless; they ask for the right comparison.
questions.explain: Those motivated enough to stay differ from those who did not, so the sample cannot be assumed representative.
questions.rule: No random selection, no assumption of representativeness.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the volunteers reflected the population at large because thousands signed up.
questions.explain: Large numbers do not give representativeness. Random selection does, and the volunteers lacked it.
questions.rule: Numbers do not replace random selection.

questions.q: What does the authors' fix require when judging how smart superforecasters are?
options: Comparing them only with other forecasters in the same tournament
Dropping all test scores and judging by tournament results alone
Comparing them with other forecasters and with the US public
Raising the gift certificate so more people volunteer
optionExplain: That would compare volunteers with volunteers, leaving the representativeness problem untouched.
The authors still use the test scores; they add the population comparison.
Only a comparison with the general population shows how unusual the group is.
Paying more would not make the volunteers a random sample.
questions.explain: Because the volunteers are unusual, their scores have to be set against the general population as well as against other forecasters.
questions.teaches: To judge how intelligent superforecasters are, the authors compare them not only with other forecasters but with the general population of the United States.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a self-selected group of volunteers cannot be assumed to reflect the population, so results must be compared with the general population.

questions.q: A town's online poll on a new park gets 900 replies, mostly from daily users. What does the authors' point on volunteers suggest?
options: Treat 900 replies as the town's view, since 900 is quite a large number
Treat the 900 replies as a self-selected group, not the town's view
Weight the daily users more, since they know the park best
Throw the poll away and ask nobody else instead
optionExplain: Large numbers do not repair self-selection.
The respondents chose themselves, so they cannot be assumed to represent everyone.
That deepens the skew rather than correcting it.
The point is to be cautious about what it shows, not to ignore all evidence.
questions.explain: A poll answered by those who chose to answer cannot be assumed to represent the town, just as the volunteers could not be assumed to represent the public.
questions.teaches: The authors say we can be quite confident their volunteers were not average people, because they spent a big chunk of free time on hard geopolitical questions for a $250 gift certificate.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a self-selected group of volunteers cannot be assumed to reflect the population, so results must be compared with the general population.

questions.q: Compared with the general population, how did superforecasters score on the intelligence and knowledge tests?
options: Better than 99% of people, in genius territory
About average, matching the general population
Better than about 50% of people, only slightly above average
Better than about 80% of people, but not off the charts
optionExplain: This would match the top 1%, which most superforecasters did not reach.
The forecasters as a group, and especially superforecasters, scored above the public.
Both groups were higher than that; the chapter gives about 70% and 80%.
Well above average, yet far from genius territory.
questions.explain: They were well above average but not extreme. The card next gives the full picture.
questions.rule: According to the authors, intelligence and knowledge help up to a point, but superforecasting does not call for genius-level scores.

questions.q: Regular forecasters beat about 70% of the population on the tests; superforecasters beat about ____ percent.
questions.explain: Superforecasters placed higher than about 80% of the population.
questions.rule: According to the authors, intelligence and knowledge help up to a point, but superforecasting does not call for genius-level scores.

questions.q: A panel assumes only people in the top 1% by IQ can forecast well. What do the authors' findings say?
options: It is correct, since superforecasters all had scores in the top 1% of people
Most superforecasters fell well short of that level, so it is not needed
It is irrelevant, since the tests measured nothing about forecasters
It holds only for the very best forecaster in the tournament
optionExplain: The text says most did not.
The authors report that most superforecasters did not reach genius territory.
The tests did show above-average scores; they just did not show genius levels.
The authors do not single out the very best as a genius; Sandy's case is a different point.
questions.explain: Superforecasters scored high but not at genius level, so a top-1% requirement would be mistaken.
questions.rule: Smart enough helps; genius is not required.

questions.q: Which jump in test scores is larger, from the public to forecasters or from forecasters to superforecasters?
options: From forecasters to superforecasters, by far
They are equal, since both groups outscored the public by the same amount
Neither, since both groups scored identically on the tests
From the public to the forecasters, as the authors note
optionExplain: Regular forecasters were about 70th percentile and superforecasters about 80th, a smaller step.
The authors say the two jumps are not equal.
The groups scored differently, though not by much between forecasters and supers.
Forecasters beat about 70% of people and superforecasters about 80%, so the jump from the public is the big one.
questions.explain: The big jump is from the public to the forecasters. The authors read this as showing returns that fade beyond a threshold.
questions.rule: Most of the gain comes early, then it flattens.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say intelligence and knowledge help forecasting but add little beyond a certain threshold.
questions.explain: That is their reading of the test results for forecasters and superforecasters.
questions.rule: Help, not decisive.

questions.q: The authors tie their finding to a hunch from Daniel Kahneman. What did the hunch say about experts?
options: High-powered experts would forecast little better than attentive newspaper readers
Subject experts would forecast far better than attentive newspaper readers would
Experts would do worse than chance, since they overthink problems
Readers of the New York Times would outscore all other groups of forecasters tested
optionExplain: This hunch matches a threshold effect: extra expertise adds little.
This is the opposite of the hunch.
The hunch was that experts would be not much better, not worse than chance.
The hunch compared experts with attentive readers, and made no claim about top rank.
questions.explain: Kahneman's hunch was that high-powered experts would not forecast much better than attentive readers of the New York Times.
questions.teaches: Daniel Kahneman once shared a hunch that high-powered subject-matter experts would not be much better forecasters than attentive readers of the New York Times.
questions.rule: According to the authors, intelligence and knowledge help up to a point, but superforecasting does not call for genius-level scores.

questions.q: What went wrong in the forecast behind the escalation of the Vietnam war, according to the authors?
options: Too much analysis delayed the decisions until it was too late
The planners lacked access to any intelligence about the region at the time
Certainty with no serious analysis, until 1967 and after the decisions
The planners were less intelligent than their critics
optionExplain: The authors say analysis came late, not that it delayed anything.
The case is not about missing information but about untested assumptions.
The authors say no serious analysis was done until 1967, years after the decisions.
The point is that these were the best and the brightest, not less intelligent.
questions.explain: The certainty was not based on serious analysis. The card next shows why the authors cite it.
questions.rule: According to the authors, smart people can forecast badly; it is how intelligence is used, not the raw amount, that matters.

questions.q: McNamara and colleagues were famously dubbed one of the best and the ____.
questions.explain: McNamara was called one of the best and the brightest, which is why the case shows cleverness is not enough.
questions.rule: According to the authors, smart people can forecast badly; it is how intelligence is used, not the raw amount, that matters.

questions.q: A brilliant lawyer predicts a merger will fail but has not examined why the other side would walk away. Which authors' lesson fits?
options: Brilliance is enough, so her prediction deserves trust
Lawyers should not forecast, since they argue for a living rather than for accuracy
The merger will fail, because brilliant people are mostly right
A sharp mind does not replace checking the assumptions behind a forecast
optionExplain: The McNamara case is told to show that brilliance is not enough.
The authors do not reject a profession; they point to unexamined assumptions.
The case shows brilliant people can be wrong with great confidence.
McNamara's team failed to analyze its assumptions critically.
questions.explain: The lesson is to examine the assumptions behind a forecast, not to lean on the forecaster's brilliance.
questions.rule: Smart and unexamined is still unexamined.

questions.q: True or false: In the McNamara case the authors point to certainty without serious analysis, not to a lack of intelligence.
questions.explain: These men were called the best and the brightest; the failing was in how the power was used.
questions.rule: The failure was in use, not in capacity.

questions.q: What does the authors' Vietnam case say about the timing of serious analysis of the key forecast?
options: None took place until 1967, years after the decisions to escalate
It was done before escalation and then ignored by the planners
It was done in 1967 and showed the planners had been right all along
It was never done at all, so the question remains open
optionExplain: The analysis of this critical forecast came well after the decisions.
The authors say no serious analysis existed before 1967.
The timing is given to show the analysis came late, not to vindicate anyone.
The analysis was done in 1967, just too late to guide the decisions.
questions.explain: The assumption that one fall would topple the region was acted on long before anyone tested it.
questions.teaches: No serious analysis of the critical Vietnam forecast was conducted until 1967, years after the decisions to escalate had been made.
questions.rule: According to the authors, smart people can forecast badly; it is how intelligence is used, not the raw amount, that matters.

questions.q: A chess master and a beginner both forecast a tournament's winner. The master gives a confident answer without checking assumptions. What should we conclude?
options: Trust the master, since rank reflects crunching power
Trust the beginner, since novices tend to forecast better
Confidence plus rank does not guarantee accuracy; method matters
Neither forecast can be judged, since forecasting is a matter of luck
optionExplain: The authors argue crunching power alone does not settle accuracy.
The authors never claim that novices beat experts.
The authors say crunching power is not what counts; how you use it does.
The authors do not take that view; they say method separates good forecasts.
questions.explain: Ability does not substitute for examining assumptions, whatever the forecaster's standing.
questions.teaches: McNamara wrote that they failed to analyze their assumptions critically, then or later, which the authors cite as the source of the flawed foundations.
questions.rule: According to the authors, smart people can forecast badly; it is how intelligence is used, not the raw amount, that matters.

questions.q: Faced with the Chicago piano-tuner puzzle, how does Enrico Fermi's approach differ from most people's?
options: He looks the answer up in a directory before making any guess at all
He breaks it into smaller questions instead of a single number
He refuses to guess at all, since the data are missing
He asks a piano expert and adopts the expert's number
optionExplain: Fermi's students had no yellow pages; the approach does not depend on looking up the answer.
Fermi expected students to estimate by breaking the question down.
Guessing is not eliminated; it is moved into visible steps.
The method depends on a visible chain of reasoning, not on adopting someone else's number.
questions.explain: Fermi asked what information would allow an answer. The card next lays out the idea.
questions.rule: According to the authors, replace one question you cannot answer with several smaller ones whose guesses you can inspect.

questions.q: Most people's first guess comes out of a black ____ with no visible reasoning.
questions.explain: The authors describe the unexamined guess as coming out of a black box.
questions.rule: According to the authors, replace one question you cannot answer with several smaller ones whose guesses you can inspect.

questions.q: To estimate the number of coffee shops in Leeds, which first move follows the Fermi approach?
options: Name the number that feels about right and move on
Search for the answer online and copy the number that is found there
Ask what facts would give the answer, such as customers per day
Wait until every needed fact is known with certainty
optionExplain: This is the black-box guess that Fermi's approach replaces.
The point of Fermi-izing is the visible reasoning, not copying a number.
Breaking the question into facts that determine the answer is the Fermi move.
Fermi-izing proceeds with rough estimates, not certainties.
questions.explain: The first step is to ask what information would allow an answer, then guess each piece.
questions.rule: Ask what would have to be true, then guess in the open.

questions.q: After Fermi-izing, what typically happens to the accuracy of the estimate compared with the first black-box guess?
options: It gets worse, since each separate guess adds a new error to the total
It tends to be more accurate than the first black-box number
It is always exact, since each sub-guess is checked
It stays the same, since a guess is a guess
optionExplain: Errors add, but the authors say the net result is better overall.
The authors say the net result tends to be a more accurate estimate.
The sub-guesses are still guesses; the claim is only that the net result tends to improve.
The authors say separating the knowable from the unknowable helps accuracy.
questions.explain: Guessing remains, but the process becomes visible and the net estimate tends to improve.
questions.rule: Guesses you can inspect beat guesses you cannot.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Fermi-izing removes the need to guess.
questions.explain: Guessing is not eliminated; it is brought into the open where it can be inspected.
questions.rule: Fermi-izing exposes guesses, it does not remove them.

questions.q: The authors say that to Fermi-ize a question you must overcome a deep-rooted fear. What is it?
options: The fear of numbers, since the method needs a lot of arithmetic
The fear of experts, since the method replaces their advice entirely
The fear of silence, since the method needs long pauses
The fear of looking dumb, since Fermi-izing dares us to be wrong
optionExplain: The fear named is of looking foolish, not of arithmetic.
The text does not say this.
Pauses appear only in the black-box description.
The authors write that Fermi-izing dares us to be wrong, so we must overcome the fear of looking dumb.
questions.explain: Putting numbers on the page invites being wrong in public, which is the fear to overcome.
questions.teaches: Fermi-izing dares us to be wrong, so we must overcome our deep-rooted fear of looking dumb.
questions.rule: According to the authors, replace one question you cannot answer with several smaller ones whose guesses you can inspect.

questions.q: What is the last step in turning the four piano facts into a number of tuners?
options: Divide total tuning hours by the hours one tuner works a year
Multiply the number of pianos by the hours each tuning takes
Add the tunings per year to the number of pianos
Divide the number of pianos by the number of people in Chicago
optionExplain: Total work divided by a tuner's annual hours gives the number of tuners.
This gives total work, which is only part of the calculation.
Adding unlike quantities does not give tuners.
That gives pianos per person, an input and not the answer.
questions.explain: The final division gives tuners. The card next shows the four facts.
questions.rule: According to the authors, total tuning work divided by one tuner's annual hours gives the number of tuners.

questions.q: Put the steps of the piano-tuner breakdown in order.
items: Estimate how many pianos Chicago has
Estimate how often a piano is tuned in a year and how long it takes
Work out the total tuning hours needed
Divide by the hours one tuner works in a year
questions.explain: Pianos, tuning frequency and duration give total work; dividing by one tuner's hours gives the number of tuners.
questions.rule: According to the authors, total tuning work divided by one tuner's annual hours gives the number of tuners.

questions.q: To estimate how many taxi drivers a city needs, which set of facts follows the piano-tuner pattern?
options: Trips a day, time per trip, and hours one driver works
City population, average age, and average income of residents
Number of cars, their colour, and their make
The number of taxi companies and their start dates
optionExplain: Total work in the city, divided by the work one worker supplies, mirrors the piano calculation.
These describe people but do not give the amount of taxi work.
These details do not combine into work done per driver.
This is a count of firms, not of work to be done.
questions.explain: Total work divided by what one worker can supply is the structure the piano example uses.
questions.rule: Total work divided by one worker's capacity.

questions.q: In the piano calculation, what happens to the estimated number of tuners if each tuning takes longer?
options: It goes down, because tuners work faster
It stays the same, because pianos are fixed
It goes up, because total tuning work rises
It cannot be told without knowing the population
optionExplain: Tuning time is the length of each job, not tuner speed in the formula.
Fixing pianos does not stop total work from rising.
Longer tuning raises total work; the divisor stays the same.
The formula depends on the stated facts, not on population directly.
questions.explain: More hours per tuning means more total hours, which means more tuners for the same tuner hours.
questions.rule: More work per job means more workers.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that exchanging one unanswerable question for four was a wasted effort.
questions.explain: They say it is not wasted: breaking the question down lets us separate the knowable from the unknowable.
questions.rule: Four easier questions beat one impossible one.

questions.q: In a related use, the authors turn the number of pianos into a smaller question about people. What do they ask first?
options: How many piano makers are there in the United States?
How many people are there in Chicago?
How many tuning appointments are on the calendar?
How many piano lessons are given in a year?
optionExplain: The authors do not bring in makers of pianos.
They break pianos into people times the share who own one, plus institutions.
Appointments are part of what the estimate is trying to produce.
Lessons are not part of the breakdown.
questions.explain: The pianos question is itself broken down into smaller ones, starting with the population.
questions.teaches: The authors break the pianos question down again, starting with how many people live in Chicago.
questions.rule: According to the authors, total tuning work divided by one tuner's annual hours gives the number of tuners.

questions.q: The authors want a number for Chicago's population but are unsure. What do they do?
options: Pick the single number that first comes to mind and then keep it
Leave the item out and estimate the tuners without it
Use the population of the largest city, New York
Set a range they are 90% sure holds it, then take the midpoint
optionExplain: That is the black-box guess the authors want to replace.
Population feeds the pianos figure, so leaving it out would break the chain.
The authors place Chicago third, after New York and Los Angeles, and do not substitute another city.
They set a 90% confidence interval and used its midpoint.
questions.explain: A confidence interval narrows a guess. The card next explains how.
questions.rule: According to the authors, name each missing number, give it a rough value and keep the guesses visible.

questions.q: A confidence interval, in the authors' sense, is a range you are ____ percent sure contains the right answer.
questions.explain: The authors define it as a range you are 90% sure contains the right answer.
questions.rule: According to the authors, name each missing number, give it a rough value and keep the guesses visible.

questions.q: You think a stadium holds between 40,000 and 60,000 fans, 90% sure. Using the midpoint rule, what single starting guess follows?
options: 40,000, the safe low end of the range
50,000, the midpoint of the range
60,000, the generous top of the range
The average of 40,000 and the previous guess
optionExplain: The low end would bias the estimate down; the authors choose the midpoint.
The authors take the midpoint when they cannot say where in the range the answer lies.
The top is as arbitrary as the bottom; the midpoint balances them.
No previous guess is given; the midpoint is the rule shown.
questions.explain: With no sign of where the answer lies, the midpoint of the range is the neutral starting guess.
questions.rule: Range first, then midpoint.

questions.q: In the authors' calculation, a tuner works 2,000 hours before travel. If travel took nothing, how many tuners would the 100,000 hours need?
options: 62.5, the number the authors reached
200, since each tuner works fewer hours
100, since 100,000 divided by 1,000 is 100
50, since 100,000 divided by 2,000 is 50
optionExplain: 62.5 includes the 20% travel reduction, to 1,600 hours.
Fewer hours would raise the number, but removing travel increases hours.
1,000 hours is not a number from the calculation.
Without subtracting travel time, a tuner works 2,000 hours, giving 50 tuners.
questions.explain: Removing the travel cut raises annual hours from 1,600 to 2,000, so fewer tuners are needed.
questions.rule: More hours per tuner means fewer tuners.

questions.q: True or false: The authors label several numbers in their piano-tuner estimate as black-box guesses.
questions.explain: They say so openly, for instance for how often pianos are tuned and how long a tuning takes.
questions.rule: Visible guesses are still guesses.

questions.q: The authors reached 62.5 tuners. What do they say to estimate for the final answer?
options: Sixty-three piano tuners in Chicago
Sixty-two piano tuners in Chicago
Fifty piano tuners in Chicago
Eighty-three piano tuners in Chicago
optionExplain: They round 62.5 to sixty-three.
Rounding 62.5 down would be a different convention than the one they state.
Fifty is what no-travel hours would give, not the authors' result.
Eighty-three is the directory listing count, a separate figure.
questions.explain: The authors round 62.5 up to sixty-three, then compare with the yellow pages.
questions.teaches: The authors' final estimate was sixty-three piano tuners in Chicago, rounded from 62.5.
questions.rule: According to the authors, name each missing number, give it a rough value and keep the guesses visible.

questions.q: How did the authors' estimate of piano tuners compare with a count from the Chicago yellow pages?
options: It was exactly right, matching the yellow pages entry for entry
It was far off, which shows guessing cannot work
It looked surprisingly close, though the listings had duplicates
It could not be checked, since the yellow pages were not available
optionExplain: Duplicates mean the benchmark is uncertain, and the numbers differ.
The authors read the gap as small given the guesswork.
The yellow pages gave eighty-three listings, with duplicates, against sixty-three.
Levitin had counted listings in the yellow pages.
questions.explain: The estimate looked surprisingly close. The card next explains what that shows.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a visible chain of rough guesses can land near the truth, which is why the habit helps forecasters.

questions.q: Levitin found ____ piano-tuner listings in the Chicago yellow pages, though many were duplicates.
questions.explain: The count was eighty-three, with duplicates, so the true number is uncertain.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a visible chain of rough guesses can land near the truth, which is why the habit helps forecasters.

questions.q: A cafe owner Fermi-izes weekly cup sales, then checks them against receipts that double-count refunds. How should she read the match?
options: As proof the method is exact, since the numbers are close
As proof the method failed, since receipts and estimate differ
As meaningless, since receipts can never check an estimate
As rough support only, since the benchmark itself has errors
optionExplain: The authors do not claim exactness from one close comparison.
Small gaps are expected with rough estimates and flawed records.
The receipts are an imperfect check, not a useless one.
The authors treat the yellow-pages count as uncertain because of duplicates.
questions.explain: A close match to an imperfect benchmark is encouraging but not proof.
questions.rule: Check estimates against data, and note the data's flaws.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the yellow pages gave an exact count of Chicago's piano tuners.
questions.explain: Many listings were duplicates, so the precise number was uncertain.
questions.rule: Even the benchmark can be fuzzy.

questions.q: How do the authors describe Fermi estimation's place in teaching?
options: They are part of the curriculum in many physics and engineering faculties
They are banned in physics classes, because they depend so heavily on guessing
They are taught only to forecasters, not to scientists
They are taught as a party game with no scientific use
optionExplain: The authors say such estimate problems are taught, for example estimating pizza eaten by a university's students.
The authors report the opposite.
The authors say physics and engineering faculties teach them.
The authors present them as serious estimation practice.
questions.explain: Estimation puzzles are part of the curriculum in many physics and engineering faculties.
questions.teaches: Fermi problems, such as estimating the square inches of pizza eaten by all University of Maryland students in a semester, are part of the curriculum in many physics and engineering faculties.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a visible chain of rough guesses can land near the truth, which is why the habit helps forecasters.

questions.q: Why did Sandy Sillman welcome Fermi estimation when the authors shared it with superforecasters?
options: It replaced the need for data in his atmospheric models and in his science
It was new to him and he found it puzzling at first
It was critical to his atmospheric-model work and part of his thinking
It was useful only for forecasting, not for his science
optionExplain: He described it as part of his thinking, not as a substitute for data.
He said it was already part of how he thinks.
He said it became a part of his natural way of thinking.
He said it was critical to his science job.
questions.explain: Sandy said Fermi estimation was so critical to his work with atmospheric models that it became part of his natural way of thinking.
questions.teaches: Sandy Sillman said Fermi estimation was critical to his work with atmospheric models and had become a part of his natural way of thinking.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a visible chain of rough guesses can land near the truth, which is why the habit helps forecasters.

questions.q: What did the tournament question about Arafat ask forecasters?
options: Whether Israel had ordered Arafat's death
Whether French or Swiss inquiries would find elevated polonium
Whether Arafat died of natural illness or poison
Whether Arafat's widow would permit further tests of his remains
optionExplain: This is the different question that many hunches answer.
It asked about the test results, not about who was responsible.
The question asked about test findings, not about the cause of death.
Permission had already been given before the question was posed.
questions.explain: The question concerned test findings. The card next reads it closely.
questions.rule: According to the authors, read a forecasting question exactly as written, because it may ask less than the story it sits in.

questions.q: The question asked whether either the French or Swiss inquiries would find elevated levels of ____ in Arafat's remains.
questions.explain: It asked about polonium findings in the remains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, read a forecasting question exactly as written, because it may ask less than the story it sits in.

questions.q: A news item asks whether an audit will find unusual payments. A reader's hunch is that the CEO is honest. Which flaw matches this case?
options: It uses a confident tone, which weakens any forecast
It ignores the firm's history, which the question requires forecasters to cover
It answers a question about the CEO's guilt, not about the audit's findings
It trusts a feeling, and a feeling cannot inform any forecast
optionExplain: Tone is not the flaw; the mismatch with the question is.
History may help later, but the first flaw is the mismatch.
The hunch about guilt does not directly answer a question about audit findings.
The authors do not rule out all hunches, just the failure to answer the question asked.
questions.explain: The hunch speaks to guilt, while the question concerns what the inquiry will find.
questions.rule: Answer the question asked.

questions.q: True or false: The tournament question asked whether French or Swiss inquiries would find elevated polonium.
questions.explain: It asked about test findings in the remains, not about who was responsible.
questions.rule: The finding, not the culprit.

questions.q: What detail about the tests could make a yes answer possible even if Israel played no part?
options: Both inquiries had to agree on a positive result for it to count
Only one of the two inquiries had to find elevated polonium
Neither inquiry could report a result before 2012
The tests were on belongings, not the body
optionExplain: The question used 'either', not 'both'.
The question says 'either the French or Swiss', so one positive suffices.
The question refers to inquiries after the exhumation, and timing is not the point.
The question was about the remains of Arafat's body.
questions.explain: Because 'either' is enough, the wording itself raises the chance of yes compared with a demand for both.
questions.teaches: Only one of the two European teams had to get a positive result for the correct answer to be yes.
questions.rule: According to the authors, read a forecasting question exactly as written, because it may ask less than the story it sits in.

questions.q: In 2006 Alexander Litvinenko, a Russian former spy, was murdered with polonium-210. How does the authors' text use this fact?
options: It proves that polonium-210 was also used to kill Arafat himself in 2004
It shows polonium-210 is harmless in small amounts
It shows Swiss researchers invented the polonium test
It made the 2012 polonium finding on his belongings look ominous
optionExplain: The text only says it was ominous, not that it was proof.
The authors say polonium-210 can be deadly if ingested.
The text gives Swiss researchers a role, but not that.
The authors say the finding was ominous because polonium-210 had been used on Litvinenko.
questions.explain: The Litvinenko case gave the polonium finding its ominous edge, without answering the question asked.
questions.teaches: Polonium-210 is a radioactive element that can be deadly if ingested, and it was used to murder Alexander Litvinenko in 2006.
questions.rule: According to the authors, read a forecasting question exactly as written, because it may ask less than the story it sits in.

questions.q: How do the authors say most people turn a hunch into a probability?
options: They match the feeling's strength to a number: a shout becomes 95%
They collect base rates and then adjust them for the case's specifics
They average the views of several friends and use that
They break the question into parts and guess each
optionExplain: Strong feeling maps straight to an extreme probability.
That is what the superforecasters do, later in the chapter.
Averaging views is not how the authors describe the hunch.
That is the Fermi approach the authors recommend instead.
questions.explain: The strength of the feeling becomes the number. The card next names this.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the strength of a hunch is not a forecast; an unexamined hunch cannot be checked for errors.

questions.q: The authors call the hunch that arrives the moment you read a question the tip-of-your-____ perspective.
questions.explain: They call it the tip-of-your-nose perspective.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the strength of a hunch is not a forecast; an unexamined hunch cannot be checked for errors.

questions.q: A fan reads a question on whether her home team will win and feels 90% certain because she loves the team. Which description fits?
options: A tip-of-your-nose forecast: the feeling's strength became the number
An outside-view forecast: she started from the base rate of home-team wins
A Fermi estimate: she broke the question into parts
A synthesis of views: she combined two opposing views
optionExplain: The feeling's strength became the probability, with no visible reasoning.
She did not look at any base rate.
She did not break it down.
She used one gut feeling.
questions.explain: A forecast from the immediate feeling, with no reasoning to inspect, is the tip-of-your-nose perspective.
questions.rule: If a number comes from the strength of a feeling, it is tip-of-your-nose.

questions.q: Sort each habit by whether it is the tip-of-your-nose approach or the Fermi-style approach.

items.t: Turn the strength of a gut feeling into a probability
Ask what would have to be true for the answer to be yes
Give a TV-pundit-style instant call
List what facts would allow an answer, then guess each

questions.explain: The hunch maps feeling to number from a black box; the Fermi style opens the reasoning to inspection.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the strength of a hunch is not a forecast; an unexamined hunch cannot be checked for errors.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that if a hunch contains an error, you will not catch it.
questions.explain: The hunch comes from a black box, so its error stays hidden.
questions.rule: Louder is not more accurate.

questions.q: The authors compare an uncaught hunch error to a fast wrong answer on the Cognitive Reflection Test. What does the comparison show?
options: Test-takers who answer fast are usually correct, so speed is a virtue
The test measures knowledge of politics
A fast first answer may be wrong, and the error goes unnoticed
Careful people should give the ten-cent answer
optionExplain: Their point is the opposite.
The test is mentioned for the quick-answer trap.
The quick answer feels right and hides its error.
Ten cents is the wrong quick answer on that test.
questions.explain: Both show how an unexamined first answer can hide an error.
questions.teaches: Blurting out 'Ten cents!' on the Cognitive Reflection Test is the authors' example of an unexamined first answer whose error you do not catch.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the strength of a hunch is not a forecast; an unexamined hunch cannot be checked for errors.

questions.q: What do the authors say is wrong with the hunch that Israel is to blame, as an answer to the tournament question?
options: It states too high a probability for the event in question
It answers a different question from the one asked
It relies on poor information about the region
It ignores that the inquiries took years to report
optionExplain: The problem is not the size of the number but the question it answers.
The question asked about polonium findings, not about who did it.
The authors do not blame information quality.
The timing is not what they flag.
questions.explain: The hunch responds to a different question. The card next names the swap.
questions.rule: According to the authors, check that your answer responds to the question actually asked, not a nearby easier one.

questions.q: The authors call the swap of a hard question for an easy one a classic bait and ____.
questions.explain: System 1 pulled a classic bait and switch.
questions.rule: According to the authors, check that your answer responds to the question actually asked, not a nearby easier one.

questions.q: Match each statement to the question it actually answers.
pairs: Will either the French or Swiss inquiries find elevated polonium?
Polonium decays quickly, so it may not be detectable
Can tests detect polonium after years?
questions.explain: Hunches about Israel address who did it; only the tournament wording and the science point address the finding.
questions.rule: According to the authors, check that your answer responds to the question actually asked, not a nearby easier one.

questions.q: A forecaster notes that the tournament asks about test results, then asks whether tests can detect polonium after years. What is she doing?
options: Making a bait-and-switch by changing the question that was asked
Copying another forecaster's answer
Starting with the tip-of-your-nose perspective
Staying with the question asked and breaking it into parts
optionExplain: She does the opposite; she holds to the question.
Nothing suggests copying.
That would mean answering from a hunch.
She stays with the asked question and unpacks it.
questions.explain: She avoids the swap by asking what the question needs to be true.
questions.rule: Stay with the question asked.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the bait and switch can be avoided by fixing the forecast at 50%.
questions.explain: They say the trap can be avoided by Fermi-izing, which means unpacking the question, not setting a fixed number.
questions.rule: Avoid the switch by unpacking, not by hedging.

questions.q: A manager asked whether Q3 sales will exceed target answers whether the sales team is good. What does the authors' lesson say?
options: Nothing, since team quality settles sales
She swapped a Q3 sales question for one about team quality
She should have predicted the opposite direction for sales
She should have asked the team for an opinion
optionExplain: Team quality may inform, but it is not the question asked.
The team-quality question is easier and nearby, which is the bait and switch.
The lesson concerns which question is answered, not which direction.
Asking is not the fix the authors describe.
questions.explain: Answering a question about a person instead of the event asked is the same swap.
questions.teaches: The authors say System 1 replaced a hard question with an easy one that was not asked, a swap that went unnoticed.
questions.rule: According to the authors, check that your answer responds to the question actually asked, not a nearby easier one.

questions.q: What was Bill Flack's first step on the Arafat question?
options: Researching Israel's motives for wanting Arafat dead
Estimating the share of poisoning suspicions that later prove true
Asking his teammates which answer they favoured
Checking whether polonium could still be detected years later
optionExplain: That belongs to a later stage, if at all.
That is a base-rate step he takes after unpacking.
Teammates helped by posting the Swiss report, but opinion polling came later.
His first step was about science, not politics.
questions.explain: His first step was detection. The card next shows his route.
questions.rule: According to the authors, unpack a question into what it would take for yes and for no, and start with the step that comes first.

questions.q: Put Bill Flack's early steps in order.
items: Ask what it would take for yes and what for no
Check that polonium can still be detected on old remains
List ways remains could have become contaminated
Note that only one of the two teams needs a positive result
questions.explain: He unpacked yes and no, checked the science first, then listed contamination routes and noticed the 'either' wording.
questions.rule: According to the authors, unpack a question into what it would take for yes and for no, and start with the step that comes first.

questions.q: To forecast whether a bridge will open by June, which first step best copies Bill Flack's style?
options: Ask what would have to be true for it to open, and for it not to
Read the contractor's press release and adopt the date it gives
Say 50% and wait for more news
Find the official responsible and ask for a promise
optionExplain: Unpacking into the conditions for yes and for no is his method.
A press release is a view, not an unpacking of the question.
A fixed number avoids the work of unpacking.
That asks for a promise, not for conditions.
questions.explain: Listing what must hold for yes and for no gives the road map.
questions.rule: Ask what it would take for yes and for no.

questions.q: True or false: Bill Flack's first step was the science of whether polonium could still be detected.
questions.explain: This step had nothing to do with politics, and he read the Swiss team's report to check it.
questions.rule: Start with the first factual condition.

questions.q: Bill listed other ways remains could be contaminated. Why did each added route matter?
options: Each route lowered it, because more stories are harder to believe
Routes did not matter, only the strongest suspect did
Each added route raised the probability of contamination
Each route matters only if tested one by one in a lab
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite.
The authors say additional routes mattered.
The authors say each additional way increased the probability.
The text uses routes to raise probability, not to require tests.
questions.explain: Several independent ways to get a positive result raise the chance that at least one happens.
questions.teaches: Each additional way Arafat's body could have been contaminated with polonium increased the probability that it was, including postmortem contamination by a Palestinian faction.
questions.rule: According to the authors, unpack a question into what it would take for yes and for no, and start with the step that comes first.

questions.q: A company asks whether a product will ship on time, and a planner lists ways delay could occur. How is that like Bill's list?
options: It shows the outcome is unlikely, since many things must go right
It replaces the base rate, which is then unnecessary
It matters only if the routes are all equally likely
Many routes to one outcome each raise its chance
optionExplain: Here the outcome is delay, and more routes to delay raise its chance.
The authors use the base rate next, not instead.
Nothing in the text requires equal likelihood.
More ways for an outcome to occur raise its probability.
questions.explain: As more separate routes lead to a result, the result becomes more probable.
questions.teaches: Bill noted that only one of the two European teams had to get a positive result for the answer to be yes, another factor nudging the probability up.
questions.rule: According to the authors, unpack a question into what it would take for yes and for no, and start with the step that comes first.

questions.q: Asked how likely the Renzetti family is to have a pet, what do superforecasters do first?
options: Find the share of American households with a pet
Study the family's names and ages for hints about their tastes
Ask whether a five-year-old can look after a pet
Take the answer to be 50%, then adjust for the family
optionExplain: They start with the base rate for the broader class.
That is the inside view, which superforecasters take second.
That is a detail of the case, and so belongs to the inside view.
Fifty percent is not derived from the class, as the base rate is.
questions.explain: They begin with the share of households. The card next names this.
questions.rule: According to the authors, begin with how common the thing is in the broader class, then adjust for the particulars.

questions.q: Match each term to what it means in the chapter.
pairs: How common something is within a broader class
Kahneman's term for starting from the base rate
The specifics of the particular case
questions.explain: The base rate is the outside view; the specifics are the inside view.
questions.rule: According to the authors, begin with how common the thing is in the broader class, then adjust for the particulars.

questions.q: To forecast whether a new restaurant will survive five years, which is the outside-view starting point?
options: The chef's training and the menu's originality
The owner's confidence that the plan will work
The share of new restaurants in similar towns that survive
The landlord's own account of the street's foot traffic and rents
optionExplain: These are details of the case: the inside view.
Confidence is a feeling about the case, not a class rate.
This is the base rate for the broader class.
This is also a detail of the specific location.
questions.explain: The outside view asks how often it happens among cases of this class.
questions.rule: Outside view: the class rate. Inside view: this case's story.

questions.q: The base rate for pets is high, but the family is small and its child is five. What do the authors do with the details?
options: Drop the base rate and use only the details of the case
Use them to adjust the starting figure up or down
Average the base rate with a hunch of 50%
Ignore the details because stories mislead
optionExplain: The base rate stays as the starting point.
The inside view adjusts the outside-view starting point.
Averaging with an arbitrary hunch is not what the authors describe.
The details are used, second, to adjust.
questions.explain: Details move the starting figure; they do not replace it.
questions.rule: Anchor on the class, adjust for the case.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say superforecasters start with the base rate and then use the case's details to adjust.
questions.explain: The details are used second, to move the outside-view figure up or down.
questions.rule: Outside first, not outside only.

questions.q: A few minutes of searching gave the authors a figure for American pet ownership. What was it?
options: About 38% of all American households own a pet
About 73% of American households own a pet
About 62% of American households own a pet
About 50% of American households own a pet
optionExplain: Thirty-eight percent is the share without pets.
Seventy-three percent is a later, narrower figure for single-family homes.
This was the outside view in the Renzetti problem.
The authors found a specific figure; fifty is not it.
questions.explain: The starting estimate is the 62% of households that own a pet.
questions.teaches: A few minutes with Google told the authors that about 62% of American households own pets, which became the starting estimate.
questions.rule: According to the authors, begin with how common the thing is in the broader class, then adjust for the particulars.

questions.q: Why, according to the authors, do smart people so often skip the outside view?
options: They doubt statistics, since most statistics are thought to be unreliable
The inside view is concrete and storyable; the outside view is bare
They lack access to base rates, which are usually secret
They believe the outside view is always less accurate
optionExplain: The authors do not say that.
The inside view lends itself to storytelling and the outside view does not.
Base rates are often easy to find.
The authors argue the opposite.
questions.explain: The inside view is vivid. The card next shows an example.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a vivid story about one case can hide a plain pattern across the class.

questions.q: Noonan was struck that Bush's approval had risen to 47% four years after he left office, equal to President ____'s.
questions.explain: The rebound put Bush level with Obama at 47%.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a vivid story about one case can hide a plain pattern across the class.

questions.q: A business reporter finds it astonishing that a new CEO's shares rose in his first year. What outside-view check would help?
options: Ask how the CEO felt about the appointment
Ask what his personal strategy is for the first year
Ask whether other CEOs would have chosen differently
Ask how shares of firms with new CEOs usually move

Strategy is a detail of the case, not the class rate.
This explores alternatives, not the base rate.
The class pattern shows whether the rise is surprising.
questions.explain: The outside-view check is the typical pattern for the class.
questions.rule: Before reading meaning into a case, check the class pattern.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Noonan's finding that Bush's rating rose was astonishing evidence for her view.
questions.explain: They say presidential approval always rises after a president leaves office, so the rise was not surprising.
questions.rule: A pattern shared by the whole class is not special evidence.

questions.q: What did the outside view show about former presidents' approval, as the authors tell it?
options: Approval always rises after a president leaves office, even Nixon's
Approval falls after a president leaves, so Bush's rise is a surprise
Approval is flat after office, so Bush was unusual
Approval depends on the party of the successor

The authors say the opposite.
The authors say it always rises.
The text gives no such claim.
questions.explain: A rise is the usual pattern, which drains Bush's rise of surprise.
questions.teaches: Presidential approval always rises after a president leaves office; even Richard Nixon's number went up.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a vivid story about one case can hide a plain pattern across the class.

questions.q: A school head is amazed that test scores rose in the year after a new principal arrived. What mistake from the chapter does this risk?
options: Reading meaning into a case without checking the class pattern
Using the base rate when the specifics matter much more to the case
Ignoring the principal's arrival as a cause
Anchoring on a number spun on a wheel
optionExplain: The authors show that missing the outside view can produce illusory meaning.
The authors say the specifics matter second, not that they matter more.
The risk is in over-reading the case.
That is a different effect, from the anchoring experiments.
questions.explain: Without checking whether scores usually rise, the head may find meaning that is not there.
questions.teaches: Noonan, a Wall Street Journal columnist and former Reagan speechwriter, is the authors' example of a smart, accomplished person who skipped the outside view.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a vivid story about one case can hide a plain pattern across the class.

questions.q: If armed clashes between two countries recur about every five years, what does the outside view suggest for any one year?
options: A 50% chance, since either it happens or it does not
A 5% chance, taking the five years as the percentage
A 20% chance of a clash
An 80% chance, since clashes are due after four quiet years
optionExplain: That ignores the recurrence rate.
Five is a number of years, not a percentage.
One clash per five years gives one in five per year.
