questions.explain: High walls were normal in that wealthy neighbourhood; the secretive occupants were the unusual part.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the analysts faced a hard judgment on partial evidence, without the answer everyone has since learned.

questions.q: A reviewer later judges the analysts knowing how events ended. What does the author's remark about Abbottabad suggest?
options: The reviewer is best placed, since the ending shows what they ought to have known
Their judgments carry no weight, since each person is bound to be biased
The ending settles whether any one of the judgments was in fact sound
The analysts did not know then what is known now, so judge them by what they knew
optionExplain: Hindsight makes the ending look foreseeable, which is the very trap the remark warns about.
The chapter values the analysts' independent judgments and welcomes their differences.
The chapter later argues that outcome alone does not settle whether a judgment was sound.
Our reading: the author's pause on what the analysts knew points to judging by the evidence at the time.
questions.explain: Our reading: the author's pause on what the analysts knew then points to judging by the evidence at the time.
questions.teaches: The author says the compound's story was later dramatized in Zero Dark Thirty, whose scenes the chapter uses to compare fictional and real attitudes to uncertainty.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the analysts faced a hard judgment on partial evidence, without the answer everyone has since learned.

questions.q: In the film scene, what does the CIA director most want from his advisers?
options: That each adviser give a very different estimate to widen the range of views
That they all reach the same conclusion about whether bin Laden is there
That no adviser quote a number when saying how likely the claim might be
That the most senior adviser overrule the others before he makes his decision
optionExplain: A wide range is what he gets, and he dislikes it, so he cannot be asking for it.
He is exasperated by the lack of agreement, which is the point of the scene.
The advisers give percentages and he objects to their disagreement, not to numbers as such.
He wants consensus from everyone, not simply the view of the senior adviser.
questions.explain: He wants agreement. The card next shows why the authors disagree.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the fictional director wants agreement as proof of correctness, but agreement is not proof.

questions.q: The advisers around the table give figures such as 60% and ____ percent, and the fictional director sighs.
questions.explain: The chapter gives 60% and 80% as the figures that go around the table.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the fictional director wants agreement as proof of correctness, but agreement is not proof.

questions.q: A manager hears three analysts say 55%, 60% and 75% that a project finishes on time. How would the film's director feel?
options: Delight that the spread offers several independent views to work with
Indifference, because estimates given in percent carry no real meaning
Frustration that they disagree, as if agreement would prove the answer
Suspicion that one adviser must be lying whenever the numbers differ
optionExplain: Delight is the authors' attitude and the real Panetta's, not the film director's.
Nothing in the scene shows him dismissing percentages as meaningless.
The fictional director wants agreement; the authors call that a natural but mistaken wish.
The scene does not accuse any adviser of lying.
questions.explain: The fictional director treats disagreement as a problem. The authors say it is a mistake.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the fictional director wants agreement as proof of correctness, but agreement is not proof.

questions.q: Put these events of the Panetta scene in the order the chapter gives them.
items: The deputy director gives 60%
The next adviser concurs at 60%
A later adviser says 80%
The director sighs that it is a mess
questions.explain: The deputy director speaks first, the next person concurs at 60%, one says 80%, and the director sighs once all have spoken.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the fictional director wants agreement as proof of correctness, but agreement is not proof.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, agreement among independent advisers would prove their conclusion correct.
questions.explain: The authors say agreement is reassuring but is not proof; they treat universal agreement as a warning sign.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the fictional director wants agreement as proof of correctness, but agreement is not proof.

questions.q: A film wants to show a leader as decisive. Which choice fits the pattern the chapter criticises?
options: The leader demands one answer and treats a spread of estimates as a failure
The leader asks each expert for a private number and then compares all of them
The leader averages the numbers first and then asks each expert what they saw
The leader invites experts to say what they believe and not what is wanted
optionExplain: This matches the fictional director's reaction to the spread of 60% and 80%.
Private numbers compared side by side use the spread; the authors approve of this.
Averaging and then asking what each saw is the approach the authors suggest.
Inviting honest beliefs is what the real Panetta did.
questions.explain: Demanding one answer and treating spread as failure is the fictional director's error.
questions.teaches: The authors point out that the film's director later tells an aide that the others will not commit to yes or no because they are cowed.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the fictional director wants agreement as proof of correctness, but agreement is not proof.

questions.q: True or false: A smart executive should treat universal agreement among advisers as a warning sign.
questions.explain: The authors say so. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, treat a spread of independent judgments as a resource to average, and unanimity as a warning flag.

questions.q: A weighted ____ of the judgments gives those you respect most more say in the group's conclusion.
questions.explain: The text proposes simple averaging, or weighted averaging when some judgments deserve more say.
questions.rule: According to the authors, treat a spread of independent judgments as a resource to average, and unanimity as a warning flag.

questions.q: Five analysts rate a merger's chance of closing at 30%, 55%, 60%, 65% and 80%. What would the authors advise a board to do?
options: Combine them, say by a simple average of 58%, and treat the spread as useful
Ask the analysts to keep talking until all of them give the same single figure
Discard 30% and 80% as unusual and use only the middle three estimates
Take the figure from the most senior analyst and set the rest aside
optionExplain: The five values add to 290, so a simple average is 58%; the authors call averaging a good start.
Pressing for one figure produces the agreement the authors treat as a warning flag.
The authors do not tell the reader to discard extremes; they treat the spread as information.
Using one person's view throws away the other judgments the executive paid for.
questions.explain: The authors recommend synthesising the array of judgments, starting with a simple average.
questions.rule: According to the authors, treat a spread of independent judgments as a resource to average, and unanimity as a warning flag.

questions.q: All six advisers independently give exactly 70%. What would the authors say the executive should suspect?
options: That the number must be right, because six separate people arrived at it
That the advisers each used a different method and hit it by pure chance
That groupthink may have taken hold, since unanimity is a warning flag
That the executive should now round the figure up to a full 100%
optionExplain: Agreement feels like proof, but the authors warn that it can signal groupthink.
Different methods agreeing by chance is possible, but the chapter does not raise it.
A smart executive expects variation among independent thinkers and treats total agreement as a flag.
Rounding to certainty would contradict the whole chapter.
questions.explain: Total agreement among independent judges is unlikely, so it should raise suspicion.
questions.rule: According to the authors, treat a spread of independent judgments as a resource to average, and unanimity as a warning flag.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say weighted averaging is wrong because it gives some advisers more say than others.
questions.explain: They suggest it: those whose judgment the executive most respects can get more say in the collective conclusion.
questions.rule: According to the authors, treat a spread of independent judgments as a resource to average, and unanimity as a warning flag.

questions.q: Why do the authors expect independent advisers to differ even on the same evidence?
options: Each of them hides their true belief in order to protect their own reputation at work
They are different people with different training, experience and personalities
Probability is meaningless, so any number is as good as any other number
They are never shown the same evidence, because staff pick what each sees
optionExplain: Nothing in the chapter suggests dishonesty; honesty is what is encouraged.
That is the authors' reason, with the note that the evidence they see likely varies somewhat too.
The chapter argues that probabilities matter a great deal.
The authors say they may have looked at the same evidence and still differ.
questions.explain: People differ in education, training, experience and personality, so some spread is to be expected.
questions.teaches: The authors add that even if all looked at the same evidence, and there is likely some variation in what they saw, it is unlikely they would reach precisely the same conclusion.
questions.rule: According to the authors, treat a spread of independent judgments as a resource to average, and unanimity as a warning flag.

questions.q: Judgments in the real meeting varied. Which range did the real Panetta recall?
options: From fifty to fifty-five percent, all clustered close around even odds
From ninety-five to one hundred percent, with every person convinced
From zero to ten percent, with every person doubtful about the claim
From as low as thirty to forty percent to ninety percent and above
optionExplain: A tight cluster at even odds would make the meeting dull; he recalled a wide spread.
Some people were far less sure than that; he recalled low figures as well.
Nobody is reported as that doubtful; the lowest figures he recalled were 30 to 40%.
He said the judgments varied everywhere in between.
questions.explain: He recalled a wide spread. The card next shows how he reacted.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the real Panetta asked for honest, varied estimates and rejected certainty.

questions.q: The real Panetta said several times in the interview: Nothing is one ____ percent.
questions.explain: His line is Nothing is one hundred percent.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the real Panetta asked for honest, varied estimates and rejected certainty.

questions.q: A department head wants honest forecasts from staff. Following the real Panetta, what should she say?
options: Give me the figure the team has agreed on so that we avoid any conflict
Tell me what you actually believe, not what you think I want to hear
Keep your own view to yourself unless you are completely certain of it
Round your estimate to yes or no so that it is easier for me to act on
optionExplain: A pre-agreed figure removes the diversity he valued.
He encouraged people not to say what they thought he wanted to hear but what they believed.
He wanted uncertain beliefs too, not only certain ones.
He was comfortable with probabilities and did not ask for yes or no.
questions.explain: The real Panetta asks for honest beliefs.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the real Panetta asked for honest, varied estimates and rejected certainty.

questions.q: True or false: Unlike his film counterpart, the real Panetta welcomed the diversity of the estimates he heard.
questions.explain: He encouraged people to say what they believed, and he saw diverse views as a critical part of his job.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the real Panetta asked for honest, varied estimates and rejected certainty.

questions.q: A colleague says: the real Panetta wanted a single consensus number. What is the mistake?
options: He welcomed diverse views and saw gathering them as a critical part of his job
He wanted no number at all and asked staff only for written opinions
He asked staff to defer to whoever in the room had the most experience of such cases
He preferred that staff say what they thought he wanted to hear
optionExplain: The authors present him as the opposite of the film's director.
He did ask for estimates, so the wish for no numbers is not his.
He asked for individual beliefs and not deference.
He said the reverse of this.
questions.explain: The real Panetta wanted honest, varied judgments.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the real Panetta asked for honest, varied estimates and rejected certainty.

questions.q: Before the Abbottabad meeting, what had the real Panetta's career given him experience of?
options: Running spy networks abroad for decades without ever briefing a leader
Rejecting every estimate that came with a probability attached to it
Working only in military roles that carried no political duties at all
Presenting diverse views to the president as chief of staff
optionExplain: The chapter describes a political career, not a career as a spymaster.
He accepted probabilities and encouraged honest estimates.
His roles included Congress and White House posts, so they were political.
He was chief of staff to President Clinton and later secretary of defense under Obama.
questions.explain: As Clinton's chief of staff he considered gathering diverse views a core part of the job.
questions.teaches: Panetta was a former congressman, chief of staff to President Clinton and secretary of defense to President Obama, and as chief of staff he saw obtaining and presenting diverse views as critical.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the real Panetta asked for honest, varied estimates and rejected certainty.

questions.q: True or false: In the film, Maya refuses to give any estimate below certainty, apart from a 95% offered to calm the room.
questions.explain: She says a hundred percent and offers ninety-five because certainty freaks the others out. The card next explains the thinking.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the fictional director and Maya think with a two-setting mental dial: yes or no, with no degrees of maybe.

questions.q: The fictional director sees only two settings on his mental ____.
questions.explain: The authors describe a mental dial with two settings.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the fictional director and Maya think with a two-setting mental dial: yes or no, with no degrees of maybe.

questions.q: A coach demands a yes or no on whether the team will win, with no hedging. Which thinking is that?
options: A three-setting dial, where maybe is allowed as a middle position
A fine-grained dial that moves in small percentage steps like 62%
A two-setting dial, with only yes and no available
A weighted average that combines several different expert estimates
optionExplain: Maybe is the third setting, and the coach has ruled it out.
Fine percentage steps are the probabilistic thinking the chapter recommends later.
Only yes and no leaves out any degree of maybe.
Averaging combines judgments, which is a different move.
questions.explain: A yes-or-no demand is a two-setting dial.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the fictional director and Maya think with a two-setting mental dial: yes or no, with no degrees of maybe.

questions.q: Suppose Maya had said fifty percent instead. How would the fictional director have taken it?
options: As wisdom, since he welcomes a spread of judgments from his advisers
As proof that the compound was empty, since a hedge suggests no one there
As weakness, since he thinks that probabilities are for weaklings
As the best use of the information that was available to the group
optionExplain: Welcoming a spread is the real Panetta's attitude, not the film's.
Nothing in the scene ties a hedge to an empty compound.
Our reading: he equates hedging with weakness, as when he says the others are cowed.
The film's director wants confidence, not careful use of information.
questions.explain: He dismisses probabilities as weakness.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the fictional director and Maya think with a two-setting mental dial: yes or no, with no degrees of maybe.

questions.q: True or false: According to the chapter, Maya's 100% shows that the film's director fully understands uncertainty.
questions.explain: He wants a clean yes or no; the authors say he has no setting for degrees of maybe.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the fictional director and Maya think with a two-setting mental dial: yes or no, with no degrees of maybe.

questions.q: After the compound was found, how did Maya show her certainty over the following weeks?
options: She filed a probability report each week showing a steadily growing percentage figure
She asked for a vote among the advisers on whether the group should wait
She stopped speaking to the director until he finally agreed with her view
She wrote the count of elapsed days on her superior's window, up to 98, 99 and 100
optionExplain: Maya does not use probabilities in the film; she speaks in certainty.
No vote is shown; she acts alone.
The film shows her marking the days, not going silent.
The film shows her marking the delay in thick red ink.
questions.explain: Her day counts on the window dramatise the frustration of certainty.
questions.teaches: After the compound was discovered, Maya was so sure bin Laden was there that she wanted it bombed to rubble immediately.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the fictional director and Maya think with a two-setting mental dial: yes or no, with no degrees of maybe.

questions.q: True or false: A forecaster who said 100% and turned out right was therefore reasonable.
questions.explain: The authors say right outcome does not make an unreasonable certainty reasonable. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, judge a forecast by whether it fits the evidence, since the outcome cannot show that.

questions.q: Maya's claim was correct but more extreme than the evidence could support, so she was right but ____.
questions.explain: The authors call her right but unreasonable.
questions.rule: According to the authors, judge a forecast by whether it fits the evidence, since the outcome cannot show that.

questions.q: A trader says 100% that a stock will rise and it does. Which judgment fits the authors' view?
options: Right but unreasonable, because no ordinary evidence supports total certainty
Wrong but reasonable, because a lucky outcome never shows any real skill
Right and reasonable, because the result itself proves that the claim was sound
Unreasonable because the stock should in fact have gone down instead
optionExplain: A 100% claim cannot be supported by the evidence, even when the outcome is right.
That label fits a wrong outcome that came from a measured forecast, which is the opposite case.
Outcome cannot prove that a forecast was reasonable; this is the process-outcome point.
Nothing in the case says the stock should have fallen.
questions.explain: Certainty beyond the evidence is unreasonable even when the event happens.
questions.rule: According to the authors, judge a forecast by whether it fits the evidence, since the outcome cannot show that.

questions.q: Suppose the intelligence community had said 60% to 70% that Saddam had weapons of mass destruction, and was wrong. How would the authors describe it?
options: Right but unreasonable, since the result is what counts in the end
Wrong but reasonable, since a measured estimate fits the evidence
Right and reasonable, since 60% to 70% is close to certainty anyway
Wrong and unreasonable, since any estimate that fails must be careless
optionExplain: That label describes Maya: the outcome matched but the certainty went beyond the evidence.
It is the mirror image of Maya's case.
The estimate would have been wrong, since Saddam had no weapons of mass destruction.
A measured estimate was reasonable; failure alone does not make it careless.
questions.explain: Scaling back to 60% or 70% would be reasonable even if it turned out wrong.
questions.rule: According to the authors, judge a forecast by whether it fits the evidence, since the outcome cannot show that.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that even a tiny chance for each alternative would add up to 1%, 2%, 5% or more.
questions.explain: That sum is why 100% was more than the evidence could support.
questions.rule: According to the authors, judge a forecast by whether it fits the evidence, since the outcome cannot show that.

questions.q: The IC was once so sure Saddam had weapons of mass destruction that it did not explore what?
options: The possibility that the weapons were larger than the reports had said
The possibility that other countries held similar weapons in secret
The possibility that he did not have such weapons at all
The possibility that the evidence was being kept in Pakistan
optionExplain: Larger weapons are a worry the community did have, not a neglected alternative.
Other countries were not the point of the passage.
The author uses this to show why fine-grained distinctions matter.
Pakistan belongs to the bin Laden case, not the Iraq case.
questions.explain: Certainty closed off exploration of the alternative, and that is why 1% versus 0% matters.
questions.teaches: The intelligence community was once so sure Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction that it did not explore the possibility that he did not.
questions.rule: According to the authors, judge a forecast by whether it fits the evidence, since the outcome cannot show that.

questions.q: In Bowden's account, what confidence level did the CIA's team leader give that bin Laden was in the compound?
options: 60%, matching the figure that another officer gave
80%, which was about where most senior DNI officers stood
95%, with a second CIA officer agreeing
50%, the phrase the president later used to sum up
optionExplain: Sixty percent was the figure of another officer, not the team leader.
Eighty percent was about where most of the Directorate of National Intelligence officers stood.
He was almost sure, at ninety-five percent.
Fifty-fifty was the president's later summary, not any officer's estimate.
questions.explain: He put it at 95%. The card next shows the whole range.
questions.rule: According to Bowden, the president heard estimates from about 30% to 95% and treated the matter as one of probability.

questions.q: The book that gives this account is The Finish, by Mark ____.
questions.explain: Mark Bowden wrote The Finish: The Killing of Osama bin Laden.
questions.rule: According to Bowden, the president heard estimates from about 30% to 95% and treated the matter as one of probability.

questions.q: A panel of five gives 95%, 80%, 80%, 60% and 40% that a product will launch on time. Which reaction echoes the president's first remark?
options: These are degrees of likelihood, so this is a matter of probability
These five numbers are mere noise, so I will set all of them aside
The highest figure comes from the most confident, so it must be right
I need all five to give me one number before I can act on any
optionExplain: The president said, this is a probability thing.
Setting the numbers aside throws away information the panel has given.
Confidence is not the same as accuracy, a point the chapter makes later.
Insisting on one number is the fictional director's mistake.
questions.explain: Treating the spread as a matter of probability is the first step.
questions.rule: According to Bowden, the president heard estimates from about 30% to 95% and treated the matter as one of probability.

questions.q: Match each source in Bowden's account to the confidence level given.
pairs: Most Directorate of National Intelligence officers
questions.explain: The team leader said 95%; most of the four senior officers about 80%; another officer 60%; some as low as 40 or 30.
questions.rule: According to Bowden, the president heard estimates from about 30% to 95% and treated the matter as one of probability.

questions.q: True or false: Bowden's account says that some officers in the room put bin Laden's presence as low as 40 or even 30%.
questions.explain: Some Directorate of National Intelligence officers were that low, and another officer said 60%.
questions.rule: According to Bowden, the president heard estimates from about 30% to 95% and treated the matter as one of probability.

questions.q: How had the four senior officers at the Directorate of National Intelligence formed their views?
options: They had voted at a meeting and then reported the single result
They had copied the CIA team leader's figure and rounded it lower
They had been told by the president which range they should give
They had reviewed the case and each written out their own opinion
optionExplain: The account describes separate written opinions, not a vote.
Their figures differ from the team leader's, so they were not copied.
Nothing in the account suggests the president set a range.
Their opinions were written out, not offhand, which is why a spread appeared.
questions.explain: Their independent, written opinions are why a spread appeared.
questions.teaches: Four senior officers at the Directorate of National Intelligence had reviewed the case and written out their own opinions before the president spoke.
questions.rule: According to Bowden, the president heard estimates from about 30% to 95% and treated the matter as one of probability.

questions.q: True or false: Bowden was impressed by the CIA's use of numbers and probabilities.
questions.explain: He was not. The card next shows his view.
questions.rule: According to Bowden, Obama found the CIA's number-heavy process confusing rather than clarifying.

questions.q: Obama said the process gave not more certainty but more ____.
questions.explain: In Bowden's account the president found more confusion.
questions.rule: According to Bowden, Obama found the CIA's number-heavy process confusing rather than clarifying.

questions.q: A firm adds a ten-step scoring system after a costly error, and managers find it yields more doubt. Which comparison fits Bowden's account?
options: A simple process that gave one clear yes or no answer each time it was used by leaders
An elaborate process meant to weigh certainty that leaves leaders more confused
A process that was dropped as soon as the original error was found
A process that gave leaders the certainty they had lacked before
optionExplain: The CIA's process was described as elaborate, not simple.
This is how Bowden describes the CIA's response to the Iraq error.
The process was instituted after the error, not dropped.
Bowden says it gave more confusion, not more certainty.
questions.explain: The CIA's elaborate process left the president with more confusion.
questions.rule: According to Bowden, Obama found the CIA's number-heavy process confusing rather than clarifying.

questions.q: According to Bowden, what would Obama be doing if he acted on this evidence?
options: Following a safe recommendation that every officer in the room shared
Taking a gamble, pure and simple, and a big one
Applying a proven formula that carried only a low risk of error
Waiting for a further round of estimates before he made any choice
optionExplain: The officers did not share a view, so no safe consensus existed.
Bowden says Obama had no trouble admitting the gamble to himself.
Bowden says the formula-like process did not help him.
The account has him decide to act, not wait.
questions.explain: Bowden says Obama saw it as a big gamble.
questions.rule: According to Bowden, Obama found the CIA's number-heavy process confusing rather than clarifying.

questions.q: True or false: Bowden ties the CIA's elaborate weighing process to its erroneous call about Saddam's weapons a decade earlier.
questions.explain: He says the error led the agency to institute an almost comically elaborate process for weighing certainty.
questions.rule: According to Bowden, Obama found the CIA's number-heavy process confusing rather than clarifying.

questions.q: What event did Bowden say led the CIA to adopt its elaborate process for weighing certainty?
options: Its failure to warn the country about the attacks of September 2001
A congressional demand that every estimate it produced must carry a number
A change of director who liked numbers a great deal more than words
Its erroneous call that Saddam was hiding weapons of mass destruction
optionExplain: The 2001 attacks are a plausible trigger, but Bowden names the Iraq call.
Nothing is said of Congress in this passage.
No change of director is mentioned.
Bowden ties the process to that error, a decade earlier.
questions.explain: The Iraq error drove the elaborate process.
questions.teaches: Bowden says the CIA's call that Saddam was hiding weapons of mass destruction, made a decade earlier, kicked off a long and very costly war and led to the weighing process.
questions.rule: According to Bowden, Obama found the CIA's number-heavy process confusing rather than clarifying.

questions.q: From Bowden's information, about what was the median of the officers' estimates?
options: Around 70%, from the limited information Bowden gives
Around 30%, the figure that the least confident officers gave
Around 50%, the number the president used when he spoke
Around 95%, the figure that the CIA team leader gave
optionExplain: It appears to have been around seventy percent.
Thirty percent was the low end of the range, not the middle.
Fifty-fifty was Obama's phrase, not the median.
Ninety-five percent was the team leader's view, one end of the spread.
questions.explain: About 70%. The card next shows how it compares with Obama's remark.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a literal 50% against a crowd median near 70% has no reasonable basis in Bowden's account.

questions.q: The chapter calls the collective view of a group of judges the wisdom of the ____.
questions.explain: The authors call the group's view the wisdom of the crowd.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a literal 50% against a crowd median near 70% has no reasonable basis in Bowden's account.

questions.q: Seven advisers give 30%, 50%, 60%, 70%, 80%, 90% and 95%. A leader says 50-50 and means it literally. What would the authors say?
options: It is wise, because splitting the difference between the views removes bias
It is correct, because the lowest and the highest numbers cancel each other out
It is misguided: the median is 70% and nothing supports 50% as more accurate
It cannot be judged, because a literal number has no link to the estimates
optionExplain: Splitting the difference sounds fair, but it is not what the median does.
The extremes do not cancel in this way; the middle value is 70%.
The median of seven values is the fourth one, which is 70%.
A literal number can be compared with the median, which is what the authors do.
questions.explain: A literal 50% against a median of 70% has no reasonable basis.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a literal 50% against a crowd median near 70% has no reasonable basis in Bowden's account.

questions.q: Which are reasons the authors give for doubting a literal fifty-fifty? Select all that apply.
options: The group's collective judgment was higher than 50%
Bowden gives no reasonable basis for thinking 50% more accurate
The number looks plucked out of the air
All officers had agreed on a figure near 50%
Obama had said he would never accept a probability
optionExplain: Correct: the median was around 70%.
Correct: the account gives no such basis.
Correct: the authors call it a number plucked out of the air.
The officers did not agree; they ranged widely.
No such statement is reported.
questions.explain: The first three are the authors' points against a literal reading.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a literal 50% against a crowd median near 70% has no reasonable basis in Bowden's account.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the officers' median estimate appears to have been around 70%, above Obama's fifty-fifty.
questions.explain: Bowden's information is sketchy, but the median appears to be about 70%.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a literal 50% against a crowd median near 70% has no reasonable basis in Bowden's account.

questions.q: How firmly do the authors hold the 70% median?
options: As an exact figure that Bowden reports from a formal vote of the officers
As a number that Obama himself announced to the whole room that day
As an average they computed from every officer's written report
As an apparent figure, inferred from information the authors call sketchy
optionExplain: Bowden does not report a vote.
Obama is quoted saying fifty-fifty, not 70%.
The authors do not have every report; they work from Bowden's account.
They say it appears to be around 70%.
questions.explain: The median is an inference from sketchy information, so it is held loosely.
questions.teaches: The authors call the information Bowden provides sketchy; the 70% median is how it appears, not a reported fact.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a literal 50% against a crowd median near 70% has no reasonable basis in Bowden's account.

questions.q: According to the authors, what do people who say fifty-fifty often mean?
options: Exactly one chance in two, worked out with care from all the evidence
That they are not sure, or maybe, rather than a literal 50%
Whatever the first speaker in the room has said before them
A request that more evidence be gathered before anything is decided
optionExplain: A literal reading is what the authors say is often not meant.
Researchers have shown that people often do not mean it literally.
Nothing in the chapter says people echo each other.
A request for evidence is a different message from maybe.
questions.explain: It often means maybe. The card next shows how this reading fits Obama.
questions.rule: According to the authors, fifty-fifty often means maybe, and when a decision does not turn on the exact number a quick maybe can be reasonable.

questions.q: People who say fifty-fifty often mean I am not sure, or in a word, ____.
questions.explain: The authors say it is often a stand-in for maybe.
questions.rule: According to the authors, fifty-fifty often means maybe, and when a decision does not turn on the exact number a quick maybe can be reasonable.

questions.q: A founder says her launch is 50-50 but would go ahead at any chance above 25%. What does the Obama reading suggest?
options: She is stating an exact probability that she has measured with some care
She is refusing to decide, since 50-50 always means a toss of a coin
She may mean maybe, since her decision holds across a wide range of odds
She has misread her own data, since founders tend to overrate their odds
optionExplain: The reading says the number is often not literal.
The reading says the opposite: it let the executive decide.
Her decision does not turn on the exact number, as in the authors' reading of Obama.
No claim about founders appears in the chapter.
questions.explain: When any significant chance triggers the action, the exact number does little.
questions.rule: According to the authors, fifty-fifty often means maybe, and when a decision does not turn on the exact number a quick maybe can be reasonable.

questions.q: True or false: On the authors' reading, Obama would still have ordered the strike if he thought the chance was 30%.
questions.explain: The authors say it may not have mattered whether the probability was 90%, 70% or perhaps even 30%.
questions.rule: According to the authors, fifty-fifty often means maybe, and when a decision does not turn on the exact number a quick maybe can be reasonable.

questions.q: True or false: The authors state as fact that Obama meant fifty-fifty as maybe.
questions.explain: The author says he suspects it but does not know.
questions.rule: According to the authors, fifty-fifty often means maybe, and when a decision does not turn on the exact number a quick maybe can be reasonable.

questions.q: Why might it be reasonable for Obama to cut the probability discussion short?
options: If any significant chance would lead him to act, refining the number wastes time
Probabilities are meaningless in a crisis, so no one should state them
The officers had refused to give him any numbers, so there was nothing left to refine
The chance was exactly one in two, and no further work could improve it
optionExplain: That is the authors' reading of his likely thinking.
The authors do not call probabilities meaningless.
The officers gave numbers, in fact many of them.
The authors say fifty-fifty may not have been literal.
questions.explain: When the action does not hinge on the number, precision adds little.
questions.teaches: The author says that, given the context, he suspects maybe is what Obama had in mind, but he cannot know.
questions.rule: According to the authors, fifty-fifty often means maybe, and when a decision does not turn on the exact number a quick maybe can be reasonable.

questions.q: What does the chapter call the state of knowledge you are in before you know how a coin toss will land?
options: The ignorance prior, the starting state before the outcome is known
The wisdom of the crowd, the pooled view of many separate and independent judges
The outside view, the stance taken from a distance on a case
The tip-of-your-nose view, the quick judgment from easy recall
optionExplain: That is the phrase the authors use for the state of knowledge before the coin lands.
The wisdom of the crowd is a group's collective view, not a state before the outcome.
The outside view is a Kahneman term that comes later in the chapter.
The tip-of-your-nose view is the lion-in-the-grass style of thinking.
questions.explain: It is the ignorance prior. The card next shows how it enters the Obama story.
questions.rule: According to the authors, falling back on the ignorance prior because estimates differ wastes the information on the table.

questions.q: Retreating to the ignorance prior means Obama did not make full use of the ____ at the table.
questions.explain: The authors say he did not make full use of the information available.
questions.rule: According to the authors, falling back on the ignorance prior because estimates differ wastes the information on the table.

questions.q: Annoyed by five forecasts that range from 30% to 80%, a manager announces 50% without using them. Which mistake is this?
options: Weighting each forecast by how much the manager respects the person who made it
Taking the median of the forecasts as the combined estimate
Falling back on the ignorance prior and discarding what the forecasts carry
Treating the disagreement as a sign that people think independently
optionExplain: Weighting uses the information, so it is not the mistake.
The median also uses the information.
The manager returns to an uninformed 50% instead of using the forecasts.
Welcoming disagreement is the attitude the authors recommend.
questions.explain: Ignoring the forecasts wastes what they know.
questions.rule: According to the authors, falling back on the ignorance prior because estimates differ wastes the information on the table.

questions.q: Match each term to what the chapter means by it.
pairs: The state of knowledge before the outcome is known
The collective judgment of many people
The third setting on a mental dial
questions.explain: The three terms sit at different points: knowledge before the facts, a group's judgment, and the third setting of the dial.
questions.rule: According to the authors, falling back on the ignorance prior because estimates differ wastes the information on the table.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Obama's mental dial had only two settings, like the fictional director's.
questions.explain: They say his dial had a third setting, maybe.
questions.rule: According to the authors, falling back on the ignorance prior because estimates differ wastes the information on the table.

questions.q: Why do the authors call falling back on the ignorance prior a mistake?
options: It gives a number that is too high to be at all plausible
It wastes information the officers had put on the table
It shows that probabilities are of no real use to any leader
It makes any agreement between the officers impossible later on
optionExplain: The mistake is not that the number is high.
The mistake lies in leaving the information unused.
The authors argue that probabilities are useful.
Agreement is not the aim; the authors welcome disagreement.
questions.explain: The wasted information is the cost.
questions.teaches: The authors say the spread of estimates was itself usable information, and the retreat meant leaving it unused.
questions.rule: According to the authors, falling back on the ignorance prior because estimates differ wastes the information on the table.

questions.q: How many settings did Tversky say most people have when dealing with probabilities?
options: Two: yes and no, with nothing in between
Five: a scale from very unlikely to very likely
Ten: one for each tenth of a probability
Three: gonna happen, not gonna happen and maybe
optionExplain: Two is the film director's dial, and Tversky's joke included maybe.
Five is the scale used by the National Intelligence Council, mentioned later.
Ten steps would already be a fine-grained dial, which Tversky did not claim.
Tversky's three settings are gonna happen, not gonna happen and maybe.
questions.explain: Three. The card next names them.
questions.rule: According to the author, most people think in three settings: it will happen, it will not, or maybe.

questions.q: Tversky's three settings were gonna happen, not gonna happen and ____.
questions.explain: The third setting is maybe.
questions.rule: According to the author, most people think in three settings: it will happen, it will not, or maybe.

questions.q: Which statements fit a three-setting dial, and which are finer-grained?

items.t: The merger will happen
The merger might happen
The merger will not happen
The merger has a 62% chance
The merger has a 7% chance

questions.explain: Will, will not and might are the three settings; 62% and 7% are fine-grained.
questions.rule: According to the author, most people think in three settings: it will happen, it will not, or maybe.

questions.q: If Tversky's remark is right, what would most people do with a forecast of 80%?
options: Hold it as exactly four chances in five, with care
Treat it as gonna happen, close to certain
Treat it as maybe, since it is not a full 100%
Reject it as a number that has no real meaning
optionExplain: Holding fine probabilities is what most people do not do on a three-setting dial.
Our reading, from the Rubin story later in the chapter: people tend to turn high probabilities into certainties.
Maybe is for middling cases; a high probability slides toward will happen.
Rejection is not the pattern the chapter describes.
questions.explain: High probabilities slide into certainty on a three-setting dial.
questions.rule: According to the author, most people think in three settings: it will happen, it will not, or maybe.

questions.q: True or false: The author says Tversky's remark was meant as a precise research finding.
questions.explain: It was an offhand joke, though the author thinks it captures a basic truth.
questions.rule: According to the author, most people think in three settings: it will happen, it will not, or maybe.

questions.q: In what setting did Tversky make the remark?
options: A National Research Council committee charged with preventing nuclear war
A tournament run by the intelligence community for its own analysts
A lecture on weather forecasting at a large university
A White House briefing for the president on events in the Middle East that year
optionExplain: The author calls it an absurdly ambitious mission for an academic committee.
The tournament came decades later and was not the setting.
The remark was not made in a lecture.
The remark was not made at a White House briefing.
questions.explain: The remark was a joke on a committee with a grand mission.
questions.teaches: Tversky made the remark thirty years earlier on a National Research Council committee charged with preventing nuclear war; he had an impish sense of humor and saw the absurdity of an academic committee out to save the world.
questions.rule: According to the author, most people think in three settings: it will happen, it will not, or maybe.

questions.q: According to the authors, when did the best minds start to think seriously about probability?
options: Early on, with the first lawgivers and philosophers of ancient Greece and Rome
Only in the twentieth century, once large computers made calculation cheap
Remarkably late, arguably as late as Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi of 1713
At the founding of the intelligence community in the years after the war
optionExplain: The ancients thought about chance, but the authors say serious thought on probability began much later.
The date the authors give is much earlier than the age of computers.
The authors say it was remarkably late, because for most of history there were no statistical models of uncertainty.
The intelligence community plays no part in this history.
questions.explain: Remarkably late, arguably 1713. The card next shows what people used before that.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the tip-of-your-nose perspective turns how easily an example comes to mind into yes, no or maybe.

questions.q: The 1713 work Ars Conjectandi was published by Jakob ____.
questions.explain: Jakob Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi is the date the authors give.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the tip-of-your-nose perspective turns how easily an example comes to mind into yes, no or maybe.

questions.q: A hiker hears a rustle and at once recalls a story of a bear attack on that trail. Which perspective is this?
options: The tip-of-your-nose perspective: ease of recalling a case drives the judgment
A weighted average of expert estimates gathered over many other trails in the region
The ignorance prior, which starts from the odds of a fair coin toss
A fine-grained estimate that separates a 60% chance from an 80% one
optionExplain: Judging by how easily an example comes to mind is the tip-of-your-nose perspective.
Averaging experts is a deliberate method, not a quick reaction to a rustle.
The ignorance prior is a state of knowledge before the outcome is known.
The authors say this quick perspective cannot reach that fine a grain.
questions.explain: Ease of recall drives the judgment.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the tip-of-your-nose perspective turns how easily an example comes to mind into yes, no or maybe.

questions.q: A shadow moves in the grass and the lion example comes to mind only weakly. What does the authors' account predict?
options: A firm no, followed by relaxing at once and walking on
A precise estimate of 63%, worked out from the shadow's size
A firm yes, followed by running as fast as possible
An unsettling middle judgment: maybe it is a lion
optionExplain: A no would need an easier recall of safe cases, not a weak recall of lions.
The perspective cannot produce so fine a number.
A strong response, not a weak one, gives a firm yes.
A weaker response gives the middle possibility.
questions.explain: A weak response produces maybe.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the tip-of-your-nose perspective turns how easily an example comes to mind into yes, no or maybe.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the tip-of-your-nose perspective cannot tell a 60% chance of a lion from an 80% chance.
questions.explain: That distinction takes slow, conscious, careful thought.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the tip-of-your-nose perspective turns how easily an example comes to mind into yes, no or maybe.

questions.q: What does the authors' account say it takes to separate a 60% chance from an 80% chance?
options: A strong gut reaction that comes to mind very quickly
Slow, conscious, careful thought
A vote among people who all share the same worry
A habit of treating every shadow as a threat
optionExplain: A gut reaction is the quick System 1 response, which gives yes, no or maybe, not degrees.
That is what the tip-of-your-nose perspective cannot supply, per the authors.
The authors do not propose a vote as the way to tell 60% from 80%.
A habit of alarm gives a yes, not a degree of chance.

questions.teaches: The tip-of-your-nose perspective cannot distinguish a 60% chance from an 80% chance; that takes slow, conscious, careful thought.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the tip-of-your-nose perspective turns how easily an example comes to mind into yes, no or maybe.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a three-setting dial was a poor fit for the problems our ancestors faced.
questions.explain: They say it suited them. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a coarse dial was a good fit for the quick decisions of ancestral life.

questions.q: On the lion dial, YES means run, MAYBE means stay alert and NO means ____.
questions.explain: The three settings were run, stay alert, relax.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a coarse dial was a good fit for the quick decisions of ancestral life.

questions.q: A driver sees a pedestrian step toward the road. Which response fits the lion-dial logic?
options: Estimate the chance to the nearest percent before touching the brake pedal
Brake at once for a clear yes, without stopping to work out the exact odds
Wait to see whether many of the other drivers react in the same way
Average the opinions of the passengers before choosing what to do

A quick, clear response is what a coarse dial supplies in an urgent moment.
Waiting for others wastes the seconds that matter.
Averaging takes too long when a decision is urgent.

questions.rule: According to the authors, a coarse dial was a good fit for the quick decisions of ancestral life.

questions.q: Suppose an ancestor tried to separate a 60% chance of a lion from an 80% chance each time. What does the authors' account suggest?
options: It would make them reliably faster at escaping every danger they met
It would have no effect on how they handled the dangers around them
It would make each predator slower to attack them in the grass
It could slow them down and get them killed

The authors say extra analysis could have a cost.
Predators are not part of the claim.
The authors say a more fine-grained analysis could slow you down and get you killed.

questions.rule: According to the authors, a coarse dial was a good fit for the quick decisions of ancestral life.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, finer distinctions were usually needed to survive in ancestral conditions.

questions.rule: According to the authors, a coarse dial was a good fit for the quick decisions of ancestral life.

questions.q: What fits modern forecasting better than the lion dial, according to this chapter?
options: Finer degrees of probability, when the question rewards precision
The same three settings, because they have served humans for so long
A single setting of maybe, applied to every question in the same way
Whichever setting the most confident person in the room recommends

questions.q: Which cut in a child's disease risk may a parent pay the most for, according to the authors?
options: 10% down to 5%, since that step removes the larger share of risk overall
Both cost the same, since each removes five points of risk

Both cuts are five points in size, so the first is not larger.
Removing the last 5% is still worth the same five points to the model.

questions.rule: According to the authors, people pay a premium for removing a risk altogether, more than the size of the reduction explains.

questions.q: According to the authors, why did our ancestors treat small chances as zero when they could?
options: They had learned from long experience that small risks never turn into real events
They had no way of noticing any danger below one chance in a hundred
Constant alert cost too much mental effort, so they needed worry-free zones
They believed lions and snakes had stopped living nearby

questions.q: How does the popular, nineteenth-century picture of science see uncertainty?
options: As the main goal that scientists work to protect and to preserve for later researchers

questions.q: When scientists say this is true, there is supposed to be an invisible ____.
questions.explain: The authors call the unspoken caveat an invisible asterisk.

questions.q: True or false: If nothing is certain, the authors conclude that the three-setting dial should keep yes and no and drop maybe.

questions.explain: Adults were in the middle, undergrads a little lower, regulars lower still and superforecasters lowest.
questions.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters score lowest on fate and sit firmly on the side that rejects it.

questions.section: But What Does It All Mean?
questions.q: True or false: The superforecasters scored near the middle of the fate scale, like adult Americans.
questions.explain: Adult Americans were mid-scale; superforecasters were lowest.
questions.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters score lowest on fate and sit firmly on the side that rejects it.

questions.section: But What Does It All Mean?
questions.q: Besides superforecasters, which groups did the researchers put the same statements to?
options: Regular forecasters, Penn undergraduates and a cross section of adult Americans
Only regular forecasters and the intelligence analysts working for the government
Professional meteorologists and leading economists
Only Penn undergraduates and Northwestern students
optionExplain: These are the three comparison groups.
Intelligence analysts were not given the statements in this chapter.
The chapter names no meteorologists or economists as respondents.
Northwestern students took part in a different experiment.
questions.explain: The same questions went to regular volunteer forecasters, Penn undergraduates and a broad cross section of adult Americans.
questions.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters score lowest on fate and sit firmly on the side that rejects it.
questions.teaches: The researchers put the same fate and probability statements to regular volunteer forecasters, undergraduates at the University of Pennsylvania and a broad cross section of adult Americans.

questions.section: But What Does It All Mean?
questions.q: What did the authors find when they compared fate scores with Brier scores?
options: No link at all between belief in fate and accuracy
A significant correlation: stronger belief in fate went with greater accuracy
A link only among undergraduates and not among forecasters
A significant correlation: stronger belief in fate went with poorer accuracy
optionExplain: There was a significant link.
The link ran the other way.
The link was among forecasters.
Fate thinking went with poorer accuracy.
questions.explain: Fate thinking went with less accuracy. The card next shows the detail.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the more a forecaster embraces probabilistic thinking, the more accurate she is.

questions.section: But What Does It All Mean?
questions.q: The authors compared individual fate scores with ____ scores, the measure of forecasting accuracy.
questions.explain: They used Brier scores.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the more a forecaster embraces probabilistic thinking, the more accurate she is.

questions.section: But What Does It All Mean?
questions.q: Two forecasters have fate scores of 2 and 7 on the 9-point scale. Which is likelier to be more accurate, per the authors?
options: The one scoring 7
They are equally accurate
The one scoring 2
Neither, because fate has no link to accuracy
optionExplain: Higher fate scores went with lower accuracy, so 7 is the less likely.
Fate scores and accuracy were linked, so they are not equally accurate.
Lower fate scores go with higher accuracy.
The authors found a significant link, so fate does bear on accuracy.
questions.explain: Low fate means more accurate.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the more a forecaster embraces probabilistic thinking, the more accurate she is.

questions.section: But What Does It All Mean?
questions.q: If a forecaster moves toward it-was-meant-to-happen thinking, what do the authors' findings predict for accuracy?
options: It will tend to rise
It will stay the same
It will tend to fall
It will become perfect
optionExplain: Rising accuracy is the reverse of the correlation the authors report.
The correlation is significant, so accuracy does not stay the same.
The correlation runs that way.
Nothing suggests perfect accuracy; the finding is a tendency.
questions.explain: Accuracy tends to fall.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the more a forecaster embraces probabilistic thinking, the more accurate she is.

questions.section: But What Does It All Mean?
questions.q: True or false: The authors say they do not know whether misery is the price of accuracy.
questions.explain: They raise the question and leave the existential issues to others.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the more a forecaster embraces probabilistic thinking, the more accurate she is.

questions.section: But What Does It All Mean?
questions.q: Why do the authors call the combined findings a depressing possibility?
options: Superforecasters turn out to be the least happy of all the groups the team studied
Finding meaning leads to both wellbeing and accuracy
Fate thinking is shown to cause forecasting errors
Meaning goes with wellbeing but against foresight, so the two might trade off
optionExplain: No such measurement is reported.
That would not be depressing.
They report a correlation, not a cause.
They raise the question of whether misery is the price of accuracy.
questions.explain: A trade-off is possible but not shown.
questions.teaches: Finding meaning in events is positively correlated with wellbeing but negatively correlated with foresight, which sets up the question of whether misery is the price of accuracy.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the more a forecaster embraces probabilistic thinking, the more accurate she is.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the demanding opening process is only the beginning of the work on a question.
questions.explain: The authors call it only the beginning; forecasts must then be updated. The card next lays out the steps.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the opening process of unpacking, comparing views and stating a precise probability is demanding, yet it only starts the work on a question.

questions.q: The authors liken the final synthesis of several views into one to the acute vision of a ____.
questions.explain: The synthesis step is described as a single vision as acute as that of a dragonfly.
questions.rule: Synthesize the views into one sharp picture.

questions.q: A manager starts from how long such hires usually stay, then adjusts for this one. Which two steps from the authors' list is she using?
options: Inside view first, then the outside view
Unpacking the question, then stating a probability
Outside view first, then the inside view
Prediction market first, then the inside view
optionExplain: The authors give the outside view first, then the inside view; the order matters because the wider class anchors the estimate.
Those are the first and last steps in the list, not the two views she is using here.
She starts with the wider class of cases and then plays up what is unique about this one.
She consults no market or crowd; she starts from a base rate for the wider class.
questions.explain: The wider class of similar hires is the outside view. The details of this person are the inside view.
questions.rule: Outside view first, then inside view.

questions.q: Put the steps in the order the authors list them.
items: Unpack the question into components
Adopt the outside view
Adopt the inside view
Compare your views with those of others
Synthesize the views into one vision
State your judgment on a finely grained probability scale
questions.explain: The list runs: unpack, separate known from unknown, take the outside view, then the inside view, compare with others, then synthesize and state a judgment.
questions.rule: Unpack first; synthesize and state a probability last.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the opening process is a fixed method that guarantees a good forecast when every step is followed.
questions.explain: The authors say it is not paint-by-numbers. Hence it is a rough, shared way of working that still demands judgment.
questions.rule: A rough method, not a guarantee.

questions.q: A team lead has her own project estimate. Beyond the inside and outside views, which extra check do the authors single out?
options: What prediction markets and other crowd methods say about the same question
Asking the most senior colleague for a single final number to adopt
Waiting for the project to finish so the estimate can be scored fairly
Dropping the outside view once the inside view has been worked out in full detail
optionExplain: The authors say to pay special attention to markets and other crowd-wisdom methods.
The authors point to crowds and markets, not to one authority.
Scoring comes after the question closes; this step is about forming the forecast.
Both views stay in the list; neither replaces the other.
questions.explain: The authors tell forecasters to compare their views with others', with special attention to prediction markets and crowd methods.
questions.teaches: The authors say to explore how your views compare with those of others, paying special attention to prediction markets and other methods of drawing wisdom from crowds.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the opening process of unpacking, comparing views and stating a precise probability is demanding, yet it only starts the work on a question.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a forecast should be revised as information changes, not filed away until the question closes.
questions.explain: Forecasts are judgments to be updated in light of changing information. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a forecast is a judgment to be revised as information changes, and an updated forecast is likely to be closer to the truth.

questions.q: The authors say forecasts are judgments that should be ____ in light of changing information.
questions.explain: Forecasts are meant to be updated as the information they rest on changes.
questions.rule: Keep the forecast in step with the evidence.

questions.q: On Wednesday a weather service gives 70% for rain on Saturday. By Friday the storm track has shifted away. What do the authors' ideas suggest?
options: Keep 70%, because changing a forecast would show that the first judgment was weak
Wait until Saturday, because only the final outcome can show whether the forecast was wrong
Drop the forecast, because new information makes any earlier number worthless to keep
Revise the Saturday forecast, since a forecast should change when its information changes
optionExplain: Revising is a sign of tracking the facts, not of an earlier flaw.
The authors want the judgment kept current, not left until the draw.
The earlier number still carries value; it needs adjusting, not discarding.
The storm track was part of the information behind the forecast.
questions.explain: A forecast stands on available information, so a change in that information calls for a change in the forecast.
questions.rule: New information, new forecast.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a forecast reflecting the latest information is likely to be closer to the truth than one that is not.
questions.explain: That is the authors' reason for updating.
questions.rule: Updated forecasts tend to be closer to the truth.

questions.q: In the IARPA tournament, how often could a forecaster change a forecast after making it?
options: Once a week, on a fixed day set by the organisers
As often as she liked, for any reason
Only when the organisers announced that new information had arrived
Twice at most, to stop forecasters from gaming the score
optionExplain: No such limit is described.
The authors say Bill could raise or lower his forecast as often as he liked.
Forecasters used their own judgment about when to update.
The authors describe no cap; Devyn Duffy later made over sixteen forecasts per question on average.
questions.explain: The tournament allowed any number of updates. That is why updating skill could matter as much as the first forecast.
questions.teaches: In the tournament a forecaster could raise or lower a forecast as often as he liked, for any reason.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a forecast is a judgment to be revised as information changes, and an updated forecast is likely to be closer to the truth.

questions.q: A company has forecast next quarter's sales. A major competitor then unexpectedly declares bankruptcy. What do the authors' examples imply?
options: Leave the sales forecast, since a competitor's problems are not the company's
Revise the expected sales to reflect the competitor's collapse
Raise it to the maximum possible, because any rival failure guarantees gains
Cancel the forecast until the bankruptcy proceedings have fully ended
optionExplain: A rival's collapse changes the market the forecast was made about.
The authors give exactly this case as a reason to update.
The authors say revise accordingly, not jump to an extreme.
A forecast is a judgment under uncertainty and can be updated now.
questions.explain: The authors' own examples are a candidate surging in the polls, which should raise his win probability, and a competitor's bankruptcy, which should revise expected sales.
questions.teaches: The authors' examples of updating: if new polls show a candidate surging into a lead, boost his chance of winning; if a competitor unexpectedly declares bankruptcy, revise expected sales accordingly.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a forecast is a judgment to be revised as information changes, and an updated forecast is likely to be closer to the truth.

questions.q: About how many forecasts per question did the superforecaster Devyn Duffy make on average in the third season?
options: About 2
About 6
Exactly 1, since good forecasts need no revision
More than 16
optionExplain: Superforecasters update far more often than this.
This is closer, but well short of what the tournament data show.
The authors say frequent updating was part of his success.
He made 2,271 forecasts on 140 questions.
questions.explain: He made 2,271 forecasts on 140 questions, which is more than 16 per question. The card next shows how he does it.
questions.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters update much more often than regular forecasters, and Devyn Duffy shows how: alerts on each question and a revision whenever the news bears on it.

questions.q: Devyn follows developments using Google ____ set to the topic of each question.
questions.explain: He sets Google alerts for terms such as Syrian refugees and the UN agency that monitors their numbers.
questions.rule: Use alerts to catch news on each question.

questions.q: One forecaster tracks coup risk where events change daily; another tracks a slow policy shift. Following Devyn, how should their alerts be set?
options: Daily for the fast-moving coup question, weekly for the slower one
Weekly for both, since frequent alerts only add noise to the process
Daily for both, because more alerts always make for better updates
None for the coup, since a coup cannot be forecast from the news
optionExplain: Devyn sets daily alerts when events may change rapidly and weekly otherwise.
Devyn matches the pace of alerts to the pace of events.
He reserves daily alerts for fast-changing situations.
Devyn's own example of a daily alert is the risk of a coup in Thailand.
questions.explain: Devyn adjusts the alert rate to how fast events may change.
questions.rule: Match the alert rate to the pace of events.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, superforecasters update much more frequently, on average, than regular forecasters.
questions.explain: The authors say this is another big reason why they are super.
questions.rule: Superforecasters update much more often.

questions.q: Which of Devyn Duffy's own explanations for his success appears in the chapter?
options: An unusual talent for the maths of probability
Years of professional work in intelligence analysis
Good luck and frequent updating
Insider contacts who passed him early news
optionExplain: His own e-mail credits a talent for doing well on tests, which he says makes him look smarter than he is.
He was a factory worker who lost his job and is now a state caseworker.
He says he would attribute his success so far to good luck and frequent updating.
He relies on public news and Google alerts.
questions.explain: Devyn attributes his success to good luck and frequent updating, with a joking nod to his skill at tests.
questions.teaches: Devyn credits his success in the tournament to good luck and frequent updating, and jokes that his talent for multiple-choice tests makes him look more intelligent than he is.
questions.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters update much more often than regular forecasters, and Devyn Duffy shows how: alerts on each question and a revision whenever the news bears on it.

questions.q: A newsroom editor wants to track a fast-moving story. According to Devyn's practice, what is the sequence after an alert arrives?
options: Collect a week of alerts, then average the news into one monthly figure
Check whether other forecasters changed theirs, then copy them
Read it when it arrives, think through what it implies, then update
Save the alerts for the final review once the question has closed
optionExplain: Devyn reads alerts as soon as they come in.
Devyn reasons about what the news implies himself.
That is the sequence the chapter describes.
Updating is done during the life of the question.
questions.explain: Devyn reads alerts at once, thinks through their implications for the future and updates.
questions.teaches: Devyn reads alerts as soon as they arrive, thinks through what they imply about the future, and then updates his forecast.
questions.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters update much more often than regular forecasters, and Devyn Duffy shows how: alerts on each question and a revision whenever the news bears on it.

questions.q: How did superforecasters' very first forecasts compare in accuracy with those of regular forecasters?
options: They were about the same, and the gap opened only as updating began
They were at least 50% more accurate
They were slightly worse, but frequent updating made up the difference
They were about 10% more accurate, a modest edge
optionExplain: This is the suspicion the authors answer.
The authors report a gap of at least 50% before any updating.
The authors report the opposite.
The gap the authors report is far larger.
questions.explain: Superforecasters led from the start, by at least 50%. The card next shows how the authors use this.
questions.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters' lead does not come from news-watching alone: their first forecasts were already at least 50% more accurate, and updating well is itself skilled work.

questions.q: The famous political scientist lost interest in the tournament when he learned it required ____.
questions.explain: He was interested until he learned the tournament required updating.
questions.rule: The suspicion centres on updating.

questions.q: A fund manager says a rival's results come only from checking the news more often. Which test mirrors the authors' reply?
options: Count how many hours a day the rival spends reading the news and watching television
See whether the rival's first call, before any updating, was already better than the others'
Assume news-watching cannot matter at all, so skill alone must explain everything she does
Ask the rival whether she believes news-watching explains her results, and trust her answer
optionExplain: That measures effort, which is the suspicion, not whether skill also matters.
The authors point out that superforecasters would have won with initial forecasts alone.
The authors concede that careful monitoring is a big advantage.
Her opinion is not evidence; the authors point to the accuracy of first forecasts.
questions.explain: If the rival was ahead before any updating, news-watching cannot be the whole explanation.
questions.rule: Test the first call, not only the later ones.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, belief updating means adjusting a forecast to whatever the latest news shows.
questions.explain: The authors say updating is not mindless adjustment to whatever is on CNN, and call belittling it a huge mistake.
questions.rule: Updating is judgment, not reflex.

questions.q: How do the authors say the skill of good updating compares with that of making the initial forecast?
options: It needs far less skill, because the hard analysis is already done
It needs different skills, mostly speed and stamina in reading news
It needs less skill, because the crowd's view can be copied
It needs the same skills and is often as demanding, sometimes more
optionExplain: This is the belittling view the authors reject.
They say the skills are the same ones used for the initial forecast.
The authors describe updating as demanding judgment, not copying.
The authors say good updating requires the same skills and can even be more challenging.
questions.explain: Updating draws on the same skills as the first forecast, and it can be harder.
questions.rule: Updating is as demanding as forecasting.
questions.teaches: Good updating requires the same skills used in making the initial forecast and is often just as demanding; it can even be more challenging.

questions.q: A senior consultant declines a contest after learning that forecasts must be refreshed over time. Which reason does the authors' anecdote match?
options: He saw a contest against people with free time to follow the news, not one of expertise
He doubted that anyone could update accurately enough to matter in such a contest
He expected updates to be scored more harshly than first forecasts in the tournament
He thought the questions were too easy to suit a consultant of his reputation
optionExplain: The consultant did not want to compete with unemployed newsjunkies.
The authors' anecdote shows disdain for updaters, not doubt about their accuracy.
No such scoring rule is mentioned.
His stated worry was the kind of competitor, not the questions.
questions.explain: He said he had no interest in competing with unemployed newsjunkies. The authors disliked the attitude but took the point.
questions.teaches: The political scientist said he had no interest in competing with unemployed newsjunkies; the authors disliked the attitude but saw the point.
questions.rule: According to the authors, superforecasters' lead does not come from news-watching alone: their first forecasts were already at least 50% more accurate, and updating well is itself skilled work.

questions.q: How did President Obama's September 2014 address on ISIL bear on the question of foreign military operations in Syria before December 1, 2014?
options: It made a no all but certain, since speeches seldom lead to action
It had no bearing, because the question had been settled earlier
It made a yes all but certain, and forecasters updated in a flurry
It made little difference, since forecasters had expected it
optionExplain: The address said action in Syria was coming.
The question was live and the announcement mattered.
The authors report a flurry of updating towards yes.
The authors describe a flurry of updating, not a shrug.
questions.explain: The speech made a yes all but certain. The card next shows why updating on it earns no special credit.
questions.rule: According to the authors, updating on news everyone can see is necessary but gives no edge; the difference lies elsewhere.

questions.q: No one can produce superior forecasts only by staying on top of what ____ knows.
questions.explain: A development clear to everyone and the response it calls for give no one an edge.
questions.rule: Common knowledge gives no edge.

questions.q: A central bank unexpectedly cuts rates on live TV. By the authors' logic, what does a forecaster earn by updating a mortgage-rate estimate on it?
options: A decisive edge, because few forecasters follow central banks closely
Nothing at all, so the forecast should be left alone to avoid any overreacting
Updating is needed, but it gives no edge, since everyone sees the same news
An edge only if the forecaster waits a week for the market to settle
optionExplain: The announcement was on live TV; its meaning is clear to everyone.
Failing to update would be an error; the point is that updating earns no edge.
The authors say a response clear to everyone does not separate forecasters.
The authors locate the edge in subtler information, not in waiting.
questions.explain: Everyone sees the headline and its meaning, so updating on it is required but not distinguishing.
questions.rule: Headline news is table stakes.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, correctly updating on a headline everyone can see is enough to produce superior forecasts.
questions.explain: They say no one can produce superior forecasts only by staying on top of what everyone knows.
questions.rule: Common knowledge is not an edge.

questions.q: According to the authors, what does make the difference between forecasters who respond to news?
options: Correctly reading subtler information, so as to zero in on the outcome sooner
Reading more news sources than anyone else, so that no headline is ever missed
Reacting sooner and more strongly than others do to headline news of any kind
Waiting for official confirmation before changing a forecast at all, whatever the news
optionExplain: The edge lies in the subtle signals others miss or misread.
More sources help catch headlines, which everyone catches anyway.
The authors warn that strong reactions can be overreactions.
Waiting is not the authors' advice; Bill Flack moved on a subtle signal.
questions.explain: The edge comes from reading subtler information correctly and so converging on the eventual outcome sooner.
questions.rule: Win on the subtle signals.
questions.teaches: What makes the difference is correctly identifying and responding to subtler information so you zero in on the eventual outcome faster than others.
