questions.q: A forecaster gave 30% to a CEO resigning this year. The CEO announces on TV he will resign next month. What response is called for?
options: A small nudge to 35%, so as not to overreact
No change until the resignation takes effect next month
A fall to 20%, since announced plans often change
A large bump, to near certainty
optionExplain: With a clear and decisive announcement, a nudge would be underreaction.
Waiting is not updating; the news already decides it.
The announcement raises the probability sharply.
In the Syria case the response was a bump up to near certainty.
questions.explain: Clear and decisive news calls for a large move. The authors describe the right update in the Syria case as a bump up to near certainty.
questions.teaches: For the Syria question, the update that the announcement called for was a bump up to near certainty.
questions.rule: According to the authors, updating on news everyone can see is necessary but gives no edge; the difference lies elsewhere.

questions.q: When the Swiss team announced a delay for more testing, what did Bill Flack do with his 60% forecast?
options: Lowered it to 40%, since a delay suggests the tests were inconclusive
Raised it cautiously to 65%
Left it alone, since the delay said nothing definite about the result
Raised it to 95%, since a delay shows polonium was found
optionExplain: He read the delay the other way.
He read the delay as a possible sign of a positive result.
He treated it as slightly diagnostic.
It was one explanation among several, so he moved only a little.
questions.explain: Bill moved up five points. The card next shows the reasoning.
questions.rule: According to the authors, smart updating reads subtly diagnostic information and moves the forecast in proportion to how much the signal supports one explanation.

questions.q: Bill Flack nudged his forecast on Arafat from 60% to ____% after the Swiss delay.
questions.explain: He raised it to 65% yes.
questions.rule: A cautious, small move.

questions.q: A company delays a promised earnings announcement to run further checks. Following Bill's reasoning, what is the wise response?
options: Ignore it, because delays are routine and tell you nothing about the test results
Ask what the delay suggests under each explanation, favour the likelier, and move a little
Treat it as proof of bad news and cut the forecast sharply at once, to be safe
Wait for the announcement, since only final results count as information at all
optionExplain: Bill treated an unexplained delay as possible evidence.
Bill weighed an explanation but kept his move small because others remained.
That is one explanation, not the only one.
Bill used the delay itself before the results came.
questions.explain: Bill treated the delay as weak evidence, favoured one explanation and moved a little.
questions.rule: Small signal, small move.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a Brier score has meaning only in relation to the difficulty of the problem.
questions.explain: On this hard question most experts were shocked by the results, so 0.36 was impressive.
questions.rule: Judge a score against the difficulty.

questions.q: How do analysts tell polonium that was introduced into a body from polonium produced by natural lead decay?
options: They compare the amount found with a typical background level for the population at large
They check whether the polonium is found in the bones or the soft tissue
They test two independent labs, and accept it if both agree
They remove all the polonium, wait for any lead to decay into more, then retest
optionExplain: The authors describe a repeat test, not a comparison of amounts.
No such step is described.
The delay was one team's second round, not a two-lab check.
If lead was the source, new polonium appears in the second test.
questions.explain: Removing the polonium and waiting shows whether lead is generating more. That is what Bill thought the delay meant.
questions.rule: A second test separates the two sources.
questions.teaches: To tell introduced polonium from lead-derived polonium, analysts remove all the polonium, wait long enough for any lead to decay into polonium, then test again.

questions.q: A forecaster scores 0.36 on a very hard question and is unsure whether that is good. Which comparison do the authors use?
options: How other forecasters did: a prediction market at 4.27% yes scored about five times worse
How the score compares with a perfect 0.00, since any gap from perfect counts as poor work
How the score compares with an easier question's 0.10, which had a smaller risk of error
How quickly the forecaster updated before the question closed, whatever the final result
optionExplain: Against a market that put yes at only 4.27%, Bill did far better.
The authors say a score has meaning only relative to the difficulty.
Difficulty differs, so that comparison would mislead.
Speed matters, but it is not the comparison the authors use here.
questions.explain: The market's 4.27% for yes gave a Brier score five times worse than Bill's, which shows how strong 0.36 was on a hard question.
questions.teaches: At the close of trading, a prediction market inside the tournament put the probability of yes at 4.27%, which translates into a Brier score five times worse than Bill's.
questions.rule: According to the authors, smart updating reads subtly diagnostic information and moves the forecast in proportion to how much the signal supports one explanation.

questions.q: True or false: Bill Flack, one of the best updaters in the tournament, still made at least one serious updating mistake.
questions.explain: Even the best updaters make mistakes, and the Abe case shows one. The card next tells the story.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a forecaster who dismisses new evidence because it conflicts with a reasonable forecast can underreact, even if the forecast was sound.

questions.q: Someone close to Abe said, unofficially, that the prime minister would visit the ____ Shrine.
questions.explain: The shrine honors Japan's war dead.
questions.rule: Name the question to recall the case.

questions.q: An analyst doubts a CEO would sell, as it makes no sense. A confidant says he will. What risk does Bill's miss warn about?
options: Believing the statement fully, on the view that insiders are always right about such things
Changing the forecast too often, on the view that every new tip is only noise
Dismissing the tip because it clashes with what a rational outsider would do
Relying on the base rate of such sales, which is too low to matter in any case
optionExplain: Bill's error was the reverse: he did not weigh the tip enough.
Bill's error was not updating at all.
That is how Bill dismissed the tip about Abe.
Bill's reasoning was not about a base rate but about what made sense.
questions.explain: Bill judged the visit senseless, so he discounted the tip. The tip deserved weight even if the visit looked unwise.
questions.rule: Do not dismiss evidence because it surprises you.

questions.q: Sort each fact: did it support Bill's initial forecast of no visit, or point toward a visit?

items.t: Visits outrage the Chinese and Korean governments
The United States constantly urges prime ministers not to go
The shrine lists about a thousand war criminals among the honored dead
Someone close to Abe said, unofficially, that he would go
Conservatives like Abe revere the shrine
Abe visited on December 26

questions.explain: Outrage in China and Korea, American urging and the war criminals listed were reasons to expect no visit. The tip, conservatives' reverence for the shrine and the actual visit pointed to a visit.
questions.rule: Weigh facts on both sides.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Bill Flack's initial forecast that Abe would not visit was unreasonable.
questions.explain: The authors call it a reasonable forecast. The error was in how he treated the later tip.
questions.rule: A sound forecast can still be updated badly.

questions.q: A forecaster hears an unofficial, well-placed tip that contradicts her forecast. From the Abe story alone, what do the authors say about potentially insightful evidence?
options: Wait for official confirmation, since unofficial sources are weak
Move by a few points at most, as large moves risk overreaction
Do not hesitate to turn the ship's wheel hard
Prefer the base rate, as individual tips rarely beat history
optionExplain: The tip was unofficial, and Bill's wait cost him.
That is the later counterweight, not the lesson of the Abe story.
That is the lesson they draw from Bill's miss, before showing the opposite danger.
The authors draw no such lesson from the Abe case.
questions.explain: The authors say stories like Bill's suggest you should not hesitate to turn the ship's wheel hard, then immediately show Doug's overcorrection.
questions.teaches: The authors say these stories suggest that if you spot potentially insightful new evidence, you should not hesitate to turn the ship's wheel hard.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a forecaster who dismisses new evidence because it conflicts with a reasonable forecast can underreact, even if the forecast was sound.

questions.q: After a teammate found a scientific report on Arctic sea ice, Doug Lorch moved his forecast from 55% yes to about what?
optionExplain: He moved to 95% yes.
He moved a lot more than that.
He moved more than that.
This is a big move, but not as big as the one he made.
questions.explain: Doug swung to 95%. The card next shows why the authors call this risky.
questions.rule: According to the authors, one convincing but dated report can tempt even a top forecaster into a sharp move that the evidence does not support.

questions.q: In the report Doug found, all but ____ of the twenty-eight projections predicted less ice.
questions.explain: Twenty-five of the twenty-eight projections pointed to less ice.
questions.rule: The report was lopsided but dated.

questions.q: A forecaster at 55% that a team will win finds a three-week-old analyst report favouring them and jumps to 95%. What does Doug's case warn?
options: A strong report should always be followed to the letter, since analysts in the field know best
Analysts' reports should be ignored, as they reflect only opinion
The report's age matters when conditions change daily, so the jump is likely too big
The jump is right if the report's authors were experts in their field
optionExplain: Doug followed a strong report and lost.
Doug's report was a sound source; the issue was the size of the move.
The authors stress that a month is a long time for a daily-changing reality.
Expertise did not stop the report from being stale.
questions.explain: A convincing report can still be stale. The shorter the horizon and the faster conditions change, the more its age matters.
questions.rule: Weigh the age of a report.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Doug's mistake was acting on a report that scientists had already withdrawn.
questions.explain: The report was not withdrawn; the catch was that it was a month old.
questions.rule: Stale, not withdrawn.

questions.q: Why was 55% a prudent opening forecast on the Arctic question?
options: The Arctic is too unpredictable for any forecaster to go much past a coin flip on it
Forecasters are told by the organisers to open every question close to 50% as a rule
In mid-August the ice extent was almost exactly last year's, and everyone expected a close call
Scientists had not tracked the ice extent closely enough to say anything about it in August
optionExplain: The question was close, not unforecastable; Doug later moved to 95% and then to 15%.
No such rule is described.
Scientists and superforecasters alike saw a close call.
Scientists track Arctic sea ice with amazing precision and report it daily.
questions.explain: With extent nearly the same as a year earlier, either outcome was plausible, so a near-even opening fit the evidence.
questions.rule: Close evidence, close forecast.
questions.teaches: Scientists track Arctic sea ice with amazing precision, reporting daily, and in mid-August 2014 the extent was almost exactly what it had been a year earlier, so everyone from scientists to superforecasters agreed the outcome would be close.

questions.q: A forecaster jumps to 95% on a stale report, then events move against its projections. According to Doug's case, what happens to the score?
options: It suffers, as Doug's did when ice loss slowed
It is unaffected, since the original 55% still counts
It improves, since moving early rewards the forecaster for taking a view
It is unaffected, since one stale report is not held against a forecaster
optionExplain: He was exposed to the full cost of a confident miss.
Scores follow the forecasts held, not only the opening one.
Doug's early, large move was costly.
The text says Doug's score suffered.
questions.explain: Over the weeks after Doug's jump, ice loss slowed. On September 15 there was more ice than a year earlier, and his score suffered.
questions.rule: Confident moves cost when wrong.
questions.teaches: In the weeks after Doug moved to 95%, ice loss slowed; on September 15 there was more ice than a year earlier, and Doug's score suffered.

questions.q: After the initial forecast, which pair of dangers does the chapter name?
options: Overconfidence and underconfidence in the first estimate
Following the crowd and ignoring the crowd
Updating too rarely and updating too often
Underreaction and overreaction to new information
optionExplain: Those concern the first estimate, not the weight given to later information.
The crowd is a source to compare with, not one of the two dangers.
This sounds right but confuses how often with how much, which is what these errors measure.
These are the two errors of weighing new information.
questions.explain: The two dangers are about the weight placed on new information. The card next defines them.
questions.rule: According to the authors, after the first forecast you can err by giving new information too little weight or too much, and both errors cost accuracy.

questions.q: Giving too little weight to new information is called ____.
questions.explain: Not giving enough weight to new information is underreaction.
questions.rule: Too little weight is underreaction.

questions.q: An investor sells her entire portfolio after reading one gloomy headline. Which of the authors' two dangers is this?
options: Underreaction, because she ignored the other headlines of the week
Overreaction, because one headline is treated as more meaningful than it is
Neither, since selling everything is a decisive and well-informed act
Underreaction, because she waited until the headline appeared before she acted
optionExplain: She acted strongly on one headline, which is the opposite error.
She adjusted far more radically than the evidence supports.
Decisiveness is not the test; the weight on the news is.
Waiting for news is not itself underreaction.
questions.explain: Treating one headline as huge is overreaction: seeing information as more meaningful than it is.
questions.rule: Overreaction means too much weight.

questions.q: Match each case to the error it shows.
pairs: Dismissing a credible tip because it seems to make little sense
Swinging from 55% to 95% on one month-old report
Moving a forecast by exactly the amount the new evidence supports
questions.explain: Dismissing a credible tip is underreaction; swinging to 95% on one dated report is overreaction; giving each poll the weight it deserves is neither.
questions.rule: Weight is the test.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, overreaction is the fault of forecasters who ignore new information.
questions.explain: Ignoring new information is underreaction. Overreaction is seeing it as more meaningful than it is.
questions.rule: Under: too little. Over: too much.

questions.q: A forecaster consistently gives new evidence a little too little weight. According to the authors, how bad can such an error get?
options: It can only slow the forecast, since errors of weight never reverse direction
In extreme cases it can destroy a perfectly good forecast
It cannot hurt accuracy, since a cautious forecaster is never badly wrong
It matters only for overreaction, as underreaction is a harmless habit
optionExplain: The authors say extreme cases can destroy a good forecast.
The authors say both errors can do so in extreme cases.
The authors say both errors can diminish accuracy.
They say both can diminish accuracy and wreck a forecast.
questions.explain: Both errors reduce accuracy, and in extreme cases either can destroy a perfectly good forecast.
questions.teaches: Both under- and overreaction can diminish accuracy, and in extreme cases both can destroy a perfectly good forecast.
questions.rule: According to the authors, after the first forecast you can err by giving new information too little weight or too much, and both errors cost accuracy.

questions.q: Why did Joshua Frankel not raise his forecast from 82% to 99% after the Syria announcement?
options: He doubted that the announced action would actually be carried out
He thought 82% was already the highest sensible figure
He disagreed with how the question was worded
Events moved fast and he was too swamped with work to stay on top of them
optionExplain: He later said the update was plainly called for.
He later said he should have gone to 99%.
No such disagreement is reported.
He said so himself.
questions.explain: He was too busy. The card next puts this in context.
questions.rule: According to the authors, some underreaction is plain neglect, such as being too busy to revise a forecast after decisive news.

questions.q: Frankel's forecast stayed at 82% when he later said it should have risen to ____%.
questions.explain: He said 99% was where it belonged.
questions.rule: Know the gap: 82 versus 99.

questions.q: A forecaster with many open questions has a hectic week and makes no changes after a decisive announcement. What kind of underreaction is this?
options: Plain neglect, a lapse of upkeep, not a thinking error
A psychological bias, because everyone who skips an update is resisting new facts
A deliberate strategy of avoiding overreaction by waiting
Not underreaction at all, since no new information was processed
optionExplain: This matches Frankel's case.
Frankel's lapse was lack of time, not resistance.
Frankel did not choose to wait; he was swamped.
Failing to process it is underreaction.
questions.explain: Frankel's lapse came from workload, not from how he read the news.
questions.rule: Some underreaction is just neglect.

questions.q: True or false: The authors describe Frankel's underreaction as having a prosaic cause: he was too swamped with work to update.
questions.explain: His lapse was workload, not a psychological bias.
questions.rule: Some underreaction is plain neglect.

questions.q: What did Frankel do after his lapse became clear?
options: He argued the question should be cancelled as unfair
He blamed the announcement for being too vague
He wrote that he had done a poor job of updating
He said nothing, as a closed question needs no review
optionExplain: No such claim is reported.
He took the blame himself.
The authors quote his blunt self-assessment.
He openly reviewed his error.
questions.explain: Frankel said he had done a poor job. Superforecasters openly note their lapses, which makes learning from them possible.
questions.rule: Name the lapse.
questions.teaches: Frankel wrote, once the question closed, that he had done a poor job of updating his forecast.

questions.q: A team keeps old forecasts live long after events have settled them. Which phrase of the authors fits the fix?
options: Turning the ship's wheel hard when evidence is insightful
Finding the middle passage between two dangers
Good housekeeping: sweeping out old forecasts
Unpacking the question into components
optionExplain: That is about the weight of news, not about upkeep.
That is about balancing under- and overreaction.
The authors say some updating reduces to this.
That is a step in the opening process.
questions.explain: Some updating is housekeeping, clearing out outdated forecasts so they do not sit uncorrected.
questions.teaches: The authors say some updating does reduce to good housekeeping, which means sweeping out old forecasts.
questions.rule: According to the authors, some underreaction is plain neglect, such as being too busy to revise a forecast after decisive news.

questions.q: Looking back, what question did Bill Flack say he had really been answering about the Yasukuni visit?
options: If I were prime minister of Japan, would I visit Yasukuni?
Will relations with China and Korea be damaged by a visit?
Will the United States object to a visit?
Is the unofficial source usually reliable?
optionExplain: He said this was the question he had been answering.
He weighed those costs, but they were not his replacement question.
That was one reason he weighed, not the substituted question.
He did not frame his error that way.
questions.explain: He answered a question about himself, not about Abe. The card next names this move.
questions.rule: According to the authors, replacing the hard question with an easier one can make real evidence look irrelevant, causing underreaction.

questions.q: Substituting an easier question for a hard one is called a bait and ____.
questions.explain: The authors recall the bait-and-switch from chapter 2.
questions.rule: Bait and switch: swap the question.

questions.q: Asked if a rival will cut prices, a manager asks whether he would, in its place. A report says the rival will. What follows?
options: He gives the report far too much weight, since it settles the question he asked
He weighs the report correctly, since his own view is the best guide
He seeks a second source before reacting, which prevents all errors of this kind
He dismisses it, because it does not fit the question he is really answering
optionExplain: It does not settle the question he is actually answering.
His view of the rival's mind is not the rival's mind.
The error lies in the question asked, not the number of sources.
This is Bill's pattern.
questions.explain: If you answer a different question, evidence about the real one looks irrelevant.
questions.rule: Check which question you are answering.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Bill's problem was that he lacked the facts about the political costs of a visit.
questions.explain: He had those facts. His problem was ignoring Abe's own feelings by answering a question about himself.
questions.rule: The facts were there; the question had changed.

questions.q: Which facts about Abe did Bill's reasoning from rational costs and benefits leave out?
options: Abe had promised the Chinese government that he would not visit the shrine as prime minister
Abe is a conservative nationalist who had visited before and wanted to go again
Abe had never been to the shrine and had no interest in it
Abe had been advised by the United States to visit
optionExplain: No such promise is reported.
These facts bear on what Abe would do.
The reverse: he had visited before.
The United States urged leaders not to go.
questions.explain: Bill's costs-and-benefits analysis was a rational PM's, but Abe is a conservative nationalist who had visited and wanted to return.
questions.rule: Model the person, not yourself.
questions.teaches: Abe is a conservative nationalist who had visited Yasukuni before, though not as prime minister, and who wanted to go again.

questions.q: Asked if a regime will fall, a forecaster asks whether she wants it to. How will she probably react to news of mass protests?
options: She will overreact to it, since protests always signal that a regime is about to fall
She will probably dismiss it, since it is irrelevant to her substituted question
She will update correctly, as the protests are visible to all
She will update by a small but correct amount, as a cautious habit
optionExplain: The substitution leads to ignoring evidence, not inflating it.
Having strayed from the real question, she misjudges the evidence.
Visibility does not fix a substituted question.
The error is in the question, not in the size of steps.
questions.explain: Straying from the real question, Bill dismissed new information because it did not bear on his replacement question.
questions.teaches: Having strayed from the real question, Bill dismissed the new information because it was irrelevant to his replacement question.
questions.rule: According to the authors, replacing the hard question with an easier one can make real evidence look irrelevant, causing underreaction.

questions.q: True or false: Hard-liners such as Earl Warren and General DeWitt insisted that the danger of sabotage had not lessened, though none had occurred.
questions.explain: They did insist, and DeWitt even read the absence of sabotage as confirming. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, belief perseverance is the pull to rationalize away facts that upset a settled belief, and in extreme cases absent evidence is read as confirmation.

questions.q: Psychologists call the clinging to a belief despite new evidence belief ____.
questions.explain: The authors use the term for the tendency to rationalize away new information that upsets settled beliefs.
questions.rule: Name: belief perseverance.

questions.q: A manager says: 'The fact that the new product has no buyers yet proves they are about to arrive.' Which pattern is this?
options: Healthy updating, because it keeps the original plan on course for longer
Overreaction, because a single missing sale is treated as decisive
A bait and switch, because the question has been replaced
Belief perseverance, reading a missing expected result as confirmation
optionExplain: A fact that went against the belief is treated as support for it.
The error is rationalizing, not overreacting to news.
The question is unchanged; the belief is protected.
It mirrors DeWitt's argument.
questions.explain: The manager treats evidence against his belief as support for it, as DeWitt did.
questions.rule: Evidence against a belief is not a confirmation of it.

questions.q: According to the authors, what usually happens when people face facts they cannot ignore?
options: They budge grudgingly, but by less than they should
They move all the way at once, since facts that cannot be ignored settle matters
They dig in as DeWitt did, which is the common response
They abandon the old belief while keeping their sense of self intact
optionExplain: Extreme obstinacy is rare; shortfall is common.
The authors say the change is likely to be less than it should be.
The authors say such extreme obstinacy is rare.
That is not the common pattern the authors describe.
questions.explain: More commonly the change is grudging and falls short. The brain likes things neat and tries to minimise disturbances.
questions.rule: Expect shortfall, not extremes.
questions.teaches: More commonly than extreme obstinacy, people confronted with facts impossible to ignore budge grudgingly, and the degree of change is likely to be less than it should be.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, extreme obstinacy like General DeWitt's is rare among people confronted with facts impossible to ignore.
questions.explain: The authors say such extreme obstinacy is rare; more commonly people budge grudgingly.
questions.rule: Extreme cases are rare.

questions.q: Earl Warren later became chief justice and a champion of civil rights. What does the authors' account imply about his stance in 1942?
options: It shows he never really held his 1942 view and was only acting for public show
It shows that belief perseverance affects only people with weak principles
At the time, security rather than civil rights was at the tip of his nose
It shows his later career proves the internment was justified
optionExplain: The authors describe real conviction.
Warren was, the authors later say, a civil libertarian at heart.
The authors say civil rights were not at the tip of his nose then.
The authors call the policy an unjust imprisonment.
questions.explain: Warren's later fame does not change what he was thinking in 1942, when security was uppermost.
questions.teaches: Warren later became governor of California and chief justice of the US Supreme Court, remembered as a liberal champion of school desegregation and civil rights, but in World War II security, not civil rights, was at the tip of his nose.
questions.rule: According to the authors, belief perseverance is the pull to rationalize away facts that upset a settled belief, and in extreme cases absent evidence is read as confirmation.

questions.q: True or false: The authors could not trace the famous line about changing your mind when the facts change to its supposed source.
questions.explain: They could not, and the leading Keynes experts think it apocryphal. The card next tells what they found.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a well-known line attributed to Keynes could not be traced and may be apocryphal, and one author publicly admitted he was wrong to repeat it.

questions.q: The authors could not trace the Keynes line to its ____, and the leading Keynes experts think it is apocryphal.
questions.explain: No one has discovered where it comes from.
questions.rule: The attribution is unverified.

questions.q: A chef learns his favourite saying was misattributed. His restaurant does not rest on it. What does the authors' account predict?
options: He can admit the mistake without much pain
He will resist the correction, since a public statement must be defended
He will feel obliged to find a new source that supports the saying
He will find it hard, as admitting error is painful whatever the stakes
optionExplain: The authors found it easy to own up for just that reason.
The authors' own case shows that low stakes make admitting error easy.
The authors confessed that they were wrong.
The authors say admitting it was not hard for them.
questions.explain: A misattributed quotation that supports nothing else is cheap to give up.
questions.rule: Low stakes make updating cheap.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say they found a primary source that proves Keynes said the line.
questions.explain: They found no source; the experts think the line is apocryphal.
questions.rule: No source was found.

questions.q: Why did the author say that admitting the Keynes error was not hard?
options: He had already been criticised for the error by several readers, so confessing was a relief
He believed the line is true in spirit, so nothing was lost
He wrote the error in a minor article that few people read
Many smart people made the same mistake, and the line was not central to his identity
optionExplain: No such criticism is reported.
The authors do not give this as a reason.
The authors say the line appears in books, including his own.
Both facts lowered the cost of admitting error.
questions.explain: Being wrong was shared with many smart people, and being right was not part of his identity.
questions.rule: Identity raises the cost of error.
questions.teaches: The author found confessing easy because many smart people had made the same mistake, so it was not embarrassing, and because the quotation was not central to his work and being right about it was not part of his identity.

questions.q: One professor repeated a catchy line; another built her career on a disputed claim. Both are shown wrong. How might the second react?
options: Her reaction will be calmer, since a career gives more experience of being wrong
Her reaction might be much less casual, because her career rests on the claim
Her reaction will be the same, since error is error
Her reaction will be to publish a retraction at once
optionExplain: The authors suggest the opposite.
The author says his own reaction might have been less casual if he had staked his career on the line.
The authors link the reaction to what is staked.
The authors suggest the stakes would make her slower to admit error.
questions.explain: The authors say that had he staked his career on the quotation, his reaction might have been less casual.
questions.teaches: If the author had staked his career on that quotation, his reaction might have been less casual.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a well-known line attributed to Keynes could not be traced and may be apocryphal, and one author publicly admitted he was wrong to repeat it.

questions.q: What have social psychologists long known about getting people to commit publicly to a belief?
options: It makes people more open to evidence, since they want to appear fair to others
It tends to freeze the belief in place and make it resistant to change
It has no effect, because beliefs depend only on evidence
It weakens the belief, since saying it aloud exposes its flaws
optionExplain: The authors say the reverse.
Public commitment hardens beliefs.
The authors say commitment matters.
Commitment strengthens resistance.
questions.explain: Commitment freezes beliefs. The card next shows the effect on a top forecaster.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the more a person is committed to a belief, the harder it is to change, which makes updating hardest on questions one cares about.

questions.q: The stronger the ____, the greater the resistance to changing a belief.
questions.explain: The authors say resistance grows with commitment.
questions.rule: Stronger commitment, greater resistance.

questions.q: One analyst announces her election forecast on TV; another keeps hers in a private notebook. Per social psychologists, who will be slower to revise?
options: The one with the notebook, since nobody has ever tested her reasoning in public
Neither, since both started from the same evidence
Both equally, since only the forecast, not the commitment, matters
The one who announced it, since public commitment freezes a belief
optionExplain: Privacy lowers commitment.
The same evidence does not mean the same commitment.
The authors say commitment affects resistance.
She has committed in public.
questions.explain: Public commitment is the stronger form, so her belief will be harder to change.
questions.rule: Public commitment hardens belief.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Jean-Pierre Beugoms does not struggle to change his mind, even on topics he knows best.
questions.explain: He says it is a challenge, especially on questions he has an investment in, such as military ones.
questions.rule: Even good updaters struggle where invested.

questions.q: According to Beugoms, what can happen when he realises he is wrong on a military question?
options: He might spend a few days in denial before critiquing himself
He updates at once, since his training at West Point makes him quick
He asks a teammate to make the change for him
He gives up forecasting military questions altogether
optionExplain: He says so himself.
He says he might spend days in denial.
No such step is reported.
He keeps answering them.
questions.explain: Even a self-aware updater may delay when the question is close to his expertise.
questions.rule: Expertise can slow updating.
questions.teaches: Beugoms says that if he realises he is wrong on a military question, he might spend a few days in denial about it before he critiques himself.

questions.q: A senior engineer feels she should do better than most on questions in her own field. Following Beugoms, how does that expectation affect her updating?
options: It lowers her investment, since expertise makes errors easy to spot
It has no effect, as expectations do not change how evidence is weighed
It raises her investment, so admitting she was wrong becomes harder
It speeds her updating, as she knows where to look
optionExplain: Beugoms' experience is the reverse.
Beugoms links his expectation to his difficulty.
Beugoms says he feels he should be doing better than most on military questions.
Beugoms says it slows him down.
questions.explain: Beugoms feels he should be doing better than most on military questions, so being wrong stings and he delays.
questions.teaches: Beugoms says he feels he should be doing better than most on military questions, which is why realising he is wrong is hard for him.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the more a person is committed to a belief, the harder it is to change, which makes updating hardest on questions one cares about.

questions.q: True or false: A belief that supports many other beliefs is harder to change than one that supports none.
questions.explain: A belief near the core holds up others, so pulling it out upsets them. The card next explains the image.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the nearer a belief sits to the core of one's self-perception, the more it supports, and the harder it is to remove.

questions.q: The authors compare our system of beliefs to the children's game ____.
questions.explain: Blocks are stacked on each other like a Jenga tower.
questions.rule: Beliefs are stacked like Jenga blocks.

questions.q: A scientist holds a view about a minor lab step and another about the theory behind her career. Where do they sit in the tower?
options: Both near the top, because beliefs about work are not about the self
Both near the core, since every belief a scientist holds is equally central
The lab step near the top; the theory near the core
The lab step near the core; the theory near the top, since theories are revisable
optionExplain: Her career theory is bound up with self-perception.
The lab step supports little.
The more a belief supports, the nearer the core it sits.
Revisability depends on what is built on it, not its type.
questions.explain: A belief that supports nothing else is near the top, and one tied to identity is near the core.
questions.rule: Position depends on what rests on the belief.

questions.q: Sort each belief: is it easy or hard to remove from the tower?

items.t: The Keynes line, a block at the apex that supports nothing else
A belief near the top of the tower
A forecast in Beugoms's specialty, lower down next to a self-perception block
A belief near the core, holding up many others
A belief at the very base of the tower
A belief that can be tossed away without disturbing other blocks

questions.explain: Blocks that support nothing else, like the Keynes line, are easy to toss; blocks that sit beside self-perception or at the base are hard to remove.
questions.rule: Core blocks resist.

questions.q: What do the authors say about removing a block at the very base of the tower?
options: There is no way to remove it without bringing everything crashing down
It can be done safely if the other blocks are shored up first
It can be done at a cost only to the blocks directly above it
It is easy, since a base block is the oldest and the least examined of all
optionExplain: The whole tower rests on it.
The authors say there is no way.
Everything is brought down.
The authors say it is the hardest.
questions.explain: A base belief holds up the rest, so removing it brings down the tower. This is why extreme commitment breeds extreme reluctance.
questions.rule: Base beliefs cannot be pulled out alone.
questions.teaches: When a block is at the very base of the tower, there is no way to remove it without bringing everything crashing down; extreme commitment leads to extreme reluctance to admit error.

questions.q: Why was it so hard for the men behind the 1942 internment to admit error?
options: They lacked any evidence that the danger of sabotage had lessened as the war went on
They had never held a public view, so there was nothing to defend in the first place
They saw the internment as a small matter with little at stake for their careers
Their commitment was massive; admitting error would have taken a sledgehammer to their tower
optionExplain: There was evidence: no sabotage occurred.
They held strong public views.
The authors stress the size of their commitment.
The authors say this of Warren.
questions.explain: Warren was, deep down, a civil libertarian; admitting he had unjustly imprisoned 112,000 people would have demolished his mental tower.
questions.teaches: Warren was deep down a civil libertarian, and admitting to himself that he had unjustly imprisoned 112,000 people would have taken a sledgehammer to his mental tower.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the nearer a belief sits to the core of one's self-perception, the more it supports, and the harder it is to remove.

questions.q: True or false: People who feel strongly about gun control typically say they would not change their position even if shown conclusive contrary evidence.
questions.explain: Kahan finds they typically say no. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, strongly held views on risk often follow identity rather than evidence, so people will not change them even for conclusive proof.

questions.q: Dan Kahan, whose research on risk judgments the authors cite, is a professor at ____ University.
questions.explain: He is a Yale professor.
questions.rule: Kahan: Yale; identity drives risk judgments.

questions.q: A reader's view on a new tax matches her social group's on every issue. How could she test whether evidence or identity drives it?
options: Count how many sources she has read on the tax, and weigh how reliable each was
Ask whether she would change her view if shown conclusive evidence against it
Check whether her view is the majority view in the country at large and among friends
Ask whether she is certain, since certainty shows evidence drove the view
optionExplain: More reading does not show whether she could be moved.
This is Kahan's test.
A majority view can still be identity-driven.
Certainty is what identity-driven views feel like.
questions.explain: Kahan asks people to imagine conclusive evidence and whether they would change their position; an identity-driven view typically would not move.
questions.rule: Imagine conclusive evidence and ask whether you would move.

questions.q: True or false: Kahan found that people with strong views typically say they would not change them even when given conclusive evidence.
questions.explain: That is the finding the authors report.
questions.rule: Strong views resist conclusive evidence.

questions.q: Why do the authors say many people refuse even to imagine conclusive evidence against their view?
options: They have studied the evidence closely and know the opposite cannot be true
The belief block is holding up many others, and removing it risks chaos
They think imagining evidence is a waste of time
They distrust professors and surveys in general
optionExplain: The authors describe reluctance, not careful study.
This links Kahan's finding to the tower image.
The reason given is the risk of chaos.
No such distrust is mentioned.
questions.explain: A block that supports many others cannot be removed without upheaval, so people will not even picture removing it.
questions.rule: Imagining a change is a threat to the tower.
questions.teaches: Such a belief block is holding up a lot of others, and taking it out risks chaos, so many people refuse even to imagine the conclusive evidence.

questions.q: A survey shows that people's views on two unrelated policies line up almost perfectly. Which explanation fits Kahan's account?
options: The two policies share a hidden logical link that careful evidence reveals to anyone
Respondents weighed the evidence on each of the two issues independently of each other
Survey questions must have been worded in the same way
Identity links the views although the two issues have no logical connection
optionExplain: The authors say the two issues have no logical connection.
Independent weighing would not produce such a match.
No such explanation is given.
Gun control and climate change have no logical connection to each other.
questions.explain: Kahan's pairing of gun control and climate views shows that identity can link issues that have no logical link.
questions.teaches: Views on gun control and climate change often correlate even though the two issues have no logical connection to each other.
questions.rule: According to the authors, strongly held views on risk often follow identity rather than evidence, so people will not change them even for conclusive proof.

questions.q: Why might non-professional forecasters update more easily than famous pundits?
options: They have little ego invested in each forecast
They have more time to read
They use better mathematical methods
They are never wrong, so there is nothing to update
optionExplain: That is the authors' claim.
Time is not the reason given.
The chapter says superforecasters rarely crunch the numbers.
Even the best updaters err.
questions.explain: Low ego investment helps, as the card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, low ego investment makes it easier for superforecasters to admit an offtrack forecast and so avoid underreaction.

questions.q: Superforecasters, being non-professionals, have little ____ invested in each forecast.
questions.explain: Little ego investment makes admitting error easier.
questions.rule: Less ego, easier updating.

questions.q: A hobbyist forecaster and a career pundit both see a forecast go off track. Which does the authors' account say will likelier update readily?
options: The pundit, since public exposure forces honesty
Both equally, since good forecasters ignore reputation
The hobbyist, because less of her reputation rides on the forecast
Neither, since updating is a matter of intelligence rather than ego
optionExplain: Public exposure raises commitment.
The authors say reputation stakes matter.
The authors say low ego investment helps superforecasters.
The authors tie updating to ego investment.
questions.explain: A forecaster with less riding on a forecast can drop it with less cost.
questions.rule: Less at stake, easier updating.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say superforecasters have no ego investment in their forecasts at all.
questions.explain: They have little ego invested, not none: the authors say they do not have zero ego investment.
questions.rule: Little is not zero.

questions.q: What could make a superforecaster's commitment to forecasts grow fast, according to the authors?
options: Winning a tournament by a large margin over every other forecaster
Working in a team with experts who keep a close watch on them
If being a superforecaster becomes part of their self-concept
Making forecasts on a large number of questions during one season
optionExplain: The authors tie growth to self-concept.
Teammates matter for reputation, but self-concept is the factor named.
Identity raises the stakes.
Volume of forecasts is not the factor named.
questions.explain: The label itself is the risk: once it is part of identity, a missed forecast threatens identity.
questions.rule: Labels become identities.
questions.teaches: Superforecasters care about their reputations among their teammates, and if 'superforecaster' becomes part of their self-concept their commitment will grow fast.

questions.q: Compare a hobbyist forecaster with a career CIA analyst or an acclaimed pundit. Who has the greater self-esteem stakes in a forecast, per the authors?
options: The career analyst or pundit, whose reputation is on the line
The hobbyist, since an amateur has more to prove to the other forecasters
Neither, since stakes do not depend on career or on public reputation
The pundit only, since analysts work in secret and have no public record
optionExplain: The authors say superforecasters' stakes are far smaller.
The authors say the opposite.
They say stakes differ greatly.
They name career CIA analysts as well.
questions.explain: Career analysts and acclaimed pundits have their reputations on the line, which makes underreaction a bigger risk.
questions.teaches: The self-esteem stakes of superforecasters are far less than those for career CIA analysts or acclaimed pundits with their reputations on the line.
questions.rule: According to the authors, low ego investment makes it easier for superforecasters to admit an offtrack forecast and so avoid underreaction.

questions.q: In the 1989 study, what happened when participants were given irrelevant facts about Robert or David as well as the stereotype-fitting facts?
options: They became more confident, since more information gives more certainty
Their estimates stayed the same, since the facts were irrelevant
They refused to give an estimate at all
They lost confidence in their stereotype-based estimates
optionExplain: More information that is irrelevant lowers confidence here.
That is what they should have done, and not what happened.
They gave estimates.
The extra facts weakened the fit.
questions.explain: They lost confidence. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, adding irrelevant facts about a person dilutes a stereotype-based judgment, even though those facts should be ignored.

questions.q: Psychologists call this effect of irrelevant information the ____ effect.
questions.explain: Irrelevant details dilute the stereotype.
questions.rule: Name: dilution effect.

questions.q: A manager rates a candidate highly from strong credentials, then learns the candidate keeps a cat. What does the dilution effect predict?
options: Her rating rises, since the extra detail shows a rounded person with real interests
Her rating drops, as the personal facts make the candidate less like a stereotype
Her rating stays unchanged, since the facts are irrelevant
Her rating becomes random, since the stereotype is lost
optionExplain: Irrelevant detail dilutes rather than strengthens.
Irrelevant facts weaken the fit.
That is the rational response, which people often fail to give.
The effect is a loss of confidence, not randomness.
questions.explain: With only fitting facts, the signal feels strong. Add irrelevant ones and the candidate looks more like a person than a stereotype.
questions.rule: Irrelevant detail dilutes.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, participants given the irrelevant facts about Robert and David lost confidence in their estimates.
questions.explain: The irrelevant facts weakened the fit with the stereotype.
questions.rule: Irrelevant facts reduce confidence.

questions.q: Diluting a stereotype might seem good since stereotypes are a source of bias. How do the authors judge the dilution effect?
options: It is a benefit, because it reduces their reliance on stereotypes in judging others
It remains a bias, as people should have ignored the irrelevant facts
It is neither, since it only changes confidence, not estimates
It is a strength of careful thinkers who consider all facts
optionExplain: The authors say it remains a bias.
Fighting fire with fire is possible but it remains a bias.
Confidence is part of the judgment.
The facts were irrelevant, so considering them is the mistake.
questions.explain: The authors say 'yes and no': bias can be fought with bias, but the dilution effect remains a bias.
questions.rule: A bias that offsets another is still a bias.
questions.teaches: The dilution effect remains a bias even though it can offset the bias of stereotypes: people should ignore meaningless noise but do not.

questions.q: A forecaster revises a sound estimate whenever an irrelevant detail turns up. What picture do the authors give of such people?
options: They steer by principle, moving only when the evidence itself has really changed
They behave like rigid anchors, which resist all information
They act as a sensible mean between two extremes
They sway in the wind, at the mercy of the next random gust of irrelevant facts
optionExplain: The authors describe the opposite.
That is underreaction.
Swaying is the error, not the middle path.
That is the authors' image.
questions.explain: Swaying with each irrelevant gust is overreaction, a common and costly mistake.
questions.teaches: The authors say people sway in the wind, at the mercy of the next random gust of irrelevant information.
questions.rule: According to the authors, adding irrelevant facts about a person dilutes a stereotype-based judgment, even though those facts should be ignored.

questions.q: In Malkiel's cited study of 66,000 households, about what did the heaviest traders earn per year when the market returned 17.9%?
options: About 11.4%
About 17.9%, matching the market
About 20%, thanks to skilful timing
About 5.0%, barely above nothing
optionExplain: They did much worse than the market.
They fell short of the market.
They earned less, not more.
They did worse than the market but not that badly.
questions.explain: The heaviest traders earned 11.4%. The card next puts this in context.
questions.rule: According to the authors, frequent trading on new information tends to earn less than old-fashioned buy-and-hold, a sign of costly overreaction.

questions.q: Malkiel likens frequent traders to players selecting and discarding cards in a game of gin ____.
questions.explain: The metaphor is gin rummy.
questions.rule: Name: gin rummy.

questions.q: A friend changes his retirement holdings daily after each headline. What do the authors' cited studies suggest about his returns?
options: Higher, since reacting quickly captures every opportunity
The same, as news changes the price immediately
Likely lower than a buy-and-hold approach
Higher, since trading volume reduces risk
optionExplain: The cited studies found the reverse.
The studies found a gap.
Many studies find that frequent traders get worse returns.
The studies found frequent trading hurt returns.
questions.explain: The cited studies found that those who trade more get worse returns.
questions.rule: More trading, worse returns.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say research has settled that overreaction by traders is the sole cause of stock market volatility.
questions.explain: They say the reasons are complex and debated; at least some is due to overreaction.
questions.rule: Overreaction is one factor.

questions.q: What did Keynes say about day-to-day fluctuations in profits of existing investments?
options: They are the best guide to a firm's value and always deserve a strong response from investors
They are significant, so the market reacts to them with good reason and in due proportion
They are ephemeral and non-significant, yet have an excessive and even absurd influence
They have little influence, since investors ignore them
optionExplain: Keynes called them ephemeral.
He called them non-significant.
Keynes saw the market overreacting to the trivial.
He said the influence was excessive.
questions.explain: Keynes thought the market gave trivial fluctuations too much weight.
questions.rule: Trivial news gets too much weight.
questions.teaches: Keynes said day-to-day fluctuations in the profits of existing investments, which are of an ephemeral and non-significant character, tend to have an altogether excessive and even absurd influence on the market.

questions.q: A trader spends hours a day reacting to news and earns less than a neighbour who holds and golfs. What do the authors' remarks suggest?
options: The effort bought worse results; they might have done better golfing
The trader's results should improve with still more hours spent watching the market
The neighbour must have lucky timing
Reaction speed explains the gap, so the trader should be faster
optionExplain: The authors say this of the heavy traders.
Heavier trading is what the study found to be worse.
The authors point to a pattern, not luck.
Speed of reaction is the problem.
questions.explain: Massive time and effort went into the trades, yet the traders would have been better off golfing.
questions.teaches: The authors remark that massive time and effort went into the heavy traders' trades and yet they would have been better off if they had gone golfing.
questions.rule: According to the authors, frequent trading on new information tends to earn less than old-fashioned buy-and-hold, a sign of costly overreaction.

questions.q: Which pair of classical images do the authors use for the opposing dangers of under- and overreaction?
options: Icarus and Daedalus
Achilles and Hector
Sisyphus and Tantalus
Scylla and Charybdis
optionExplain: This pair concerns flight and a father's warning.
These are warriors, not twin dangers.
These are figures of endless punishment.
The authors use this old pair of dangers.
questions.explain: They use Scylla and Charybdis. The card next explains the choice.
questions.rule: According to the authors, good updating means steering a middle course between giving new information too little weight and too much.

questions.q: The authors say good updating is all about finding the middle ____.
questions.explain: It is the passage between the two dangers.
questions.rule: Find the middle passage.

questions.q: A forecaster with modest commitment is tempted to swing hard on every report. Which error do the authors see as her greater risk?
options: Underreaction, since her low stakes make her careless about what the news says
Overreaction, since little commitment leaves her free to move too far
Neither, since only experts are at risk of either
Both equally, since commitment does not matter
optionExplain: Low stakes make updating easier.
Modest commitment makes overreaction the greater risk.
The authors expect superforecasters to be at risk.
The authors link commitment to the type of error.
questions.explain: Low commitment frees a forecaster to move easily, which raises the risk of overreaction.
questions.rule: Low commitment raises overreaction risk.

questions.q: True or false: Given superforecasters' modest commitment, the authors expect overreaction to be a greater risk for them than underreaction.
questions.explain: Low commitment frees a forecaster to move easily.
questions.rule: Low commitment points to overreaction.

questions.q: In the authors' account of Scylla and Charybdis, what were the two dangers?
options: Two storms in the Atlantic, one off each coast of Spain, far apart
A rock shoal off Italy and a whirlpool on the coast of Sicily
Two sirens whose songs lured sailors from their course
Two islands, one rich and one barren, between which ships could trade
optionExplain: Not the authors' account.
These are the authors' details.
That is a different myth.
Not the authors' account.
questions.explain: Scylla was a rock shoal off the coast of Italy and Charybdis a whirlpool on the coast of Sicily, not far away; sailors who strayed too far in either direction were doomed.
questions.rule: Two dangers, close together.
questions.teaches: Scylla was a rock shoal off the coast of Italy and Charybdis a whirlpool on the coast of Sicily, not far away; sailors were doomed if they strayed too far in either direction.

questions.q: Which case do the authors give of the greater risk, overreaction, for forecasters with modest commitment?
options: Bill Flack discounting the tip about Abe's planned visit to the shrine
Joshua Frankel failing to revise because he was swamped with work
Earl Warren insisting that the danger had not lessened
Doug Lorch's team swinging from 55% to 95% on one month-old report
optionExplain: That was underreaction.
That was underreaction.
That was belief perseverance.
It is the example the authors give.
questions.explain: The authors point to Doug and his team as an overreaction.
questions.teaches: The authors cite Doug Lorch and his team swinging from 55% to 95% on a single, month-old report as an overreaction.
questions.rule: According to the authors, good updating means steering a middle course between giving new information too little weight and too much.

questions.q: How long does Tim Minto typically spend on an initial forecast?
options: Several hours
About forty-five minutes
A full working day
Five to fifteen minutes
optionExplain: He takes less time than some top forecasters.
More than he says.
Far more than he says.
That is his stated routine.
questions.explain: He takes five to fifteen minutes. The card next shows what he does afterwards.
questions.rule: According to the authors, Tim Minto's routine is a quick first pass followed by daily revisits, a second opinion and a search for contrary evidence.

questions.q: The next day Tim Minto comes back to a question and forms a ____ opinion.
questions.explain: He takes another look the next day.
questions.rule: Revisit and form a second opinion.

questions.q: A new forecaster wants to copy Tim. After a quick first pass on a question, what routine fits?
options: Stay with the first judgment unless a major headline forces a change of mind
Come back the next day for a second opinion and seek contrary evidence
Spend the whole first day on one question and then leave it
Wait for a prediction market to move before looking again
optionExplain: Tim revisits the question without waiting for headlines.
That is Tim's pattern.
Tim spends only minutes on the first pass.
Tim looks for contrary evidence himself.
questions.explain: Tim's habit is a quick start, then a second look and a search for contrary evidence.
questions.rule: Revisit, and seek what contradicts you.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Tim Minto spends hours on every initial forecast, far more than other top forecasters.
questions.explain: He typically spends five to fifteen minutes, less than some other top forecasters.
questions.rule: Updating, not the first pass, is his strength.

questions.q: About how many forecasts does Tim Minto typically make on a question by the time it closes?
options: One or two, since he only updates after big events
A dozen, and sometimes forty or fifty
About four, one a week for a month
Over a hundred on every question
optionExplain: He updates constantly.
On the Afghan troop-presence question he made seventy-seven.
He makes many more.
The most the authors report is seventy-seven.
questions.explain: He usually makes about a dozen forecasts, sometimes forty or fifty, and seventy-seven on one question about US troops in Afghanistan.
questions.rule: Updating often is Tim's habit.
questions.teaches: By the time a question closes, Tim Minto has usually made a dozen forecasts, sometimes forty or fifty, and on the Afghanistan troop question he made seventy-seven.

questions.q: A manager sees an analyst changing his estimates dozens of times per question. What do the authors say about how this might look?
options: It proves the analyst is indecisive and underreacting to what he reads
It shows skill, since more forecasts always mean more accuracy
It shows overreaction, as any frequent updating is overreaction
It may look like overreaction, though the size of the changes matters
optionExplain: Many changes do not imply underreaction.
The size of changes also matters.
Frequency alone does not prove overreaction.
The authors say so before explaining the size of Tim's changes.
questions.explain: It may look as though Captain Minto is sailing straight for the Charybdis of overreaction, but the magnitude of his changes tells a different story.
questions.teaches: It may look as though Captain Minto is sailing straight for the Charybdis of overreaction, but the magnitude of his constant course corrections is what makes a big difference.
questions.rule: According to the authors, Tim Minto's routine is a quick first pass followed by daily revisits, a second opinion and a search for contrary evidence.

questions.q: On the Syrian refugee question, about how large was Tim Minto's average update?
options: About 3.5%
About 12%
About 20%
About 35%
optionExplain: His changes were tiny.
That is much bigger than his typical step.
Far bigger than his typical step.
He made no swings of thirty or forty points.
questions.explain: His average update was about 3.5%. The card next shows why that matters.
questions.rule: According to the authors, many small updates let a forecaster keep the value of both the prior forecast and the new information.

questions.q: Over three months, Tim Minto changed his forecast on the Syrian refugee question ____ times.
questions.explain: The chart shows thirty-four changes, each small on average.
questions.rule: Small steps.

questions.q: Ana moves her estimate about four points per new poll; Ben moves about thirty-five. Whose style matches the superforecasters'?
options: Ben's, because big moves show conviction
Neither, because superforecasters do not change their minds on polls
Ana's, because they update often and in small increments
Ben's, because large moves capture new information faster
optionExplain: Big moves risk overreaction.
They update frequently.
Superforecasters update in smaller increments.
Fast but at the cost of losing the prior information.
questions.explain: Ana's pattern of frequent small changes is the style the authors report in superforecasters.
questions.rule: Small, frequent steps.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, superforecasters update more often than other forecasters but in larger increments.
questions.explain: They update more often and in smaller increments.
questions.rule: More often, in smaller steps.

questions.q: Why did Tim's pattern of many small updates keep him safe between the two dangers?
options: Small updates are always correct, since they avoid mistakes of every kind in the forecast
Frequent updating alone prevents both errors, whatever the size of each step
Few small updates risk underreaction and many large ones overreaction; many small ones avoid both
Small updates mean each new forecast ignores the old information
optionExplain: They sometimes led him away from the answer.
The size of the steps is the key.
That is the authors' reasoning.
The reverse: they preserve the old information.
questions.explain: A few small updates would put him on a heading for underreaction; many large updates could tip him toward overreaction; many small ones slip safely between.
questions.rule: Many and small together.
questions.teaches: A few small updates would have put Tim on a heading for underreaction, and many large updates could have tipped him toward overreaction; many small updates slipped safely between Scylla and Charybdis.

questions.q: A forecaster rebuilds her estimate each day entirely around the newest poll. What does she lose, according to the authors?
options: The value of the old information that underpinned her prior forecast
The value of the new information, which she ignores
The ability to forecast, since polls are noise
Nothing, since the newest poll contains all the old information as well
optionExplain: A forecaster so impressed by new information loses the value of the old.
She weights only the new.
The authors do not say polls are noise.
The newest poll does not hold the earlier knowledge.
questions.explain: A forecaster who ignores new information loses its value, and one who relies on it entirely loses the value of the old; balance keeps both.
questions.teaches: A forecaster so impressed by new information that he bases his forecast entirely on it will lose the value of the old information that underpinned his prior forecast.
questions.rule: According to the authors, many small updates let a forecaster keep the value of both the prior forecast and the new information.

questions.q: In the authors' Senate example, news of a Colorado poll lifts a 60% forecast. Roughly how large is the final update?
options: Ten points, to 70%
One point, to 61%
Fifteen points, to 75%
Four points, to 64%
optionExplain: That is the cap, not the final figure.
That is the bottom of the first range.
Above the cap they set.
The authors settle on 4%.
questions.explain: They settle on 4 percentage points. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: According to the authors, bound the size of the update, then narrow the range with questions until a figure emerges, however boring the result.

questions.q: The authors call such tiny changes in a forecast units of ____.
questions.explain: Units of doubt are the small increments.
questions.rule: Name: units of doubt.

questions.q: At 30% that a bill passes, a forecaster hears a swing legislator back it. She caps the gain, asks questions, settles on 6. Which method?
options: Jumping to the legislator's side because she is a key vote in the chamber
Setting a ceiling, then narrowing the range with questions about the news
Copying the crowd's estimate of the bill's chances
Waiting for the vote since only the outcome gives information
optionExplain: She did not jump.
This mirrors the Senate example.
She reasoned from the news.
She updated now.
questions.explain: She capped the update, asked questions that sharpen the size and settled on a figure.
questions.rule: Cap, question, narrow, settle.

questions.q: Put the steps of the authors' Senate example in order.
items: Accept the update must be more than zero
Set a ceiling of about 10%
Ask questions about the other races, trends and timing
Narrow the range to 3% to 7%
Settle on 4% and raise 60% to 64%
questions.explain: The update must exceed zero; consider how many other races must tip and set a ceiling; ask about the news; narrow the range; settle on a figure and apply it.
questions.rule: Cap, question, narrow, settle.

questions.q: True or false: In the authors' example, the Colorado poll was judged to justify a jump of about ten points.
questions.explain: Ten was the ceiling; they settled on four.
questions.rule: The cap is not the answer.

questions.q: If many more races look winnable than needed for a majority, where in the range should the update sit?
options: Toward the lower end, since so many options dilute the weight of any single poll
Toward the higher end, since a win in one race matters more when others can tip
At the cap, since many winnable races mean certainty
At zero, since extra races make Colorado irrelevant
optionExplain: The authors say the reverse.
The authors say 'lots more than needed' suggests the higher end.
The cap is an upper bound, not the answer.
The update must be more than zero.
questions.explain: If the answer is lots more than needed, it suggests the higher end of the range; if barely enough, the lower end.
questions.teaches: If lots more races look winnable than needed to take a Senate majority, the authors say that suggests the higher end of the range; if barely enough, it points toward the lower end.
questions.rule: According to the authors, bound the size of the update, then narrow the range with questions until a figure emerges, however boring the result.

questions.q: Your back is to a billiard table. A friend says a second ball stopped left of the first. What does that tell you?
options: Its exact position on the table, to within a few inches
Nothing, because one comparison between two balls is too weak to tell you anything
It is certainly on the right half
It is not on the extreme left edge, and a little likelier on the right
optionExplain: The clue is far too coarse.
A weak clue still shifts the odds.
The clue only tilts the odds a little.
The clue is trivial but not nothing.
questions.explain: The answer is a small tilt, not a location. The card next shows how repeated clues add up.
questions.rule: According to the authors, many small bits of information, each slightly favouring one answer, can slowly narrow the range of the truth without ever removing uncertainty.

questions.q: Repeating the process narrows the range but leaves some ____ in place.
questions.explain: Some uncertainty remains after each round.
questions.rule: Narrow, but not to zero.

questions.q: A detective gathers many weak clues, each slightly favouring suspect A. Which feature of the billiards example matches?
options: Each small clue shifts the odds a little; many together close in without certainty
One clue is enough to settle the case, provided the right one is found early
Weak clues should be ignored until a strong one arrives to confirm them
Many clues together remove all doubt about the identity of the culprit
optionExplain: That is the point of the example.
The example uses many weak clues.
Each clue is not nothing.
Uncertainty is never eliminated entirely.
questions.explain: Many small clues steadily narrow the range.
questions.rule: Weak clues add up.

questions.q: Three more balls each land to the left of the first. What happens to your belief that the first ball is on the right side?
options: It jumps to certainty after the third report
It stays the same, since the reports repeat each other
It rises a little more with each report, without reaching certainty
It falls, since the first ball must then be somewhere on the left side
optionExplain: Uncertainty is never eliminated.
Each is a new scrap of information.
Each repeat increases the likelihood a little more.
Left reports suggest the first ball is on the right.
questions.explain: Each new left report tilts the odds a bit further.
questions.rule: Repetition accumulates.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, repeating the billiards procedure slowly narrows the range but leaves some uncertainty in place.
questions.explain: You zero in on the truth, but some uncertainty remains.
questions.rule: Narrow, never zero.

questions.q: A piece of evidence seems almost worthless, so a forecaster ignores it. What does the billiards example say?
options: It is worthless unless it is later confirmed by a much stronger and clearer clue
It should be given as much weight as a decisive clue
It is not nothing: it already rules out an extreme and tilts the odds a tad
It matters only if the friend is an expert
optionExplain: The example shows weak clues are useful.
It tilts the odds only a tad.
Even a trivial scrap carries some information.
The example does not turn on expertise.
questions.explain: The answer tells you the first ball is not on the extreme left edge and makes the right side a tad likelier.
questions.teaches: The friend's first answer, though almost trivial, tells you the first ball is not on the extreme left edge and makes it just a tad more likely to be on the right side of the table.
questions.rule: According to the authors, many small bits of information, each slightly favouring one answer, can slowly narrow the range of the truth without ever removing uncertainty.

questions.q: According to the authors, on which two things should a new belief depend?
options: The latest news and how many forecasters agree with it
The prior belief and the diagnostic value of the new information
How confident you feel and how fast the news arrived
The base rate alone, since new information mostly adds noise to the estimate
optionExplain: Neither is the theorem's input.
These are the two inputs.
Confidence and speed are not the inputs.
The theorem uses the diagnostic value of the new information.
questions.explain: The theorem multiplies the prior by the diagnostic value. The card next puts it in words.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a new belief combines the prior belief with the diagnostic value of the new information, rather than replacing one with the other.

questions.q: In words, posterior odds equal the likelihood ratio times the ____ odds.
questions.explain: The prior odds are the odds before the new information.
questions.rule: Prior odds times likelihood ratio.

questions.q: Two forecasters see the same news. One started at 90% and the other at 10%. Per the theorem, should they end at the same figure?
options: Yes, since the same news has the same effect on everyone who sees it
No, since the new belief depends on the prior and the news
Yes, since good forecasters ignore their priors
No, but only because one forecaster is less skilled
optionExplain: The news has the same diagnostic value, but the priors differ.
The prior is one of the two inputs.
The prior is part of the formula.
Different priors alone give different results.
questions.explain: The same diagnostic value applied to different priors gives different new beliefs.
questions.rule: News is weighed against the prior.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The diagnostic value of the new information
The updated belief after the new information
questions.explain: The prior is the belief before the new information; the likelihood ratio is the diagnostic value of the new information; posterior odds are the updated belief.
questions.rule: Prior, evidence, posterior.

questions.q: True or false: According to the theorem, the new belief depends only on the new information.
questions.explain: It depends on the prior belief as well as the diagnostic value of the new information.
questions.rule: Old and new both count.

questions.q: A forecaster treats her prior as only a number and discards it when news arrives. What does the authors' wording suggest she loses?
options: Only the final figure, which she can recompute
Nothing, as the news contains the old knowledge
Only the sense of her original confidence
All the knowledge that informed her prior
optionExplain: The prior carries more than the figure.
The news adds to the prior; it does not replace it.
More than a feeling is lost.
The prior carries that knowledge with it.
questions.explain: The authors speak of the prior belief and all the knowledge that informed it.
questions.teaches: The prior belief carries with it all the knowledge that informed it.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a new belief combines the prior belief with the diagnostic value of the new information, rather than replacing one with the other.

questions.q: Starting from the base rate for defense-secretary nominees, what prior did Jay Ulfelder put on Hagel being confirmed?
optionExplain: Only one of 24 nominees had been rejected.
That was the pundit's view, not the base rate.
The base rate was higher.
That is the figure after the poor hearing.
questions.explain: The prior was 96%. The card next shows how the hearing changed it.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an experienced forecaster starts from the base rate and lets bad news pull the figure down by only as much as the news is diagnostic.

questions.q: Only one of ____ official nominees for defense secretary had been rejected by the Senate.
questions.explain: The base rate was 23 out of 24, or about 96%.
questions.rule: Base rate: 96%.

questions.q: Of twenty comparable startups, 15 survived three years. A new one gets a bad review. What is the first step in Ulfelder's manner?
options: Start from the review itself and treat it as the whole of the answer for the startup
Ignore the review because base rates settle every case
Start from the survival base rate as the prior, then adjust for the review
Average the review and the base rate without weighing either
optionExplain: He starts from the base rate.
He adjusts for the new information.
That is Ulfelder's method.
He weighs by diagnostic value.
questions.explain: Ulfelder started with how often similar nominees were confirmed and then adjusted.
questions.rule: Prior first, then adjust.

questions.q: True or false: Ulfelder obtained the exact figures for how often failing and successful nominees perform poorly at hearings.
questions.explain: He did not have the numbers, so he assumed them, tilting the assumptions towards the sceptic.
questions.rule: Assumptions, not data.

questions.q: Why did Ulfelder tilt his assumptions heavily in favour of Tom Ricks?
options: Because Ricks had strong data on how nominees perform at hearings
Because he wanted his own forecast to match Ricks's forecast of the outcome
If Ricks could not win on those generous numbers, he could not win at all
Because the base rate said Hagel would fail
optionExplain: Ulfelder lacked the numbers.
He concluded Ricks's estimate was way off.
