It is a stress test.
The base rate favoured confirmation.
questions.explain: Giving the sceptic generous numbers makes the conclusion robust.
questions.rule: Test the opposing view on its best terms.
questions.teaches: Ulfelder tilted his estimates heavily in Ricks's favour, so that if Ricks could not be vindicated with those numbers he could not be vindicated at all.

questions.q: Tom Ricks said Hagel's chances were 50-50 and falling about 2% for each day the committee did not vote. How did Ulfelder's method differ?
options: He anchored on the 96% base rate and adjusted for the hearing, reaching 83%
He agreed with Ricks that it was 50-50, because the hearing had gone badly
He ignored the hearing altogether and kept the 96% base rate
He used a steady daily decline of 2% for each day, as Ricks did
optionExplain: He ended far above Ricks's 50-50.
He concluded Ricks's estimate was way off.
His forecast fell to 83%.
That was Ricks's approach.
questions.explain: Ricks offered a steady daily decline from 50-50; Ulfelder started from the base rate and adjusted once.
questions.teaches: Tom Ricks put Hagel's withdrawal at 50-50 but declining by the day, saying that every business day the Senate Armed Services Committee did not vote the likelihood of Hagel becoming defense secretary declined by about 2%.
questions.rule: According to the authors, an experienced forecaster starts from the base rate and lets bad news pull the figure down by only as much as the news is diagnostic.

questions.q: True or false: Superforecasters rarely work through Bayes' theorem explicitly when they update.
questions.explain: They rarely crunch the numbers so explicitly. The card next explains what they do instead.
questions.rule: According to the authors, you can update the Bayesian way by weighing evidence in proportion to its strength, without writing the formula.

questions.q: What matters more to superforecasters than the theorem is Bayes' core insight of updating in proportion to the weight of the ____.
questions.explain: Update in proportion to the weight of the evidence.
questions.rule: Weigh evidence in proportion.

questions.q: A math-averse analyst fears she must learn the formula to update well. What do the authors tell her?
options: Yes, since without the formula her updates cannot be trusted at all
Yes, but she may look it up each time
No, since evidence never needs weighing
No: follow the insight of updating in proportion to the evidence
optionExplain: The authors say no formula is required.
The authors say she need not use it at all.
Weighing the evidence is the insight.
Algebra is not required.
questions.explain: The authors say the formula is not required; the spirit is.
questions.rule: Spirit over formula.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Tim Minto used Bayes' theorem to compute each of his hundreds of updates.
questions.explain: He knows it but did not use it even once.
questions.rule: The theorem is not the method.

questions.q: How does Tim Minto describe his own grasp of Bayes' theorem?
options: He has memorised it word for word and applies it to every one of his forecasts
He has a better intuitive grasp than most but could not write it from memory
He has never heard of it and learned the spirit by trial
He thinks it is wrong and uses a different method
optionExplain: He did not use it once.
That is his own description.
He knows the theorem.
He appreciates the Bayesian spirit.
questions.explain: He says he probably has a better intuitive grasp than most people, but could not write it from memory.
questions.rule: Intuition can outrun notation.
questions.teaches: Minto says he likely has a better intuitive grasp of Bayes' theorem than most people, even though he would probably fail to write it down from memory.

questions.q: Why do numerate superforecasters rarely work through the theorem explicitly?
options: They do not know the theorem, since it is not taught to forecasters
They could use it if worth the trouble, but rarely find it so
The theorem is wrong for forecasting problems of this kind
They are not numerate enough to apply it to their own forecasts
optionExplain: Many know it.
The authors say many know it and could use it.
The authors do not say so.
The authors call them a numerate bunch.
questions.explain: The authors say superforecasters are numerate and could deploy the theorem, but rarely crunch the numbers so explicitly.
questions.teaches: The superforecasters are a numerate bunch: many know about Bayes' theorem and could deploy it if they felt it was worth the trouble, but they rarely crunch the numbers so explicitly.
questions.rule: According to the authors, you can update the Bayesian way by weighing evidence in proportion to its strength, without writing the formula.

questions.q: After Doug Lorch found that the sea ice report was failing, what did he do?
options: Lowered his forecast from 95% in many small steps over the following days
Stayed at 95% until the question closed
Raised his forecast to 99%
Dropped the report and made a new forecast, 55% and then 15%
optionExplain: He chose a fresh forecast instead.
That would have been worse.
The gap with reality pointed the other way.
He took a fresh look.
questions.explain: He made a new forecast. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the many-small-updates guideline is a principle with caveats: when the basis of a forecast fails, make a fresh forecast.

questions.q: Doug fell back to his opening 55% and then dropped to ____%.
questions.explain: He then resumed small updates from there.
questions.rule: 55 then 15.

questions.q: A forecaster's 95% rests entirely on one source that new data show is failing. What does Doug's case suggest?
options: Take a fresh look, set the source aside and forecast anew, then resume small updates
Lower the forecast by one point a day until it settles near the middle
Hold at 95% since a source should be trusted until it is formally withdrawn by its authors
Raise the forecast, since the source is now more informative
optionExplain: That is what Doug did.
Doug's case shows this would be too slow.
His source was failing against the data.
The data contradicted the source.
questions.explain: When the basis of a forecast fails, small steps from the old position carry the error along.
questions.rule: Replace a failed basis.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say many small updates is the right approach in every circumstance.
questions.explain: They say it is not a skeleton key; sometimes it is exactly the wrong thing to do.
questions.rule: Principles have caveats.

questions.q: What did Doug compare when he decided to ditch the report?
options: The report against other forecasters' latest forecasts on the same question that week
The report against the opening forecast alone
Recent ice data and data for the previous twelve years, set against the projections
His own earlier forecasts from the previous twelve years of tournaments
optionExplain: He compared data.
He compared the report to data.
He saw a big and widening gap.
He compared projections to data.
questions.explain: He compared recent and previous-year data with the projections and saw a big and widening gap.
questions.rule: Check the basis against reality.
questions.teaches: Doug looked at the most recent data and data for the previous twelve years, compared them with the scientists' projections and saw a big and widening gap.

questions.q: What does the authors' use of Orwell's sixth rule say about forecasting rules?
options: Follow every rule exactly, since rules protect the forecaster against error
Treat all six of Orwell's rules as fixed laws, whatever the case may be
Break any rule sooner than do something outright barbarous; so would superforecasters
Rules are useless, so forecasters should invent their own each time
optionExplain: Orwell's sixth rule says the opposite.
The sixth rule says to break the others when needed.
The authors draw this parallel.
The authors keep broad principles.
questions.explain: Orwell's sixth rule is to break any of the rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous. The authors say superforecasters likewise break rules rather than make a barbarous forecast.
questions.teaches: George Orwell's sixth rule in 'Politics and the English Language' was to break any of the rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous.
questions.rule: According to the authors, the many-small-updates guideline is a principle with caveats: when the basis of a forecast fails, make a fresh forecast.

questions.q: According to the authors, what drove Mary Simpson to take forecasting seriously?
options: She had missed the 2007-08 crisis and felt she should do better
She had won an earlier contest and wanted to defend her title
She wanted a second career after leaving her utility company
She had been hired by the project to coach other volunteers
optionExplain: Right: a costly miss in her own field, plus the sense that she should be better, set her off.
Plausible for a winner's story, but the chapter describes a failure, not a win.
Retirement features in her story, but only because her savings were hit by the crash.
She volunteered for the project; the chapter does not say she coached anyone.
questions.explain: Simpson's story starts with a failure, not a success. The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: Failure can be the spur.

questions.q: Simpson realized the size of the financial crisis only when ____ Brothers declared bankruptcy in September 2008.
questions.explain: The chapter dates her realization to the Lehman Brothers bankruptcy, which was too late for her savings.
questions.rule: Simpson saw the crisis only at Lehman.

questions.q: A veteran restaurant buyer misjudged a sharp drop in diners and lost money. Which reaction resembles Simpson's?
options: Blame the drop on events that nobody could ever foresee
Stop making demand predictions and order a fixed amount
Resolve to study how forecasts like hers could improve
Switch to a new supplier and hope the drop reverses soon
optionExplain: Appealing, since the crisis surprised many experts, but it excuses rather than improves.
This avoids forecasting; Simpson took up more of it.
Right: Simpson wanted to think more about forecasting after her miss.
This changes a detail but not the buyer's own judgment.
questions.explain: Simpson answered her miss by working on her forecasting skill, not by excusing or avoiding it.
questions.rule: Treat a miss as a reason to improve.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Simpson had the background to understand the economy yet still missed the crisis.
questions.explain: She held an economics PhD and had managed financial affairs, which is why the miss frustrated her.
questions.rule: A miss despite expertise stings, and motivates.

questions.q: Beyond protecting her savings, what else does the chapter say pushed Simpson to improve?
options: A promise to colleagues that she would publish a forecast
A wish to prove that economists could not predict anything
A request from the utility that employed her to lead a team
A feeling that she should be better at it because she could
optionExplain: Nothing in the chapter mentions a promise or publication.
That is the opposite of her attitude: she wanted to be better, not to show it was hopeless.
She had semiretired and worked as an independent consultant by then.
Right: the authors say it was the sense that she should, because she could.
questions.explain: The chapter says self-interest was not the only motive: she felt she should improve because she was able to.
questions.rule: Ability can create an obligation to improve.
questions.teaches: Simpson's motive was not only financial self-interest: she felt she should be better at forecasting because she could.

questions.q: Two analysts missed a market fall that most experts missed. Ana shrugs. Ben studies how he forecasts. Who acts like Simpson?
options: Ana, since a miss that most experts shared needs no review
Ben, since a shared miss is still a reason to think harder
Neither, since Simpson turned to a team for help
Both, since each accepts the miss in some way
optionExplain: A shared miss is comforting, but Simpson did not take comfort from it.
Right: Simpson missed it like most experts, yet wanted to think more about forecasting.
Simpson did volunteer for a project, but the story is about her own drive to improve.
Accepting a miss is not the same as acting on it; only one analyst did.
questions.explain: Simpson was in a crowd of experts who missed the crisis, and she still used her miss as the start of improvement.
questions.rule: A shared miss is still a miss worth studying.
questions.teaches: Simpson's miss was shared by most experts in her field, yet she still wanted to think more about forecasting.

questions.q: A person says I am bad at math and treats this as a permanent fact about themselves. What does Dweck call this belief?
options: A growth mindset
A calibrated mindset
A pragmatic mindset
A fixed mindset
optionExplain: The opposite: a growth mindset says effort and learning can build ability.
Calibration is about matching confidence to accuracy, a different matter.
Pragmatic is a trait the authors list for superforecasters, not Dweck's term.
Right: believing abilities are fixed, only revealed and never built, is the fixed mindset.
questions.explain: Dweck's two terms divide on whether ability can be built. The card next sets them out.
questions.rule: Fixed means ability is revealed, not built.

questions.q: Dweck defines a growth mindset as believing that your abilities are largely the product of ____.
questions.explain: A growth mindset ties ability to effort: you grow to the extent you are willing to work hard and learn.
questions.rule: Growth mindset: ability grows with effort.

questions.q: A new hire fails her first client pitch. Which remark shows a growth mindset in Dweck's sense?
options: Some people are born closers, and I am not one
My talent will show itself in time if I wait
I will ask what went wrong and rework the pitch
One failure shows I should be doing something else
optionExplain: This treats persuasion as a fixed gift, the fixed mindset.
This treats talent as something revealed rather than built, also a fixed view.
Right: she treats the failure as information for building the skill.
Reading one failure as proof of limits is how the authors describe the fixed mindset.
questions.explain: A growth mindset reads a setback as a prompt to work and learn; a fixed mindset reads it as a verdict.
questions.rule: Setbacks are prompts, not verdicts.

questions.q: Which statements fit a growth mindset and which a fixed mindset, as the authors describe them?

items.t: You can grow to the extent you are willing to work hard and learn
Abilities can only be revealed, not created and developed
I am bad at math, like being left-handed
Abilities are largely the product of effort
A setback shows that my limits have been revealed

questions.explain: The growth view makes ability a product of effort and learning; the fixed view treats it as given, to be revealed.
questions.rule: Ask whether ability is built or only revealed.

questions.q: True or false: Dweck defines a growth mindset as the belief that abilities are entirely the product of effort.
questions.explain: The definition says largely, not entirely; it leaves room for other factors.
questions.rule: Largely is not entirely.

questions.q: A trainer assumes every new analyst already believes skill is built by effort. According to the authors reporting Dweck, is that assumption safe?
options: No, because many people hold a fixed mindset
Yes, because the belief is so obvious that nearly everyone holds it
Yes, because anyone who studies math at school learns it
No, because only people with high scores ever hold it
optionExplain: Right: the authors say the growth mindset is far from universal, and many hold a fixed one.
It seems obvious, which is why the authors mention that some may think so, but research shows otherwise.
School requires math study, but the authors say it can deepen a fixed belief instead.
The chapter links the mindsets to beliefs, not to test scores.
questions.explain: Though it may seem too obvious to state, Dweck's research shows the growth mindset is far from universal.
questions.rule: Do not assume the growth mindset is common.
questions.teaches: Although it may seem too obvious to need saying, Dweck's research shows that the growth mindset is far from universal.

questions.q: A teenager is sure she is bad at drawing and that this cannot change. How hard will she most likely practise, on the authors' account?
options: Harder than others, to prove herself wrong
Not hard, since practice seems pointless
As hard as anyone, since belief and effort are unrelated
Hard at first, then less as she improves
optionExplain: Some people do this, but the authors say the fixed belief discourages effort.
Right: if limits are fixed, trying hard looks pointless, so she will hold back.
The point is that belief shapes effort; they are related.
The authors describe giving up after setbacks, not easing off after progress.
questions.explain: The belief makes effort look futile, and the next card shows how that closes the loop.
questions.rule: If effort looks pointless, you will not try.

questions.q: The authors say the belief I am bad at math becomes self-____.
questions.explain: A belief that produces the conditions for its own truth is self-fulfilling.
questions.rule: The belief brings about its own proof.

questions.q: After one flat loaf, Dev decides he is no baker and cannot become one. Following the authors' reasoning, what comes next?
options: He bakes more often, since every failure shows what to fix
He rarely bakes, reads each flop as proof, and does not improve
He improves anyway, since baking is a skill of the hands and eyes
He asks a baker for advice, because belief helps learning
optionExplain: This is how a growth mindset behaves, not the fixed belief Dev holds.
Right: a fixed belief leads to little effort and to setbacks read as proof.
Skill may be learnable, but the authors say the belief stops him from learning it.
Seeking advice fits a growth mindset; Dev has decided it is pointless.
questions.explain: Dev's belief leads him to try little, and when he does, any flop confirms it.
questions.rule: Fixed beliefs shut the door on effort.

questions.q: Put the authors' chain of reasoning for the fixed belief in order.
items: The person believes he is bad at math and always will be
He sees no point in trying hard to improve
A setback is taken as further proof that limits are revealed
He wants to stop wasting his time as soon as possible
His potential for improvement is never realized
questions.explain: The authors move from belief to little effort, to setbacks read as proof, to quitting, to unrealized potential.
questions.rule: Belief, little effort, proof, quitting.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a fixed-mindset person who is forced to study math treats a setback as a signal to try harder.
questions.explain: The authors say he takes any setback as further proof that his limits have been revealed.
questions.rule: A setback is read as proof, not a prompt.

questions.q: A manager tells a struggling employee, You are not a natural at this. Which effect on the employee fits the authors' account?
options: Effort will rise, since the remark challenges the employee
No change, since remarks have no effect on belief
Effort may fall, since a trait that is fixed can't be changed
Skill will rise, since honesty clarifies one's limits
optionExplain: Challenge motivates only if ability seems changeable.
The chapter's point is that beliefs about ability affect behavior.
Right: if ability seems immutable, trying seems pointless.
The authors say a belief in limits blocks improvement.
questions.explain: Fixed beliefs treat weakness as unchangeable, so effort looks pointless.
questions.rule: Labeling someone a non-natural can lower effort.
questions.teaches: The authors compare the fixed belief to being left-handed or female or tall: an immutable feature of who a person is, which is why effort seems futile.

questions.q: In Dweck's study, some fifth graders lost interest when puzzles got harder. What does the chapter say set them apart from the others?
options: Their raw puzzle-solving talent
Their age and year in school
Their enjoyment of the easy puzzles
Their mindset about ability
optionExplain: A natural guess, but the chapter says talent did not explain it.
All were fifth graders, so this does not separate them.
All the children enjoyed the easy puzzles.
Right: the key factor was mindset.
questions.explain: The chapter points to mindset, not talent. The card next gives the study.
questions.rule: Mindset, not talent, drove persistence.

questions.q: True or false: In Dweck's study, the fifth graders enjoyed the easy puzzles.
questions.explain: They did; the split appeared only when the harder puzzles arrived.
questions.rule: The split appears at difficulty.

questions.q: In a chess club, some equally skilled juniors drop out after losing to stronger players while others stay. Which explanation does Dweck's study favor?
options: Differences in mindset about whether ability can grow
Differences in raw chess talent among the juniors
Differences in how much they enjoyed easy games
Differences in the strength of their opponents
optionExplain: Right: equally able children can differ in how they react to difficulty because of mindset.
The juniors are described as equally skilled, so talent cannot explain the split.
Easy games are enjoyed by all, as in the puzzle study, so they do not separate groups.
Opponents are the same challenge for all the juniors.
questions.explain: As with the puzzle children, equal ability can come with different reactions, and mindset explains the gap.
questions.rule: Same ability, different mindset, different persistence.

questions.q: Even when children are matched for puzzle talent, Dweck's results suggest their reactions to hard puzzles still differ because of ____.
questions.explain: The chapter says that even among equally adept children, some were turned off and others intrigued; the key factor was mindset.
questions.rule: Equal talent still left a mindset gap.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the children who gave up on the harder puzzles lacked puzzle-solving talent.
questions.explain: The authors say the difference was not talent; even equally adept children split by mindset.
questions.rule: Do not read giving up as lack of talent.

questions.q: A teacher wants a quick sign of which pupils relish a tough task. In Dweck's study, what did a growth-mindset child do?
options: Finished the puzzles faster than anyone else
Declined to continue so as to protect a good record
Asked for the puzzle names so a parent could buy more
Asked for easier puzzles to build confidence
optionExplain: Speed is not what the chapter reports.
Declining an offer to take puzzles home was what the fixed-mindset children did.
Right: one child asked for the names so their mom could buy more when these ran out.
The growth-mindset children liked the harder puzzles even more.
questions.explain: A child who wanted to buy more of the harder puzzles shows the appetite for challenge; those who declined to take puzzles home showed the opposite.
questions.rule: Wanting more of the hard task signals growth mindset.
questions.teaches: In the study, the children who lost interest turned down an offer to take puzzles home, while one growth-mindset child asked for the puzzle names so a parent could buy more.

questions.q: In Dweck's brain-scan experiment, which feedback failed to engage fixed-mindset volunteers?
options: Information that could help them improve
Being told that their answer was right
Being told that their answer was wrong
Being scanned while answering the questions
optionExplain: Right: they cared about the verdict but not the information to improve.
They were fully engaged by right-or-wrong feedback.
Verdicts, right or wrong, engaged them.
They took part in the hard questions without any reported disengagement.
questions.explain: The scans showed attention to the verdict only. The card gives the details.
questions.rule: Verdicts engaged them; improvement tips did not.

questions.q: Fixed-mindset volunteers were fully engaged when told whether their answers were right or ____.
questions.explain: They engaged with the verdict, right or wrong, but not with information that could help them improve.
questions.rule: Verdict yes, improvement information no.

questions.q: After a mock exam, each student gets a mark and a page of tips. Who fits the fixed-mindset pattern?
options: The student who reads the tips before looking at the mark
The student who rereads both and asks the tutor questions
The student who ignores the mark and rewrites the exam
The student who reads the mark and skips the tips
optionExplain: This student values the information to improve, like growth-mindset volunteers.
Interest in both mark and tips shows learning as a priority.
This student cares about the learning more than the verdict.
Right: attention to the verdict only is the pattern the scans showed.
questions.explain: The fixed-mindset volunteers cared about the verdict and passed over what could help them.
questions.rule: Look for who ignores the improving information.

questions.q: Which information held fixed-mindset volunteers' attention, and which held only growth-mindset volunteers?

items.t: Being told an answer was right
Being told an answer was wrong
Information that could help improve their answers
Learning the right answer after a miss

questions.explain: Verdicts engaged the fixed-mindset volunteers; the information that could stretch knowledge engaged only the growth-mindset volunteers.
questions.rule: Verdicts versus improvement.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, fixed-mindset volunteers were as engaged by the information that could help them improve as by the verdict.
questions.explain: They engaged with the verdict; what failed to hold them was information that could help them improve.
questions.rule: They cared about verdicts, not learning.

questions.q: A forecasting tournament closes a question. Which behavior is the opposite of the fixed-mindset pattern in the scans?
options: Checking only whether your forecast was right
Being as keen to know how to do better as how you did
Skipping the postmortem when the forecast was right
Posting your score to the group and moving on
optionExplain: Checking only the verdict is the fixed-mindset pattern.
Right: the chapter says superforecasters, unlike the fixed-mindset subjects, are keen to know how to improve.
Skipping the review is also verdict-only behavior.
Reporting a score without examining what to improve is verdict-only.
questions.explain: The authors contrast superforecasters with Dweck's fixed-mindset subjects: they want to know how to improve, not only how they did.
questions.rule: Seek the lesson as well as the score.
questions.teaches: Whenever a question closes, superforecasters are, unlike Dweck's fixed-mindset subjects, as keen to know how they can do better as to know how they did.

questions.q: A 1945 profile called Keynes consistently inconsistent. What did it mean by that?
options: He reversed himself readily when circumstances warranted
He repeated the same investing mistakes in every decade
He held a theory of money that differed from his investing
He changed his views only after losing his clients' money
optionExplain: Right: he reversed positions without guilt and even rebuked less nimble minds.
His mistakes were followed by changes, not repeated.
The chapter describes changing views, not a gap between theory and investing.
He changed his mind whenever circumstances seemed to call for it, not only after losses.
questions.explain: The profile praised his readiness to contradict himself. The card gives the context.
questions.rule: Consistently inconsistent means changing as the facts change.

questions.q: A 1945 profile described Keynes as consistently ____.
questions.explain: The label turns a usual criticism into praise: Keynes reversed himself whenever circumstances called for it.
questions.rule: Consistent in updating, inconsistent in views.

questions.q: A fund manager says, I do not reverse a call, because consistency builds trust. How does that compare with Keynes's attitude?
options: Keynes would share it, since his record rested on consistency
Keynes would be indifferent, since reversals had no effect on him
Keynes would see it as a limit, since he changed his mind readily
Keynes would value it only for family money
optionExplain: His one steady belief was that he could do better, not that his views stayed fixed.
He prided himself on reversals and urged others to follow his lead.
Right: he took pride in admitting mistakes and adopting new beliefs.
The chapter gives no split between family money and other money.
questions.explain: Keynes treated reversal as a virtue, so a rule against reversing would cut against his practice.
questions.rule: Keynes prized readiness to reverse.

questions.q: In the legend, Churchill cabled Keynes, Am coming around to your point of view. How did Keynes reply?
options: Welcome aboard. The facts have not changed.
Sorry to hear it. Have started to change my mind.
Thank you. I never change my mind on principle.
Please wait. I must review the evidence first.
optionExplain: He is the one said to be changing, not holding to the facts.
Right: the reply shows his joke about his own readiness to change.
This is the reverse of the profile's portrait.
The legend has a quip, not a request to wait.
questions.explain: The authors cite the legend to show how readily Keynes would drop a view he had just persuaded someone to share.
questions.rule: He changed his mind even as others came around.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Keynes felt guilty about reversing his positions.
questions.explain: The profile says he felt no guilt and even used reversals to rebuke less nimble-minded people.
questions.rule: Reversal was not a source of shame.

questions.q: Which workplace policy best reflects Keynes's remark that there is no harm in being wrong if one is promptly found out?
options: Keep forecasts private so misses cause no embarrassment
Avoid forecasting anything that could turn out wrong
Reward staff for never revising a published view
Review forecasts regularly so misses surface quickly
optionExplain: Private forecasts hide misses, so nobody finds them out.
Avoiding forecasts avoids errors but also the learning.
Rewarding no revision rewards sticking to errors.
Right: the point is to find errors promptly, so a miss costs little.
questions.explain: Keynes wrote in 1933 that there is no harm in being sometimes wrong, especially if one is promptly found out.
questions.rule: Being found out early limits the cost of being wrong.
questions.teaches: Keynes wrote in 1933 that there is no harm in being sometimes wrong, especially if one is promptly found out.

questions.q: After his bad currency calls in 1920, how did Keynes respond?
options: He kept to safe assets such as real estate for the rest of his life
He stopped investing for others and returned to economics
He embraced new ideas, such as moving King's College into stocks
He repeated his currency strategy more cautiously
optionExplain: The chapter says he did not retreat to the safe and easy.
He went on managing money for others for decades.
Right: he did not retreat to the safe and easy, and pressed on with new ideas.
The chapter says he found new directions, not a more careful version of the old one.
questions.explain: Keynes treated failure as a prompt to try new approaches. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Failure was a prompt to try again differently.

questions.q: After 1929 Keynes concluded that stock prices can differ from the true ____ of companies.
questions.explain: He decided that an investor should study a company's business, capital and management to judge its underlying value.
questions.rule: Prices are not always true value.

questions.q: A farm co-op loses heavily on a commodity bet. Which response most resembles Keynes after 1929?
options: Examine which assumption failed and change the approach
Quit trading and put all funds in the safest assets
Double the bet to win back the loss quickly
Treat the loss as bad luck and change nothing
optionExplain: Right: Keynes subjected his thinking to scrutiny and found a faulty assumption.
The chapter says Keynes did not retreat to the safe and easy, and retreat would skip the analysis.
This is gambling rather than learning from the failure.
Blaming luck would skip the scrutiny that led him to value investing.
questions.explain: Keynes's response was to test his assumptions after a blow, find the flaw and rebuild.
questions.rule: Hunt the faulty assumption after a loss.

questions.q: Match each event in Keynes's investing life to what followed.
pairs: He moved King's College into stocks
He judged one key assumption wrong
questions.explain: The chapter links these events in order: a near wipe-out, a bold new departure, and a rethink after the crash.
questions.rule: Match failure with its response.

questions.q: True or false: After the 1929 crash, Keynes concluded that stock prices reliably reflect the true value of companies.
questions.explain: He concluded the opposite: stock prices do not always reflect true value, so investors should study the business.
questions.rule: Prices can differ from underlying value.

questions.q: A home buyer reasons: asking prices can differ from true value, so I will study the building's condition and finances. Whose idea is this?
options: Diversification, which spreads a buyer's money across many unrelated assets
Value investing, which Benjamin Graham developed in the US
Market timing, which means trying to buy right before a rise in price
Hedging, which means betting against your own forecast to limit the damage
optionExplain: Spreading risk is sound practice, but the buyer here studies value, not spreads risk.
Right: judge underlying value by studying the thing, as Keynes did.
The buyer is not predicting price moves, but judging what the building is worth.
Hedging offsets risk; it does not ask what the thing is really worth.
questions.explain: Studying underlying value rather than trusting price is the idea Graham called value investing, which became the cornerstone of Warren Buffett's fortune.
questions.rule: Study underlying value, not just price.
questions.teaches: About the same time as Keynes, Benjamin Graham developed the same approach in the United States and called it value investing; it became the cornerstone of Warren Buffett's fortune.

questions.q: A baby tilts her head too far back and flops onto a pillow. According to the authors, why does her mother let it happen?
options: The pillow makes falling painless, so the lesson is free
Sitting up is something babies learn only by being held
The mother wants to see how well the baby reacts
The flop teaches her not to tilt that far
optionExplain: The pillow softens the fall, but the point is what the baby learns.
The authors say babies learn it by trying, not by being held.
The chapter gives the mother a teaching purpose, not a test.
Right: the initial flop delivers the conceptual breakthrough.
questions.explain: The flop is the lesson. The card next gives the whole cycle.
questions.rule: The failure is part of learning.

questions.q: Put the steps of the learning cycle in the authors' order.
items: Try
Fail
Analyze
Adjust
Try again
questions.explain: The authors give the sequence as try, fail, analyze, adjust, try again.
questions.rule: Try, fail, analyze, adjust, try again.

questions.q: A new driver clips a cone while parallel parking. Which response follows the cycle?
options: Practise only in empty lots until the fear passes
Read about parking until the first try can be perfect
Work out what she misjudged, adjust the angle and try again
Stop trying, since the cone shows she lacks the knack
optionExplain: Avoiding the problem skips the analysis of what went wrong.
The authors say reading is no substitute for trying, and this skips the trying.
Right: analyze the failure, adjust, and go again.
Treating the failure as a verdict is the fixed mindset, not the cycle.
questions.explain: She fails, works out what went wrong, adjusts and tries again.
questions.rule: Learn from the failure, then try again.

questions.q: A trainee fighter pilot gets excellent classroom teaching and many hours in advanced simulators. What do the authors say is still needed?
options: Another year of classroom study
Many hours in the air
Another simulator of higher quality
Only a written test of the rules
optionExplain: The authors say classroom instruction alone is not enough.
Right: pilots need hours in the air, the more the better.
Even advanced simulators are not enough, they say.
A test measures knowledge, not the skill gained by doing.
questions.explain: Instruction and simulators do not replace real flying time.
questions.rule: Real practice cannot be skipped.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a mother who lets her baby flop onto a pillow lets it learn not to tilt that far.
questions.explain: The mother could skip the drama, but the flop delivers the conceptual breakthrough.
questions.rule: Do not remove the useful failure.

questions.q: A bank sends new traders to a month of lectures and then to the trading floor. What would the authors say about the lectures alone?
options: They are not enough, since skills are learned by doing
They are enough, since trading is mainly a thinking job
They are harmful, since lectures prevent the trainees from failing
They are enough if the lecturers are expert traders themselves
optionExplain: Right: the authors name bankers with surgeons and executives as people who need practice.
Even the most demanding skills, the authors say, need doing.
The authors do not say lectures harm; they say lectures are not enough.
Expert teaching does not replace practice, just as classroom teaching does not replace flying.
questions.explain: The authors say the point holds for surgeons, bankers and business executives alike.
questions.rule: No skill escapes the need for practice.
questions.teaches: The authors say the same holds for surgeons, bankers and business executives: classroom learning alone does not produce the skill.

questions.q: Polanyi wrote a precise physics description of riding a bicycle. Did he say it tells a person how to ride?
options: Yes, because the description is exact enough to follow
Yes, if the learner first studies enough physics
No, because the physics of cycling is not understood
No, because you cannot apply such a rule while riding
optionExplain: The description is precise, but precision does not make it usable on the bicycle.
Knowing more physics does not give the feel of balance.
Polanyi's point is that the rule is known but not enough, not that it is unknown.
Right: you can't adjust your path to a ratio while riding, and the rule omits other factors.
questions.explain: Polanyi's answer was no. The card says why.
questions.rule: A rule can be exact and still not teach the skill.

questions.q: The kind of knowledge that we only get from bruising experience is called ____ knowledge.
questions.explain: The authors call it tacit knowledge: it cannot be fully captured in words and conveyed to others.
questions.rule: Tacit knowledge comes from doing.

questions.q: Mia reads three books on swimming and understands every stroke. What would the authors expect when she first enters deep water?
options: She will swim well, since she understands every stroke
She will swim well if she remembers the books word for word
She will still need to practise, as knowing is not doing
She will fail for good, since books made her overconfident
optionExplain: Understanding the strokes in words is what Polanyi's description shows is not enough.
Memory of the words does not supply the feel the skill needs.
Right: tacit knowledge only comes from trying.
The authors do not say books doom the learner, only that they cannot replace trying.
questions.explain: As with cycling, written understanding does not give the skill of doing.
questions.rule: Understanding in words is not the skill.

questions.q: Suppose a cyclist tried to follow Polanyi's rule by calculating the curve for each unbalance and speed. What does Polanyi say would happen?
options: He would ride more smoothly than before
He would ride well, but slowly
He would not move at all
He would fall off the machine
optionExplain: The rule is too crude to improve riding in practice.
Polanyi gives no hint that it would work slowly.
He says you would fall off, not stand still.
Right: Polanyi says you would fall off because the formula leaves out other factors.
questions.explain: Polanyi says that if you could apply the rule you would fall, since other factors matter in practice.
questions.rule: The formula omits what the rider needs.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a rider who has mastered cycling can explain it well enough that others skip the falls.
questions.explain: They say such a rider would succeed no better than Polanyi at explaining how to stay upright.
questions.rule: Experts cannot hand over tacit knowledge in words.

questions.q: A firm trains junior forecasters with only a reading list. What do the authors say about reading alone?
options: It is no substitute for the experience of forecasting
It is enough if the books are the best available
It is harmful, since books mislead forecasters
It is enough for people with a growth mindset
optionExplain: Right: learning to forecast requires trying to forecast.
The authors say even the best books are no substitute for experience.
They tell readers not to burn their books, so books are not called harmful.
A growth mindset still needs trying; the cycle depends on doing.
questions.explain: The authors say it should be equally obvious that learning to forecast requires trying to forecast.
questions.rule: Books cannot replace doing.
questions.teaches: The authors say it should be as obvious that learning to forecast requires trying to forecast as that learning to ride requires riding: reading books on forecasting is no substitute for the real thing.

questions.q: By roughly how much did mastering the authors' training booklet improve forecasting accuracy in randomized experiments?
options: About 1%
About 10%
About 50%
About 90%
optionExplain: Too small: the authors call it a meaningful gain from one tiny booklet.
Right: the authors report an improvement of roughly 10%.
Too large: it is a modest gain from a short booklet.
Far too large: the booklet helps, but no booklet transforms a forecaster.
questions.explain: The chapter reports a gain of roughly 10%. The card gives the full finding.
questions.rule: Guidelines give a real but modest boost.

questions.q: The authors say that mastering their training guidelines can improve accuracy by roughly ____ percent.
questions.explain: The experiments found a gain of roughly 10% from mastering one tiny booklet.
questions.rule: About 10% from the booklet.

questions.q: Sam has played online poker daily for years without ever reading about common errors. What does the chapter suggest adding?
options: Learn the common errors and best practices, then play on
Stop playing for now and study the theory of poker alone
Play more hands per day without changing anything else
Switch games so that earlier habits do not carry over
optionExplain: Right: informed practice combines knowledge and doing.
The authors say don't burn your books, but they also stress practice, so quitting practice is wrong.
More of the same practice is not informed practice.
Changing games throws away the experience; the problem is that it was uninformed.
questions.explain: Knowledge of best practices makes each hour of practice teach more.
questions.rule: Add knowledge to practice.

questions.q: Match each contributor to the role the authors give it.
pairs: Help draw the right lessons from personal experience
Fills abstract public knowledge with real-world content
Showed a gain of roughly 10% from the booklet
questions.explain: Guidelines and experience feed each other, and the experiments are the evidence for the gain.
questions.rule: Each helps the other.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that mastering their training booklet and practising each make the other more useful.
questions.explain: People who read the booklet benefited more from practice, and people who practiced benefited more from the booklet.
questions.rule: Books and practice work together.

questions.q: Why do the authors say their training guidelines make personal experience more useful?
options: They give forecasters fixed rules that replace their own judgment
They remove the need for any feedback on past forecasts
They help strike the right balance of outside and inside views
They help forecasters avoid being wrong on any question
optionExplain: The guidelines inform judgment; the authors do not describe them as replacing it.
The chapter stresses feedback as separate and essential.
Right: the guidelines help draw the right lessons and balance the outside and inside views.
Being wrong is not removed by guidelines; they improve accuracy by roughly 10%.
questions.explain: The authors say the guidelines help us draw the right lessons from experience and strike the right balance between outside and inside views.
questions.rule: Guidelines focus the lessons of experience.
questions.teaches: The authors say the training guidelines help forecasters draw the right lessons from personal experience and strike the right balances between the outside and inside views, while experience gives pallid abstractions real-world content.

questions.q: As police officers gain years of experience judging who is lying, what does research say happens to their accuracy and confidence?
options: Accuracy and confidence rise together
Confidence grows faster than accuracy
Accuracy falls while confidence stays level
Confidence falls as accuracy rises
optionExplain: This would follow if experience gave feedback, which it does not here.
Right: officers grow confident faster than they grow accurate.
The authors do not report accuracy falling.
The gap widens in the other direction, with confidence rising.
questions.explain: Experience without clear feedback raises confidence more than accuracy. The card gives the reasons.
questions.rule: Confidence can outrun accuracy.

questions.q: Experience helps only when it is accompanied by clear and timely ____.
questions.explain: Without clear feedback on whether judgments were right, experience does not improve them.
questions.rule: Experience needs feedback.

questions.q: A hiring manager interviews hundreds of candidates but does not learn how any hire performed. What do the authors' ideas predict?
options: More accuracy over time as the interviews pile up
Less confidence as the doubts accumulate
Steady accuracy and steady confidence
More confidence over time without more accuracy
optionExplain: Accuracy comes from feedback, not just repetition.
Confidence grows with experience when feedback is missing.
The officers' case shows confidence rising with experience.
Right: no feedback means experience cannot sharpen judgment, but confidence still grows.
questions.explain: Like the officers, the manager gets no clear feedback, so confidence outgrows accuracy.
questions.rule: No feedback, no learning, more confidence.

questions.q: In controlled tests of lie detection, what happens to the gap between officers' confidence and skill as they become more experienced?
options: It stays the same
It shrinks slowly
It disappears after about five years
It grows
optionExplain: If the gap were fixed, experience would have no effect on confidence.
A shrinking gap would need feedback, which is missing.
The chapter reports no such point.
Right: the gap grows as officers assume experience has made them better.
questions.explain: Experience raises confidence without raising accuracy, so the gap widens.
questions.rule: The gap widens with unchecked experience.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors' reading of research, police officers tend not to get better at spotting lies with experience.
questions.explain: Without clear feedback, experience does not improve their judgment, though their confidence grows.
questions.rule: Years on the job are not skill.

questions.q: A talent scout judges teenagers and learns who became a star only after ten years, when many factors have intervened. Why is this poor feedback?
options: The result comes too quickly to be believed
The result comes late and is tangled with other factors
The result is always the same, so nothing is learned
The result is clear but the scout ignores it
optionExplain: Delay is the problem here, not speed.
Right: as with trials and plea bargains, delay and many factors blur the lesson.
The result varies, but delay and other factors hide what the scout got right.
The problem is the structure of the feedback, not the scout's attitude.
questions.explain: The authors note that resolution of an officer's judgment may take months or years and many factors could have gone into it.
questions.rule: Late, tangled outcomes teach little.
questions.teaches: When a case is eventually resolved, a huge range of factors could have gone into the outcome, so even a verdict seldom tells an officer clearly whether the judgment was right.

questions.q: Which of these groups does the chapter say generally avoids overconfidence?
options: Police officers and experienced judges
Business executives and seasoned investors
Meteorologists and seasoned bridge players
Teachers and university professors
optionExplain: Police officers are the chapter's example of overconfidence.
The chapter does not name these groups as well calibrated.
Right: both get clear, prompt feedback.
The chapter does not discuss these groups here.
questions.explain: Meteorologists and bridge players both see their errors quickly. The card explains why that matters.
questions.rule: Prompt feedback keeps confidence honest.

questions.q: Calibration is how closely your ____ matches your accuracy.
questions.explain: A well calibrated person is as confident as they are accurate.
questions.rule: Calibration: confidence matches accuracy.

questions.q: Which worker is best placed to become well calibrated, by the chapter's reasoning?
options: A weather presenter whose forecast is checked next morning
A policy adviser whose predictions resolve in ten years or so
A columnist who predicts that things might change
A consultant whose clients never report the results
optionExplain: Right: clear and prompt feedback is what calibration needs.
Long delays make feedback weak and tangled.
Vague predictions give no clear feedback.
With no results reported, there is no feedback.
questions.explain: Calibration grows where results are clear and quick, as in the weather presenter's case.
questions.rule: Look for quick, clear results.

questions.q: Which settings give clear, prompt feedback, and which give slow or unclear feedback?

items.t: A meteorologist calls for rain tomorrow
A bridge player estimates tricks before a hand
An officer judges a suspect, with the trial months away
A forecaster says something might happen
A forecaster states a date and a number

questions.explain: Quick, checkable results give clear feedback; long delays and vague claims do not.
questions.rule: Speed and clarity give feedback.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say overconfidence is an immutable law of human nature.
questions.explain: They say it is not immutable: meteorologists and bridge players generally avoid it.
questions.rule: Overconfidence can be avoided.

questions.q: Which of these gives the clearest signal that you have failed?
options: An officer waiting months for a trial
A vague forecast that something could happen
A boy skinning his knee when he falls off a bike
A forecast judged years later from memory
optionExplain: Waiting months blurs the feedback.
A vague forecast cannot be judged.
Right: he knows at once, so he can think about what went wrong and adjust.
Memory years later is unreliable.
questions.explain: The authors say to learn from failure we must know when we fail, as the baby, the boy and the golfer do.
questions.rule: Knowing you failed comes first.
questions.teaches: To learn from failure we must know when we fail, as the baby who flops, the boy who skins his knee and the accountant who putts into a sand trap do; because they know, they can think about what went wrong and adjust.

questions.q: A forecaster says a default could happen next year. Why can that forecast not be scored?
options: It states a probability, and probabilities cannot be scored
Could covers almost any outcome, so none can show it wrong
It looks too far ahead for anyone to check
It was made by a single person rather than by a group
optionExplain: Probabilities can be scored; this is the point of Brier scores later in the chapter.
Right: a word like could can mean almost anything.
Distance in time is a separate barrier from vagueness.
The number of forecasters is not the issue.
questions.explain: Could, might and may stretch to fit any result. The card sets out the problem.
questions.rule: Vague words cannot be scored.

questions.q: Vague terms like probably and likely make it impossible to ____ forecasts.
questions.explain: If a term can mean almost anything, no result can show a forecast was right or wrong.
questions.rule: Vague forecasts cannot be judged.

questions.q: Which forecast could be judged without argument when the year ends?
options: Sales may well improve in the second half
Sales are likely to look better soon
Sales could see a significant rise at some point
Sales will be 5% above June's level by December
optionExplain: May well improve is elastic and can fit any result.
Likely and soon are open to stretching.
Significant and some point are fuzzy.
Right: a number and a date let anyone check the result.
questions.explain: Only a precise claim with a measurable outcome and date can be checked.
questions.rule: Make it checkable.

questions.q: A forecaster judges her own vague forecast. According to the authors, what happens to the problem?
options: It gets worse, as she can stretch the words to fit
It disappears, since she knows well what she meant
It stays the same as it would with an impartial judge
It becomes smaller as her confidence grows
optionExplain: Right: the chapter says it makes the problem even worse.
Knowing what she meant makes it easy to claim it fit.
The chapter says the self-judge makes it worse.
Confidence is not what shrinks the problem.
questions.explain: Even an impartial observer would struggle, and when the forecaster is the judge it is worse.
questions.rule: Do not judge your own vague forecasts.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say an impartial observer can extract meaningful feedback from vague forecasts without difficulty.
questions.explain: They say even an impartial observer would struggle.
questions.rule: Vagueness hurts every judge.

questions.q: Which phrase is as fuzzy as the chapter's example from Steve Ballmer?
options: A product will gain 8% share by June
A product will gain significant share
A product will lose 2% share by March
A product will hold exactly its share this year
optionExplain: This has a number and a date.
Right: significant has no measure, like Ballmer's wording.
Also measurable and datable.
Also checkable at year end.
questions.explain: The authors cite Ballmer's reference to significant market share as sounding precise but being fuzzy as fog.
questions.rule: Words that sound precise may not be.
questions.teaches: The authors give Steve Ballmer's reference to “significant market share” as a phrase that may sound precise but on close inspection proves as fuzzy as fog.

questions.q: Students rated a personality profile 4.2 out of 5 for fit. What was unusual about the profile?
options: Each profile was written by the students about themselves
It was based on a long interview with each student
Everyone received the same one, made of vague statements
It came from a test of the students' brain activity
optionExplain: The profile came from Forer, not from the students.
There was no interview; the profile was assembled from a book.
Right: Forer gave everyone the same profile built from vague astrology statements.
The test was a personality test, not a brain scan.
questions.explain: The profile was the same for all and made of vague statements. The card gives the details.
questions.rule: Vague statements fit everyone.

questions.q: Vague statements that seem to fit everyone illustrate the ____ effect, named for a psychologist.
questions.explain: The effect is named for Bertram Forer.
questions.rule: The Forer effect.

questions.q: A company quiz gives every employee the same paragraph: You value harmony but can be firm. Most rate it accurate. Which effect explains this?
options: The Forer effect: vague wording stretches to fit anyone
Self-fulfilling belief: staff become what the quiz says
Fixed mindset: staff think their traits cannot change
Growth mindset: staff believe they can build harmony
optionExplain: Right: elastic wording seems personal to each reader.
The paragraph does not cause the trait; it merely fits.
Mindset is about beliefs on changing ability, not fit of a profile.
Mindset is not what the rating shows.
questions.explain: Everyone stretches the vague paragraph to fit their self-image.
questions.rule: Vague statements seem personal.

questions.q: Which statements are vague and elastic, and which are precise and checkable?

items.t: You have a great need for people to like and admire you
Something could happen in the region soon
Unemployment will exceed 6% in June
The incumbent will win by more than 3 points
Prices may move in either direction

questions.explain: Elastic statements fit any outcome; precise ones can be shown wrong.
questions.rule: Precise claims can fail.

questions.q: True or false: Forer gave every student the same vague profile.
questions.explain: He assembled the profile from vague statements in an astrology book and gave it to everyone.
questions.rule: The fit was imagined.

questions.q: A forecaster who predicted that inflation could rise reviews her forecast after prices climb and judges it correct. What does the Forer effect warn?
options: She has proved that her vague forecast was in fact precise
She should trust her own judgment more, since it was right
Her forecast was accurate because she chose a cautious word
She may stretch vague words to fit while feeling objective
optionExplain: Could rise is not precise; it would fit almost anything.
The warning is about trust in self-judgment of vague claims.
Caution does not make a vague claim scorable.
Right: vague language is elastic, and the judge may not notice stretching it.
questions.explain: The students thought they were judging the test objectively yet stretched the vague language, so self-judgment of vague forecasts is unreliable.
questions.rule: Don't kid yourself.
questions.teaches: The students believed they were judging the test objectively, yet stretched the vague statements to fit their self-images.

questions.q: You estimated an event at 30%, and it then happened. When you later try to recall your estimate, which way will it probably drift?
options: Downward, away from the outcome
Upward, toward the outcome
It will stay exactly at 30%
It will drift randomly in either direction
optionExplain: The slant runs toward the result, not away.
Right: knowing the outcome slants memory toward it.
Memory is not fixed; the outcome pulls it.
The drift is predictable in direction.
questions.explain: Knowing the outcome slants memory toward it. The card names the effect.
questions.rule: Memory bends toward the result.

questions.q: Hindsight bias is also described as the feeling that you knew the outcome all ____.
questions.explain: People feel they saw the outcome coming because knowing it reshapes their memory of their earlier view.
questions.rule: I knew it all along.

questions.q: After a startup collapses, an investor who backed it says the collapse was bound to happen. Which effect is at work?
options: The Forer effect, as vague words fit any result
Calibration, as her confidence matches her accuracy
Value investing, as she studied the business
Hindsight bias, as the known outcome reshapes her memory
optionExplain: The Forer effect is about vague profiles fitting everyone.
Calibration is about matching confidence to accuracy over many judgments.
Value investing is about judging underlying worth before investing.
Right: the known result skews her recollection of her earlier view.
questions.explain: She recalls a view shaped by the outcome, not the view she held beforehand.
questions.rule: Outcome rewrites memory.

questions.q: In Fischhoff's research, people recall their earlier estimate after learning the outcome. What happens when they try hard not to let the outcome sway them?
options: The slant still appears
The slant vanishes entirely
The slant reverses direction
The slant appears only for rare events
optionExplain: Right: the outcome slanted estimates even when people tried not to let it.
Effort did not remove it.
The direction stays the same.
The chapter does not limit the effect to rare events.
questions.explain: Knowing the outcome consistently slanted the estimate, even with effort.
questions.rule: Effort of will does not remove the bias.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say hindsight bias disappears when people try not to let the outcome sway their recollection.
questions.explain: They say the knowledge consistently slanted the estimate even when people tried to prevent it.
questions.rule: Trying is not enough.

questions.q: In 1991 a Saturday Night Live skit joked that Democrats feared running against President Bush. What does it show about the received view?
options: Bush's reelection looked a coin flip, so many Democrats ran
Bush's reelection looked doubtful after the Gulf War
Bush's reelection looked close to certain, so few top Democrats ran
Bush's reelection looked certain, so Clinton was expected to win
optionExplain: The skit shows the opposite of a coin flip.
The skit stresses how popular the incumbent was.
Right: leading Democrats stayed out and cleared the way for the obscure governor of Arkansas.
Clinton was obscure, not the expected winner.
questions.explain: The skit captured the received wisdom that Bush was certain to win, which is why many people later misremember how likely they thought a Bush loss was.
questions.rule: Check old records, not memory.
questions.teaches: A 1991 Saturday Night Live skit captured the received wisdom that Bush 41 was certain to win, which is why leading Democrats stayed out and cleared the way for Bill Clinton.

questions.q: Experts later recalled their 1988 estimates of the Soviet Party losing power. By how much were the recalled figures too high on average?
options: 3 percentage points
31 percentage points
10 percentage points
70 percentage points
optionExplain: Far too small: the chapter calls the effect quite big.
Right: the average recalled number was 31 points higher than the correct figure.
A guess that is too small for the gap the chapter reports.
This was one expert's extreme case, not the average.
questions.explain: The gap was 31 points on average. The card gives the study.
questions.rule: Memory shifts a lot toward the outcome.

questions.q: On average the experts recalled a number ____ percentage points higher than the correct figure.
questions.explain: The average error was 31 percentage points.
questions.rule: 31 points on average.

questions.q: In 1988 an expert put the chance of the Party losing its monopoly at 10%. Which later recollection fits the study?
options: That she had thought it 40% or 50% likely
That she had thought it 10% likely, as before
That she had thought it 2% likely
That she had not made any estimate
optionExplain: Right: the chapter gives a 10% expert who might remember 40% or 50%.
Accurate recall was not the typical result.
The slant went toward the outcome, not away.
The experts did recall estimates; they were just wrong.
questions.explain: Knowing the Soviet Union fell moved her memory toward a higher figure.
questions.rule: The memory moves toward what happened.

questions.q: Match each item in Tetlock's Soviet study to the right detail.
pairs: Experts were asked to recall them in
Average recalled number exceeded the real one by
The Party losing its power monopoly
questions.explain: The estimates came before the collapse, the recall came after it, and the gap averaged 31 points.
questions.rule: Separate when the estimate and the recall were made.

questions.q: True or false: The experts' recalled estimates were on average 31 percentage points higher than the figures they had given.
questions.explain: Knowing the Soviet Union had fallen moved their memory toward a higher figure.
questions.rule: Memory drifts toward the outcome.

questions.q: A manager says she will recall her forecasts when results arrive. What does Tetlock's study suggest about trusting memory?
options: Memory is reliable for experts, though not for beginners
Memory fails only for low-probability events such as a collapse
Even experts misremember badly, so record forecasts at the time
Memory is fine as long as the forecast was made with confidence
optionExplain: The study was of experts, and they erred.
The study's example included 10% and 20% estimates, but nothing limits the effect to them.
Right: written records guard against the drift of memory toward outcomes.
Confidence at the time does not protect the recollection.
questions.explain: One expert who gave 20% recalled 70%, so records made at the time are needed.
questions.rule: Write it down at the time.
questions.teaches: One expert who put the probability at 20% recalled it as 70%, which shows why hindsight bias is also called the I knew it all along effect.

questions.q: Tim Minto's forecast on Syrian refugee flows got a Brier score of 0.07. How did the chapter describe it?
options: A middling result, like a shot that hits the rim
A poor result, like a ball thrown at the wrong hoop
An unscoreable result, because the wording was vague
An excellent result, a nothing-but-net free throw
optionExplain: The chapter reserves the rim sounds for the dark, unscored shooter.
The poor result was Minto's other score, 1.46, on Abe.
The wording was clear, which is why it could be scored.
Right: the chapter calls it clear, precise, meaningful and excellent.
questions.explain: Lower Brier scores are better, and 0.07 was excellent. The card gives the full picture.
questions.rule: Scores show hits and misses.

questions.q: Minto's 0.07 was the forecasting equivalent of a nothing-but-____ free throw.
questions.explain: The chapter compares the excellent score to a free throw that goes in without touching the rim.
questions.rule: Nothing but net.

questions.q: A sales team forecasts in vague words and later recalls them from memory. What would turn the lights on for them?
options: Hold a longer team meeting before each forecast is made
Rate forecasts as good when the outcome was good
Ask the most senior member to judge all forecasts
Write numeric probabilities with dates and score them
optionExplain: A longer meeting adds discussion but not feedback.
Rating by outcome is the trap the chapter warns about later.
A senior judge faces the same vagueness and memory limits.
Right: clear wording and scoring give feedback that memory cannot distort.
questions.explain: Clear, scored forecasts let results speak. Vague words and memory do not.
questions.rule: Make forecasts clear and score them.

questions.q: Which practices turn the lights on for a forecaster, and which leave them off?

items.t: A numeric probability scored with a Brier score
A forecast saying something might happen
Recalling old forecasts from memory
A written forecast with a clear question and deadline

questions.explain: Scoring and clear wording create feedback; vague words and memory hide it.
questions.rule: Clear and scored, or dark.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Minto's Brier score of 0.07 on Syrian refugee flows was an excellent result.
questions.explain: They call it clear, precise and meaningful, the equivalent of a nothing-but-net free throw.
questions.rule: Higher scores are worse.

questions.q: Why can a veteran who has shot thousands of free throws with the lights on learn from sounds in the dark, but not a novice?
options: The veteran has learned to link sounds to results
The veteran can still see the ball in the dark
The veteran counts only the swishes he hears
The novice never hears the sounds at all in the dark
optionExplain: Right: the veteran learned the links when he could see.
The dark means no one sees the ball.
Counting only hits would give no way to learn from misses.
The novice hears the sounds but cannot interpret them.
questions.explain: In the dark, a novice cannot tell a swish from an underthrown ball; with practice and no feedback he only grows more confident.
questions.rule: Feedback gives meaning to signals.
questions.teaches: A novice who throws balls in the dark for weeks may grow more confident (I've practiced so much I must be excellent) without getting any better.

questions.q: A bridge player is well calibrated when bidding. According to the authors, what should we expect for business forecasting?
options: Full carry-over, since calibration is a general skill
Carry-over only if the player is highly intelligent
Little or no carry-over to business forecasting
Carry-over only for political forecasts
optionExplain: Calibration is not a general skill, on the authors' account.
The chapter ties transfer to context, not intelligence here.
Right: judgment calibrated in one context transfers poorly, if at all.
The chapter says transfer is poor in any other context.
questions.explain: Calibration is context-bound. The card gives the details.
questions.rule: Calibration does not travel well.

questions.q: Research shows that judgment calibrated in one context transfers ____, if at all, to another.
questions.explain: Calibration in one setting does not carry over well to others.
questions.rule: Transfers poorly.

questions.q: A chess master wants to forecast elections more accurately. What do the authors' ideas suggest?
options: Play more chess to sharpen her general judgment
Forecast elections repeatedly and check results
Study chess openings that resemble campaigns
Wait until her intelligence is high enough
optionExplain: Chess calibration is context-bound, like bridge.
Right: practise the type you want to improve, with feedback.
Resemblance does not carry over calibration.
The authors point to practice, not waiting.
questions.explain: To get better at one kind of forecasting, do that kind.
questions.rule: Practise the target kind.

questions.q: A pilot is well calibrated about turbulence on short flights. How well will this calibration carry over to forecasting currency moves?
options: Fully, since both involve probabilities
Partly, in proportion to flying hours
Poorly, if at all
Better than for a non-pilot by a wide margin
optionExplain: Both involve probabilities, but calibration does not depend on that.
The chapter does not link transfer to hours of experience.
Right: context-bound calibration transfers poorly.
The chapter gives no support for a large advantage.
questions.explain: Calibration earned in one context does not move well to another.
questions.rule: Different context, little carry-over.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say skill from bridge bidding makes people noticeably better at political forecasting.
questions.explain: They say to forget it: calibration in one context transfers poorly, if at all.
questions.rule: No shortcuts.

questions.q: Which reaction to a missed forecast do the authors recommend?
options: Note the miss and avoid questions of that kind
Blame bad luck and keep the same method
Wait until more evidence arrives before deciding
Say Wow, I got that one wrong and think about why
optionExplain: Avoiding the kind of question forgoes the practice that improves it.
Blaming luck prevents the review of the method.
Waiting delays the feedback that practice needs.
Right: a cheerful willingness to admit the miss and ask why.
questions.explain: The authors prescribe a cheerful willingness to say, Wow, I got that one wrong. I'd better think about why.
questions.rule: Admit the miss, then ask why.
questions.teaches: The authors recommend a cheerful willingness to say “Wow, I got that one wrong. I’d better think about why.”

questions.q: After finding his old comments too sparse to reconstruct his thinking, what did Jean-Pierre Beugoms do?
options: He stopped reviewing his old forecasts altogether
He started leaving longer comments on forecasts
He asked teammates to write his comments for him
He moved to forecasting fewer questions overall
optionExplain: He kept reviewing, which is why he found the problem.
Right: he started leaving more and longer comments to examine his thinking.
The chapter does not say teammates wrote his comments.
The chapter does not say he forecast fewer questions.
questions.explain: He fixed the record at the source. The card gives both examples.
questions.rule: Leave notes for the future review.

questions.q: After a question closes, superforecasters often write a ____ with teammates to examine what went wrong.
questions.explain: The authors describe lengthy postmortems shared online among teammates.
questions.rule: Review after the question closes.

questions.q: A product team lost a bid after assuming a rival could not match its price. Which step mirrors Devyn Duffy's lesson?
options: Check that assumption with someone who knows rival costs
Defend the assumption as reasonable given the facts known
Drop price as a factor in all of the later bids
Credit the loss to bad luck and move on to the next bid
optionExplain: Right: reexamine assumptions and ask experts if you can find them.
Defending it repeats the unquestioned assumption.
Dropping price confuses one failed assumption with the whole factor.
Calling it luck skips the postmortem.
questions.explain: Duffy's lesson was to ask experts and reexamine assumptions from time to time.
questions.rule: Question assumptions of expertise.

questions.q: Match each person or group to the lesson or habit the chapter attaches to them.
pairs: Leave fuller comments to critique your thinking
questions.explain: Each shows a different part of analysis after the result: testing assumptions, keeping a record, and sharing the review.
questions.rule: Assumptions, record, sharing.

questions.q: True or false: Duffy wrote that his team had not done nearly enough to question its polonium assumption.
questions.explain: He said they did not question the assumption, for example by asking an expert.
questions.rule: The assumption was not tested.

questions.q: Why might a forecaster write detailed notes on a question the day it is announced?
options: So a later postmortem can rebuild her thinking
So that her teammates will agree with the forecast
So the notes can replace the forecast itself
So she can avoid having the forecast scored later
optionExplain: Right: notes made early make the review possible.
Notes do not secure agreement.
Notes record reasoning; they do not replace the forecast.
Scoring still happens whatever notes she keeps.
questions.explain: The authors say Beugoms in effect prepares for the postmortem from the moment the question is announced.
questions.rule: Prepare the postmortem at the start.
questions.teaches: In effect, Beugoms prepares for the postmortem from the moment the tournament question is announced.

questions.q: Devyn Duffy's team aced the Guinea elections question. What did he say in his postmortem?
options: They deserved full credit for their forecasting method
They should have forecast a different outcome entirely
They had been unlucky not to score even higher marks
They had been lucky, as protests nearly stopped the vote
optionExplain: He said the team could not take all the credit.
Their forecast was right, so no different outcome was needed.
He said the team was lucky, not unlucky.
Right: the protests nearly prevented the elections, so the team lucked out.
questions.explain: He credited luck as well as skill. The card gives the details.
questions.rule: Admit luck when you succeed.

questions.q: Duffy said that with Guinea, his team ____ out as well as being skilled.
questions.explain: He wrote that they lucked out, too.
questions.rule: We lucked out.

questions.q: A manager picks a risky supplier, and it delivers on time by chance. What do the authors' ideas suggest she do?
options: Treat the good result as proof the choice was wise
Repeat the same choice, since it worked well once
Ask if the decision was sound apart from its result
Skip the review, since nothing went wrong this time
optionExplain: This is the mistake the authors warn about.
Repeating it relies on the same flaw.
Right: a good outcome does not show the decision was good.
A review of a lucky success can still reveal flaws.
questions.explain: A good result may hide flaws in thinking. The review looks at the reasoning.
questions.rule: Judge reasoning, not just result.

questions.q: Which comments acknowledge luck, and which credit skill alone after a good result?

items.t: We were right, but the protests nearly stopped the vote
We were right, so our method is proven
We lucked out on this one
We were right, so no review is needed

questions.explain: Duffy's style acknowledges how close the result came to going the other way.
questions.rule: Say how it nearly went wrong.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say people assume a bad decision when a decision is followed by a good outcome.
questions.explain: They say people assume the decision was good, which isn't always true.
questions.rule: Good outcome does not mean good decision.

questions.q: Which statement does the chapter support about people who succeed?
options: They are usually quick to credit luck for part of success
They are usually not open to the idea that luck helped
They credit luck only on the occasions when they lose
They credit luck for the result more than the method
optionExplain: The chapter says the opposite, which is why Duffy stands out.
Right: the successful are not usually so open to that idea.
The chapter does not link luck to losing.
The chapter says successful people tend not to credit luck.
questions.explain: The authors say that unlike Duffy, the successful are not usually open to the idea that they didn't entirely earn their success.
questions.rule: Duffy is the exception.
questions.teaches: The authors say the successful are not usually so open to the idea that they didn't entirely earn their success, which makes Duffy's willingness to say we lucked out unusual.

questions.q: In Tetlock's research, how did experts treat what-if scenarios suggesting their failed forecast was nearly right?
options: They welcomed them like an old friend
They dismissed them as speculative
They ignored them as irrelevant
They accepted them only when others agreed
optionExplain: Right: the experts welcomed the almost-right tale.
The dismissal was for the almost-wrong tales.
They responded strongly, not with indifference.
The chapter reports no dependence on others' agreement.
