questions.explain: Experts accepted the stories that rescued their forecasts. The card gives the full pattern.
questions.rule: Welcome flattering what-ifs, doubt threatening ones.

questions.q: Experts were open to I was almost ____ scenarios but rejected I was almost wrong alternatives.
questions.explain: They welcomed scenarios that made a failed forecast look nearly right.
questions.rule: Almost right is welcome.

questions.q: After a lost bet a pundit says a few votes would have made her right; after a win she rejects that tale. Which pattern?
options: Open to every counterfactual, whichever way it points
Closed to every counterfactual, whichever way it points
Open to almost-right stories, closed to almost-wrong ones
Open to almost-wrong stories only
optionExplain: She treats the two kinds differently, so she is not open to all.
She accepts one kind, so she is not closed to all.
Right: she welcomes what saves her misses and rejects what threatens her hits.
She welcomes almost-right, the opposite of this option.
questions.explain: The pundit shows the asymmetry Tetlock found among experts.
questions.rule: Judge what-ifs evenly.

questions.q: Which kind of what-if did experts welcome, and which did they dismiss as speculative?

items.t: A better-organised coup would have kept the Party in power
A small tweak would have made a correct forecast fail
A less drunk set of plotters would have changed the result
A butterfly-effect event could easily have overturned a hit

questions.explain: The experts welcomed what-ifs that rescued failed forecasts and dismissed those that undermined correct ones.
questions.rule: Welcome rescuers, dismiss threats.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say experts dismissed every counterfactual scenario as speculative.
questions.explain: They welcomed scenarios under which their failed forecast would have been right; they dismissed the ones that threatened their correct forecast.
questions.rule: Selective, not uniform.

questions.q: An analyst predicted Quebec would leave Canada, and it did not. By the pattern in Tetlock's study, which what-if would she most welcome?
options: A tale where a small tweak keeps Quebec in more firmly
A tale where a small tweak makes Quebec leave
A tale that says no forecast could have been right
A tale that says her forecast was a pure guess
optionExplain: That would show her forecast needed no rescue; it did not fail.
Right: she would welcome the tale that makes her failed forecast look nearly right.
Experts did not accept stories that denied any forecast could succeed.
Calling it a guess would hurt her, not rescue her.
questions.explain: The three questions were the Party in the Soviet Union, a violent overthrow of apartheid and Quebec's separation, and the answers all came out no.
questions.rule: Spot the flattering what-if.
questions.teaches: Tetlock's three questions were whether the Communist Party would stay in power in the Soviet Union, whether apartheid would be violently overthrown, and whether Quebec would separate from Canada; the answers were no, no and no.

questions.q: How long does the try-fail-analyze-adjust cycle typically take on a bicycle, compared with forecasting?
options: Hours on a bicycle; several days in forecasting at most
Seconds in both cases, though forecasting is harder
Months in both cases, though forecasting is riskier
Seconds on a bicycle; months or years in forecasting
optionExplain: The chapter gives seconds for the bicycle.
Forecasting loops are far longer than seconds.
The bicycle loop is far shorter than months.
Right: the loop is fast on a bike and slow in forecasting.
questions.explain: The loop is fast for riding and slow for forecasting. The card sets out both differences.
questions.rule: Loop length differs greatly.

questions.q: In forecasting, the role of ____ is bigger than in bicycling.
questions.explain: Chance plays a bigger role, so best practices improve the odds less reliably.
questions.rule: Chance matters more.

questions.q: A cyclist and a forecaster both follow best practices yet suffer a bad outcome. Which is more likely a sign of poor practice?
options: The forecaster's, since forecasting is harder
The cyclist's, since chance plays a smaller role
Equally likely, since both followed best practices
Neither, since outcomes never reflect practice
optionExplain: Forecasters should be more tentative, so a bad outcome says less about practice.
Right: cyclists following best practices can usually expect excellent outcomes.
The authors say the two differ in chance.
Practice improves odds in both.
questions.explain: For forecasters, best practices improve the odds less reliably, so a bad outcome tells less.
questions.rule: Chance weakens the signal.

questions.q: Because the forecasting loop takes months or years, what happens to a forecaster's feedback compared with a cyclist's?
options: It arrives faster, since forecasts are written down
It arrives at the same speed as a cyclist's
It arrives much later and more rarely
It does not arrive at all
optionExplain: Writing helps clarity but cannot speed up results.
The loop lengths differ greatly.
Right: a long loop means slow feedback.
Feedback does arrive, but late.
questions.explain: A loop of months or years means feedback comes late.
questions.rule: Slow loop, slow feedback.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the analogy between forecasting and bicycling is pretty good but imperfect.
questions.explain: They note the loop is slower in forecasting and chance plays a bigger role.
questions.rule: Analogies have limits.

questions.q: Given the slow loop and the large role of chance, what do the authors say a forecaster needs besides a growth mindset?
options: A lot of grit
A lot of luck
A faster feedback loop
A bigger team
optionExplain: Right: even with a growth mindset, a forecaster needs a lot of grit.
Luck is the problem, not the remedy.
The loop's length is a given, not a choice.
The authors name grit, not team size.
questions.explain: The authors say that even with a growth mindset the forecaster has to have a lot of what Angela Duckworth dubbed grit.
questions.rule: Slow loops need grit.
questions.teaches: Even with a growth mindset, the forecaster who wants to improve has to have a lot of what the authors' colleague Angela Duckworth dubbed grit.

questions.q: How do the authors define grit?
options: A quick recovery from each mistake without needing to review it
A belief that abilities are the product of effort
A habit of changing views whenever new facts arrive
Passionate perseverance of long-term goals despite frustration and failure
optionExplain: Recovery speed is not the definition; grit is about perseverance.
That is the growth mindset, a related idea.
That describes updating, a different trait.
Right: grit is perseverance toward long-term goals through frustration and failure.
questions.explain: Grit is perseverance over the long term. The card gives examples.
questions.rule: Grit means perseverance.

questions.q: Grit is passionate perseverance of long-term ____, even in the face of frustration and failure.
questions.explain: The definition centers on long-term goals pursued through setbacks.
questions.rule: Perseverance toward long-term goals.

questions.q: A learner takes up a language, falters for months, and keeps studying despite little visible progress. Which trait does she show?
options: Hindsight bias, as she reads her progress backward in time
Calibration, as her confidence closely matches her accuracy
Value investing, as she studies the underlying worth of things
Grit, as she persists toward a long-term goal
optionExplain: Hindsight bias concerns memory of past estimates.
Calibration concerns matching confidence to accuracy.
Value investing concerns judging company worth.
Right: persistence through frustration toward a long-term goal.
questions.explain: She keeps going through frustration, as Kilkenny did.
questions.rule: Persevere through the frustration.

questions.q: Which behaviors show Anne Kilkenny's grit, according to the chapter? Select all that apply.
options: Forecasting all 150 questions in year 3
Staying with it after high-confidence forecasts ended badly
Withdrawing once her accuracy fell
Writing back to the UN agency to ask how often data were updated
optionExplain: Right: she forecast every question despite a team that did little.
Right: her accuracy plunged and she kept at it.
Wrong: she kept at it when her accuracy plunged.
Right: she queried the agency twice and persisted when the answer was in French.
questions.explain: Kilkenny's grit shows in the volume of work, her persistence after bad outcomes, and her follow-up with the data source.
questions.rule: Grit is visible in what you keep doing.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Anne Kilkenny is already a superforecaster.
questions.explain: They say she isn't a superforecaster, at least not yet, though her results are impressive.
questions.rule: Not yet.

questions.q: Readers flood an author with I knew it all along emails. Which response mirrors Kilkenny's reaction to her Palin email adulation?
options: Thank the readers and take credit for having predicted it
Question how anyone could know that, since feelings pose as knowledge
Reply to each of the readers with her own detailed predictions about it
Delete the emails because they come from partisan readers
optionExplain: Taking credit would be revelling in the adulation, which she resisted.
Right: she kept her head and questioned how anyone could know from a glimpse.
The chapter does not say she replied with predictions.
She scrutinized rather than discarded.
questions.explain: Kilkenny arched a skeptical eyebrow at partisan praise; the authors say such astute observation, with careful research, helps make a superforecaster.
questions.rule: Question praise that looks like knowledge.
questions.teaches: Kilkenny, amid partisan praise for her Palin email, noted that feelings were masquerading as knowledge; the authors say such critical, psychologically astute observation, plus careful research, helps make a superforecaster.

questions.q: Which factor do the authors say is the strongest predictor of becoming a superforecaster?
options: Raw intelligence measured by standard tests
Years of experience in politics or government
Commitment to updating and self-improvement
Formal training in statistics and probability
optionExplain: Intelligence is the closest rival, about a third as powerful.
The authors do not name political experience as the strongest predictor.
Right: perpetual beta is the strongest predictor.
The authors do not name statistics training as the strongest predictor.
questions.explain: Perpetual beta tops the list, ahead of intelligence. The card explains the term.
questions.rule: Updating and self-improvement matter most.

questions.q: Computer programmers use the term perpetual ____ for a program that is improved without end.
questions.explain: A perpetual beta is a program not meant for a final release, used, analyzed and improved without end.
questions.rule: Perpetual beta.

questions.q: A company keeps its product design in constant testing and improves it monthly; no version is final. Which phrase from the chapter fits?
options: Perpetual beta
Consistently inconsistent
Value investing
Nothing but net
optionExplain: Right: use, analyze, and improve without end.
That describes Keynes changing his mind.
That describes judging worth of a company.
That describes an excellent forecast score.
questions.explain: Perpetual beta describes work that is never finished and always improved.
questions.rule: Never final, always improving.

questions.q: Two applicants have similar intelligence, but one is more committed to updating and self-improvement. By the authors' finding, who is likelier to become a superforecaster?
options: The more committed one
The other one
Both equally likely
Neither, since intelligence decides
optionExplain: Right: perpetual beta is roughly three times as powerful a predictor as intelligence.
Without a commitment edge, nothing here favors the other.
Commitment predicts more strongly than intelligence.
Intelligence is the closest rival, not the main predictor.
questions.explain: With intelligence equal, the commitment gap is the stronger predictor.
questions.rule: Commitment counts for more.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say perpetual beta is roughly three times as powerful a predictor of superforecasting as intelligence.
questions.explain: Intelligence is the closest rival, and perpetual beta is the stronger predictor.
questions.rule: Perpetual beta beats intelligence.

questions.q: According to the authors, how well can a high IQ make up for a lack of dedication to growing one's synapses?
options: Fully, since intelligence outweighs any amount of dedication
Not easily: it is difficult, however high the IQ
Partly, in proportion to the size of the IQ score
Not at all, since IQ is irrelevant to forecasting
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite.
Right: no matter how high one's IQ, it is difficult to compensate.
The authors do not give a proportion.
The authors say intelligence matters but is not the strongest predictor.
questions.explain: The predictive power of perpetual beta suggests that no matter how high one's IQ it is difficult to compensate for lack of dedication to the personal project of growing one's synapses.
questions.rule: Dedication is hard to replace.
questions.teaches: The predictive power of perpetual beta suggests that, no matter how high one's IQ, it is difficult to compensate for lack of dedication to the personal project of growing one's synapses.

questions.q: According to the authors, how does an actively open-minded person treat beliefs?
options: As treasures to be protected from every challenge
As fixed facts about the world to be defended
As feelings that need no testing or checking
As hypotheses to test, not treasures to guard
optionExplain: This is the attitude the portrait rejects.
Fixed facts to defend is also the closed view.
Feelings masquerading as knowledge are what Kilkenny doubted.
Right: the portrait describes beliefs as hypotheses to test.
questions.explain: Active open-mindedness treats beliefs as testable. The card lists the full portrait.
questions.rule: Test beliefs; don't guard them.

questions.q: Match each philosophic trait to the authors' gloss.
pairs: What happens does not have to happen
questions.explain: The three outlook traits are caution, humility and a nondeterministic view of events.
questions.rule: Cautious, humble, nondeterministic.

questions.q: A colleague says, My view on the merger is settled, so please don't challenge it. Which trait from the portrait is lacking?
options: Numeracy
Grit
Active open-mindedness
Dragonfly-eyed synthesis
optionExplain: Numeracy is comfort with numbers, not openness.
Grit is perseverance, not openness to challenge.
Right: beliefs are hypotheses to test, not treasures to guard.
Dragonfly-eyed synthesis concerns valuing diverse views, close in spirit but a method trait.
questions.explain: Refusing challenge treats a belief as a treasure; the portrait says to treat beliefs as hypotheses.
questions.rule: Beliefs are hypotheses.

questions.q: Which traits belong to the portrait's methods of forecasting, and which to its work ethic?

items.t: Pragmatic
Probabilistic
Grit
Growth mindset
Thoughtful updater

questions.explain: Method traits describe how they forecast; work-ethic traits describe how they keep at it.
questions.rule: Method versus work ethic.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say every superforecaster has every attribute in the composite portrait.
questions.explain: They say not every superforecaster has every attribute; there are many paths and ways to compensate.
questions.rule: A sketch of the typical case.

questions.q: A firm screens candidates against the portrait. What does the authors' sketch leave out entirely?
options: Intelligence, since the sketch has no place for it
Numeracy, since it has to be tested separately later
Other people, since we seldom judge the future alone
Humility, since it varies too widely between people
optionExplain: Intelligence appears in the portrait.
Numeracy appears in the portrait.
Right: the chapter ends noting that other people are missing from the sketch.
Humility appears in the portrait.
questions.explain: The authors say another element is missing entirely: other people, because we are a social species and decide together.
questions.rule: The sketch is of individuals.
questions.teaches: The sketch leaves out other people: we seldom make judgments about the future in isolation, and the next question is what happens when superforecasters work in groups.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: In the 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion, what happened to the exiles who landed in Cuba?
options: They held the beach for weeks, then escaped by sea to the Guatemalan base
They reached the Escambray Mountains and joined other local anti-Castro fighters for months
Cuban troops surrounded them, and within three days all were dead or taken prisoner
They held the coast until American soldiers landed to relieve them
optionExplain: Plausible for a failed landing, but no sea escape is described; the force was wiped out or captured.
This was the contingency plan, but the mountains lay about 80 miles away across swamp and jungle.
Right: the force was overwhelmed within three days.
Secrecy depended on no American soldiers landing, so none came.
questions.explain: About 1,400 men faced 20,000 soldiers and were finished in three days. The card next shows why the authors blame the plan.
questions.rule: Judge a failure by asking what in the plan could have been seen in advance.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: The contingency plan sent the guerrillas to the ____ Mountains, 80 miles from the landing site across swamp and jungle.
questions.explain: The fallback came from the first version of the plan, which landed the men at the foot of the mountains. After the switch, the distance was 80 miles of swamp and jungle.
questions.rule: A backup plan must be rechecked when the main plan changes.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: A bakery moves its depot across town but keeps the old fallback route for breakdowns. Which Bay of Pigs flaw does this repeat?
options: A fallback built for the original site was not rechecked after the site changed
The operation was carried out by staff who had not been properly trained
A secret plan was published in a newspaper and the organisers went ahead with it anyway
Advisers were replaced by outsiders shortly before the key decision was made
optionExplain: Right: like the Escambray fallback, the old route no longer fits the new location.
The authors say the problem was the plan, not execution or training.
That also happened in 1961, but it is a different flaw from the stale fallback.
Kennedy's advisers were mostly the same people in both crises; no replacement is described.
questions.explain: The Bay of Pigs fallback assumed a landing site that had since been changed. The bakery's fallback assumes a depot that has since moved.
questions.rule: When one part of a plan changes, recheck every part that depended on it.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: Suppose the planners had asked how guerrillas would reach the Escambray Mountains from the new landing site. What would they have found?
options: A short open road along the coast, so the fallback would have worked as planned
Mountains beside the new beach, so the fallback needed no change
Soviet soldiers already posted along the route to the mountains
About 80 miles of swamp and jungle, which made the retreat unrealistic
optionExplain: That was true of the first landing site, not the switched one.
The first plan landed the men at the foot of the mountains; the switch ended that.
Soviet troops arrived on the island only after the fiasco.
Right: the distance and terrain made the fallback hopeless.
questions.explain: One simple question about distance and terrain would have exposed the flaw. The authors later imagine exactly such a questioning exchange.
questions.rule: A plain question about the facts can expose a flaw a confident group misses.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the Bay of Pigs failed mainly because the landing force carried out a sound plan badly.
questions.explain: The authors write that the problem was not one of execution but the plan, which was harebrained and full of flaws that should have been spotted.
questions.rule: Blame the plan, not only the execution.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: A city council learns a newspaper has exposed its secret plan. Which reaction repeats what the authors say happened in Washington?
options: Members stop the plan at once and rewrite it from the beginning with outside advice
Members voice concern but decide it matters little, and the plan goes ahead
Members split into two camps and vote the plan down by a narrow margin
Members blame the newspaper and quietly drop the plan the next week
optionExplain: Reconsideration is exactly what did not happen in 1961.
Right: this matches the concern without reconsideration that Schlesinger recalled.
No split vote is described; the group stayed in step.
The plan was not dropped; the invasion went ahead.
questions.explain: Schlesinger recalled that concern arose but the idea took hold around the cabinet table that exposure would not much matter so long as no American soldiers fought.
questions.rule: Exposure prompted concern but no rethink; the planners treated it as harmless.
questions.teaches: After the Times exposure, the planners felt concern but did not reconsider, because the idea took hold that it would not matter if no American soldiers took part in the fighting.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: True or false: After the Bay of Pigs, Kennedy replaced most of his advisers before the Cuban missile crisis.
questions.explain: He did not; the cast of both episodes was mostly the same. The card next shows what changed instead.
questions.rule: Look at how a group works, not only at its members.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: The authors say that groups can be wise, or mad, or ____.
questions.explain: Groups can be wise, mad, or both; what decides it is the group's own way of working.
questions.rule: Groups can be wise, mad, or both.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: A coaching staff wins the league one year and loses badly the next with the same people. Which point from the authors fits best?
options: Results can change with how the group works, even when its members stay the same
Results track individual ability, so some staff members must have lost their skill
A group that wins once has proven chemistry and will keep winning with the same people
Replacing the staff is the only dependable way to bring about a change in results
optionExplain: Right: the Kennedy case shows the same people can do very different work.
The Kennedy cast kept their abilities; the difference came from the process.
The same advisers who failed in 1961 succeeded in 1962, so past success is no guarantee.
Kennedy did not replace his team, and the result still changed.
questions.explain: Kennedy's advisers were mostly unchanged, yet their results swung from fiasco to triumph, so the process is the first place to look.
questions.rule: When results swing with the same members, examine the process.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: Match each title to what the authors say about it.
pairs: Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds
Janis's 1972 study of the Bay of Pigs and the missile crisis
questions.explain: The chapter sets the two crowd titles side by side: one praises collective judgment, the other chronicles collective folly. Janis's book examined both Kennedy episodes.
questions.rule: Crowds can be wise and mad; Janis studied both Kennedy episodes.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: A manager studies why one project team failed. Which approach follows the authors' lesson from the Kennedy cases?
options: Treat the failure as proof that teams make decisions worse than individuals
Treat the last success as proof that this team can be trusted to decide
Weigh the harm and the benefit teams can bring, rather than seeing only one
Look only at who sat on the team and ignore how they worked together
optionExplain: Managers who focus on the negative miss what teams can add.
The same cast did both; one success does not guarantee the next.
Right: the authors say managers need to see both sides of group work.
The Kennedy cases show that who is in the group does not decide the outcome.
questions.explain: The authors say managers tend to focus on either the negative or the positive of working in groups, but need to see both.
questions.rule: Keep both the upside and the downside of teams in view.
questions.teaches: Managers tend to focus on either the harm or the benefit of working in groups, but the authors say they need to see both.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the Kennedy cases show that a group is wiser than any individual in it by default.
questions.explain: The authors conclude that groups can be wise, mad, or both. The same group produced both a fiasco and a triumph.
questions.rule: Groups are not wise by default.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: Which best describes groupthink as the psychologist Irving Janis used the term?
options: A crowd of strangers averaging separate guesses to reach a better estimate
A close-knit group whose shared illusions block critical thinking
A leader forcing a group to accept a plan through rank and threats of dismissal
Members arguing so fiercely that the group can never settle on a decision
optionExplain: That describes the wisdom of crowds, which is a different mechanism.
Right: cohesion and shared illusions are the core of Janis's idea.
Groupthink is unconscious and comes from getting along, not from force.
The opposite danger, rancor and dysfunction, is a different failure.
questions.explain: Janis was describing groups that get along too well. The card next gives the authors' account.
questions.rule: Groupthink is agreement without questioning.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: The authors say groups that get along too well do not question assumptions or confront ____ facts.
questions.explain: Pleasant agreement replaces examination of awkward facts.
questions.rule: Cosy agreement avoids awkward facts.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: A board of close friends approves every proposal in minutes, and nobody asks about costs. Which point from the authors does this show?
options: Separate judgments are being averaged so that individual errors cancel out
Precision questioning is being used to dissect vague claims tactfully
A prediction market is pooling many views into one reliable price
Quick agreement is being treated as proof that each proposal is sound
optionExplain: Averaging needs independent judgments, which this board is not producing.
Nobody is asking questions here, so no questioning is taking place.
No market is involved; this is a single close group.
Right: the board takes its own unanimity as a sign it is right.
questions.explain: The board is pleasantly agreeing and reading the agreement as correctness, which is the pattern Janis described.
questions.rule: Agreement is not evidence of being right.
questions.hint: Which choice has the group questioning nothing?

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: Sort each sign by whether it points to groupthink or to a questioning team.

items.t: Everyone agrees, and the agreement is taken as proof the plan is sound
Assumptions go untested because the group gets along so well
Members raise doubts and the others weigh them
Weak points of a plan are probed before it is approved
The group shares an illusion that nothing can go wrong
Disagreement is welcomed and examined

questions.explain: Groupthink replaces questioning with comfortable agreement, while a questioning team probes assumptions and welcomes dissent.
questions.rule: Ask whether agreement came after questioning or instead of it.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Janis meant something more precise than the vague catchphrase groupthink has become.
questions.explain: Janis described cohesive groups developing shared illusions that interfere with critical thinking. Agreement alone does not qualify.
questions.rule: Groupthink is a mechanism, not agreement alone.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: At a school meeting nobody objects to a schedule change, and the head concludes everyone finds it reasonable. What step of groupthink is this?
options: Members have each submitted separate private judgments that are then averaged together
A devil's advocate has challenged the schedule and been answered fully
Silence is read as agreement, and agreement is read as proof of correctness
The head has asked precise questions to find out what members think
optionExplain: Nobody has been asked for a private judgment here.
No challenger appears in the scene.
Right: the group moves from no objection to everyone agrees to it must be right.
Asking nothing is the point: the head infers views from silence.
questions.explain: The authors describe the Bay of Pigs reasoning this way: nobody objected, which was taken to mean everyone thought the plan reasonable, so it must be.
questions.rule: Absence of objection is not agreement, and agreement is not proof.
questions.teaches: In the Bay of Pigs reasoning, the absence of objection was taken to mean everyone thought the plan reasonable, so it must be.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: After the Bay of Pigs, which change did Kennedy's advisers adopt for the missile crisis?
options: Protocol and hierarchy were set aside so that anyone could question anything
Every adviser was replaced by outside specialists in each relevant field of expertise
Meetings closed once the group agreed, to show unity to the Soviet Union
The president chaired every session and opened with his preferred plan
optionExplain: Right: the advisers were encouraged to question freely.
The cast was mostly the same; outsiders were brought in only occasionally.
Cozy unanimity was the problem the inquiry identified.
The president sometimes left the room, and he kept his lean to himself.
questions.explain: The inquiry blamed cozy unanimity, so the fixes aimed at freer questioning. The card next lists them.
questions.rule: Fix the culture of questioning first.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: Sorensen and Robert Kennedy were assigned the job of intellectual ____, pressing every bone of contention.
questions.explain: The role was to stop errors arising from too superficial an analysis.
questions.rule: Give someone the job of pressing every point.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: A hospital director wants honest debate over a risky merger. Which step follows the Kennedy approach?
options: Hold the vote right away so that no one has time to lobby colleagues
Open each meeting by stating the preferred option, so the group knows where it stands
Name a devil's advocate to press weak points, and set rank aside during discussion
Invite only the heads who agreed in earlier talks to keep the peace
optionExplain: A rushed vote leaves no room for probing.
Stating a preference first narrows the discussion; Kennedy withheld his.
Right: this copies the watchdog and no-hierarchy steps.
Inviting only those who agree recreates cozy unanimity.
questions.explain: Kennedy's team named challengers and relaxed hierarchy so that the weak points were pressed rather than left unspoken.
questions.rule: Assign challengers and soften rank.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: Match each device to how it appeared in Kennedy's missile-crisis process.
pairs: Sorensen and Robert Kennedy pressing every bone of contention
Robert Kennedy asking sharp, sometimes rude questions
Generalists with a license to question
Participants speaking beyond their own area of expertise
questions.explain: Each device attacks cozy unanimity from a different side: a job, a style, a license, and new voices.
questions.rule: Several devices work together against unanimity.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: Why did Kennedy keep to himself his early view that preemptive air strikes might be needed?
options: So the Soviet Union would not learn of the options under review
So the strikes would not become the focus of the discussion
So that his brother could take the lead in presenting the plan
So the committee would end its work quickly and in agreement
optionExplain: Secrecy from Moscow is not the reason given.
Right: the authors say there is less true give-and-take when the president is present.
No such handover is described.
The aim was wider discussion, not a fast consensus.
questions.explain: By the end of the first day the committee had seriously discussed ten alternatives, and the president's own thinking began to change.
questions.rule: A leader's stated view can steer a discussion; withholding it widens the options.
questions.teaches: Kennedy kept his preemptive-strike view private so it would not dominate the talk; by the end of day one the committee had seriously discussed ten alternatives and his thinking began to change.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: A team member is asked to play devil's advocate at the next meeting. What cost does the Kennedy case suggest she may face?
options: She will lose all influence, so the role should be given to the most junior member present
She will make the group less accurate, because arguing divides the team
She will face no cost, because the role is respected and carries no friction
She may become unpopular with some colleagues, though the role still serves the group
optionExplain: The Kennedy case does not tie the role to the junior; Robert Kennedy was the president's brother.
The process improved decisions despite the friction.
The text says Robert Kennedy took on unpopularity.
Right: Robert Kennedy accepted the role at the expense of becoming unpopular.
questions.explain: Robert Kennedy took the role avidly, at the expense of becoming unpopular with some associates.
questions.rule: Challenging roles can cost goodwill.
questions.teaches: Robert Kennedy accepted the watchdog role avidly even at the expense of becoming unpopular with some of his associates.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: In a team, what does cognitive loafing mean?
options: Members disagreeing so sharply that they cannot work together on anything at all
Members repeating each other's research to make sure it is correct
Members copying the leader's view in order to be seen as loyal
Members easing off the hard work because others will do the heavy lifting
optionExplain: That is rancor, a different danger.
Duplicating work is the opposite of loafing.
That is deference, a different problem.
Right: loafing means leaving the effort to others.
questions.explain: Loafing is about effort, not conflict. The card next sets it beside groupthink.
questions.rule: Loafing is effort left to others.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: The authors worried that cognitive loafing and ____ could reinforce each other in a team.
questions.explain: Loafing lets members skip the work, and groupthink lets them take agreement as a finished job.
questions.rule: The two risks feed each other.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: In a study group, three students stop reading the papers because a fourth summarises them each week. Which risk is this?
options: Cognitive loafing, since others will do the heavy lifting
Groupthink, since shared illusions block critical thinking
Collective folly, since a dominant voice sets every view
Precision questioning, since vague claims are being dissected
optionExplain: Right: the three have stopped making their own effort.
Groupthink concerns shared illusions among those who do engage.
A single dominant voice is a different mechanism, discussed later.
No one is questioning anything here.
questions.explain: The students let the fourth carry the load, so effort is being withheld.
questions.rule: Notice who is no longer doing the work.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: A team already skips the hard work, then members quickly agree. What do the authors expect?
options: The agreement will correct the loafing, since all views now match and nothing is left unchecked
The loafing will fade, because agreeing takes effort from every member
The tendencies reinforce each other, so agreement seems to show the work is done
The two will cancel, leaving the team no worse than before
optionExplain: Agreement does not repair missing effort.
Agreement is easy and takes less effort, not more.
Right: the two feed each other.
The authors describe reinforcement, not cancellation.
questions.explain: Unchecked agreement lets members feel done while little real work has happened.
questions.rule: Quick agreement can hide missing effort.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if a group's agreement is ill-founded, the group slips into self-righteous complacency.
questions.explain: Unanimity is a powerful force; when it is not backed by good reasons, the group becomes complacent rather than correct.
questions.rule: Agreement is not proof.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: Which thought best captures how loafing and groupthink feed each other in a committee?
options: We disagree, so each of us must check everything
We all agree, so there is nothing left to check
The chair has decided, so there is nothing to discuss
We have the data, so the numbers can decide for us
optionExplain: That would drive more work, not less.
Right: agreement is treated as completion of the task.
Deference to the chair is a different dynamic.
Letting data decide is not loafing or groupthink.
questions.explain: The authors give the reasoning in the chapter: if we all agree, our work is done.
questions.rule: The thought we all agree, so we are done turns agreement into an excuse to stop.
questions.teaches: In the authors' account, the two tendencies meet in the thought that everyone agrees, so the work is done.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: True or false: Averaging many people's judgments works best when each person forms a judgment before hearing the others.
questions.explain: Separate judgments keep errors random, so they cancel in the average. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Separate judgments, then combine.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: Aggregation can only do its magic when people form judgments ____, so that errors are more or less random.
questions.explain: Independence makes errors random, and random errors cancel in an average.
questions.rule: Independence lets errors cancel.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: Ten coworkers estimate a project cost in a shared chat where the boss posts first. Which effect threatens the average?
options: Ten separate estimates average out the errors, so accuracy rises sharply whatever the boss posts first
Later estimates drift toward the boss's, so errors stop being random and cancel less
Precision questions reveal the thinking behind each estimate before it posts
Members avoid cognitive loafing because the boss has posted a number to check
optionExplain: That describes independent estimates, not a chat anchored on the boss.
Right: anchoring on one voice removes independence.
Nothing in the scene is questioning the estimates.
A boss's number does not change whether the others' errors are independent.
questions.explain: Once members follow one voice, their errors become the same error, and an average cannot cancel a shared mistake.
questions.rule: Anchoring on one voice turns many guesses into one.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: True or false: Ten coworkers who write private estimates before discussing are more likely to have random errors that cancel in the average.
questions.explain: Private first judgments keep errors independent, which is the condition under which aggregation works.
questions.rule: Collect judgments before discussion begins.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: What do the authors say American home buyers in 2005 talked themselves into believing?
options: That mortgage debt would be forgiven by the government
That tulip bulbs were a safer investment than houses
That prices would stay flat for a full decade to come
That real estate prices could only go up
optionExplain: No such belief is described.
Tulip bulbs belong to the seventeenth-century Dutch example, not to 2005.
The belief was in constant rises, not stagnation.
Right: the authors give this as an example of collective folly.
questions.explain: The authors pair that belief with Dutch investors in the seventeenth century, who became convinced a tulip bulb was worth more than a laborer's annual salary.
questions.rule: When a group talks itself into one belief, errors pile up.
questions.teaches: Collective folly includes Dutch investors in the seventeenth century, who believed a tulip bulb was worth more than a laborer's annual salary, and American home buyers in 2005, who believed real estate prices could only go up.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: Which panel member poses the independence problem the authors describe?
options: A member who asks precise questions about vague claims
A member who thanks colleagues for constructive criticism
A member whose credentials lead others to fall into line
A member who shares sources and invites push-back openly
optionExplain: Precise questions help others reason; they do not replace their judgment.
Thanking critics encourages independent views.
Right: deference to credentials replaces separate judgment.
Inviting push-back protects independence.
questions.explain: The authors list a loudmouth, a bully, a superficially impressive talker, and someone with credentials that cow others into line.
questions.rule: Watch for voices that get others to give up their own judgment.
questions.teaches: The authors name the figures who can erode independence: a loudmouth who dominates, a bully, a superficially impressive talker, and someone whose credentials cow others into line.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: How were forecasters assigned to work alone or in teams in year 1?
options: The top performers from earlier seasons chose their own teammates
Volunteers who wanted teamwork were placed together in groups
At random, with several hundred in each condition
Organisers matched people by profession to build balanced teams
optionExplain: Year 1 began before any superforecaster had been identified.
Self-selection would bias the comparison.
Right: random assignment lets the groups be compared fairly.
No matching by profession is described.
questions.explain: Random assignment is what lets the comparison say something about teams. The card next gives the setup.
questions.rule: Randomise, then compare.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: The authors took the advice of Archie ____ and ran an experiment on teams.
questions.explain: With both outcomes plausible, they chose to test rather than guess.
questions.rule: When you do not know, test.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: A firm cannot tell whether open-plan seating raises output. Which step follows the authors' approach?
options: Randomly assign staff to two layouts and compare their results
Ask managers which layout they believe works better and adopt it
Move the whole firm to open plan and compare with last year
Let each employee choose a layout and compare the two groups
optionExplain: Right: random assignment tests the question directly.
Opinion is the guess the authors chose not to rely on.
A before-and-after comparison mixes in every other change.
Self-chosen groups differ in ways other than the layout.
questions.explain: The authors faced two plausible stories and no evidence, so they let random assignment decide.
questions.rule: Where stories conflict, run a comparison.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: Sort each point by whether it is an argument for teams or against them.

items.t: Members can share information and perspectives
Aggregation of different judgments is critical to accuracy
Members may let others do the heavy lifting
Friendly forecasters may fall into groupthink
Unanimity can breed self-righteous complacency
A group that keeps questioning can be more than the sum of its parts

questions.explain: The authors found strong arguments on both sides, which is why they ran an experiment.
questions.rule: List both sides before testing.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: Besides curiosity, why did the authors build teams into the research?
options: Teams were cheaper to score than individual forecasters
Important real-world forecasts are seldom made without discussing them with others
The sponsor had required teams as part of the tournament rules
Earlier research on university committees had already shown that teams were more accurate
optionExplain: Cost is not the stated reason.
Right: understanding forecasting in the real world meant understanding it in groups.
No such rule is described.
The authors say they did not know the answer.
questions.explain: Realism and curiosity were the two reasons given.
questions.rule: Study the setting as people really work.
questions.teaches: Besides curiosity, the authors wanted to understand real-world forecasting, where people seldom make important forecasts without discussing them with others.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: A school tests teacher teams but wants individual accountability. Which feature of the authors' setup should it copy?
options: Score only the team as a whole and discard every individual member's result
Score only the team leader and credit the team with it
Score each person separately and never report a team score
Score each person individually and pool the scores into a team score
optionExplain: The authors kept individual scores.
Teams were not scored on a leader alone.
A team score was created by pooling.
Right: individuals were scored, and scores were pooled for the team.
questions.explain: Forecasters could see how both they and their team were doing.
questions.rule: Keep individual and team scores both visible.
questions.teaches: Team members were still scored as individuals, with individual scores pooled into a team score, and forecasters could see both their own result and their team's.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: True or false: The authors told teams not to take their own agreement, in itself, as proof that they are right.
questions.explain: That was one of the primer's warnings. The card next gives the full primer.
questions.rule: Agreement is not proof.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: The authors urged teams to practice constructive ____, a phrase from Intel's Andy Grove.
questions.explain: The aim is confrontation of ideas that stays constructive.
questions.rule: Confront ideas, not people.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: You doubt a teammate's forecast. Which reply fits the primer?
options: Stay quiet, because the rest of the team has already agreed with it and doubts would slow things down
Say you disagree and ask what evidence supports it, without criticising the person
Say the forecast is silly and move on to a prediction of your own
Accept it, since agreement itself is a sign the forecast is right
optionExplain: That is deference, which the primer warns against.
Right: this is cooperative but not deferential.
A personal shot adds heat, not light.
The primer says agreement alone is not proof.
questions.explain: The primer asks for challenge without hostility: the claim is questioned, the person is respected.
questions.rule: Challenge the claim, respect the person.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: Sort each behaviour by the danger it belongs to.

items.t: Everyone defers to avoid friction
Agreement is taken as proof of being right
Disagreement turns into personal attacks
Members stop cooperating after an argument
Doubts are never raised at all
Criticism targets the person, not the claim

questions.explain: The primer warned of two opposite failures: too much agreement, and too much hostility.
questions.rule: Two opposite dangers need two opposite cautions.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: How does the primer describe the place of pointed questions in a team?
options: As essential to a team as vitamins are to a human body
As a last resort for teams whose trust has broken down
As a courtesy to leaders who need to feel in control
As a risk to be limited, since they can slow a team down
optionExplain: Right: the authors call pointed questions as essential as vitamins.
They are routine nourishment, not a last resort.
They are not described as a courtesy.
The primer wants more of them, not fewer.
questions.explain: Questions supply what a team needs to stay healthy.
questions.rule: Pointed questions keep a team healthy.
questions.teaches: The primer likens pointed questions to the vitamins a human body needs.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: A manager wants a team that neither agrees on everything nor fights. Which primer instruction should she copy?
options: Avoid raising doubts once a majority has agreed on the answer
Make sure every decision is unanimous before the team moves on
Let the loudest member settle each dispute to prevent a long clash
Disagree without being disagreeable, and never stop doubting
optionExplain: That is deference to majority, the groupthink risk.
Unanimity is what the primer says not to trust.
Letting one voice settle it undermines independence.
Right: this holds both cautions together.
questions.explain: Both ends are covered: keep doubting, and keep the doubting civil.
questions.rule: Hold both cautions at once.
questions.teaches: The primer says consensus is not always good and disagreement is not always bad, so neither should be judged on its face.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: A teammate says soccer's popularity is declining and you doubt it. Which reply do the authors favor?
options: That is a silly thing to say about a game that millions of people love around the world
What evidence shows its popularity is declining, and over what time frame?
I don't think so; I really believe the opposite is true today
What do you mean by that? I am not sure I follow your claim
optionExplain: A personal shot adds heat, not light.
Right: it zeroes in on evidence and time frame.
It states disagreement without saying why.
It lowers the temperature but is too vague to probe.
questions.explain: The right reply asks for evidence and a time frame. The card next sets out the full approach.
questions.rule: Ask something that can be answered with facts.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: Precision questions reveal the ____ behind a conclusion so that it can be probed and tested.
questions.explain: They open up the reasoning rather than decide the matter.
questions.rule: Questions expose reasoning.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: A colleague says customers are unhappy lately. Which reply is a precision question?
options: You always exaggerate customer problems, don't you, every single time?
I don't think so, our customers seem fine to me
What do you mean? I'm not sure I understand you
Which customers, unhappy about what, and since when?
optionExplain: A personal shot adds heat.
A bare disagreement does not say why.
A vague query does not target the claim.
Right: it targets who, what and when.
questions.explain: Who, what and when are the loose terms in the claim, and each can be answered with facts.
questions.rule: Target the loose term.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: Match each reply to the soccer-decline claim to what the authors say about it.
pairs: A personal shot that adds heat, not light
Lowers the temperature but is too vague
What evidence shows the decline, and over what time frame?
Zeroes in and reveals the thinking
questions.explain: Only the last reply gives the other person something specific to answer.
questions.rule: Specific beats vague, hostile or empty.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: According to the authors, when is precision questioning most often missing?
options: When the team has not met face to face
When the topic is unfamiliar to the speaker
When it is needed most
When the group has a leader who forbids it
optionExplain: Meeting face to face is not the factor named.
Unfamiliarity is not the cause given.
Right: despite a long history, it is often not used when needed most.
No leader ban is described.
questions.explain: The practice goes back to Socrates, yet the authors say it is often not used at the moment it matters most.
questions.rule: Good practice is easy to forget under pressure.
questions.teaches: Good teachers have practised precision questioning since Socrates, but it is often not used when it is needed most.

questions.section: To Team or Not to Team?
questions.q: An engineer says the bridge is unsafe. After you ask precise questions, what do the authors say you gain?
options: A view of the thinking behind the claim, even if the answers do not settle it
A final ruling on whether the bridge is safe, which settles the dispute for good
A way of showing the engineer is wrong without argument
A shorter meeting, because the claim is dropped
optionExplain: Right: the answers expose the reasoning so it can be tested.
The authors say the answers will not settle the matter.
Questions are not a trick to win.
No time saving is claimed.
questions.explain: The authors note that the answers will not settle the matter but will reveal the thinking behind the conclusion.
questions.rule: Questions expose; testing decides.
questions.teaches: Precise questions will not settle the matter, but they reveal the thinking behind the conclusion so it can be probed and tested.

questions.q: By how much were teams more accurate than individuals, on average, at the end of year 1?
options: About 23%
About 5%
About 50%
About 75%
optionExplain: Right: the authors report 23%.
Too small; teams did better than this.
50% is a later figure, for superforecasters moving onto superteams.
Far above what was found.
questions.explain: Teams beat individuals by 23% in year 1. The card next explains the risk that came with it.
questions.rule: Year 1: teams were 23% more accurate.

questions.q: In business circles, the hubris that afflicts highly accomplished people is called ____ disease.
questions.explain: The authors use CEO disease for success undermining the habits that produced it.
questions.rule: Success can erode its own causes.

questions.q: A star surgeon joins a team of equal stars and starts assuming her judgment is right because it is hers. Which risk is this?
options: Cognitive loafing, as others will do the heavy lifting of the surgical work
Hubris from acclaim, which can undermine the habits that earned it
A shortage of diversity among the specialists
Rancor from members who disagree too sharply
optionExplain: She is not leaving work to others.
Right: this is the CEO disease the authors worry about.
Diversity is a separate issue the chapter raises later.
Nobody is arguing in the scene.
questions.explain: The surgeon trusts her judgment because it is hers, which is the hubris the authors feared.
questions.rule: Praise can replace the habits that earned it.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, being told they are exceptional and grouped with other stars leaves superforecasters' habits of mind unaffected.
questions.explain: The authors say success can bring acclaim that undermines the habits of mind that produced it; that risk is why they worried.
questions.rule: Success can undo itself.

questions.q: What did the authors say was a plus of superteams not meeting face to face?
options: Members could rely on tone of voice and body language to settle each disagreement quickly
Members worked harder to avoid being seen as loafing in person
Members felt closer from the first week without any extra effort
Distance could make it easier to manage disputes and keep a critical perspective
optionExplain: Online teams do not hear tone of voice.
Being seen in person is not the point.
The text says teams had to work to build closeness.
Right: the authors list this as the plus of distance.
questions.explain: Distance can make disputes easier to manage and a critical perspective easier to keep.
questions.rule: Distance cuts both ways.
questions.teaches: Because the teams did not meet face to face, distance could make disputes easier to manage and a critical perspective easier to keep.

questions.q: An online expert group whose members have not met in person starts trading insults. Which minus of distance does this show?
options: The group cannot gather any information, because it works only online
Online discussion can degenerate into poisonous harangues
Members rely on tone of voice that cannot be heard
Members lack a primer on teamwork
optionExplain: Information can be shared online.
Right: the authors name this as a risk of distance.
Tone of voice is not mentioned.
A primer is a remedy, not the cause.
questions.explain: Strangers who never meet are easier to disregard, and online talk can turn into harangues.
questions.rule: Distance can foster conflict as well as calm.
questions.teaches: On the minus side, it is easier to disregard people we have never met, and distance could even foster conflict, as online discussion can degenerate into poisonous harangues.

questions.q: True or false: Some superforecasters in new teams held back from criticising teammates, fearing offence or feeling intimidated.
questions.explain: Some held back, intimidated by credentials or fearful of causing offence. The card next tells how it eased.
questions.rule: Even experts hold back among strangers.

questions.q: Rosenthal described teammates circling a disagreement without saying it directly as dancing ____.
questions.explain: They were afraid of giving offense, so they used careful words.
questions.rule: Politeness can hide disagreement.

questions.q: New volunteers on a charity board hide their doubts behind soft hints. Which step used by superteams applies?
options: Say openly that push-back is welcome, and thank people for constructive criticism
Appoint the most senior volunteer to decide each issue quickly
Ask all members to vote right away without any discussion of their reasons for it
Remove sensitive subjects from the agenda to keep the peace
optionExplain: Right: the superteams made criticism welcome and rewarded it.
Deference to rank deepens the problem.
Without reasons, nothing is probed.
Avoiding sensitive subjects is the taboo effect.
questions.explain: Explicit invitations and thanks made it safe to speak plainly.
questions.rule: Invite and reward push-back.

questions.q: True or false: In Rosenthal's account, once members thanked one another for constructive criticism, the dancing around gradually diminished.
questions.explain: Explicit invitations and thanks made it safe to speak plainly, and the circling faded.
questions.rule: Reward critics and the circling fades.

questions.q: What did Rosenthal say team members told one another to assure others that criticism was welcome?
options: That they would never take criticism personally, however sharply it was put
That they preferred written comments to spoken ones
That they wanted push-back if a teammate saw something they had missed
That they expected agreement unless proven wrong
optionExplain: No such promise is quoted.
No preference for written comments is described.
Right: this is his account.
Agreement was not the aim.
questions.explain: Everybody said they wanted push-back if a teammate saw something they did not.
questions.rule: Ask for push-back in so many words.
questions.teaches: Team members explicitly told one another they wanted push-back if a teammate saw something they had missed.

questions.q: A polite question is taken as hostile by a teammate. Which point from Elaine Rich's account explains this?
options: Anonymous questions are always safer than questions with a name
People take things differently, so a helpful inquiry can seem an aggressive criticism
Experts do not mind being questioned by strangers who have no relevant credentials of their own
Questions about easy topics cause the most conflict
optionExplain: Nothing says anonymity is always safer.
Right: she said the same question can land very differently.
She herself was intimidated.
The charged topics were passionate ones.
questions.explain: She found it difficult to question strangers: what one person sees as helpful inquiry another may take as aggressive criticism.
questions.rule: The same words can be received differently.
questions.teaches: Elaine Rich noted that what one person considers a helpful inquiry another may take as aggressive criticism.

questions.q: In a premortem, what is the team asked to do?
options: Rank the members' forecasts and drop the weakest one
Meet after the failure to assign blame to the right person
Assume a course of action has failed and explain why
Vote on the plan and record each member's reasons
optionExplain: Ranking forecasts is not what a premortem does.
Looking back to assign blame happens after a failure; a premortem looks ahead.
Right: the failure is imagined in advance.
A vote does not ask for imagined failure.
questions.explain: The team starts from the supposition that the plan failed. The card next gives the authors' account.
questions.rule: Imagine the failure, then explain it.

questions.q: The usual team fixes include bringing in outsiders, suspending ____, and keeping the leader's views under wraps.
questions.explain: These are the steps Kennedy's team took after the Bay of Pigs.
questions.rule: Soften rank to hear dissent.

questions.q: A project lead fears staff will not criticise her launch plan. Which premortem step fits?
options: Tell the team to imagine the launch has failed and ask them to explain why
Ask each person to send her a short note supporting the plan
Hold a review a month after launch to find who made errors
Present the plan again more slowly and in more detail so that doubts are easier to see
optionExplain: Right: this is the premortem as described.
Supportive notes invite agreement, not doubt.
A review after launch looks back; a premortem looks ahead.
Repeating a plan does not give staff a safe route to doubt.
questions.explain: The exercise lets people voice doubts as part of the task rather than as an attack on the lead.
questions.rule: Make doubt part of the assignment.

questions.q: Which are among the usual solutions the authors list for team problems?
options: Bring in outsiders
Suspend hierarchy
Keep the leader's views under wraps
Give the leader a veto over every dissent
Require every decision to be unanimous
optionExplain: Right: fresh perspectives are on the list.
Right: rank can inhibit candid talk.
Right: the leader's view can steer discussion.
A leader's veto over dissent would silence challenge; it is not among the remedies.
Unanimity is what the authors warn against trusting.
questions.explain: The three standard remedies each reduce the pull of rank and of the leader's own opinion.
questions.rule: Three standard remedies work on rank and the leader's opinion.

questions.q: Why does a premortem help doubts to come out?
options: Members gain a vote that can overrule the leader on any plan they doubt
Members feel safe voicing doubts about the leader's plan
Members are rewarded with shares in the outcome
Members can avoid explaining their own forecasts
optionExplain: No vote is described.
Right: assuming failure frees members to say what worries them.
No reward is described.
The exercise asks for explanation, not exemption.
questions.explain: Because the failure is assumed, a doubt becomes part of the exercise rather than an attack on the leader.
questions.rule: Assumed failure makes doubt safe.
questions.teaches: A premortem makes team members feel safe to express the doubts they may have about the leader's plan.

questions.q: A leaderless volunteer network wants candid debate. Which usual fix has nothing to work on?
options: Imagining that a plan has failed and then explaining why it failed in detail
Bringing in outsiders to offer fresh views
Asking members to challenge claims with precise questions
Keeping the leader's views under wraps, since there is no leader
optionExplain: A premortem works without a leader.
Outsiders can join any group.
Precise questions need no leader.
Right: with no leader, nothing can be withheld.
questions.explain: Superteams began with no leaders and no norms, so remedies that adjust leaders and norms had little to adjust.
questions.rule: Fit the fix to the structure the team has.
questions.teaches: The superteams did not start with leaders and norms, which created other challenges than the ones the usual solutions address.

questions.q: Marty Rosenthal wanted to fill gaps in his team without seeming to take over. What did he mostly do?
options: He led by example, explaining his own forecasts in more detail
He assigned each teammate a task and set weekly deadlines
He asked the researchers to appoint a team leader for the group
He stayed silent so that the others would fill the gaps
optionExplain: Right: he modelled the behaviour he wanted.
Giving orders among strangers can backfire.
No request to the researchers is described.
Silence would not improve the discussions.
questions.explain: He chose example over instruction. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Model what you want.

questions.q: Rosenthal described his way of shaping the team as leading from ____.
questions.explain: He led by example rather than by instruction.
questions.rule: Lead by example.

questions.q: In a new online hobby group nobody leads and posts are thin. Which move follows Rosenthal's approach?
options: Announce rules for posting and assign roles to each member of the group
Post your own reasoning in detail and invite comments on it
Wait until a moderator is appointed by the site owners
Ask members to vote on who should be the group's leader
optionExplain: Announcing rules is the taking over he avoided.
Right: this models the behaviour wanted.
Waiting leaves the gap unfilled.
A leadership vote among strangers is the stepping forward he feared.
questions.explain: Explaining his own work in detail showed others what a useful post looks like and invited reply.
questions.rule: Show what good looks like.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, giving directions as a stranger is the safest way to start a leaderless team.
questions.explain: The authors say that among strangers this can backfire; Rosenthal led by example instead.
questions.rule: Directions from a stranger can backfire.

questions.q: What did Rosenthal organise to settle who did what in his team?
options: A written vote by e-mail on the preferred division of labour among all members
A meeting at the university where each member gave a talk
A rota in which the most active member decided each week
A conference call to hash out workloads, with the details handled by him
optionExplain: No e-mail vote is described.
The face-to-face meetings were at conferences, for another purpose.
No rota is described.
Right: the call plus his handling of details.
questions.explain: Most of the team signed up for the call's plan.
questions.rule: Offer to carry the details.
questions.teaches: Rosenthal organised a conference call to hash out workloads, handling the details himself, and most of the team signed up.

questions.q: A coordinator explains her own work and runs a call that settles workloads. What might she expect, going by Rosenthal's account?
options: Resistance because she has taken over
Stronger commitment to the team from members
Fewer questions about each member's forecasts
A rapid end to disagreement among the group
optionExplain: The feedback was that people loved it.
Right: the feedback was warm and commitment grew.
He wanted more explaining, not less.
Disagreement was still wanted.
questions.explain: Rosenthal reported that people loved the call and felt a little stronger commitment to the team.
questions.rule: Shared planning builds commitment.
questions.teaches: After the call, the feedback was that people loved it, and Rosenthal thought they felt a little stronger commitment to the team.

questions.q: What was the unofficial goal of the Wharton and Berkeley conferences?
options: To pick out next year's best forecasters for prizes
To add a human dimension to the teams
To train forecasters in a new scoring method
To announce which team had won the tournament
optionExplain: No prize selection is described.
Right: the authors call it the unofficial goal.
The researchers presented data, not training.
No such announcement is described.
questions.explain: The official goal was sharing knowledge. The card next describes the human side.
questions.rule: Meeting adds a human dimension.

questions.q: The official goal of the conferences was to share ____, with researchers presenting data and superforecasters offering their views.
questions.explain: The sharing of knowledge was the stated reason; the human dimension was the unofficial one.
questions.rule: Official and unofficial goals can differ.

questions.q: A remote team lead has funds for one gathering. Which choice follows the authors' account?
options: A cancelled gathering, since in-person contact weakens critical thinking
A training day that bars social time to keep the focus on work
A social gathering for teammates, since contact may help them push back
A gathering open only to the team's leader and its top scorers
optionExplain: The authors do not say contact weakens critique.
Rosenthal's social event helped, in his view.
Right: Rosenthal's barbecue is an example.
Excluding most of the team does not build belonging.
questions.explain: A modest personal touch made push-back easier, in Rosenthal's view.
questions.rule: A little social contact can help a remote team.

questions.q: True or false: Rosenthal thinks his modest efforts, such as the barbecue, made no difference to his team's willingness to push back.
questions.explain: He thinks they did make a difference: they helped the team push back on each other and feel committed to share information.
questions.rule: Closeness can make challenge easier.

questions.q: What worry did Elaine Rich express as her sense of responsibility grew?
options: Being outvoted by teammates with stronger credentials whenever the team took a vote
Being asked to lead the team before she was ready
Being blamed for the team's forecasts when they failed
Being a freeloader who reads others' posts without sharing her own research
optionExplain: Her worry was about contributing, not voting.
No leadership request is described.
Blame is not mentioned.
Right: she felt she had to shoulder her part of the burden.
questions.explain: She called not offering thoughts and research a temptation she had to resist.
questions.rule: Belonging makes you feel obliged to contribute.
questions.teaches: As her sense of belonging grew, Elaine Rich felt she had to share her part of the burden rather than freeload by reading what others wrote.

questions.q: A newcomer does well in a group and her confidence rises. What does Elaine Rich's account suggest happens next?
options: She becomes less likely to share her own research with the rest of the group
Her sense of responsibility to the group grows with her confidence
She leaves the group to work alone on harder questions
She stops questioning the views of teammates she knows
optionExplain: She felt more duty to share, not less.
Right: confidence and responsibility rose together.
She found the team more stimulating than working alone.
Questioning became easier.
questions.explain: She did well, which boosted her confidence, and her sense of responsibility grew with it.
questions.rule: Success can deepen commitment as well as pride.
questions.teaches: Elaine Rich did well, which boosted her confidence, and her sense of responsibility grew with it.

questions.q: True or false: On the best teams, effort rose as commitment grew, even though the workload was divided.
questions.explain: The authors found this on the best teams, the opposite of what a division of labor suggests. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Shared work can raise effort.

questions.q: Most teams have a nucleus of five or ____ members who do most of the work.
questions.explain: A small core carries most of the effort.
questions.rule: A small core does most of the work.

questions.q: A volunteer group splits its tasks, and members start spending more hours as they feel committed. Which pattern is this?
options: Cognitive loafing, as members take it easy
Effort rising with commitment even though the work is divided
Groupthink, as members share illusions
Division of labor reducing everyone's effort, as the workload is split among members
optionExplain: Loafing would show falling effort.
Right: this matches the best superteams.
Nothing here shows shared illusions.
That is the expected result, which did not occur.
questions.explain: The authors saw workloads divided and effort grow as commitment grew.
questions.rule: Commitment can outweigh the saving from dividing work.

questions.q: A member treats forecasting as work, not play, on a team that divides the work. What would the authors expect?
options: Less effort needed from each person, as division of labor would suggest
More effort, because every task becomes more interesting once it is shared out
No change, because effort is fixed by ability
Conflict, because division of work leads to rancor
optionExplain: Right: the expected drop applies when forecasting is seen as work.
Interest in the task is the play attitude.
The authors describe effort as responsive to commitment.
No link to rancor is described.
questions.explain: The authors note the expected reduction applies at least if the person approaches forecasting as work, not play.
questions.rule: Attitude shapes whether shared work reduces effort.

questions.q: True or false: Elaine Rich said teammates could support each other, help each other or build on ideas, and called it a rush.
questions.explain: She said the team work was tons more work but that sharing it felt like a rush, not a burden.
questions.rule: Work can feel like play when shared.
questions.teaches: Elaine Rich said that on the team you could be supporting each other, helping each other or building on ideas, and called it a rush.

questions.q: A newcomer asks why team work was more stimulating than solo work. Which reasons did Elaine Rich give?
options: The team had a leader who set clear rules for everyone to follow from the start
The prizes for team winners were larger than for individuals
The work was lighter once tasks were shared among five or six
You can support each other, help each other and build on ideas
optionExplain: The superteams began without leaders.
No prize difference is described.
She said the work was tons more, not lighter.
Right: she cited mutual support and building on ideas.
questions.explain: She said it was a rush to support and help each other and build on ideas.
questions.rule: Building together is rewarding.
questions.teaches: Elaine Rich said teammates could support each other, help each other, and build on ideas, and called it a rush.

questions.q: On the Honduras election question, how did Paul Theron respond to polls giving Castro a slight lead?
options: He ignored the polls and relied on his knowledge of investment markets
He consulted a specialist and an obscure analysis, then favoured Hernández
He followed the polls and left the research to his teammates, as most members did
He asked his team to vote on which candidate to prefer
optionExplain: He did research rather than ignore the polls.
Right: he dug further and changed his forecast.
He did the research himself and shared it.
No team vote is described.
questions.explain: The expert said the polls were dodgy. The card next gives the account.
questions.rule: Dig before you settle.

questions.q: A political scientist told Theron that, although polls showed Castro ahead, the polls were ____.
questions.explain: The expert doubted the quality of the polls.
questions.rule: Check the quality of the polls.

questions.q: A team member finds a rare expert source on a question. Which behaviour does the Honduras account illustrate?
options: Sharing everything learned with teammates so all benefit
Keeping the source private to protect an edge in the scores
Waiting until the team has voted on whether the source is worth sharing
Posting only the final forecast, not the reasoning behind it
optionExplain: Right: Theron shared everything he learned.
Theron shared, so teammates benefited.
No vote is described.
Teams benefited from reasoning, not conclusions alone.
questions.explain: Theron's effort paid off for him and for the others.
questions.rule: Share what you find.

questions.q: True or false: Theron shared everything he learned with his teammates, who benefited too.
questions.explain: Sharing is how one member's effort became the team's gain.
questions.rule: Sharing is how one member's work becomes the team's.

questions.q: What reason did Theron give for why a team gathers information better than one person?
options: A team can outvote the individual researchers who disagree with the majority and so settle disputes
A team avoids the cost of paying for each source it needs
A team makes each member more confident in their own forecast
Each member brings something different, so no individual could cover as much ground
optionExplain: He did not mention voting.
Cost is not his point.
His point is coverage, not confidence.
Right: he said even unlimited hours would be less fruitful given different research styles.
questions.explain: Theron said no individual could cover as much ground as a good team, even with unlimited hours, given different research styles.
questions.rule: Different styles cover more ground.
questions.teaches: Theron said no individual could cover as much ground as a good team, even with unlimited hours, because each member brings a different research style.

questions.q: A forecaster changes her forecast after a specialist calls the polls dodgy. How should the effort be judged, per the Honduras account?
options: By how long she spent contacting specialists and reading their published analyses
By whether her teammates agreed with her new forecast
By whether the changed forecast proves more accurate, as when Hernández won
By how prominent the specialist is in the field
optionExplain: Time spent does not show accuracy.
