Teammate agreement does not show accuracy.
Right: Theron's effort paid off because Hernández won.
Prominence does not show accuracy.
questions.explain: Hernández won, so Theron's considerable effort paid off.
questions.rule: Judge effort by results.
questions.teaches: Hernández won the election, so Theron's change of forecast and his considerable effort paid off.

questions.q: True or false: According to Theron, one individual with unlimited hours could match the ground a good team covers.
questions.explain: Theron said even with unlimited hours an individual would be less fruitful, given different research styles.
questions.rule: Teams cover more ground.

questions.q: On average, how much more accurate did year-1 superforecasters become after joining superteams in year 2?
options: About 50%
About 10%
About 23%
About 100%
optionExplain: Right: the authors report 50%.
Too low.
23% was the gain of year-1 teams over individuals.
Far above what was found.
questions.explain: Superteams brought a 50% gain. The card next separates it from the 23% figure.
questions.rule: 50%: superforecasters on superteams.

questions.q: A superforecaster placed on a superteam in year 2 became, on average, 50% more ____.
questions.explain: The measure is accuracy.
questions.rule: The gain is in accuracy.

questions.q: A top performer joins an elite team the next year. What does the authors' result lead you to expect?
options: No change at all, since top performers have little room left to improve
On average a large gain in accuracy, roughly half again
A drop, since elite teams breed hubris
A small gain of about a tenth
optionExplain: The result was a gain.
Right: the average gain was about 50%.
Hubris was feared but did not defeat the gain.
The gain was much larger than a tenth.
questions.explain: On average, superforecasters became 50% more accurate on superteams.
questions.rule: Elite teams helped elite individuals.

questions.q: True or false: The 23% figure and the 50% figure describe the same comparison.
questions.explain: The 23% figure compares year-1 teams with individuals. The 50% figure compares superforecasters on superteams in year 2 with their own earlier accuracy.
questions.rule: Keep the two comparisons apart.

questions.q: What did an analysis in year 3 show about superteams?
options: A smaller gain of about 10%
No gain, since the first result was chance
The same 50% result
A gain that applied only to the best teams
optionExplain: It matched the year-2 result.
It confirmed, not overturned.
Right: year 3 repeated the finding.
No such split is reported.
questions.explain: An analysis in year 3 got the same result.
questions.rule: The result held in a second year.
questions.teaches: An analysis in year 3 got the same result of about 50% greater accuracy.

questions.q: A startup argues remote teams of strangers cannot work well. How does the superteam result bear on this?
options: It proves remote teams of strangers always beat teams that meet in person and know each other
It shows strangers cannot work together online without a leader to direct the work
It shows online teams do well only on easy questions where the answer is not in doubt
Online superteams of strangers improved markedly, which the authors found startling
optionExplain: The authors do not compare with in-person teams.
The superteams had no leaders at the start.
No such limit to easy questions is described.
Right: the authors found the result startling given the loose connection.
questions.explain: Given that these were strangers tenuously connected in cyberspace, the authors found the result startling.
questions.rule: Loose online ties can still yield strong teams.
questions.teaches: The authors found the 50% result startling because the teams were collections of strangers tenuously connected in cyberspace.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the 50% gain was found only in year 2 and not repeated.
questions.explain: An analysis in year 3 got the same result.
questions.rule: The finding was repeated.

questions.q: A contract pays $1 if an event occurs and trades at 40 cents. What probability does the price suggest, in theory?
options: Roughly 40%
Roughly 4%
Roughly 60%
Roughly 100%
optionExplain: Right: the price tracks the market's estimate of the probability.
Too low by a factor of ten.
60% would imply a price of 60 cents.
100% would imply a price of a dollar.
questions.explain: A 40-cent price on a $1 contract suggests about 40%. The card next gives the logic.
questions.rule: Price approximates probability.

questions.q: A prediction-market contract pays nothing if the outcome does not occur and ____ if it does.
questions.explain: The $1 payout is what links price to probability.
questions.rule: The payout is $1 or nothing.

questions.q: A contract on a local election trades at 30 cents. You believe the chance is 55%. What does the authors' logic suggest?
options: Sell, since the price shows that the event is unlikely
Buy, since the price is below your estimate; your buying pushes the price up
Wait, since the price cannot move until the vote is held and the result is known
Ignore it, since a market cannot beat your own estimate
optionExplain: Selling would lock in a loss if you are right.
Right: buying when the price is too low moves the price toward the probability.
Prices move with trading.
The market incorporates many views; yours adds one.
questions.explain: Each trader's judgment enters the price through trading.
questions.rule: Trade on the gap between price and belief.

questions.q: A new event suggests the favoured candidate will not win. What happens to the contract price?
options: The price holds, as traders ignore new events
The price rises, as traders buy in a panic
There is a rush to sell and the price declines
The contract is cancelled until the outcome is known
optionExplain: Traders respond to news.
Bad news for the favourite lowers demand.
Right: the authors say a rush to sell lowers the price.
No cancellation is described.
questions.explain: Selling pressure lowers the price in line with the revised judgments.
questions.rule: News moves prices through trading.

questions.q: What do the authors say about the strong version of the efficient market hypothesis?
options: It has been proven by a battalion of Nobel laureates who developed the underlying theory
It is correct, since prediction markets never lose their collective minds or misprice anything
It is false, since anyone can consistently beat markets with effort
It is hard to square with psychology and experience, yet markets remain hard to beat
optionExplain: The authors call the theory impressive but not proven perfect.
They say markets sometimes lose their collective minds.
They say consistently beating markets is very hard.
Right: they accept both points.
questions.explain: Markets make mistakes, but few can plausibly claim to have consistently beaten them.
questions.rule: Markets are imperfect but hard to beat.
questions.teaches: The authors call the strong efficient market hypothesis hard to square with psychology and experience, since markets make mistakes, but note that consistently beating markets is still very hard.

questions.q: A forecasting site lets users trade contracts on weather events. What gives traders reason to scrutinise each other's views?
options: Traders are told to praise each other's contributions in the site's discussion forum
Each trade puts money behind a view, so being wrong costs the trader
A moderator checks each trader's reasoning before a trade
Traders vote weekly on which view is correct
optionExplain: Praise is the opposite of second-guessing.
Right: incentives create second-guessing.
No moderator is part of the market logic.
Voting is not trading.
questions.explain: If you agree with my judgment you will not sell; if you think I am wrong, you will.
questions.rule: Markets give people reasons to second-guess each other.
questions.teaches: Markets create incentives for people to relentlessly second-guess each other: if you agree with a buyer you hold, and if you think the buyer is wrong you sell.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the strong form of the efficient market hypothesis is well supported by psychology and experience.
questions.explain: The authors say the strong version is hard to square with what psychology and experience have taught.
questions.rule: Do not take the strong form for granted.

questions.q: Before the results, what did most economists expect when superteams faced prediction markets?
options: That the two would tie, since both aggregate many views
That the superteams would win by a small margin
That neither would beat the average of solo forecasts
That the markets would beat the superteams easily
optionExplain: No tie was expected.
Economists favoured the markets.
Markets were expected to do far better than the crowd.
Right: the authors say most economists thought it was no contest.
questions.explain: Economists trust markets as aggregators, so they expected markets to mop the floor with superteams. The card next gives the results.
questions.rule: Experts expected markets to win.

questions.q: In the comparison, the wisdom of the crowd was the ____ average of all forecasts made by people working alone.
questions.explain: Each solo forecast counted equally.
questions.rule: The crowd figure was a simple average.

questions.q: Put these from lowest to highest accuracy in the authors' comparison.
items: Wisdom of the crowd (average of solo forecasts)
Ordinary teams
Prediction markets
Superteams
questions.explain: Each step up was reported each year: teams about 10% above the crowd, markets about 20% above teams, superteams 15% to 30% above markets.
questions.rule: Crowd, teams, markets, superteams.

questions.q: A forecasting firm has an average of solo guesses, a trading market and a team of experts. By the authors' ordering, which scores lowest?
options: The average of solo guesses
The trading market, which cannot use the public's views
The team of experts, which loses independence
None, because all three methods score the same
optionExplain: Right: the crowd average is the lowest in the authors' ordering.
Markets beat ordinary teams in the study.
Ordinary teams beat the crowd average.
The differences were reported each year.
questions.explain: Teams beat the crowd average, and markets beat teams.
questions.rule: The crowd average was the baseline.

questions.q: What objection did the authors expect from finance colleagues about their prediction markets?
options: That the markets used traders who had no real interest in the questions they were asked about
That the markets lacked liquidity: no real money at stake and too few traders
That the markets were run by companies with no experience
That the markets only covered questions about the economy
optionExplain: Interest is not the issue raised.
Right: the authors call this a testable idea.
Inkling and Lumenogic are named without criticism of their experience.
The questions covered complex global events.
questions.explain: Real money was not at stake and there was no critical mass of traders; the authors say this may be right and is worth testing.
questions.rule: Thin markets may understate what real markets can do.
questions.teaches: Finance colleagues may protest that the markets lacked liquidity, with no real money at stake and no critical mass of traders; the authors say this may be right and is a testable idea.

questions.q: A skeptic says the superteam win proves prediction markets are useless. Which caveat do the authors offer?
options: Markets lost only because they were run by commercial firms with little experience
Markets were beaten only in the first year of the contest
Markets still did a pretty good job of forecasting complex global events
Markets were never compared with ordinary teams at all
optionExplain: No such reason is given.
Results were clear-cut each year.
Right: the authors stress that markets did well.
Markets beat ordinary teams by about 20%.
questions.explain: The authors say it is important to recognise that, while superteams beat the markets, the markets did well.
questions.rule: Beating a benchmark does not make it poor.
questions.teaches: While superteams beat prediction markets, the authors stress that the markets did a pretty good job of forecasting complex global events.

questions.q: True or false: In the authors' comparison, superteams beat prediction markets by 15% to 30%.
questions.explain: That is the margin the authors report, each year.
questions.rule: Superteams beat the markets by 15% to 30%.

questions.q: In Edmondson's best surgical teams, what did the nurse do without hesitation?
options: Asked the surgeon to hand over the operation to a senior colleague
Told the surgeon he had left a sponge behind the pancreas
Stopped all operations until a hospital review had taken place
Waited until after the operation to report the mistake privately
optionExplain: No handover is described.
Right: she corrected a higher-up, because it was safe to do so.
Stopping all operations is not described.
Hesitation was not part of the best teams.
questions.explain: The point is that the nurse spoke up. The card next explains why she could.
questions.rule: Safe teams speak up at once.

questions.q: Edmondson's best teams felt it was psychologically ____ to correct higher-ups.
questions.explain: Safety, not rank, decided whether she spoke.
questions.rule: People speak up when it is safe.

questions.q: A junior pilot promptly tells the captain about a missed checklist item. Which team culture does this reflect?
options: One where junior members are expected to defer to rank and wait to be asked
One where members avoid disagreement to keep unity
One where it is psychologically safe to correct higher-ups
One where members seek credit from the leader
optionExplain: Deference would keep her quiet.
Avoiding disagreement would keep her quiet.
Right: speaking up promptly signals safety.
Credit-seeking is not the sign described.
questions.explain: A culture where correction is safe lets errors surface quickly.
questions.rule: Safety lets errors surface.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, superteams encouraged members to challenge each other respectfully, admit ignorance and request help.
questions.explain: They avoided the extremes of groupthink and flame wars, building minicultures that made these behaviours normal.
questions.rule: Respectful challenge, not suppression.

questions.q: Reading a team's chat logs, which sign would suggest a shared purpose, according to the authors?
options: Members avoid mentioning each other's names
Members post longer messages than other teams
Members reply to every message within an hour
Members say our more often than my
optionExplain: No such sign is given.
Length is not the sign.
Reply time is not the sign.
Right: the authors say the superteams said our more than my.
questions.explain: One sign of the shared purpose was linguistic: superteams said our more than my.
questions.rule: Shared purpose shows up in pronouns.
questions.teaches: One sign of a shared purpose on the superteams was linguistic: members said our more than my.

questions.q: True or false: Put high-AOM people together and you will get a high-AOM team.
questions.explain: The authors say teams were not merely the sum of their parts: team AOM depends on how members communicate. The card next explains.
questions.rule: A team is not the sum of its members.

questions.q: How a group thinks collectively is an ____ property of the group itself, not only of its members.
questions.explain: It arises from the patterns of communication among members.
questions.rule: Team thinking is emergent.

questions.q: Five open-minded experts form a panel but do not discuss anything with one another. What do the authors' ideas predict?
options: The panel will do less well than its open-minded members suggest
The panel will match the average of its members' open-mindedness
The panel will gain, because experts need no outside voices to improve their views
The panel will be excellent because it avoids groupthink
optionExplain: Right: open-minded people who do not engage are less than the sum of their parts.
That would be the sum-of-parts view the authors reject.
Isolation removes the gains of exchange.
Avoiding groupthink is not enough; engagement is needed.
questions.explain: The group's open-mindedness lives in how members communicate, which here is absent.
questions.rule: Open minds need engagement.

questions.q: Match each item to how the authors describe it.
pairs: Probed by surveying the person's own thinking
Probed by surveying attitudes toward the group and patterns of interaction
Arises from communication among members, not only their individual thinking
questions.explain: The team measure looks at the group and how members interact, because that is where the property lives.
questions.rule: Measure the team at the team level.

questions.q: A panel of strongly opinionated people engage one another in pursuit of the truth. What do the authors expect?
options: Less than the sum of its parts, because of clashing opinions
More than the sum of its opinionated parts
Exactly the sum of its parts, because opinions cancel out
A split group, because opinionated people cannot cooperate
optionExplain: Opinionated members who engage are the good case.
Right: engagement in pursuit of truth adds value.
The authors reject the sum-of-parts view.
The point is that they can cooperate.
questions.explain: A group of opinionated people who engage one another in pursuit of the truth will be more than the sum of its parts.
questions.rule: Engaged debate can lift a group above its parts.
questions.teaches: A group of opinionated people who engage one another in pursuit of the truth will be more than the sum of its opinionated parts.

questions.q: True or false: The authors found a correlation between a team's AOM and its accuracy.
questions.explain: They call this little surprise; the harder question is what makes a team more or less open-minded.
questions.rule: Team AOM and accuracy went together.

questions.q: In Adam Grant's categories, what does a matcher do?
options: Gives as much as he gets
Gives more than he receives
Gives less than he takes
Gives only when asked
optionExplain: Right: matchers keep things even.
That is a giver.
That is a taker.
Not part of Grant's categories.
questions.explain: Matchers balance giving and getting. The card next describes all three types.
questions.rule: Giver, matcher, taker.

questions.q: Grant calls people who give less than they take ____.
questions.explain: Takers take more than they give.
questions.rule: Takers give less than they take.

questions.q: A colleague shares his spreadsheet template with everyone, hoping others will follow. Which type is he, and why might it pay off?
options: A matcher, since he is only returning what he once received from his colleagues
A taker, since he wants others to share in return for what he has put in
A chump, since freeloaders will use it and give nothing back
A giver, whose example can improve others' behaviour and so help everyone
optionExplain: A matcher gives only in proportion to receiving.
A taker gives less than he takes.
The authors say givers are not chumps.
Right: the authors say a giver's example can raise the behaviour of others.
questions.explain: Deliberate generosity can change how others behave, benefiting everyone.
questions.rule: Generosity can be a strategy.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, givers are chumps who end up worse off than others.
questions.explain: The authors cite Grant's finding that givers tend to come out on top, and say none of their superteam givers is a chump.
questions.rule: Givers tend to come out on top.

questions.q: What happened to superteam givers Doug Lorch and Tim Minto, according to the authors?
options: Both were removed from their teams for giving away too much of their time and tools
Each had the best individual score in his year, and each man's team won
Both scored lowest because they spent time helping others
Both won the individual prize but their teams placed last
optionExplain: No removal is described.
Right: Lorch led in year 2 and Minto in year 3.
They topped the chart.
Their teams won.
questions.explain: Lorch distributed programming tools; Minto contributed an analysis for automatic tweaks to forecasts over time.
questions.rule: Givers can also top the table.
questions.teaches: Doug Lorch, who shared programming tools, had the best individual score in year 2, and Tim Minto, who shared an analysis of automatic tweaks, topped year 3; each man's team won.

questions.q: A manager asks whether to reward a colleague who spends hours helping others. What reading do the authors' views support?
options: Giving always costs the giver something real and so should be discouraged in teams
Giving helps only when everyone else is also a giver
Deliberate giving can set a useful example, as Rosenthal's did
Giving is useful only for leaders of large teams
optionExplain: The authors say it can help the giver too.
A giver's example can change others.
Right: the authors stress that giving was deliberate.
Rosenthal had no formal leadership role.
questions.explain: Rosenthal was generous in a deliberate effort to change the behaviour of others for the benefit of all.
questions.rule: Give deliberately, not blindly.
questions.teaches: Marty Rosenthal was not indiscriminately generous with his time and effort; he gave deliberately to change the behaviour of others for the benefit of all.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the superteam results give organizations a simple recipe for smarter decisions.
questions.explain: They say it is not that simple: replication in an organization would be a challenge. The card next gives the cautions.
questions.rule: No simple recipe.

questions.q: Singling out some staff for special status may be ____ inside an organization, the authors warn.
questions.explain: Labelling some as super can split a workplace.
questions.rule: Special status can divide.

questions.q: A CEO plans to hand-pick her ten best analysts, form one team and expect better forecasts. Which caution applies?
options: Teams of top performers always lose to the plain average of solo forecasts in the study
Groups should never be formed from people in different functions
Singling people out may be divisive, and there is no guarantee of results
Hand-picking analysts guarantees groupthink in every case
optionExplain: The authors found superteams beat the crowd.
Cross-functional teams can be disruptive, but the authors do not forbid them.
Right: these are the authors' cautions.
The authors do not say groupthink is guaranteed.
questions.explain: The authors list divisiveness, disruption and no guarantee.
questions.rule: Pilot a team design before relying on it.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, their conclusions about superteams are solid and complete.
questions.explain: They call the work on superteams in its infancy and say solid conclusions take time.
questions.rule: Early work, open questions.

questions.q: One of the best superforecasters left no comments for teammates. What reason did he give?
options: He had no time to read other people's work
He did not want to risk groupthink
He thought his teammates were not accurate enough
He was banned by the team from commenting
optionExplain: Time is not the reason given.
Right: this is one of the eccentric exceptions.
No such judgment is described.
No ban is described.
questions.explain: There were exceptions, such as a few teams that were not mutually supportive but still did well.
questions.rule: Exceptions warn against a single formula.
questions.teaches: Some eccentric exceptions existed: a few teams that were not mutually supportive did well, and one of the best superforecasters refused to comment for teammates so as not to risk groupthink.

questions.q: What do the authors say combining uniform perspectives produces?
options: More of the same
A sharp rise in accuracy
A split among members
A bias toward the loudest
optionExplain: Right: identical views add nothing new.
That requires differing views.
Not what the authors say.
Not what the authors say.
questions.explain: Uniform views add nothing. The card next explains Page's phrase.
questions.rule: Aggregation needs difference.

questions.q: Scott Page coined the phrase that diversity trumps ____.
questions.explain: The phrase puts diversity above ability.
questions.rule: Page: diversity trumps ability.

questions.q: A hiring panel is five graduates of the same school with the same training. What does the authors' point predict?
options: Combining their views adds a lot, since they all agree with one another so strongly
Combining their views adds little, since they share the same perspective
Combining their views will exceed any single member's by a wide margin
Combining their views gives the best result, since they are all able
optionExplain: Agreement is not information.
Right: uniform perspectives produce more of the same.
Slight variation gives only slight improvement.
Ability alone does not guarantee a gain.
questions.explain: Without differences, aggregation has nothing new to combine.
questions.rule: Choose for difference as well as ability.

questions.q: True or false: The authors conclude that team builders should drop ability and choose only for diversity.
questions.explain: The authors call that a false dichotomy; the choice is the mix of ability and diversity that works in each situation.
questions.rule: Mix ability and diversity.

questions.q: A team's members differ only slightly in outlook. What improvement do the authors expect from combining them?
options: Only a slight improvement
A large gain, because slight differences compound
No improvement at all, because they agree
A fall in accuracy, since they overlap
optionExplain: Right: slight variation gives slight improvement.
Large gains need real differences.
Slight differences still add something.
Overlap does not harm accuracy.
questions.explain: The authors say that slight variation produces slight improvement, while differing perspectives make the magic work.
questions.rule: The gain scales with the difference.
questions.teaches: Combining uniform perspectives produces more of the same, and slight variation produces only slight improvement; it is the diversity of perspectives that makes the magic work.

questions.q: Obama's advisers gave estimates from 30% to 95% that the tall man was bin Laden. About what did the average come to?
options: Roughly 70%
Roughly 40%
Roughly 55%
Roughly 90%
optionExplain: Right: the authors say the advisers averaged roughly 70%.
Too low for estimates mostly over 50%.
Too low.
Too high.
questions.explain: Most estimates were well over 50%, and the average was roughly 70%. The card next shows why the authors think it should be higher.
questions.rule: Average first, then ask what was missing.

questions.q: The extremizing algorithm works superbly, but its effectiveness depends on ____.
questions.explain: The more diverse the team, the more distinct scraps of information it holds.
questions.rule: Extremizing needs diversity.

questions.q: Six analysts with different data rate a merger's success at 60% to 80%, each pointing the same way. What does the authors' logic suggest?
options: A combined view below the plain average, because their data overlap so much and cancel
A combined view above the plain average, because each holds scraps the others lack
The plain average is exactly right, because every view counts equally
No combined view is possible, since the data differ
optionExplain: Overlap would justify less extremizing, not a lower figure.
Right: if they pooled their scraps, each would likely raise the estimate.
Equal weight ignores the unshared information.
Aggregation exists to combine differing data.
questions.explain: Because the scraps mostly point the same way, giving all of them to everyone would raise estimates.
questions.rule: Pooled scraps beat a plain average.

questions.q: A team of clones, whose members all hold identical information, is to be extremized. What do the authors advise?
options: As much as possible
Only a little
Not at all
Only in the first year
optionExplain: That would suit a highly diverse team.
Even a little would add error.
Right: with no diversity, there are no hidden scraps.
Timing is not the factor.
questions.explain: If everyone already knows everything, the average already reflects all information.
questions.rule: No diversity, no extremizing.
questions.teaches: A team with zero diversity, whose members are clones, should not be extremized at all.

questions.q: A team shares information very well. How much did extremizing help such superteams, per the authors?
options: A great deal, because sharing creates extreme views
It hurt them, because extremizing punishes sharing
It helped them more than any other team
Not much, because sharing reduced diversity
optionExplain: Sharing lowers diversity.
No harm is described.
Regular teams gained more.
Right: they were good at sharing, so little diversity remained.
questions.explain: Regular teams shared less, so extremizing gave them major gains, enough to pass some superteams, and extremizing a large pool of regular forecasters produced tournament-winning results.
questions.rule: Extremizing gains track information not yet shared.
questions.teaches: Extremizing gave regular forecasting teams major gains, enough to pass some superteams, and extremizing a large pool of regular forecasters produced tournament-winning results.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say extremizing works equally well whatever the diversity of the team.
questions.explain: They say its effectiveness depends on diversity, and a team of clones should not be extremized at all.
questions.rule: Diversity decides how much extremizing helps.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, these tools will not replace analysts or the officials who synthesize their conclusions.
questions.explain: The authors say the tools should be on decision makers' desks, but there will always be a need for a chief executive to be surrounded by a smart team of advisers.
questions.rule: The tools support, not replace, advisers.

questions.q: Which set of qualities do people say an effective leader needs, in near-universal agreement?
options: Patience, a love of debate and a habit of hearing every side first
Charm, a loud voice and a record of never having been wrong once
Confidence, decisiveness and a vision the group can work toward
Obedience, caution and a talent for writing very detailed plans
optionExplain: Patience and debate help forecasters, but they are not the leader qualities the authors name.
Charm may help, but the authors list confidence, not a perfect record.
Right: these are the three basic points the authors say nearly every list contains.
Obedience and caution are not among the three agreed qualities.
questions.explain: The authors name confidence, decisiveness and vision. The card next shows why superforecasting seems to threaten each.
questions.rule: Know the three leader traits before judging the clash.

questions.q: Leaders who think so long that they cannot act risk what the authors call analysis ____.
questions.explain: The authors use analysis paralysis for endless deliberation, which a decisive leader must avoid.
questions.rule: Decisiveness means sizing up, deciding and moving on.

questions.q: A founder keeps reopening a product choice to weigh each new report, and her team stops building. Which leader quality is under strain?
options: Decisiveness, because the team needs a decision so that work can move on
Vision, because the team no longer shares any goal to strive for together
Confidence, because a founder who reads reports cannot believe in her plan
Humility, because a leader who revises too often has too much of it
optionExplain: Right: the authors say leaders cannot ruminate endlessly; they must decide and move on.
The goal may still be shared; the stall comes from not deciding.
Reading reports does not by itself erode belief in the plan; the issue is delay.
The authors do not treat humility as a leader flaw to be cured.
questions.explain: The scenario is analysis paralysis, which strains decisiveness.
questions.rule: Endless review is what decisiveness rules out.

questions.q: True or false: The authors conclude that leaders must give up superforecaster habits in order to lead.
questions.explain: They say the contradiction is more apparent than real, and that the superforecaster model can make good leaders superb.
questions.rule: The authors say the dilemma can be resolved.

questions.q: Match each feature of superforecasting to the leader requirement it seems to threaten.
pairs: Readily changing one's mind or admitting error
questions.explain: Each of the authors' three questions pairs one superforecaster habit with one leader need.
questions.rule: Each habit seems to strain a different leader need.

questions.q: According to the authors, the approach that resolves the dilemma has a history. Put its stages in order, earliest first.
items: Articulated by a nineteenth-century Prussian general
Perfected by the German army of World War II
Made foundational doctrine by the modern American military
Deployed by many successful corporations today
questions.explain: The authors trace one approach from a Prussian general through the German army and the American military into business.
questions.rule: The answer to the dilemma is an old organisational approach that has spread.
questions.teaches: The approach that resolves the dilemma was first set out by a nineteenth-century Prussian general and later became doctrine in the modern American military and in many corporations.

questions.q: True or false: Moltke's own wording of the idea was more nuanced than the slogan soldiers use today.
questions.explain: Moltke wrote that no plan of operations extends with certainty beyond the first encounter with the enemy's main strength; the slogan is a snappier later form. The card next shows his version.
questions.rule: Moltke's original is more careful than the slogan.

questions.q: Moltke wrote that no plan of operations extends with ____ beyond the first encounter with the enemy's main strength.
questions.explain: He did not say plans fail at once; he said they cannot be trusted with certainty past the first encounter with the main enemy force.
questions.rule: Never entirely trust your plan.

questions.q: Rain ruins the schedule of an outdoor wedding. Which planner's stance matches Moltke's?
options: Throw away planning altogether, since no schedule can ever be made to work
Hold to the schedule exactly, on the grounds that all events resemble each other
Write more binding rules for every kind of weather so that nothing differs
Treat the schedule as a guide, expect changes, and improvise as needed
optionExplain: Moltke did not conclude that planning is pointless; he said not to trust a plan fully.
He said two cases never are exactly the same, so rigid adherence misleads.
Moltke thought binding rules for all circumstances are impossible.
Right: a plan helps, yet it should not be trusted entirely, and improvisation is essential.
questions.explain: Moltke's lesson is to plan and to hold the plan loosely.
questions.rule: Plan, then be ready to improvise.

questions.q: How does Moltke's original statement differ from the soldiers' slogan?
options: It says that plans fail even before the first soldier has met any enemy at all
It limits the claim to what comes after the first clash with the main enemy force
It tells commanders to avoid detailed plans because such plans always fail on contact
It is the same claim, shortened, with exactly the same meaning as before
optionExplain: Moltke placed the limit at the first encounter with the main force, not before it.
Right: the original is narrower and more careful.
He did not say plans always fail; he said they cannot be trusted with certainty.
The authors stress the original is more nuanced than the slogan.
questions.explain: The authors note that the slogan is snappier but loses nuance.
questions.rule: Check whether a famous slogan keeps the original's limits.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Moltke saw himself as a visionary directing his army like chess pieces.
questions.explain: They say he was no Napoleon and never saw himself that way; his approach to leadership was entirely different.
questions.rule: Moltke did not see command as moving pieces.

questions.q: A trainer wants a war game that shows chance. According to the authors, what did the Prussian military invent to do this?
options: Maps with fixed routes, so that students could memorise the right path
Board games with dice, to add the element of chance chess lacks
Sealed orders opened only after a battle had been won or lost
Chess variants with extra pieces, so that players had more choices
optionExplain: Fixed routes would remove surprise, the opposite of the aim.
Right: the Prussians appreciated uncertainty and invented dice games to add chance.
Sealed orders are not mentioned in the text.
Extra pieces add options, not chance; chess lacks chance and the dice supplied it.
questions.explain: Prussian planners built chance into their games.
questions.rule: Training can build uncertainty in on purpose.
questions.teaches: The Prussian military long appreciated uncertainty and invented board games with dice to add the element of chance that chess lacks.

questions.q: In German war academies of Moltke's era, what happened when an instructor gave his view of a scenario?
options: Students noted it down, since the instructor held the single right answer
Students stayed silent, because criticism was kept for senior generals
Students voted, and the majority view replaced the instructor's decision
Students could challenge it; the instructor was a comrade among others
optionExplain: That describes other nations of the era, including the United States.
Even generals' views were scrutinised, so juniors did speak.
The text describes discussion and criticism, not binding votes.
Right: even the instructor's views could be challenged.
questions.explain: The card next shows how the academies differed from rote teaching.
questions.rule: Good training invites challenge.

questions.q: In German war academies, scenarios were laid out and students were invited to suggest ____ and discuss them collectively.
questions.explain: Students proposed solutions and argued about them instead of being handed the right answer.
questions.rule: Students proposed; they were not just told.

questions.q: Which hospital training session is closest to the German war academy method?
options: Residents propose treatments, and the senior doctor's plan can be questioned
Residents memorise the head surgeon's treatment list and repeat it on request
Residents watch the senior doctor decide and ask no questions until their exams
Residents follow a printed script for every case, whatever the patient presents
optionExplain: Right: proposing and debating solutions, with the instructor open to challenge, is the method described.
That mirrors the other nations, where students nodded and memorised.
Silence until exams is the opposite of expected disagreement.
A script for every case removes the thinking the academies wanted.
questions.explain: The method puts student reasoning at the centre.
questions.rule: Look for proposals, debate and challenge.

questions.q: True or false: A junior officer in Moltke's army could criticise the result of a large maneuver before the attending general spoke.
questions.explain: The authors report that junior officers were regularly asked for opinions and criticised outcomes before the general had the floor.
questions.rule: Junior views counted.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Moltke's officers were taught only military subjects, so they had no schooling in critical thinking.
questions.explain: Besides military training they received what we would now call a liberal arts education stressing critical thinking, and even military courses expected hard thinking.
questions.rule: Officers were taught to think, in military and other subjects.

questions.q: A firm wants managers trained as Moltke's officers were. Besides professional training, what education did those officers receive?
options: A short course on obeying orders without comment, to build firm discipline in the ranks
A rotation through each rank so that they would know every duty well
What we would call a liberal arts education, stressing critical thinking
A course on mathematics only, since war is a matter of numbers
optionExplain: Obedience without comment is the opposite of what the academies taught.
Rotation through ranks is not mentioned in the text.
Right: the authors say it resembled a liberal arts education with an emphasis on critical thinking.
Mathematics only is not described; the education was broad.
questions.explain: Breadth of education supported independent judgment.
questions.rule: Teach thinking skills as well as the job.
questions.teaches: In addition to their military training, Moltke's officers received what we would now consider a liberal arts education with an emphasis on critical thinking.

questions.q: At Zorndorf in 1758, how did the cavalry general Seydlitz answer the king's order to attack?
options: He attacked at once, then asked the king to forgive the delay in his advance
He sent back a request for a written order and waited until it arrived
He passed the order to a subordinate and kept his own forces out of the fight
He refused, judging the time wrong, and attacked later when it seemed right
optionExplain: He did not attack at once; he refused three messages.
No written order is mentioned.
Seydlitz commanded his own cavalry; no hand-off is described.
Right: he held back until he judged the moment right, and the attack then turned the battle.
questions.explain: The card next gives the whole story.
questions.rule: A commander on the spot may judge timing better than the one who sent the order.

questions.q: Seydlitz told the king his ____ was at the king's disposal after the battle, but he would use it meanwhile.
questions.explain: The remark played on the threat to take his head; he meant to use it to judge the right moment.
questions.rule: Use your head, even when ordered otherwise.

questions.q: A director tells a project lead to ship on Friday. The lead thinks two more test days are needed. Which response fits the lesson?
options: Comply in silence and note the objection afterwards, to protect her position
Explain why the date is wrong and hold back only if the reason is good
Ignore the date and ship whenever she likes, since she knows the product best
Ask the director for the order in writing, so that any blame can be shifted
optionExplain: Silent compliance gives up the thinking the officers were expected to do.
Right: the lesson is to think, discuss, criticise, and disobey only with a good reason.
The lesson is not that subordinates may do as they please; a good reason is needed.
Shifting blame is not what the story models; Seydlitz put his own head at stake.
questions.explain: She argues first, and refuses only for a strong reason.
questions.rule: Challenge openly; disobey only with good reason.

questions.q: Which behaviours fit the lesson of the Seydlitz story, and which do not?

items.t: Questions an order and explains the concern to the superior
Refuses an order after careful thought, for a stated good reason
Ignores an order because it is inconvenient
Carries out every order without any thought of its merits

questions.explain: The story rewards thinking and reasoned refusal, not blind obedience and not casual defiance.
questions.rule: Neither blind obedience nor casual defiance.

questions.q: True or false: The Seydlitz story supports disobeying an order only when an officer has a good reason.
questions.explain: The authors say disobedience is for when you absolutely must, and with a good reason.
questions.rule: Disobedience needs a good reason.

questions.q: A company wants a story to teach judgment. According to Muth, how did Prussian officers keep the Seydlitz story alive?
options: They carved it on regimental monuments, so every new recruit would see it each day
They kept it in the king's private archive, for use only by the senior generals
They retold it in lectures, the mess and letters, as shared cultural knowledge
They taught it only to cavalry units, since Seydlitz had commanded cavalry
optionExplain: Monuments are not mentioned.
The story was widely shared, not locked in an archive.
Right: Muth says it was retold countless times in lectures, the mess and correspondence.
The text says it was general cultural knowledge in the officer corps.
questions.explain: Stories carried the lesson through the whole corps.
questions.rule: A culture is passed on by retelling its stories.
questions.teaches: According to Muth, Seydlitz-like stories were collective cultural knowledge in the Prussian officer corps, retold countless times in lectures, the officers' mess and letters between comrades.

questions.q: True or false: The Wehrmacht manual of 1935 treated waiting for more information in a tense situation as a sign of strong leadership.
questions.explain: It said the opposite: such waiting is seldom a sign of strong leadership and more often a sign of weakness. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Waiting under pressure can be weakness.

questions.q: An imperfect decision made in ____ was better than a perfect one made too late.
questions.explain: The point is timing: a decision that arrives too late loses its value.
questions.rule: A timely decision beats a late perfect one.

questions.q: A shift manager has ten minutes to reassign staff after a fire alarm, with partial reports. Which approach matches the Wehrmacht view?
options: Decide now on what is known, since waiting for reports costs more than a flawed choice
Wait for every report to arrive, because a sound decision needs all of the facts first
Delay and consult everyone, since a shared choice is always the safest one to make
Pick at random, because information gathered under time pressure is useless anyway
optionExplain: Right: when time is short, act on what is known; waiting is more often weakness.
Waiting for every report is the habit the manual criticises in tense situations.
Consulting everyone consumes the time that the situation does not give.
The manual still values clarifying the situation; it does not call information useless.
questions.explain: The time available sets the style of decision.
questions.rule: Under time pressure, a decision in time wins.

questions.q: According to the authors, how would the same army decide when it has days before a move?
options: More leisurely and complex, since circumstances set the time available
In the same abrupt way, since speed was the only value the army ever held
Not at all, until the commander in chief had approved the plan in person
By vote of the whole staff, because that was how the army ruled itself
optionExplain: Right: decisions could be leisurely and complex when time permitted.
Speed was valued when bullets were flying, not as a fixed style.
Waiting for the commander in chief is the centralised habit the chapter argues against.
Voting is not mentioned in the text.
questions.explain: The style of decision follows the time available.
questions.rule: Match deliberation to the time you have.

questions.q: True or false: According to the manual, clarifying the enemy situation is an obvious necessity.
questions.explain: The manual criticises waiting for information in a tense situation, not seeking it.
questions.rule: Seek information, but do not wait on it past the point of use.

questions.q: A coach cannot decide whether to wait for scouting or send the team out now. Which maxim from the 1935 manual applies?
options: The first criterion in war remains complete knowledge of the other side
The first criterion in war remains the approval of the supreme commander
The first criterion in war remains decisive action
The first criterion in war remains agreement among all the subordinates
optionExplain: The manual says waiting for information is more often weakness, not strength.
Waiting for the supreme commander is the opposite of the approach described.
Right: the manual puts decisive action first.
Agreement by all is not mentioned; the manual ranks decisive action first.
questions.explain: The manual ends the discussion with a ranking of values.
questions.rule: When in doubt about timing, act decisively.
questions.teaches: The 1935 Wehrmacht manual declared that the first criterion in war remains decisive action.

questions.q: According to Wehrmacht doctrine, what changes in a leader's mindset once a decision has been made?
options: The leader invites fresh debate on the decision at every new report received
The leader hands the choice to subordinates, who then redo it from scratch
Doubts are set aside, and the leader acts with resoluteness once decided
The leader keeps weighing odds, so that the plan can be dropped at any time
optionExplain: Reopening debate at each report is the opposite of the sharp line the Wehrmacht drew.
The leader keeps ownership of the decision; subordinates choose how to carry it out.
Right: after deliberation comes implementation, with resolve.
Continued weighing is the deliberation phase; implementation is supposed to be resolute.
questions.explain: The card next sets out the line between deliberating and acting.
questions.rule: Deliberate, then commit.

questions.q: Moltke wrote that if one wishes to attack, then half ____ are out of place.
questions.explain: He asked for resolute attack; half measures undermine it.
questions.rule: Once you act, act fully.

questions.q: A team lead picked a launch plan, then keeps voicing doubts in front of the team. What advice fits the Wehrmacht view?
options: Voice doubts in the deliberation stage, then lead the launch with calm and resolve
Keep sharing every doubt with the team, since honesty requires it at all times, even then
Never revisit the plan after launch, whatever new facts come in during the work itself
Hand the launch to the team and let them decide again whether to go ahead
optionExplain: Right: doubt belongs in the thinking stage; the doing stage needs resolve.
Honesty about uncertainty has its place before the decision, not in the middle of carrying it out.
The manual says a plan can be dropped when circumstances demand a new decision.
The leader does not hand back the decision; only the method is for the team.
questions.explain: Separate the thinking stage from the doing stage.
questions.rule: Voice doubts before the decision, not during execution.

questions.q: True or false: The command manual said a course of action must not be abandoned without overriding reason.
questions.explain: It also said that inflexibly clinging to a course can lead to failure.
questions.rule: Resolve has an exception: an overriding reason.

questions.q: Sort each activity into the stage of the Wehrmacht line it belongs to.

items.t: Weighing the uncertainty and complexity of the situation
Asking whether the plan itself might be wrong
Carrying out the attack without half measures
Showing calm and assurance to the troops

questions.explain: Questioning belongs before the decision; resolve and assurance belong to carrying it out.
questions.rule: Each stage has its own mindset.

questions.q: A new sergeant must keep a unit's trust in a confusing situation. What does Moltke advise officers to show?
options: Open doubt, so that the soldiers see that the officer is honest
Constant activity, so that the soldiers never have a moment of rest
Strict silence, so that the soldiers cannot learn what is uncertain
Calm and assurance, which earn the trust of the soldier
optionExplain: Open doubt would spread the uncertainty that the leader is meant to contain.
Constant activity is not what the text says.
Silence is not described; the officer shows assurance, not secrecy.
Right: Moltke wanted officers to show calm and assurance to earn trust.
questions.explain: Moltke linked visible assurance to trust.
questions.rule: Appearing steady is part of leading.
questions.teaches: Moltke told officers to show calm and assurance to earn the trust of the soldier, and said that in a fog of uncertainty one's own decision is the one thing that must be certain.

questions.q: Under Auftragstaktik, what does a commander tell a subordinate?
options: How to proceed in every step, leaving the goal for the subordinate to infer
What the goal is, leaving the choice of how to reach it to the subordinate
Nothing at all, so that the subordinate must set the goal and the means
Both the goal and a fixed method, with permission needed for any change
optionExplain: That reverses the principle.
Right: the goal is given; the method is left to those on the spot.
The commander still sets the goal; otherwise the army would lose coherence.
A fixed method with permission to change it is the command-and-control style.
questions.explain: The card next states the principle in the authors' words.
questions.rule: Goal from above, method from below.

questions.q: The English name for the principle of Auftragstaktik is mission ____.
questions.explain: The term is mission command.
questions.rule: Auftragstaktik means mission command.

questions.q: A hotel manager must have rooms ready for a conference group arriving at three. Which instruction follows mission command?
options: Clean floors in this order, using these supplies, and report each room completed
Rooms must be ready by three because the group arrives then; the team decides how
Do whatever seems best, without telling anyone why the three o'clock deadline exists
Ask the manager before changing the cleaning order, whatever the situation turns up
optionExplain: A fixed sequence tells the team how and not why.
Right: it gives the goal and the reason, and leaves the method to the team.
Without a stated goal and reason the team cannot judge what matters.
Needing approval for changes is the opposite of pushing decisions down.
questions.explain: The instruction states the aim and leaves the means open.
questions.rule: State what and why; leave how.

questions.q: According to the authors, what would happen if units on the ground made strategic decisions as well?
options: The army would move faster as a whole, because every unit chooses its best goal
The army would match the enemy's choices, since each unit senses the enemy first
The army would grow stronger, as strategy would be shaped by the best-informed
The army would lose coherence and become many tiny units pursuing separate ends
optionExplain: Speed in local action is the benefit of choosing the method, not the goal.
Local sight of the enemy helps tactics, not coherent strategy.
Those on the ground do not see the bigger picture, so they lack the strategic view.
Right: decentralised strategy would break the army into units with separate aims.
questions.explain: That is why the goal stays with the top.
questions.rule: Decentralise the method, not the strategy.

questions.q: True or false: Auftragstaktik means each unit sets its own goals, so long as it acts quickly.
questions.explain: Commanders still tell subordinates the goal. What moves down the hierarchy is the choice of how to achieve it.
questions.rule: The goal stays central.

questions.q: True or false: In the Wehrmacht, judgment about how to reach the commander's goal was expected right down to the lowliest private.
questions.explain: The authors say soldiers at every rank were told what the commander wanted and expected to use judgment about how.
questions.rule: Judgment was expected at every rank.
questions.teaches: Auftragstaktik was not limited to senior officers: right down to junior officers, NCOs and the lowliest private, soldiers were told what the commander wanted and expected to use judgment about how.

questions.q: In the authors' Wehrmacht example, what is the captain told about taking the town?
options: To take it, because that cuts a key road enemy reinforcements would use
To take it by a set route from the southwest, then seize the canal bridge
To take it without being told why, since the reason is not his business
To take it only after sending a report to HQ and awaiting its choice of route
optionExplain: Right: he gets the goal and the reason, and chooses how.
The set route belongs to the command-and-control version.
Not being told why is also the command-and-control version.
Waiting for HQ is the opposite of mission command.
questions.explain: The card next sets the two versions side by side.
questions.rule: The purpose is part of the order.

questions.q: In the Wehrmacht version, taking the town would sever a key ____ that the enemy needed to reach the region beyond.
questions.explain: The purpose gave the captain a reason to judge what mattered.
questions.rule: A stated purpose guides improvisation.

questions.q: A courier is told to deliver a parcel to a street address. The road is closed. Which version of the order helps him most?
options: Take Route 9, turn at the bakery, and hand the parcel to the receptionist at the desk
Deliver the parcel to the street address and do not ask what it contains or why
The parcel holds medicine a clinic needs by five, so choose any route to it
If the road is closed, stop and phone the dispatcher for a fresh route
optionExplain: A fixed route fails when the road is closed.
Not knowing the contents leaves him unable to judge what matters.
Right: knowing the purpose lets him choose a new way.
Phoning the dispatcher is the move the command-and-control captain is left with.
questions.explain: Goal and reason make improvisation safe.
questions.rule: Give the purpose, and the person can adapt.

questions.q: On the road to the town, the Wehrmacht captain finds a bridge HQ believed destroyed. According to the authors, what does he do?
options: He asks HQ whether to cross it, and waits for the answer before moving on with the attack
He leaves it alone, because the order named only the town and nothing about any bridges
He uses it to attack at once, since a bridge is a gift to the side that finds it first
He destroys it himself, since it could carry enemy reinforcements, without asking HQ
optionExplain: Asking HQ is the order-following captain's habit.
The aim is to stop reinforcements, so ignoring the bridge defeats it.
Using the bridge for his own attack does not serve the stated purpose.
Right: knowing why the town matters, he acts at once.
questions.explain: Understanding the purpose lets him see what the bridge means.
questions.rule: Know the aim, spot the threat, act.

questions.q: True or false: The captain given only a route is certain to cope well when the town differs from HQ's picture.
questions.explain: The authors say he will be unsure what to do other than ask HQ for new orders.
questions.rule: A route without a reason fails when the picture changes.

questions.q: True or false: Moltke observed that when events differ greatly from what orders assumed, subordinates feel uncertain and trust in their superiors is shaken.
questions.explain: The authors quote Moltke saying it shakes the trust of subordinates and gives units a feeling of uncertainty.
questions.rule: Orders that ignore the possibility of surprise erode trust.
questions.teaches: Moltke observed that when things happen entirely differently from what orders from higher headquarters presumed, it shakes the trust of subordinates and gives units a feeling of uncertainty.

questions.q: At Eben Emael, what happened to the lieutenant commanding the operation, Rudolf Witzig?
options: His glider crashed on the fort's roof, and he was captured soon after the guns fell
His glider landed 100 kilometres off target in Germany, and he came later by another
He directed the assault by radio from a base, then flew in after the surrender came
He was replaced on the eve of the attack by the sergeant who took the roof
optionExplain: He was not captured; he reached the fort later.
Right: he was out of the fight at first and joined late.
The troops flew in radio silence; no direction by radio is described.
No replacement was named beforehand; a sergeant took charge when the lieutenant was lost.
questions.explain: The card next gives the whole account.
questions.rule: Plans break; initiative continues.

questions.q: With the lieutenant missing, a ____ took charge of the troops on the fort's roof and knocked out the Belgian guns.
questions.explain: A non-commissioned officer led the attack without waiting for orders.
questions.rule: Initiative reached below officer level.

questions.q: A project leader's flight is cancelled; a senior technician takes charge and finishes the installation. Which feature of Eben Emael is this?
options: A team ignores the aim of the mission and follows a leader's earlier script
A commander micromanages from the rear and controls each action directly
A subordinate takes charge when the commander is lost and finishes the mission
A unit waits until fresh instructions arrive from headquarters before it moves again
optionExplain: Following an old script is the opposite of improvising.
Direct control from the rear is the style the chapter argues against.
Right: the sergeant did the same when Witzig's glider was lost.
Waiting for new orders is the habit of command and control.
questions.explain: The mission continued because someone on the spot judged and acted.
questions.rule: Understand the aim well enough to carry on without the commander.

questions.q: Which actions show Auftragstaktik at work, and which show the opposite habit?

items.t: A sergeant takes charge after the commander is lost and completes the task
A sergeant improvises an attack with commandeered vehicles
A unit halts until headquarters sends a fresh plan
A captain repeats the set route even after the town has changed

questions.explain: The Eben Emael sergeants acted on the aim; waiting for HQ or repeating the route shows the other style.
questions.rule: Initiative on the spot marks mission command.

questions.q: True or false: The authors tell the Eben Emael story to show initiative at every level of the Wehrmacht.
questions.explain: They use it to show the reverse of the mindless machine.
questions.rule: The case contradicts the machine image.

questions.q: Before the invasion of Belgium and France, a senior officer ordered divisions across the borders and the Meuse. How did he say to do it?
options: He said it was up to them; he did not care how they did it
He supplied a detailed timetable that each division had to follow
He said each division must clear its route with headquarters first
He gave each division a fixed set of roads and a list of bridges
optionExplain: Right: the order stated the goal and left the method to the commanders.
A detailed timetable would tell them how.
Clearing the route would give the decision back to headquarters.
Fixed roads and bridges dictate the method.
questions.explain: Even a major operation was ordered by goal.
questions.rule: Big stakes do not require detailed orders.
questions.teaches: On 10 May 1940 a senior officer told the commanders of the assault into Belgium and France to cross the German and Belgian borders and the Meuse, and said he did not care how they did it.

questions.q: True or false: The Nazis inherited the Wehrmacht rather than creating it.
questions.explain: The authors stress this to correct the picture of a machine built by the regime. The card next gives their case.
questions.rule: Check where an organisation came from before judging it.

questions.q: The authors say that enough Wehrmacht officers were both superforecasters and ____ that the army achieved great success.
questions.explain: They use the pair to say that judgment and decisive leadership were combined.
questions.rule: Superforecasting and leading can be combined.

questions.q: A reviewer sees staff in matching uniforms marching in step and concludes they cannot think for themselves. Which lesson applies?
options: Appearance can mislead; look at how the organisation actually makes decisions
Appearance is a reliable guide, since uniforms show how thinking is organised
Organisations that march in step must be weaker than those that do not
An organisation serving a bad cause cannot be effective at any level
optionExplain: Right: the newsreel image hid the independent thinking inside the army.
The authors use the Wehrmacht to show that appearance misleads.
Marching is not evidence of weakness either; the point is that the image says little.
The authors reject the link between a bad cause and poor competence.
questions.explain: Judge decision making by how it works, not how it looks.
questions.rule: Do not read an organisation's thinking from its image.

questions.q: According to the authors, how could a heavily outnumbered army conquer most of Europe and hold it for years?
options: Its soldiers followed orders so exactly that no unit ever deviated from the plan at all, anywhere
Its generals made every important choice at headquarters, with great speed and little debate
Enough officers, mainly at operational and tactical levels, joined judgment to decisive leadership
Its leaders avoided any doubt in their minds, since doubt weakens an army in the field
optionExplain: Exact obedience is the image the authors reject.
Centralised choices are the style that Moltke's principles oppose.
Right: this is the authors' explanation.
The doctrine allowed doubt before the decision.
questions.explain: The explanation lies in who held judgment and where.
questions.rule: Look for judgment in the ranks.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say every officer of the Wehrmacht was both a superforecaster and a superleader.
questions.explain: They say not all were, but enough were, especially at the operational and tactical levels.
questions.rule: Enough, not all.

questions.q: A coach wants a motto for a bold team. According to the Wehrmacht manual, what must take precedence over boldness and daring?
options: Strict obedience to the written plan, whatever the situation shows
Good judgment
Speed in action, so that an enemy is never given time to react
Careful avoidance of risk, so that nothing can be lost by chance
optionExplain: The manual asks for independent decisions, not strict obedience.
Right: the manual says great success requires boldness and daring, but good judgment must take precedence.
Speed is valued, but the manual ranks judgment above boldness.
Daring is also required; the manual does not ask for risk avoidance.
questions.explain: Boldness works best when guided by judgment.
questions.rule: Judgment ranks above daring.
questions.teaches: The Wehrmacht manual said great success requires boldness and daring, but good judgment must take precedence.

questions.q: At Normandy, why did the German reserve tanks not move quickly against the landings?
options: They had run out of fuel after weeks of fighting along the coast road
Their commanders judged the landings a feint and held the tanks back for later
The Allies had destroyed the roads, so that no tank column could pass through
They could move only on Hitler's personal command, and no one woke him
optionExplain: Fuel is not mentioned in the text.
The text shows no commander's judgment; the tanks awaited Hitler.
Road damage is not mentioned.
Right: control was centralised in one man who was asleep.
questions.explain: The card next gives the account.
questions.rule: Centralised control can stall action.

questions.q: Hitler directed that the reserves could only move on his personal ____.
questions.explain: The rule made the reserves wait for one man.
questions.rule: A single point of command is a single point of delay.

questions.q: A chain requires the CEO's sign-off for any local price change. During a storm, stores wait for hours. Which Normandy lesson applies?
options: A strong chief who approves every move assures faster and safer action
Delay at the centre is acceptable, since lower levels see only a small part
When one person must approve every move, action waits for that person
Approval from the top is needed only when the weather is calm and clear
optionExplain: The Normandy case shows the reverse.
Lower levels do lack the wider picture, but the cost here was lost time at the moment it mattered.
Right: the German reserves waited for Hitler, as the stores wait for the CEO.
The lesson is not tied to weather; it is about who holds the power to act.
questions.explain: Centralised approval turns a sleeping chief into a stalled organisation.
questions.rule: Decisions pushed down are not stopped by a missing chief.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the Wehrmacht failed only because Hitler took control of operations.
questions.explain: They say it was overwhelmed in part by superior resources, and also made blunders, often because of Hitler's control.
questions.rule: Two causes, not one.

questions.q: True or false: Under Moltke's principles, the German reserves at Normandy would not have needed one man's personal command to move.
questions.explain: Mission command pushes decisions down so commanders on the spot can act. Hitler's order broke that.
questions.rule: Moltke's rule would have freed the reserves.

questions.q: The authors call the German defeat at Normandy ironic. What made it so?
options: It vindicated Moltke, a German general, through defeat by an American of German descent
It showed a German general beaten by a rival from a country with far fewer men to field
It proved that superior numbers, and not command style, decide the outcome of every battle
It showed an American general who copied German tactics in every detail of his plans
optionExplain: Right: Eisenhower, an American general of German descent, understood Moltke's philosophy better than Germany's Supreme Commander.
The point is Moltke's vindication, not the size of the countries.
The authors cite resources as one cause, not the sole cause.
No copying of tactics is described; Eisenhower understood the philosophy.
questions.explain: A nineteenth-century German general was proved right by a German loss.
questions.rule: Principles can be vindicated by those who break them.
questions.teaches: The authors call it ironic that Moltke was vindicated by the German defeat at Normandy, at the hands of Eisenhower, an American general of German descent who understood Moltke's philosophy better than Germany's Supreme Commander.

questions.q: True or false: After publishing an article on tanks, the young Eisenhower was praised by the army for his new ideas.
questions.explain: He was told his ideas were wrong and dangerous and threatened with court-martial. The card next gives the account.
questions.rule: Inventive thinking was punished.

questions.q: The orders for the American landings in North Africa were the size of a Sears Roebuck ____.
questions.explain: The comparison shows how long and detailed American orders were.
questions.rule: Detailed orders leave little room for initiative.

questions.q: An engineer writes a memo proposing a new method and is told to keep it to herself or be disciplined. Which army habit is this?
options: Giving subordinates the goal and letting them choose for themselves how to reach it
Training officers by open discussion, where even the teacher may be challenged by students
Punishing a junior who argues against doctrine, as with Eisenhower's tank article
Pushing decisions down the hierarchy so that people on the spot can act on their own
optionExplain: That is mission command, the opposite habit.
That describes the German war academies.
Right: this matches the reprimand Eisenhower received.
That also describes mission command.
questions.explain: The reprimand shows a culture that shut down criticism.
questions.rule: Suppressing dissent is the opposite of mission command.

questions.q: If American orders were long and detailed, what room did they leave for individual initiative, according to the authors?
options: Little room, because few choices were left to those carrying them out
Plenty of room, since detail only helps those who must decide quickly under fire
Room only for generals, since the orders came down from the highest levels
Room for initiative that was welcomed and rewarded at every rank of the army
optionExplain: Right: detailed orders leave the subordinate little to decide.
Detail fixes the method, so there is less to decide, not more.
The text does not limit initiative to generals.
The text says initiative was valued despite the training, not because of it.
questions.explain: Detailed orders and little initiative go together.
questions.rule: Detail in orders reduces initiative.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say some American officers valued initiative despite their training, not because of it.
questions.explain: They say there were smart and creative American officers who did so.
questions.rule: Initiative existed, against the system.

questions.q: Patton wrote: “Tell them what to do, and they will surprise you with their ingenuity.” Which principle does this capture?
options: The spirit of command and control: give the method, hold the goal back
The spirit of consensus: decide only after everyone has agreed on a plan
The spirit of delay: give no orders until the facts are fully known
The spirit of Auftragstaktik: give the goal, leave the method
optionExplain: That reverses it.
Consensus is not what the quote says.
The quote says nothing about delay.
Right: Patton captured the spirit of Auftragstaktik.
questions.explain: Patton was one officer who valued initiative.
questions.rule: Tell people what, not how.
questions.teaches: George Patton was one smart American officer who captured the spirit of Auftragstaktik, writing that you should never tell people how to do things.

questions.q: After ordering the D-Day invasion to go ahead, what did Eisenhower do first?
options: He ordered all subordinates to sign a pledge that their plans were complete
He wrote a note taking personal responsibility, to be released if it failed
He wrote a note asking the president to delay the landings by a few more days
He waited for each commander to report that the weather forecast was right
optionExplain: No pledge is mentioned.
Right: the note accepted blame in advance.
The order was irrevocable; the note did not seek delay.
The text describes the note, not waiting on commanders.
questions.explain: The card next shows what this says about his leadership.
questions.rule: Take responsibility in advance.

questions.q: Like Moltke, Eisenhower understood that a cool and assured appearance could do more to spread ____ than false claims of certainty.
questions.explain: A steady manner builds morale without pretending that things are certain.
questions.rule: Calm builds confidence; false certainty does not.

questions.q: A surgeon is anxious before a risky operation. Which behaviour is closest to Eisenhower's?
options: Tell the team the operation is certain to succeed, so that they all feel safe and calm
Stay steady with the team, while privately accepting the risk and the blame
Show the team every doubt, so that they feel the full burden of the decision at hand
Cancel the operation until all risk has been removed from the plan by more study
optionExplain: False claims of certainty are what the authors say Eisenhower avoided.
Right: assured manner outside, honest acceptance of uncertainty inside.
Showing every doubt would not spread confidence.
Waiting for all risk to vanish is analysis paralysis; Eisenhower gave the order.
questions.explain: Calm for the troops, honest within.
questions.rule: Look steady without claiming certainty.

questions.q: True or false: A leader like Eisenhower would take criticism from subordinates seriously, and admit it when a subordinate had been right.
questions.explain: The authors say he respected well-founded criticism and readily acknowledged mistakes.
questions.rule: Welcome well-founded criticism.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Eisenhower showed the troops his private moods, since leaders should look as they feel.
questions.explain: In private he could be moody and brooding; with the troops he kept a smile and a steady word.
questions.rule: Outward calm is deliberate.

questions.q: In 1954 Ridgway advised against intervening in Vietnam. Why did President Eisenhower respect his judgment?
options: Ridgway had won the largest battles of the Pacific war while under his own personal command
Ridgway was the army's most senior general and so outranked every other adviser in the room
Ridgway had agreed with Eisenhower on every question that came up during the whole war
In 1943 Ridgway had resisted the Rome drop order, and Eisenhower later judged him right
optionExplain: No Pacific battles are mentioned.
Rank is not the reason given.
Ridgway's value lay in having disagreed and being right.
Right: Eisenhower remembered that his earlier objection had been correct.
questions.explain: A record of well-founded disagreement earned a hearing.
questions.rule: Credit those who disagreed correctly.
questions.teaches: Eisenhower respected the army chief of staff Matthew Ridgway's 1954 advice against intervening in Vietnam, because in 1943 Ridgway had resisted the order to drop an airborne division on Rome and Eisenhower later decided he had been right.

questions.q: In which year did mission command become part of official American military doctrine?
optionExplain: Right: 1982, in the years of Cold War tension and Soviet numerical superiority.
1944 was the year of the Normandy invasion; the US learnt the lesson later.
1956 was the war between Israel and Egypt.
2003 was the invasion of Iraq, long after the doctrine was adopted.
questions.explain: The card next explains why the time had come.
questions.rule: Doctrine adopted under pressure.

questions.q: An Israeli slogan of the era said that plans are a ____ for change.
questions.explain: The slogan expressed the mission-command attitude to plans.
questions.rule: Plans are starting points for change.

questions.q: A small firm faces a rival with ten times its staff. Which step matches what NATO did in the early 1980s?
options: Copy the rival's rigid plans, since larger forces know best how to win wars
Give up local initiative, so that all choices are made at headquarters
Study methods that let a smaller force do more, even those of past rivals
Avoid learning from any former opponent, however effective it was in the field
optionExplain: Rigid plans do not make a smaller force more effective.
Centralisation is the opposite of mission command.
Right: when outnumbered, NATO studied approaches that made a force more effective, including old Wehrmacht generals' advice.
NATO consulted even former opponents.
questions.explain: Pressure from numbers prompted a search for a better method.
questions.rule: Learn from former opponents when pressed.

questions.q: True or false: An Israeli officer would be likely to praise a division whose plans were mostly foiled if its objectives were still met.
questions.explain: The authors quote an officer proudly noting that almost all the plans were foiled but all objectives were attained.
questions.rule: Objectives matter more than plans.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the US army was quick to adopt the Wehrmacht's lessons after World War II.
