questions.explain: They say it was slow; Israel appreciated individual initiative first and the US adopted mission command in 1982.
questions.rule: The US learnt late.

questions.q: An Israeli officer commented on a division in the 1956 war with Egypt. What did he say about its plans and results?
options: The plans were followed closely, and most objectives were met, though rather more slowly than hoped
The plans were foiled and the objectives were also missed, leaving the division short of its aim
The plans were drawn up late, though the objectives were still met on time in the end
Almost all the plans were foiled, yet all objectives were attained, faster than expected
optionExplain: That describes rigid execution, not the officer's remark.
The remark was proud, not a report of failure.
The remark concerned foiled plans, not late drafting.
Right: the officer praised success despite foiled plans.
questions.explain: The result shows plans as a platform, not a script.
questions.rule: Judge a plan by whether the objective was reached.
questions.teaches: An Israeli officer proudly said that in the 1956 war with Egypt almost all of a division's plans were foiled but all objectives were attained in full, and faster than expected.

questions.q: In the 2003 thunder run, what did the armoured column do and at what cost?
options: It besieged the city for weeks and lost most of its armoured vehicles
It raced to the captured airport and lost only one vehicle
It turned back at the airport after taking heavy losses and low ammunition
It waited at the edge of Baghdad for new orders from the capital
optionExplain: The run was a quick raid, not a siege.
Right: the Iraqis were caught off guard.
The column got through; the brigade a few days later ran low on ammunition and still stayed.
The point was action by the commanders on the spot, not waiting for orders.
questions.explain: The card next gives the second run and the Mosul case.
questions.rule: Surprise and speed were the key.

questions.q: In Mosul, General David Petraeus informed his superiors in Baghdad what he was doing but did not ask ____.
questions.explain: He informed, and acted on his own initiative.
questions.rule: Inform, but do not wait for permission.

questions.q: A regional sales manager meets a market shock. Her director is unreachable for days. Which move resembles Petraeus in Mosul?
options: She waits for instructions, since a plan from above is safest in a crisis of this kind
She hides her actions, so that no one can say she exceeded her role in the company
She improvises a response from her own knowledge and tells the director what she does
She copies her last year's plan exactly, since it succeeded in a calm year before
optionExplain: Waiting is the habit the chapter argues against.
Petraeus informed his superiors; he did not hide anything.
Right: act on the spot and keep the superior informed.
Mosul called for improvising new strategies, not repeating old plans.
questions.explain: Initiative with transparency.
questions.rule: Act and inform.

questions.q: True or false: In the second thunder run, ground commanders decided to stay in the government district despite running low on ammunition.
questions.explain: The authors call this a gutsy call that helped ensure the rapid collapse of Iraqi defences.
questions.rule: Commanders on the spot made the critical call.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the military leadership did not forecast the insurgency that followed the fall of Baghdad.
questions.explain: The insurgency was not forecast, and for months or years leaders had little idea how to respond.
questions.rule: Local initiative filled a forecasting gap.

questions.q: In 2007 Petraeus received overall command in Iraq. What did he do, and what followed?
options: He brought in flexible officers and spread his Mosul methods; violence fell
He replaced the Mosul methods with a rigid national plan, and violence held steady
He kept his officers in their old posts and waited for orders, and violence fell
He gave up the Mosul approach to follow headquarters, and violence rose then fell
optionExplain: Right: like-minded commanders and the Mosul strategies were extended across the country.
That reverses what he did.
He brought in new officers rather than leave the old posts.
He extended his Mosul approach rather than give it up.
questions.explain: He scaled up a local success.
questions.rule: Spread what works through like-minded people.
questions.teaches: The insurgency that blossomed after the fall of Baghdad was not forecast by the military leadership, which for months or years had little idea how to respond.

questions.q: Petraeus disliked live-fire exercises that were choreographed. What was wrong with a script, in his view?
options: Commanders met no surprises, so training did not prepare them to improvise
The script cost too much, because real weapons and explosives were used
The script let junior officers make choices that belonged to the generals above
The script exposed the plans to the enemy, who could learn them in advance
optionExplain: Right: reality brings surprises, so training must too.
Safety drove the script; cost is not the complaint.
The complaint was lack of surprise, not who made choices.
Enemy knowledge is not mentioned.
questions.explain: The card next gives the aim of his training.
questions.rule: Train for surprise.

questions.q: Petraeus called the divide between doers and thinkers a false ____.
questions.explain: He holds that leaders must be both thinkers and doers.
questions.rule: Doers and thinkers are not rivals.

questions.q: A bank wants its branch managers ready for crises. Which plan follows Petraeus's approach?
options: Give each manager a binder with a step for every crisis imaginable in advance
Repeat the same rehearsed drill each year until it can be done blind
Run drills with unscripted surprises that are safe yet force improvisation
Keep managers away from any experience that might make them uncomfortable at work
optionExplain: A binder with every step is the script he rejected.
A repeated drill removes surprise.
Right: unscripted but safe surprises develop flexible leaders.
Comfort is what he wants to push people out of.
questions.explain: Exercises should force improvisation.
questions.rule: Practise surprise safely.

questions.q: True or false: Petraeus would likely say that boldness alone settles which move is right.
questions.explain: He says the bold move is the right move except when it is the wrong move; a leader must first figure out the right move.
questions.rule: Boldness serves judgment.

questions.q: True or false: According to Petraeus, officers should be sent to top universities mainly to acquire a body of knowledge.
questions.explain: He says knowledge is a secondary benefit; the main aim is to meet very different basic assumptions, which trains mental flexibility.
questions.rule: Meeting other ways of thinking trains flexibility.

questions.q: Which statement is closest to Petraeus's view of Hamlet and Henry V in Peters's contrast?
options: Henry V is the model: commanders should decide quickly and not deliberate
Leaders must be both: work out the right move, then carry it out boldly
Hamlet is the model: commanders should consider every side before acting
Neither is useful: commanders should follow regulations without deliberating
optionExplain: That is Peters's view.
Right: he rejects the split between doers and thinkers.
Petraeus wants decisive execution too.
He wants flexible thinking, not obedience to regulation.
questions.explain: The contrast belongs to Peters; Petraeus rejects the choice.
questions.rule: Do not choose between thinking and doing.

questions.q: Petraeus sends officers to top universities. What does he say the experience gives them?
options: Mastery of the technical subjects needed for the highest staff posts in the army
Contacts in civilian life who can later help the army with its supplies and funds
Experience of lectures whose content would be applied directly in combat situations
Meeting bright people whose assumptions differ, which trains flexibility
optionExplain: He calls knowledge a secondary benefit.
Contacts are not mentioned.
The benefit is not direct application.
Right: the benefit is meeting different assumptions and conclusions.
questions.explain: Intellectual surprises train like battlefield ones.
questions.rule: Seek out different assumptions.
questions.teaches: Petraeus sends officers to top universities mainly to meet very bright people with different basic assumptions, since grappling with other ways of thinking trains mental flexibility like encountering shocks on a battlefield.

questions.q: Which executive offered a near-perfect summary of mission command: we tell people what we want but not how?
options: Jeff Bezos, the founder who set leadership principles for all of Amazon's staff
Damian McKinney, the former Royal Marine who designed a Walmart leadership academy
William Coyne, a senior vice president of research and development at 3M
Helmuth von Moltke, the Prussian general who wrote of the green table
optionExplain: Bezos is quoted on disagreeing and committing, a different part of the principle.
McKinney designed the academy and spoke about command and control in companies.
Right: Coyne said they do not tell people how to achieve the goals.
Moltke is the origin of the idea, not a business executive.
questions.explain: The card next gives all three firms.
questions.rule: Goal from above, method from below.

questions.q: One of Jeff Bezos's leadership principles at Amazon is: have backbone; disagree and ____.
questions.explain: Leaders challenge decisions they doubt, then commit wholly once the decision is made.
questions.rule: Challenge first, then commit.

questions.q: Design-team members argue hard against a proposal; the lead decides to proceed and all then work to make it succeed. Which principle is this?
options: Disagree and commit: challenge before the decision, then back it fully
Consensus rule: nothing proceeds until every member agrees on the plan
Command and control: the lead gives each member a fixed list of steps
Analysis paralysis: the team keeps reopening the proposal after the decision
optionExplain: Right: the team challenges, then commits.
Consensus would stop the work before it begins.
Fixed step lists are the command-and-control style.
Reopening the decision is the paralysis the chapter warns against.
questions.explain: Challenge and commitment each have their stage.
questions.rule: Disagree before, commit after.

questions.q: Why did Walmart create a leadership academy, according to the authors?
options: It wanted to copy the army's rank structure for its head office
It had lost managers to rivals who offered better pay and benefits
It was building stores more slowly than rivals and needed new ideas
It was building stores faster than it could develop store managers
optionExplain: The academy took a philosophy, not a rank structure.
Pay is not mentioned.
The company was building quickly, not slowly.
Right: the need was to prepare managers for promotion sooner.
questions.explain: The academy answered a shortage of managers.
questions.rule: Train for the growth you plan.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Walmart's academy was based on a civilian business school's curriculum.
questions.explain: They say it was modelled on military academies, with the mission command philosophy at its foundation.
questions.rule: The academy followed a military model.

questions.q: Besides asking leaders to disagree and commit, what does the Amazon principle say leaders will not do for social cohesion?
options: Argue: leaders keep their objections to themselves for the team's sake
Compromise: leaders do not compromise for the sake of social cohesion
Commit: leaders hold back their effort until the whole team is willing
Decide: leaders leave the choice to the group until a majority is found
optionExplain: The principle obliges leaders to challenge decisions respectfully.
Right: the principle says leaders have conviction and do not compromise for the sake of social cohesion.
Once a decision is determined, they commit wholly.
Nothing in the principle sets a majority rule.
questions.explain: Respectful challenge comes before the group's comfort.
questions.rule: Do not trade the right answer for harmony.
questions.teaches: The Amazon principle also says leaders have conviction and are tenacious, and do not compromise for the sake of social cohesion.

questions.q: True or false: Damian McKinney said companies are more focused on command and control than their military counterparts.
questions.explain: He told the Financial Times so, calling it ironic. The card next gives the context.
questions.rule: Check which side holds the tighter control.

questions.q: McKinney said companies were more focused than the military on what he called command and ____.
questions.explain: Command and control is the top-down style of orders and obedience.
questions.rule: Command and control is the top-down style.

questions.q: A retired officer joins a firm where every expense needs three signatures. Which advice would she most likely give?
options: Add a fourth signature, as the army does, to protect the firm
Cut the signatures and let teams choose how to meet shared goals
Stress rank and status so that people know whose word counts
Write longer procedures so that no one needs to use any judgment
optionExplain: The army the authors describe does not rely on piling up approvals.
Right: ex-officers advise worrying less about status and empowering teams.
Advisers tell executives to worry less about status.
Longer procedures remove judgment, the opposite of the advice.
questions.explain: The advice is to empower, not to control.
questions.rule: Empower people to choose the how.

questions.q: Sort each habit by the style it shows.

items.t: Orders spell out every step and the reason is not given
Subordinates must ask for approval before any change of method
The goal and purpose are stated and the method is left open
People on the spot may improvise toward a shared aim

questions.explain: The first two keep decisions at the top; the last two push them down.
questions.rule: Spot the style by who chooses the method.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the modern military image of mechanical obedience is accurate and still fits its leaders.
questions.explain: They call that image laughably out of date.
questions.rule: The old image is out of date.

questions.q: Ex-military officers advise executives. According to the authors, what do they often tell executives to do?
options: Worry more about rank and status, and make sure every employee defers to a superior
Worry less about shared goals and let every team pick its own objectives at will
Worry more about written procedure and have every step approved by someone above
Worry less about status and more about empowering teams to choose how to reach goals
optionExplain: That reverses it.
The goals stay shared; only the method is left to teams.
More written procedure is command and control.
Right: the advice is to empower people and teams.
questions.explain: Advisers bring mission command to firms.
questions.rule: Empower people within shared goals.
questions.teaches: Ex-military officers advising corporations often tell executives to worry less about status and more about empowering their people and teams to choose the best ways to achieve shared goals.

questions.q: Which trait do the authors say many of the book's admired leaders and thinkers showed?
options: Strong self-assurance, in some cases a large ego
Modesty about their own abilities, in nearly every case
Hesitancy in deciding, from a fear of being wrong
Deference to authority, in the form of obedience to rank
optionExplain: Right: the authors point to self-confidence in Petraeus, Keynes, Soros and others.
That is the opposite of the picture they give.
These leaders acted boldly.
Cochrane, for one, called out the most eminent authorities.
questions.explain: The card next gives the examples.
questions.rule: Confidence and good judgment can coexist.

questions.q: Soros's most famous bet, shorting the British pound in 1992, earned him an estimated $1.1 ____.
questions.explain: He sold sterling worth almost $10 billion to make it.
questions.rule: Soros acted boldly under pressure.

questions.q: A colleague says confident people cannot be good forecasters. Which point from the chapter answers best?
options: Only people who doubt themselves ever make a forecast worth reading in the end
Confidence in one's own judgment has no place anywhere in a forecaster's work
Judges the authors admire, such as Keynes and Soros, were very self-assured
Good forecasters hide their confidence from other people, so it goes unseen
optionExplain: The authors do not argue that doubt makes forecasts worthwhile.
They say confidence can inspire determined action.
Right: the examples show confidence alongside good judgment.
Nothing in the chapter suggests hiding confidence.
questions.explain: The examples answer the claim directly.
questions.rule: Confidence alone does not spoil judgment.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say Eisenhower, the plainspoken man from Abilene, had a substantial ego.
questions.explain: They say he had no shortage of self-regard.
questions.rule: Plain speech does not mean lack of ego.

questions.q: Match each figure to the detail the authors give about his self-assurance.
pairs: Thought he was the smartest man in the room
Had the chutzpah to call out the most eminent authorities
Shorted the British pound in 1992 under extreme pressure
questions.explain: Each detail is one of the authors' examples.
questions.rule: Three self-assured judges.

questions.q: Eisenhower repeatedly refused the presidential nomination. What made him change his mind before 1952?
options: He saw that his party would offer him the post without any fight at all that year
He saw that Truman would not run, and no strong rival was left in the race
He saw that a long army career had left him no other path to useful work
He saw that an isolationist would likely win and that he alone could stop that
optionExplain: Both parties had begged him earlier, and he refused.
Truman had even offered to step aside for him.
He sincerely did not want the job; a sense of duty changed his mind.
Right: he thought only he could stop it, and the biographer says he decided he was the best.
questions.explain: His self-regard showed in his belief that he alone could do it.
questions.rule: Self-assurance can turn into a sense of duty.
questions.teaches: Eisenhower sincerely did not want the presidency, but in 1952 he decided that only he could stop an isolationist from winning, and a biographer wrote that he decided he was the best and would have to serve.

questions.q: According to the authors, what is the humility that good judgment requires?
options: A sense that you are less talented or intelligent than most of the people around you
A recognition that reality is complex and that human judgment is full of mistakes
A habit of deferring to whoever has the highest rank or the longest record of success
A refusal to take firm positions, so that no one can later prove you wrong
optionExplain: That is self-doubt, which the authors set apart from intellectual humility.
Right: it is intellectual humility, not self-doubt.
Deference to rank is not what they describe.
Avoiding firm positions would prevent determined action, which the authors also want.
questions.explain: The card next states the difference.
questions.rule: Humility about the world, not about your worth.

questions.q: The humility needed for good judgment is not self-doubt but ____ humility.
questions.explain: The authors define it as recognising complexity and fallibility.
questions.rule: It is intellectual humility.

questions.q: Which surgeon shows the humility the authors describe?
options: One who doubts her ability and avoids any operation that could go wrong
One who is sure she is right since she believes it and her record is long
One confident in her skill who still reviews errors because medicine is complex
One who defers to senior surgeons in every decision, whatever the evidence says
optionExplain: That is self-doubt, not intellectual humility.
That is Duke's shortcut: belief proves itself.
Right: confidence in ability combined with an awareness of complexity and error.
Deference is not the humility described.
questions.explain: Intellectual humility sits with confidence.
questions.rule: Be confident in skill, humble about judgment.

questions.q: Duke warns about the shortcut: I am successful, so my belief proves I am right. What danger does she see?
options: You look at reality from the tip of your nose
You will always lose to a more cautious opponent at the table
You will spend too long thinking and then decide too late
You will lose the confidence that determined action requires
optionExplain: Right: a belief in your own judgment cannot check itself.
The shortcut is not about opponents' caution.
The shortcut skips thinking, rather than prolonging it.
The shortcut inflates confidence, rather than draining it.
questions.explain: Confidence cannot prove itself right.
questions.rule: A belief is not evidence for itself.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say you cannot think highly of yourself and be intellectually humble.
questions.explain: They say it is quite possible to do both, and that the combination can be wonderfully fruitful.
questions.rule: High self-regard and humility can coexist.

questions.q: Sort each thought into intellectual humility or self-doubt.

items.t: Reality is complex and even geniuses make many mistakes
I am untalented and unworthy of this decision
I am good at this, but my judgment still needs checking
I am not intelligent enough to have a view

questions.explain: The first and third accept fallibility without denying ability; the second and fourth deny ability.
questions.rule: Doubting the world is not doubting yourself.

questions.q: In his second inaugural, Lincoln urged firmness in the right as God lets us see it. How do the authors read this?
options: Fierce conviction, joined with an admission that our own vision is limited
Plain uncertainty, since a leader who says this has not yet made a decision
Pure self-confidence, because Lincoln claimed to see the right as God does
A call to wait, until a divine sign made the right course clear to everyone
optionExplain: Right: the authors call it fierce conviction and a humble acknowledgment.
Lincoln said to strive on to finish the work, which is determined.
The phrase admits that vision is limited.
He urged striving on, not waiting.
questions.explain: Conviction and humility were in the same sentence.
questions.rule: Resolve and humility can be joined.
questions.teaches: The authors read Lincoln's “as God gives us to see the right” as a statement of fierce conviction that also humbly acknowledges that our vision is limited, our judgment flawed, and even our firmest belief may be wrong.

questions.q: Why do the authors say they used the Wehrmacht as an illustration even though it makes us squirm?
options: Because no other organisation in history ever made use of mission command so well
Because its cause deserves credit for the competence of its officers and men
Precisely because it makes us squirm, which is the discomfort forecasters must face
Because few readers will have strong feelings about it either way, the authors thought
optionExplain: They say other organisations could illustrate the point.
They call the cause the evilest in modern history.
Right: the authors answer with the squirm itself.
They expect readers to have strong feelings.
questions.explain: The card next sets out their reasoning.
questions.rule: Discomfort is the test.

questions.q: The authors say there is no divinely mandated link between morality and ____.
questions.explain: A bad cause can still be served with skill.
questions.rule: Moral standing does not predict competence.

questions.q: An analyst assumes a hated regime's army must be incompetent. According to the authors, what error is this?
options: Giving the opponent too much credit, which risks wasting a good deal of the analyst's time
Assuming moral weakness and cognitive weakness go together, so underestimating the foe
Letting a firm moral view guide the analysis, which risks making it too accurate
Judging competence by results alone, which risks overlooking the opponent's motives
optionExplain: Underestimating, not overestimating, is the danger.
Right: the authors call it seeing illusory correlations.
A moral view that distorts the facts lowers accuracy.
Results are a sound guide to competence; motives are another question.
questions.explain: Keep moral and factual judgments apart.
questions.rule: Do not assume the evil are inept.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say it is logically contradictory to call the Wehrmacht both horrific and effective.
questions.explain: They say there is no logical contradiction, only a psychological tension.
questions.rule: The tension is felt, not logical.

questions.q: True or false: A forecaster who cannot cope with the dissonance of admiring an enemy's skill is likely to underestimate that enemy.
questions.explain: The authors say forecasters who cannot cope risk the most serious forecasting error: underestimating the opponent.
questions.rule: Dissonance can distort forecasts.

questions.q: What did F. Scott Fitzgerald say marks a first-rate intelligence, in the passage the authors quote?
options: The ability to ignore feelings in order to reach a quick decision
The ability to follow a plan to the end without any change at all
The ability to settle on one idea and drop its opposite for good
The ability to hold two opposed ideas in mind and still function
optionExplain: Fitzgerald did not praise ignoring feelings to decide quickly.
The passage concerns two ideas, not a plan.
The point is keeping both ideas, not dropping one.
Right: this is the capacity the authors say a superforecaster needs.
questions.explain: The authors apply Fitzgerald to the Wehrmacht.
questions.rule: Hold two opposed ideas without freezing.
questions.teaches: In “The Crack-Up” F. Scott Fitzgerald observed that a first-rate intelligence can hold two opposed ideas in mind at once and still function, which the authors say forecasters need in order to separate feelings from factual judgments.

questions.q: True or false: Superforecasters who excel at self-criticism are immune to letting their values shape a forecast.
questions.explain: The authors say even they sometimes conflate facts and values. The card next gives two cases.
questions.rule: Feelings can leak into forecasts.

questions.q: Doug Lorch let his loathing of the ____ regime lead him to the wishful conclusion that the rebels would take Aleppo.
questions.explain: The evidence said the rebels were outgunned, but his feelings pointed the other way.
questions.rule: A strong dislike can pull a forecast.

questions.q: A forecaster dislikes a company and predicts it will fail, despite strong sales figures. Which error from the chapter is this?
options: Giving too much weight to the sales figures and too little to rumour in the market
Choosing a company whose results could not be measured against a deadline date
Letting feelings about the company lead to a wishful conclusion against the evidence
Changing the forecast too quickly after reading new facts about the company's sales
optionExplain: The error runs the other way: facts were underweighted.
The case does not concern whether results can be measured.
Right: this mirrors Lorch's wishful conclusion.
The fault is the refusal to follow the evidence.
questions.explain: Wishes are not evidence.
questions.rule: Check whether a wish is writing your forecast.

questions.q: True or false: Frankel noticed at the time he made the forecast that optimism was influencing him.
questions.explain: The authors say he did not sense it then; he only realised later.
questions.rule: Bias can be invisible while it is acting.

questions.q: Sort each statement into a factual judgment or a feeling about the regime.

items.t: The rebels are outgunned by the government forces
The regime deserves to fall for what it has done
The regime's army has so far resisted every assault
It would be wonderful to see the regime collapse

questions.explain: A forecast needs the factual judgments; the feelings belong apart.
questions.rule: Keep facts and feelings in separate columns.

questions.q: A couple of weeks before the closing date, what made Frankel realise that optimism had shaped his North Korea forecast?
options: A talk with a friend whose relatives escaped North Korea in the Korean War
A new report from analysts who had tracked the nuclear programme closely for years
A review of his earlier results, which showed a clear pattern of optimism in his forecasts
A message from the question's organisers, who advised him to revise his forecast soon
optionExplain: Right: the conversation made him see it, and he flipped his forecast.
No such report is mentioned.
No review of earlier results is mentioned.
No message from organisers is mentioned.
questions.explain: An outside view revealed the bias.
questions.rule: Another person's view can expose hidden hope.
questions.teaches: Frankel realised his optimism only a couple of weeks before the closing date, through a conversation with a friend whose family members had escaped North Korea at the time of the Korean War, and he then flipped his forecast.

questions.q: According to Tetlock, what mainly explains why superforecasters forecast so well?
options: The hard work: research, self-criticism and repeated updating
Intelligence scores far above the range of other forecasters
An inborn open-minded temperament that other people cannot acquire by effort
A run of good luck that happened to last for several years
optionExplain: Right: Tetlock stresses what they do over what they are.
Their scores are above average but, he says, not off the charts.
They score higher on open-mindedness, but he does not call it inborn or unlearnable.
By summer 2014 it was clear they were not merely superlucky.
questions.explain: Tetlock's answer is a bit of both, with the weight on what superforecasters do. The card next gives the list.
questions.rule: Skill rests more on practice than on rare traits.

questions.q: Asked whether superforecasters are different kinds of people or do different kinds of things, Tetlock answered: a bit of ____.
questions.explain: He says they score somewhat above average on intelligence and open-mindedness, yet what makes them good is chiefly what they do.
questions.rule: The answer is both, weighted toward what they do.

questions.q: A manager wants sharper forecasts from her sales team. Following Tetlock's account, which plan fits best?
options: Build habits of research, self-criticism and updating in the team
Replace the team with people who score highest on standard intelligence tests
Wait for individuals who show a natural gift for confident hunches
Hire only people with an open-minded personality and train nobody
optionExplain: Right: the habits are what Tetlock says make superforecasters good, and habits can be taught.
Intelligence helps a little, but Tetlock says it is not off the charts and not the main factor.
Hunches are the fast intuitions that careful checking is meant to correct.
Open-mindedness helps, but Tetlock gives the work as the main cause, so training matters.
questions.explain: Tetlock's list is a list of activities. A manager can ask for them directly.
questions.rule: Aim at the activities, not at finding a special type.

questions.q: Sort each item into what superforecasters ARE or what they DO, as Tetlock describes them.

items.t: Somewhat above average in intelligence
Somewhat above average in open-mindedness
Gathering and combining other perspectives
Making granular judgments
Relentless updating of forecasts
Self-criticism and careful thought

questions.explain: Tetlock gives two traits, both above average without being extreme, and a longer list of activities. He says the activities matter more.
questions.rule: Traits are the starting point; the activities are the main cause.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says superforecasters score far off the charts on intelligence, and this explains their success.
questions.explain: He says they score higher than average but are not off the charts, and that what they do matters more than what they are.
questions.rule: Do not turn above average into off the charts.

questions.q: A bank finds two traders who beat the market for years. Before asking whether they are a different kind of person, what should it settle?
options: Whether their personality tests differ from those of colleagues
Whether their record is too steady to put down to luck alone
Whether they work longer hours than the others on the floor
Whether their intelligence scores sit far off the charts
optionExplain: That question comes after skill is shown to exist, and Tetlock does not rest his answer on tests.
Right: Kahneman asked his question once it was clear the superforecasters were not merely superlucky.
Hours are one possible habit, but the first step is to rule out luck.
Tetlock says superforecasters do not score off the charts, so this would not explain it.
questions.explain: Kahneman posed the people-or-practice question after the evidence had ruled out simple luck. Asking what explains skill makes sense only once skill is shown.
questions.rule: Rule out luck first, then ask what explains the skill.
questions.teaches: Kahneman put his question in summer 2014, once it was clear that superforecasters were not merely superlucky.

questions.q: True or false: According to Tetlock, continuous self-scrutiny is exhausting even for the best forecasters.
questions.explain: He says the effort of constant checking is exhausting, and the feeling of knowing is seductive. The card next explains why that matters.
questions.rule: Careful thinking costs effort.

questions.q: Conscious reflection that can catch mistakes from rapid, unconscious thinking is called System ____ in the chapter.
questions.explain: System 2 is the conscious reflection; System 1 is the rapid unconscious operation that produces the mistakes.
questions.rule: System 2 checks, System 1 answers fast.

questions.q: A pilot checks every dial by hand through a ten-hour shift and misreads one near the end. Which part of Tetlock's account fits?
options: Conscious reflection works best when the person has been tired for hours
The feeling of knowing was missing, so nothing felt wrong
Constant self-scrutiny is tiring, which makes a late slip more likely
Fast intuition was switched off completely, so the dial was unreadable
optionExplain: Tetlock says the opposite: tiredness makes reflection harder to sustain.
The feeling of knowing is present when a wrong answer feels right, which is the danger.
Right: the chapter says continuous self-scrutiny is exhausting.
Intuition is not switched off; it is the source of quick answers that checking must catch.
questions.explain: The pilot's lapse matches the point that effortful checking is hard to keep up. The chapter links this to forecasters.
questions.rule: Effort-heavy checking fades first.

questions.q: A rushed forecaster feels certain of an answer. According to Tetlock's account, what is likely to happen to her check?
options: The certainty will trigger a more careful second check
Training will have removed any feeling of certainty already
The slip will not matter because past scores protect her ranking
She may skip it, because the feeling of knowing is seductive
optionExplain: Certainty usually does the reverse; it makes checking feel unnecessary.
Tetlock says the feeling of knowing remains tempting even for the best.
He warns that a slipup can hurt a forecaster, not protect her.
Right: a strong feeling of knowing makes checking feel unnecessary.
questions.explain: The feeling of knowing is what leads a forecaster to skip the check. That is why Tetlock calls it seductive.
questions.rule: A strong feeling of certainty is a cue to check, not to skip.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock and Kahneman agree that superforecasters risk a blown forecast through a System 2 slipup.
questions.explain: The chapter says Tetlock and Kahneman agree about this. They differ on how far training can protect people.
questions.rule: They agree on the risk; they differ on the remedy.

questions.q: A top chess player calculates every move but plays a fast, tired move in a final game. Which result does Tetlock's account match?
options: No loss, because her earlier effort has become permanent
A deliberate change of style that shows how adaptable she is
A costly slip, like a forecaster's tumble down the rankings
A gain, because quick intuition beats careful checking in a final game
optionExplain: Earlier effort does not store up; each slip counts.
Nothing in the account suggests a slip is a choice.
Right: the chapter says one System 2 slipup can mean a blown forecast and a tumble down the rankings.
Tetlock does not say intuition beats checking.
questions.explain: The account says one slip can mean a blown forecast and a nasty tumble down the rankings. A final-game slip has the same shape.
questions.rule: In a ranked contest one lapse can cost a lot.
questions.teaches: A System 2 slipup can mean a blown forecast and a nasty tumble down the rankings.

questions.q: In the 2014 interview Tetlock discusses, what did General Flynn say about the level of conflict in the world?
options: That it was a calm pause between two much larger wars
That it was prolonged societal conflict, pretty unprecedented
That conflict was fading, as it had after the Cold War ended in 1991
That it matched the average level of the last few decades
optionExplain: Flynn said the environment was uncertain and dangerous, not calm.
Right: Flynn called it a prolonged and pretty unprecedented period of societal conflict.
That matches what the data show, not what Flynn said.
Flynn described the period as unusual, not typical.
questions.explain: Flynn made a sweeping claim about conflict, and Tetlock tests it. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: A bold claim invites a check.

questions.q: Kahneman's WYSIATI stands for What You See Is All ____.
questions.explain: The phrase names the habit of treating whatever is in front of you as the whole picture.
questions.rule: WYSIATI: what you see is all there is.

questions.q: A shopkeeper sees three rude customers one Monday and tells staff that customers grow ruder every year. Which check fits Tetlock's point?
options: Ask staff to describe the three rude customers in much more detail
Rely on the strong feeling that the claim is true
Look for records that count rude incidents across many years
Wait to see if the next day's customers are ruder
optionExplain: More detail about the same three sharpens what is in view but does not widen it.
The feeling is the very thing that WYSIATI says should not be trusted alone.
Right: the claim is about a trend, so only a longer record can test it.
One more day is still a small sample from the same desk.
questions.explain: Flynn judged a worldwide trend from what crossed his desk. The shopkeeper does the same from one Monday, and a wider record is the remedy.
questions.rule: Test a claim about a trend against a record of the trend.

questions.q: Suppose Flynn had searched for reports on global conflict before the interview. According to Tetlock, what would he have found?
options: Interstate wars falling since the 1950s, civil wars since the early 1990s
Interstate wars rising since the 1950s and civil wars rising since the early 1990s
Interstate wars rising while civil wars fell after the Cold War
No reliable reports, since violence has not been quantified
optionExplain: Right: the reports show declines in both, and battle deaths fell with a few blips.
That reverses the direction the reports show.
That mixes the two trends; interstate wars also declined.
Many reports have quantified global violence since World War II.
questions.explain: A short search would have turned up the declines. Tetlock says Googling the conflict trends would have been enough.
questions.rule: A quick check can overturn a confident impression.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says Flynn's claim about unprecedented societal conflict can be checked against data.
questions.explain: Much of the interview was too vague to judge, but the final line is an empirical claim that reviews of global violence can test.
questions.rule: Separate the checkable claim from the vague talk.

questions.q: A veteran auditor accepts a client's figures because they feel right, though she knows to check assumptions. What does Flynn's case suggest?
options: She lacked the training in checking assumptions that Flynn, an intelligence officer, had
It happens only to people who have not read enough
Skill does not guard her when a belief does not feel like an assumption
More hours of reading would have prevented it
optionExplain: Flynn was a lifelong intelligence officer who knew the importance of checking assumptions.
Flynn read reports for hours; the error came from what the reading did not cover.
Right: Tetlock says Flynn knew assumptions should be checked, but his did not feel like one.
Flynn already read two to three hours each day.
questions.explain: The case shows that skill at checking does not help when the belief never feels like an assumption.
questions.rule: What feels like fact escapes the checking habit.
questions.teaches: Flynn, a lifelong intelligence officer who knew the importance of checking assumptions, did not check because his conclusion did not feel like an assumption.

questions.q: True or false: Knowing that the two Müller-Lyer lines are equal in length does not stop the top one from looking longer.
questions.explain: Tetlock says even after measuring, you cannot see the lines as equal. The card next draws the lesson.
questions.rule: Knowing is not the same as seeing.

questions.q: We can only monitor the answers that bubble up into consciousness and, when we can, use a ____ to check.
questions.explain: The ruler stands for any deliberate check on what intuition produces.
questions.rule: Check intuitive answers with a deliberate test.

questions.q: A restaurant's 4.9 rating rests on nine reviews, yet it still feels like a sure thing. Which move matches Tetlock's advice?
options: Stop feeling the pull by deciding that the rating means nothing
Ignore the number because awareness removes the feeling
Avoid thinking about restaurants until the feeling fades
Notice the pull, then check how many reviewed and who they were
optionExplain: Tetlock says feelings from an illusion cannot be switched off by decision.
He says even knowing an illusion is one does not remove it.
Avoidance does not check anything; the feeling returns with the next rating.
Right: the feeling stays, so the remedy is to check what it rests on.
questions.explain: You cannot stop the sure-thing feeling, so you test its basis, as you would measure the two lines.
questions.rule: Do not try to stop the feeling; check what it tells you.

questions.q: Match each item to its role in Tetlock's argument.
pairs: The egocentric view that cannot be switched off
Equal lines that still look different once measured
A deliberate check on the answers that bubble up
questions.explain: The perspective is the cause, the illusion shows it cannot be switched off, and the ruler stands for the check that is left.
questions.rule: Name the cause, the demonstration and the remedy.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock concludes that, since illusions cannot be switched off, checking our answers is pointless.
questions.explain: He concludes the opposite: because we cannot stop the illusion, we monitor the answers and use a ruler to check them.
questions.rule: Unstoppable does not mean uncheckable.

questions.q: A driver must brake within half a second and has no time to verify what she sees. What does Tetlock's account imply?
options: The illusion fades once she knows it might be wrong
She can reflect carefully, since slow reflection fits in half a second
The impression stands, because checking needs time and capacity
Her impression is accurate because it came to her fast
optionExplain: Tetlock says knowing it is an illusion does not switch it off.
Reflection takes time and effort, which she lacks in half a second.
Right: Tetlock says we use the ruler when we have the time and cognitive capacity.
Speed gives no guarantee of accuracy; the Müller-Lyer lines look wrong at a glance.
questions.explain: Checking is a use of time and capacity. When both run out, the impression is all that remains.
questions.rule: A check needs time and capacity.
questions.teaches: Using a ruler to check an impression is possible only when we have the time and the cognitive capacity.

questions.q: On how far training can protect people against biases, how does Tetlock compare his view with Kahneman's?
options: He is more pessimistic and thinks that training cannot help anyone at all
He holds the same view and sees no difference between them
He thinks biases switch off once a person understands them
He is more optimistic that people can inoculate themselves somewhat
optionExplain: The reverse of what he says; he is the more hopeful.
The chapter says he and Kahneman agree about the slipup risk but not about training.
He says even knowing an illusion does not switch it off.
Right: Tetlock is the more optimistic of the two, though only to some degree.
questions.explain: Tetlock is more hopeful about training than Kahneman. The card next sets out the claim.
questions.rule: Hopeful, but hedged.

questions.q: Tetlock thinks smart, dedicated people can ____ themselves to some degree against certain cognitive illusions.
questions.explain: The word is inoculate. It implies partial protection, not immunity.
questions.rule: Inoculation is partial protection.

questions.q: A firm can recruit and train talented people to resist bias, or rely on its processes alone. Which does Tetlock's reasoning favour?
options: Rely on processes alone, since training cannot reduce any bias in people
Train everyone equally and skip recruiting for talent entirely
Wait for evidence that biases can be switched off first
Recruit and train people to resist biases, since firms gain from it
optionExplain: That is Kahneman's more pessimistic direction, not Tetlock's.
Tetlock speaks of talented, dedicated people, so recruiting matters too.
Tetlock does not say biases can be switched off, only partly resisted.
Right: his argument is that if training helps, organizations gain from recruiting and training talented people.
questions.explain: The practical upshot of Tetlock's optimism is recruiting and training. This is advice from the authors, not a settled result.
questions.rule: If training helps, recruit and train for it.

questions.q: Suppose training could not reduce bias at all. What would follow for Tetlock's advice to organizations?
options: The case would grow stronger, since training would then be needed more
The case for recruiting and training for bias resistance would weaken
The case would be unchanged, since it never depended on the training
The case would turn into a case for making people immune
optionExplain: Advice to train cannot get stronger if training does nothing.
Right: his advice is conditional on his view being right.
He says if he is right, organizations will have more to gain, so it does depend on it.
Immunity is not what he claims.
questions.explain: The conclusion is conditional: if Tetlock is right, organizations gain. If not, the gain disappears.
questions.rule: A conditional conclusion falls with its condition.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock and Kahneman agree on the slipup risk, but Tetlock is more optimistic about training.
questions.explain: He says he is more optimistic that smart, dedicated people can inoculate themselves to some degree.
questions.rule: Read the hedges: some degree, certain illusions.

questions.q: Two scientists disagree about whether a diet works and agree to design one study together. Which Kahneman practice is this?
options: Scope insensitivity, answering an easier question than the one that was asked
Inoculation, building partial protection against an illusion
Adversarial collaboration, working with people who hold different views
WYSIATI, treating what is in view as the whole picture
optionExplain: That is a bias, not a way of working with a rival.
That is Tetlock's term for resisting illusions, not for collaborating.
Right: Kahneman practises adversarial collaboration, as with Gary Klein on expert intuition and Barbara Mellers on superforecasters.
That is a cognitive illusion, not a research practice.
questions.explain: Kahneman resolves disputes by working with those who disagree. He did so with Gary Klein on expert intuition and with Mellers on superforecasters.
questions.rule: Settle a dispute by designing a test together.
questions.teaches: Kahneman practises adversarial collaboration, as he did with Gary Klein on expert intuition and with Barbara Mellers on superforecasters.

questions.q: Groups were asked what they would pay to clean up some lakes in Ontario, or all 250,000. What did the averages show?
options: About 250,000 times more for the larger cleanup
Roughly double for the larger cleanup
About the same amount, near $10 for each
Less for the larger cleanup, because it seemed hopeless to attempt
optionExplain: A fair expectation if people multiplied, but they did not.
A plausible compromise, but the answers were about equal.
Right: both groups gave about $10 on average.
Reasonable-sounding, but the study did not find a drop.
questions.explain: The averages were close to equal. The card next gives Kahneman's explanation.
questions.rule: People's bids barely moved with size.

questions.q: Instead of the question asked, people answer an easier one about their feelings. Tetlock calls this a classic ____ and switch.
questions.explain: The hard question is how much a harm is worth in money. The easier one is how bad it makes you feel.
questions.rule: Bait and switch: a hard question swapped for an easy one.

questions.q: A town hears that a spill harmed 500 ducks, then 50,000. Gifts are about equal both times. Which idea fits?
options: Scope insensitivity: the gift follows the feeling, not the duck count
WYSIATI: residents judged only from what was in front of them, ignoring the stated numbers
A System 2 slipup: residents grew tired of checking the facts
Inoculation: residents trained themselves to resist the bias
optionExplain: Right: the number of ducks changed a hundredfold and the gift barely moved.
Related in spirit, but WYSIATI is about drawing conclusions from what you see, not about ignoring a stated size.
Nothing here is about fatigue in checking.
Inoculation would mean the gifts did follow scope.
questions.explain: A hundredfold change in the count left the gift flat, which is the pattern of the lake and bird studies.
questions.rule: If the size changes and the response does not, suspect scope insensitivity.

questions.q: In the bird study the number rose from 2,000 to 20,000 to 200,000. What did average willingness to pay do?
options: It stayed near $80 each time
It rose in line with the number of birds
It doubled with each tenfold increase
It fell as the numbers grew larger
optionExplain: Right: each group gave about $80.
That would be sensitivity to scope.
A modest rise would still be sensitivity; the study found none.
Even a fall would be a response to scope.
questions.explain: Tenfold rises left the amount near $80. This shows the pattern the lake study showed.
questions.rule: A flat answer across big changes in size marks scope insensitivity.

questions.q: True or false: Kahneman explains the results by saying people respond to a prototype image such as an oil-soaked duck.
questions.explain: He says the prototype evokes an emotional response, and people answer how bad it makes them feel.
questions.rule: A feeling, not a calculation, sets the amount.

questions.q: A charity shows one hungry child, then says 10,000 children need help. Gifts barely rise. What does Kahneman's account say donors map onto dollars?
options: A careful estimate of the cost of helping each hungry child
The total number of children, discounted for doubt
Their level of trust in the charity's accounts
The intensity of the emotion the prototype image evokes
optionExplain: That would be a calculation, which scope insensitivity replaces.
That would make gifts grow with the count, which is what does not happen.
Trust is not part of Kahneman's explanation.
Right: Kahneman wrote that the prototype evokes an affective response, and its intensity is mapped onto the dollar scale.
questions.explain: The feeling's intensity is converted into an amount, so the donor answers how bad it makes them feel.
questions.rule: The amount follows the feeling's intensity.
questions.teaches: Kahneman wrote that the prototype evokes an affective response whose intensity is then mapped onto the dollar scale.

questions.q: Regular forecasters were asked whether Assad's regime would fall within three months, or within six. What did they say on average?
options: About 40% for three months and 41% for six months
About 20% for three months and 41% for six months
About 41% for three months and about 24% for six months
About 15% for three months and 24% for six months
optionExplain: Right: their answers were almost identical across the two time frames.
A rise like that would show sensitivity to the time frame, which they lacked.
A fall with a longer window makes no sense, and is not what they said.
These are the superforecasters' figures, not the regular forecasters'.
questions.explain: The two answers were almost the same, so the time frame made little difference. The card next sets out why that matters.
questions.rule: Nearly equal answers across time frames signal scope insensitivity.

questions.q: In Tetlock's account, the time frame of a forecast is its ____.
questions.explain: The longer the window, the more likely the event, so a sensitive forecaster's probability should rise with the window.
questions.rule: Time frame is scope.

questions.q: Asked about flooding within one week and within one year, a forecaster says 30% to both. What does Tetlock's account suggest?
options: She is scope sensitive, because the two answers match each other exactly
She may be answering on the strength of evidence, ignoring the window
She has avoided bait and switch by keeping her answer steady
She has given the one answer that the evidence allows for both windows
optionExplain: Matching answers are the warning sign, not the sign of sensitivity.
Right: a year is a larger window than a week, so a probability that does not change is suspect.
Keeping the number steady is the bait and switch, answering an easier question.
A longer window should allow more chances, so one answer for both is odd.
questions.explain: Equal answers for a week and a year suggest she weighed the evidence and skipped the time frame, as most regular forecasters did.
questions.rule: A probability that ignores the window deserves a second look.

questions.q: Match each group and time frame to the average probability it gave that the Assad regime would fall.
questions.explain: Regular forecasters barely moved between windows, while superforecasters gave a clearly higher figure for the longer window.
questions.rule: Compare the change between windows, not just the levels.

questions.q: In 2012 the arguments for and against Assad's fall felt roughly equal. What did that weighing leave out?
options: The sources, which the weighing should have listed before anything else
The time frame, which weighing the arguments alone cannot supply
The rebels' strength, which the weighing treated as zero
The regional allies, which the weighing counted twice
optionExplain: Sources are not what the passage says was missing.
Right: the arguments could be balanced and still say nothing about when.
Rebel momentum was among the arguments weighed.
Allies were among the arguments against a fall, counted once.
questions.explain: Balanced arguments give a rough 50% with no deadline attached. Without a time frame the number cannot answer a question about timing.
questions.rule: Arguments tell you which way, not how soon.
questions.teaches: Weighing the arguments for and against Assad's fall, which felt roughly equal, yields about 50% but says nothing about the time frame.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says superforecasters showed perfect scope sensitivity in the Assad questions.
questions.explain: He says it was not perfect scope sensitivity, a tricky thing to define, but good enough to surprise Kahneman.
questions.rule: Quote the result at its true strength.

questions.q: Two analyst groups each saw only one version of a question, three or twelve months, yet their answers differed sensibly. What does this suggest?
options: Each copied the other, since the answers moved together
Each saw both versions, so they compared them directly
Each weighed the time frame, perhaps by picturing other deadlines
Each ignored the time frame and answered only from the strength of evidence
optionExplain: Nothing in the setup lets them copy one another.
The design means no one was asked both versions.
Right: Tetlock reasons that superforecasters thought about other time frames themselves, since no one was asked both.
Ignoring the time frame would give equal answers, as with regular forecasters.
questions.explain: Because no one saw both versions, differing answers point to people who imagined the other time frame on their own.
questions.rule: Between-group differences with no direct comparison suggest the habit of imagining other time frames.
questions.teaches: Because no one was asked both the three- and six-month versions, the superforecasters' different answers suggest they also thought about other possible time frames.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says his team's guidelines taught superforecasters about scope before they had thought about the problem themselves.
questions.explain: He says superforecasters were already talking about the problem, though not with that term. The card next gives the guidance.
questions.rule: The practice came from both sides.

questions.q: The guidelines urge forecasters to mentally ____ with the question asked, for example by moving the cutoff date.
questions.explain: Tinkering means changing a detail of the question in your head and seeing whether your answer moves.
questions.rule: Tinker with the question and watch the answer.

questions.q: A forecaster is asked if a share price will pass $50 by December. Which step follows the guidelines?
options: Ask how her answer changes if the date were June or the target were $45
Ask whether her first answer feels right and keep it if it does feel right
Ask colleagues to settle on a single number before she goes on
Ask whether the company's chief executive will resign by December
optionExplain: Right: she varies the date and the target to see whether her model responds.
A feeling of rightness is what the exercise is meant to test.
Agreement among colleagues does not test sensitivity to the details.
A different question altogether is not a variation of this one.
questions.explain: The guidelines' own examples change a cutoff date or a target price. The share-price question invites the same moves.
questions.rule: Vary the date or the target and see if the answer moves.

questions.q: After tinkering, a forecaster finds her answer would be the same for a six-month or a twelve-month cutoff. What should she conclude?
options: Her model may be ignoring the time frame, so she should recheck it
Her model is robust, so the check is complete and nothing more is needed
The time frame is irrelevant to this kind of question
She has reached perfect scope sensitivity and need not check again
optionExplain: Right: an unchanged answer across very different windows is the scope-insensitivity signal.
Robustness here would mean the answer moved sensibly.
A longer window gives more room for the event, so it matters.
Equal answers across windows show the opposite of sensitivity.
questions.explain: The exercise exists to expose answers that stay flat when they should move. Our reading: a flat answer calls for a recheck.
questions.rule: A flat answer to a changed question is a warning sign.

questions.q: True or false: According to Tetlock, superforecasters were discussing scope insensitivity-type problems before his team gave the topic a name.
questions.explain: He says they were talking about the problems, though not with that term, before his team studied them.
questions.rule: Practice can precede the theory that names it.

questions.q: A hospital's best nurses use a habit the trainers later write into the manual, which then improves other nurses. Which relationship did Tetlock describe?
options: The guidelines came first and shaped the habit alone
The habit stayed private and the guidelines ignored it
Practice and guidelines shaped each other, as with superforecasters
The habit was invented by the trainers and handed down to the nurses
optionExplain: That reverses the order; the practice was there first.
In Tetlock's account the guidelines used what superforecasters did.
Right: Tetlock says superforecasters' thinking informed the guidelines as much as the guidelines informed their thinking.
The superforecasters were already raising the problems.
questions.explain: The influence ran both ways between the superforecasters and the guidelines.
questions.rule: Good practice can feed training, and training can feed practice.
questions.teaches: Tetlock says the superforecasters' thinking informed his team's training guidelines as much as the guidelines informed their thinking.

questions.q: In Tetlock's golfer example, how do the first few tries at a new stance go?
options: Awkward, needing a mental checklist, with something still forgotten
They feel natural at once, since the body knows what to do
They go smoothly after one lesson once the steps are understood
They prove hopeless, which is why most golfers give the stance up in the end
optionExplain: Right: the first three tries are laborious, then it gets easier with practice.
The example stresses awkwardness at first.
One lesson is not enough; she is corrected on the first and again on the third try.
She keeps at it and succeeds; the example is not about giving up.
questions.explain: The golfer starts with a laborious checklist and ends with graceful habit. The card next draws the lesson.
questions.rule: Practice makes effort automatic.

questions.q: A golfer who keeps at it eventually buries the instructions in System ____ and does it all gracefully.
questions.explain: The steps start as conscious System 2 checking and end as automatic System 1 operation.
questions.rule: Practised steps migrate to System 1.

questions.q: A new analyst runs a checklist on every report. After a year she does most of it without thinking. Which idea fits?
options: Her System 2 has stopped working and System 1 took over
She has become immune to every bias the checklist was meant to cover
She has given up checking in favour of her intuition
A System 2 correction has become habitual, part of her System 1
optionExplain: The checking still happens, now without effort.
Tetlock claims partial protection at most, not immunity.
She still checks; the checks have become automatic.
Right: practice has made the correction second nature.
questions.explain: Her checks have moved from effortful to automatic, as the golfer's stance did. The checks are the same; the effort is not.
questions.rule: Habit lightens the effort without removing the correction.

questions.q: Match each example in Tetlock's account to the point it illustrates.
pairs: A golfer learning to stand at the tee
A skill moving from System 2 to System 1 through practice
An early stage of a skill that is automatic for adult readers
A tool that lightens the load without relying on habit
questions.explain: The golfer and the child show practice making effort automatic, while software offers a different way to cut the load.
questions.rule: Two routes to a lighter load: practice and tools.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says that once a correction becomes habitual, superforecasting stops being hard work.
questions.explain: He says superforecasting remains hard work, and that those who do it well expect to stumble.
questions.rule: Habit helps; it does not end the effort.

questions.q: A researcher builds a script that shows her articles from sources she usually disagrees with. Which kind of aid from the chapter is this?
options: A habit that has become second nature through repetition
A software tool that corrects a pull toward the like-minded
A thought experiment that varies the time frame of a question
A ruler that checks an illusion by measuring it directly
optionExplain: A habit comes from practice, not from software.
Right: Doug Lorch's news-source selection program was designed to correct the System 1 bias in favour of the like-minded.
That exercise tinkers with the question asked.
The ruler is a check on a visual illusion.
questions.explain: Software can do part of the correcting so that the forecaster does not have to. Lorch's program was built for the like-minded bias.
questions.rule: Tools can carry some of the load.
questions.teaches: Doug Lorch built a news-source selection program to correct the System 1 bias in favour of the like-minded.

questions.q: In Tetlock's story of a European four centuries ago, what stunned him?
options: A flock of white swans larger than any he had seen
A black swan brought back on a ship from Australia
A white swan with unusual markings seen in Europe
A swan that could not fly, sold at a harbour market
optionExplain: Size and shape varied in what he imagined, but all swans were white.
Right: his experience held only white swans.
Markings are not the point; colour is.
Flight is not part of the story.
questions.explain: He had seen only white swans, so a black one was outside what he could imagine. The card next draws out the metaphor.
questions.rule: Experience sets the limits of what we can picture.

questions.q: Taleb says a black swan must be not only surprising but also ____.
questions.explain: Tetlock reports that a black swan must be impactful, so an event with trivial effects would not qualify.
questions.rule: A black swan is both unimaginable and impactful.

questions.q: Which event best fits Tetlock's description of a black swan?
options: A collapse from a cause nobody imagined, with huge effects
An election result that polls had put at a 45% chance
A storm forecast days ahead that caused the expected damage
A minor surprise in a busy field with no lasting effect
optionExplain: Right: unimagined before it happened, and impactful.
A result with a 45% chance was easily imaginable.
A forecast storm is neither unimagined nor a surprise.
Lasting effect is missing, so Taleb would not count it.
questions.explain: Two tests apply: it could not be imagined beforehand, and its effects were large.
questions.rule: Both conditions must hold: unimaginable and impactful.

questions.q: Sort each case by whether it fits the black swan metaphor as Tetlock describes it.

items.t: An event nobody could imagine beforehand, with huge effects
A European meets a black swan after seeing only white ones
A flood that experts warned of a week in advance
A small surprise that left nothing changed

questions.explain: The first two are outside experience and, in the first case, impactful. The last two are either expected or unimportant.
questions.rule: Test for unimaginable beforehand and impactful afterwards.

questions.q: True or false: According to Tetlock, Taleb counts any surprise at all as a black swan.
questions.explain: A black swan must also be impactful; surprise alone does not suffice.
questions.rule: Surprise is necessary; impact is also required.

questions.q: A farmer who has seen only dry autumns for fifty years cannot picture a flood. Which part of the swan story does this mirror?
options: A surprise counts as a black swan only if it is also impactful
A black swan arrives on a ship from far away
Experts should have predicted the event in time
Experience limits the range of events a person can picture
optionExplain: True of Taleb's definition, but the farmer's case is about imagination.
The ship is a detail of the story, not its point.
Nothing in the farmer's case implies experts could have predicted it.
Right: the European pictured swans of every size and shape, yet all white, because experience had shown no others.
questions.explain: The European's imagination varied in size and shape but stayed white, because his experience was all white. The farmer's imagination is bounded the same way.
questions.rule: What we can picture is bounded by what we have seen.
questions.teaches: The European imagined swans that varied in size and shape but were all white, because his experience had taught him all swans are white.

questions.q: As Tetlock reports it, how does Taleb's view bear on the forecasting tournaments?
options: They are a fool's errand, since what matters cannot be forecast
They are useful, since black swans can be forecast with practice
They are redundant, since forecasting has already been perfected
They are sound, but need longer time frames in order to work
optionExplain: Right: that is Tetlock's summary of what the critique implies for his work.
Taleb denies that black swans can be forecast.
He does not say forecasting is perfected.
He does not ask for longer time frames; he says what matters cannot be forecast.
questions.explain: Taleb's view makes the whole research programme look pointless. The card next gives the argument.
questions.rule: If only jumps matter and jumps cannot be forecast, forecasting does not matter.

questions.q: Per Taleb, history does not crawl; it makes ____.
questions.explain: That line carries his claim that sudden, large events drive history.
questions.rule: History makes jumps, in Taleb's view.

questions.q: An investor says only rare shocks move markets, so tracking quarterly earnings is pointless. Which of Taleb's claims does this echo?
options: Forecasting is feasible for anyone who follows a particular formula closely
Slow change adds up to large effects across centuries
What matters cannot be forecast; what can be forecast does not matter
Experts do better at short horizons than at long ones
optionExplain: That is the claim on the opposite side of Tetlock's false dichotomy.
That is Tetlock's counter-point about crawling, not Taleb's claim.
Right: the investor treats what can be tracked as unimportant.
Tetlock makes that point about horizons, but it is not the investor's argument.
questions.explain: The investor accepts only jumps as important, so everyday tracking looks pointless.
questions.rule: Jumps only, so little to forecast that matters.

questions.q: Match each position in this debate to what it says.
pairs: Black swans alone decide history, so forecasting is bunk
The other half of the false dichotomy
Forecasting is feasible if you follow my formula
Both extremes are mistaken, and Taleb's points are serious
questions.explain: Tetlock places Taleb at one end and a formula-confident forecaster at the other, then rejects both.
questions.rule: Name both extremes before rejecting them.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock dismisses Taleb's critique as shallow and not worth a reply.
questions.explain: Tetlock says he respects Taleb and thinks the critique makes deep points future tournaments must struggle to address.
questions.rule: Take the strongest form of a critique seriously.

questions.q: A pundit rejects both my model is infallible and all prediction is bunk, yet co-writes a paper with a critic. Whom does she resemble?
options: Taleb, who holds that only jumps matter in history
A formula believer, who thinks forecasting works by method
Flynn, who judged the world from what lay on his desk
Tetlock, who respects Taleb and co-wrote a paper with him
optionExplain: Taleb stands at one end of the dichotomy.
The formula believer is the other end.
Flynn is Tetlock's example of WYSIATI, not of balanced dialogue.
Right: Tetlock says he and Taleb cowrote a paper on a key area where they agree.
questions.explain: Tetlock engages with his critic while rejecting both ends of the dichotomy.
questions.rule: Engage the critic and keep the point of agreement.
questions.teaches: Tetlock and Taleb have cowritten a paper on a key area where they agree.

questions.q: True or false: According to Tetlock, a 1994 plot to crash a hijacked jet into the Eiffel Tower was broken up.
questions.explain: Tetlock cites it as evidence that using planes as weapons was conceivable. The card next lays out the case.
questions.rule: Check whether the event was conceivable beforehand.

questions.q: In 1998 the US Federal Aviation Administration examined a scenario of hijacked ____ cargo planes crashed into the World Trade Center.
questions.explain: That scenario predates 9/11 by three years.
questions.rule: The scenario had been examined years earlier.

questions.q: A firm calls its main supplier's bankruptcy a black swan, though auditors flagged the risk two years earlier. By Tetlock's strict test, what is it?
options: A true black swan, since it still came as a surprise to the managers
A black swan, since the bankruptcy had large consequences
More like a gray swan, because it was not inconceivable beforehand
Neither, since a bankruptcy cannot surprise anyone at all
optionExplain: Surprise to some managers is not the test; inconceivability beforehand is.
Impact is only one of the two requirements.
Right: the warning shows the event could be conceived, which fails the strict test.
Surprise to some is possible; the point is that it was conceivable.
questions.explain: Auditors had raised the possibility, as security circles had raised airplane attacks before 9/11.
questions.rule: A prior warning makes an event gray, not black.

questions.q: Apply the strict definition to history's famous black swans, event by event. What does Tetlock expect to happen to their number?
options: It grows, since each event looks stranger when it is examined closely
It shrinks, since many of them were conceived of beforehand
It stays the same, since surprise is what defines them
It falls to zero, since every one of them was predicted
optionExplain: Closer scrutiny finds precedents rather than more strangeness.
Right: if black swans must be inconceivable, a rare species becomes much rarer.
On the strict test surprise alone does not suffice.
Being conceived beforehand is not the same as being predicted.
questions.explain: The strict test removes cases like 9/11. Tetlock says the rare species suddenly becomes a lot rarer.
questions.rule: A stricter definition means fewer qualifying cases.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says the Richardson exchange shows security experts in August 2001 thought an airplane could not be used as a bomb.
questions.explain: Richardson answered that the tactic was very much under consideration and some groups would probably use it before long.
questions.rule: Read what the expert actually said.

questions.q: A blackout is called a black swan, though engineers had warned of such blackouts for a decade. Which chapter case does this mirror?
options: Flynn's reading of conflict data from the stack of reports on his own desk
The golfer who buries instructions in System 1
World War I, preceded by over a decade of worry about great-power war
The lakes study in which bids stayed near $10
optionExplain: Flynn's case is about checking claims, not conceivability.
The golfer shows habit, not conceivability.
Right: Tetlock says World War I was also preceded by more than a decade of fretting and so fails the unimaginability test.
The lakes study is about scope, not black swans.
questions.explain: A decade of warnings means the event was conceivable. Tetlock makes the same point about World War I.
questions.rule: Years of warnings show an event was conceivable.
questions.teaches: World War I, also called a black swan, was preceded by more than a decade of fretting about the danger of war among the great powers.

questions.q: According to Tetlock, what does the first IARPA tournament show about superforecasters' skill at spotting gray or black swans?
options: That they spot them better than regular forecasters do
That they spot them no better than pure chance would
Nothing either way; they may be clueless or astonishingly adept
That they spot them only when the event is under a year away from now
optionExplain: The data cannot support that claim.
Equally, the data cannot support this claim.
Right: the tournament's questions cannot tell us.
No time limit like that is reported; the problem is rarity of the events.
questions.explain: The tournament cannot speak to rare events. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Absence of evidence is not evidence of failure.

questions.q: Taleb also offers a more modest definition of a black swan: a highly improbable ____ event.
questions.explain: The modest definition drops the demand that the event be inconceivable but keeps its large impact.
questions.rule: Modest definition: highly improbable and consequential.

questions.q: A weather bureau has checked 5,000 daily rain forecasts. Following Tetlock's reasoning, what can it not conclude from them?
options: Whether its 70% days saw rain about 70% of the time
How well it forecasts a once-in-a-thousand-years storm
Whether it is well calibrated on everyday rain
How its accuracy compares with its record from last year
optionExplain: Frequent events give enough data to check this.
Right: such storms are too rare to build a record of forecasts about them.
Calibration on frequent events can be judged from a large sample.
Comparing yearly accuracy on common events is possible.
questions.explain: Short-horizon, frequent questions allow calibration to be judged. A once-in-a-thousand-years storm cannot be judged that way.
questions.rule: Skill can only be measured where outcomes recur.

questions.q: A tournament's questions concern events with a 0.1% chance. What does Tetlock's reasoning imply about the time needed for enough data?
options: A few months, since forecasts can be made quickly by one analyst
About a year, as with the first IARPA tournament
No time, since rare events are easy to calibrate
Decades or centuries, since such events almost never happen
optionExplain: Forecasts are quick to make, but outcomes are what take time.
The first tournament dealt with frequent events, not rare ones.
Rarity makes calibration harder, not easier.
Right: collecting enough occurrences of a 0.1% event takes a very long time.
questions.explain: The scarcity of outcomes sets the time needed, not the speed of making forecasts.
questions.rule: The wait is for outcomes, not forecasts.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says the first tournament proves that superforecasters cannot spot black swans.
questions.explain: He says the tournament tells us nothing about it either way: they may be as clueless as anyone or astonishingly adept.
questions.rule: No evidence of skill is not evidence of no skill.

questions.q: A bank tests risk officers on 2,000 routine loan-default forecasts. A director says this shows they can spot a once-in-a-century crisis. What follows?
