options: Frequent events were tested; a rare, impactful crisis is harder still
The claim stands, since 2,000 forecasts is a large sample of loan cases
The claim fails only if the officers were wrong on defaults
The claim stands, since crises resemble routine defaults
optionExplain: Right: the test cannot say anything about events too rare to occur in the sample.
Size of sample does not make rare events appear.
Even perfect accuracy on defaults would leave rare events untested.
Tetlock treats rare, consequential events as a separate case.
questions.explain: Requiring the events to be impactful as well as highly improbable multiplies the difficulty of gathering data.
questions.rule: Frequent-event skill does not certify rare-event skill.
questions.teaches: Requiring events to be impactful as well as highly improbable multiplies the difficulty of gathering enough data.

questions.q: According to Tetlock, what do global growth rates of 1% a year in the nineteenth century and 2% in the twentieth show?
options: Slow, steady change can add up to unprecedented wealth
Growth is driven mainly by rare sudden jumps in technology
Growth rates cannot be forecast by anyone over long periods
Wealth in the twenty-first century is spread evenly across society
optionExplain: Right: small yearly changes, compounded, transformed the world.
That is Taleb's emphasis, not what these rates show.
Tetlock says nothing of the kind here.
Tetlock makes no claim here about how wealth is spread across people.
questions.explain: Tetlock uses these rates to argue that slow change is not trivial. The card next sets out the argument.
questions.rule: Compounding turns small steady change into large change.

questions.q: Tetlock says history does sometimes jump, but it also ____.
questions.explain: He accepts Taleb's jumps and adds slow movement as a second force.
questions.rule: History jumps and crawls.

questions.q: A planner says only sudden disasters matter for a city's future. Which example from Tetlock answers her best?
options: A European meets a black swan after seeing only white ones
A 1994 plot to crash a hijacked jet into the Eiffel Tower was broken up
Growth of 1% to 2% a year turned past squalor into present wealth
A general judges the world from reports stacked on his desk
optionExplain: That illustrates the idea of a black swan, which is a jump.
That is a conceivability case about a sudden attack.
Right: slow compounding growth shows that gradual change can transform a society.
That illustrates WYSIATI, not slow change.
questions.explain: A planner who watches only for jumps misses the changes that accumulate year after year.
questions.rule: Watch the crawl as well as the jump.

questions.q: A forecaster correctly anticipates slow trends such as growth in average wealth. By Tetlock's argument, is her work trivial?
options: No, since slow incremental change can be profoundly important
Yes, since only black swans change the course of history
Yes, since slow trends are already known to everyone
No, since slow trends matter far more than any single sudden jump could
optionExplain: Right: slow change added up to the wealth of today's world.
That is Taleb's view, which Tetlock argues against.
Tetlock gives no reason to think slow trends are universally known.
Tetlock concedes that history does sometimes jump, so he does not rank slow change above jumps.
questions.explain: Tetlock places both jumps and slow change among the forces that matter.
questions.rule: Slow does not mean trivial.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says slow, incremental change can be profoundly important.
questions.explain: He says history sometimes jumps but also crawls, and slow change can matter profoundly.
questions.rule: He adds crawling to jumping, not one for the other.

questions.q: A public-health official says only pandemics shape population health, so no steady trend matters. Which of Tetlock's examples best answers her?
options: The sudden fall of a government within a single week
A hijacked plane striking a tower on a sunny morning
A swan from Australia that surprised a European
The inch-worm advance in life expectancy
optionExplain: That is a jump, not a slow trend.
That is another jump, a surprise attack.
That is the black swan metaphor, which is about surprise.
Right: Tetlock names the inch-worm advance in life expectancy as an example of slow change that matters.
questions.explain: Life expectancy has advanced slowly but has changed lives profoundly.
questions.rule: Steady health gains show slow change at work.
questions.teaches: Tetlock cites the inch-worm advance in life expectancy as another case of slow change that matters.

questions.q: Vinod Khosla spreads many investments and expects most to fail. What payoff does he hope for?
options: Steady modest returns from most of the investments he makes
One or two rare start-ups that yield a Google-size fortune
A forecast that beats rivals by a few percentage points
Protection against loss in case every single bet fails
optionExplain: That describes the forecasting approach, not his.
Right: he accepts many failures in return for a rare huge winner.
That also describes the forecasting approach.
He expects most bets to fail and accepts the losses.
questions.explain: Khosla's strategy lives on rare huge wins. The card next compares it with another way.
questions.rule: Many small losses, one huge win.

questions.q: Tetlock says the approach of beating rivals by forecasting more accurately is the one used by the best ____ players.
questions.explain: Judging odds a little better than the others wins more often, in modest amounts.
questions.rule: Poker players profit from small edges in accuracy.

questions.q: A fund buys many risky start-ups, expecting most to fail, hoping for one huge winner. Which approach is this?
options: Black swan investing, as Khosla practises it
Accurate forecasting, as the best poker players use it
Scope-sensitive forecasting, adjusting odds to time frames
Inoculation, building protection against a cognitive illusion
optionExplain: Right: this is spreading bets for a rare outsized payoff.
Poker players profit from small edges in accuracy, not from rare jackpots.
That is about matching probabilities to time frames, not investing style.
Inoculation is partial protection against bias.
questions.explain: The fund's pattern is Khosla's: many bets, most failing, one hoped-for fortune.
questions.rule: Spread bets for a rare outsized payoff is black swan investing.

questions.q: Sort each feature by the investing approach it describes in Tetlock's account.

items.t: Spread bets, expecting most to fail
Hope for one Google-size winner
Judge 68% where others say 60%
Pays off more often, with modest returns
Fortunes are amassed slowly
The way Taleb traded before becoming an author

questions.explain: One approach lives on rare huge wins, the other on frequent small ones.
questions.rule: Rare and huge versus frequent and modest.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says black swan investing and accurate forecasting are different, with neither superior.
questions.explain: He says neither is superior nor inferior; it is different.
questions.rule: Different is not better.

questions.q: A friend declines a 90% chance of failing but joins a 10% chance of changing the world. What does this show?
options: That people calculate odds correctly whatever wording is used to present them
That friends avoid the forecasting approach of poker players
That Taleb's way of trading is unsuited to ordinary people
How a bet is framed changes how people feel about the same odds
optionExplain: The two descriptions are of the same odds, yet feelings differ.
The scheme is not about poker.
Nothing in the chapter says that.
Right: Khosla observed that people dislike a 90% chance of failing but love a 10% chance of changing the world.
questions.explain: Khosla's remark shows why many lack the stomach for black swan investing: the same odds feel different when worded as failure or as a chance to change the world.
questions.rule: Wording sets the feeling about identical odds.
questions.teaches: Khosla remarked that people dislike a 90% chance of failing but love a 10% chance of changing the world, which describes the same bet.

questions.q: What does Tetlock say we mean today by the storming of the Bastille?
options: Only the mob taking the prison on the single day of July 14, 1789, and nothing after
The mob action of July 14 plus the events that spiraled into the Revolution
Only the later revolution, with the prison day itself set aside
The national holiday celebrated in France each year on that date
optionExplain: Tetlock says we mean something much bigger than that day.
Right: the label covers the event together with its consequences.
The label includes the prison day as the starting point.
The holiday is a result, not the meaning of the phrase.
questions.explain: The label stretches to cover what followed. The card next draws out what that means for black swans.
questions.rule: The name of an event grows to include its consequences.

questions.q: The sociologist Duncan ____ wrote that the more you want to explain about a black swan, the broader you must draw its boundaries.
questions.explain: Watts's point is that the boundaries of the event widen with what we want explained.
questions.rule: Draw the boundaries wider to explain more.

questions.q: A company calls its product recall a black swan, meaning the recall plus the lawsuits and the brand collapse. Which idea fits?
options: A strict black swan that was inconceivable before it happened
Black swan status comes from the event plus its consequences
A gray swan that others had imagined in some detail beforehand
An inch-worm advance, slow change that adds up over time
optionExplain: Nothing here tests conceivability.
Right: the recall alone was small, but its chain of consequences makes the label fit.
The label is about consequences, not about earlier warnings.
The chain here is a rapid sequence, not a slow crawl.
questions.explain: The wider the boundaries drawn around the recall, the more black swan-like it appears.
questions.rule: Consequences widen the event.

questions.q: Suppose the Taliban had handed over bin Laden after the evidence request. How would 9/11 look, in Tetlock's reading?
options: Unchanged, since the attacks alone were the whole event
A tragedy, but not the opening shot in a decade of wars
Larger, since the Taliban's help would have added to it
Forgotten, since a tragedy without wars is not remembered
optionExplain: Tetlock says the consequences are part of what we mean by 9/11.
Right: Tetlock says we would see it differently without the invasion and the hunt.
Handing over bin Laden would have shortened the chain, not lengthened it.
Tetlock calls it a tragedy certainly, so it would not be forgotten.
questions.explain: Since the consequences make the swan, different consequences make a different swan.
questions.rule: Change the consequences and the event changes.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says superforecasters have been shown to foresee the 9/11 attacks themselves.
questions.explain: He says there may be no evidence that they can foresee events like 9/11. His claim is about forecasting the consequences.
questions.rule: Do not stretch the claim from consequences to the shock.

questions.q: A volcano erupts. Which question matches the kind of consequence question Tetlock says superforecasters can answer?
options: Will an eruption nobody could imagine ever happen?
Will the government declare an evacuation zone within two weeks?
Will historians call it the greatest natural event of the century?
On which exact day will the next eruption begin?
optionExplain: That repeats the unforecastable shock question.
Right: it asks about a definite consequence within a window, like the Taliban and bin Laden questions.
That is not a definite question with a clear resolution.
That asks for the timing of a shock, not a consequence.
questions.explain: Tetlock's examples are about responses and moves after the shock, each with a definite answer.
questions.rule: Forecast the consequences you can pin down.
questions.teaches: Tetlock cites forecastable questions such as whether the US would threaten military action if the Taliban did not hand over bin Laden, whether the Taliban would comply, and whether bin Laden would flee.

questions.q: In Tetlock's EPJ research, what happened to the accuracy of expert predictions about five years out?
options: It held as high as it had been at one year
It rose, as experts gained confidence over time
It fell below chance, so experts were reliably wrong
It declined toward chance
optionExplain: Accuracy fell as the horizon grew.
Confidence may rise, but accuracy did not.
Falling toward chance is not falling below it.
Right: by five years out experts did little better than chance.
questions.explain: Accuracy decays with distance. The card next gives Tetlock's explanation.
questions.rule: Accuracy decays toward chance as the horizon lengthens.

questions.q: Tetlock says limits on predictability follow from the ____ dynamics of nonlinear systems.
questions.explain: Small causes can ripple into large effects, which is what limits foresight.
questions.rule: Butterfly dynamics limit predictability.

questions.q: A magazine's cover story predicts the world economy in ten years. What does Tetlock's agreement with Taleb and Kahneman imply?
options: It is reliable if enough experts contributed to it
Beyond the obvious, no evidence supports it, apart from lucky hits
It is reliable if the magazine has a strong record
It is reliable for economics, though not for geopolitical questions
optionExplain: More experts do not produce evidence of skill at that horizon.
Right: the three agree there is no evidence of skill at that horizon.
A record on short horizons does not carry over.
Tetlock names geopolitical or economic forecasters alike.
questions.explain: With many forecasts and many forecasters, some hits will land by luck, so they prove nothing.
questions.rule: At long horizons a hit is not evidence of skill.

questions.q: Thousands of forecasters each make several ten-year predictions. What does Tetlock's reasoning lead you to expect?
options: Most predictions correct, because there are so many
No hits at all, because the horizon is too long
A few lucky hits, which would not show real skill
Hits that cluster among the most senior experts
optionExplain: Numbers do not make forecasts correct.
Chance will produce some correct calls.
Right: with so many forecasts, chance alone yields some hits.
Seniority is not given as a predictor.
questions.explain: Lucky hits are inevitable whenever lots of forecasters make lots of forecasts.
questions.rule: Count the luck before crediting skill.

questions.q: True or false: Linton Wells's piece, sent on by Rumsfeld, predicted the 2001 terrorist attacks.
questions.explain: The piece argued that the future is hard to predict and was sent five months before 9/11. It did not predict the attacks.
questions.rule: A warning about uncertainty is not a prediction.

questions.q: A government must by law publish a twenty-year security forecast every four years. What does Tetlock say about such rituals?
options: They are sound, since the law forces experts to improve
They are harmless, since nobody relies on them in practice
They are rare, since institutions know the limits of forecasts
They persist even in institutions that should know better
optionExplain: Improvement by compulsion is not what he says.
He sees them as a notable error, not a harmless one.
He says this sort of forecasting is common.
Right: Tetlock says such forecasting is common even within institutions that should know better.
questions.explain: Congress requires the Defense Department to produce a twenty-year forecast every four years, the Quadrennial Defense Review. It prompted Linton Wells's rebellious article.
questions.rule: Institutional habit can outlast the evidence.
questions.teaches: Congress requires the Defense Department to produce a twenty-year forecast every four years, the Quadrennial Defense Review, which prompted Linton Wells to write his article.

questions.q: Linton Wells's closing advice about the future was to plan for what?
options: A future very little like what we expect
A future that closely extends current trends
A future whose key events experts will name in time
A future decided by whichever side spends most
optionExplain: Right: he was sure it would be very little like what we expect.
That is the expectation he warns against.
Naming events in advance is what he doubts.
Spending is not part of his argument.
questions.explain: Wells advises accepting surprise and planning for it. The card next draws out the advice.
questions.rule: Expect to be surprised.

questions.q: Eisenhower said plans are useless but ____ is indispensable.
questions.explain: The plan may fail on contact, but the thinking that produced it prepares people.
questions.rule: The act of planning matters more than the plan.

questions.q: A town on a river cannot predict which year its next big flood will come. Which step follows the chapter's advice?
options: Postpone all preparation until a forecast names the year
Prepare adaptable responses for different kinds of floods
Bet the budget on the single flood scenario most experts name
Predict the exact year and prepare only for that one
optionExplain: Waiting for a forecast that cannot come leaves the town unprepared.
Right: when timing cannot be forecast, build adaptability and resilience.
A single scenario is exactly the bet that a surprise defeats.
That relies on the forecast the chapter says cannot be made.
questions.explain: The advice is to prepare for surprise in general when the timing cannot be known.
questions.rule: When you cannot forecast, make yourself adaptable.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning in this part of the chapter.
pairs: Preparing for a future unlike the one expected
questions.explain: Resilience is the lower bar; antifragility adds gain from shocks.
questions.rule: Resilient survives; antifragile improves.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock cites Eisenhower's remark in support of planning for surprise.
questions.explain: Eisenhower said plans are useless but planning is indispensable, and Tetlock uses it to back preparing for surprise.
questions.rule: Read both halves of the remark.

questions.q: A principal drafts responses for a fire, then a flood, then a power cut, without predicting which comes. Which exercise from the chapter is this?
options: Tinkering with the time frame of a question to test its scope
Imagining several blows and rehearsing a response to each
Spreading bets in the hope of one huge winner
Measuring two lines to check an optical illusion
optionExplain: That exercise tests scope sensitivity.
Right: Danzig suggests imagining a smack in the ear, then a kick in the shin, and thinking how to respond to each.
That is black swan investing.
That is the ruler check for the Müller-Lyer illusion.
questions.explain: The principal rehearses several different blows instead of picking one. That is Danzig's exercise in practice.
questions.rule: Rehearse several blows, not one forecast.
questions.teaches: Danzig's exercise is to imagine reality giving you a smack in the ear and think how you would respond, then assume it gives a kick in the shin.

questions.q: Why, according to Tetlock, do big new buildings in Tokyo need advanced earthquake engineering that some other regions do not?
options: Tokyo is prone to big quakes, so the costly standard makes sense there
Tokyo's earthquakes can be timed exactly, so builders prepare each time
Poorer countries cannot afford such standards, whatever the risk
Seismologists have shown the standard pays off in every region
optionExplain: Right: the cost is justified by how likely and how big the quakes are.
Tetlock says the timing cannot be predicted with precision.
He ties the choice to risk, not just to wealth.
He says the standard makes less sense where big quakes are less likely.
questions.explain: The cost is worth paying only where the odds are high enough. The card next draws out the general point.
questions.rule: Pay for protection where the odds justify it.

questions.q: For decades the United States kept the capacity to fight ____ wars at once, but not three or four.
questions.explain: The two-war doctrine rested on a judgment about how likely it was that two wars would come together.
questions.rule: Doctrine rests on a probability judgment.

questions.q: A coastal village weighs a costly sea wall against once-in-a-century waves. According to Tetlock, what should the decision rest on?
options: A promise that the next big wave will not come within this decade
A rule to protect against every disaster that can be imagined
A wish to match the defences of the nearest big city
An explicit judgment of how likely and how large such waves are
optionExplain: Nobody can promise that, and a promise is not an estimate.
Protecting against everything is the alien-invasion trap, too costly.
A big city faces different odds.
Right: costly preparation needs priorities, and priorities need probabilities.
questions.explain: Spending on protection must be weighed against its likelihood and size, as with Tokyo's quakes.
questions.rule: Weigh the cost of protection against the odds.

questions.q: A country now judges that fighting two wars at once is very unlikely. What does Tetlock's reasoning say about the two-war doctrine?
options: Its justification weakens, since it rested on that likelihood
Its justification grows, since a rare event needs more preparation
Its justification is unchanged, since doctrines do not rest on odds
It should be widened to cover three wars at once
optionExplain: Right: the doctrine was based on a judgment about likelihood.
A rarer event justifies less spending, not more.
Tetlock says such doctrines hinge on probabilities.
Three wars were excluded for being less likely, not more.
questions.explain: Change the probability and the case for the expense changes. Our reading: the same logic would apply to any such doctrine.
questions.rule: Policy follows probability.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says that preparing for surprises frees planners from having to make probability judgments.
questions.explain: He says preparation is costly and sets priorities, which puts planners back in the forecasting business.
questions.rule: Priorities need probabilities.

questions.q: A budget memo gives a probability for a rare event that is really a guess. What does Tetlock say to do?
options: Leave the number unexplained so it looks authoritative
Drop the number altogether, since a guess cannot inform any decision at all
Say it is a guess, since knowing our ignorance beats false confidence
Replace it with a certainty so the plan reads cleanly
optionExplain: Hidden guesses are what he warns against.
He wants guesses stated openly, not removed.
Right: Tetlock says that if a probability is nothing but a guess, we should say so.
Certainty would hide the uncertainty.
questions.explain: Explicit judgments can be examined for accuracy. If one is only a guess, saying so keeps everyone honest.
questions.rule: Label guesses as guesses.
questions.teaches: Tetlock says that if a probability judgment is nothing but a guess, because that is the best we can do, we should say so.

questions.q: In the 1980s and early 1990s, what did many people believe about Japan, according to Tetlock?
options: That its economy would stagnate for several decades
That it would soon be overtaken by Germany
That it would soon dominate the global economy
That its growth would match America's only slowly
optionExplain: That is what happened, not what many believed.
Germany is not part of the story.
Right: the belief was prevalent, and its later decline looks obvious in hindsight.
The belief was that Japan would lead, not trail.
questions.explain: A confident view from the past that now looks strange. The card next draws the lesson.
questions.rule: Yesterday's confident view can look absurd today.

questions.q: In forecasting, Tetlock calls ____ bias the cardinal sin.
questions.explain: Hindsight bias makes the past seem more predictable than it was.
questions.rule: Hindsight bias is the cardinal sin.

questions.q: After a surprise election result, every pundit explains why it was bound to happen. Which bias does Tetlock link to this?
options: Scope insensitivity, which ignores the size of the stakes
Hindsight bias, which makes a surprise look predictable
WYSIATI, which judges from what lies in front of you only
Fat tails, which mistake extremes for typical cases
optionExplain: Nothing here is about the size of the problem.
Right: pundits who did not predict the result now find it explicable.
WYSIATI concerns drawing conclusions from limited evidence.
Fat tails concern the shape of a distribution.
questions.explain: The pundits make the past look foreseeable after the event. That encourages overconfidence about the next one.
questions.rule: After the fact, check whether anyone said it beforehand.

questions.q: A reader believes the past was fully predictable. What does Tetlock expect her to believe about the next decade?
options: That it is less predictable than it really is
That it is exactly as predictable as the past was
That its course depends only on chance and so cannot be studied
That it is more predictable than it really is
optionExplain: Hindsight bias works the other way.
She thinks it is more predictable than that, and the past was less predictable than she believes.
That is a different, pessimistic view.
Right: brushing off surprises in the past makes the future look easier to foresee.
questions.explain: Belief in a predictable past leads to overconfidence about the future.
questions.rule: A neat past breeds a confident future.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says China might become the world's leading economic power.
questions.explain: He says it might, and uses the Japan case to warn against certainty either way.
questions.rule: Warning against certainty is not a prediction.

questions.q: After a company fails, its advisers insist the warning signs were plain, though none warned beforehand. Which case in the chapter does this mirror?
options: Flynn's reading of conflict from the reports on his desk
Khosla's spreading of bets across many start-ups
Experts surprised by Gorbachev who then called it predictable
Wells's advice to plan for a future unlike the one that is expected
optionExplain: Flynn's case is about checking claims against data.
Khosla's case is about investing style.
Right: those experts quickly became convinced it was explicable, even predictable, though they had not predicted it.
Wells's advice is about planning for surprise.
questions.explain: The advisers, like the experts after Gorbachev, rewrite their own record to make the surprise look foreseeable.
questions.rule: Surprised experts often rewrite their record.
questions.teaches: Experts stunned by the Gorbachev surprise quickly became convinced that it was perfectly explicable, even predictable, although they had not predicted it.

questions.q: If US household wealth followed a classic bell curve, how likely would a billionaire household be, according to Tetlock?
options: About one in 700,000 households
About one in 100,000
A one-in-trillions occurrence
About one in a hundred
optionExplain: That is the figure under the true fat-tailed distribution.
That is far likelier than a bell curve allows.
Right: a bell curve would make billionaires virtually non-existent.
Far too common for a bell curve.
questions.explain: On a bell curve, extremes almost vanish. The card next shows what the real distribution does.
questions.rule: A bell curve makes extremes vanishingly rare.

questions.q: A distribution that permits much more extreme outcomes than a bell curve, as wealth does, is called ____-tailed.
questions.explain: In a fat-tailed distribution the extreme ends carry far more probability than a bell curve gives them.
questions.rule: Fat tails mean more extremes.

questions.q: A city's daily rainfall sits near the average, yet rare floods are far larger than a bell curve allows. Which description fits?
options: A bell curve, since most days are close to the average
A thin-tailed distribution, since extremes were rare in the records
An antifragile distribution, since floods strengthen the city
A fat-tailed distribution: extremes beyond what a bell curve allows
optionExplain: Most days near average is true of a bell curve, but the extremes here exceed what it allows.
Rare is not the same as bell-curve rare; the floods are bigger than that.
Antifragile describes systems that gain from shocks, not distributions.
Right: ordinary days near the average do not rule out far larger extremes.
questions.explain: A bell curve cannot produce floods much larger than the typical day. Fat tails can.
questions.rule: Judge a distribution by its extremes, not only its middle.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it describes a bell curve assumption or a fat-tailed reality.

items.t: Men's heights, mostly between five and six feet
A one-in-trillions chance of a billionaire household
Nearly five hundred billionaires in the United States
A one-in-700,000 chance of a billionaire household

questions.explain: The first two are what a bell curve gives. The last two describe the actual distribution of wealth.
questions.rule: Compare the extremes each model implies.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says US household wealth has a fat-tailed distribution, not a bell curve.
questions.explain: Wealth is not distributed normally; it allows far more extreme outcomes.
questions.rule: Do not assume a bell curve.

questions.q: A town's tallest resident is nine feet and shortest three, in line with a bell curve. A researcher says incomes will behave alike. What follows?
options: No: wealth is fat-tailed, while height's extremes stay near typical
Yes, since all human quantities follow a bell curve
Yes, since the tallest and shortest prove the model
No, since neither height nor wealth has a typical value to speak of
optionExplain: Right: the shortest man ever was just under three feet and the tallest just under nine, which is a narrow spread compared with wealth.
Tetlock's wealth example shows that not all quantities do.
Heights fit the bell curve but say nothing about incomes.
Both have typical values; the difference is how far extremes stray.
questions.explain: Height's extremes stay near its typical range. Wealth's extremes do not.
questions.rule: Extremes behave differently from quantity to quantity.
questions.teaches: The shortest man ever was just under three feet tall and the tallest just under nine feet, so even the extremes of height stay close to the typical range.

questions.q: In Tetlock's 1914 story, how does the official react to the forecaster's warning of a ten-million-death war?
options: He treats it as likely and starts planning for it at once
He treats it as vanishingly improbable and dismisses the forecaster
He treats it as improbable but acts to head it off anyway
He treats it as impossible because no war has ever killed a million
optionExplain: Under his assumption the warning looks very unlikely.
Right: his bell-curve assumption makes the warning look absurd.
He sees no reason to act on something he finds absurd.
His assumed worst case was about a million deaths, not zero beyond that.
questions.explain: The assumption sets the verdict. The card next shows how a different distribution changes it.
questions.rule: The assumed distribution decides what looks absurd.

questions.q: Tetlock compares the change in odds to a lottery moving from one in five million to one in ____.
questions.explain: Under a fat-tailed view the warning goes from absurd to a risk worth acting on, as the lottery odds do.
questions.rule: A jump in odds can change your behaviour.

questions.q: A risk manager assumes yearly losses follow a bell curve, so a loss ten times the average seems near impossible. What does Tetlock's story suggest?
options: If losses are fat-tailed, such a loss may be far likelier
Her estimate is safe, since averages are reliable guides to risk
Her estimate is too high, since huge losses cannot occur
Her estimate is right, since bell curves fit every risk
optionExplain: Right: the official's error was to assume a bell curve where the tail is fat.
Averages mislead when the tails are fat.
That reverses the effect of fat tails.
Not every quantity fits a bell curve; wealth does not.
questions.explain: A mistaken bell-curve assumption makes the tail risk look far smaller than it is.
questions.rule: Check the shape of the distribution before dismissing an extreme.

questions.q: Suppose the 1914 official had used a fat-tailed distribution. How would he have rated the forecaster's warning, in Tetlock's story?
options: Likely, so he would have started preparing at once
Impossible, since fat tails forbid very large wars
Still improbable, but thousands of times more probable than before
Exactly as improbable as before, since the underlying data are the same
optionExplain: Tetlock does not say it would become likely.
Fat tails make extreme events likelier, not forbidden.
Right: Tetlock says he would still have seen the forecast as improbable, but much more probable.
A different distribution changes the probability.
questions.explain: The same history, read through a different distribution, gives a very different risk.
questions.rule: A change of distribution can multiply a probability.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says that under a fat-tailed view the forecaster's warning would have become likely.
questions.explain: He says the warning would still have seemed improbable, though thousands of times more probable than before.
questions.rule: More probable is not the same as probable.

questions.q: A town has seen no flood above two metres. If its flood sizes are actually fat-tailed, what changes?
options: A much larger flood becomes impossible within any lifetime
A much larger flood becomes as common as a two-metre one
A much larger flood remains as unlikely as the bell curve implies
A much larger flood stays rare but could occur in a lifetime
optionExplain: Fat tails raise the odds of extremes, not lower them.
They make extremes likelier, not typical.
That is the bell-curve view, which fat tails replace.
Right: fat tails raise the odds of large outliers without making them common, as with Tetlock's twelve-foot man.
questions.explain: If height had a fat-tailed distribution, a twelve-foot man, then a fifteen-foot man, would still be very unusual but could conceivably occur in a lifetime.
questions.rule: Fat tails make big outliers rare but real.
questions.teaches: If height were fat-tailed, meeting a twelve-foot man, then a fifteen-foot man, would still be very unusual but could conceivably occur in one's lifetime.

questions.q: True or false: In Kahneman's thought experiment, there was only a 12.5% chance that Hitler, Stalin and Mao would all have been born male.
questions.explain: Each had a 50% chance, and half cubed is 12.5%. The card next explains the point of the exercise.
questions.rule: Small chances multiply into large effects.

questions.q: Kahneman's thought experiment gives an 87.5% chance that at least one of the three leaders would have been born ____.
questions.explain: The 87.5% is the complement of the 12.5% chance that all three were male.
questions.rule: At least one female is the complement of all male.

questions.q: A manager says her company's success was inevitable. Which idea in the chapter challenges this?
options: The actual outcome is one of many once-possible worlds
Fat tails make every outcome equally likely to occur
A bell curve guarantees the average outcome will occur
Scope insensitivity makes large outcomes look small to us
optionExplain: Right: the past did not have to unfold as it did.
Fat tails make extremes likelier, not all outcomes equal.
Nothing guarantees the average outcome.
That is a bias about magnitudes, not about alternative histories.
questions.explain: Counterfactual thinking shows how easily things could have gone differently.
questions.rule: Ask what else could have happened.

questions.q: Suppose Anna Hitler had been born in 1889. In Tetlock's account, what might have followed?
options: Nothing would have changed, since the movement made the outcome fixed in advance
A calmer century, since no woman could have led anything
The same war, with a milder outcome for Europe's cities
World War II might never have happened, or a shrewder dictator done worse
optionExplain: Tetlock says the effects could have been enormous.
He does not say that.
He gives no reason to expect a milder outcome.
Right: the ripple effects are unknowable but potentially enormous.
questions.explain: A small change at the start can cause very large differences later, but the direction is unknowable.
questions.rule: Small causes, unknowable effects.

questions.q: If Hitler had invaded the Soviet Union earlier in 1941, what does Tetlock say about World War II's death toll?
options: It would have been lower, since the war would have ended sooner
Far more than sixty million, given fat-tailed casualty risks
It would have been about the same, since the outcome was fixed
It would have been close to a hundred thousand, the historical average
optionExplain: Tetlock does not claim an earlier invasion would end the war sooner.
Right: war casualties are fat-tailed, so far worse outcomes were once possible.
He says the possibilities were real and numerous, not fixed.
The hundred-thousand average belonged to the official's mistaken bell curve.
questions.explain: Tetlock says World War II could have claimed far more than sixty million lives if Hitler had invaded earlier in 1941 or grasped the atomic bomb's power.
questions.rule: Real history is one outcome among darker ones.
questions.teaches: Because war casualties are fat-tailed, World War II could have claimed far more than sixty million lives if Hitler had invaded earlier in 1941 or grasped the power of the atomic bomb.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says counterfactual history proves that the future is random.
questions.explain: He says counterfactuals highlight how open the possibilities were and instill humility. They are not proof of randomness.
questions.rule: Humility is not the same as proof.

questions.q: A pilot says a near-miss could have ended in disaster. Which example in the chapter matches that feeling of many possible outcomes?
options: Flynn reading intelligence reports each morning at his desk
Khosla spreading bets over many start-ups, expecting most of them to fail
Kennedy in the Cuban missile crisis, weighing peace against annihilation
Wells predicting that 2010 would look little like expectations
optionExplain: Flynn's case is about checking claims against data.
Khosla's case is about investing style.
Right: Tetlock says prudent leaders feel this in their bones, as Kennedy did.
Wells's point is that the future will differ from expectations, not about an array of past outcomes.
questions.explain: Kennedy realized the crisis had an array of possible outcomes, ranging from peace to a nuclear war that could have killed hundreds of millions.
questions.rule: Prudent leaders see the range of outcomes.
questions.teaches: Kennedy realized the Cuban missile crisis had outcomes ranging from peace to nuclear annihilation, which could have pushed the toll of World War III into the hundreds of millions.

questions.q: How does Tetlock describe human foresight in his closing lines?
options: Useless beyond the next few days, so planning should replace it entirely
Stronger than Kahneman and Taleb admit across every horizon
Fixed by nature, so training cannot improve it at all
Puny in the big scheme, but nothing to sniff at on the human scale
optionExplain: Tetlock says accurate forecasts are possible on some developments.
He agrees with them about the limits.
He believes effort can improve it.
Right: modest, but real.
questions.explain: Tetlock combines humility with a claim of real, effortful skill. The card next gives the argument.
questions.rule: Humble, not hopeless.

questions.q: Tetlock says people can make accurate forecasts, with considerable ____, about at least some developments that matter.
questions.explain: The claim is bounded: some developments, and only with considerable effort.
questions.rule: Accuracy takes effort.

questions.q: A strategist says the future is radically open, so no forecasting is worth doing. Which reply fits Tetlock's conclusion?
options: Humility is unwarranted, since long-range forecasting has now been solved
Planning is worthless, so forecasts are all that is left to rely on
An open future makes every forecast equally likely to be right
Humility should not hide that careful work can give accurate forecasts
optionExplain: Tetlock agrees there is no evidence of long-range foresight.
He endorses planning for surprise.
Open does not mean all forecasts are equal.
Right: the open future calls for humility, not abandonment of effort.
questions.explain: Tetlock keeps both: humility about the long run and effort on questions that can be answered.
questions.rule: Humility is not abstention.

questions.q: Match each person to the emphasis Tetlock gives them in this chapter.
pairs: Black swans and fat tails make much of history unforecastable
Minds crave certainty and need hard System 2 work to resist illusions
Effortful accuracy is possible on some developments that matter
questions.explain: Each critic presses on a different point, and Tetlock's reply is bounded.
questions.rule: Know each position before judging.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock concludes that, since long-range forecasting fails, forecasting should be abandoned.
questions.explain: He concludes that humility should not obscure that people can make accurate forecasts about some developments with considerable effort.
questions.rule: A limit on range is not a ban.

questions.q: A researcher treats her two strongest critics as possible collaborators, not enemies. Whose approach does this resemble?
options: Flynn's toward the data on conflict trends
Tetlock's toward Kahneman and Taleb, as potential collaborators
The 1914 official's toward the forecaster who warned him of world war
Khosla's toward companies he expects to fail
optionExplain: Flynn did not check the data.
Right: Tetlock says they are far enough apart empirically and close enough philosophically for collaboration.
The official dismissed the forecaster as a crackpot.
Khosla's case is an investing style, not a stance toward critics.
questions.explain: Tetlock sees the critiques as the strongest challenges and still finds common ground.
questions.rule: Treat the strongest critic as a possible partner.
questions.teaches: Tetlock calls Kahneman's and Taleb's critiques the strongest challenges to superforecasting and says they are far enough apart empirically and close enough philosophically for communication and collaboration.

questions.q: Before Scotland’s 2014 referendum, pundits disagreed about what would decide the vote. What did the authors call the one highly probable outcome?
options: That the yes campaign would win narrowly after a late surge in the polls
That the polls would hold steady from the first month to the vote itself
That economic fears would outweigh nationalist feeling among Scottish voters
That pundits would explain the result at once, whatever it was
optionExplain: The polls did swing toward yes for a while, but no won widely, and the authors do not call a yes win probable.
The polls shifted rapidly two weeks before the vote, so steadiness was not the safe bet.
Some pundits expected this and others expected the reverse; the authors treat neither as the highly probable outcome.
Right: whatever happened, pundits would immediately explain why.
questions.explain: Pundits were split on the cause, yet all could be counted on to explain the result afterwards. The card next shows what the authors make of that habit.
questions.rule: Expect instant explanations after any outcome.

questions.q: The authors call hindsight-tainted analyses after major events a ____ end.
questions.explain: Analyses written in hindsight leave out too much, so the authors say they lead nowhere.
questions.rule: Hindsight analysis is a dead end for learning.

questions.q: After one election upset, an analyst announces a general law of voter behaviour. Which flaw would the authors point to?
options: It prefers explanations based on money to explanations based on national identity
It ignores the polls, which are the only valid evidence about elections
It treats the analyst’s own forecast as less important than the actual result
It builds a general law from one event with many causes, leaving most out
optionExplain: The authors take no side between economics and identity; they object to the one-factor story either way.
The authors never say polls are the only valid evidence; the problem is the leap from one case.
The flaw is not about the analyst’s own forecast; the card is about explaining one event after it happens.
Right: many factors were at work, so a one-factor law leaves too much out.
questions.explain: A single event with many causes cannot support a sweeping law. That is the move the authors call misguided.
questions.rule: Do not turn one result into a law.

questions.q: Sort each response to a surprising result: does it fit the authors’ advice or the hindsight habit?

items.t: Asking what to adjust in one’s view of how the world works
Admitting one was unsure of the outcome beforehand
Noting that many factors were at work in the result
Writing as though the result had been obvious all along
Declaring that one factor beats another in all places
Explaining the result at once with a single neat cause

questions.explain: The advice treats the result as data about one’s model. The habit supplies a tidy story that the result seems to prove.
questions.rule: Ask what the result changes, not what it proves.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say every event, even a surprising one, is an opportunity to improve our mental models.
questions.explain: They say every event is an opportunity to learn and improve the models from which we derive our expectations of the future.
questions.rule: Learn from events without over-explaining them.

questions.q: A shop thrives in one town and an analyst says low prices beat service in every town. How would the authors rate that step?
options: As sound, since one clear success shows which factor matters most everywhere
As the same size of error as explaining the single town alone
As harmless, since analysts only describe the past and predict nothing
As even more misguided than explaining the single town with one cause
optionExplain: It feels sound because the success was real, but the many causes in one town do not carry to other towns.
The authors rank the leap to other places as worse than the one-event story, not equal to it.
The analyst is making a claim about other towns, which is a prediction, so this does not describe the step.
Right: the authors call concluding that a winning factor will win elsewhere even more misguided.
questions.explain: The authors say it is even more misguided to conclude that because economics trumped nationalism here, it will do so elsewhere. Spreading a one-event story to new places adds a second error.
questions.rule: A one-event story travels worse than it seems.
questions.teaches: The authors say it is even more misguided to conclude that because economics trumped nationalism in Scotland, it will do so elsewhere.

questions.q: After Scotland voted no, how did the political scientist Daniel Drezner respond to the surprise?
options: He wrote an analysis explaining why nationalism or economics had been bound to prevail
He argued that his earlier post had already forecast the margin correctly
He blamed the pre-vote polls for failing to show the true state of opinion
He admitted he had been unsure and resolved to make clear, scored predictions in future
optionExplain: That is the habit he poked fun at; he did not do it.
He admitted his forecast was unclear, so he made no such claim.
The chapter does not report him blaming the polls.
Right: he confessed uncertainty and said he wanted to keep score.
questions.explain: Drezner gave a rare reaction among pundits: he owned his uncertainty. The card next sets out what he concluded.
questions.rule: Own your uncertainty, then make it scorable.

questions.q: Drezner said he would make a clear prediction and offer a confidence ____ about it.
questions.explain: A prediction plus a confidence interval gives something definite to score.
questions.rule: A clear prediction needs a stated confidence.

questions.q: A columnist writes that a merger ‘could fail’. Which rewrite lets readers score the claim, on Drezner’s logic?
options: The merger will probably face serious problems at some point in the coming years
Many mergers in this sector end badly, so readers should be cautious about this one
The merger carries real risk, and the strain between the two firms is already visible
I put 70% on the merged firm’s shares closing below today’s price on 31 December
optionExplain: No date, no measure and no number: it could never be shown wrong.
A general caution about mergers says nothing definite about this one.
It sounds concrete, but the risk has no size or deadline, so nothing could settle it.
Right: it has a probability, a measure and a date, so the result can be checked.
questions.explain: A scorable forecast says what will happen, by when, and how confident the forecaster is.
questions.rule: Scorable means definite, dated and quantified.

questions.q: A forecast is too vague to say what it predicted. What does the outcome then tell the forecaster about changing his thinking?
options: Which assumptions to drop, because every outcome exposes the error behind it
How much to trust the polls, because they were the likely source of error
Nothing definite, because it is not clear what the forecast got right or wrong
That he should adopt the opposite view, because the outcome contradicted him
optionExplain: It feels like outcomes always teach, but without a clear forecast nothing marks an error.
Polls were not the issue in Drezner’s case; his own wording was.
Right: Drezner asked what he had forecast and how to change his thinking, and neither was clear.
Flipping views presumes a clear miss, which a vague forecast cannot show.
questions.explain: Drezner saw that he could not tell what he had forecast, so he could not tell how to adjust. Vagueness removes the lesson.
questions.rule: No clear forecast, no clear lesson.

questions.q: True or false: According to the chapter, Drezner had forecast before the vote that yes would win the Scottish referendum.
questions.explain: He had thought no would win, but his post argued why yes might win. That mismatch is why his forecast was unclear.
questions.rule: Mixed messages cannot be scored.

questions.q: A pundit calls an upset result a ‘teachable moment’ but does not state what he had predicted. What does the chapter’s logic say is missing?
options: A rival pundit who made the opposite prediction and was right
A larger sample of past upsets from which to draw a general rule
A confident tone, so that readers take the lessons seriously
A scorable forecast, so there is nothing definite to adjust from
optionExplain: A rival’s success is not what makes lessons possible; clear scoring is.
More cases might help, but the chapter’s point is about clarity of the forecast itself.
Confidence of tone is not feedback; Drezner asked for numbers.
Right: without a stated prediction there is no clear error to learn from.
questions.explain: Drezner himself called the result a teachable moment for punditry and asked what one does with data points like this to adjust one’s worldview. The answer in the chapter is to keep score.
questions.rule: A teachable moment needs a scorable forecast.
questions.teaches: Drezner himself called the result a teachable moment for punditry and asked what to do with such data points to adjust one’s worldview.

questions.q: Which reason does the chapter give for taking forecasting tournaments seriously, even though they have scores and leaderboards?
options: Winning the tournament carries public prestige for top forecasters
Tournament questions are chosen to be more interesting than ordinary forecasts
Entrants are paid according to how well they place on the leaderboard
Forecasts feed costly decisions in business, government and security
optionExplain: The chapter does not argue from prestige.
The questions were screened for difficulty and relevance, but interest is not the argument here.
Payment is not the reason the chapter gives.
Right: the stakes are real because decisions depend on forecasts.
questions.explain: The chapter links forecasting to prosperity, policy and peace. The card next states the claim and the formula the authors draw from it.
questions.rule: Forecasts steer real decisions.

questions.q: The authors’ short formula for seeing better is: forecast, ____, revise.
questions.explain: You need a measurement of the forecast against the outcome before you can revise.
questions.rule: Forecast, measure, revise.

questions.q: A hospital board wants better triage forecasts. Which plan follows the authors’ formula?
options: Rank staff by title and give the most senior the final say on every forecast made
Ask senior staff to explain each missed case in detail once the case has closed
Keep forecasts general so that no individual can be blamed for a miss
Log each forecast with a probability, score it against the outcome, then adjust
optionExplain: Titles are among the criteria the authors say are used instead of testing.
Explanations after the fact are the hindsight habit the chapter warns about.
Generality avoids blame but makes measurement impossible.
Right: it forecasts, measures against outcomes, and revises.
questions.explain: The formula needs all three steps. Skipping the measurement leaves the other two with nothing to work from.
questions.rule: Do all three steps.

questions.q: Match each field to what good forecasting can decide there, as the chapter puts it.
pairs: The difference between prosperity and bankruptcy
Policies that boost communities versus ones with unintended consequences and wasted taxes
The difference between peace and war
questions.explain: The chapter names three domains with real stakes. Each pairs a good outcome with a bad one that depends on foresight.
questions.rule: Stakes are real in every domain.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a disastrous invasion of Iraq would certainly have been averted had intelligence not claimed certainty.
questions.explain: The chapter uses the modal word might: a disastrous invasion might have been averted. It does not claim that it would have been.
questions.rule: Notice the modal word: might.

questions.q: A think tank issues only broad forecasts such as ‘tensions will rise’. By the chapter’s reasoning, why does this block learning?
options: Broad forecasts attract fewer readers, so fewer people check them
Such forecasts are rarely right, so forecasters slowly lose confidence in them
They can never be proven wrong, so nothing forces anyone to revise a model
Broad forecasts need larger tournaments, which few think tanks can run
optionExplain: Readership is not the issue the authors raise.
The point is not accuracy; a forecast too fuzzy to fail is also too fuzzy to teach.
Right: only when we are proven wrong so clearly that we cannot deny it do we adjust.
Size of tournament plays no part in the argument.
questions.explain: The authors say fuzzy thinking can never be proven wrong, and only when we are proven wrong so clearly that we can no longer deny it to ourselves will we adjust our mental models.
questions.rule: A forecast that cannot fail cannot teach.
questions.teaches: Fuzzy thinking can never be proven wrong, and only a clear, undeniable miss pushes people to adjust their mental models.

questions.q: Tetlock imagines consumers of forecasting changing how they treat pundits. What would they ask a pundit before heeding him?
options: How his view compares with the latest published polls
How many awards and degrees he holds
How good the story is that he tells about the future
How his past predictions fared
optionExplain: Matching polls is not the test he describes.
Credentials are what they would stop being satisfied with.
Good stories are exactly what gulls consumers, according to Tetlock.
Right: they would ask about the track record and reject answers made of anecdotes and credentials.
questions.explain: The change Tetlock imagines moves the question from who the pundit is to how his forecasts have scored. The card next gives the full picture.
questions.rule: Ask for the record, not the résumé.

questions.q: Tetlock compares the hoped-for change to the evidence-based ____ revolution.
questions.explain: He expects forecasters to be tested rigorously, as pills now are.
questions.rule: Compare forecasting with tested medicine.

questions.q: A company is choosing between two consultants: one offers vivid stories and credentials, the other a record of scored forecasts. What fits Tetlock’s hope?
options: Choose the one with credentials, since expertise matters most in a new field
Hire neither, since no forecaster can be tested in advance
Choose the storyteller, since stories help managers remember advice
Ask both for their record of scored forecasts and weigh that above credentials
optionExplain: Credentials are what Tetlock says should stop being enough.
The chapter says forecasters can and should be tested.
Good stories are what gull consumers according to the chapter.
Right: he hopes consumers will ask how past predictions fared.
questions.explain: Tetlock’s hope is that buyers of forecasts will behave like buyers of tested drugs. A scored record is the evidence.
questions.rule: Buy forecasts on evidence.

questions.q: Suppose testing becomes the standard expectation for forecasters. What does Tetlock say they themselves would gain?
options: Higher fees, because tested forecasters can charge more for their work
Protection from blame, because test results excuse any single miss
Clear feedback, the only route to improving their foresight
Freedom from competition, because untested rivals would be shut out
optionExplain: The chapter does not argue from fees.
Cover against blame is the opposite of what testing offers; it exposes misses.
Right: higher expectations benefit them because only clear feedback lets them improve.
The chapter does not say rivals would be shut out.
questions.explain: Tetlock argues that forecasters, like Drezner, should welcome higher expectations, because testing produces the feedback they need.
questions.rule: Testing is how forecasters improve.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says the evidence-based forecasting revolution is sure to come.
questions.explain: He says it could be huge, but also that nothing may change and that he is modestly optimistic.
questions.rule: Hope is not prediction.

questions.q: A reader finishes the book and wants forecasting to change. What role does Tetlock give her?
options: She is a critic, whose main job is to show that the research fails
She is a bystander, since change depends on intelligence agencies alone
She is a future tournament entrant, since only entrants can drive change
She belongs to the attentive public that helps decide the outcome
optionExplain: He invites readers to judge the outlook, not to refute the research.
He doubts intelligence agencies will lead; the public’s expectations matter.
Entering a tournament is not what he asks of readers.
Right: he says the attentive public will decide, and readers can make the final forecast.
questions.explain: Tetlock says whether his research proceeds amid tumultuous change or a stagnant status quo will be decided by what political scientists call the attentive public. He is modestly optimistic and leaves the final forecast to readers.
questions.rule: Readers help decide the outcome.
questions.teaches: Tetlock says the attentive public, as political scientists call it, will decide whether his research proceeds amid change or stagnation.

questions.q: Lenin’s phrase ‘kto, kogo’ literally means ‘who, whom’. What did he use it to say?
options: That the winners of a debate are whoever speaks first and loudest
That every statement should be sorted into true or false before use
That politics is a contest over who does what to whom
That each person must ask whom they serve before they begin to speak
optionExplain: Debate is only one place the contest happens; he meant power.
He cared about power, not sorting statements by truth.
Right: it is shorthand for who does what to whom.
Serving someone is a subtler idea; his phrase is about who prevails over whom.
questions.explain: The phrase reduces politics to a struggle for power. The card next shows what that means for forecasting.
questions.rule: Kto-kogo means who does what to whom.

questions.q: Kto-kogo is Lenin’s shorthand for ‘Who does what to ____?’
questions.explain: Kto means who and kogo means whom.
questions.rule: Kto is the doer; kogo is the one done to.

questions.q: A party strategist publishes a poll forecast designed to discourage rival volunteers. Which view of forecasting does this fit?
options: The accuracy view, since the strategist is trying to predict the result
The tournament view, since the forecast is public and open to scoring
The hindsight view, since the forecast is built after the event
The kto-kogo view, since the forecast serves the strategist’s side first
optionExplain: Accuracy is not the strategist’s aim; the effect on rivals is.
Publishing is not scoring; no one measures the forecast against outcomes.
The forecast comes before the event, so hindsight is not in play.
Right: the forecast is a move in the contest, not an attempt to see what is coming.
questions.explain: On the kto-kogo view the test of a forecast is whether it advances one’s side.
questions.rule: Ask whose interests the forecast serves.

questions.q: Sort each statement: does it express the accuracy view or the kto-kogo view of forecasting?

items.t: Forecasts are judged by how well they match what happens
The exclusive goal of forecasting is to be accurate
Scores and track records show who forecasts well
A forecast succeeds if it advances the tribe’s interests
Evidence and argument are adornments to a struggle for power
Being the kto matters more than being right

questions.explain: The accuracy view, which Tetlock took as his stance in chapter 1, ranks forecasts by fit with events. The kto-kogo view ranks them by what they do for one side.
questions.rule: Two goals, two ways of judging a forecast.

questions.q: True or false: On the kto-kogo view, accuracy is pushed aside whenever the pursuit of power requires it.
questions.explain: Accurate forecasts are welcome when they help the forecaster’s side, and pushed aside if power requires something else.
questions.rule: Describing a view is not endorsing it.

questions.q: If kto-kogo fully described forecasting, what would follow for efforts to reform it?
options: Reform would be urgent, since forecasting would then be failing its main goal
Reform would matter only to researchers, since users would not care
Reform would succeed quickly, since power-seekers adopt whatever works
Reform would be unnecessary, as forecasting already serves its purpose
optionExplain: Under this view the main goal is power, which forecasting already serves.
The view does not distinguish researchers from users in this way.
The view predicts the opposite: tools that do not serve power are dropped.
Right: on this perspective there is no need to reform forecasting, and it will not change.
questions.explain: The authors draw the pessimistic conclusion from the view: forecasting will not change because it already serves its primary purpose well. That is why the view is the strongest force against reform.
questions.rule: Kto-kogo implies no reform.
questions.teaches: On the kto-kogo perspective there is no need to reform forecasting, and it will not change, because it already serves its primary purpose well.

questions.q: In 2014 many Democrats turned against Nate Silver. According to the chapter, what changed?
options: He announced that he would join a Republican campaign, which cost him support
His track record fell sharply after the 2012 election, so his methods were doubted
He began to publish forecasts without probabilities, which made them harder to trust
His forecasts pointed to a Republican Senate, which suited their side less
optionExplain: The chapter reports no such announcement.
The chapter says the track record was the same, not worse.
Nothing in the chapter says his format changed.
Right: same forecaster, same record, but his forecasts stopped aligning with partisan purposes.
questions.explain: The chapter shows that the same forecaster was prophet one year and stumblebum the next because of which side his forecast helped. The card next draws the lesson.
questions.rule: Same record, different welcome.

questions.q: Tetlock says he swept the point under the rug in chapter ____, when he called accuracy the sole concern.
questions.explain: In chapter 1 he said the exclusive goal of forecasting should be accuracy. This chapter admits that is often not the case.
questions.rule: Accuracy is one goal among several.

questions.q: A bank analyst warns clients about a powerful party’s rise and is fired at once. Which chapter case matches?
options: Nate Silver’s 2014 Senate forecast, which many Democrats turned against
Daniel Drezner’s post, which poked fun at the confident insta-analysis of pundits
The Santander Brasil analyst, fired for a warning about a candidate
Ernest Codman’s cartoon of dignitaries, which cost him his Harvard teaching post
optionExplain: Silver kept his job; the case is about partisan reaction, not a bank’s clients.
Drezner was not punished; he wrote a confession.
Right: the forecast displeased a powerful party, and the analyst was dismissed whether or not it was accurate.
Codman’s story concerns medicine and a cartoon, not a forecast.
questions.explain: In the Brazilian case, whether the forecast was accurate did not matter in the slightest. What mattered was the relationship with potential future presidents.
questions.rule: Forecasts can be punished for who they displease.

questions.q: Jonathan Schell’s 1982 warning of nuclear holocaust was not accurate but rallied readers. What would a kto-kogo view say of it?
options: That it failed, since the holocaust did not occur
That it succeeded, since it did exactly what it was supposed to do
That it was neutral, since a forecast cannot change behaviour
That it was dishonest, since all inaccurate forecasts are lies
optionExplain: Failure is judged by accuracy; the view judges by effect.
Right: Schell wanted to rouse readers to join the disarmament movement, and he did.
The view says forecasts are tools for moving people.
The chapter does not call Schell dishonest; it says the view looks at purpose.
questions.explain: Schell wanted to rouse readers to join the disarmament movement, and he did. Lenin would say his forecast did exactly what it was supposed to do, even though it was not accurate.
questions.rule: Judge a forecast by its purpose and you may excuse a miss.
questions.teaches: Jonathan Schell’s 1982 holocaust warning was not accurate, but it rallied readers to the disarmament movement, so a kto-kogo reading counts it a success.

questions.q: True or false: Democrats turned on Nate Silver in 2014 because his track record had worsened since 2012.
questions.explain: The chapter says same forecaster, same track record. His forecasts stopped fitting partisan purposes.
questions.rule: Reaction to a forecast can change while the record stays the same.

questions.q: A coach says his team will certainly win, to lift morale, and then loses. Whose defence does this echo?
options: Silver’s, who held to his stated probabilities
Drezner’s, who admitted that his forecast was unclear
Morris’s, who called his landslide forecast a duty
Codman’s, who argued that outcomes should be recorded
optionExplain: Silver defended a probability; the coach states a certainty for effect.
Drezner confessed uncertainty; the coach does not.
Right: Morris said the campaign was falling apart and it was his duty to say what he said.
Codman wanted records of results; he did not forecast.
questions.explain: Dick Morris forecast a Romney landslide in 2012 and, after being mocked, said the campaign was falling apart and it was his duty to say so. Tetlock adds that Morris may have lied about having lied, but that the defence seemed plausible to him says a lot about his kto-kogo world.
questions.rule: Morale can be a reason to forecast.
questions.teaches: Dick Morris defended his failed Romney-landslide forecast as a duty given a falling-apart campaign; that he thought it plausible shows the kto-kogo world he works in.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock thinks Lenin’s kto-kogo view is entirely wrong about forecasting.
questions.explain: He concedes that Lenin had a point, though he calls him a tad dogmatic. The card next shows where he draws the line.
questions.rule: Concede the point, dispute the extent.

questions.q: Tetlock calls Lenin a tad ____, meaning he held his view too rigidly.
questions.explain: The charge is rigidity: people want power, but they also value other things.
questions.rule: Dogmatic means too rigid.

questions.q: A colleague says every report here is written to please the boss, so improving accuracy is pointless. Which reply fits Tetlock’s answer to Lenin?
options: Agree, since power decides everything and accuracy cannot compete with it
Disagree, since reports are never written to please anyone in practice
Agree, since the boss will always value accuracy above personal loyalty
Grant that self-interest matters, but people value other things too
optionExplain: That is the dogmatic view Tetlock rejects.
Tetlock concedes self and tribe matter, so he would not deny it entirely.
This reverses the problem; he does not say bosses always favour accuracy.
Right: it grants the point and adds the qualification that can make all the difference.
questions.explain: Tetlock’s reply accepts that power matters while refusing to treat it as the only thing that matters.
questions.rule: Grant the motive, deny that it is the only one.

questions.q: Sort each statement: does Tetlock concede it to the kto-kogo view, or dispute it?

items.t: Self and tribe matter
Forecasting can be co-opted to advance the interests of a group
People do want power
Power is the only thing people value
Accuracy is never welcome in any forecast
Reform of forecasting is therefore pointless in every case

questions.explain: Tetlock gives the view its factual core and denies its extreme edges. People want power, but not only power.
questions.rule: Concede the core, reject the extreme.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock rejects the claim that forecasting can ever be co-opted to serve a tribe.
questions.explain: He says that if forecasting can be co-opted to advance self and tribe, it will be. His objection is to the claim that nothing else matters.
questions.rule: He admits co-option happens.

questions.q: A union leader says a safety forecast was bent to help management. Which expectation follows from Tetlock’s concession?
options: That such bending is impossible if a forecast carries a probability
That such bending is rare, because forecasters value accuracy above all
That such bending shows forecasting should be abandoned as a tool
That such bending is to be expected whenever it can advance self or tribe
optionExplain: A number does not rule out co-option; the chapter makes no such claim.
He does not say bending is rare.
He concludes the opposite: reform is still worth pursuing.
Right: he says that if forecasting can be co-opted to advance their interests, it will be.
questions.explain: Tetlock concedes that if forecasting can be co-opted to advance self and tribe, it will be. His hope rests on the other things people value, not on denying co-option.
questions.rule: Expect co-option wherever it is possible.
questions.teaches: Tetlock concedes that if forecasting can be co-opted to advance self and tribe, it will be.

questions.q: A century ago, the Boston doctor Ernest Codman proposed that hospitals record which facts about each patient?
options: Each patient’s family background, income and reputation
Each patient’s ailment, treatment and the end result of the case
Each doctor’s years of training, prizes and social standing
Each hospital’s building costs, staffing levels and daily meals
optionExplain: Social standing is what Codman’s plan set aside.
Right: ailment, treatment and, most important, the end result.
The plan disregarded a physician’s reputation and social standing; it looked at outcomes.
Costs were a source of resistance, not the thing recorded.
questions.explain: Codman wanted evidence about outcomes. The card next tells how the idea fared.
questions.rule: Record outcomes, not status.

questions.q: Codman called his proposal for recording outcomes the End ____ System.
questions.explain: The name points to the final outcome of each case, which he considered most important to record.
questions.rule: The end result is what counts.

questions.q: A city proposes publishing each clinic’s patient outcomes so residents can compare them. Which element of Codman’s idea does this repeat?
options: Asking each clinic to explain its misses after the fact in private
Staging a public protest against respected leaders in the field
Ranking clinicians by bedside manner and by social standing in town
Releasing outcome statistics so consumers can choose
optionExplain: His plan was public and numerical, not private and verbal.
His cartoon was a stunt that backfired at first; it was not the proposal.
Codman’s plan disregarded bedside manner and social standing.
Right: Codman wanted statistics released so consumers could choose on evidence.
questions.explain: Publishing outcomes so users can choose is the heart of Codman’s system.
questions.rule: Publish results so users can choose.

questions.q: Which were reasons hospitals and physicians resisted Codman’s plan? Select all that apply.
options: Hospitals would have to pay for record keepers
Physicians saw nothing in it for themselves
Keeping score could damage their reputations
The statistics Codman published were shown to be false
Patients refused to have their cases recorded
optionExplain: Right: the cost fell on hospitals.
Right: they were already respected and gained nothing from scoring.
Right: published outcomes could only hurt reputations that were already high.
The chapter gives no such finding.
The chapter does not report patient refusal.
questions.explain: The resistance came from cost and from interest. It was not about the data being wrong.
questions.rule: Resistance often follows interest.

questions.q: True or false: The uproar over Codman’s 1915 cartoon helped spread interest in Codman’s system.
questions.explain: The hue and cry created a nationwide buzz, and a growing number of hospitals implemented his scheme.
questions.rule: A setback can still spread an idea.

questions.q: A researcher’s scoring scheme threatens senior people in her field. What approach does the authors’ account of evidence-based medicine suggest?
options: Out-argue the senior people at public meetings and shame them into compliance
Wait for the senior people to retire, since only new staff will accept scoring
Rely on reason and a relentless focus on the shared goal
Keep the scheme private until it can be introduced as a complete system
optionExplain: Shaming is a form of storming the ramparts, which the authors say is not how it was done.
The authors do not say change waited for retirements.
Right: that is how Codman, Cochrane and others overcame entrenched interests.
Codman published statistics and promoted his ideas; secrecy was not the method.
questions.explain: The authors say that if kto-kogo were the decisive force, evidence-based medicine, a threat to everyone who was anyone in the hierarchy, would have been stillborn. Codman, Archie Cochrane and others overcame entrenched interests with reason and a relentless focus on making the sick well.
questions.rule: Reason and a clear aim can beat entrenched interest.
questions.teaches: If kto-kogo were decisive, evidence-based medicine would have been stillborn; Codman, Archie Cochrane and others won with reason and a relentless focus on making the sick well.

questions.q: The chapter says rapid advances in one kind of technology catalysed the shift toward evidence-based decisions. Which kind?
options: Information technology, which lets us count and test like never before
Medical technology, which made hospital records far cheaper to keep
Transport technology, which made distant institutions easier to compare
Broadcast technology, which carried the best expert advice to more people
optionExplain: Right: we can count and test like never before.
Medicine is one example of the shift, not the technology behind it.
The chapter does not mention transport.
Spreading expert advice is the old model the shift moves away from.
questions.explain: The chapter ties several movements to one enabler. The card next puts them together.
questions.rule: Information technology made counting cheap.

questions.q: The ____ Foundation is renowned for the rigor of its evaluations.
questions.explain: It is cited as a charitable foundation that insists on clear goals and measures.
questions.rule: Funders increasingly demand evaluation.

questions.q: A foundation keeps funding a project because its leader is admired, though no results are shown. Which shift in the chapter does this go against?
options: Funding contingent on stringent evaluation
Hiring only people who hold a doctorate in an applied field
Moving all decisions to a single central committee for speed
Replacing paid staff with volunteers who work on short contracts
optionExplain: Right: foundations increasingly expand programmes that deliver and close those that fail.
The chapter says nothing about doctorates.
The shift is about evidence, not about who decides.
Staffing models are not the subject.
questions.explain: Funding by reputation is the old model. The chapter describes funders moving to evaluation.
questions.rule: Evaluate, then fund.

questions.q: Sort each basis for a decision: authority and intuition, or quantification and analysis.

items.t: Do this because I think it will work and I am an expert
Follow the head coach’s hunch about how hard to train
Hire on title and a good feeling after the interview
Test the options and count the results
Use research on human performance to design practice
Fund programmes only after stringent evaluation

questions.explain: The chapter sets decisions made on the strength of an expert’s say-so against decisions made on measured results.
questions.rule: Count and test rather than trust authority.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say politicians will still weigh partisan advantage even as rigorous policy analysis grows.
questions.explain: They say politics will always be politics, yet rigorous analysis has made a real difference in government policy.
questions.rule: More analysis does not end politics.
