questions.q: A coach in a hot climate bans water during practice, trusting tradition. Which example from the chapter does this echo?
options: Don Shula’s Colts, who practised without access to water
John Madden’s Raiders, who practised at midday in full pads
Ernest Codman, who published hospital statistics at his own cost
Nate Silver, whose forecasts were reviled by one party
optionExplain: Right: Shula insisted that his players practise without access to water.
Madden’s case is about midday August practice in full pads, not water.
Codman’s story is about hospital outcomes.
Silver’s story is about partisan reaction to forecasts.
questions.explain: James Surowiecki, quoted in the chapter, cites Madden and Shula as gut-informed techniques that are going the way of bloodletting, now that training is data-driven.
questions.rule: Gut-informed training is giving way to data.
questions.teaches: Surowiecki cites John Madden’s midday full-pads practice and Don Shula’s no-water rule as gut-informed techniques going the way of bloodletting.

questions.q: Someone forecasts a 70% chance of an event and it does not happen. What does the wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy conclude?
options: That the forecast was wrong
That the forecaster should have said 100%
That the 70% figure was correct by chance alone
That the event must have been less likely than 50%
optionExplain: Right: a 30% outcome happened, but the fallacy treats the miss as proof of error.
A higher number would not be more accurate; it would be less calibrated.
One result neither confirms nor refutes the figure, but this is not what the fallacy says.
A single result does not show the probability was below 50%.
questions.explain: The fallacy treats any miss on the favoured side as an error. The card next shows why it matters for intelligence agencies.
questions.rule: A 70% forecast is not wrong when the 30% happens.

questions.q: The idea that a 70% forecast was wrong because the event did not happen is the wrong-side-of-____ fallacy.
questions.explain: Maybe is the 50% line; the fallacy treats landing on the other side of it as being wrong.
questions.rule: Don’t score a probability by one outcome.

questions.q: A risk office replaces ‘30% chance of default’ with ‘default is possible’ after a client complains. Which chapter pattern is this?
options: Choosing a fuzzy phrase over a number so as to avoid unfair blame
Raising an alarm at the slightest sign of trouble to avoid a repeat
Releasing outcome statistics so that consumers may compare providers
Making a clear prediction with a confidence interval to keep score
optionExplain: Right: this is the Kent problem. Use a number and risk being blamed; stay fuzzy and stay safe.
That describes the community after missing a threat, not a change in wording.
That is Codman’s idea, the opposite direction.
That is Drezner’s resolve, the opposite direction.
questions.explain: Replacing a number with a vague phrase is the self-protective move the authors describe.
questions.rule: Vagueness protects the forecaster and costs the user.

questions.q: Match each situation to how the chapter says the intelligence community was blamed or reacted.
pairs: Blamed for failing to connect the dots and underestimating the risk
Blamed for connecting unconnected dots and overestimating the weapons risk
Raises alarms at the slightest sign of trouble
questions.explain: The community is blamed in opposite directions and each time swings to the opposite extreme. The authors say this does nothing to improve it.
questions.rule: Opposite blame pulls forecasters to opposite errors.

questions.q: True or false: Sherman Kent’s proposal to attach numerical ranges to forecasts went nowhere, partly because of the wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy.
questions.explain: The fallacy was a big reason: use a number and risk unfair blame, stay vague and stay safe.
questions.rule: Numerical ranges threatened forecasters with blame.

questions.q: A director of national intelligence, after a missed revolution, cites improving Brier scores. What does the chapter say about this defence?
options: It would work well, since statistics are harder to dispute than words
It would work only if the scores were also better than the superforecasters’
It would cover the missed event, since improvement over time is what matters
It would leave the director without cover, since numbers invite the fallacy
optionExplain: Tetlock imagines the hearing as a failure of cover.
He imagines the director even claiming to catch the superforecasters, and it does not help.
The director’s remark that improvement matters is what the hearing would mock.
Right: lacking cover the next time they blow a big call is exactly the vulnerability.
questions.explain: Tetlock imagines a director at a hearing citing solid Brier scores, significant improvement and even catching up with the superforecasters, while a terrible event followed. Numbers would leave the community vulnerable and lacking cover.
questions.rule: Numbers can remove the cover that vagueness gives.
questions.teaches: Tetlock imagines a director citing improving Brier scores at a hearing after a missed event, and sees that numbers would leave the community lacking any cover.

questions.q: A decade before the tournament, where would Tetlock have placed the intelligence community on a list of organisations likely to get serious about forecasting?
options: At the top of those that needed to, but were least likely to
In the middle of the list, since it had mixed incentives
At the top of those most likely to, given its need for accuracy
At the bottom of those that needed to, as it had little to gain
optionExplain: Right: it most needed to but was least likely to, because of kto-kogo.
Tetlock places it at an extreme, not in the middle.
He expected the opposite: need did not translate into willingness.
He thinks it had much to gain in the long run.
questions.explain: The community was the hardest case for the hope. The card next explains why that makes the tournament a good sign.
questions.rule: Hard cases are the best evidence of change.

questions.q: Tetlock calls the IARPA tournament perhaps the best ____ to hope for change.
questions.explain: The tournament shows even the intelligence community was willing to try scoring.
questions.rule: The tournament itself is evidence for hope.

questions.q: A hospital known for fierce resistance to audits suddenly funds an audit pilot. By Tetlock’s reasoning, how much hope does this give?
options: A good deal, since resistance was most likely there
None, since an institution that resisted before will resist again
A little, since only a pilot at a friendly hospital would be convincing
A great deal, since one pilot ensures that audits become permanent
optionExplain: Right: change in the least likely place is encouraging, as with the intelligence community.
That is the kto-kogo pessimism the chapter argues against.
The reasoning goes the other way: the unfriendly case is the better evidence.
Tetlock stops short of certainty.
questions.explain: The less likely a backer, the more a backing tells you. Tetlock draws hope without claiming certainty.
questions.rule: Surprising backers are informative.

questions.q: Sort each fact: does it support hope for the intelligence community, or caution?

items.t: The community funded the IARPA tournament
The director of National Intelligence showed strong interest in scorekeeping
Scorekeeping is dangerous to the community in the short run
Numbers leave analysts open to the wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy
Blame-game ping-pong discourages long-term investment
Evidence-based forecasting should help its work in the long run

questions.explain: The chapter weighs short-run risk against long-run gain. The tournament is the sign that the second may win.
questions.rule: Weigh the risks and the signs separately.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says the community took up scorekeeping because it carries no short-run risk for analysts.
questions.explain: He says evidence-based forecasting is dangerous for the community in the short run; the surprise is that it funded the tournament anyway.
questions.rule: The surprise is the willingness despite the risk.

questions.q: A reformer says funding from a once-hostile institution proves the change is secure. Which part of Tetlock’s attitude does this overlook?
options: That it could all be undone in a heartbeat, whatever the long run holds
That hostile institutions should never be asked for money on principle
That only the director’s personal interest counts, not the funding itself
That success is certain once a single tournament has been run
optionExplain: Right: he says it could all be undone in a heartbeat, yet calls the change amazing and welcome.
Tetlock welcomes the funding; he does not object to its source.
He cites both the funding and the director’s interest as encouraging.
He does not claim certainty.
questions.explain: Tetlock adds that it could all be undone in a heartbeat. Still, he calls the change amazing and welcome, and says history may be on the side of reform in the long run.
questions.rule: Welcome the change and expect it to be fragile.
questions.teaches: Tetlock says the change could be undone in a heartbeat, yet calls it amazing and welcome, adding that history may be on our side in the long run.

questions.q: In 1976 Tetlock chose between Oxford and the United States. What did his adviser Peter Suedfeld urge him to do?
options: Take the Oxford scholarship and study the humanities in England
Stay in Canada and finish a second degree at his university
Go to the United States and commit to the scientific method
Work for a few years in business before choosing his field
optionExplain: That was the road not taken; Suedfeld called it a terrible idea.
The chapter gives no such advice.
Right: he went the scientific route, hesitantly.
The chapter does not mention a gap of years.
questions.explain: The choice shapes the imagined objection. The card next sets out what a humanist would say.
questions.rule: Tetlock might have been the objector.

questions.q: Not everything that counts can be ____, goes the famous saying the imagined humanist cites.
questions.explain: The saying continues: and not everything that can be counted counts.
questions.rule: Counting is not the same as mattering.

questions.q: A school ranks teachers only by test-score gains and dismisses a mentor whose strengths do not show in scores. Which worry does this illustrate?
options: Numbers assigned to things they cannot capture
Scores treating false alarms the same as misses
Experts explaining results only after they happen
Intelligence agencies avoiding numbers to avoid blame
optionExplain: Right: the mentor’s strengths are uncaptured by the measure.
That is the Brier flaw, a different issue.
That is the hindsight habit.
That is the wrong-side-of-maybe problem.
questions.explain: The humanist worry is that a number replaces what it cannot capture.
questions.rule: Check that the number captures what matters.

questions.q: Match each voice in the humanists’ objection to what it contributes.
pairs: Urged Tetlock to go to the US and commit to the scientific method
A cultural critic who said metrics are assigned to phenomena that cannot be measured
Not everything that counts can be counted, and not everything countable counts
questions.explain: Each source plays a different part: the adviser shows the fork in Tetlock’s life, the critic gives the objection, and the saying sums it up.
questions.rule: Keep the voices straight.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says the humanists’ objection contains no truth.
questions.explain: He says he feels there is a lot of truth in the perspective, and that too many people treat numbers as sacred totems.
questions.rule: He agrees with part of it.

questions.q: A critic fears dashboards are replacing seasoned judgment in a hospital. Whose worry in the chapter does this echo?
options: Paul Saffo’s, who found the tournament’s questions too small to matter
Leon Wieseltier’s, who warned of quantification replacing wisdom
Daniel Drezner’s, who confessed his own vague predictions
Peter Suedfeld’s, who urged the scientific method
optionExplain: Saffo’s worry was that the questions were too small, not that numbers displace wisdom.
Right: Wieseltier wrote that where wisdom once was, quantification will now be.
Drezner called for more scoring, not less.
Suedfeld advised the scientific path.
questions.explain: Wieseltier, writing in the New York Times, put it poetically: where wisdom once was, quantification will now be. Tetlock quotes him as the sharpest form of the objection.
questions.rule: Wieseltier fears numbers displacing wisdom.
questions.teaches: Wieseltier wrote in the New York Times that where wisdom once was, quantification will now be.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says a hospital could report 100% survival and still be doing badly.
questions.explain: A hospital could achieve that by turning away the sickest patients. The card next gives Tetlock’s point.
questions.rule: A crude measure can be gamed.

questions.q: The truly numerate know that numbers are ____, nothing more.
questions.explain: A tool can be good or bad, and needs to be checked.
questions.rule: Numbers are tools.

questions.q: A call centre reports 100% of customers satisfied, after hanging up on unhappy callers. Which lesson from the chapter applies?
options: A crude measure can look perfect by excluding the hardest cases
Satisfaction can never be measured, so no score should be used
The score is accurate if it reaches 100% on a large sample
Calls should be reviewed after the event, once outcomes are known
optionExplain: Right: like the hospital that turned away the sickest, the score is gamed.
Tetlock says numbers need improving, not abandoning.
A perfect score from a bad measure is a warning sign, not proof.
Hindsight review is not the point here; the measure itself is flawed.
questions.explain: A number that ignores the hard cases flatters the one who reports it. That is why numbers need constant scrutiny.
questions.rule: Ask what a number leaves out.

questions.q: A hospital adopts survival rate alone as its score. What behaviour does the chapter’s example predict?
options: More investment in the care of the sickest patients
Turning away the sickest patients to protect the score
More careful recording of each case’s treatment details
Lower prices to attract healthier patients from rivals
optionExplain: The example predicts the opposite.
Right: that is how it could boast 100% survival.
Nothing in the example concerns recording details.
Prices are not part of the example.
questions.explain: People respond to what is counted. A crude score invites ways of meeting it without improving care.
questions.rule: Scores shape behaviour.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says a well-designed scoring system, once built, no longer needs revision.
questions.explain: He says numbers must be constantly scrutinised and improved, and that the process is unending.
questions.rule: Improvement is unending.

questions.q: A manager treats her team’s dashboard as divine insight and does not revisit it. Which attitude does Tetlock criticise?
options: Treating numbers like sacred totems offering divine insight
Using any numbers at all when judging people’s work
Replacing a metric with a better one after testing it
Showing the metric to the team before the quarter ends
optionExplain: Right: he says far too many people treat numbers like sacred totems.
He does not object to using numbers.
Replacing metrics is what he recommends.
Sharing metrics is not criticised.
questions.explain: Tetlock says far too many people treat numbers like sacred totems offering divine insight, and that constant scrutiny is unnerving precisely because it is unending.
questions.rule: Do not worship the metric.
questions.teaches: Far too many people treat numbers like sacred totems offering divine insight, and the scrutiny numbers need is unnerving because it never ends.

questions.q: Which flaw of Brier scores does Tetlock admit?
options: They cannot be used for questions with more than two outcomes
They reward forecasters who make very few forecasts
They treat false alarms the same as misses
They ignore how confident the forecaster was
optionExplain: The chapter does not claim this.
The chapter does not raise this point.
Right: but people usually care far more about misses.
Brier scores do use the stated probability; this is not his criticism.
questions.explain: Equal weighting is the flaw Tetlock names. The card next gives his fix.
questions.rule: Equal weights may not match what matters.

questions.q: Tetlock suggests telling forecasters in advance that false positives will cost one-____ as much as false negatives.
questions.explain: The example weights misses ten times as heavily as false alarms.
questions.rule: Announce the weighting before forecasting.

questions.q: A flood office will score river-level warnings. Missing a flood is far worse than a false alarm. Which fix fits Tetlock’s approach?
options: Drop scoring altogether, since a perfect rule cannot be built
Score only the false alarms, since misses are hard to count
Announce in advance a heavier penalty for misses than false alarms
Ask forecasters to explain each flood afterwards in a written report
optionExplain: Tetlock says a scoring system that needs tweaking is still a big improvement.
Ignoring misses would make the problem worse.
Right: the ground rules are set beforehand, so forecasters adjust their judgments.
Written reports after the fact are the hindsight habit.
questions.explain: Telling forecasters the rules in advance lets the score reflect what the users care about.
questions.rule: Set the weights before the forecasts.

questions.q: Match each item to its part in Tetlock’s defence of scoring.
pairs: Treats false alarms the same as misses
Tell forecasters the ground rules in advance
Flawed, yet a huge advance on whimsical loan decisions
questions.explain: He admits a flaw, offers an easy fix, and compares the whole system with credit scores, which also improved on guesswork.
questions.rule: Flawed is not the same as worthless.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock calls Brier scoring a work in progress.
questions.explain: He says he cannot claim his scoring system is perfect, only that it is a big improvement.
questions.rule: Improvement, not perfection.

questions.q: A conference invites a speaker mainly for the number of books sold. Which of Tetlock’s targets does this exemplify?
options: A flaw in the way the Brier score is calculated
A criterion now used to judge forecasters
A step in the fix for weighting false alarms
A loan officer’s whimsical judgment about a borrower
optionExplain: Book sales have nothing to do with Brier scores.
Right: Tetlock lists titles, confidence, story-spinning skill, books sold, CNN appearances and time at Davos.
The fix concerns announcing penalty weights.
That is the credit-score comparison, a different domain.
questions.explain: Tetlock says the criteria used nowadays are titles, confidence, skill at spinning a story, number of books sold, CNN appearances and time spent at Davos. His scoring system improves on all of them.
questions.rule: Prestige is not a test of accuracy.
questions.teaches: Forecasters are now judged by titles, confidence, story-spinning, books sold, CNN appearances and time at Davos, which Brier scoring improves on.

questions.q: Paul Saffo called the IARPA North Korea rocket question trivial. Which question did he say was more fundamental?
options: Will North Korea conduct another nuclear test before the year ends?
Will the Korean armistice of 1953 be formally renounced soon?
How does this all turn out?
Which Pentagon colonels will advise on the next crisis?
optionExplain: That is one of the small questions Tetlock later uses in a cluster.
That is one of the events in the build-up, not Saffo’s question.
Right: he wanted the whole story rather than one launch.
Saffo mentioned colonels only as those who might find the rocket question interesting.
questions.explain: Saffo preferred the big picture to a single event. The card next sets out the dilemma his remark raises.
questions.rule: Big questions matter, but they are hard to score.

questions.q: Tetlock says the big question matters, but it can’t be ____, whereas the little question can.
questions.explain: Scoring needs an answer that can be checked against an outcome. Saffo’s answer was too vague.
questions.rule: Only definite questions can be scored.

questions.q: A city asks whether downtown will thrive and whether a new cafe will open by June. How do these fit Tetlock’s dilemma?
options: Both are small questions, and neither could be scored
The first is big and hard to score; the second is small and scorable
The first is small and scorable; the second is big and hard to score
Both are big questions, and both could be scored with a probability
optionExplain: The first is plainly broad and vague.
Right: the cafe question has a date and a yes or no outcome.
This reverses the pair.
The cafe question is narrow, not big.
questions.explain: Breadth and scorability pull in opposite directions. The big downtown question is important but vague; the cafe question is clear but narrow.
questions.rule: Check both importance and scorability.

questions.q: Sort each question: big and hard to score, or small and scorable?

items.t: How does this all turn out?
What will the next decade bring for the economy?
Where is the Korean peninsula heading?
Will North Korea attempt a multistage rocket launch between 7 January and 1 September 2013?
Will the central bank raise rates before 31 March?
Will the election be held by 1 October?

questions.explain: Big questions have no single outcome to check. Small ones name an event and a date, so they can be scored.
questions.rule: A date and an outcome make a question scorable.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says he could not tell, even later, whether Saffo’s answer was right, because it was too vague to judge.
questions.explain: He writes that even today he does not know. That is typical, he says, of answers to big, important questions.
questions.rule: Vague answers cannot be judged.

questions.q: A critic says the tournament’s questions were chosen only because they were easy to score. What does the chapter say about how they were chosen?
options: Experts screened them for difficulty and relevance
A lottery drew them from a long list prepared by the researchers themselves
Forecasters voted for the ones they thought they could answer best
Analysts submitted the ones with the answers they already believed
optionExplain: Right: the screening kept them hard and relevant, though narrower than the big questions.
The chapter describes expert screening, not a lottery.
Forecasters did not choose them.
The chapter does not say this.
questions.explain: Tetlock calls the charge unfair: the questions were screened by experts to be difficult and relevant to active problems on analysts’ desks. They are still more narrowly focused than the big questions.
questions.rule: Narrow does not mean irrelevant.
questions.teaches: The tournament’s questions had been screened by experts to be both difficult and relevant to active problems on intelligence analysts’ desks.

questions.q: Which painting technique does Tetlock compare to answering a big question with many small ones?
options: Cubism, which shows an object from several angles at once
Collage, which pastes cut-out pieces onto a single surface
Pointillism, which builds a picture from tiny dabs of paint
Impressionism, which captures a scene in a few loose strokes
optionExplain: Cubism is about viewpoints, not accumulation of small marks.
Collage uses pieces of other material, not dots.
Right: each dot adds little, but patterns emerge as the dots collect.
Loose strokes are not what Tetlock describes.
questions.explain: Dots build a portrait or landscape. The card next applies the same idea to questions.
questions.rule: Many small dots make a picture.

questions.q: Tetlock calls his approach Bayesian question ____.
questions.explain: He likes the name because of its family resemblance to the Bayesian updating of chapter 7.
questions.rule: Cluster small questions around a big one.

questions.q: To judge whether a firm is heading for trouble, which approach follows Tetlock’s clustering?
options: Ask many small dated questions, such as a missed earnings target
Ask one broad question and have experts argue about how it will turn out
Wait for the firm to fail and then explain the signs in hindsight
Ask the firm’s directors how confident they are that all will be well
optionExplain: Right: each small question adds a little, and the answers accumulate.
One broad question is the unscorable big question, argued without a test.
That is the hindsight habit the chapter calls a dead end.
Confidence is not evidence and cannot be scored by itself.
questions.explain: A cluster replaces one unscorable question with several scorable ones that bear on it.
questions.rule: Small questions add up.

questions.q: In the Korea example, more of the small questions resolve yes. What happens to the likelihood of ‘This is going to end badly’?
options: It falls, since each yes shows that the crisis has peaked
It rises, since the answers are cumulative
It stays put, since no single question settles the big one
It becomes impossible to judge once there are many answers
optionExplain: The chapter says the opposite: yeses escalate the conflict.
Right: the more yeses, the likelier the answer is that it ends badly.
No single question settles it, but together they move the odds.
Many answers make the picture clearer, as in pointillism.
questions.explain: Each yes pushes the odds a little, and together they move the answer. Tetlock compares the process to Bayesian updating.
questions.rule: Cumulative evidence moves the odds.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says each small question adds little on its own, but patterns emerge as the answers accumulate.
questions.explain: That is the point of the pointillism comparison: no dot alone, but together a picture.
questions.rule: Accumulation is the method.

questions.q: Tetlock wants to test clustering in future research. Why can the clusters that arose in the tournament not already prove it works?
options: They were too small to give results that a scientist could analyse
They arose more from events than from a deliberate diagnostic strategy
They were scored by IARPA staff rather than by independent judges
They covered only questions about North Korea, so no pattern could be seen
optionExplain: The chapter does not say the clusters were too small.
Right: the clusters arose as a consequence of events, not as a planned strategy.
The chapter says nothing about who scored them.
The chapter does not limit the clusters to North Korea.
questions.explain: There were question clusters in the tournament, but they arose more as a consequence of events than as a diagnostic strategy. Tetlock wants to develop the concept and see how effectively clusters of little questions answer unscorable big ones.
questions.rule: A planned test is needed, not accidental clusters.
questions.teaches: Clusters appeared in the tournament more as a consequence of events than as a diagnostic strategy, so Tetlock wants to develop and test the concept.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock intended the name Good Judgment Project to say that accurate forecasting and good judgment are the same thing.
questions.explain: The name seems to imply that, he says, but it is not what he intended. The card next explains the difference.
questions.rule: Do not equate foresight with judgment.

questions.q: Tetlock says foresight is one ____ of good judgment, not all of it.
questions.explain: Others include things that cannot be counted, such as moral judgment.
questions.rule: Foresight is only part of judgment.

questions.q: A firm makes the top scorer in a forecasting contest its ethics adviser, reasoning that forecasting skill is good judgment. How would Tetlock respond?
options: Foresight is one element of good judgment, not all of it
The appointment is sound, since the top scorer has proved good judgment
Forecasting contests rank accuracy, so top scorers must be dishonest
Top scorers should never be asked for advice on anything but forecasts
optionExplain: Right: other elements, such as moral judgment, are not captured by forecasting scores.
That is the equation Tetlock says he did not intend.
The chapter makes no such claim.
Tetlock does not bar them from other roles; he says forecasting skill is not the whole.
questions.explain: A forecasting score measures foresight. It cannot show moral judgment or the other parts of good judgment.
questions.rule: A score covers one element only.

questions.q: Sort each ability: can a forecasting score capture it, or is it a part of good judgment that it cannot?
groups: A forecast score can capture it

items.t: Giving a probability that an event occurs by a set date
Revising a probability when new facts arrive
Being well calibrated across many predictions
Deciding what is morally right to do
Weighing the values at stake in a policy
Judging whether a question deserves to be asked

questions.explain: Scores handle probabilities and outcomes. Moral judgment and question-asking are further elements the chapter says are not counted.
questions.rule: Good judgment has parts a score misses.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says some elements of good judgment cannot be counted.
questions.explain: He names moral judgment as an element that cannot be run through a scientist’s algorithms.
questions.rule: Not every part of judgment is countable.

questions.q: A forecaster answers every posed question superbly but does not pose any. Which element does the chapter say is missing?
options: Asking good questions, since someone must pose them first
Moral judgment, since questions cannot be asked without moral rules
Calibration, since a forecaster who never asks cannot be well calibrated
Hindsight, since only the past shows which questions mattered
optionExplain: Right: Tetlock calls asking good questions another critical dimension of good judgment.
Moral judgment is a different element named in the chapter.
Calibration is a feature of answers, not of asking.
Hindsight is the habit the chapter distrusts.
questions.explain: Tetlock says another critical dimension of good judgment is asking good questions. A farsighted forecast flagging disaster or opportunity cannot happen until someone thinks to pose the question.
questions.rule: Someone has to ask the question first.
questions.teaches: Asking good questions is another critical dimension of good judgment, since a forecast flagging disaster or opportunity cannot happen until someone poses the question.

questions.q: How does Tetlock suggest identifying a good question once time has passed?
options: Count how many forecasters answered it correctly
Check whether the pundit who asked it later turned out to be right
Ask whether you wish you had thought of it earlier
Measure how many readers shared the column that raised it
optionExplain: Correct answers measure forecasters, not the question.
A good question need not come with a good forecast, as Friedman shows.
Right: you smack your forehead and say ‘If only I had thought of that before!’
Popularity is not Tetlock’s test.
questions.explain: Tetlock judges a question by what it later reveals. The card next gives the test and his example.
questions.rule: Judge a question by what it reveals later.

questions.q: Tetlock calls his test of a good question the smack-the-____ test.
questions.explain: The reaction on reading the question later is to smack one’s forehead.
questions.rule: A good question is one you wish you had asked.

questions.q: Years later, a manager says ‘If only we had asked whether the town depended on a single employer!’ Which test does this describe?
options: The wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy applied to a forecast
The smack-the-forehead test applied to a question
The kto-kogo view applied to a partisan forecast
Codman’s system applied to a hospital
optionExplain: That fallacy concerns scoring probabilities after one outcome.
Right: the question would have drawn attention to a key driver of later events.
Kto-kogo concerns forecasting as a contest for power.
That is Codman’s outcome-recording idea.
questions.explain: The test is a reaction to a question’s value once events have shown which drivers mattered.
questions.rule: A good question points at a key driver.

questions.q: Suppose a question’s key drivers only become visible years later. When can the smack-the-forehead test be applied to it?
options: Before anyone has answered it, from its wording alone
Only at the moment when the first forecaster scores it
After time has passed and the drivers have shown themselves
Never, since drivers can only be seen in hindsight
optionExplain: The test needs time to pass.
Scoring forecasts is a different activity.
Right: the test is read after time has passed.
Time reveals the drivers, so the test can be used then.
questions.explain: The test is retrospective by design: a question earns its mark by what later events show.
questions.rule: The test needs hindsight on the question, not the answer.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says Friedman’s 2002 question passes the test because Friedman correctly foresaw that the invasion would go well.
questions.explain: The question passes because it drew attention to key drivers such as sectarianism. Friedman’s expectations were presumably quite different from what happened.
questions.rule: A good question is not a good forecast.

questions.q: A commentator poses a question that later proves central, yet backs a policy whose results he misjudged. What does the Friedman parallel imply?
options: That the question was probably not a good one
That asking well does not require forecasting well
That the commentator must have changed his mind after the event
That good questions can only come from people who forecast well
optionExplain: Friedman’s case shows that a good question can come with a poor forecast.
Right: Friedman’s question passes even though he backed the invasion on different expectations.
Nothing in the case says Friedman changed his mind.
The chapter suggests the abilities often come apart.
questions.explain: Tetlock says it is remarkable that Friedman’s question passes, because Friedman became a strong supporter of the invasion in part on expectations presumably quite different from what happened.
questions.rule: Asking and forecasting are separate skills.
questions.teaches: Friedman became a strong supporter of the invasion partly on expectations presumably quite different from what happened, which makes his question’s pass remarkable.

questions.q: What is Tetlock’s best scientific guess about whether superforecasters are also superquestioners?
options: They are always the same people, since both need an open mind
They often are not, since the two abilities may need different mindsets
They are the same when the questions concern science and not politics
They cannot be compared because no one has studied superquestioners
optionExplain: Tetlock says the opposite: we do not know and he guesses otherwise.
Right: he guesses the recipes differ.
The chapter makes no such split between science and politics.
He offers a guess; he does not refuse to compare.
questions.explain: Tetlock rejects the easy assumption. The card next sets out what he thinks and how sure he is.
questions.rule: Do not assume the two skills go together.

questions.q: Tetlock admits that we don’t actually ____ whether a superforecaster is also a superquestioner.
questions.explain: He calls the pairing an assumption and gives only a best scientific guess.
questions.rule: Treat the link as unproven.

questions.q: A newsroom has an analyst who forecasts superbly. Should it assume she will also pose its best questions?
options: Yes, since good forecasters grasp which drivers matter most
Yes, since the two skills draw on the same habits of thought
No, since Tetlock’s guess is that the two skills often do not coincide
No, since forecasters are barred by design from asking questions
optionExplain: That is the assumption Tetlock says we cannot make.
That is the same assumption stated another way.
Right: it is an unsupported assumption, and he guesses the abilities often differ.
Nothing bars forecasters from asking questions.
questions.explain: Tetlock’s guess is that the two abilities often come from different mindsets, so skill in one does not show skill in the other.
questions.rule: Skill at answering does not show skill at asking.

questions.q: If Tetlock’s guess is right, what follows for a team that wants both abilities?
options: It may need different people for each, since the skills often do not coincide
It should hire only superforecasters and ask them to pose the questions too
It can drop question-asking, since forecasting skill will cover it
It should train every member to do both at the same level
optionExplain: Right: complementary strengths may sit in different heads.
That repeats the assumption his guess denies.
He says question-asking is a critical element of good judgment.
The guess suggests such training may not produce both.
questions.explain: If the skills rarely coincide, the team gains by pairing people. The next idea turns this into a call for cooperation.
questions.rule: Pair complementary strengths.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock presents his view of superquestioners as a best scientific guess, not as a settled finding.
questions.explain: He writes that we do not actually know, and calls the idea his best scientific guess.
questions.rule: Respect the stated confidence.

questions.q: A team lead wants one member to pose questions and another to forecast them. Which pairing follows Tetlock’s guess?
options: A foxy, eclectic thinker to pose questions and a confident big-idea thinker to forecast
A confident big-idea thinker to pose questions and a foxy, eclectic thinker to forecast
Two foxy thinkers, one to ask and one to answer, for the sake of agreement
Two big-idea thinkers, one to ask and one to answer, for the sake of speed
optionExplain: This reverses his pairing.
Right: superb question generation often seems to go with hedgehog-like incisiveness, and superb forecasting with foxy eclecticism.
Tetlock links the two tasks to different mindsets.
He links the two tasks to different mindsets, not the same one.
questions.explain: Tetlock says superb question generation often seems to accompany hedgehog-like incisiveness and confidence in a Big Idea, while superb forecasting reflects foxy eclecticism and sensitivity to uncertainty.
questions.rule: Questioners lean hedgehog; forecasters lean fox.
questions.teaches: Superb question generation often seems to accompany hedgehog-like incisiveness and a Big Idea; superb forecasting goes with foxy eclecticism and sensitivity to uncertainty.

questions.q: How does Tetlock read Friedman’s December 2014 warning of surprises after the fall in oil prices?
options: As a precise forecast that superforecasters should try to beat
As a hindsight explanation of events that had already happened
As evidence that Friedman was slippery and should be ignored
As a question for forecasters rather than a forecast of its own
optionExplain: Tetlock says it is vague, so it cannot be scored.
The column looks ahead; it is not an after-the-fact story.
He acknowledges the charge but chooses a more useful reading.
Right: it is an attempt to draw forecasters’ attention to something worth thinking about.
questions.explain: Tetlock turns a vague column into a pointer. The card next gives the larger idea.
questions.rule: Treat vague warnings as questions.

questions.q: Tetlock calls for a Tom-____ symbiosis between superquestioners and superforecasters.
questions.explain: Tom stands for the pundit Tom Friedman and Bill for the superforecaster Bill Flack, the pair contrasted at the start of the book.
questions.rule: Questioners and forecasters need each other.

questions.q: An energy analyst writes that falling prices will bring ‘surprises’ for exporting states. How would Tetlock suggest forecasters treat this?
options: Dismiss it, since a prediction without dates or numbers is worthless
Score it as a forecast and mark it as wrong, since nothing happened
Rewrite it as specific, scorable questions about particular states and dates
Wait until a surprise occurs and then count it as a hit for the analyst
optionExplain: Tetlock does not dismiss the column; he reads it as a question.
It is too vague to score as a forecast.
Right: the warning points forecasters toward questions they can answer.
That would credit a vague forecast after the fact, the habit he criticises.
questions.explain: The forecasters’ job is to turn the pointer into specific questions they can answer with calibrated probabilities.
questions.rule: Make the vague question specific.

questions.q: Match each party to what Tetlock says it offers the other.
pairs: Provocative questions that sharpen forecasters’ foresight
Well-calibrated answers that fine-tune questioners’ mental models
questions.explain: Each side supplies what the other lacks. The frame that sets them against each other is the last false dichotomy.
questions.rule: Complementary, not rival.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says Friedman’s oil column should be read as a precise, scorable forecast.
questions.explain: He says it is a vague warning of unspecified surprises in unspecified time frames, so as a forecast it is not terribly helpful.
questions.rule: Read it as a question.

questions.q: A reader asks whether superforecasters could beat Friedman’s predictions. How does Tetlock treat the question?
options: As the main test of whether superforecasting works
As unknown and beside the point, given complementary strengths
As already settled in favour of superforecasters by the tournament
As already settled in favour of Friedman by his column on oil
optionExplain: He says it is beside the point, not central.
Right: it is both unknown and, for present purposes, beside the point.
He says it is unknown.
He says it is unknown.
questions.explain: Tetlock says whether superforecasters can outpredict Friedman is both unknown and, for present purposes, beside the point. They should acknowledge each other’s strengths rather than dwell on alleged weaknesses.
questions.rule: Do not turn the pairing into a contest.
questions.teaches: Whether superforecasters can outpredict Friedman is both unknown and, for present purposes, beside the point; each side should use the other’s strengths.

questions.q: In 2014, how did the signatories who answered Bloomberg’s questions say they felt about their 2010 letter to Bernanke?
options: Some conceded the letter had been mistaken, while others held to it
They split into camps, with most saying they would now word it more carefully
They said unanimously that they were right and would not change a word
They declined to comment and said the letter had been misquoted
optionExplain: Those who responded were unanimous.
None said they would reword it; they stood by every word.
Right: every respondent said they were right.
The chapter reports that they did reply.
questions.explain: The replies are the point of the story. The card next sets out the two kinds of reason they gave.
questions.rule: Unanimity here shows no one updated.

questions.q: Those who replied to Bloomberg said they wouldn’t change a ____ of the 2010 letter.
questions.explain: They stood by every word, even though the dollar did not weaken and inflation did not rise.
questions.rule: No change of position at all.

questions.q: A forecaster warns of ‘a risk of recession’, sees none for years, and says the risk remains. Which reason from the chapter does this echo?
options: Looking at the wrong measure of the outcome
Pointing to the loose wording of the original warning
Counting only the results that favour one’s side
Citing a better track record than one’s critics have
optionExplain: That is James Grant’s kind of reply, not this one.
Right: Niall Ferguson noted the word ‘risk’ and the absence of a date, so the warning is not proved wrong.
The chapter does not describe this move in the replies.
Nothing in the replies compares track records.
questions.explain: A claim that a risk exists, with no date, is compatible with any outcome. That makes it impossible to fail.
questions.rule: Risk with no date cannot fail.

questions.q: Sort each reply: does it say the wrong measure was used, or that the wording was not refuted?

items.t: Inflation is plentiful on Wall Street, not at the checkout counter
Critics checked prices where the effect does not show
Look for the effect in a different place than the critics did
The letter spoke of a risk, and a risk remains
The letter named no date, so time has not run out
Nothing in the wording says the warning has failed

questions.explain: The first kind of reply disputes where to look; the second says the letter, as written, cannot be shown wrong.
questions.rule: Two ways to avoid being wrong.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says the later weakening of the dollar and rise of inflation proved the letter wrong.
questions.explain: The dollar did not weaken and inflation did not rise, yet the wording was so vague that it was impossible to say definitively that the letter was wrong.
questions.rule: Vague wording blocks a clear verdict.

questions.q: A fund manager says his bear-market warning still stands because he said ‘risk’ and gave no date. Whose argument is he following?
options: James Grant’s, who said inflation was on Wall Street
Niall Ferguson’s, who stressed ‘risk’ and the lack of a date
Daniel Drezner’s, who promised to give a confidence interval
Paul Krugman’s, who catalogued his opponents’ failures
optionExplain: Grant argued that the wrong measure was being used.
Right: Ferguson said to note the word ‘risk’ and the absence of a date.
Drezner did the opposite: he committed to scorable forecasts.
Krugman’s role in the chapter is attacking forecasting failures.
questions.explain: James Grant argued that there is plenty of inflation, not at the checkout counter but on Wall Street. Niall Ferguson said to note the word ‘risk’ and the absence of a date, so there is still a risk of currency debasement and inflation.
questions.rule: Hedged wording blocks scoring.
questions.teaches: James Grant said the inflation was on Wall Street, not at the checkout counter; Niall Ferguson said to note the word ‘risk’ and the absence of a date.

questions.q: A Minneapolis Fed president, an Austerian, announced that events had shown the Keynesians were closer to the truth. What happened?
options: It was taken as routine, since economists often revise their views
It provoked a fierce reply from fellow Austerians who rejected it
It made headlines, since people so rarely adjusted their thinking
It led both camps to sign a joint statement about what they learned
optionExplain: The chapter says the opposite: it was newsworthy because it was rare.
The chapter does not report such a reply.
Right: the headline could have been ‘Man Changes His Mind in Response to Evidence’.
The chapter reports no joint statement.
questions.explain: That a change of mind made headlines shows how rare it was. The card next sets out the failure Tetlock sees.
questions.rule: Updating is rare enough to be news.

questions.q: Tetlock says the failure was one of ____, not necessarily of substance.
questions.explain: People wrote down beliefs and waited, yet no one budged.
questions.rule: The process, not the answer, failed.

questions.q: Two analysts publish opposing growth forecasts, wait three years, and neither changes position despite the data. What failure would Tetlock name?
options: A failure of substance, because at least one of them must be wrong
A failure of process, because the debate produced no updating
A failure of measurement, because the forecasts were too precise
A failure of arithmetic, because the forecasts used different units
optionExplain: Tetlock stays agnostic on substance; the problem is that no one updated.
Right: beliefs were written down, time passed, and no one budged.
Precision is what he asks for.
The scenario gives no sign of unit errors.
questions.explain: The mark of failure is not who was right but that the exchange taught no one anything.
questions.rule: A debate that teaches no one has failed.

questions.q: Put in order what Tetlock says should happen in a debate like Keynesians versus Austerians.
items: Each side states its predictions in writing
Time passes and outcomes arrive
Predictions are compared with what actually happened
Those shown to be wrong say so and adjust their thinking
questions.explain: The comparison of predictions with outcomes comes before any adjustment, and none of it can start unless the predictions were written down.
questions.rule: State, wait, compare, adjust.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says he is not claiming that the letter writers were wrong on substance.
questions.explain: He says he is agnostic on issues outside his field. His objection is to the failure of process.
questions.rule: Process failure is not the same as being wrong.

questions.q: Two commentators each publish lists of the other’s failed forecasts, and neither learns. Which description from the chapter fits?
options: A debate between great minds that clarified the issues for readers
A food fight between rival fraternities, with nothing learned
A model adversarial collaboration run under the rules of science
A tournament in which forecasts were scored by a neutral party
optionExplain: That is what the exchange could have been, not what it was.
Right: nobody seemed to have learned anything beyond how to defend their original position.
It lacked the good faith and ground rules of the Kahneman-Klein case.
No neutral scoring was involved.
questions.explain: Paul Krugman hammered opponents for their failures and Niall Ferguson hammered back with a catalogue of Krugman’s alleged failures. Tetlock says it looked less like a debate between great minds and more like a food fight between rival fraternities.
questions.rule: Hammering opponents is not learning.
questions.teaches: Krugman and Ferguson hammered each other over forecasting failures, which Tetlock says looked like a food fight between rival fraternities, with nobody learning beyond defending their position.

questions.q: Which pair of psychologists does Tetlock cite as a model of adversarial collaboration?
options: Daniel Kahneman and Gary Klein
Peter Suedfeld and Philip Tetlock
Carol Dweck and Daniel Kahneman
Gary Klein and Paul Saffo
optionExplain: Right: they developed apparently contradictory schools yet met to reconcile them.
Suedfeld was Tetlock’s adviser, not a collaborator in this sense.
Dweck appears in other chapters, not this model.
Saffo is the futurist who found the tournament question trivial.
questions.explain: The Kahneman-Klein case shows rivals cooperating under scientific rules. The card next applies it to forecasting.
questions.rule: Rivals can design tests together.

questions.q: Tetlock says the key to a forecast question that tests a disagreement is ____.
questions.explain: Vague claims cannot be scored; precise ones can.
questions.rule: Precision makes a test possible.

questions.q: Two economists disagree on whether a tax cut will ‘boost growth’. Which question best fits Tetlock’s approach?
options: Will the tax cut turn out to be good for the economy over time?
Will the economy feel noticeably stronger once the tax cut is in place?
Will GDP growth top 3% in the year after the cut, by official figures?
Will most economists agree in the end that the tax cut was useful?
optionExplain: No benchmark and no period: it cannot be scored.
‘Feel stronger’ is a feeling, not a measure.
Right: it names an amount, a benchmark and a period.
Agreement of experts is not a measure of the outcome.
questions.explain: Tetlock’s test is how much, measured by what benchmark, over what period. The right question answers all three.
questions.rule: Amount, benchmark, period.

questions.q: Sort each wording: precise enough to score, or too ambiguous?

items.t: Will consumer prices, by the official index, rise more than 5% over three years?
Will the euro close below one dollar on 31 December 2026?
Will the official unemployment rate exceed 8% in March?
Will the policy cause inflation?
Will inflation become a problem at some point?
Will the economy do badly in the long run?

questions.explain: A scorable question has a measure, a threshold and a date. The ambiguous ones leave all three open.
questions.rule: Measure, threshold and date.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says Kahneman and Klein discussed why their views differed and how they could be reconciled.
questions.explain: That is the Kahneman-Klein model he proposes for forecasting.
questions.rule: They talked their differences through.

questions.q: Why did Kahneman and Klein collaborate even though each was a threat to the other’s legacy?
options: Because they committed to playing by scientific ground rules
Because a funder required them to share a laboratory
Because their schools turned out to have been identical
Because they agreed to avoid questions that could be scored
optionExplain: Right: they were committed to scientific ground rules, so they met to reconcile their views.
The chapter gives no such reason.
Their schools were apparently contradictory.
The collaboration was meant to test and reconcile, not to avoid scoring.
questions.explain: Tetlock notes that each man’s school threatened the other’s legacy, but both were committed to playing by scientific ground rules, so they got together to discuss why their views differed.
questions.rule: Shared ground rules make rivalry productive.
questions.teaches: Kahneman and Klein each threatened the other’s legacy, yet their commitment to scientific ground rules let them collaborate.

questions.q: In a forecasting contest between two camps, each is right on some questions and wrong on others. What does Tetlock say this shows?
options: That the contest was badly designed and produced no useful result
That reality is more mixed than either side thought
That one side should be declared the winner by points
That forecasts cannot settle any real dispute between camps
optionExplain: He calls the split decision a feature, not a bug.
Right: a split decision tells both sides that reality is more mixed.
Declaring a winner would not capture a mixed result.
He thinks many questions can help settle a dispute.
questions.explain: A mixed result is informative, not a failure. The card next states the claim and its catch.
questions.rule: A split decision is informative.

questions.q: Tetlock says that if the goal is learning, not ____, a split decision is progress.
questions.explain: The aim is to learn what is true, not to celebrate a win.
questions.rule: Aim for learning.

questions.q: Two school-reform camps run a joint test: one wins on test scores, the other on attendance. Which verdict fits Tetlock?
options: Progress: reality is more mixed than either side thought
Failure: a split result settles nothing and wastes the effort
Victory for the camp whose result was easier to measure
Draw: both camps should keep their views exactly as before
optionExplain: Right: a split decision, if learning is the goal, counts as progress.
Tetlock calls this a feature, not a bug.
Ease of measurement does not decide which camp is right.
Keeping views unchanged is the failure the chapter describes.
questions.explain: Tetlock expects mixed outcomes and welcomes them. Each camp learns where it was right and where it was not.
questions.rule: Welcome the mixed verdict.

questions.q: Suppose the loudest voices on each side are invited to join an adversarial test. What does Tetlock expect?
options: They will welcome it because the test will prove their side right
They will have zero interest in adversarial collaboration
They will join if the moderator promises them time on television
They will design the best tests because they know the issues well
optionExplain: Tetlock says strident voices have no interest in adversarial collaboration.
Right: he says they have zero interest.
The chapter does not mention such an offer.
He looks instead to the less voluble, more reasonable voices.
questions.explain: The catch is who takes part. Tetlock looks to the quieter, reasonable voices instead.
questions.rule: Look beyond the loudest voices.

questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says a single well-chosen bet can resolve a complex theoretical dispute.
questions.explain: He says a single bet cannot, just as a single dot is not a painting. It takes many questions and clusters.
questions.rule: One bet is one dot.

questions.q: In a transparent forecasting test, a participant whose forecasts failed rationalises away the facts. What does Tetlock expect?
options: He will pay a reputational price, while others honourably say they were wrong
He will keep his reputation, because the test results will be forgotten
He will be barred from taking part in future tests by the moderator
He will be praised, since refusing to concede shows strength of conviction
optionExplain: Right: rationalisers pay a reputational price, and others do the honorable thing.
The point of the open test is that everyone can watch.
The chapter does not mention a ban.
The chapter says the opposite.
questions.explain: Tetlock says that when the results run against their beliefs some will rationalise away the facts but will pay a reputational price, while others will do the honorable thing and say ‘I was wrong’. The rest of us can watch and get a little wiser.
questions.rule: Open tests make rationalising costly.
questions.teaches: When results run against their beliefs some will rationalise away the facts but will pay a reputational price, while others will say ‘I was wrong’.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: In the epilogue, what small correction did Bill Flack make to the book's description of him?
options: His Brier score had been rounded up in the first chapter of the manuscript
He had joined the forecasting tournament a year later than the manuscript said
He was born in Kansas City, Missouri, so he is not quite a native of Nebraska
He had grown up in Omaha and had never lived anywhere outside Nebraska
optionExplain: A Brier score is mentioned, but the correction is not about it.
Plausible for a correction, but the text gives a different one.
Right: he was born elsewhere and moved to Nebraska at seven.
This reverses the correction: his family moved to Nebraska when he was seven.
questions.explain: The correction concerns his birthplace; the epilogue reads such care as precision. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a superforecaster is exact about small facts and honest about what he does not know.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: The epilogue calls Flack's habit of knowing what he does not know intellectual ____.
questions.explain: Intellectual humility means knowing what you do not know and respecting those who do.
questions.rule: Humility is part of what makes him a superforecaster.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A forecaster is asked about politics in a country she has not studied. Which reply fits the humility the epilogue describes?
options: I would have to look up the basics first, and specialists know the country far better
My record is strong, so I can skip the specialists and rely on my own instincts
Nobody can say anything useful about a country like that, so I will not forecast
I will give a confident answer straight away so no one thinks I am unprepared
optionExplain: Right: it admits the gap and respects those who fill it.
Confidence from a record is tempting, but it ignores what she does not know.
This is giving up, not humility; Flack still forecasts hard questions.
This hides the gap rather than admitting it.
questions.explain: Humility admits the gap in knowledge and respects those with deep knowledge.
questions.rule: Admit the gap, then go and fill it.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: Match each behaviour of Flack to what the epilogue says it shows.
pairs: Saying he would have to search the web for a minor country's leader
Holding a Brier score that backs his forecasts on tough questions
questions.explain: The correction shows precision, the Davos remark shows humility, and the Brier score is the evidence of an outstanding record.
questions.rule: According to the authors, a superforecaster is exact about small facts and honest about what he does not know.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: True or false: The epilogue says pundits such as Tom Friedman have Brier scores showing records as strong as Flack's.
questions.explain: The epilogue says Flack has the Brier score to prove his record, and that the Tom Friedmen of the world do not.
questions.rule: Flack's record is scored; the pundits' records are not.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A forecaster with a scored record meets a regional specialist who has deep knowledge but no scored record. Which attitude is Flack's?
options: Dismiss the specialist, because only a scored record deserves a hearing in forecasting
Value the specialist's deep knowledge while still trusting a scored record of his own
Defer entirely to the specialist, because his own record counts for little
Copy the specialist's number, because deep knowledge outranks any scored record
optionExplain: Flack's humility runs the other way: he respects deep knowledge.
Right: he respects what the specialist knows and does not give up his own evidence.
Flack is humble, but he does not discount his record.
He values such knowledge, but he does not say it replaces a record.
questions.explain: The epilogue says Flack respects people with in-depth knowledge and calls it valuable, even though they lack a Brier score.
questions.rule: Respect knowledge you lack without discarding evidence you have.
questions.teaches: The epilogue says Flack respects people with in-depth knowledge, such as the Tom Friedmen of the world, and calls that knowledge valuable.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: How does Flack say he treats the good pundits whose forecasts he reads?
options: As authorities whose conclusions he adopts once they have been tested against the news
As lawyers who make the best case for an outcome, whose arguments he then weighs
As rivals whose forecasts he tries to beat on the same questions in the same season
As sources he ignores, since they are not scored and he trusts only his own record
optionExplain: Adopting a view whole is what he says bad pundits ask readers to do.
Right: lawyers putting forth the best argument.
The epilogue does not describe pundits as rivals in a contest.
He says he does not dismiss pundits; he uses them.
questions.explain: He sees good pundits as advocates in an adversarial system. The card next shows how he uses them.
questions.rule: According to the authors, treat a pundit's argument as evidence to weigh, not as a pronouncement to obey or ignore.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: Flack compares good pundits to lawyers in an ____ judicial system.
questions.explain: In an adversarial system each side puts forth its best argument and the judge or jury weighs them.
questions.rule: Pundits argue; the forecaster weighs.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: Three analysts argue, with data, for different sales results next quarter. Which approach matches Flack's use of pundits?
options: Adopt the forecast of the most senior analyst, since seniority reflects judgment
Ignore all three, because none of them has a scored record of forecasting
Weigh all three arguments, check background facts, then make his own forecast
Average the three headline numbers without reading the reasons behind them
optionExplain: Deferring to one voice treats the pundit's word as a pronouncement.
Flack does not dismiss pundits; he uses their arguments.
Right: arguments are weighed and he forms his own forecast.
This skips the arguments, which are what Flack weighs.
questions.explain: Flack forms his own forecast from a weighted sum of the arguments after checking the background.
questions.rule: Weigh arguments; do not copy numbers.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: Sort each pundit habit: bad or good for Flack's purposes?

items.t: Issues a forecast with no supporting argument
Backs a forecast with anecdotes rather than useful facts
Expects readers to treat the forecast as word from Mt. Sinai
Argues the case for why an outcome will happen
Puts forth the best argument for a forecast
Supplies facts a reader can check and build on

questions.explain: Flack rejects pronouncements and anecdotes, and values pundits who argue their case so that he can weigh it.
questions.rule: According to the authors, treat a pundit's argument as evidence to weigh, not as a pronouncement to obey or ignore.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: True or false: The epilogue says Flack forms his forecast by weighing and adding to the pundits' arguments, not by deferring to any single pundit.
questions.explain: Flack describes a weighted sum of everybody's arguments, with further digging into background, ending in his own forecast.
questions.rule: According to the authors, treat a pundit's argument as evidence to weigh, not as a pronouncement to obey or ignore.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A famous commentator will not enter a scored tournament. According to the authors, how might the commentator still help forecasters?
options: By pitching forecasting questions for aspiring forecasters to try
By checking the final forecasts of the tournament winners before they are published
By choosing which forecasters' scores will be released to the public
By replacing weak forecasts with the commentator's own strong hunches
optionExplain: Right: the baseball image has strategic thinkers pitching and forecasters batting.
Nothing in the epilogue gives pundits a role as checkers.
Scoring is not described as the commentator's job.
The epilogue does not suggest swapping in unscored hunches.
questions.explain: The authors note that Friedman pitched questions on Iraq in 2002, and that some of his 2014 questions on petro-states may prove tricky to hit.
questions.rule: Unscored thinkers can still supply good questions.
questions.teaches: The authors say Friedman pitched questions on Iraq in 2002 and petro-states in 2014, the latter possibly tricky to hit.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: If a run of overconfident forecasts went badly, how does Flack say he would probably respond?
options: He would stop forecasting until the uncertainty in the world had reduced
He would treat the run as bad luck and leave his approach exactly as it was
He would doubt that he had ever been a competent superforecaster at all
He would become more cautious and less prone to extreme forecasts
optionExplain: He keeps going; he treats the setback as feedback.
He admits luck matters, but he says the score would change his behaviour.
He says it would not shatter his image of himself as competent.
Right: caution follows overconfidence.
questions.explain: He says the score would make him more cautious. The card next explains the cycle behind this.
questions.rule: According to the authors, treat success as partly luck, expect slumps, and let score feedback change how you forecast.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: The authors say that Flack is perpetual ____.
questions.explain: Perpetual beta names the cycle of try, fail, analyze, adjust and try again.
questions.rule: Keep trying, failing, analysing and adjusting.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A salesperson hit her targets for three years, then missed after giving clients very confident forecasts. Which response is perpetual beta?
options: Blame the market and keep the method unchanged, since the earlier years proved it
Study what the miss shows about her confidence, adjust, and try again
Decide her earlier success was worthless and stop making forecasts
Wait for luck to turn and make the same bold forecasts as before
optionExplain: This ignores the feedback, as if luck played no part in the success.
Right: try, fail, analyze, adjust, try again.
Flack's own reaction is to adjust, not to quit or deny past skill.
Hoping for luck skips the analyse and adjust steps of the cycle.
questions.explain: The cycle requires using the feedback to adjust, then trying again.
questions.rule: Use the miss; do not hide from it.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A forecaster's hot streak came in a phase of irreducible uncertainty. What do the authors say statistics suggest next?
options: The streak will continue, because a hot streak shows rising skill
The streak will fade only if the forecaster stops using the same method
Massive regression to the mean, so the streak is likely to fade
Nothing can be said, because phases of uncertainty cannot be described
optionExplain: In such phases luck outweighs skill, so a streak is weak evidence of rising skill.
The fading comes from the statistics, not from a change of method.
Right: luck trumps skill in those phases, so statistics point to regression to the mean.
The authors do say what statistics suggest: regression to the mean.
questions.explain: In phases where luck trumps skill, the authors say the statistics favour regression to the mean.
questions.rule: According to the authors, treat success as partly luck, expect slumps, and let score feedback change how you forecast.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: True or false: Flack says a few overconfident forecasts gone wrong could hit his Brier score hard but probably not shatter his self-image.
questions.explain: He says such misses could separate a terrific season from a terrible one, but would make him more cautious rather than shatter his self-image.
questions.rule: A bad run corrects behaviour, not identity.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A coach scores her match predictions each season. According to Flack's view, what can a score tell her that wins and losses cannot?
options: Whether she tends to be underconfident or overconfident, so she can adjust
Which of her players will be most skilled in the following season
Whether a good season came from skill rather than from luck, with certainty
When a phase of irreducible uncertainty will end and skill will count again
optionExplain: Right: Flack says the Brier score tells him about over- and underconfidence.
A score is about her forecasting, not about her players.
Flack himself says luck played a part, and a score does not separate them with certainty.
Nothing in the epilogue says a score reveals when such phases end.
questions.explain: Flack says the Brier score gives him feedback on whether he is under- or overconfident, and he changes his forecasting in response.
questions.rule: Scores diagnose confidence, not just success.
questions.teaches: Flack says the Brier score gives feedback on whether he is under- or overconfident, and he modifies his forecasting behaviour in response.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: The first commandment advises aspiring superforecasters to concentrate on questions of which difficulty?
options: The hardest questions, because the biggest uncertainty offers the biggest payoff
The easiest questions, because rules of thumb give quick and reliable wins
A middle band, where hard work pays off the most
Only questions on topics the forecaster already knows well from earlier work
optionExplain: The commandment warns against cloudlike questions that no model can master.
The commandment also warns against wasting time on clocklike questions.
Right: neither easy nor impenetrable.
The commandment is about difficulty, not familiarity with the topic.
questions.explain: The advice is to avoid both ends of the difficulty range. The card next names the middle band.
questions.rule: According to the authors, put effort into the Goldilocks zone, where questions are neither clocklike nor cloudlike.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: The authors tell forecasters to focus on the ____ zone of difficulty, where effort pays off the most.
questions.explain: Goldilocks zone is the authors' phrase for questions neither too easy nor too hard.
questions.rule: Aim at the middle band of difficulty.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A retail analyst weighs four questions. Which one sits best in the Goldilocks zone?
options: Will the shop open at its posted hour tomorrow, as it has done every day so far?
What will one currency's exchange rate be on a date twelve years from now?
Which firm not yet founded will dominate retail thirty years from now?
Will a rival chain announce a flagship closure within six months, given falling sales?
optionExplain: A rule of thumb answers this; it is clocklike.
Even fancy models fail at this; it is cloudlike.
The field of possibilities is unknown, as with the 2028 election.
Right: there is evidence to work with and the field is narrow enough.
questions.explain: Effort can pay here: the question is neither answered by a rule of thumb nor beyond any model.
questions.rule: According to the authors, put effort into the Goldilocks zone, where questions are neither clocklike nor cloudlike.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: Sort each question as the authors would: clocklike or cloudlike?

items.t: What time the first train leaves on a fixed timetable tomorrow
Whether a toy shop sells more in December than in March, as every year
Whether the sun will rise on a given day
Who will win a national election twelve years from now
A currency's exchange rate on a date many years ahead
The exact oil price on a date far in the future

questions.explain: Clocklike questions yield to simple rules of thumb. Cloudlike ones, such as far-off elections or markets with a reputation for unpredictability, defeat even fancy models.
questions.rule: According to the authors, put effort into the Goldilocks zone, where questions are neither clocklike nor cloudlike.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: True or false: The authors say a class of outcomes often shows its predictability only after you try for a while to gain traction.
questions.explain: They say we usually do not discover how unpredictable outcomes are until we have spun our wheels for a while, so triage is a judgment call.
questions.rule: According to the authors, put effort into the Goldilocks zone, where questions are neither clocklike nor cloudlike.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A city planner debates forecasting local housing demand next year; nobody knows whether it is predictable. What do the authors say to weigh?
options: Only whether the topic has a general reputation for being unpredictable
Which would cost more here: failing to try on a predictable topic, or wasting effort on an unpredictable one
Whether a simple rule of thumb already exists that gets close to the answer
Whether other planners have already attempted a forecast on the same topic
optionExplain: Reputations count, but the authors say predictability is usually found by trying.
Right: the two basic errors set the question.
A rule of thumb marks a clocklike question, which is not the only case worth effort.
Other attempts are not the test the commandment gives.
questions.explain: The authors name two errors: failing to try to predict the potentially predictable, and wasting time on the unpredictable, and ask which would be worse.
questions.rule: Weigh the cost of each error.
questions.teaches: The authors name two basic errors in triage, failing to try on the predictable and wasting time on the unpredictable, and ask which would be worse in your situation.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: In Peter Backus's estimate of potential partners in London, which figure did he start from before narrowing down?
options: The number of women he had met in the previous year, as a sample of the whole
The number of single women who had joined dating sites in his borough
The number of university graduates living in London who were his own age
The population of London, about six million
optionExplain: He used proportions of the whole population, not his own contacts.
This is a narrow count he would have to estimate by filtering.
Graduates are one of his filters, not his starting point.
Right: he began with the whole population and applied filters.
questions.explain: He started from the population and applied proportions. The card next shows the method.
questions.rule: According to the authors, split a hard question into parts, guess each part in the open, and let the pieces build a number you can check.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: The authors say superforecasters see ____-izing, named for a physicist, as part of the job.
questions.explain: Fermi-izing means ballparking answers by splitting a problem into knowable and unknowable parts.
questions.rule: Break it up and guess in the open.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A founder wants to estimate how many coffee shops a mid-sized town can support. Which first step follows the second commandment?
options: Wait for a full survey of every shop before making any estimate at all
Split it: residents, share who buy coffee out, visits each week, shop capacity
Declare it unknowable and pick a round number that feels about right
