Ask three friends for gut figures and average them without any breakdown
optionExplain: This hides ignorance behind a delay; the commandment says to make best guesses.
Right: sub-problems flush out ignorance and assumptions.
Vague guessing keeps the assumptions hidden instead of exposed.
Without sub-problems no assumption can be examined or corrected.
questions.explain: Decompose into parts you can estimate, so that assumptions are exposed and testable.
questions.rule: Split, guess, expose assumptions.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: Backus multiplies several fractions together. If he doubled only the share he finds attractive, what would happen to his estimate?
options: The pool would rise by five percentage points and no more
The pool of potential partners would roughly double
The pool would stay the same, as the other fractions cancel the change
The pool would halve, because a higher standard means fewer matches
optionExplain: The share enters as a multiplier, not as an amount added at the end.
Right: a chain of multiplied fractions scales with each part.
Nothing in the chain cancels it; the other fractions are unchanged.
Doubling the share of women he finds attractive raises the count.
questions.explain: Because the parts are multiplied, doubling one part doubles the result, which shows which assumptions matter most.
questions.rule: According to the authors, split a hard question into parts, guess each part in the open, and let the pieces build a number you can check.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: True or false: The authors say remarkably good probability estimates often arise from remarkably crude series of assumptions and guesstimates.
questions.explain: They call this the surprise: crude, openly stated assumptions can still give good estimates that can be scored.
questions.rule: A Fermi estimate is rough by design.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: Which of these does the commandment cite as a kind of question superforecasters answered quantitatively by Fermi-izing?
options: Questions about Lasorda's choice of pitchers
Questions about who won the 1952 election in 1940
Questions about Arafat's autopsy
Questions about the planning habits of Summers's research assistants
optionExplain: Lasorda appears in a later commandment, as a coach quoted on management.
This is the triage example of a question that cannot be forecast.
Right: Arafat's autopsy is one of the listed topics.
Summers appears under the outside view, not Fermi-izing.
questions.explain: The authors list Arafat's autopsy, bird-flu epidemics, oil prices, Boko Haram, the Battle of Aleppo and bond-yield spreads as questions answered by Fermi-izing.
questions.rule: Fermi-izing was used on real tournament questions.
questions.teaches: The authors say superforecasters Fermi-ized questions about Arafat's autopsy, bird-flu epidemics, oil prices, Boko Haram, the Battle of Aleppo and bond-yield spreads.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: What question do the authors say superforecasters ask to take the outside view?
options: How would I feel if my forecast turned out to be wrong in this case?
What features of this case make it different from every earlier case?
Which expert holds the most inside information about this particular case?
How often do things of this sort happen in situations of this sort?
optionExplain: This is about feelings, not about base rates.
This is the inside view, which looks at the particulars of the case.
Insider knowledge feeds the inside view, not the comparison class.
Right: it asks for the comparison class.
questions.explain: The outside view asks how often such things happen in such situations. The card next sets it against the inside view.
questions.rule: According to the authors, set your expectation from the comparison class, then adjust for evidence about the particular case.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: When bosses ask how long a project will take, employees tend to underestimate: the authors call this the ____ fallacy.
questions.explain: The planning fallacy is underestimating how long a task will take, often by a factor of two or three.
questions.rule: Plans run late more often than their makers expect.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A contractor says a kitchen refit will take three weeks. Which step takes the outside view?
options: Count the days in the contractor's own schedule again, step by step
Look up how long refits of this kind took in comparable homes
Trust the contractor because the plan is detailed and the crew is friendly
Ask the contractor to promise the date in writing before work begins
optionExplain: Re-checking this one plan is an inside-view exercise.
Right: a comparison class tells you how such jobs usually go.
A detailed plan is still one case seen from within.
A promise says nothing about how long such jobs take.
questions.explain: Comparing with similar jobs is the outside view; reviewing this one plan is the inside view.
questions.rule: Start from similar cases.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: By Summers's correction, how long should he expect a task to take if the research assistant says two days?
options: Four days
Two weeks
Four weeks
Four months
optionExplain: This only doubles the number; Summers also moved up a time unit.
A step up in units from days would be to weeks, but the rule doubles first.
Right: double it to four, then move to the next unit up.
The correction moves up one unit only, from days to weeks.
questions.explain: Summers doubled the estimate and moved to the next higher unit, so an hour became two days and two days became four weeks.
questions.rule: According to the authors, set your expectation from the comparison class, then adjust for evidence about the particular case.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: True or false: The authors say Summers would adjust his correction if an employee astonished him by delivering on time.
questions.explain: He would weigh the outside-view expectation of tardiness against evidence that this employee is an exception.
questions.rule: According to the authors, set your expectation from the comparison class, then adjust for evidence about the particular case.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A manager knows her team's past estimates ran late, so she stretches new ones by a fixed factor. What does she share with Summers?
options: She replaces every estimate with the average of all past estimates
She trusts each estimate because the team knows its own project best
She uses the inside view of each project, studying its steps in detail
She takes the outside view toward her team's estimates, treating them as a class
optionExplain: Summers corrected the estimate rather than replacing it.
Summers did not trust employee estimates at face value.
Her fixed factor ignores the details of each project.
Right: her factor comes from how such estimates behave.
questions.explain: The authors call Summers's rule a nerd joke: he took the outside view toward employees' estimates, because employees fail to take the outside view themselves.
questions.rule: A correction factor is itself an outside view.
questions.teaches: Summers's correction is itself an outside view: he treated the employees' estimates as a class that runs late, because the employees themselves failed to take the outside view.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: According to the authors, how do the best forecasters tend to move their estimates when news comes in?
options: In large swings, so that each new report is reflected at once and in full
Not at all until a decisive event settles the question one way or the other
Only between three levels: unlikely, maybe and likely, to stay readable
Often in small steps, such as from 0.6 to 0.65
optionExplain: Large swings happen only after diagnostic signals.
Waiting for decisive news is the underreacting the commandment warns about.
The commandment says an uncertainty dial needs more than three settings.
Right: incremental steps are typical.
questions.explain: Small, frequent adjustments mark the best forecasters. The card next adds the exception.
questions.rule: According to the authors, move estimates in small steps on weak signals, jump on diagnostic ones, and use more than three settings of doubt.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: The authors compare belief updating to brushing and ____ in dental hygiene.
questions.explain: Belief updating can be boring and uncomfortable, but it pays off in the long run, like flossing.
questions.rule: Updating is routine upkeep.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A forecaster puts a bill's passage at 0.60. A minor committee delay appears. Which revision fits the authors' description?
options: Move from 0.60 to about 0.55
Drop to 0.05 at once, since any delay is a warning sign of failure
Stay at 0.60 whatever happens, to avoid being pushed around by news
Move to 0.95 so as to hedge against the delay in case it matters
optionExplain: Right: a weak signal earns a small, scorable shift.
A minor signal does not justify a jump.
This is underreacting; fine adjustments are what the authors praise.
Moving the wrong way with no new evidence is not hedging; it is noise.
questions.explain: A weak signal calls for a small step. The numbers matter because words cannot capture such shifts.
questions.rule: Small signals, small steps.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: If the new signal is diagnostic rather than minor, what do superforecasters do, according to the authors?
options: Hold their estimate until a second source confirms it in detail
Still move by five points, so that their method stays consistent
Move their estimates quickly
Return to fifty-fifty, because strong news makes the case less clear
optionExplain: The authors say superforecasters know how to jump when signals are diagnostic.
The step size follows the strength of the signal.
Right: superforecasters jump on diagnostic signals.
Strong, diagnostic news makes the case clearer, not less clear.
questions.explain: Superforecasters move fast in response to diagnostic signals, and the authors say they value and cultivate this skill.
questions.rule: According to the authors, move estimates in small steps on weak signals, jump on diagnostic ones, and use more than three settings of doubt.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: Match each forecasting move to what the authors say it shows.
pairs: A small step on a weak signal
Moving fast on a diagnostic signal
Answering a hard question with maybe
Vague verbiage that hides subtle distinctions
questions.explain: Small numeric steps catch fine distinctions, jumps answer diagnostic news, and maybe discards the distinctions.
questions.rule: According to the authors, move estimates in small steps on weak signals, jump on diagnostic ones, and use more than three settings of doubt.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the president's fifty-fifty remark was the most informative way to report the bin Laden estimates.
questions.explain: They say that if the same estimates had been basketball odds, the president would probably have said between three to one and four to one.
questions.rule: Fifty-fifty hides finer shades.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: Why, per the authors, might a president think in odds about a basketball tournament but not about a raid?
options: Presidents have no time for security odds and only have time for sports
Basketball outcomes are settled by clocks and rules, so odds are only possible there
National security questions are all cloudlike, so numbers could not help
Different norms govern different thought processes: scorable odds are routine in sports, not in national security
optionExplain: Time is not the explanation they give.
The authors blame norms, not a difference in how outcomes are settled.
They say the rigor is missing, not that the questions are all hopeless.
Right: norms differ between fields.
questions.explain: The authors say reducing complex hunches to scorable probabilities is de rigueur in sports but not national security, and they add that slam dunk implies willingness to offer infinite odds.
questions.rule: Do not reserve rigor for trivial pursuits.
questions.teaches: The authors say scorable probabilities are routine in sports but not in national security because different norms govern different thought processes, and that slam dunk implies offering infinite odds.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: In the fifth commandment, what should a devout dove or devout hawk list in advance?
options: The sources that would prove their own side right once the facts are known
The signs that would nudge them toward the other side
The names of the experts on their own side who would back their view
The likely outcomes of the crisis, ranked from most to least pleasant
optionExplain: The commandment asks for evidence against one's view, not for it.
Right: pre-committing to signs that could change your mind.
Listing allies does not test the view.
Pleasantness of outcomes is not the point; the signs are.
questions.explain: Each side names signs that would nudge it toward the other. The card next explains the aim.
questions.rule: According to the authors, name the best counterargument and the signs that would move you, then merge the views into one judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: The authors call the nuanced hybrid of a dove and a hawk a dove-____.
questions.explain: A dove-hawk has a nuanced view of when tougher or softer policies are likelier to work.
questions.rule: Combine views instead of choosing a side.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A manager is sure price rises lift profit; a colleague is sure they cost customers. Which step follows the fifth commandment?
options: Back whichever view has more supporters among the staff and move on
Average the two opinions to a middle position and stop there
Each lists the signs that would move them toward the other view
Ask the chief executive to settle it by choosing one of the two views
optionExplain: Counting supporters skips the clash of causal forces.
A mechanical average is not the synthesis the authors describe.
Right: pre-listing signs makes each side take the counterargument seriously.
Handing off the choice avoids the work of weighing both forces.
questions.explain: Each side should say in advance what evidence would nudge it toward the other, which opens a path to synthesis.
questions.rule: Name the signs that would change your mind.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: Match each term to the authors' description.
pairs: One view meets another and another, merged into a single image
A hybrid with a nuanced view of when tougher or softer policies work
questions.explain: Dialectics joins two views; dragonfly eye joins many; the dove-hawk is the person who has done the joining well.
questions.rule: According to the authors, name the best counterargument and the signs that would move you, then merge the views into one judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: True or false: The authors say synthesis follows paint-by-number rules once the arguments have been listed.
questions.explain: They say there are no paint-by-number rules: synthesis is an art that reconciles irreducibly subjective judgments.
questions.rule: No formula for synthesis.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A hiring panel of four members holds four different views of a candidate. How does dragonfly eye differ from classical dialectics?
options: Many views, not two, must be merged into a single image
Dialectics merges many views, while dragonfly eye keeps only two views apart
Dragonfly eye drops the minority views, leaving the strongest one alone
Dragonfly eye merges views by a fixed rule, where dialectics relies on judgment
optionExplain: Right: more than two views are synthesized.
The authors describe the opposite.
The authors speak of synthesizing all the views.
The authors say there is no fixed rule here.
questions.explain: The authors contrast classical dialectics, where a thesis meets an antithesis, with dragonfly eye, where one view meets another and another and all must be merged into one image.
questions.rule: Dragonfly eye extends dialectics from two views to many.
questions.teaches: Classical dialectics joins a thesis and an antithesis, while dragonfly eye must merge one view after another into a single image.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: When a forecast succeeds, what do the authors advise about a postmortem?
options: Run it only if the success was by a wide margin and fully confirmed later
Skip it, because a correct forecast shows the reasoning behind it was sound
Run one as well, since offsetting errors may have produced the success
Run it only for failures, since a success gives no flaws to look for
optionExplain: Margin is not the test; a lucky success may look wide.
The authors say success does not always imply sound reasoning.
Right: successes can hide errors.
The commandment says not to forget postmortems on successes.
questions.explain: Offsetting mistakes can give a right answer for the wrong reasons. The card next gives the full balance.
questions.rule: According to the authors, avoid both rushing and dawdling, and run postmortems on failures and successes alike.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: The seventh commandment says long-term accuracy requires good scores on both calibration and ____.
questions.explain: The commandment pairs calibration with resolution.
questions.rule: Two scores, not one.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A fund manager's call proved right, but two of her assumptions were wrong in opposite directions. What do the authors advise?
options: Treat it as proof that her method works and use the same method again
Review the call anyway, because offsetting errors may have produced the success
Discard the method, since any wrong assumption makes the result worthless
Wait for another success before deciding whether a review is worth doing
optionExplain: The authors warn this sets you up for a nasty surprise.
Right: success can come from luck by offsetting errors.
The advice is to examine the reasoning, not to throw it away.
A single lucky success is exactly what a postmortem should test.
questions.explain: The authors say not all successes imply that the reasoning was right; she may have lucked out.
questions.rule: Check successes too.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: Sort each response to a failure: learning too little, or learning too much?

items.t: Overlooking flaws in your basic assumptions
Excusing the failure instead of owning it
Skipping the postmortem because the error looks random
Dropping a basically sound approach after one minor technical slip
Treating a small technical mistake with big effects as proof the approach was wrong

questions.explain: The authors say learning too little is the more common error, but a minor technical mistake with big ramifications can lead to learning too much.
questions.rule: According to the authors, avoid both rushing and dawdling, and run postmortems on failures and successes alike.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A forecaster treats every success as proof of sound reasoning and keeps the same approach. What do the authors warn?
options: She will gain steadily better calibration through repeated confirmation
She will learn too much from her failures and abandon sound methods
She is setting herself up for a nasty surprise
She will become decisive, which the authors count as a sufficient virtue
optionExplain: Confirmation by luck does not improve calibration.
The question concerns successes, not failures.
Right: lucky successes can hide flawed reasoning.
The seventh commandment says decisiveness must be balanced with prudence.
questions.explain: The authors say that confidently reasoning along the same lines, after a success that may be luck, sets you up for a nasty surprise.
questions.rule: According to the authors, avoid both rushing and dawdling, and run postmortems on failures and successes alike.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the more common mistake after a failure is to learn too much from it.
questions.explain: They say the more common error is to learn too little from failure and overlook flaws in basic assumptions.
questions.rule: Under-learning is the common slip.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A smoke-alarm team cut false alarms last month, then missed a real fire. What would the seventh commandment advise next?
options: Switch to reacting only to the most recent mistake, to keep the rules simple
Cut false alarms further, since misses are less costly than false alarms
Accept the miss as bad luck and keep the current settings as they are
Look for ways to reduce both misses and false alarms, not only the latest kind of error
optionExplain: The commandment says avoiding only the most recent mistake is not enough.
This treats one error type as the only one that counts.
A postmortem and balance are the commandment's answer, not acceptance.
Right: tamp down both types of error.
questions.explain: The authors say it is not enough to avoid the most recent mistake: forecasters must find ways to tamp down both misses and false alarms, to the degree the world permits.
questions.rule: Do not fight only the last error.
questions.teaches: The authors say avoiding only the most recent mistake is not enough: forecasters must reduce both misses and false alarms, as far as the world permits.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: Which of these is one of the three team skills named in the ninth commandment?
options: Shared blame, so that no single member bears a forecasting error alone
Majority voting, so the largest group settles each disagreement fairly
Anonymous polling, so that no one is influenced by seniority in the group
Perspective taking
optionExplain: The commandment is about argument and questioning, not blame.
A vote ends debate; it is not a skill the commandment names.
Nothing in the commandment mentions anonymity.
Right: perspective taking is one of the three.
questions.explain: The three are perspective taking, precision questioning and constructive confrontation. The card next defines them.
questions.rule: According to the authors, practise perspective taking, precision questioning and constructive confrontation, and mind the fine lines in leading.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: Learning to disagree without being disagreeable is called ____ confrontation.
questions.explain: Constructive confrontation is the third team skill.
questions.rule: Disagree, but with respect.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: In a meeting, Priya restates a rival's argument so well that the rival says that is exactly what she meant. Which skill is this?
options: Micromanagement, because she took over the rival's job of making the case
Precision questioning, because she made the rival's point clearer than before
Constructive confrontation, because she has met the rival's view head on
Perspective taking
optionExplain: The commandment names micromanaging as a fault of leaders, not this.
That skill is about asking questions to clarify arguments, not restating them.
Confrontation is about disagreeing well; restating is about understanding.
Right: understanding the other side so well you can state it to its satisfaction.
questions.explain: The test of perspective taking is stating the other side's case to its satisfaction.
questions.rule: State their case so they agree.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: Match each team skill to its description from the commandment.
pairs: Reproducing the other side's argument to its satisfaction
Helping others clarify arguments so they are not misunderstood
questions.explain: The three skills differ: restating the other side, clarifying through questions, and disagreeing respectfully.
questions.rule: According to the authors, practise perspective taking, precision questioning and constructive confrontation, and mind the fine lines in leading.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: True or false: The ninth commandment says the line between a rigid group and a decisive one can be a fine one.
questions.explain: It lists three fine lines: suggestion versus meddling, rigid versus decisive, and scatterbrained versus open-minded.
questions.rule: According to the authors, practise perspective taking, precision questioning and constructive confrontation, and mind the fine lines in leading.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A project lead reviews every line of her team's work each day. Which side of the Lasorda image the authors quote is she on?
options: Holding it too loosely, which lets it fly away and be lost
Holding the dove too tightly, which kills it
Holding it gently, which is the balance the image recommends
Not holding a dove at all, since the image is about sport, not teams
optionExplain: Daily review of every line is the opposite of loose.
Right: too tight a grip stifles the team.
The image warns against excess in either direction; daily review of everything is excess.
The authors quote it as a picture of managing people.
questions.explain: The authors quote Tommy Lasorda: managing is like holding a dove, and a tight grip kills it while a loose one loses it.
questions.rule: Management fails at either extreme.
questions.teaches: Tommy Lasorda compared managing to holding a dove in the hand: held too tightly it dies, held too loosely it is lost.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: The appendix is titled Ten Commandments. How many numbered guidelines does it actually list?
options: Ten, with the tenth urging the reader to master the error-balancing bicycle
Eleven, the last being not to treat commandments as commandments
Twelve, with a final one on the Goldilocks zone of difficulty
Nine, with the team skills as the last item in the list
optionExplain: This is the tenth item, but another follows it.
Right: the numbering runs to eleven.
The Goldilocks zone is the first item, not an extra one.
The list continues past the team skills.
questions.explain: The numbering runs from one to eleven, and the final item warns against treating the list as commandments. The card next explains.
questions.rule: According to the authors, practise with unambiguous feedback, balance opposing errors, and treat the list as guidelines.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: The authors say you cannot learn to ride a ____ by reading a physics textbook.
questions.explain: The bicycle image says skill comes from doing, with feedback, not from reading.
questions.rule: Learning requires doing.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A trainee reads three forecasting manuals without making a scored forecast. Which point from the tenth commandment applies?
options: Learning requires doing, with feedback that leaves no doubt whether you succeed or fail
Triage: she should pick questions that are neither clocklike nor cloudlike
Perspective taking: she should restate what the manuals say in her own words
Fermi-izing: she should break each manual into smaller and simpler parts
optionExplain: Right: practice with clear feedback is what is missing.
Triage is about choosing questions, not about practice.
Restating the manuals is still reading, not practice with feedback.
Splitting manuals into parts is still reading, not doing.
questions.explain: Reading about forecasting is not practice; she needs scored forecasts and feedback.
questions.rule: Do, and get clear feedback.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: Sort each activity: deliberative practice, or going through the motions?

items.t: Making scored forecasts and studying the feedback
Forecasting regularly and checking each result against the outcome
Making forecasts, then reviewing where each went right or wrong
Reading the news and tossing out casual probabilities
Making forecasts that are never checked against outcomes
Reading manuals about forecasting without making forecasts

questions.explain: The authors call for deep, deliberative practice with feedback, not casual probabilities tossed out after reading the news.
questions.rule: According to the authors, practise with unambiguous feedback, balance opposing errors, and treat the list as guidelines.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: True or false: The authors say a forecaster who follows the commandments dutifully no longer needs to think about the case in front of him.
questions.explain: They say superforecasting requires constant mindfulness, especially when dutifully following the commandments.
questions.rule: Rules do not replace thinking.

questions.unitTitle: Epilogue and Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.section: Appendix: Ten Commandments for Aspiring Superforecasters
questions.q: A trainer insists forecasters follow the list mechanically in every case. Which reasoning do the authors quote against that?
options: Rules slow forecasters down, and speed matters more than care in practice
Rules are useful only to beginners and experts should drop them entirely
Binding rules are impossible, since two cases will never be exactly the same
Rules should be made longer, so that more cases are covered by them
optionExplain: The authors do not argue from speed.
They call guidelines the best we can do, not a beginner's tool.
Right: no two cases are exactly alike.
More rules would not change that cases are never exactly alike.
questions.explain: The authors quote Helmuth von Moltke's warning that binding rules are impossible because two cases will never be exactly the same.
questions.rule: Guidelines, not commandments.
questions.teaches: The authors quote Helmuth von Moltke: it is impossible to lay down binding rules because two cases will never be exactly the same.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which sentence comes closest to the main claim of Superforecasting?
options: Nobody can predict anything, so forecasts should be left out of decisions
A few gifted people can see decades ahead, and nobody else can learn how
Foresight is a measurable skill built on learnable habits, within limits
Computers will soon replace human forecasters on every kind of question
optionExplain: This is the debunkers' view; the authors accept limits but reject futility.
The authors say superforecasters are not oracles and that the skill can be learned.
Right: the authors argue foresight is real, bounded, and the product of habits.
The authors expect blending machines and judgment, not replacement.
questions.explain: The authors take a middle path: foresight is real and learnable, but limited. The card next sets out the claim.
questions.rule: Foresight is real, learnable and bounded.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The authors say foresight is not a mysterious gift but the product of particular ways of thinking, gathering information and ____ beliefs.
questions.explain: Chapter 1 names three kinds of habit: thinking, gathering information and updating beliefs.
questions.rule: The skill sits in what people do.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A colleague says a rival's analyst is a born forecaster whom nobody could copy. Which reply fits the authors?
options: Her record may reflect habits of thought that careful people can learn
Agreed, foresight is inborn, so hiring the right people is the only route
Her results show that only people with very high IQs can forecast well
Analysts are best left alone, since habits cannot be copied or taught
optionExplain: Right: the authors say foresight comes from what people do, not from who they are.
This is the gift view the authors reject in chapter 1.
The authors say intelligence matters up to a point but does not explain superforecasters.
They say the habits can be learned and cultivated.
questions.explain: The second conclusion of chapter 1 is that the habits can be learned and cultivated.
questions.rule: Look for habits before assuming a gift.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: the authors claim superforecasters can reliably foresee events decades ahead.
questions.explain: Chapter 1 says they are not gurus or oracles; their measured skill covers about three months to a year and a half.
questions.rule: The claim has a time limit.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: If foresight comes from habits rather than traits, what do the authors expect of a determined newcomer who adopts the habits?
options: No gain at all, because only the traits of superforecasters matter here
Instant superforecaster status, since adopting the habits is enough alone
A gain only if the newcomer already has a genius-level IQ to begin with
Accuracy can improve, since the habits are open to determined people
optionExplain: The authors reject this: they say what matters is what superforecasters do.
They say habits can be learned; they do not promise instant status.
The authors say superforecasters are smart but not off the charts.
Right: they say any intelligent, thoughtful, determined person can learn the habits.
questions.explain: Habits are open to anyone, but the authors promise improvement, not instant expertise.
questions.rule: Habits can be learned; mastery takes effort.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A firm doubts that any short training can help its analysts. What did the authors report from the tournament?
options: An hour of reading improved accuracy by roughly 10% across the year
No training helped; only years of experience improved accuracy
A year of full-time coursework was needed for any measurable gain
A short tutorial improved accuracy by about 60%, matching superforecasters
optionExplain: Right: the tutorial took about sixty minutes and improved accuracy by roughly 10%.
The authors report a gain from a short tutorial.
The tutorial took about an hour, not a year.
The roughly 60% figure is the superforecasters' lead, not the tutorial's gain.
questions.explain: The authors call 10% modest but achieved at little cost, and say modest gains add up over time.
questions.rule: A small cost can buy a lasting gain.
questions.teaches: A tutorial that took about sixty minutes to read improved accuracy by roughly 10% through the tournament year, a modest gain at little cost.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which order best follows the book's case for superforecasting?
options: Describe the habits first, then ask whether anyone has scored the forecasters
Argue that limits make forecasting futile, then show the habits regardless
Show forecasts can be scored, show some score well, then give the habits
Show the teams, then argue that individual forecasters do not matter much
optionExplain: Habits come after the skill is shown, not before.
The authors accept limits but do not argue forecasting is futile.
Right: scoring, then results, then habits makes the case in a sensible order.
The book keeps individuals central and treats teams as one later step.
questions.explain: A case is easier to follow when evidence for the skill comes before its explanation. The card next lays out the steps.
questions.rule: Show the skill before explaining it.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Put the steps of the book's case in order, as this card reads it.
items: Forecasts can be scored fairly
A tournament shows some forecasters beat the rest
Superforecasters share learnable habits
The authors test the claim against limits and objections
questions.explain: Each step needs the one before: scoring makes the tournament result possible, and the habits explain a skill already shown.
questions.rule: Measure, show, explain, test.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reviewer accepts the habits as sensible but doubts that the people are skilled. Which step answers the doubt?
options: The habits step, because a list of sensible habits is itself the evidence
The limits step, because black swans show who has real skill
The leadership chapter, because military examples show who is skilled
The tournament step: scored forecasts compared with a control group
optionExplain: Sensible-sounding habits are not evidence; the authors say convincing methods still need tests.
The limits step narrows the claim; it does not show skill.
The military chapter illustrates principles; it does not measure forecasters.
Right: the scored, compared results show the skill the habits are meant to explain.
questions.explain: The reviewer asks about evidence of skill, which the scored tournament step supplies.
questions.rule: Ask which step answers the objection.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Suppose forecasts in the tournament could not be scored. What would follow for the habit chapters in this reading?
options: Nothing, since habits are valid whether or not accuracy is ever measured
Their claims would lose support, as habits could not be tied to accuracy
They would gain support, since unscored habits cannot be disproved by anyone
They would stand, because the epilogue's guidelines can be scored instead
optionExplain: The chain makes habits depend on a skill that scoring has shown.
Right: without scored results, a claim that habits explain accuracy has nothing to rest on.
A claim that cannot be disproved is not stronger; chapter 2 treats unlosable claims as a warning sign.
The guidelines are meant to be practised with feedback, which also needs scoring.
questions.explain: Chapter 2 warns that a claim which can never be shown wrong earns no trust, so unscored habits would earn none either.
questions.rule: Unscored habits are untested habits.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: in this reading, the habit chapters come after the tournament result they try to explain.
questions.explain: Chapter 4 shows the superforecasters' lead; chapters 5 to 9 then ask what they do differently.
questions.rule: Result first, explanation second.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A skeptic wants to rank superforecasters by IQ alone to find the best. Which finding from the explain step speaks to this?
options: The authors found IQ useless; the top forecasters were all below average in it
Intelligence was the strongest predictor, ahead of every habit studied
Perpetual beta was about three times as strong a predictor as intelligence
Every superforecaster scored in the top 1% on the intelligence tests
optionExplain: The authors say intelligence helps; they do not say it is useless.
The authors rank perpetual beta ahead of intelligence.
Right: the authors call perpetual beta roughly three times as powerful a predictor as its closest rival, intelligence.
The authors say most superforecasters fall well short of genius territory.
questions.explain: The explain step names commitment to updating and self-improvement as the strongest predictor.
questions.rule: Effort and updating outweigh raw intelligence.
questions.teaches: The authors call perpetual beta, the degree of commitment to belief updating and self-improvement, roughly three times as powerful a predictor of rising to superforecaster as its closest rival, intelligence.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: What do the book's cases of unchecked medicine, vague forecasts and unscored intelligence analysis have in common?
options: Each involved experts who knew their claims were false but made them anyway
Each failed because the people involved lacked intelligence or training
Each was cured by replacing human judgment with computer models
Confident judgments were never put to a test that could show them wrong
optionExplain: The authors describe honest confidence, not deceit.
The people were capable; the missing piece was testing.
The authors suggest blending machines and judgment, not replacement.
Right: in each case, confidence stood in for a fair test.
questions.explain: The shared thread is missing tests. The card next names it.
questions.rule: Confidence is not a test.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Chapter 1 says that without measurement there is no revision, and without ____ there can be no improvement.
questions.explain: The loop runs forecast, measure, revise; each missing step stops the next.
questions.rule: No revision, no improvement.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A consultancy publishes forecasts like markets may see significant turbulence soon. By the book's logic, what stops anyone scoring them?
options: Terms and time frame are undefined, so no outcome could count as a miss
Only election forecasts can be scored; forecasts about markets cannot
Consultancies are exempt from scoring because their clients are private firms
Probabilities cannot be scored by any method, however they are stated
optionExplain: Right: vague terms and missing time frames make a forecast untestable.
Chapter 3 says forecasts of many kinds can be scored once precise.
The book gives no such exemption; it complains that scoring is rarely demanded.
The Brier score exists to score probability forecasts.
questions.explain: Chapter 3 treats vague wording and missing time frames as smaller obstacles than probability, but they still block judging.
questions.rule: Make the claim precise before scoring it.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each chapter to the point it adds about testing.
pairs: Without measurement there is no revision
Random assignment lets a difference in outcome be traced to the treatment
Forecasts need precise terms before they can be scored
The intelligence community is held to process, not accuracy
Practice helps only with clear, timely feedback
questions.explain: Each chapter adds a different piece of the same point: testing needs measurement, a comparison, precision, accuracy checks and feedback.
questions.rule: One point, five pieces.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: the authors say following a checklist of good process does not replace checking whether forecasts turn out accurate.
questions.explain: Chapter 4 says process standards are sensible but do not replace checking forecasts against what happens.
questions.rule: Process is not accuracy.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A clinic ranks surgeons only by how many of their patients survive. What does the Codman example in chapter 12 warn about?
options: A crude score can be gamed, such as by turning away the sickest patients
Any survival score proves a surgeon's skill, so such a ranking is dependable
Scoring surgeons is pointless because their outcomes are mostly down to luck
Scores should be kept secret to protect surgeons' reputations from damage
optionExplain: Right: a score that tracks only survival can let a hospital boast 100% while refusing the sickest patients.
The authors warn that numbers need scrutiny.
The authors defend scoring, with scrutiny.
The point of Codman's system was to publish end results.
questions.explain: Measurement is the hinge, but the measure itself must be checked for what it fails to capture.
questions.rule: Test the test.
questions.teaches: Tetlock notes that a crude version of Codman’s system tracking only patient survival could let a hospital boast that 100% of its patients live while turning away the sickest, so scoring systems need constant scrutiny.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: If a group of forecasters topped the scores only through luck, what would you expect in the following year?
options: They would fall back toward the average
They would stay at the top at the same rate
They would improve further as their confidence grows
They would split evenly between top and bottom
optionExplain: Right: luck does not repeat, so extreme results drift back toward the average.
Staying put at the same rate would point to skill.
Confidence does not raise accuracy.
Nothing in the logic of luck predicts a mirror-image split.
questions.explain: Extreme results from luck tend to regress. The card next shows how the authors use this check.
questions.rule: Luck regresses; skill persists.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The authors judge the superforecasters mostly skilled, though not ____.
questions.explain: Individuals slip back somewhat each year, so the authors stop short of calling anyone infallible.
questions.rule: Mostly skill is not pure skill.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A fund manager beats the market two years running. By the book's luck check, what would best support skill?
options: A vivid and confident interview in which the manager explains both wins
A persuasive story about why the strategy should keep beating the market
Top managers on a large list staying near the top across several years
The manager's best single month, which is the strongest of the last year
optionExplain: Confidence feels convincing, but it is not a record.
A story linking causes to results after the fact says little; the authors say to ask how many tried.
Right: consistency among many contestants over time is the book's test for skill.
One extreme month is the kind of result that regresses.
questions.explain: The luck check looks for persistence across many people and years, not for a convincing account of one success.
questions.rule: Look for persistence across many, not one story.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each finding into the group it supports.

items.t: The lead over regular forecasters widened over the years
A question resolved yes when a fishing-boat captain stabbed an officer shortly before the deadline
About 70% of superforecasters stayed in the top group each year
Oil prices depend on many tangled, nonlinear factors
Foxes beat hedgehogs on both calibration and resolution
Individuals slip back somewhat from one year to the next

questions.explain: The first three findings are strands of the case for skill. The last three show why the authors keep luck in the picture.
questions.rule: Count both skill and luck.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: the authors say luck played no part in the superforecasters' results.
questions.explain: They say the superforecasters were mostly skilled, and that quirky events and tangled systems mean luck must play a part on some questions.
questions.rule: Mostly skill leaves room for luck.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: In pure guessing, how likely is it that 70% of one year's top group stays in the top group next year?
options: About 1 in 3, as among the real forecasters
Under 1 in 100,000,000, practically never
About 1 in 2, like a fair coin flip
About 1 in 100, a rare but plausible streak
optionExplain: That is the figure the authors give for the real forecasters, whose year-to-year correlation is about 0.65.
Right: with no skill, the authors put such consistency below 1 in 100,000,000.
If luck alone ruled, such consistency would be far rarer than a coin flip.
Even a rare streak is far more likely than this.
questions.explain: Consistency like the superforecasters' would be astronomically unlikely among guessers, which is why the authors read it as skill.
questions.rule: The more skill, the more persistence.
questions.teaches: For coin-flip guessers, whose year-to-year correlation is 0, the chance of seeing 70% of the top group stay at the top is under 1 in 100,000,000; for forecasters, with a correlation of about 0.65, it is about 1 in 3.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: When many people each guess a quantity separately, how does their average usually compare with a typical individual guess?
options: The average is worse, because the errors add up
The average is usually better than the typical guess
The two are equally accurate, whoever the guessers are
The average is better only if every guesser is an expert
optionExplain: Errors that point in different directions cancel rather than add.
Right: valid information adds up while random errors cancel.
Averaging does improve on the typical guess.
The ox example involved fairgoers, not experts.
questions.explain: Averaging beats the typical guess because scattered errors cancel. The card next links this to other parts of the book.
questions.rule: Combined views beat the typical single view.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The authors use the ____ eye as their picture of many lenses, each with its own view, synthesized into one clear image.
questions.explain: A dragonfly eye has thousands of lenses; the brain synthesizes their views into one picture.
questions.rule: Many lenses, one image.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Five people privately estimate a launch cost before any meeting. Which idea from chapter 9 does this protect?
options: Extremizing, since private answers are pushed toward 100% or zero
The planning fallacy, since private estimates are doubled for safety
Groupthink, since privacy builds the cohesion that avoids questioning
Independence, so errors stay random and can cancel when averaged
optionExplain: Extremizing is a separate step that pushes an aggregate toward certainty.
The planning fallacy is about underestimating time, not about privacy.
Groupthink is cohesion replacing questioning; privacy works against it.
Right: separate judgments keep errors random, so averaging can cancel them.
questions.explain: Chapter 9 says aggregation can only do its magic when people form judgments independently.
questions.rule: Collect views before discussion.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each idea to the setting where the book applies it.
pairs: One person making a second judgment of their own
Many separate guessers whose average is taken
A group that discusses and shares research
Rivals agreeing on forecasts that test their dispute
questions.explain: The same logic of combining views appears at four scales: one head, a crowd, a team and a pair of rival camps.
questions.rule: Same logic, four scales.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: chapter 9 says independent judgments make errors more or less random, so they cancel out when averaged.
questions.explain: Group discussion can destroy independence, so the same error repeats across the group and mistakes pile up instead of canceling.
questions.rule: Independence keeps errors random.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Five equally skilled analysts read the same sources and share one view. What does the diversity point say combining them adds?
options: Little, because combining uniform perspectives only produces more of the same
A great deal, because five skilled analysts reliably outperform any single one
Accuracy, because averaging cancels errors whatever the source of the views
Accuracy, once their forecasts are pushed toward 100% or zero by extremizing
optionExplain: Right: the authors say the key word is different; uniform views add nothing new.
Ability alone does not guarantee a gain when the views are alike.
Errors cancel only when they point in different directions.
Extremizing helps most when members hold different pieces of information, not the same view.
questions.explain: Aggregation needs differing perspectives; skill without difference gives more of the same.
questions.rule: Different, not just able.
questions.teaches: Scott Page coined the phrase diversity trumps ability; the authors put ability first in building superteams and did not design for diversity, so if Page is right, making diversity the key to membership might have improved the results.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: According to the authors, what is the best way to become a better forecaster?
options: Read widely on psychology until knowledge of the biases becomes second nature
Memorise a manual of rules and apply them carefully to every question
Practise forecasting with clear feedback, balancing opposing errors
Copy the forecasts of the best-known pundits and track how they perform
optionExplain: Knowing the biases helps little without practice.
The authors say you cannot become a superforecaster by reading training manuals.
Right: skill comes from practice with unambiguous feedback.
The authors treat pundits' arguments as evidence to weigh, not forecasts to copy.
questions.explain: The authors compare forecasting to riding a bicycle: it is learned by doing. The card next gathers the habits.
questions.rule: Practise with feedback.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each habit to what it asks of the forecaster.
pairs: Break a hard question into parts and guess each one
Start from how often such cases happen, then adjust
Move estimates in small steps on weak signals
Look hard at where the reasoning went wrong, even after successes
Spend effort where it is likely to pay off
questions.explain: Each habit is a practical step that the middle chapters introduce and the epilogue collects.
questions.rule: Each habit has a plain job.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A manager must estimate how long a new project will take. Which guideline applies?
options: Make one confident estimate from the details of this project's plan
Ask how long similar projects took, then adjust for this one
Wait until the project ends, then run a postmortem to set the estimate
Have the team meet and agree on a single figure without dissent
optionExplain: That starts from the inside view; the authors say to start outside.
Right: start from the base rate for the class, then adjust for what is special.
A postmortem is for learning afterwards, not for setting the estimate.
Agreement without dissent is the groupthink the authors warn about.
questions.explain: The outside view comes first, and the inside view then adjusts it.
questions.rule: Start from the class, then adjust.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A decisive fact arrives that overturns the basis of a forecast. What does the guideline on updating suggest?
options: Keep adjusting by tiny steps, since small steps suit every case
Hold the forecast steady until more evidence arrives to confirm it
Round the forecast to fifty-fifty, since the position is now unclear
Make a large move, since a strong signal calls for a jump
optionExplain: The authors say small updates are a principle with caveats, not a skeleton key.
Waiting under-reacts to a strong signal.
Fifty-fifty is a stand-in for maybe, not a response to strong evidence.
Right: forecasters update in small steps on weak signals and jump on diagnostic ones.
questions.explain: The guideline balances under-reaction against over-reaction; the size of the move follows the strength of the signal.
questions.rule: Match the move to the signal.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: the authors say their guidelines are binding rules that cover every forecasting case.
questions.explain: The last item says not to treat commandments as commandments; guidelines are the best that can be done where nothing is certain or exactly repeatable.
questions.rule: Guidelines, not laws.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A forecaster reviews only the forecasts that failed. What would the authors add?
options: Review the successes too, since a hit may come from errors that offset
Nothing, because a success shows that the process was sound and complete
Stop reviewing altogether, because outcomes are mostly down to luck anyway
Review successes instead of failures, because hits teach more than misses
optionExplain: Right: the authors say to run postmortems on successes too, since you may have lucked out.
A hit can come from luck, so success alone does not show the process worked.
The authors keep learning from outcomes while accepting luck.
The authors want both failures and successes examined.
questions.explain: Learning from outcomes means checking the reasoning behind hits as well as misses.
questions.rule: Examine wins as well as losses.
questions.teaches: The authors say to do postmortems on successes too, because you may have lucked out through offsetting errors.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which stance does Tetlock take in the debate between debunkers and defenders of expert forecasting?
options: Forecasting is futile, and experts only create false comfort
Expert foresight is dependable once experts are scored
The debate cannot be settled, so he takes no position
Real limits exist, yet some foresight can be cultivated
optionExplain: This is the debunkers' view, which Tetlock says goes too far.
Scoring showed modest foresight in some experts, not general dependability.
He takes a clear position between the two camps.
Right: he accepts the limits and still believes foresight can be built.
questions.explain: Tetlock labels his position optimistic skeptic. The card next shows how the book keeps both halves.
questions.rule: Accept limits without giving up.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Tetlock calls his stance between debunkers and defenders that of an optimistic ____.
questions.explain: The skeptic half accepts real limits; the optimist half holds that foresight can be cultivated.
questions.rule: Skeptic about limits, optimist about skill.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A magazine cites the book to back its forecast of the world order in 2040. What fits Tetlock's own limits?
options: The book's tournament results extend to any horizon the editors choose
The citation is sound whenever the magazine's forecasters have scored well before
The book reports no evidence of foresight ten years out beyond the obvious
The citation is sound if enough experts contribute, since crowds beat individuals
optionExplain: The tournament looked months to about a year and a half ahead, not decades.
A record on short horizons does not carry over to ten years or more.
Right: Tetlock agrees with Kahneman and Taleb that no such evidence exists.
More contributors do not create evidence of skill at a horizon where none exists.
questions.explain: The book's evidence is about short horizons, so citing it for 2040 stretches it.
questions.rule: Do not stretch evidence past its horizon.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A tournament adds 500 questions about one-in-a-thousand events over three years. What does Tetlock's reasoning predict about its data?
options: Plenty of events will occur, giving a clear verdict on skill
Almost none will occur, leaving too little data to judge skill
Superforecasters will do worst, since rare events defeat careful thinking
Cases will resolve evenly yes and no, giving a fair test of calibration
optionExplain: Events that improbable almost never happen in so short a time.
Right: highly improbable events almost never happen, so data pile up over decades or longer.
The problem is a lack of data, not a known weakness of superforecasters.
An even split would require events far more common than one in a thousand.
questions.explain: Calibration needs many cases; very rare events supply too few to score.
questions.rule: Rare events starve the data.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says we do not know whether superforecasters are good at spotting rare, high-impact events.
questions.explain: He says they may be as clueless as anyone or astonishingly adept, and that we should not fool ourselves.
questions.rule: The gap is in the evidence, not a verdict.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A planner must prepare for events beyond any forecasting horizon. What does Tetlock advise?
options: Plan for adaptability and resilience instead of betting on a forecast
Adopt the forecast of the most senior expert and plan firmly around it
Skip planning altogether, since nothing beyond the horizon can be known
Extremize the best available forecast, then build the plan around that
optionExplain: Right: beyond the horizon, plan for surprise by building adaptability and resilience.
Seniority does not create foresight where none exists.
He keeps planning but changes its form.
Extremizing sharpens a forecast; it does not create foresight beyond the horizon.
questions.explain: Tetlock turns a limit on forecasting into a way of planning.
questions.rule: Where you cannot forecast, prepare to adapt.
questions.teaches: Beyond the forecasting horizon, Tetlock advises planning for surprise through adaptability and resilience, and notes that such preparation is costly, so judging probabilities still matters.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: What does Tetlock hope buyers of forecasts will start to demand?
options: More vivid forecasts told as persuasive stories that are easy to follow
Proof of accuracy from rigorous testing, as buyers expect of a medicine
Forecasts only from credentialed experts with the highest academic degrees
Faster forecasts, with any testing left until after they have been used
optionExplain: The authors criticise pundits who win attention with good stories.
Right: he hopes buyers will ask forecasters to prove accuracy as they expect a pill to be tested.
Credentials are not evidence of accuracy; the book contrasts them with track records.
Testing after use would not help buyers choose.
questions.explain: Tetlock hopes for an evidence-based revolution in forecasting. The card next gives the reasons for hope and for doubt.
questions.rule: Demand tested track records.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: According to chapter 1, the missing measurement of forecasts is mostly a ____-side problem.
questions.explain: Governments, business and the public do not ask for evidence of accuracy, so little is supplied.
questions.rule: No demand, no scoring.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A city council hires a consultancy whose reports do not give dates or probabilities. Which advice from the book applies?
options: Trust the firm's reputation, since a famous name predicts accurate forecasts
Ask for precise, dated forecasts and a record of how earlier ones scored
Ask for vivid narratives so the council can follow the logic of each report
Wait for events to unfold, then judge which parts of each report held up
optionExplain: Fame is not a track record; the book contrasts the two.
Right: precise, dated forecasts can be scored, and a record shows accuracy.
Stories persuade, but they do not show accuracy.
Judging after the fact invites hindsight bias and vague wording.
questions.explain: A buyer who wants tested forecasts must ask for forecasts that can be tested.
questions.rule: Ask for forecasts that can be scored.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Why does the book expect an agency under constant blame to resist scoring?
options: Calculating the scores is too costly for an agency of that size to afford
Analysts believe their craft is too intuitive to be measured at all
Numbers expose analysts to unfair blame, so fuzzy wording feels safer
Rivals inside the agency would use scores to win bigger budgets
optionExplain: The book gives fear of blame, not cost, as the reason.
The authors do not attribute resistance to a belief that craft cannot be measured.
Right: a likely event that fails to occur can be called a miss, while fuzzy words keep analysts safe.
Budgets are not the book's explanation.
questions.explain: Chapter 12 ties resistance to the wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy and the cycle of blame.
questions.rule: Fear of blame favours fuzzy words.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: the authors say hospitals welcomed Codman's end-result system from the start.
questions.explain: Hospitals balked at the cost and physicians feared for their reputations; Codman met entrenched resistance before the idea spread.
questions.rule: Resistance came first.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reformer proposes publishing a hospital's results and is shunned by colleagues. What does the Codman story suggest?
options: The idea is doomed, since resistance from insiders settles the matter
The reformer should drop the idea until insiders ask for it
The reformer is wrong, since colleagues' resistance shows the idea fails
Resistance may be fierce, yet a sound idea with a clear goal can win
optionExplain: Codman's idea was resisted and still prevailed.
Waiting for insiders to ask would have meant waiting a very long time.
Resistance shows a threat to insiders, not that the idea fails.
Right: the authors use Codman to show a score-keeping idea can win despite fierce resistance.
questions.explain: The authors use Codman to argue that power struggles are not the whole story.
questions.rule: Resistance is not the last word.
questions.teaches: Codman was pushed out of Massachusetts General Hospital, yet the uproar over his 1915 cartoon spread his ideas and hospitals went on to adopt them.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: How far ahead did most questions in the IARPA tournament look?
options: Several decades, to test long-range foresight
Under one week, to give very fast feedback
More than one month and less than one year
Exactly ten years, matching a usual planning cycle
optionExplain: The authors say the skill does not stretch to decades.
Weekly questions would be too short for the forecasts the tournament wanted.
Right: most questions fell between one month and one year.
Ten years is beyond the horizon the authors say they can support.
questions.explain: The horizon of the questions limits what the results show. The card next lists this and other limits.
questions.rule: Know the horizon of the evidence.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The roughly 2,800 volunteers who completed testing cannot be assumed to be a ____ sample of the population.
questions.explain: Only motivated people stayed to be tested, so the group is self-selected.
questions.rule: Self-selected is not random.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A firm reads that superteams were 50% more accurate and plans to rebuild every department around them. What do the authors say?
options: Go ahead, since a 50% average gain is a guarantee for any organization
Do it only in departments that already employ proven superforecasters
Avoid teams entirely, since the findings show groups lose accuracy
Treat it as promising but not a recipe, since replication is hard
optionExplain: The authors say there is no guarantee of results.
The authors do not limit the caution to departments without superforecasters.
Teams helped in the authors' tests; the caution is about replication.
Right: the authors call the work young and say replication in organizations would be a challenge.
questions.explain: A strong result in one setting does not guarantee the same gain elsewhere.
questions.rule: Promising is not proven everywhere.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each limit to what it restricts.
pairs: Foresight at decades is not shown
Results cannot be assumed to hold for the general population
It is not an official comparison with intelligence analysts
Skill at spotting rare, high-impact events is not shown
They are not a recipe for organizations
questions.explain: Each limit narrows a different part of the claim; none says the skill is absent.
questions.rule: A limit narrows; it does not erase.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: the authors say the 30% figure for superforecasters against intelligence analysts came secondhand from an unnamed participant.
questions.explain: Chapter 4 reports it as a Washington Post item quoting an unnamed participant, and the authors say a direct comparison would be closely guarded.
questions.rule: Secondhand figures carry less weight.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A study of volunteers who finished a hard course reports gains. What did the authors do about their own self-selected volunteers?
options: They compared the volunteers' test scores with the general population's
They assumed the volunteers matched the population, since all were adults
They dropped volunteers who scored above the population average on tests
They tested only volunteers who had already finished a forecasting course
optionExplain: Right: they compared the volunteers' intelligence and knowledge scores with those of the public.
Adulthood does not make volunteers representative.
Dropping high scorers would hide the very difference being studied.
Nothing in the book describes such a restriction.
questions.explain: A self-selected sample cannot be assumed representative, so it helps to compare it with a wider group.
questions.rule: Compare a selected group with a wider one.
questions.teaches: The authors compared their volunteers with the general population: regular forecasters scored higher on the intelligence and knowledge tests than about 70% of the population, and superforecasters higher than about 80%.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: How does Tetlock respond to Taleb's claim that black swans make the tournament a fool's errand?
options: He dismisses it, since black swans are too rare to matter for decisions
He accepts it fully and says the tournament should be abandoned at once
He says the tournament did cover rare events and found superforecasters adept
He respects it, calls it a false choice, and grants a gap on rare events
optionExplain: He treats Taleb's critique as serious, not as something to dismiss.
He rejects the all-or-nothing conclusion.
He says the opposite: the tournament cannot show skill at rare events.
Right: he calls it a false dichotomy yet agrees the tournament cannot speak to rare events.
questions.explain: Tetlock answers part of the objection and concedes part. The card next sets out the replies.
questions.rule: Answer some, concede some.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Tetlock says Taleb's critique offers a false ____ between forecasting working by formula and forecasting being bunk.
questions.explain: He rejects both extremes: forecasting is neither a formula that always works nor worthless.
questions.rule: Reject the two extremes.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A critic says your score counts only small questions, so it ignores what matters. Which reply from chapter 12 fits?
options: Score a cluster of small questions that add up toward the big one
Drop the small questions and score only the biggest questions directly
Reply that big questions do not matter because they cannot be scored
Say scores cannot mislead, since numbers are a sacred form of insight
optionExplain: Right: Tetlock proposes scoring many tiny but pertinent questions that close in on the big one.
The biggest questions are the hardest to score, which is the dilemma.
Tetlock does not say the big questions are unimportant.
Tetlock says numbers are tools, not sacred insight.
questions.explain: Tetlock answers Saffo's challenge by building up from small, scorable questions.
questions.rule: Build big answers from small scored questions.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each point by how the book handles it (our reading).

items.t: A short tournament cannot show skill at spotting rare events
The choice between a forecasting formula and bunk is a false dichotomy
Numbers can be applied where they do not belong
A cluster of small questions can approach a big question
The questions that matter most are the hardest to score
Power-seeking is real but not the only motive in forecasting

questions.explain: Our reading: the first, third and fifth points are conceded; the others are replies that argue against the objection.
questions.rule: Concede what is true; answer what is not.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Tetlock says the humanists' objection to counting has no merit.
questions.explain: He says there is a lot of truth in it, since numbers are sometimes applied where they do not belong, though he does not give up measuring forecasts.
questions.rule: Part-agreement is not rejection.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Two rival camps run a joint forecast test and each wins some questions. How does Tetlock read that result?
options: As a failure, because a fair test should crown a single winning side
As a feature, because reality is more mixed than either side thought
As a sign the questions were badly chosen and the test should be rerun
As proof that forecasting cannot settle any dispute between rival camps
optionExplain: Tetlock does not expect one side to win everything.
Right: he calls a split decision a feature, not a bug.
A mixed result is the expected outcome over many questions.
A mixed result teaches both sides something.
questions.explain: A split decision shows that each camp had some merit, which is the learning the test is for.
questions.rule: Success is what both sides learn.
questions.teaches: Tetlock calls a split decision across many questions a feature, not a bug, because it shows reality is more mixed than either side thought; the approach also presumes good faith from the participants.

questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A debate is full of strident voices that reject joint testing. What does Tetlock's reply predict?
options: They will join once the questions are made precise enough to answer
They will improve the test, since conflict sharpens every forecast
It will not take hold there; he bets on quieter, reasonable voices
The test will still work, since outcomes decide the winner regardless
optionExplain: Strident voices have no interest in adversarial collaboration.
Conflict without good faith does not produce a useful test.
Right: he looks to less voluble and more reasonable voices instead.
Without willing participants there is no joint test to run.
questions.explain: The approach needs willing participants, so it works only where good faith exists.
