questions.rule: Good faith is a precondition.

questions.q: In the diagram, coin-toss guessers form a symmetric bell. A reader says the right tail shows real talent. What corrects this?
options: The peak sits at 50/50, so the typical guesser has no talent and the thin tails can safely be ignored
The left tail mirrors the right, with as many very bad guessers, so chance alone explains both ends
The right tail is much lower than the peak, so too few guessers are there to count as truly skilled
The tails run down to the floor of the chart, so nobody actually reaches the extreme results shown
questions.explain: The curve is symmetric: very bad guessers are as common as very good ones. That is what pure luck produces, so an extreme high score alone does not show skill.
optionExplain: Tempting because the peak is at 50/50, but the tails are part of the luck pattern; ignoring them is not what corrects the reader.
Right: the matching tail of very bad guessers shows the extremes arise from chance, not talent.
A tail being small is true of the left tail too; size does not separate skill from luck.
The curve only approaches the floor; the chart shows guessers at the extremes, so this misreads it.
questions.rule: According to the authors, extreme results among many people can arise from luck alone.

media.alt: Symmetric bell curve of many people guessing coin tosses. The horizontal axis is the number of correct guesses, the vertical axis the number of guessers at each level. A dashed line at the peak is labelled 50/50. The thin left tail is labelled very bad guessers and the thin right tail very good guessers.

questions.q: In the diagram, which figure completes the grid?
options: A diamond holding an x
A rectangle holding an x
A star holding an x
A star holding a plus
questions.explain: The third row uses the x, and it already holds a diamond and a rectangle. The third column holds a diamond and a rectangle, so the missing shape is the star. Finding such rules is what the authors call fluid intelligence.
optionExplain: The x is right, but the bottom row already has a diamond, so a second diamond breaks the one-of-each rule.
The x is right, but the bottom row already has a rectangle, so a second one repeats a shape.
Right: the star is the one shape missing from the bottom row and the last column, and the row symbol is an x.
The star is right, but a plus belongs to the middle row, while the bottom row uses an x.
questions.rule: According to the authors, fluid intelligence is raw reasoning power, measured by finding the rules behind patterns.

media.alt: Three-by-three grid of outlined shapes, each holding a small symbol, with the bottom-right cell blank. Row 1 holds a rectangle, a star and a diamond, each with a minus. Row 2 holds a star, a diamond and a rectangle, each with a plus. Row 3 holds a diamond and a rectangle, each with an x, then the blank cell. Each row and column holds all three shapes once. Eight candidate figures sit below as possible answers.

questions.q: In the diagram, the probability line ends near 1. A reader says every change moved toward that end value. What fits the line?
options: Several drops, such as one in mid-February, moved away from the end value, yet the overall trend still rose
The line barely moved during January, so he waited for February before taking any news into account
Each change was far too small to matter, so the final climb came from one single very large update
The line rose steadily from the first day, so no change before March ever moved against the trend
questions.explain: The line dips more than once, including a drop to near 0.55 in mid-February, then climbs in small steps. Some updates went the wrong way, but the trend was mostly right.
optionExplain: Right: the dips are visible, and the later rise is a sequence of small steps.
The line already wobbles between about 0.6 and 0.75 through January, so he was updating from the start.
The late rise is many small steps, not one large jump.
The line falls several times before March, so it did not rise steadily.
questions.rule: According to the authors, many small updates carry the trend even if some new forecasts move away from the answer.

media.alt: Line chart of one forecaster’s probability on the vertical axis, 0 to 1, from January to March, with a dashed line at 1. The line starts a little above 0.5 and wobbles between about 0.6 and 0.75 through January and early February. It dips to near 0.55 in mid-to-late February, jumps back to about 0.72, then climbs in many small steps to almost 1 by the end of March.

questions.q: In the diagram, what shows the net-worth curve allows more extreme outcomes than a bell curve?
options: Its peak sits left of the bell's peak, so wealth spreads evenly around its typical value like height
Its peak is lower than the bell's, so it holds fewer households overall than the bell curve does
Its line is drawn thicker than the bell's outline, so wealth is measured more precisely than height
Its right-hand stretch stays far above the bell, so very rich households are much likelier than a bell allows
questions.explain: Out at the far right the bell has dropped to the floor while the net-worth curve is still well above it. That thick tail is what makes extreme outcomes likelier than a bell curve would.
optionExplain: The curve is lopsided, with a long right stretch, so it is not an even spread like height.
The two curves describe the same set of households; a lower peak does not mean fewer of them.
Line thickness is only drawing style and says nothing about measurement.
Right: the tail height at the right end is the feature that marks a fat tail.
questions.rule: According to Tetlock, a fat-tailed distribution makes extreme outcomes far likelier than a bell curve would.

media.alt: Chart of number of households (vertical axis) against a quantity, with two curves. A shaded symmetric bell, labelled normal distribution such as height, has a dashed median line at its peak. A thick curve labelled fat tail, such as net worth, peaks lower and further left, then trails in a long stretch to the right, far above the bell, which has dropped to the floor there.

questions.q: True or false: In the diagram, one yes among the four smaller questions is enough to settle the big question.
questions.explain: The big question sits above four smaller ones, and their answers are cumulative. Each yes makes the bad outcome likelier, but no single small question settles it.
questions.rule: According to Tetlock, small questions add up; none nails the big one down alone.

media.alt: Tree diagram: a dark oval at the top asks whether there will be another Korean war. Arrows point down from it to four lighter ovals in a row, each a smaller question: missile launches, nuclear tests, cyber attacks and artillery shelling.

cover.alt: Book cover: bold condensed black title lettering on white, slanting in perspective, with thin streaks of purple and cyan lines rushing toward the right edge like speed lines.
